questions.question: A maintenance coordinator asks Claude to build a small internal issue-tracking artifact. Staff disagree about whether unresolved issues or the newest reports should appear first. No live integration is needed for the initial trial. What is the most useful next step?

options.label: A
options.text: Demonstrate both orderings and ask staff to choose their preferred visual presentation.

options.label: B
options.text: Have the sponsor choose from mockups and use satisfaction with that design as the gate.

options.label: C
options.text: Default to recency for the trial because chronology avoids deciding which issues are important.

options.label: D
options.text: Observe staff using a small prototype on representative handovers before choosing the ordering.

questions.explanation:
✅ The correct option is: Observe staff using a small prototype on representative handovers before choosing the ordering.

The decision is about the ordering that supports real handovers, not about which mock-up looks nicest. A representative prototype lets staff encounter the trade-off in context and produces behavioural evidence before the team commits. In this scenario, the key concept is prototype observation. The best answer is the one that directly tests, protects, or controls that concept before the workflow moves forward. It therefore addresses the decision that actually matters, rather than merely improving presentation, speed, or confidence.

❌ Why the Other Options Are Wrong:

Demonstrate both orderings and ask staff to choose their preferred visual presentation - This does not directly test, preserve, or apply the specific requirement stated in the scenario. It may be a reasonable supporting activity, but it does not provide the evidence, control, or accountable decision needed before the work proceeds.

Have the sponsor choose from mockups and use satisfaction with that design as the gate - This does not directly test, preserve, or apply the specific requirement stated in the scenario. It may be a reasonable supporting activity, but it does not provide the evidence, control, or accountable decision needed before the work proceeds.

Default to recency for the trial because chronology avoids deciding which issues are important - This does not directly test, preserve, or apply the specific requirement stated in the scenario. It may be a reasonable supporting activity, but it does not provide the evidence, control, or accountable decision needed before the work proceeds.

📚 Key Concepts to Remember for the Exam:

1) Prototype testing and evidence-based iteration.
2) Identify the claim, decision, or boundary that the scenario actually asks you to control.
3) Prefer the option that creates evidence or preserves the required control before a consequential action.

questions.question: A community broadband team revises a prompt after installation requests were mislabeled. The revision will become the shared default if it fixes that failure without weakening established categories. Which TWO checks provide the most decision-relevant evidence? Select TWO.

options.label: A
options.text: Repeat the installation cases used during editing and treat a clean rerun as sufficient evidence for release.

options.label: B
options.text: Evaluate representative held-out installation requests that were not used to design the revised classification instructions.

options.label: C
options.text: Compare the old and revised prompts for specificity and completeness, preferring whichever version contains more explicit category wording overall.

options.label: D
options.text: Have a second reviewer inspect the revised prompt and predict which request types it will classify correctly.

options.label: E
options.text: Run the established cross-category regression test set and examine whether previously reliable request labels have weakened.

questions.explanation:
✅ The correct option is: Evaluate representative held-out installation requests that were not used to design the revised classification instructions. AND Run the established cross-category regression test set and examine whether previously reliable request labels have weakened.

A revised prompt should be assessed on examples that did not shape the edit and on the established cases it must not damage. This separates a genuine improvement from memorising the failure examples. In this scenario, the key concept is held-out and regression evaluation. The best answer is the one that directly tests, protects, or controls that concept before the workflow moves forward. It therefore addresses the decision that actually matters, rather than merely improving presentation, speed, or confidence.

❌ Why the Other Options Are Wrong:

Repeat the installation cases used during editing and treat a clean rerun as sufficient evidence for release - This does not directly test, preserve, or apply the specific requirement stated in the scenario. It may be a reasonable supporting activity, but it does not provide the evidence, control, or accountable decision needed before the work proceeds.

Compare the old and revised prompts for specificity and completeness, preferring whichever version contains more explicit category wording overall - More output or more variants do not establish that the governing condition has been met. The scenario still requires the specified evidence, test, source check, or accountable approval before a decision can be trusted.

Have a second reviewer inspect the revised prompt and predict which request types it will classify correctly - A prompt instruction cannot override the source, policy, permission, or tool capability that governs this decision. The workflow must align with the controlling rule, not merely state a preference for a different outcome.

📚 Key Concepts to Remember for the Exam:

1) Use held-out cases plus regression tests before promoting a shared prompt.
2) Identify the claim, decision, or boundary that the scenario actually asks you to control.
3) Prefer the option that creates evidence or preserves the required control before a consequential action.

📌 References:

Claude documentation - https://docs.anthropic.com/en/docs/build-with-claude/develop-tests

questions.question: An analyst asks Claude to produce a register of exceptions to a courier's standard delivery promise. A reviewer samples twelve listed entries and confirms that every sampled quotation and clause reference is accurate. The register will be described as comprehensive. Which additional control addresses the most important remaining claim?

options.label: A
options.text: Confirm that the twelve sampled clauses came from the policy version named in the register.

options.label: B
options.text: Ask a second reviewer to repeat the accuracy check on the same twelve sampled entries.

options.label: C
options.text: Search the complete policy systematically, using a defined exception taxonomy, for qualifying exceptions absent from the register.

options.label: D
options.text: Standardize verified entries so every exception follows a consistent editorial pattern.

questions.explanation:
✅ The correct option is: Search the complete policy systematically, using a defined exception taxonomy, for qualifying exceptions absent from the register.

Checking sampled entries establishes that listed claims are accurate; it does not establish that every qualifying exception was found. A systematic search against a stated taxonomy directly tests the completeness claim. In this scenario, the key concept is completeness versus accuracy. The best answer is the one that directly tests, protects, or controls that concept before the workflow moves forward. It therefore addresses the decision that actually matters, rather than merely improving presentation, speed, or confidence.

❌ Why the Other Options Are Wrong:

Confirm that the twelve sampled clauses came from the policy version named in the register - This does not directly test, preserve, or apply the specific requirement stated in the scenario. It may be a reasonable supporting activity, but it does not provide the evidence, control, or accountable decision needed before the work proceeds.

Ask a second reviewer to repeat the accuracy check on the same twelve sampled entries - This does not directly test, preserve, or apply the specific requirement stated in the scenario. It may be a reasonable supporting activity, but it does not provide the evidence, control, or accountable decision needed before the work proceeds.

Standardize verified entries so every exception follows a consistent editorial pattern - This does not directly test, preserve, or apply the specific requirement stated in the scenario. It may be a reasonable supporting activity, but it does not provide the evidence, control, or accountable decision needed before the work proceeds.

📚 Key Concepts to Remember for the Exam:

1) Accuracy and completeness are separate claims and need separate controls.
2) Identify the claim, decision, or boundary that the scenario actually asks you to control.
3) Prefer the option that creates evidence or preserves the required control before a consequential action.

📌 References:

Claude documentation - https://docs.anthropic.com/en/docs/build-with-claude/prompt-engineering/overview

questions.question: A distributor uses Claude to draft operating instructions from approved equipment manuals. An editor has confirmed that the draft is readable and all cited pages exist. One paragraph tells workers to bypass a sensor during cleaning, but the manual's cited passage concerns inspection by a technician. Who should review this discrepancy before release?

options.label: A
options.text: An equipment or safety specialist, checking applicability to these workers and this cleaning task.

options.label: B
options.text: An experienced end user, checking whether the draft's sequence resembles how workers currently clean the equipment.

options.label: C
options.text: The editor, reviewing the complete cited passage and aligning the paragraph's terminology with that source.

options.label: D
options.text: The scheduler, confirming the cleaning step fits within the available shift interval.

questions.explanation:
✅ The correct option is: An equipment or safety specialist, checking applicability to these workers and this cleaning task.

The issue is not prose quality or the existence of a citation. It is whether the cited material actually authorizes workers to bypass a safety control during this task, which requires relevant technical or safety expertise. In this scenario, the key concept is expert review of applicability. The best answer is the one that directly tests, protects, or controls that concept before the workflow moves forward. It therefore addresses the decision that actually matters, rather than merely improving presentation, speed, or confidence.

❌ Why the Other Options Are Wrong:

An experienced end user, checking whether the draft's sequence resembles how workers currently clean the equipment - This does not directly test, preserve, or apply the specific requirement stated in the scenario. It may be a reasonable supporting activity, but it does not provide the evidence, control, or accountable decision needed before the work proceeds.

The editor, reviewing the complete cited passage and aligning the paragraph's terminology with that source - This does not directly test, preserve, or apply the specific requirement stated in the scenario. It may be a reasonable supporting activity, but it does not provide the evidence, control, or accountable decision needed before the work proceeds.

The scheduler, confirming the cleaning step fits within the available shift interval - This does not directly test, preserve, or apply the specific requirement stated in the scenario. It may be a reasonable supporting activity, but it does not provide the evidence, control, or accountable decision needed before the work proceeds.

📚 Key Concepts to Remember for the Exam:

1) Source relevance and operational applicability need subject-matter review.
2) Identify the claim, decision, or boundary that the scenario actually asks you to control.
3) Prefer the option that creates evidence or preserves the required control before a consequential action.

questions.question: A conference organizer wants Claude to shorten session-description approval. Drafting takes 10 minutes, but descriptions then spend two days in correction rounds because speakers' titles and biographies were not confirmed before drafting. Which redesign most directly addresses the observed cause of rework?

options.label: A
options.text: Switch to a faster model to reduce the amount of time spent generating each session description.

options.label: B
options.text: Collect and confirm title and biography fields before drafting, with a clear owner for missing information.

options.label: C
options.text: Extend the drafting prompt with more detailed style rules so speaker confirmations are less likely to change wording.

options.label: D
options.text: Have Claude generate three description variants so approvers can select a preferred version more quickly.

questions.explanation:
✅ The correct option is: Collect and confirm title and biography fields before drafting, with a clear owner for missing information.

The delays occur because input facts are unresolved before drafting, so faster generation or more variants would not eliminate the correction cycle. Confirming the source fields and assigning an owner removes the known cause. In this scenario, the key concept is upstream cause removal. The best answer is the one that directly tests, protects, or controls that concept before the workflow moves forward. It therefore addresses the decision that actually matters, rather than merely improving presentation, speed, or confidence.

❌ Why the Other Options Are Wrong:

Switch to a faster model to reduce the amount of time spent generating each session description - Changing the model does not by itself correct the missing evidence, conflicting requirement, or control failure described in the scenario. The workflow needs the stated validation or decision boundary, not simply a different model tier.

Extend the drafting prompt with more detailed style rules so speaker confirmations are less likely to change wording - More output or more variants do not establish that the governing condition has been met. The scenario still requires the specified evidence, test, source check, or accountable approval before a decision can be trusted.

Have Claude generate three description variants so approvers can select a preferred version more quickly - More output or more variants do not establish that the governing condition has been met. The scenario still requires the specified evidence, test, source check, or accountable approval before a decision can be trusted.

📚 Key Concepts to Remember for the Exam:

1) Fix the upstream information gap rather than optimizing the visible drafting step.
2) Identify the claim, decision, or boundary that the scenario actually asks you to control.
3) Prefer the option that creates evidence or preserves the required control before a consequential action.

📌 References:

Claude documentation - https://docs.anthropic.com/en/docs/build-with-claude/prompt-engineering/overview

questions.question: A consultant uses Claude for two clients. One requires dates as day-month-year; the other requires year-month-day. Both also need the consultant's general preference for concise writing. Which setup applies these requirements at the intended scope?

options.label: A
options.text: Put both date rules in personal preferences and ask Claude to infer the client from each document.

options.label: B
options.text: Keep all three rules in one shared Project and switch its date instruction before each client task.

options.label: C
options.text: Keep concise writing as a general preference and each client's date rule in that client's respective Project instructions.

options.label: D
options.text: Put the writing preference in each chat and identify each client's date rule in its Project description.

questions.explanation:
✅ The correct option is: Keep concise writing as a general preference and each client's date rule in that client's respective Project instructions.

A personal preference is appropriate for a durable cross-client style choice, whereas each date format is client-specific and belongs in that client Project. This avoids conflicting instructions and keeps the rule available to all chats for that client. In this scenario, the key concept is instruction scope. The best answer is the one that directly tests, protects, or controls that concept before the workflow moves forward. It therefore addresses the decision that actually matters, rather than merely improving presentation, speed, or confidence.

❌ Why the Other Options Are Wrong:

Put both date rules in personal preferences and ask Claude to infer the client from each document - This relies on Claude to validate its own output. A model response is not independent evidence, so it cannot establish that the underlying source, rule, calculation, or date is correct. The required check must be made against the relevant authoritative input.

Keep all three rules in one shared Project and switch its date instruction before each client task - This leaves the identified defect or uncertainty in place rather than resolving it before the output is relied on. A caveat, repeated draft, or later correction does not make an unsupported or incomplete result safe to use.

Put the writing preference in each chat and identify each client's date rule in its Project description - This does not directly test, preserve, or apply the specific requirement stated in the scenario. It may be a reasonable supporting activity, but it does not provide the evidence, control, or accountable decision needed before the work proceeds.

📚 Key Concepts to Remember for the Exam:

1) Place instructions at the narrowest scope that reliably needs them.
2) Identify the claim, decision, or boundary that the scenario actually asks you to control.
3) Prefer the option that creates evidence or preserves the required control before a consequential action.

📌 References:

Claude documentation - https://support.claude.com/en/articles/9519177-how-can-i-create-and-manage-projects

questions.question: A product team moves a six-week planning discussion into a fresh chat. The transfer summary records a preferred launch date and the reasons for it, but omits a decision log entry stating that release is conditional on passing an accessibility audit. The new chat has not begun. What is the best continuity safeguard?

options.label: A
options.text: Retain the concise transfer summary and ask the new chat to identify any likely unstated launch dependencies.

options.label: B
options.text: Amend the transfer material with the verified audit condition and its status before continuing the plan.

options.label: C
options.text: Move the preferred date later by one sprint so the omitted condition is less likely to affect release.

options.label: D
options.text: Attach the full transcript without highlighting the decision, allowing the new chat to reconstruct relevant constraints.

questions.explanation:
✅ The correct option is: Amend the transfer material with the verified audit condition and its status before continuing the plan.

The audit condition is a release constraint, not a detail Claude should infer. Put the verified dependency and current status into the transfer material before work continues so the new chat starts from accurate governing context. In this scenario, the key concept is verified continuity. The best answer is the one that directly tests, protects, or controls that concept before the workflow moves forward. It therefore addresses the decision that actually matters, rather than merely improving presentation, speed, or confidence.

❌ Why the Other Options Are Wrong:

options.text: When the source log has no owner for an issue, the completed handover labels that issue's owner as unassigned.

options.text: The handover remains brief enough for a busy supervisor while preserving all operational context that might later prove useful during the shift.

questions.question: A repair marketplace is exploring ways to reduce missed appointments. Customer interviews describe several possible causes but do not establish which intervention will work. Which TWO prompt instructions best preserve creative range while keeping proposals distinguishable from evidence? Select TWO.

options.text: Generate varied interventions from plausible causes, including mechanisms other than additional reminder messages.

options.label: B
options.text: Use the intervention mentioned most often across the customer interviews as the standard pattern for every proposed solution.

options.label: C
options.text: Rewrite each proposal as a confirmed customer requirement before comparing implementation effort and operational feasibility.

options.label: D
options.text: For each proposed mechanism, label its assumptions and specify observations that would strengthen or weaken it.

options.label: E
options.text: Rank every proposed idea by expected impact before analysis, then omit hypotheses that cannot receive a confident numerical score.

That preserves creativity while preventing a proposal from being presented as established customer evidence. In this scenario, the key concept is hypothesis discipline. The best answer is the one that directly tests, protects, or controls that concept before the workflow moves forward. It therefore addresses the decision that actually matters, rather than merely improving presentation, speed, or confidence.

Use the intervention mentioned most often across the customer interviews as the standard pattern for every proposed solution - This does not directly test, preserve, or apply the specific requirement stated in the scenario. Rewrite each proposal as a confirmed customer requirement before comparing implementation effort and operational feasibility - This does not directly test, preserve, or apply the specific requirement stated in the scenario. questions.question: A user receives a message saying their Claude usage allowance resets at 3:00 p.m. It is 2:30 p.m. Even a new chat containing one short sentence cannot be submitted. Which response best matches this situation?

options.label: A
options.text: Move the same account to Desktop and retry without attachments.

options.label: B
options.text: Remove previous attachments and open another chat to recover the allowance.

options.label: C
options.text: Start a new Project with shorter instructions and turn off unnecessary tools.

options.label: D
options.text: Wait for the reset or use an authorized allowance option.

questions.explanation:
✅ The correct option is: Wait for the reset or use an authorized allowance option.

A new chat, device, attachment removal, or shorter instruction does not create allowance when the account is blocked until a stated reset. The legitimate choices are to wait or use an authorized option. In this scenario, the key concept is usage limits. The best answer is the one that directly tests, protects, or controls that concept before the workflow moves forward. It therefore addresses the decision that actually matters, rather than merely improving presentation, speed, or confidence.

Move the same account to Desktop and retry without attachments - This does not directly test, preserve, or apply the specific requirement stated in the scenario. It may be a reasonable supporting activity, but it does not provide the evidence, control, or accountable decision needed before the work proceeds.

Remove previous attachments and open another chat to recover the allowance - Removing information or a control does not resolve the governing issue and can make the resulting work less traceable or less safe. The right response is to correct the authoritative material or apply the relevant safeguard.

Start a new Project with shorter instructions and turn off unnecessary tools - A prompt instruction cannot override the source, policy, permission, or tool capability that governs this decision. The workflow must align with the controlling rule, not merely state a preference for a different outcome.

options.label: B
options.text: Keep prices, destinations, and structure unchanged; replace delivery guarantees with the supplied shipment estimates throughout the announcement.

options.label: A
options.text: Add more clean documents from the original pilot population to improve confidence under the same narrow conditions.

options.label: B
options.text: Sample the difficult document types and terminology conflicts that the expanded workflow is expected to encounter.

options.label: C
options.text: Define pass thresholds for terminology accuracy and end-to-end handling time before examining the new results.

options.label: D

options.text: Share a chat transcript and let the colleague create future conversations from its copied content.

Grant edit access and add an instruction asking the colleague not to change shared configuration - A prompt instruction cannot override the source, policy, permission, or tool capability that governs this decision. questions.question: Claude reports that first-attempt collection success across two parcel-locker locations was 85%, averaging Location A's 90% (9 of 10) and Location B's 80% (80 of 100). options.label: A
options.text: 85.0%, because equal weighting prevents the busier location from dominating the reported performance.

options.label: B
options.text: 90.0%, because the smaller location's result is less affected by variation in daily collection volume.

options.label: C
options.text: 80.9%, because 89 successful first attempts occurred among 110 individual collection attempts.

options.label: D
options.text: 80.0%, treating the larger location as the combined operating result.

questions.explanation:
✅ The correct option is: 80.9%, because 89 successful first attempts occurred among 110 individual collection attempts.

The report is about all attempts, so calculate successes divided by total attempts: 9 plus 80 over 10 plus 100, or 89/110. Averaging location rates assigns equal weight to unequal volumes and answers a different question. In this scenario, the key concept is weighted aggregation. The best answer is the one that directly tests, protects, or controls that concept before the workflow moves forward. It therefore addresses the decision that actually matters, rather than merely improving presentation, speed, or confidence.

questions.question: A research coordinator has documented a Claude workflow and prepared an approved example output. Before colleagues take over, she wants to learn whether the documentation is sufficient. Which test gives the strongest evidence?

options.label: A
options.text: Demonstrate a new case while colleagues follow the documentation and record any step the demonstration adds to it.

options.label: B
options.text: Have colleagues annotate the documentation with questions, then ask the coordinator to clarify every uncertainty they identify.

options.label: C
options.text: Have a colleague run an unseen case from the instructions and assess it against agreed criteria.

options.label: D
options.text: Ask colleagues to reproduce the approved example and check whether their output matches its wording and section structure.

questions.explanation:
✅ The correct option is: Have a colleague run an unseen case from the instructions and assess it against agreed criteria.

An unseen case run by a colleague tests whether the documentation alone is sufficient, rather than whether someone can imitate a demonstration or approved wording. Agreed criteria make the assessment objective. In this scenario, the key concept is independent execution test. The best answer is the one that directly tests, protects, or controls that concept before the workflow moves forward. It therefore addresses the decision that actually matters, rather than merely improving presentation, speed, or confidence.

❌ Why the Other Options Are Wrong:

Demonstrate a new case while colleagues follow the documentation and record any step the demonstration adds to it - This does not directly test, preserve, or apply the specific requirement stated in the scenario. It may be a reasonable supporting activity, but it does not provide the evidence, control, or accountable decision needed before the work proceeds.

Have colleagues annotate the documentation with questions, then ask the coordinator to clarify every uncertainty they identify - This does not directly test, preserve, or apply the specific requirement stated in the scenario. It may be a reasonable supporting activity, but it does not provide the evidence, control, or accountable decision needed before the work proceeds.

Ask colleagues to reproduce the approved example and check whether their output matches its wording and section structure - This relies on Claude to validate its own output. A model response is not independent evidence, so it cannot establish that the underlying source, rule, calculation, or date is correct. The required check must be made against the relevant authoritative input.

📚 Key Concepts to Remember for the Exam:

1) Test handover documentation with an independent person and a novel case.
2) Identify the claim, decision, or boundary that the scenario actually asks you to control.
3) Prefer the option that creates evidence or preserves the required control before a consequential action.

Claude documentation - https://docs.anthropic.com/en/docs/build-with-claude/develop-tests

questions.domain: Domain 6: Governance, Risk, and Responsible Use
questions.question: A team discovers that a Claude-generated product comparison sent to a customer overstated a compatibility claim. The internal reviewer had approved it without opening the linked source. Which response best supports accountability?

options.label: A
options.text: Update the internal comparison and notify the customer if they ask about compatibility again.

options.label: B
options.text: Send the customer a correction and make the required source check a recorded step before future release.

options.label: C
options.text: Send a correction, then keep the approval process unchanged because the individual reviewer has now been reminded.

options.label: D
options.text: Explain the model's error to the customer and replace the reviewer with an additional automated source check.

questions.explanation:
✅ The correct option is: Send the customer a correction and make the required source check a recorded step before future release.

The customer received an overstated claim, so accountability requires timely correction. Requiring and recording source inspection before release addresses the control failure that permitted the claim. In this scenario, the key concept is correction and prevention. The best answer is the one that directly tests, protects, or controls that concept before the workflow moves forward. It therefore addresses the decision that actually matters, rather than merely improving presentation, speed, or confidence.

❌ Why the Other Options Are Wrong:

Update the internal comparison and notify the customer if they ask about compatibility again - This does not directly test, preserve, or apply the specific requirement stated in the scenario. It may be a reasonable supporting activity, but it does not provide the evidence, control, or accountable decision needed before the work proceeds.

Send a correction, then keep the approval process unchanged because the individual reviewer has now been reminded - This leaves the identified defect or uncertainty in place rather than resolving it before the output is relied on. A caveat, repeated draft, or later correction does not make an unsupported or incomplete result safe to use.

Explain the model's error to the customer and replace the reviewer with an additional automated source check - This does not directly test, preserve, or apply the specific requirement stated in the scenario. It may be a reasonable supporting activity, but it does not provide the evidence, control, or accountable decision needed before the work proceeds.

📚 Key Concepts to Remember for the Exam:

1) Correct external errors and strengthen the failed release control.
2) Identify the claim, decision, or boundary that the scenario actually asks you to control.
3) Prefer the option that creates evidence or preserves the required control before a consequential action.

Claude documentation - https://docs.anthropic.com/en/docs/build-with-claude/prompt-engineering/overview

options.label: B
options.text: Add neutral training examples to the knowledge base and let the relative number of examples determine the tone.

options.label: C
options.text: Set neutral tone in Project instructions for generation and identify the scripts as factual references rather than style examples.

options.label: D
options.text: Delete the sales scripts and rely on the model's general product knowledge to replace their factual content.

questions.explanation:

Project instructions should establish the neutral generation requirement, while the sales scripts can remain factual references rather than implicit tone examples. Renaming or counting examples does not clearly control behaviour. In this scenario, the key concept is separating facts from style. The best answer is the one that directly tests, protects, or controls that concept before the workflow moves forward. It therefore addresses the decision that actually matters, rather than merely improving presentation, speed, or confidence.

Rename the Project to emphasize neutral training and leave its instructions and reference materials unchanged - This leaves the identified defect or uncertainty in place rather than resolving it before the output is relied on. A caveat, repeated draft, or later correction does not make an unsupported or incomplete result safe to use.

Add neutral training examples to the knowledge base and let the relative number of examples determine the tone - This does not directly test, preserve, or apply the specific requirement stated in the scenario. It may be a reasonable supporting activity, but it does not provide the evidence, control, or accountable decision needed before the work proceeds.

Delete the sales scripts and rely on the model's general product knowledge to replace their factual content - Removing information or a control does not resolve the governing issue and can make the resulting work less traceable or less safe. questions.question: A cooperative has fixed the purpose and scoring criteria for a supplier decision. It needs an evidence table from submissions, a scored comparison, and a shortlist memo. Which TWO workflow choices create the strongest control points between these dependent products? Select TWO.

options.label: A
options.text: Generate all three products in one pass, then validate the evidence after the shortlist has been approved.

options.label: B
options.text: Verify the completed evidence table against the original supplier submissions before using it as controlled input to scoring.

options.label: C
options.text: Have every stage reinterpret the original submissions independently so disagreements broaden the analysis.

options.label: D
options.text: Review and approve the scored comparison against the agreed rubric before using those results to draft the shortlist memo.

options.label: E
options.text: Draft the shortlist recommendation before scoring, then extract only the submission evidence needed to justify the suppliers already selected for advancement.

questions.explanation:
✅ The correct option is: Verify the completed evidence table against the original supplier submissions before using it as controlled input to scoring. AND Review and approve the scored comparison against the agreed rubric before using those results to draft the shortlist memo.

Verify the evidence table before scoring, then approve scoring against the rubric before drafting the shortlist. These controls prevent unverified facts or unapproved scores from quietly propagating downstream. In this scenario, the key concept is stage gates. The best answer is the one that directly tests, protects, or controls that concept before the workflow moves forward. It therefore addresses the decision that actually matters, rather than merely improving presentation, speed, or confidence.

❌ Why the Other Options Are Wrong:

Generate all three products in one pass, then validate the evidence after the shortlist has been approved - This places the check or correction too late, after the decision or output has already become harder to control. The relevant evidence or approval must be applied before the consequential action occurs.

Have every stage reinterpret the original submissions independently so disagreements broaden the analysis - This does not directly test, preserve, or apply the specific requirement stated in the scenario. It may be a reasonable supporting activity, but it does not provide the evidence, control, or accountable decision needed before the work proceeds.

Draft the shortlist recommendation before scoring, then extract only the submission evidence needed to justify the suppliers already selected for advancement - This does not directly test, preserve, or apply the specific requirement stated in the scenario. It may be a reasonable supporting activity, but it does not provide the evidence, control, or accountable decision needed before the work proceeds.

📚 Key Concepts to Remember for the Exam:

1) Validate each controlled input before it becomes the next stage’s foundation.
2) Identify the claim, decision, or boundary that the scenario actually asks you to control.
3) Prefer the option that creates evidence or preserves the required control before a consequential action.

questions.question: A wholesale team uses Claude to prepare catalog copy from a verified product table. After copy and reseller sheets are drafted, a product manager changes the pack size for one item. Several documents use that field. Which workflow response best prevents inconsistent versions?

options.label: A
options.text: Update the source table and recheck each dependent output that uses the changed pack size.

options.label: B
options.text: Edit the reseller sheet first and keep the catalog unchanged until its next scheduled revision cycle.

options.label: C
options.text: Regenerate every document from the old table with a prominent note describing the new pack size.

options.label: D
options.text: Correct the catalog paragraph and ask reseller staff to report any mismatches they encounter later.

questions.explanation:
✅ The correct option is: Update the source table and recheck each dependent output that uses the changed pack size.

Change the approved source first, then identify and recheck every output dependent on the altered field. Local edits, delayed corrections, or notes create competing versions of the same fact. In this scenario, the key concept is source-of-truth propagation. The best answer is the one that directly tests, protects, or controls that concept before the workflow moves forward. It therefore addresses the decision that actually matters, rather than merely improving presentation, speed, or confidence.

❌ Why the Other Options Are Wrong:

Edit the reseller sheet first and keep the catalog unchanged until its next scheduled revision cycle - This leaves the identified defect or uncertainty in place rather than resolving it before the output is relied on. A caveat, repeated draft, or later correction does not make an unsupported or incomplete result safe to use.

Regenerate every document from the old table with a prominent note describing the new pack size - This does not directly test, preserve, or apply the specific requirement stated in the scenario. It may be a reasonable supporting activity, but it does not provide the evidence, control, or accountable decision needed before the work proceeds.

Correct the catalog paragraph and ask reseller staff to report any mismatches they encounter later - This does not directly test, preserve, or apply the specific requirement stated in the scenario. It may be a reasonable supporting activity, but it does not provide the evidence, control, or accountable decision needed before the work proceeds.

📚 Key Concepts to Remember for the Exam:

1) Update the source of truth and trace changes through all dependencies.
2) Identify the claim, decision, or boundary that the scenario actually asks you to control.
3) Prefer the option that creates evidence or preserves the required control before a consequential action.

questions.question: An employee-experience team may upload de-identified survey feedback to an approved Claude workspace. options.label: A
options.text: Generalize or remove identifying details under the applicable policy, escalating when useful de-identification remains uncertain.

options.label: B
options.text: Upload the original comments and instruct Claude to suppress sensitive details only in its visible response.

options.label: C
options.text: Assess whether combinations of role, event, and context could allow colleagues to re-identify a respondent.

options.text: Treat the feedback as de-identified because the structured table no longer contains direct name fields.

Treat the feedback as de-identified because the structured table no longer contains direct name fields - More output or more variants do not establish that the governing condition has been met. Replace each removed name with a random identifier while preserving the distinctive narrative details unchanged - Removing information or a control does not resolve the governing issue and can make the resulting work less traceable or less safe. questions.question: A team is considering a third-party Skill that formats public workshop notes. Its sample output is useful, but the package includes scripts that contact an external service, and policy requires review of third-party automation. Which TWO checks are necessary before enabling it? Select TWO.

options.label: A
options.text: Treat widespread adoption as evidence that the package satisfies the organization's own automation requirements.

options.label: B
options.text: Remove explanatory comments from the package so Claude's instructions become the only visible behavior controls.

options.label: C
options.text: Run the package first on genuine workshop notes from multiple events, allowing reviewers to assess formatting quality and consistency under realistic operating conditions.

options.label: D
options.text: Inspect the commands the embedded scripts execute and the information they may transmit beyond the organization's approved environment.

options.label: E
options.text: Verify the package's source and complete the formal review required by the organization's third-party automation policy before activation.

questions.explanation:
✅ The correct option is: Inspect the commands the embedded scripts execute and the information they may transmit beyond the organization's approved environment. AND Verify the package's source and complete the formal review required by the organization's third-party automation policy before activation.

External scripts may execute commands and transmit information, so their behaviour and provenance require inspection and formal approval before activation. Sample quality alone does not address those risks. In this scenario, the key concept is third-party automation review. The best answer is the one that directly tests, protects, or controls that concept before the workflow moves forward. It therefore addresses the decision that actually matters, rather than merely improving presentation, speed, or confidence.

Treat widespread adoption as evidence that the package satisfies the organization's own automation requirements - This does not directly test, preserve, or apply the specific requirement stated in the scenario. It may be a reasonable supporting activity, but it does not provide the evidence, control, or accountable decision needed before the work proceeds.

Run the package first on genuine workshop notes from multiple events, allowing reviewers to assess formatting quality and consistency under realistic operating conditions - This does not directly test, preserve, or apply the specific requirement stated in the scenario. questions.question: A sourcing team uses an approved connector whose available tools can search and read supplier records but cannot modify them. Staff want Claude to update a supplier's address in that source system after drafting a correction. Which configuration decision is appropriate?

options.label: A
options.text: Use an authorized write-capable integration for source updates, or keep that step with staff in the source system.

options.label: B
options.text: Put an address-update procedure in Project instructions and retain the connector's existing read-only tool set.

options.label: C
options.text: Give Claude an example of a successful update response so it can complete the missing action consistently.

options.label: D
options.text: Save the corrected address in Project knowledge so future searches replace the original source record.

questions.explanation:
✅ The correct option is: Use an authorized write-capable integration for source updates, or keep that step with staff in the source system.

A read-only connector cannot update the supplier source just because instructions request it. Use an approved write-capable integration or perform the controlled update with staff in the source system. In this scenario, the key concept is tool capability. The best answer is the one that directly tests, protects, or controls that concept before the workflow moves forward. It therefore addresses the decision that actually matters, rather than merely improving presentation, speed, or confidence.

❌ Why the Other Options Are Wrong:

Put an address-update procedure in Project instructions and retain the connector's existing read-only tool set - This leaves the identified defect or uncertainty in place rather than resolving it before the output is relied on. A caveat, repeated draft, or later correction does not make an unsupported or incomplete result safe to use.

Give Claude an example of a successful update response so it can complete the missing action consistently - This does not directly test, preserve, or apply the specific requirement stated in the scenario. It may be a reasonable supporting activity, but it does not provide the evidence, control, or accountable decision needed before the work proceeds.

Save the corrected address in Project knowledge so future searches replace the original source record - This does not directly test, preserve, or apply the specific requirement stated in the scenario. It may be a reasonable supporting activity, but it does not provide the evidence, control, or accountable decision needed before the work proceeds.

Treat purchase histories as covered by the original approval when the final messages omit customer names - This does not directly test, preserve, or apply the specific requirement stated in the scenario. questions.question: A glassworks has approval to use Claude for internal production planning. A manager proposes extending the same workflow to draft supplier price challenges that will be sent externally. The approval covers neither external correspondence nor commercial negotiation. What should happen first?

options.label: A
options.text: Proceed, since the workflow, the workspace and the reviewing staff all remain unchanged.

options.label: B
options.text: Proceed with a few low-value suppliers and seek approval on the strength of those results.

options.label: C
options.text: Proceed once each drafted challenge is reviewed by the manager owning that supplier relationship.

options.label: D
options.text: Obtain approval covering external correspondence and commercial negotiation before the extended workflow is used.

questions.explanation:
✅ The correct option is: Obtain approval covering external correspondence and commercial negotiation before the extended workflow is used.

The existing approval is limited to internal production planning. Supplier price challenges are external correspondence and commercial negotiation, which the approval explicitly does not cover. The first action is to obtain approval that covers that new use before any external draft is sent. That preserves the stated governance boundary rather than treating an internal approval as transferable.

❌ Why the Other Options Are Wrong:

Proceed, since the workflow, the workspace and the reviewing staff all remain unchanged - The same tools and reviewers do not expand the scope of the existing approval. The new work is a different use: external commercial correspondence.

Proceed with a few low-value suppliers and seek approval on the strength of those results - Running a pilot still sends unapproved external commercial correspondence. Results after the fact cannot create the missing approval.

Proceed once each drafted challenge is reviewed by the manager owning that supplier relationship - A relationship owner reviewing the draft is useful quality control, but it is not the missing approval for external correspondence and commercial negotiation.

1) Apply the stated requirement or boundary before optimizing secondary concerns.
2) Prefer checkable evidence over a model's confidence, a plausible-looking output, or repeated generation.
3) Keep the governing source, approval, and review step aligned with the decision being made.

questions.question: A packaging supplier's classification prompt has run unchanged for a year against a stored set of labelled cases. The team learns that the underlying model has been updated. Nothing has been reported as wrong. What should they do?

options.label: A
options.text: Wait until someone reports a misclassification before running any test of the prompt.

options.label: B
options.text: Ask Claude whether the update affects how it applies the classification rules.

options.label: C
options.text: Rewrite the prompt for the updated model before the next classification run.

options.label: D
options.text: Run the stored labelled cases again and compare against the recorded results.

questions.explanation:
✅ The correct option is: Run the stored labelled cases again and compare against the recorded results.

The correct choice directly addresses the controlling requirement in the scenario. It applies the relevant evidence, boundary, or success condition before the work moves to a consequential next step. That makes it stronger than an answer that merely improves presentation, increases speed, or assumes that a plausible output has already been validated.

Wait until someone reports a misclassification before running any test of the prompt - This does not directly test, preserve, or apply the specific requirement stated in the scenario. It may be a reasonable supporting activity, but it does not provide the evidence, control, or accountable decision needed before the work proceeds.

Ask Claude whether the update affects how it applies the classification rules - This relies on Claude to validate its own output. A model response is not independent evidence, so it cannot establish that the underlying source, rule, calculation, or date is correct. The required check must be made against the authoritative input.

Rewrite the prompt for the updated model before the next classification run - Changing the model does not by itself correct the missing evidence, conflicting requirement, or control failure described in the scenario. questions.question:
A marketing associate sends Claude one combined request for an email draft, a price update, testimonials, and a call to action. The reply covers only the email in full and barely touches the rest.

What should the associate do differently?

options.label: A
options.text: Break the request into separate prompts, one for each requirement, and combine the finished pieces afterward.

options.label: B
options.text: Resend the same combined request again, assuming a second attempt will naturally cover every requirement.

options.label: C
options.text: Ask Claude to expand the existing draft's length, assuming a longer version will include the missing requirements.

options.label: D
options.text: Ask Claude to focus only on refining the email's headline instead of addressing the other requirements.

questions.explanation:
CORRECT: Break the request into separate prompts, one for each requirement, and combine the finished pieces afterward.

Combining an email draft, a price update, testimonials, and a call to action into one request left Claude with several distinct deliverables to juggle at once, and only the first one was carried through completely. Turning each requirement into its own prompt lets Claude give full attention to one deliverable at a time, then the associate assembles the finished pieces.

Exam Guide Mapping

-
Domain: Domain 1: Prompting and Task Execution (14%)

-
Objective: Apply task decomposition techniques to structure complex requests

INCORRECT: Resend the same combined request again, assuming a second attempt will naturally cover every requirement.

Resubmitting the exact same combined request does not change the fact that four distinct deliverables are still competing for attention in a single ask. The same pattern, one requirement handled well and the rest shortchanged, is likely to repeat.

INCORRECT: Ask Claude to expand the existing draft's length, assuming a longer version will include the missing requirements.

Lengthening the same draft might add more words, but nothing about a longer response guarantees the price update, testimonials, and call to action are actually included rather than more detail on the email alone. This would only help if the added length were specifically directed at the missing requirements, which is really the same fix as decomposing the request.

INCORRECT: Ask Claude to focus only on refining the email's headline instead of addressing the other requirements.

Narrowing attention to just the headline ignores the three other requirements entirely rather than resolving them, leaving the price update, testimonials, and call to action unaddressed. This trades one gap for another instead of fixing the underlying issue.

questions.question:
An operations professional sends Claude a single line request to improve our onboarding process. The response reads like generic industry advice, with no reference to the team's current situation.

What should the professional do next?

options.label: A
options.text: Revise the prompt to include the current process steps, the specific improvement goal, and any known constraints.

options.label: B
options.text: Accept the response as useful general guidance, since industry best practices likely apply well to most onboarding programs overall.

options.label: C
options.text: Ask Claude to make the same response sound more specific and detailed without changing what was actually asked.

options.label: D
options.text: Ask Claude to compare onboarding practices across five other companies instead of describing our own process.

questions.explanation:
CORRECT: Revise the prompt to include the current process steps, the specific improvement goal, and any known constraints.

A single line prompt names only the topic, improving onboarding, and leaves out the team's current process, the specific goal for the change, and any constraints Claude should work within. That missing context is exactly why the response reads like generic industry advice instead of tailored recommendations. Supplying those three details turns an open ended request into one Claude can answer specifically.

Exam Guide Mapping

-
Domain: Domain 1: Prompting and Task Execution (14%)

-
Objective: Create effective prompts for business and technical tasks

INCORRECT: Accept the response as useful general guidance, since industry best practices likely apply well to most onboarding programs overall.

General industry practices are not the same as advice tailored to this team's actual process, since the response never engaged with the team's current steps or constraints at all. Treating broad, unanchored guidance as useful overlooks that the prompt gave Claude nothing specific to build on.

INCORRECT: Ask Claude to make the same response sound more specific and detailed without changing what was actually asked.

Asking for a more specific sounding tone changes word choice, not the missing information itself, so the reply could still lack any real detail about this team's process. This would only become a genuine fix if the follow up also supplied the process steps, goal, and constraints, which is the same solution under different wording.

INCORRECT: Ask Claude to compare onboarding practices across five other companies instead of describing our own process.

Comparing practices across other companies produces a different kind of research entirely, rather than describing this team's own onboarding process, goal, and constraints as the original request needed. It sidesteps the gap instead of closing it.

questions.question:
A communications specialist asks Claude to draft a client-facing announcement about a policy change. The draft uses formal legal style phrasing and several unexplained internal acronyms that clients will not recognize.

What should the specialist do next?

options.label: A
options.text: Give Claude feedback on the mismatch and ask for a plain language revision aimed at everyday, non-expert readers.

options.label: B
options.text: Send the announcement as drafted, since it accurately explains the policy change in full detail.

options.label: C
options.text: Ask Claude to spell out the acronyms in parentheses while leaving the rest of the legal style phrasing completely unchanged.

options.label: D
options.text: Ask Claude to shorten the announcement to a single sentence, without addressing the phrasing at all.

questions.explanation:
CORRECT: Give Claude feedback on the mismatch and ask for a plain language revision aimed at everyday, non-expert readers.

The draft's formal legal phrasing and unexplained internal acronyms are signs it was written for an internal, expert audience rather than the clients who will actually read it. Giving Claude that specific feedback and asking for a plain language revision aimed at everyday readers lets it revise using context it already has, rather than starting over.

Exam Guide Mapping

-
Domain: Domain 1: Prompting and Task Execution (14%)

-
Objective: Iterate prompts to improve output quality

INCORRECT: Send the announcement as drafted, since it accurately explains the policy change in full detail.

Explaining the policy in full detail is not the same as explaining it in language clients can follow, since the draft's legal phrasing and internal acronyms are exactly what a general audience would struggle with. Completeness does not fix a readability mismatch.

INCORRECT: Ask Claude to spell out the acronyms in parentheses while leaving the rest of the legal style phrasing completely unchanged.

Spelling out acronyms addresses one symptom while leaving the deeper problem, dense legal style phrasing throughout the rest of the announcement, completely untouched. This would only become adequate if the specialist also asked for the legal phrasing itself to be simplified, which is essentially the same revision requested a different way.

INCORRECT: Ask Claude to shorten the announcement to a single sentence, without addressing the phrasing at all.

Cutting the announcement to one sentence removes detail without addressing why the existing phrasing and acronyms are hard for clients to follow. A shorter announcement written in the same dense style would still confuse the same readers.

questions.question:
A project manager pastes three vendor proposals into Claude and asks which one is best. The reply names a winner, but its justification shifts between price, speed, and reputation across paragraphs.

What should the manager add to the prompt?

options.label: A
options.text: Name the specific factors the proposals should be judged against, such as cost, timeline, and risk tolerance.

options.label: B
options.text: Accept the named winner as final, since Claude reviewed the full text of all three proposals.

options.label: C
options.text: Ask Claude to restate its recommendation once more so the justification sounds more consistent, without changing what was actually evaluated.

options.label: D
options.text: Ask Claude to rank the vendors alphabetically instead of evaluating which proposal is strongest.

questions.explanation:
CORRECT: Name the specific factors the proposals should be judged against, such as cost, timeline, and risk tolerance.

A justification that shifts between price, speed, and reputation from paragraph to paragraph shows Claude was never told which factors should actually decide the comparison. Naming specific criteria, such as cost, timeline, and risk tolerance, gives Claude a consistent basis to evaluate all three proposals against rather than switching rationale midway.

INCORRECT: Accept the named winner as final, since Claude reviewed the full text of all three proposals.

Reviewing the full text of each proposal is not the same as judging them against a consistent standard, since the shifting justification shows no stable criteria were ever applied. Full document coverage does not guarantee a defensible recommendation.

INCORRECT: Ask Claude to restate its recommendation once more so the justification sounds more consistent, without changing what was actually evaluated.

Asking for the recommendation to be restated only changes how confidently it sounds, not what it was actually based on, so the same shifting rationale could easily persist in different words. This would only fix the problem if the manager also specified which criteria to judge by, which is the real solution here.

INCORRECT: Ask Claude to rank the vendors alphabetically instead of evaluating which proposal is strongest.

Ranking vendors alphabetically ignores the comparison entirely and produces an ordering that has nothing to do with which proposal is actually strongest. It sidesteps the evaluation task rather than fixing how it was set up.

questions.question:
A market analyst asks Claude one open ended question about electric vehicle trends and gets back a reply that jumps between unrelated countries, decades old statistics, and unverified anecdotes with no clear focus.

What should the analyst do differently?

options.label: A
options.text: Narrow the question by specifying a target region, time period, and source type before asking again.

options.label: B
options.text: Treat the reply as adequate coverage, since it does mention multiple electric vehicle markets across different points in time.

options.label: C
options.text: Ask Claude to present the same information as a bulleted list so it reads as more organized.

options.label: D
options.text: Ask Claude to translate the reply into a different language, assuming that will make the trends easier to compare.

questions.explanation:
CORRECT: Narrow the question by specifying a target region, time period, and source type before asking again.

The scattered reply, jumping across countries, mixing decades old data, and leaning on unverified anecdotes, signals that the original question never set a region, a timeframe, or a required evidence type. Narrowing the question along exactly those three dimensions gives Claude a defined scope to answer within instead of ranging freely across the topic.

Exam Guide Mapping

-
Domain: Domain 1: Prompting and Task Execution (14%)

-
Objective: Create effective prompts for business and technical tasks

INCORRECT: Treat the reply as adequate coverage, since it does mention multiple electric vehicle markets across different points in time.

Mentioning multiple markets and time periods is not the same as answering within a defined scope, since the reply's scattershot coverage is itself evidence that no clear region, timeframe, or evidence type was ever established. Treating breadth as adequacy misses the actual gap in the original question.

INCORRECT: Ask Claude to present the same information as a bulleted list so it reads as more organized.

Reformatting the same unscoped information into a list changes its presentation, not its substance, so the same mix of unrelated countries, eras, and anecdotes would simply appear in a tidier layout. This would only add real value if the reorganization also grouped the content by a chosen region and time period, at which point it becomes the same underlying fix.

INCORRECT: Ask Claude to translate the reply into a different language, assuming that will make the trends easier to compare.

Translating the reply changes its language, not its scope, so the same unfocused mix of countries, eras, and anecdotal claims carries over untouched into the translated version. The comparison problem was never about language in the first place.

options: Narrow the question by specifying a target region, time period, and source type before asking again.
Treat the reply as adequate coverage, since it does mention multiple electric vehicle markets across different points in time.

What should the officer do next?

options.label: A
options.text: Send Claude the group's target length and a past successful letter, then ask for a shorter, warmer revision.

options.label: B
options.text: Send the draft to donors as is, since it still communicates the fundraising appeal's core message clearly.

options.label: C
options.text: Ask Claude to cut the draft down to a single paragraph without giving any other direction.

options.label: D
options.text: Ask Claude to add the donor's name in bold at the top of the same letter to personalize it.

questions.explanation:
CORRECT: Send Claude the group's target length and a past successful letter, then ask for a shorter, warmer revision.

The reply came back three times longer than the group typically sends and noticeably more formal, both signs that Claude was never told a target length or shown what the organization's voice actually sounds like. Supplying a length target and a past successful letter gives Claude a concrete standard to draft against instead of guessing.

Exam Guide Mapping

-
Domain: Domain 1: Prompting and Task Execution (14%)

-
Objective: Iterate prompts to improve output quality

INCORRECT: Send the draft to donors as is, since it still communicates the fundraising appeal's core message clearly.

Communicating the core message is not the same as matching the length and tone this organization's donors expect, since sending a reply that reads far longer and more formal than usual risks feeling off brand regardless of whether the facts are correct.

INCORRECT: Ask Claude to cut the draft down to a single paragraph without giving any other direction.

Adding a bolded donor name changes a cosmetic detail while leaving the underlying length and tone mismatch fully intact, since personalizing a greeting does not address why the letter reads three times longer and more formal than the group's usual style.

questions.question:
A product manager asks Claude one question that both requests brainstorming for new features and immediately asks for the single top pick. The reply returns just one suggestion with no other ideas shown.

What should the manager do differently?

options.label: A
options.text: Separate the request into two steps, first generate a range of ideas, then pick the best one.

options.label: B
options.text: Accept the single suggestion as final, since Claude typically has strong instincts about which features matter most for users.

options.label: C
options.text: Ask Claude to expand on the same suggestion with more supporting detail and specific examples.

options.label: D
options.text: Ask Claude to rank the single suggestion against competitor products instead of generating any new ideas.

questions.explanation:
CORRECT: Separate the request into two steps, first generate a range of ideas, then pick the best one.

The single prompt asked Claude to brainstorm and immediately pick a favorite in the same breath, so no real spread of ideas existed before a choice was made. Separating generation from selection gives Claude room to produce several distinct concepts first, with picking a top choice handled as its own later step.

Exam Guide Mapping

-
Domain: Domain 1: Prompting and Task Execution (14%)

-
Objective: Apply task decomposition techniques to structure complex requests

INCORRECT: Accept the single suggestion as final, since Claude typically has strong instincts about which features matter most for users.

Claude's general instincts on other tasks do not make one ungenerated pick reliable here, since the prompt never allowed a real set of ideas to form before the top choice was named. Treating a single early guess as sound skips the brainstorming step entirely.

INCORRECT: Ask Claude to expand on the same suggestion with more supporting detail and specific examples.

Expanding the same suggestion with more detail produces a richer description of one idea, not a set of alternatives to weigh. This would only serve the manager's actual goal if the added detail took the form of several distinct new ideas rather than more support for the single one already given.

INCORRECT: Ask Claude to rank the single suggestion against competitor products instead of generating any new ideas.

Ranking the lone suggestion against competitors evaluates an idea that was never really chosen from a broader set, rather than creating the wider pool of features the manager actually asked to brainstorm. This adds a comparison, not variety.

questions.question:
An HR professional asks Claude to summarize employee survey results and receives three dense paragraphs of prose. The professional needs to paste the results directly into presentation slides as short bullet points.

What should the professional do next?

options.label: A
options.text: Resubmit the request specifying that the summary should be delivered as short bullet points suitable for slides.

options.label: B
options.text: Copy the paragraphs into the slides as is, since the prose does capture the survey results accurately.

options.label: C
options.text: Ask Claude to add line breaks between sentences in the same paragraphs, assuming that alone will make them look like a bullet list.

options.label: D
options.text: Ask Claude to expand the summary with additional statistical detail, assuming a longer summary will be easier to present.

questions.explanation:
CORRECT: Resubmit the request specifying that the summary should be delivered as short bullet points suitable for slides.

The reply came back as three dense paragraphs of prose, but the professional actually needs short bullet points ready to paste into slides, a mismatch that shows the original request never specified the output format. Resubmitting with an explicit bullet point requirement gives Claude the missing constraint it needs to match the deliverable to its actual use.

Exam Guide Mapping

-
Domain: Domain 1: Prompting and Task Execution (14%)

-
Objective: Iterate prompts to improve output quality

INCORRECT: Copy the paragraphs into the slides as is, since the prose does capture the survey results accurately.

Copying the accurate paragraphs directly into the slides ignores that the professional needs short bullet points, not dense prose, regardless of whether the content itself is correct. Accuracy of the summary does not solve a format mismatch between what was delivered and what the slides require.

INCORRECT: Ask Claude to add line breaks between sentences in the same paragraphs, assuming that alone will make them look like a bullet list.

Adding line breaks between existing sentences only visually separates the same long, wordy prose rather than condensing it into short, punchy bullet phrasing appropriate for slides. This option would only work if the professional also asked Claude to rewrite each point as a short standalone phrase, which is effectively the format specification needed in the first place.

INCORRECT: Ask Claude to expand the summary with additional statistical detail, assuming a longer summary will be easier to present.

Expanding the summary with more statistical detail adds length in the same prose format, doing nothing to address why the current shape does not fit directly into slides. More detail in paragraph form is no easier to present than less detail in the same form.

questions.question:
A curriculum coordinator asks Claude for a one page science fact sheet for parents. It includes a specific temperature statistic absent from the classroom's vetted materials.

What should the coordinator do before distributing it?

options.label: A
options.text: Verify the statistic against a reliable, vetted source before including it in the fact sheet for parents.

options.label: B
options.text: Distribute the fact sheet as is, since the statistic reads consistently with general scientific knowledge on the topic.

options.label: C
options.text: Soften the statistic's wording with an approximate qualifier, without checking whether the number itself is accurate.

options.label: D
options.text: Remove every statistic from the fact sheet entirely, including ones the coordinator can already confirm are accurate.

questions.explanation:
CORRECT: Verify the statistic against a reliable, vetted source before including it in the fact sheet for parents.

The fact sheet is headed for parents, but one specific statistic is not backed by any of the classroom's vetted reference materials. Verifying that number against a reliable outside source closes the gap before the statistic reaches an audience that will take it at face value.

Exam Guide Mapping

-
Domain: Domain 2: Output Evaluation and Validation (21%)

-
Objective: Apply fact-checking and validation techniques

INCORRECT: Distribute the fact sheet as is, since the statistic reads consistently with general scientific knowledge on the topic.

Reading consistently with general scientific knowledge does not confirm that a specific number is correct, since the same missing sourcing problem still applies. Fluent, plausible sounding phrasing is not a substitute for actually checking where the figure came from.

INCORRECT: Soften the statistic's wording with an approximate qualifier, without checking whether the number itself is accurate.

Adding a qualifier like approximately softens the claim's tone but leaves the number itself unverified, so an inaccurate statistic could still reach parents just phrased more cautiously. This option would only resolve the issue if the coordinator paired the softer wording with an actual check of the source, which is the verification step already needed.

INCORRECT: Remove every statistic from the fact sheet entirely, including ones the coordinator can already confirm are accurate.

Removing every statistic, including ones the coordinator can already confirm, discards useful and verifiable information rather than addressing the one unsupported number. The fix should target the specific unverified claim, not eliminate all quantitative content.

questions.question:
A supply chain manager asks Claude to summarize a vendor contract's risk clauses. The summary covers payment terms and delivery timelines but never mentions termination or liability, which the manager knows the contract addresses.

What should the manager do next?

options.label: A
options.text: Ask Claude to specifically summarize the termination and liability clauses before relying on the summary.

options.label: B
options.text: Treat the summary as complete, since it already captures the two most commonly negotiated contract terms.

options.label: C
options.text: Ask Claude to make the same summary longer overall, without pointing to which clauses were left out.

options.label: D
options.text: Escalate the entire contract to legal for a full manual review, bypassing any further use of the summary.

questions.explanation:
CORRECT: Ask Claude to specifically summarize the termination and liability clauses before relying on the summary.

The summary leaves out termination and liability, two clauses the manager already knows exist in the contract, even though it covers payment and delivery in full. Asking Claude to specifically address the omitted clauses closes that known gap before the manager treats the summary as a complete risk picture.

Exam Guide Mapping

-
Domain: Domain 2: Output Evaluation and Validation (21%)

-
Objective: Evaluate Claude-generated outputs for accuracy and completeness

INCORRECT: Treat the summary as complete, since it already captures the two most commonly negotiated contract terms.

Covering the two most commonly negotiated terms is not the same as covering every clause the manager already knows matters, since termination and liability were left out entirely. A partial summary does not become complete just because it addresses familiar territory.

INCORRECT: Ask Claude to make the same summary longer overall, without pointing to which clauses were left out.

Making the summary longer without naming which clauses are missing could simply add more detail to the sections already covered, leaving termination and liability untouched. This option would only close the gap if the added length were specifically directed at the omitted clauses, which is the same fix the manager actually needs.

INCORRECT: Escalate the entire contract to legal for a full manual review, bypassing any further use of the summary.

Escalating the entire contract to legal abandons a summary that is mostly complete over one identifiable, fixable gap. A quick follow up request targeting the missing clauses resolves the issue without discarding the AI assisted summary altogether.
