questions.question:
A grant writer asks Claude to draft prior research support for a proposal. The draft attributes a specific line to a named foundation report the writer cannot locate anywhere.

What should the writer do before submitting it?

options.label: A
options.text: Confirm the quoted line and report actually exist by checking the foundation's own published materials.

options.label: B
options.text: Include the line as written, since it reads as specific and authoritative enough to be genuine.

options.label: C
options.text: Remove the quotation marks around the line but keep the same claimed source and wording in the proposal.

options.label: D
options.text: Delete every reference to prior research support from the section, including any studies the writer can independently confirm.

questions.explanation:
CORRECT: Confirm the quoted line and report actually exist by checking the foundation's own published materials.

A specific attributed line tied to a named foundation report that the writer cannot locate anywhere is a warning sign of a fabricated detail, since Claude can generate confident sounding, specific looking citations that do not correspond to any real source. Checking the foundation's own published materials confirms whether the line and report genuinely exist before it goes into a submitted proposal.

Exam Guide Mapping

-
Domain: Domain 2: Output Evaluation and Validation (21%)

-
Objective: Identify hallucinations, inconsistencies, and biases in responses

INCORRECT: Include the line as written, since it reads as specific and authoritative enough to be genuine.

Sounding specific and authoritative is exactly the kind of surface confidence a fabricated citation can carry, so it is not evidence that the line or report is real. Including it on that basis risks putting an unverifiable claim into a proposal that funders may scrutinize closely.

INCORRECT: Remove the quotation marks around the line but keep the same claimed source and wording in the proposal.

Removing the quotation marks changes the line from a direct quote to a paraphrase but keeps the same unverified source and claim in the proposal. This option would only address the underlying risk if the writer also confirmed the foundation report exists, which is the verification step already required.

INCORRECT: Delete every reference to prior research support from the section, including any studies the writer can independently confirm.

Deleting every reference to prior research, including studies the writer can independently confirm, discards legitimate support the proposal may need over one unverified line. The fix should target the specific unconfirmed attribution, not remove all research references.

questions.question:
A financial analyst asks Claude to summarize a quarterly earnings report. One paragraph states revenue grew 12 percent while a later paragraph, describing the same period, states revenue declined slightly.

What should the analyst do next?

options.label: A
options.text: Compare both revenue figures against the original earnings report to determine which one is accurate.

options.label: B
options.text: Use whichever figure appears first in the summary, since it was likely generated most carefully.

options.label: C
options.text: Ask Claude to pick one of the two figures and restate it consistently throughout the summary.

options.label: D
options.text: Send the summary to the compliance team for review without first checking either figure.

questions.explanation:
CORRECT: Compare both revenue figures against the original earnings report to determine which one is accurate.

Two paragraphs describing the same period give contradictory revenue figures, a 12 percent increase in one place and a slight decline in another, so at least one of them must be wrong. Comparing both numbers against the original earnings report is the only way to determine which figure, if either, actually reflects the source data.

Exam Guide Mapping

-
Domain: Domain 2: Output Evaluation and Validation (21%)

-
Objective: Identify hallucinations, inconsistencies, and biases in responses

INCORRECT: Use whichever figure appears first in the summary, since it was likely generated most carefully.

Assuming the first figure mentioned is the most carefully generated has no real basis, since both numbers come from the same response and either one could be the error. Position within the summary says nothing about which figure matches the original report.

INCORRECT: Ask Claude to pick one of the two figures and restate it consistently throughout the summary.

Picking one figure and restating it consistently fixes the appearance of the contradiction without confirming that the chosen number is actually correct. This would only resolve the real problem if the choice were based on checking the original report, which is the verification step still missing.

INCORRECT: Send the summary to the compliance team for review without first checking either figure.

Escalating to compliance before doing any basic verification skips a check the analyst can easily perform directly against the earnings report. Involving compliance may still be warranted later, but it does not substitute for first confirming which of the two figures is accurate.

questions.question:
A public health communicator asks Claude to draft an FAQ about a new vaccine. The draft states a specific efficacy percentage the communicator has not seen in any agency publication.

What should the communicator do before the FAQ is published?

options.label: A
options.text: Verify the efficacy percentage against an authoritative source, such as the CDC or WHO, before publishing.

options.label: B
options.text: Publish the FAQ as drafted, since Claude generally provides accurate figures on well known medical topics.

options.label: C
options.text: Add a footnote saying figures may vary, without confirming what the actual efficacy percentage is.

options.label: D
options.text: Remove every specific number from the FAQ entirely, including figures the communicator can already independently confirm are accurate.

questions.explanation:
CORRECT: Verify the efficacy percentage against an authoritative source, such as the CDC or WHO, before publishing.

A specific efficacy percentage that does not appear in any agency publication the communicator has seen is exactly the kind of claim that needs outside confirmation before it reaches the public. Checking the figure against an authoritative source like the CDC or WHO ensures a health related FAQ is not built on an unverified number.

Exam Guide Mapping

-
Domain: Domain 2: Output Evaluation and Validation (21%)

-
Objective: Apply fact-checking and validation techniques

INCORRECT: Publish the FAQ as drafted, since Claude generally provides accurate figures on well known medical topics.

General reliability on well known topics does not confirm that this particular efficacy percentage is correct, since a specific figure absent from any agency source could still be inaccurate. Publishing a public facing health claim on that assumption skips the verification the situation calls for.

INCORRECT: Add a footnote saying figures may vary, without confirming what the actual efficacy percentage is.

A footnote acknowledging that figures may vary flags uncertainty without resolving it, since the actual efficacy percentage still goes unconfirmed. This would only become adequate if the footnote were paired with an actual check against an authoritative source, which is the verification step itself.

INCORRECT: Remove every specific number from the FAQ entirely, including figures the communicator can already independently confirm are accurate.

Removing every specific number, including ones the communicator can already confirm as accurate, discards verified information over one unconfirmed figure. The fix should target the specific unverified efficacy percentage, not eliminate every number the FAQ contains.

questions.question:
An HR business partner asks Claude to draft a termination letter that cites specific policy violations by the employee. The draft reads polished and professional.

What should the partner do before sending it?

options.label: A
options.text: Have HR leadership or legal review the letter for accuracy and compliance before it is sent.

options.label: B
options.text: Send the letter as drafted, since it reads polished and uses a professional, confident tone throughout.

options.label: C
options.text: Ask Claude to soften a few of the letter's harsher sounding phrases before sending it out.

options.label: D
options.text: Route the letter through outside legal counsel for a full contract review before any HR staff see it.

questions.explanation:
CORRECT: Have HR leadership or legal review the letter for accuracy and compliance before it is sent.

A termination letter that cites specific policy violations directly affects someone's employment and carries legal exposure for the organization, so a polished tone alone does not confirm the content is accurate or compliant. Having HR leadership or legal review it before sending catches errors and risk that professional sounding phrasing can mask.

Exam Guide Mapping

-
Domain: Domain 2: Output Evaluation and Validation (21%)

-
Objective: Determine when human review or additional verification is required

INCORRECT: Send the letter as drafted, since it reads polished and uses a professional, confident tone throughout.

Reading polished and confident is a surface quality of the writing, not evidence that the cited policy violations are accurate or that the letter meets legal requirements. A high stakes, employment ending document needs more than fluent phrasing before it goes out.

INCORRECT: Ask Claude to soften a few of the letter's harsher sounding phrases before sending it out.

Softening a few harsh sounding phrases changes tone, not whether the underlying policy violations are stated accurately or the letter is legally sound. This would only address the real risk if paired with an actual review of the letter's substance by HR leadership or legal.

INCORRECT: Route the letter through outside legal counsel for a full contract review before any HR staff see it.

Routing the letter through outside legal counsel for a full contract review is a heavier process than this situation typically needs, since standard HR or legal review is normally sufficient. Reaching for a disproportionate level of scrutiny is not the calibrated step here.

questions.question:
A compliance officer asks Claude to summarize a new data privacy regulation. Most of the summary matches materials the officer already knows, but one bullet cites an unusually specific penalty amount never seen elsewhere.

What should the officer do next?

options.label: A
options.text: Verify that one specific penalty figure against the regulation's official text, even though the rest matches known material.

options.label: B
options.text: Accept the entire summary as reliable, since most of it matches materials the officer already knows well.

options.label: C
options.text: Reverify every bullet in the summary in equal depth, rather than focusing extra scrutiny on the one unusual figure.

options.label: D
options.text: Add a caveat noting that figures should be confirmed independently, without checking the penalty amount itself.

questions.explanation:
CORRECT: Verify that one specific penalty figure against the regulation's official text, even though the rest matches known material.

Most of the summary lines up with materials the officer already trusts, but the unusually specific penalty amount stands apart as a claim with no prior confirmation and real regulatory stakes if wrong. Verifying that one figure against the regulation's official text targets the actual risk without re-checking content that is already known to be reliable.

Exam Guide Mapping

-
Domain: Domain 2: Output Evaluation and Validation (21%)

-
Objective: Apply fact-checking and validation techniques

INCORRECT: Accept the entire summary as reliable, since most of it matches materials the officer already knows well.

Trusting the whole summary because most of it matches known material overlooks that one specific claim, the penalty figure, has no such backing and carries its own risk if incorrect. Overall familiarity does not extend automatically to every individual detail in the response.

INCORRECT: Reverify every bullet in the summary in equal depth, rather than focusing extra scrutiny on the one unusual figure.

Reverifying every bullet in equal depth spends effort on content the officer already recognizes as accurate while giving the one genuinely uncertain figure no more scrutiny than everything else. This would be the right instinct only if directed specifically at the unusual penalty amount rather than spread evenly across the summary.

INCORRECT: Add a caveat noting that figures should be confirmed independently, without checking the penalty amount itself.

A caveat about confirming figures independently shifts the verification burden onto whoever reads the summary later instead of resolving whether the specific penalty amount is accurate now. It leaves the actual claim unchecked while sounding like a responsible addition.

questions.question:
A support lead asks Claude to adapt an internal troubleshooting guide for non-technical customers. The customer facing version still includes internal error codes and engineering shorthand throughout.

What should the lead do next?

options.label: A
options.text: Ask Claude to revise the guide again, replacing the error codes and shorthand with plain language customers can follow.

options.label: B
options.text: Publish the guide as is, since it still covers the exact same troubleshooting steps customers actually need to resolve their issue.

options.label: C
options.text: Ask Claude to add a glossary defining the error codes at the end of the same guide.

options.label: D
options.text: Ask Claude to add more troubleshooting steps to the guide, assuming extra steps will make it clearer for customers.

questions.explanation:
CORRECT: Ask Claude to revise the guide again, replacing the error codes and shorthand with plain language customers can follow.

Internal error codes and engineering shorthand surviving into the customer facing version show the adaptation never actually changed the language itself, even though it targets the right audience on paper. Asking for a further revision that replaces that jargon with plain language is what actually closes the gap between the internal draft and a customer ready guide.

Exam Guide Mapping

-
Domain: Domain 2: Output Evaluation and Validation (21%)

-
Objective: Edit, adapt, refine, and compare outputs for the intended audience

INCORRECT: Publish the guide as is, since it still covers the exact same troubleshooting steps customers actually need to resolve their issue.

Covering the correct steps does not mean customers can understand them, since the error codes and shorthand are precisely the kind of language a non-technical reader will struggle to follow. Matching the content is not the same as matching the audience.

INCORRECT: Ask Claude to add a glossary defining the error codes at the end of the same guide.

A glossary appended at the end helps a reader decode the jargon after the fact but leaves the body of the guide just as dense as before. This would only match the correct fix if the glossary were paired with rewriting the body itself in plain language, rather than replacing it.

INCORRECT: Ask Claude to add more troubleshooting steps to the guide, assuming extra steps will make it clearer for customers.

Adding more steps increases the guide's length without touching the actual problem, which is word choice, not step count. More content written in the same jargon heavy style does nothing to make it clearer for a non-technical reader.

A proposal writer asks Claude for three different opening paragraphs for a client pitch, each written in a different tone. The client is known to prefer formal, understated communication.

What should the writer do before choosing one?

options.label: A
options.text: Compare the three paragraphs specifically against the client's known preference for formal, understated communication.

options.label: B
options.text: Pick whichever paragraph appears first in Claude's response, since first drafts are usually the strongest option.

options.label: C
options.text: Ask Claude which of the three paragraphs it recommends most, and use that choice without independent comparison.

options.label: D
options.text: Ask Claude to merge all three paragraphs into one single opening instead of choosing between them.

questions.explanation:
CORRECT: Compare the three paragraphs specifically against the client's known preference for formal, understated communication.

Three paragraphs in three different tones only become a real choice once measured against something concrete, and the client's known preference for formal, understated communication is exactly that standard. Comparing each option against that specific preference is what turns three interchangeable drafts into one defensible pick.

Exam Guide Mapping

-
Domain: Domain 2: Output Evaluation and Validation (21%)

-
Objective: Edit, adapt, refine, and compare outputs for the intended audience

INCORRECT: Pick whichever paragraph appears first in Claude's response, since first drafts are usually the strongest option.

The order paragraphs appear in has no connection to which tone actually fits this client, so treating the first one as automatically strongest ignores the one detail that should decide the choice.

INCORRECT: Ask Claude which of the three paragraphs it recommends most, and use that choice without independent comparison.

Asking for a recommendation without supplying the client's preference leaves Claude to guess at the same standard the writer already knows. This would only become adequate if the writer first gave Claude the formal, understated preference to judge against, at which point it is the same comparison stated differently.

INCORRECT: Ask Claude to merge all three paragraphs into one single opening instead of choosing between them.

Merging three differently toned paragraphs together risks producing an inconsistent opening rather than one that matches the client's preferred style. It avoids the actual choice instead of making it.

An operations analyst asks Claude to build a 40 row monthly expense tracking template the team will reuse and edit every month. Claude returns the template as plain text directly in the chat window.

What should the analyst do next?

options.label: A
options.text: Ask Claude to deliver the template as a structured, downloadable spreadsheet the team can reuse and edit directly.

options.label: B
options.text: Copy the plain text template into an email as is, since it already lists every expense category the team currently tracks each month.

options.label: C
options.text: Ask Claude to reformat the same plain text response with bullet points for easier reading in the chat.

options.label: D
options.text: Ask a developer to build a custom expense tracking application through the API instead of this template.

questions.explanation:
CORRECT: Ask Claude to deliver the template as a structured, downloadable spreadsheet the team can reuse and edit directly.

A 40 row template the team will reuse and edit every month is exactly the kind of significant, self-contained, reusable deliverable that calls for a structured format rather than plain text buried in the chat window. Asking Claude to deliver it as a downloadable spreadsheet matches the format to how the team actually intends to use it.

Exam Guide Mapping

-
Domain: Domain 2: Output Evaluation and Validation (21%)

-
Objective: Organize and curate information and select appropriate output formats (artifacts, inline, structured data)

INCORRECT: Copy the plain text template into an email as is, since it already lists every expense category the team currently tracks each month.

Having the right categories listed does not make plain text in an email editable or reusable month after month, since the team still lacks a structured file they can update directly. Content coverage is not the same as a usable format.

INCORRECT: Ask Claude to reformat the same plain text response with bullet points for easier reading in the chat.

Bulleted plain text is easier to read but still lives inside the chat window rather than as an editable, downloadable file. This would only meet the team's need if it were paired with an actual structured, downloadable format, which is the fix already required.

INCORRECT: Ask a developer to build a custom expense tracking application through the API instead of this template.

Commissioning a custom application through the API is a far heavier build than a recurring expense template needs, when a platform native structured output already solves the reuse and editing requirement directly.

A researcher asks Claude to synthesize five industry reports into one competitive landscape summary. The response returns five separate paragraphs, each mirroring one report's original structure, with no comparison across them.

What should the researcher do next?

options.label: A
options.text: Ask Claude to reorganize the content around shared themes so it compares the five reports directly.

options.label: B
options.text: Accept the five paragraphs as sufficient, since each one accurately reflects the details of its own source report.

options.label: C
options.text: Ask Claude to add transition sentences between the same five paragraphs without changing their underlying structure.

options.label: D
options.text: Ask Claude to summarize only one of the five reports instead of covering all five sources.

questions.explanation:
CORRECT: Ask Claude to reorganize the content around shared themes so it compares the five reports directly.

Five paragraphs that each mirror one report's own structure, with no comparison across them, is a rundown of sources rather than a synthesized competitive landscape. Reorganizing the content around shared themes is what actually produces the cross report comparison the researcher originally asked for.

Exam Guide Mapping

-
Domain: Domain 2: Output Evaluation and Validation (21%)

-
Objective: Organize and curate information and select appropriate output formats (artifacts, inline, structured data)

INCORRECT: Accept the five paragraphs as sufficient, since each one accurately reflects the details of its own source report.

Each paragraph being accurate to its own source does not add up to a synthesized summary, since accuracy within a single report says nothing about whether the reports were actually compared against one another.

questions.question:
An operations coordinator asks Claude whether a new scheduling tool will integrate with the team's legacy system. Claude replies with complete certainty that it will work seamlessly, citing no test or source.

What should the coordinator do before proceeding?

options.label: A
options.text: Verify the integration through testing or documentation, since confidence is not proof of compatibility.

options.label: B
options.text: Proceed with the integration as planned, since Claude expressed no uncertainty about the outcome.

options.label: C
options.text: Ask Claude to state its confidence level as a percentage before deciding whether to proceed with the integration project.

options.label: D
options.text: Cancel the integration project entirely, since Claude was unable to cite a specific source.

questions.explanation:
CORRECT: Verify the integration through testing or documentation, since confidence is not proof of compatibility.

Claude answered with complete certainty but cited no test or source, and a confident tone by itself says nothing about whether the two systems will actually work together. Testing the integration directly or checking technical documentation is what confirms compatibility, rather than the phrasing Claude used.

Exam Guide Mapping

-
Domain: Domain 2: Output Evaluation and Validation (21%)

-
Objective: Apply fact-checking and validation techniques

INCORRECT: Proceed with the integration as planned, since Claude expressed no uncertainty about the outcome.

The absence of hedging language is a feature of how the answer was worded, not evidence that the systems are actually compatible, so proceeding on that basis skips the verification the situation needs.

INCORRECT: Ask Claude to state its confidence level as a percentage before deciding whether to proceed with the integration project.

A self reported percentage is still self reported, no more grounded in an actual test or document than the original confident sentence was. This would only help if paired with independent verification, which is the actual fix needed here.

INCORRECT: Cancel the integration project entirely, since Claude was unable to cite a specific source.

Cancelling the project outright discards a potentially workable integration over an unverified claim, when a quick test or documentation check could confirm compatibility without abandoning the project.

questions.question: A recruiter starts a new chat for every resume screened, pasting in the same interview rubric and job description each time before Claude can score the candidate. What should the recruiter do instead?

options.label: A
options.text: Move this recurring screening work into a Project holding the rubric and job description permanently.

options.label: B
options.text: Keep opening a new chat for each resume, since Claude scores candidates correctly once the rubric is pasted in.

options.label: C
options.text: Bookmark one chat conversation for reuse, without changing how the rubric gets supplied to Claude.

options.label: D
options.text: Stop using Claude for candidate screening and have the hiring team review every resume manually.

questions.explanation:
CORRECT: Move this recurring screening work into a Project holding the rubric and job description permanently.

Pasting the same rubric and job description into a new chat before every single resume is the sign of a recurring task without a home for its shared context. A Project keeps that rubric and description in place permanently, so each new screening starts with them already available.

Exam Guide Mapping

-
Domain: Domain 5: Configuration and Knowledge Management (12%)

-
Objective: Configure Claude Projects with instructions and knowledge sources

-
Domain: Domain 2: Output Evaluation and Validation (21%)

-
Objective: Organize and curate information and select appropriate output formats (artifacts, inline, structured data)

INCORRECT: Keep opening a new chat for each resume, since Claude scores candidates correctly once the rubric is pasted in.

Scoring correctly once the rubric is supplied does not remove the actual cost here, which is re-supplying that same rubric and job description for every single candidate.

INCORRECT: Bookmark one chat conversation for reuse, without changing how the rubric gets supplied to Claude.

A bookmarked conversation is still one fixed thread tied to whichever candidate it started with, not a source Claude draws on for a new screening. This would only become the real fix if the rubric and description lived somewhere Claude pulls from automatically for each new chat, which is what a Project provides.

An events planner asks Claude one quick question for a venue recommendation weighing weather, group size, budget, and reviews across an entire region. The reply names only one venue with no comparison shown.

What should the planner do differently?

options.label: A
options.text: Turn on Research so Claude gathers and compares venues across the region against all four criteria.

options.label: B
options.text: Book the named venue directly, since it was the only concrete option Claude provided.

options.label: C
options.text: Ask Claude for three more venue names in the same reply, without weighing them against the stated criteria.

options.label: D
options.text: Call ten venues in the region directly instead of asking Claude for any further help.

questions.explanation:
CORRECT: Turn on Research so Claude gathers and compares venues across the region against all four criteria.

Weighing weather, group size, budget, and reviews across an entire region needs more than a single quick question can deliver, which is why only one venue came back with no real comparison. Research runs the deeper, multi source investigation needed to gather and weigh options against all four criteria at once.

Exam Guide Mapping

-
Domain 3: Product and Model Selection (12%)

-
Objective: Select appropriate Claude product features (Projects, research mode, chat, artifacts)

-
Domain 4: Workflow Integration and Solution Design (16%)

-
Objective: Leverage Claude for research, planning, and process optimization

INCORRECT: Book the named venue directly, since it was the only concrete option Claude provided.

Being the only option offered is not the same as being evaluated against weather, group size, budget, and reviews, so booking it skips the comparison the planner actually needs before deciding.

INCORRECT: Ask Claude for three more venue names in the same reply, without weighing them against the stated criteria.

More names widen the list but still leave every option unweighed against the four stated criteria. This would only become the real fix if those additional venues were also evaluated against weather, size, budget, and reviews, which is exactly what Research already does.

questions.question:
An e-commerce team uses Claude's most capable and expensive model tier to add simple category labels to thousands of product photos each week. The tagging backlog keeps growing and costs keep rising.

What should the team do?

options.label: A
options.text: Move this simple, high volume tagging work to a faster, lower cost model tier.

options.label: B
options.text: Keep the top tier model on every photo, since its category labels have never been wrong.

options.label: C
options.text: Process the same photos in smaller weekly batches while keeping the same top tier model.

options.label: D
options.text: Pause the tagging project entirely and have staff label the photos by hand instead.

questions.explanation:
CORRECT: Move this simple, high volume tagging work to a faster, lower cost model tier.

A growing backlog and rising costs on simple category labeling point directly to a task running on a tier built for harder problems than it actually has. Moving this repetitive, high volume work to a faster, lower cost tier matches the model to the complexity the task really involves.

Exam Guide Mapping

-
Domain 3: Product and Model Selection (12%)

-
Objective: Differentiate between Claude model types (Haiku, Sonnet, Opus)

-
Objective: Align model selection with task requirements (cost, speed, quality)

INCORRECT: Keep the top tier model on every photo, since its category labels have never been wrong.

Label accuracy was never the stated problem, so keeping the same tier does nothing to address the growing backlog or the rising costs the team is actually facing.

INCORRECT: Process the same photos in smaller weekly batches while keeping the same top tier model.

Smaller batches change scheduling, not cost or speed per photo, so the same higher tier keeps being paid for on every image regardless of batch size. This would only help if the tier itself changed for this category of work, which is the actual fix needed.

INCORRECT: Pause the tagging project entirely and have staff label the photos by hand instead.

Reverting to fully manual tagging abandons a task Claude handles well at the right tier, trading a simple model mismatch for a much slower manual process.

questions.question:
A legal team asks Claude's fastest, most economical model tier to draft a regulatory risk memo covering conflicting rules across four jurisdictions. The memo treats the conflicting rules as if they agree.

What should the team do?

options.label: A
options.text: Have the most capable model tier draft this memo instead, given the conflicting rules involved.

options.label: B
options.text: Accept the memo as drafted, since it does name all four jurisdictions and cites relevant statutes throughout.

options.label: C
options.text: Ask the same fast, economical tier to add more citations to the same memo.

options.label: D
options.text: Cancel this memo and have outside counsel draft the entire analysis from scratch.

questions.explanation:
CORRECT: Have the most capable model tier draft this memo instead, given the conflicting rules involved.

Flattening genuinely conflicting rules across four jurisdictions into apparent agreement shows the fastest, most economical tier under delivered on the reasoning depth this one-off memo actually needed. Assigning the most capable tier available matches the model to the legal complexity involved.

Exam Guide Mapping

-
Domain 3: Product and Model Selection (12%)

-
Objective: Differentiate between Claude model types (Haiku, Sonnet, Opus)

-
Objective: Align model selection with task requirements (cost, speed, quality)

-
Domain 7: Troubleshooting and Optimization (10%)

-
Objective: Identify, diagnose, and resolve issues with underperforming prompts or poor outputs

INCORRECT: Accept the memo as drafted, since it does name all four jurisdictions and cites relevant statutes throughout.

Naming jurisdictions and citing statutes correctly does not mean the actual conflicts between their rules were captured, which is the specific problem the memo has.

INCORRECT: Ask the same fast, economical tier to add more citations to the same memo.

More citations can make the memo look more thorough without resolving the fact that it still treats conflicting rules as if they agree. This would only fix the real issue if the added detail actually reconciled or flagged the conflicts, which a more capable tier is suited to do.

INCORRECT: Cancel this memo and have outside counsel draft the entire analysis from scratch.

Discarding the memo and starting over externally abandons work Claude can handle well once assigned the right tier, rather than fixing the specific mismatch that caused the problem.

questions.question:
An operations coordinator handles a daily mix of drafting, light analysis, and quick summaries, and keeps toggling between the fastest tier and the most capable one for each task, losing time deciding.

What single default is most reasonable?

options.label: A
options.text: Set the mid tier, balanced model as the everyday default and switch only when a task clearly demands otherwise.

options.label: B
options.text: Keep the most capable tier as the permanent default for everything, since it can handle any task that comes up.

options.label: C
options.text: Pick a different tier at random each morning to avoid overthinking the choice on any given day.

options.label: D
options.text: Route every task through both tiers and compare the two outputs before deciding which to keep.

questions.explanation:
CORRECT: Set the mid tier, balanced model as the everyday default and switch only when a task clearly demands otherwise.

A daily mix of moderate tasks with no single extreme requirement, some drafting, some light analysis, some summaries, is exactly what the balanced mid tier is designed to cover. Making it the standing default ends the constant per task toggling and reserves a deliberate switch for the occasional job that truly needs more speed or more capability.

Exam Guide Mapping

-
Domain 3: Product and Model Selection (12%)

-
Objective: Align model selection with task requirements (cost, speed, quality)

-
Domain 7: Troubleshooting and Optimization (10%)

-
Objective: Optimize workflows for efficiency and effectiveness

INCORRECT: Keep the most capable tier as the permanent default for everything, since it can handle any task that comes up.

Defaulting to the most capable tier for quick summaries and light drafting over provisions those tasks, spending extra cost and latency on reasoning depth they never call for. Capability headroom is not free when most of the day's work does not need it.

INCORRECT: Pick a different tier at random each morning to avoid overthinking the choice on any given day.

Choosing randomly detaches the model from the task entirely, so some days simple work runs on an overpowered tier and other days heavier work runs on one too light. A default should fit the typical workload, not be left to chance.

INCORRECT: Route every task through both tiers and compare the two outputs before deciding which to keep.

Running every task twice and comparing doubles the effort for work that a single balanced tier handles well on the first pass. This would only make sense if each task's requirements were genuinely unknown, which is not the case for a familiar daily routine.

questions.question:
A consultant has one very long chat where a client engagement's decisions and context now need to carry into next month's separate work streams. Relying on that single thread to hold everything feels increasingly fragile.

What is the best approach?

options.label: A
options.text: Capture the durable context in a Project so it persists across future chats rather than living in one thread.

options.label: B
options.text: Keep everything in the single long chat and simply scroll back whenever earlier context is needed.

options.label: C
options.text: Copy the entire chat transcript into a document and re-paste all of it into every future conversation.

options.label: D
options.text: Delete the long chat and rebuild the context from memory at the start of each new work stream.

questions.explanation:
CORRECT: Capture the durable context in a Project so it persists across future chats rather than living in one thread.

Context that must survive across separate future work streams should not depend on a single conversation that grows fragile as it lengthens. Moving the durable decisions and background into a Project gives them a persistent home that every new chat in that Project can draw on, which is what carrying context forward actually requires.

Exam Guide Mapping

-
Domain 3: Product and Model Selection (12%)

-
Objective: Select appropriate Claude product features (Projects, research mode, chat, artifacts)

-
Objective: Understand and manage context limitations and memory considerations (when to restart, summarize, or persist)

Domain 5: Configuration and Knowledge Management (12%)

-
Objective: Configure Claude Projects with instructions and knowledge sources

INCORRECT: Keep everything in the single long chat and simply scroll back whenever earlier context is needed.

Leaning on one ever growing thread is precisely the fragility the consultant already senses, since a single chat is not built to anchor context that needs to span multiple future engagements. Scrolling back also does nothing to make that context available in the separate work streams to come.

INCORRECT: Copy the entire chat transcript into a document and re-paste all of it into every future conversation.

Re-pasting a full transcript into every new chat reintroduces the same bulk each time and burns context space on material that is mostly irrelevant to the immediate task. This would only approach the right idea if the context lived somewhere Claude draws on selectively, which a Project already handles.

INCORRECT: Delete the long chat and rebuild the context from memory at the start of each new work stream.

Deleting the thread throws away the very record of decisions the consultant needs to preserve, and rebuilding from memory each time invites gaps and errors. The goal is to retain that context reliably, not to reconstruct it repeatedly by hand.

INCORRECT: Keep everything in the single long chat and simply scroll back whenever earlier context is needed.

Leaning on one ever growing thread is precisely the fragility the consultant already senses, since a single chat is not built to anchor context that needs to span multiple future engagements. Scrolling back also does nothing to make that context available in the separate work streams to come.

INCORRECT: Copy the entire chat transcript into a document and re-paste all of it into every future conversation.

Re-pasting a full transcript into every new chat reintroduces the same bulk each time and burns context space on material that is mostly irrelevant to the immediate task. Deleting the thread throws away the very record of decisions the consultant needs to preserve, and rebuilding from memory each time invites gaps and errors. The goal is to retain that context reliably, not to reconstruct it repeatedly by hand.

questions.question:
A small business owner must choose between two markets to expand into next quarter and wants to weigh demand signals, competition, and regulatory hurdles for each before committing.

How should Claude best support this decision?

options.label: A
options.text: Use Claude to gather and synthesize the demand, competition, and regulatory factors, then make the call themselves.

options.label: B
options.text: Have Claude pick the winning market outright and commit to whichever one it names.

options.label: C
options.text: Use Claude only to word the final announcement after the market is chosen by other means.

options.label: D
options.text: Skip structured research and expand into both markets at once to avoid having to choose.

questions.explanation:
CORRECT: Use Claude to gather and synthesize the demand, competition, and regulatory factors, then make the call themselves.

A planning decision like a market choice is best supported by having Claude assemble and organize the relevant evidence, demand, competition, and regulatory hurdles, so the owner decides from a clearer picture. Claude informs the decision by doing the research legwork while the judgment stays with the person accountable for it.

Exam Guide Mapping

-
Domain 4: Workflow Integration and Solution Design (16%)

-
Objective: Leverage Claude for research, planning, and process optimization

-
Domain 6: Governance, Risk, and Responsible Use (15%)

-
Objective: Identify appropriate and inappropriate use cases

INCORRECT: Have Claude pick the winning market outright and commit to whichever one it names.

Delegating the final commitment to Claude hands off a consequential business decision that depends on the owner's risk appetite, resources, and goals. Research support is meant to inform that call, not replace the person making it.

INCORRECT: Use Claude only to word the final announcement after the market is chosen by other means.

Limiting Claude to polishing the announcement wastes its most useful contribution here, which is synthesizing the comparative evidence before the decision. This would be the right scope only if the research were already done, which it is not.

INCORRECT: Skip structured research and expand into both markets at once to avoid having to choose.

Expanding into both markets sidesteps the decision rather than informing it, committing scarce resources on two fronts precisely to dodge the analysis that should guide the choice. Avoiding the comparison does not make it unnecessary.

questions.question:
A logistics manager already uses Claude to draft the weekly shipment summary, but the underlying approval process still requires five manual handoffs between departments before shipments are released.

What should the manager do next?

options.label: A
options.text: Have Claude map the five-handoff approval process to find steps that can be shortened or removed.

options.label: B
options.text: Consider the process already optimized, since the weekly summary itself now goes out much faster.

options.label: C
options.text: Ask Claude to write a more polished version of the same five-handoff approval memo.

options.label: D
options.text: Instruct Claude to remove all five handoffs immediately, without first reviewing what each one accomplishes for compliance or quality control.

questions.explanation:
CORRECT: Have Claude map the five-handoff approval process to find steps that can be shortened or removed.

Claude is currently used only to draft the summary, a content task, while the actual bottleneck, five manual handoffs before release, has never been examined. Mapping that approval process is a more valuable next use of Claude, aimed at the delay itself rather than the document describing it.

Exam Guide Mapping

-
Domain 4: Workflow Integration and Solution Design (16%)

-
Objective: Leverage Claude for research, planning, and process optimization

-
Objective: Integrate Claude into existing workflows to augment or redesign them

INCORRECT: Consider the process already optimized, since the weekly summary itself now goes out much faster.

A faster summary document says nothing about the approval process that actually delays shipments, since drafting the summary and clearing the five handoffs are two separate parts of the workflow.

INCORRECT: Ask Claude to write a more polished version of the same five-handoff approval memo.

Polishing the memo's wording leaves the five handoffs themselves completely unexamined. This would only start addressing the delay if the request also looked at whether those handoffs are necessary, which is the mapping step already needed.

INCORRECT: Instruct Claude to remove all five handoffs immediately, without first reviewing what each one accomplishes for compliance or quality control.

Cutting steps before understanding what each one accomplishes risks removing a real control along with the delay. A considered redesign starts with mapping the process, not eliminating parts of it sight unseen.

questions.question:
A product team asks Claude to design a new user onboarding flow. After reviewing the first draft, the team notices new users would need to complete eight steps before reaching any real value.

What should the team do next?

options.label: A
options.text: Share that specific friction point with Claude and iterate on a shorter path to value.

options.label: B
options.text: Launch the eight-step flow as designed, since Claude generally produces well organized onboarding sequences.

options.label: C
options.text: Ask Claude to add encouraging language to each of the eight steps without changing their number.

options.label: D
options.text: Discard this draft entirely and have the team design the onboarding flow from scratch without Claude.

questions.explanation:
CORRECT: Share that specific friction point with Claude and iterate on a shorter path to value.

The team has identified a concrete problem, eight steps before any real value, which is exactly the kind of specific feedback that makes an iteration effective. Giving Claude that detail and asking for a shorter path builds directly on the first draft instead of starting over.

Exam Guide Mapping

-
Domain 4: Workflow Integration and Solution Design (16%)

-
Objective: Use Claude to support solution design, development, and iteration

-
Objective: Leverage Claude for research, planning, and process optimization

INCORRECT: Launch the eight-step flow as designed, since Claude generally produces well organized onboarding sequences.

General reliability on other onboarding flows does not override the specific problem just identified in this draft, where new users face eight steps before reaching value.

INCORRECT: Ask Claude to add encouraging language to each of the eight steps without changing their number.

Friendlier wording does not reduce the eight steps themselves, so the core friction the team identified remains untouched. This would only help if paired with actually cutting or reordering steps, which is the real fix needed.

INCORRECT: Discard this draft entirely and have the team design the onboarding flow from scratch without Claude.

Starting over abandons a draft that is largely workable over one identified issue, when a single round of targeted feedback would resolve it faster than redesigning from nothing.

questions.explanation:

questions.question:
A team lead wants to convince a skeptical, non-technical vice president to approve using Claude for drafting client proposals. The lead's first pitch was full of terms like tokens, context windows, and model parameters.

What should the lead do differently?

options.label: A
options.text: Reframe the pitch around concrete business outcomes, like proposal turnaround time and consistency, instead of technical terms.

options.label: B
options.text: Repeat the same technical pitch again, since a thorough explanation should eventually persuade a careful reviewer.

options.label: C
options.text: Trim the same technical terms down into fewer, shorter slides without changing what the pitch is actually about.

options.label: D
options.text: Drop the proposal entirely rather than pitch Claude's adoption to the vice president again.

questions.explanation:
CORRECT: Reframe the pitch around concrete business outcomes, like proposal turnaround time and consistency, instead of technical terms.

The first pitch leaned on terms like tokens and context windows, which speak to how Claude works rather than what a non-technical vice president actually cares about. Reframing around turnaround time and consistency matches the message to the outcomes that will actually drive the approval decision.

Exam Guide Mapping

-
Domain 4: Workflow Integration and Solution Design (16%)

-
Objective: Communicate Claude's value and limitations to stakeholders

-
Domain 6: Governance, Risk, and Responsible Use (15%)

-
Objective: Follow organizational AI policies and governance standards

INCORRECT: Repeat the same technical pitch again, since a thorough explanation should eventually persuade a careful reviewer.

Repeating a pitch that already failed to land does nothing to address why it did not connect with a non-technical audience in the first place.

INCORRECT: Trim the same technical terms down into fewer, shorter slides without changing what the pitch is actually about.

Shortening the slides changes format, not content, so the same jargon that lost the VP the first time is still what the pitch is built around. This would only work if the underlying framing shifted to business terms, which is the real fix.

INCORRECT: Drop the proposal entirely rather than pitch Claude's adoption to the vice president again.

Abandoning the pitch after one attempt gives up on a case that a better framed pitch could still make successfully.

CORRECT: Set accurate expectations by noting that human review is still needed alongside Claude's help.

questions.question:
A marketing team's Project instructions tell Claude to write in the brand's distinctive voice, but no style guide or past campaign examples were ever uploaded to the project's knowledge base. Output still reads generic.

What should the team do?

options.label: A
options.text: Upload the brand style guide and past campaign examples to the project's knowledge base.

options.label: B
options.text: Accept the generic output as adequate, since the instructions already mention the brand's distinctive voice.

options.label: C
options.text: Rewrite the same instructions using stronger adjectives like distinctive and bold, without adding any reference material.

options.label: D
options.text: Abandon the Project entirely and paste brand guidelines into a brand new chat every time instead.

questions.explanation:
CORRECT: Upload the brand style guide and past campaign examples to the project's knowledge base.

Instructions describing a distinctive voice give Claude a label to aim for but no actual example of what that voice looks like, which is why the output still reads generic. Adding the style guide and past campaigns to the knowledge base gives Claude real material to draw on alongside the instructions already written.

Exam Guide Mapping

-
Domain 5: Configuration and Knowledge Management (12%)

-
Objective: Configure Claude Projects with instructions and knowledge sources

INCORRECT: Accept the generic output as adequate, since the instructions already mention the brand's distinctive voice.

Naming a trait in the instructions is not the same as showing Claude what that trait actually looks like in practice, so accepting generic output overlooks the real gap.

INCORRECT: Rewrite the same instructions using stronger adjectives like distinctive and bold, without adding any reference material.

Stronger adjectives describe the goal more emphatically but still leave Claude without any concrete example of the brand's voice. This would only work if paired with the actual reference material, which is the real fix.

INCORRECT: Abandon the Project entirely and paste brand guidelines into a brand new chat every time instead.

Abandoning the Project discards the persistent knowledge base it already offers in favor of manually re-pasting material every single chat, the opposite of what a Project is meant to solve.

options.label: B
options.text: Keep everything in the same shared Project, since Claude usually references the correct department's content.

options.label: C
options.text: Rename the uploaded files with clearer department labels while keeping them in the same shared Project.

options.label: D
options.text: Delete all uploaded knowledge from the Project and have every department paste content manually each time instead.

questions.explanation:
CORRECT: Split the knowledge base into separate, department focused Projects instead of one shared Project.

Mixing HR, engineering, and sales material into a single shared Project is why an HR question sometimes pulls in unrelated content. Splitting the knowledge base into separate, department focused Projects keeps each one's retrieval scoped to relevant material only.

Exam Guide Mapping

Domain 5: Configuration and Knowledge Management (12%)

Objective: Inform, maintain, and update Claude configurations, knowledge sources, and instructions

INCORRECT: Keep everything in the same shared Project, since Claude usually references the correct department's content.

questions.question:
An analyst wants Claude's Google Drive connector to watch a shared folder overnight and summarize any new files without anyone opening a chat.

What should the analyst understand about how the connector actually works?

options.label: A
options.text: Recognize the connector only works inside an active chat, requiring someone to ask each time.

options.label: B
options.text: Assume the connector already watches the folder continuously once it's connected, with no further prompting needed.

options.label: C
options.text: Ask Claude, in one chat, to promise it will keep checking the folder every night from now on.

options.label: D
options.text: Give up on using Claude for this folder entirely and check new files manually every morning instead.

questions.explanation:
CORRECT: Recognize the connector only works inside an active chat, requiring someone to ask each time.

Claude's connectors act only when someone is in a conversation asking for that information, with no background process watching a folder overnight on its own. Understanding that scope is what tells the analyst this hands off, overnight monitoring simply is not something the connector does.

Exam Guide Mapping

-
Domain 5: Configuration and Knowledge Management (12%)

-
Objective: Manage uploaded knowledge and connectors (e.g., Google Drive, Gmail)

INCORRECT: Assume the connector already watches the folder continuously once it's connected, with no further prompting needed.

Connecting the integration only gives Claude permission to read the folder when asked; it does not create any ongoing, unprompted monitoring of what happens inside it overnight.

INCORRECT: Ask Claude, in one chat, to promise it will keep checking the folder every night from now on.

A promise made in a single conversation has no effect once that conversation ends, since Claude does not carry an active presence forward into future nights on its own. This would only work if paired with something that runs independent of a live chat, which the standard connector does not provide.

INCORRECT: Give up on using Claude for this folder entirely and check new files manually every morning instead.

Abandoning Claude here discards a genuinely useful way to search and summarize files on request, over a background monitoring capability the connector was never going to provide in the first place.

questions.question:
A sales rep asks Claude, using the Gmail connector, to reply to ten client emails and expects each reply to send automatically once drafted.

What should the rep understand about this workflow?

options.label: A
options.text: Recognize that Claude only drafts replies, so the rep must review and send each one manually.

options.label: B
options.text: Assume all ten replies will send automatically once Claude finishes drafting them.

options.label: C
options.text: Ask Claude to mark the drafts as high priority so Gmail sends them automatically without any manual step.

options.label: D
options.text: Stop using Claude for these replies and write all ten emails manually from scratch.

questions.explanation:
CORRECT: Recognize that Claude only drafts replies, so the rep must review and send each one manually.

Claude's Gmail connector creates drafts directly in the rep's account but never sends a message on its own, regardless of how many replies are involved. Knowing that means the rep still has to open and send each of the ten drafts personally.

Exam Guide Mapping

-
Domain 5: Configuration and Knowledge Management (12%)

-
Objective: Manage uploaded knowledge and connectors (e.g., Google Drive, Gmail)

INCORRECT: Assume all ten replies will send automatically once Claude finishes drafting them.

Finishing a draft is not the same as sending it, since the connector is built to stop at the draft stage every time, with sending left entirely to the person using it.

INCORRECT: Ask Claude to mark the drafts as high priority so Gmail sends them automatically without any manual step.

Priority marking changes how a message is flagged in an inbox, not whether it gets sent, so this does nothing to move any of the ten drafts out of the outbox on its own.

INCORRECT: Stop using Claude for these replies and write all ten emails manually from scratch.

Abandoning Claude's drafts throws away real time savings over a sending step that only takes a moment once the rep understands it is required.

questions.question:
A support team's Project instructions say only to be helpful and professional when answering customer questions. Responses vary widely in length, tone, and format across different conversations.

What should the team do to improve consistency?

options.label: A
options.text: Rewrite the instructions with specific guidance on tone, response length, and required format.

options.label: B
options.text: Keep the same instructions, since they do mention being helpful and professional.

options.label: C
options.text: Add the word consistent to the existing instructions without specifying what that means in practice.

options.label: D
options.text: Remove the custom instructions entirely and let each agent word their own responses freely.

questions.explanation:
CORRECT: Rewrite the instructions with specific guidance on tone, response length, and required format.

Being helpful and professional names a general attitude but gives Claude no concrete standard for tone, length, or format, which is exactly why responses vary so widely from one conversation to the next. Rewriting the instructions with specific guidance on those three dimensions gives Claude an actual standard to apply consistently.

Exam Guide Mapping

-
Domain 5: Configuration and Knowledge Management (12%)

-
Objective: Create effective system-level instructions

INCORRECT: Keep the same instructions, since they do mention being helpful and professional.

Mentioning helpful and professional does not specify tone, length, or format, which are the actual sources of the variation the team is seeing.

INCORRECT: Add the word consistent to the existing instructions without specifying what that means in practice.

Naming consistency as a goal does not tell Claude what a consistent response actually looks like. This would only help if it were followed by concrete guidance on tone, length, and format, which is the real fix needed.

INCORRECT: Remove the custom instructions entirely and let each agent word their own responses freely.

Removing the instructions eliminates even the loose guidance currently in place, working against the consistency the team is actually trying to achieve.

questions.question:
A training coordinator wants Claude to draft first-pass, anonymized session summaries from workshop notes, with a human editor reviewing each summary before it is shared internally.

What should the coordinator do?

options.label: A
options.text: Proceed with this use case, since it is well scoped, anonymized, and includes human review.

options.label: B
options.text: Skip the human editor's review and share Claude's summaries directly, since anonymized notes carry little risk.

options.label: C
options.text: Proceed with this use case, but drop the anonymization step to save time before human review.

options.label: D
options.text: Block this use case entirely, since any AI generated content about training sessions carries some risk.

questions.explanation:
CORRECT: Proceed with this use case, since it is well scoped, anonymized, and includes human review.

A first-pass, anonymized summary with a human editor checking it before anything is shared internally has exactly the three features that make a use case genuinely appropriate: a bounded task, protected personal details, and a review step before distribution. That combination is reason enough to proceed.

Exam Guide Mapping

-
Domain 6: Governance, Risk, and Responsible Use (15%)

-
Objective: Identify appropriate and inappropriate use cases

INCORRECT: Skip the human editor's review and share Claude's summaries directly, since anonymized notes carry little risk.

Removing the review step removes exactly the safeguard that catches errors before a summary goes out, regardless of how low risk the anonymized notes themselves seem.

INCORRECT: Proceed with this use case, but drop the anonymization step to save time before human review.

Keeping the human review while dropping anonymization removes the safeguard that protects individual privacy in the notes. This would only remain appropriate if anonymization were restored, since dropping it changes what made the use case safe in the first place.

INCORRECT: Block this use case entirely, since any AI generated content about training sessions carries some risk.

Treating this bounded, safeguarded use case as if it carried the same risk as an unscoped one forgoes a legitimate, low-risk application of Claude.

questions.question:
An employee wants to upload a database of customer health records to Claude to flag which customers are likely to cancel a health plan, without checking whether this handling of health data is permitted.

What should the employee do?

options.label: A
options.text: Pause and confirm with compliance or legal whether this use of health data is permitted.

options.label: B
options.text: Upload the database as planned, since the analysis itself seems like a reasonable business goal.

options.label: C
options.text: Remove customer names from the file, then upload the remaining health records without any further review or approval.

options.label: D
options.text: Cancel the entire retention analysis project rather than pursue it through any channel.

questions.explanation:
CORRECT: Pause and confirm with compliance or legal whether this use of health data is permitted.

Uploading regulated health records to flag likely cancellations, without ever checking whether this handling is permitted, is exactly the kind of use case that needs a governance check before any data moves. Pausing to confirm with compliance or legal addresses the actual open question, whether this handling is permitted at all, rather than assuming it is.

Exam Guide Mapping

-
Domain 6: Governance, Risk, and Responsible Use (15%)

-
Objective: Apply data sensitivity, regulatory, and privacy considerations

INCORRECT: Upload the database as planned, since the analysis itself seems like a reasonable business goal.

A reasonable sounding business goal does not establish that this specific handling of regulated health data is actually permitted under the relevant rules.

INCORRECT: Remove customer names from the file, then upload the remaining health records without any further review or approval.

Stripping names addresses direct identifiers, but health data can still be regulated and re-identifiable through other details, and skipping review altogether leaves the underlying permission question unanswered. This would only become adequate if paired with an actual compliance check, which is the real fix.

INCORRECT: Cancel the entire retention analysis project rather than pursue it through any channel.

Abandoning the project outright skips the one step, a compliance check, that could show whether some version of this analysis is workable.

questions.question:
A project manager wants to upload a customer support spreadsheet containing names, email addresses, and ticket categories to Claude for trend analysis, but organizational policy restricts sharing regulated personal data.

Which two actions should the manager take before uploading?

options.label: A
options.text: Remove or replace the customer names and email addresses with anonymized identifiers before uploading.

options.label: B
options.text: Confirm with the team that the remaining ticket category and resolution data no longer identifies any individual.

options.label: C
options.text: Keep the names and email addresses in the file, but rename the column headers to something less obvious.

options.label: D
options.text: Cancel the trend analysis entirely rather than upload any part of the spreadsheet.

options.label: E
options.text: Upload the spreadsheet as is, since the analysis itself is only about internal support trends.

questions.explanation:
CORRECT: Remove or replace the customer names and email addresses with anonymized identifiers before uploading.

Names and email addresses are direct identifiers, exactly the kind of regulated personal data the policy restricts, so replacing them with anonymized identifiers is the core step that lets the analysis proceed without exposing anyone's identity.

CORRECT: Confirm with the team that the remaining ticket category and resolution data no longer identifies any individual.

Once direct identifiers are removed, checking that what remains cannot indirectly identify someone is what actually confirms the data is safe to use, rather than assuming removal alone is sufficient.

Exam Guide Mapping

-
Domain 6: Governance, Risk, and Responsible Use (15%)

-
Objective: Apply data sensitivity, regulatory, and privacy considerations

INCORRECT: Keep the names and email addresses in the file, but rename the column headers to something less obvious.

Renaming a column header changes its label, not the personal data sitting underneath it, so the names and email addresses remain fully exposed regardless of what the column is called.

INCORRECT: Cancel the trend analysis entirely rather than upload any part of the spreadsheet.

Cancelling the whole analysis discards a legitimate use case over a data handling problem that anonymization can actually solve.

INCORRECT: Upload the spreadsheet as is, since the analysis itself is only about internal support trends.

The internal nature of the analysis does not change the fact that the file still contains regulated personal data the policy specifically restricts from being shared.

questions.question:
A consultant drafted a confidential client strategy document using a personal Claude account and later worries the content might be used to train future models.

What should the consultant do to address this concern?

options.label: A
options.text: Check the account's training setting, then turn it off or delete the chat.

options.label: B
options.text: Assume no personal Claude account can ever affect model training, regardless of any settings.

options.label: C
options.text: Rename the conversation to something generic, without changing any privacy or training settings at all.

options.label: D
options.text: Stop using Claude for any client work going forward, regardless of account type or settings.

questions.explanation:
CORRECT: Check the account's training setting, then turn it off or delete the chat.

On a personal account, whether a chat can be used for training depends on that account's own model training setting, and either turning that setting off or deleting the specific chat excludes it from future training. That directly addresses the consultant's actual concern.

Exam Guide Mapping

-
Domain 6: Governance, Risk, and Responsible Use (15%)

-
Objective: Apply data sensitivity, regulatory, and privacy considerations

INCORRECT: Assume no personal Claude account can ever affect model training, regardless of any settings.

Personal accounts can be included in training specifically when the user has opted into that setting, so assuming it never applies is not reliably true.

INCORRECT: Rename the conversation to something generic, without changing any privacy or training settings at all.

A different title has no bearing on whether the underlying content is eligible for training, since that depends entirely on the account's training setting, not the conversation's name. This would only help if paired with actually checking or changing that setting, which is the real fix.

INCORRECT: Stop using Claude for any client work going forward, regardless of account type or settings.

Discarding Claude entirely gives up a useful tool over a concern that adjusting one setting, or deleting the specific chat, already resolves without abandoning future work.

questions.question:
An organization's AI usage policy requires every Claude-drafted marketing post to be reviewed by an editor before publishing. A marketing associate, working under a deadline, published several posts directly without that review.

What should the associate do now?

options.label: A
options.text: Flag the published posts for editor review now and follow the step going forward.

options.label: B
options.text: Leave the posts as published, since they read fine and no one has complained.

options.label: C
options.text: Ask an editor to review future posts only when there happens to be extra time.

options.label: D
options.text: Report the incident to senior leadership as a major policy breach requiring a formal investigation.

questions.explanation:
CORRECT: Flag the published posts for editor review now and follow the step going forward.

The policy requires editor review before publishing, and skipping it under deadline pressure is the specific lapse here. Flagging the already published posts for review now and following the step going forward restores compliance without overreacting to what happened.

Exam Guide Mapping

-
Domain 6: Governance, Risk, and Responsible Use (15%)

-
Objective: Follow organizational AI policies and governance standards

INCORRECT: Leave the posts as published, since they read fine and no one has complained.

The absence of complaints does not satisfy a policy requirement that exists independent of whether anyone has noticed a problem yet.

INCORRECT: Ask an editor to review future posts only when there happens to be extra time.

Treating review as optional depending on available time makes the requirement conditional on convenience, when the policy applies regardless of workload. This would only align with the policy if review happened every time, not just when time allows.

INCORRECT: Report the incident to senior leadership as a major policy breach requiring a formal investigation.

Escalating to a formal investigation treats a straightforward compliance lapse, fixable by reviewing the posts now and following the step going forward, as a far bigger event than it actually is.

A benefits team is unsure whether a new regulation about automated decision-making applies to Claude-assisted eligibility recommendations that a human always finalizes.

What should the team do given this uncertainty?

options.text: Raise the specific question to compliance or legal for a definitive answer before proceeding.

options.label: B
options.text: Assume the human final decision step means the new regulation cannot possibly apply here.

options.label: C
options.text: Add a disclaimer to the recommendations mentioning the new regulation, without resolving whether it applies.

options.label: D
options.text: Halt all eligibility work across the entire department until the regulation is fully repealed.

questions.explanation:
CORRECT: Raise the specific question to compliance or legal for a definitive answer before proceeding.

Genuine ambiguity about whether a new regulation covers this specific, human-finalized use case is exactly the kind of open governance question that needs a definitive answer from compliance or legal, rather than the team guessing in either direction on their own.

Exam Guide Mapping

-
Domain 6: Governance, Risk, and Responsible Use (15%)

-
Objective: Follow organizational AI policies and governance standards

INCORRECT: Assume the human final decision step means the new regulation cannot possibly apply here.

That is an assumption about how the regulation works, not a confirmed answer, and assuming away the ambiguity is exactly what should be avoided in this situation.

INCORRECT: Add a disclaimer to the recommendations mentioning the new regulation, without resolving whether it applies.

Acknowledging that the regulation exists is not the same as determining whether it actually applies to this use case. This would only resolve the real question if it were paired with an actual compliance or legal determination, which is the fix needed.

Responding to uncertainty about one specific use case by shutting down far more work than the open question actually concerns is a disproportionate reaction to genuine ambiguity.

questions.question:
A bank's marketing team uses Claude to draft loan offers, and the drafts include better rates for wealthier zip codes and higher rates for lower income zip codes, mirroring historical lending patterns.

Which two actions should the team take?

options.label: A
options.text: Review whether the criteria producing different offers reflect legitimate factors or repeat historical discriminatory lending patterns.

options.label: B
options.text: Have compliance or fair lending specialists review the criteria before any offers are sent to customers.

options.label: C
options.text: Change the wording of the offers to sound friendlier, while keeping the same underlying criteria unchanged.

options.label: D
options.text: Send the offers as drafted, since Claude generated them and presumably reflects neutral market data.

options.label: E
options.text: Stop offering loans in the lower income zip codes entirely to avoid the appearance of unequal treatment.

questions.explanation:
CORRECT: Review whether the criteria producing different offers reflect legitimate factors or repeat historical discriminatory lending patterns.

questions.question:
An analyst pastes a spreadsheet with sales figures, headcount trends, and regional expenses, then asks Claude to analyze our Q3 data. The response focuses heavily on headcount trends instead of the sales figures the analyst needed.

What caused this response?

options.label: A
options.text: The request never named which metric mattered, so Claude picked a plausible angle instead.

options.label: B
options.text: Claude fabricated the headcount trends instead of using the sales figures actually in the spreadsheet.

options.label: C
options.text: Conclude that Claude selected the wrong section for no identifiable reason and move on.

options.label: D
options.text: Assume the spreadsheet was too large for Claude to process the sales figures correctly.

questions.explanation:
CORRECT: The request never named which metric mattered, so Claude picked a plausible angle instead.

The request said only to analyze our Q3 data, without naming sales, headcount, or expenses as the priority, even though the spreadsheet contains all three. Claude's focus on headcount trends is a reasonable reading of an underspecified request, which means the missing metric specification, not an error in the response itself, is the actual cause.

Exam Guide Mapping

-
Domain 7: Troubleshooting and Optimization (10%)

-
Objective: Identify, diagnose, and resolve issues with underperforming prompts or poor outputs

INCORRECT: Claude fabricated the headcount trends instead of using the sales figures actually in the spreadsheet.

The headcount trends were already present in the uploaded spreadsheet, so referencing them is drawing on real data the analyst provided, not inventing content. This isn't a fabrication problem, it's a case of genuine data that simply wasn't the section the analyst wanted highlighted.

INCORRECT: Conclude that Claude selected the wrong section for no identifiable reason and move on.

Treating the selection as unexplainable skips a diagnosis that's actually available directly from the prompt: an ambiguous request left the choice of metric open.

INCORRECT: Assume the spreadsheet was too large for Claude to process the sales figures correctly.

Nothing in the situation points to a size or processing limitation, and introducing a technical constraint with no evidence behind it skips the simpler explanation already visible in the prompt.
