questions.question:
A policy analyst asks Claude to summarize the key points of a 40 page report and receives a summary so general it could describe almost any similar report, missing specific figures and named provisions.

What should the analyst do next?

options.label: A
options.text: Ask for a summary that includes specific figures, named provisions, and section references from this report.

options.label: B
options.text: Ask Claude to make the summary longer so more of the report's content is naturally included.

options.label: C
options.text: Accept the summary as adequate, since it does cover the general themes of the report.

options.label: D
options.text: Ask Claude to add more transition sentences between the same general points already given.

questions.explanation:
CORRECT: Ask for a summary that includes specific figures, named provisions, and section references from this report.

A summary generic enough to fit almost any similar report is missing exactly the specific figures, named provisions, and references that would tie it to this particular document. Asking explicitly for those elements adds the concrete constraints that actually resolve the vagueness.

Exam Guide Mapping

-
Domain 7: Troubleshooting and Optimization (10%)

-
Objective: Identify, diagnose, and resolve issues with underperforming prompts or poor outputs

INCORRECT: Ask Claude to make the summary longer so more of the report's content is naturally included.

A longer response can add more words without necessarily pulling in the specific figures or named provisions that were missing, since length alone doesn't direct Claude toward report-specific detail. This would only fix the vagueness if the added length were explicitly aimed at those elements, which is the real fix.

INCORRECT: Accept the summary as adequate, since it does cover the general themes of the report.

Covering general themes accurately doesn't make up for the absence of the specific figures and provisions the analyst actually needs from this report.

INCORRECT: Ask Claude to add more transition sentences between the same general points already given.

More transitions connect the same general points more smoothly but add no new specific content, leaving the underlying vagueness fully intact.

questions.question:
A team runs dozens of quick, well defined daily eligibility checks but has effort set to Max for every single one, and turnaround keeps lagging with no noticeable gain in accuracy.

What should the team do?

options.label: A
options.text: Lower the effort level for this routine, high volume task to speed up turnaround.

options.label: B
options.text: Keep effort at Max, since higher effort always produces more thorough results regardless of the task.

options.label: C
options.text: Keep effort at Max, but ask Claude to write shorter responses to save some time.

options.label: D
options.text: Turn off effort settings entirely and let every future task run with no consistent configuration.

questions.explanation:
CORRECT: Lower the effort level for this routine, high volume task to speed up turnaround.

Routine, well defined eligibility checks are exactly the kind of task where a lower effort level performs just as well while responding faster. Lowering the effort level for this high volume, simple task directly fixes the lagging turnaround without giving up quality the task doesn't need.

Exam Guide Mapping

-
Domain 7: Troubleshooting and Optimization (10%)

-
Objective: Optimize workflows for efficiency and effectiveness

INCORRECT: Keep effort at Max, since higher effort always produces more thorough results regardless of the task.

Higher effort helps most on complex or ambiguous problems, but for quick, well defined checks it adds reasoning time without a meaningful accuracy gain, so treating more effort as unconditionally better regardless of task type doesn't hold here.

INCORRECT: Keep effort at Max, but ask Claude to write shorter responses to save some time.

Shortening the response changes output length, not how much reasoning Claude does at Max effort, so the slow turnaround caused by the effort level itself remains unresolved.

INCORRECT: Turn off effort settings entirely and let every future task run with no consistent configuration.

Removing all consistency in configuration replaces one clear, fixable mismatch with an unpredictable setup that could just as easily run too high or too low for any future task.

questions.question: A developer asks Claude for a 60 line Python script, then requests three edits, each time receiving the whole script retyped as plain text in the chat. Which two actions should the developer take to work with this code efficiently?

options.label: A
options.text: Have Claude create the script as an artifact so future edits update it directly.

options.label: B
options.text: Recognize that a substantial, reusable piece of code like this is what artifacts are designed for.

options.label: C
options.text: Continue requesting the full script in chat each time, since copying it manually is straightforward enough.

options.label: D
options.text: Ask Claude to only show the changed lines in future replies, while still keeping everything in the chat window.

options.label: E
options.text: Set up a dedicated code repository and continuous integration pipeline before making any further edits.

questions.explanation:
CORRECT: Have Claude create the script as an artifact so future edits update it directly.

Retyping the entire 60 line script for every edit is the classic sign that this content belongs in an artifact, which holds a single editable version so requests turn into direct edits instead of full retypes each time.

CORRECT: Recognize that a substantial, reusable piece of code like this is what artifacts are designed for.

A 60 line script needing multiple rounds of edits is exactly the kind of significant, self-contained, reusable content artifacts exist for, so recognizing that fit is what should guide the developer's choice of feature going forward.

Exam Guide Mapping

-
Domain 3: Product and Model Selection (12%)

-
Objective: Select appropriate Claude product features (Projects, research mode, chat, artifacts)

INCORRECT: Continue requesting the full script in chat each time, since copying it manually is straightforward enough.

Manually copying and merging changes across repeated full script pastes wastes exactly the effort artifacts exist to avoid, and risks copy errors piling up across edits.

INCORRECT: Ask Claude to only show the changed lines in future replies, while still keeping everything in the chat window.

Showing only the changed lines reduces repetition somewhat, but the code still lives only as plain chat text with no single editable copy, so the developer still has to reconstruct the full file by hand. This would only approach the fix if the code actually moved into an editable artifact.

INCORRECT: Set up a dedicated code repository and continuous integration pipeline before making any further edits.

options.label: A
options.text: Request the research step first, confirm it is accurate, then have Claude draft and polish in separate follow-up messages.

options.label: B
options.text: Treat the one-pager as complete, since Claude addressed the research, drafting, and polishing all within a single response.

options.label: C
options.text: Ask Claude to re-check the price points already in the draft, without separately re-running or verifying the underlying research figures first.

questions.question:
A communications specialist asks Claude to draft a press release in the company's usual style and brand guidelines, without attaching either document. The draft reads polished but nothing like the company's established voice.

What should the specialist do next?

options.label: A
options.text: Attach the brand guidelines and a few past press releases so Claude has the referenced material to match.

options.label: B
options.text: Accept the current draft, since it already reads polished and professional for a press release.

options.label: C
options.text: Resend the exact same request, assuming a second attempt will pick up on the brand's established voice.

options.label: D
options.text: Add a mandatory second editorial review before every future release, without changing what Claude was given to work with.

questions.explanation:
CORRECT: Attach the brand guidelines and a few past press releases so Claude has the referenced material to match.

The draft cannot match a voice it was never shown, since neither the brand guidelines nor any past releases were part of the request. Supplying that reference material gives Claude something concrete to match its language and structure against, instead of guessing at what the usual style means.

Exam Guide Mapping

-
Domain 1: Prompting and Task Execution (14%)

-
Objective: Create effective prompts for business and technical tasks

INCORRECT: Accept the current draft, since it already reads polished and professional for a press release.

A polished, professional tone is not the same thing as matching this company's specific established voice, and the draft's fluency does not resolve that gap. Accepting it as is means the mismatch the specialist noticed goes uncorrected.

INCORRECT: Resend the exact same request, assuming a second attempt will pick up on the brand's established voice.

Sending the identical request again does not change what information Claude has to work from, so the brand guidelines and past examples remain just as absent as before. The same generic result would likely follow.

INCORRECT: Add a mandatory second editorial review before every future release, without changing what Claude was given to work with.

A review step might catch a mismatch after the fact, but it does nothing to give Claude the material it needs to get the voice right the first time. The underlying gap, missing reference documents, stays exactly the same going forward.

questions.question:
A financial analyst asks Claude to summarize quarterly results for the leadership team. The summary reads casual and oversimplified, closer to a general newsletter than an executive review.

What should the analyst do next?

options.label: A
options.text: Give Claude feedback on the mismatch and request a more rigorous, data-driven revision suited to an executive audience.

options.label: B
options.text: Send the summary as is, since executives generally prefer summaries that are quick and easy to read.

options.label: C
options.text: Ask Claude to add a few more industry terms to the same summary without changing its overall depth or structure.

options.label: D
options.text: Have Claude rewrite the summary at twice the length, assuming the extra length alone will read as more executive.

questions.explanation:
CORRECT: Give Claude feedback on the mismatch and request a more rigorous, data-driven revision suited to an executive audience.

An executive review calls for a more analytical, evidence-based tone than a general newsletter, and the summary's casual, oversimplified phrasing does not meet that bar. Pointing out the mismatch and asking specifically for a more rigorous, data-driven revision tells Claude exactly what register this audience expects.

Exam Guide Mapping

-
Domain 1: Prompting and Task Execution (14%)

-
Objective: Iterate prompts to improve output quality

INCORRECT: Send the summary as is, since executives generally prefer summaries that are quick and easy to read.

Executives reading a quarterly review typically expect depth and precision, not the breezy tone that suits a general newsletter. Assuming otherwise sends a summary that does not match what this particular audience actually needs.

INCORRECT: Ask Claude to add a few more industry terms to the same summary without changing its overall depth or structure.

A few extra technical terms sprinkled into an otherwise casual summary changes vocabulary without changing the underlying depth or rigor the leadership team is looking for. The summary could still read as oversimplified even with more jargon added.

INCORRECT: Have Claude rewrite the summary at twice the length, assuming the extra length alone will read as more executive.

Length and executive tone are not the same thing, so doubling the word count could just produce a longer version of the same casual, oversimplified summary. Nothing about extra length guarantees more analytical depth.

questions.question:
An operations lead asks Claude to compare three software vendors on cost, implementation speed, and support quality. The recommendation shifts each time two of those factors point in different directions.

What should the lead do differently?

options.label: A
options.text: Specify which factor should carry the most weight when cost, speed, and support quality conflict with each other.

options.label: B
options.text: Accept whichever vendor the latest comparison favors, since all three factors were already named.

options.label: C
options.text: Ask Claude to list the same three factors again in a clearer format without indicating which one matters most.

options.label: D
options.text: Weight cost as the deciding factor for this one comparison, but leave priority unspecified for future vendor decisions.

questions.explanation:
CORRECT: Specify which factor should carry the most weight when cost, speed, and support quality conflict with each other.

Naming cost, speed, and support quality did not stop the recommendation from shifting, because nothing tells Claude which factor should win when they point in different directions. Specifying that priority turns three competing signals into one that can be applied consistently.

Exam Guide Mapping

-
Domain 1: Prompting and Task Execution (14%)

-
Objective: Create effective prompts for business and technical tasks

INCORRECT: Accept whichever vendor the latest comparison favors, since all three factors were already named.

Whichever vendor a given comparison favors really just reflects which factor happened to be weighted more heavily that time, not a stable answer. Treating it as final ignores that the underlying priority was never actually set.

INCORRECT: Ask Claude to list the same three factors again in a clearer format without indicating which one matters most.

Restating cost, speed, and support quality in a cleaner format does not resolve which one should matter most when they disagree. The recommendation would likely keep shifting for the same reason it did before.

INCORRECT: Weight cost as the deciding factor for this one comparison, but leave priority unspecified for future vendor decisions.

Picking a winner this time only patches this one comparison, leaving the same undefined priority ready to produce another inconsistent recommendation on the next vendor decision. The underlying gap in guidance never actually gets fixed.

questions.question:
A technical writer asks Claude to draft a feature announcement using the product's exact internal terminology and section structure. The draft reads clearly but uses generic terms and its own organization instead.

What should the writer do next?

options.label: A
options.text: Share the team's terminology glossary and a template showing the required section structure.

options.label: B
options.text: Publish the draft as is, since the generic terms are still understandable to most readers.

options.label: C
options.text: Ask Claude to swap in a few product-specific words without providing the glossary or the structural template.

options.label: D
options.text: Ask Claude to expand the announcement into a much longer document covering unrelated features as well.

questions.explanation:
CORRECT: Share the team's terminology glossary and a template showing the required section structure.

Root cause: Claude wasn't missing skill, it was missing information. Without a glossary or structural template, it defaults to clear, generic writing, which is exactly what happened.

Fix: Give Claude the actual terminology list and a template showing the required sections. Now it has concrete conventions to match instead of guessing at your product's house style.

Watch out for: partial fixes (swapping a few words, adding unrelated content) treat the symptom, not the missing context.

Exam Guide Mapping

-
Domain 1: Prompting and Task Execution (14%)

-
Objective: Iterate prompts to improve output quality

INCORRECT: Publish the draft as is, since the generic terms are still understandable to most readers.

Readers being able to follow the announcement does not mean it uses this product's required terms and structure, which is the specific standard the writer needs to meet. Understandable and on-convention are two different bars.

INCORRECT: Ask Claude to swap in a few product-specific words without providing the glossary or the structural template.

Swapping in a handful of product-specific words changes surface vocabulary without providing the glossary or template that would fix the section structure too. The announcement would likely still drift from the required conventions overall.

INCORRECT: Ask Claude to expand the announcement into a much longer document covering unrelated features as well.

Adding more content about unrelated features has nothing to do with matching the terminology and structure this specific announcement was supposed to follow. It adds length without addressing the gap the writer actually noticed.

questions.question:
A procurement analyst asks Claude in one message to weigh the pros and cons of two shipping vendors and recommend which to choose. The pros and cons list feels thin before the recommendation appears.

What should the analyst do next?

options.label: A
options.text: Ask for a full pros-and-cons analysis first, then request the recommendation as a separate follow-up question.

options.label: B
options.text: Accept the recommendation as final, since Claude already weighed the pros and cons before giving it.

options.label: C
options.text: Ask Claude to add a few more bullet points to the same combined pros-and-cons-and-recommendation response.

options.label: D
options.text: Schedule a full, formal stakeholder review meeting before allowing Claude to compare the two vendors any further at all.

questions.explanation:
CORRECT: Ask for a full pros-and-cons analysis first, then request the recommendation as a separate follow-up question.

What went wrong: Combining "compare" and "recommend" into one ask compresses both into a single pass, so Claude rushes toward a pick instead of fully developing the analysis first.

Fix: Split it into two turns. First request the complete pros-and-cons comparison alone, then ask for the recommendation once that analysis is on the table.

Pattern recognition: This is task decomposition. Breaking a compound request into sequential steps gives each one full attention, and the final answer inherits a stronger foundation instead of a rushed one.

Exam Guide Mapping

-
Domain 1: Prompting and Task Execution (14%)

-
Objective: Apply task decomposition techniques to structure complex requests

INCORRECT: Accept the recommendation as final, since Claude already weighed the pros and cons before giving it.

A recommendation that follows a thin pros-and-cons list is only as solid as that list, and treating it as final ignores that the analysis behind it never actually had room to develop. The shallow reasoning carries straight through to the pick.

INCORRECT: Ask Claude to add a few more bullet points to the same combined pros-and-cons-and-recommendation response.

Adding a couple more bullets to the same combined request still asks Claude to analyze and decide in one pass, which is the actual source of the thin analysis. More bullets do not fix a structure that rushes past the analysis itself.

INCORRECT: Schedule a full, formal stakeholder review meeting before allowing Claude to compare the two vendors any further at all.

A formal stakeholder meeting is a heavier process than this two-vendor comparison actually calls for, and it does not address the real issue: asking Claude to analyze and recommend in the same request. The fix here is a smaller prompting change, not a bigger process.

questions.question:
An HR coordinator asks Claude to summarize a new overtime policy for a team memo. The summary states the policy takes effect on a specific date next month.

Before sending the memo, what should the coordinator do?

options.label: A
options.text: Confirm the effective date against the official policy document, since specific dates can be outdated or fabricated regardless of tone.

options.label: B
options.text: Send the memo as written, since Claude usually states dates only when it is confident they are correct.

options.label: C
options.text: Reword the date more cautiously, such as expected to take effect soon, without checking whether the date itself is accurate.

options.label: D
options.text: Delay sending the memo indefinitely until every policy detail in the company has been independently re-verified.

questions.explanation:
CORRECT: Confirm the effective date against the official policy document, since specific dates can be outdated or fabricated regardless of tone.

A specific effective date is exactly the kind of detail that can be stale or fabricated no matter how confident it sounds, since it depends on timing Claude cannot reliably know. Checking it against the actual policy document is what confirms the memo is safe to send.

Exam Guide Mapping

-
Domain 2: Output Evaluation and Validation (21%)

-
Objective: Identify hallucinations, inconsistencies, and biases in responses

-
Objective: Apply fact-checking and validation techniques

INCORRECT: Send the memo as written, since Claude usually states dates only when it is confident they are correct.

Confidence in how a date is phrased says nothing about whether that date is actually correct, since fabricated details can read just as smoothly as accurate ones. Sending the memo on that basis leaves the real risk unchecked.

INCORRECT: Reword the date more cautiously, such as expected to take effect soon, without checking whether the date itself is accurate.

Softer phrasing changes how certain the date sounds without changing whether the date itself is right, so an inaccurate effective date could still reach the team. The underlying fact still needs to be checked, not just hedged.

INCORRECT: Delay sending the memo indefinitely until every policy detail in the company has been independently re-verified.

Holding the memo hostage to a full re-verification of every policy detail goes well beyond the one figure actually in question here. The overtime memo does not need every unrelated policy fact checked to address this specific risk.

questions.question:
A compliance analyst asks Claude to summarize a new expense reimbursement policy for employees. The summary explains the standard rules clearly but never mentions the exceptions process outlined in the policy.

What should the analyst do next?

options.label: A
options.text: Request that the summary specifically cover the exceptions process, since employees need that section to know their options.

options.label: B
options.text: Distribute the summary to employees as is, since it accurately and clearly covers the policy's standard rules.

options.label: C
options.text: Add a single line noting that exceptions may exist, without describing what the exceptions process actually involves.

options.label: D
options.text: Replace the summary entirely with the full, unedited policy document, so employees can find any section on their own.

questions.explanation:
CORRECT: Request that the summary specifically cover the exceptions process, since employees need that section to know their options.

Employees who fall outside the standard rules are exactly the ones who need the exceptions process explained, and that section is the one the summary left out entirely. Asking for it by name is what gets that specific gap filled.

Exam Guide Mapping

-
Domain 2: Output Evaluation and Validation (21%)

-
Objective: Evaluate Claude-generated outputs for accuracy and completeness

INCORRECT: Distribute the summary to employees as is, since it accurately and clearly covers the policy's standard rules.

Covering the standard rules accurately does not help the subset of employees whose situation depends on the exceptions process, which is the part still missing. Distributing it as is leaves that group without what they actually need.

INCORRECT: Add a single line noting that exceptions may exist, without describing what the exceptions process actually involves.

Acknowledging that exceptions exist without explaining what the process actually involves tells an employee there is a door without saying how to open it. The substance of the missing section is still absent.

INCORRECT: Replace the summary entirely with the full, unedited policy document, so employees can find any section on their own.

Handing employees the full, unedited policy defeats the purpose of asking for a summary in the first place, and it is a much bigger change than the one section that was actually missing. The targeted gap could have been closed without discarding the summary altogether.

questions.question:
A marketing writer asks Claude to draft a blog post, and the draft states that a recent survey found most customers prefer a specific feature, without naming the survey.

What should the writer do before publishing?

options.label: A
options.text: Have Claude identify the survey behind the claim, or verify the statistic independently, since it cannot otherwise be confirmed.

options.label: B
options.text: Publish the blog post as written, since survey-based claims are common in marketing content.

options.label: C
options.text: Soften the wording to say some customers instead of most customers, without confirming whether a survey exists at all.

options.label: D
options.text: Remove all statistics from the blog post going forward, even ones drawn from the company's own verified internal data.

questions.explanation:
CORRECT: Have Claude identify the survey behind the claim, or verify the statistic independently, since it cannot otherwise be confirmed.

A claim tied to a survey that is never named cannot be checked against anything, which is a different problem from a claim that is merely confident. Tracking down the actual survey, or verifying the statistic another way, is what turns an untraceable claim into a checkable one.

"Verify with citations: Make Claude's response auditable by having it cite quotes and sources for each of its claims. You can also have Claude verify each claim by finding a supporting quote after it generates a response. If it can't find a quote, it must retract the claim." - Resource

Exam Guide Mapping

Domain 2: Output Evaluation and Validation (21%)

-
Objective: Apply fact-checking and validation techniques

INCORRECT: Publish the blog post as written, since survey-based claims are common in marketing content.

How common survey-based claims are in marketing writing has no bearing on whether this particular survey actually exists. Publishing it as written leaves an unverifiable claim sitting in front of readers.

INCORRECT: Soften the wording to say some customers instead of most customers, without confirming whether a survey exists at all.

Weakening most to some changes how strong the claim sounds without addressing that there is still no traceable survey behind it. The statistic remains just as unconfirmed as before, only phrased more cautiously.

INCORRECT: Remove all statistics from the blog post going forward, even ones drawn from the company's own verified internal data.

Banning all statistics, including ones already drawn from the company's own verified data, throws out claims that were never in question to deal with the one that was. The fix belongs to this specific unnamed-source claim, not to statistics as a category."

questions.question:
A strategy analyst asked Claude last month for a competitor's total number of retail locations and received one figure. Asking the identical question again this week returns a noticeably different total.

What should the analyst do?

options.label: A
options.text: Check both figures against the competitor's own public disclosures or another primary source, rather than assuming either answer is correct.

options.label: B
options.text: Use the more recent answer, since Claude's newer responses tend to reflect its latest available information.

options.label: C
options.text: Ask Claude which of the two totals is correct, and use whichever answer it happens to state with more apparent confidence.

options.label: D
options.text: Average the two conflicting totals together and use that blended number in the strategy report.

questions.explanation:
CORRECT: Check both figures against the competitor's own public disclosures or another primary source, rather than assuming either answer is correct.

A newer answer is not automatically a more accurate one, since either response could be the one that drifted from the real number. Comparing both figures against the competitor's own disclosures or another primary source is what actually settles which total, if either, is right.

Exam Guide Mapping

Domain 2: Output Evaluation and Validation (21%)

-
Objective: Apply fact-checking and validation techniques

INCORRECT: Use the more recent answer, since Claude's newer responses tend to reflect its latest available information.

Nothing about a response being more recent means it reflects better information, since Claude does not track this competitor's real-time store count between requests. Treating recency as a stand-in for accuracy leaves the actual discrepancy unresolved.

INCORRECT: Ask Claude which of the two totals is correct, and use whichever answer it happens to state with more apparent confidence.

Asking Claude to judge between its own two answers just produces a third statement of confidence, not new evidence about which total is correct. The analyst still has no way to know if that pick is right without checking an outside source.

INCORRECT: Average the two conflicting totals together and use that blended number in the strategy report.

Splitting the difference between two unverified numbers produces a total that was never actually reported anywhere, which is worse than either original figure. Blending unverified data does not make it more accurate.

questions.question:
A talent acquisition specialist asks Claude to draft a posting for a director-level role. The draft repeatedly describes the ideal candidate as a decisive, assertive leader who commands a room.

What should the specialist do before posting it?

options.label: A
options.text: Revise the language to focus on required skills and outcomes, removing wording that reflects gendered leadership stereotypes.

options.label: B
options.text: Post the listing as written, since assertive and decisive are reasonable qualities to want in a director-level candidate.

options.label: C
options.text: Add a sentence encouraging candidates of all backgrounds to apply, while leaving the rest of the description unchanged.

options.label: D
options.text: Remove every adjective describing leadership qualities from the posting, leaving only the role's technical requirements.

questions.explanation:
CORRECT: Revise the language to focus on required skills and outcomes, removing wording that reflects gendered leadership stereotypes.

Repeatedly framing the ideal candidate as forceful and commanding leans on traits stereotypically coded as masculine, which can discourage qualified candidates who do not fit that mold. Reworking the posting around the skills and outcomes the role actually requires removes that coded framing.

"Bias evaluations: We check whether Claude consistently provides reliable, accurate responses across different contexts and users... We also test responses on topics such as jobs and healthcare to identify whether the inclusion of identity attributes like gender, race, or religion result in biased outputs." - Resource

Domain 2: Output Evaluation and Validation (21%)

-
Objective: Edit, adapt, refine, and compare outputs for the intended audience

-
Objective: Determine when human review or additional verification is required

INCORRECT: Post the listing as written, since assertive and decisive are reasonable qualities to want in a director-level candidate.

Wanting decisive, capable leadership is reasonable, but the specific repeated framing here leans on stereotyped language rather than describing the qualities the role needs. Posting it as written carries that coded framing forward.

INCORRECT: Add a sentence encouraging candidates of all backgrounds to apply, while leaving the rest of the description unchanged.

An added invitation to apply does not change the stereotyped language earlier in the same posting, which is what a candidate actually reads first. The core wording that prompted the concern is still there.

INCORRECT: Remove every adjective describing leadership qualities from the posting, leaving only the role's technical requirements.

Stripping out every leadership-related adjective removes legitimate, relevant descriptions along with the stereotyped ones, leaving the posting far less informative than it needs to be. The fix here is rewording, not deleting the category altogether.

questions.question:
A financial advisor asks Claude to draft a client memo explaining a specific tax rate that applies to a proposed investment.

Before sending the memo to the client, what should the advisor do?

options.label: A
options.text: Verify the cited tax rate against current, authoritative tax guidance before the memo reaches the client.

options.label: B
options.text: Send the memo as drafted, since tax rates are widely known figures Claude would likely state correctly.

options.label: C
options.text: Ask Claude to restate the same tax rate in simpler terms for the client, without checking whether the rate itself is accurate.

options.label: D
options.text: Round the cited tax rate to the nearest whole number so it reads as an approximation rather than an exact figure.

questions.explanation:
CORRECT: Verify the cited tax rate against current, authoritative tax guidance before the memo reaches the client.

A specific tax rate is a factual detail with real financial consequences for the client, and Claude cannot guarantee it reflects current tax rules. Checking it against authoritative guidance before the memo goes out is what confirms the client is getting accurate information.

Domain 2: Output Evaluation and Validation (21%)

-
Objective: Evaluate Claude-generated outputs for accuracy and completeness

-
Objective: Determine when human review or additional verification is required

INCORRECT: Send the memo as drafted, since tax rates are widely known figures Claude would likely state correctly.

Being a commonly known category of figure does not guarantee this particular cited rate is current or correctly applied to this situation. Sending the memo on that assumption skips the actual check the figure needs.

INCORRECT: Ask Claude to restate the same tax rate in simpler terms for the client, without checking whether the rate itself is accurate.

Restating the same number in friendlier language changes how it reads without changing whether the rate itself is accurate. The client would still receive an unverified figure, just phrased more simply.

INCORRECT: Round the cited tax rate to the nearest whole number so it reads as an approximation rather than an exact figure.

Rounding the rate makes it look like a rough estimate rather than a precise figure, but it does nothing to confirm whether the underlying number is correct in the first place. Precision and accuracy are not the same thing here.

questions.question:
A competitive analyst reviews a Claude-drafted market report showing a competitor's market share dropped sharply this quarter, contradicting a stable figure the analyst recalls from last quarter's report.

What should the analyst do?

options.label: A
options.text: Verify the disputed market share figure against the original source data, rather than assuming either number is correct.

options.label: B
options.text: Accept the new figure, since a decline in market share is a plausible outcome for any given quarter.

options.label: C
options.text: Ask Claude to double check its own math on the new figure without comparing it against the original source data.

options.label: D
options.text: Delete the disputed figure from the report entirely rather than determining which number is accurate.

questions.explanation:
CORRECT: Verify the disputed market share figure against the original source data, rather than assuming either number is correct.

A figure that directly contradicts something the analyst already recalls seeing is a specific, checkable discrepancy, not a routine unfamiliar number. Verifying it against the original source data is what determines whether the new figure, the old one, or neither is accurate.

Domain 2: Output Evaluation and Validation (21%)

-
Objective: Identify hallucinations, inconsistencies, and biases in responses

-
Objective: Apply fact-checking and validation techniques

INCORRECT: Accept the new figure, since a decline in market share is a plausible outcome for any given quarter.

A market share decline being generally plausible does not confirm that this specific figure is accurate, especially when it contradicts a number the analyst has already seen elsewhere. Plausibility is not the same as verification.

INCORRECT: Ask Claude to double check its own math on the new figure without comparing it against the original source data.

Checking its own arithmetic only confirms Claude did the calculation correctly on whatever inputs it used, not that those inputs match the original source data. The contradiction with last quarter's figure would remain unresolved.

INCORRECT: Delete the disputed figure from the report entirely rather than determining which number is accurate.

Removing the figure avoids the discrepancy instead of resolving it, and it leaves the report without a data point the analysis may actually need. The contradiction still has not been checked against anything.

questions.question:
A support team asks Claude to draft a public-facing troubleshooting article for a login error. The published draft still references an internal codename for the login system and an internal ticket queue number.

What should the team do before publishing?

options.label: A
options.text: Revise the article to remove the internal codename and ticket reference, using only customer-facing terminology throughout.

options.label: B
options.text: Publish the article as is, since the troubleshooting steps themselves are accurate and easy to follow.

options.label: C
options.text: Add a glossary at the bottom of the article defining the internal codename and ticket queue number for readers.

options.label: D
options.text: Restructure the entire article into a completely different format and tone, without addressing the internal codename or ticket reference at all.

questions.explanation:
CORRECT: Revise the article to remove the internal codename and ticket reference, using only customer-facing terminology throughout.

Customers reading a public article have no use for an internal codename or ticket queue number, and their presence signals the draft was never adapted for an outside audience. Removing them and describing the system only in customer-facing terms is what actually fixes that.

Domain 2: Output Evaluation and Validation (21%)

-
Objective: Edit, adapt, refine, and compare outputs for the intended audience

-
Objective: Determine when human review or additional verification is required

INCORRECT: Publish the article as is, since the troubleshooting steps themselves are accurate and easy to follow.

Accurate troubleshooting steps do not change the fact that internal-only references are still sitting in a document meant for customers. Publishing it as is leaves that specific problem untouched.

INCORRECT: Add a glossary at the bottom of the article defining the internal codename and ticket queue number for readers.

Explaining an internal codename to customers still exposes internal terminology they were never meant to see, and it adds confusion rather than removing it. The reference itself needed to come out, not be footnoted.

INCORRECT: Restructure the entire article into a completely different format and tone, without addressing the internal codename or ticket reference at all.

Changing the article's format and tone has nothing to do with the internal codename or ticket number still sitting in the text. The actual problem the team noticed remains exactly where it was.

questions.question:
A communications team asks Claude for three draft options responding to a public service disruption. One draft uses a noticeably more casual, joking tone than the organization's other public statements have ever used.

What should the team do before choosing?

options.label: A
options.text: Compare each draft against the organization's own established public communication style before selecting one.

options.label: B
options.text: Select whichever draft reads most creatively, since a distinctive tone could help this statement stand out.

options.label: C
options.text: Ask Claude to tone down the jokes in the casual draft, without checking it against the organization's prior statements.

options.label: D
options.text: Require legal sign-off on every future public statement regardless of tone, even routine operational updates.

questions.explanation:
CORRECT: Compare each draft against the organization's own established public communication style before selecting one.

Whether a draft fits depends on how this organization has actually communicated publicly before, not on how any one draft reads in isolation. Comparing all three against that established precedent is what confirms which option actually belongs to this organization's voice.

"If your product relies on a specific voice, re-evaluate style prompts against the new baseline. For instance, if your product voice is warmer or more conversational, add: Use a warm, collaborative tone." Resource

Domain 2: Output Evaluation and Validation (21%)

-
Objective: Edit, adapt, refine, and compare outputs for the intended audience

-
Objective: Determine when human review or additional verification is required

INCORRECT: Select whichever draft reads most creatively, since a distinctive tone could help this statement stand out.

Standing out is not the same goal as matching how this organization has always communicated during a service disruption. Choosing for creativity risks picking the one draft that breaks from established precedent.

INCORRECT: Ask Claude to tone down the jokes in the casual draft, without checking it against the organization's prior statements.

Softening the jokes still leaves the question of whether the resulting tone actually matches this organization's prior public statements, since that comparison was never made. The draft could still land outside the established style.

INCORRECT: Require legal sign-off on every future public statement regardless of tone, even routine operational updates.

Mandating legal review for every routine statement addresses a much bigger scope than the one tone mismatch actually spotted here. The specific comparison against communication precedent still never happens under this approach.

questions.question:
An operations coordinator asks Claude for a weekly compliance checklist that the team will edit and check off. Claude delivers the checklist as plain text within the chat, with no separate copy to update.

What should the coordinator do?

options.label: A
options.text: Request the checklist as a persistent, editable document instead, so the team can update and reuse it every week.

options.label: B
options.text: Copy the checklist text into a new document each week, since the content itself is accurate and complete.

options.label: C
options.text: Ask Claude to make the checklist look more visually organized within the chat, without changing how it is stored.

options.label: D
options.text: Build a custom internal application for managing this checklist before using Claude for it at all.

questions.explanation:
CORRECT: Request the checklist as a persistent, editable document instead, so the team can update and reuse it every week.

A checklist the team edits and checks off weekly needs one persistent copy that carries updates forward, not a fresh block of chat text each time. Requesting it as an editable, reusable document is what actually supports that recurring use.

Domain 3: Product and Model Selection (12%)

-
Objective: Select appropriate Claude product features (Projects, research mode, chat, artifacts)

-
Objective: Understand and manage context limitations and memory considerations (when to restart, summarize, or persist)

INCORRECT: Copy the checklist text into a new document each week, since the content itself is accurate and complete.

Manually recreating a new document from the chat text every single week works, but it recreates the same copying effort each time instead of giving the team one reusable copy that carries its own history forward. The underlying request, something persistent and reusable, still is not met.

INCORRECT: Ask Claude to make the checklist look more visually organized within the chat, without changing how it is stored.

Better visual organization inside the chat does not change the fact that there is still no separate, persistent copy for the team to edit and check off. The storage and reuse problem remains exactly as it was.

INCORRECT: Build a custom internal application for managing this checklist before using Claude for it at all.

A full custom application is a much larger build than a recurring checklist actually requires, and it reaches past what this task calls for. A persistent document handles the same need without the added development effort.
references: [What are artifacts and how do I use them?](https://support.claude.com/en/articles/9487310-what-are-artifacts-and-how-do-i-use-them)

questions.question:
A researcher asks Claude to summarize five customer interview transcripts. The response repeats each interview's points separately in full, with no comparison of where interviewees agreed or disagreed.

Which two changes should the researcher request?

(choose two)

options.label: A
options.text: Group the interview findings around shared themes rather than listing each interview separately.

options.label: B
options.text: Call out the specific points where interviewees' responses agreed or disagreed with each other.

options.label: C
options.text: Shorten each interview's summary to the same fixed length, regardless of how much relevant content it contains.

options.label: D
options.text: Ask Claude to state its overall confidence in the summary's accuracy before using it.

options.label: E
options.text: Present the five interviews in the order they were conducted, without changing how the content itself is organized.

questions.explanation:
CORRECT: Group the interview findings around shared themes rather than listing each interview separately.

Organizing around shared themes is what turns five separate interview write-ups into an actual synthesis, letting a reader see the findings that cut across interviewees instead of five parallel summaries.

CORRECT: Call out the specific points where interviewees' responses agreed or disagreed with each other.

Naming where responses actually agreed or disagreed is what a synthesis is for, and it is exactly the comparison missing from a response that just repeats each interview in isolation.

Domain 2: Output Evaluation and Validation (21%)

-
Objective: Organize and curate information and select appropriate output formats (artifacts, inline, structured data)

-
Objective: Identify hallucinations, inconsistencies, and biases in responses

INCORRECT: Shorten each interview's summary to the same fixed length, regardless of how much relevant content it contains.

Trimming every summary to a matching length changes how much space each interview takes up without creating any comparison between them. The interviews would still sit side by side, unsynthesized.

INCORRECT: Ask Claude to state its overall confidence in the summary's accuracy before using it.

A stated confidence level describes how sure Claude is, not whether the interviews have actually been compared to one another. The missing synthesis is still missing either way.

INCORRECT: Present the five interviews in the order they were conducted, without changing how the content itself is organized.

Keeping the interviews in their original chronological order preserves the same side-by-side structure that caused the problem in the first place. Nothing about the underlying organization actually changes.

options.label: B
options.text: Proceed with the purchase decision as planned, since Claude specifically said no additional setup is required.

options.label: C

options.label: D

CORRECT: Check Salesforce's or Slack's official integration documentation to confirm what setup the connection actually requires.

How confidently a compatibility claim is stated says nothing about whether the specific setup details are correct, and integrations between two products often involve configuration steps that are easy to state incorrectly. -

Confidence in the phrasing does not verify the claim itself, and proceeding on that basis risks a purchase decision built on an unconfirmed setup assumption. The actual requirements still have not been checked anywhere official.

A list of benefits describes what the integration could offer without ever confirming whether the no-setup-required claim is actually accurate. The specific question the coordinator needed answered is still unresolved.

questions.question:
A marketing team has a Project set up with the current brand guidelines and campaign history loaded. Team members keep starting brand-new chats outside the Project and pasting in the same background details each time.

What should the team do?

options.label: A
options.text: Have the team start their chats from within the existing Project instead of creating new standalone chats.

options.label: B
options.text: Continue as is, since pasting the details manually still gives Claude the same information each time.

options.label: C
options.text: Ask each team member to save the pasted details as a personal note they copy into every new chat.

options.label: D
options.text: Create a brand-new Project for every single campaign, in addition to the one that already exists.

questions.explanation:
CORRECT: Have the team start their chats from within the existing Project instead of creating new standalone chats.

The Project already holds the guidelines and campaign history that people keep repasting, so the fix is simply working from inside it, where that material is already loaded for every chat automatically.

Domain 3: Product and Model Selection (12%)

-
Objective: Select appropriate Claude product features (Projects, research mode, chat, artifacts)

-
Objective: Understand and manage context limitations and memory considerations (when to restart, summarize, or persist)

INCORRECT: Continue as is, since pasting the details manually still gives Claude the same information each time.

Pasting the same details manually can convey the same information, but it recreates effort the Project was already built to eliminate, and it is easy to paste an outdated or incomplete version by hand.

INCORRECT: Ask each team member to save the pasted details as a personal note they copy into every new chat.

A personal copy-paste note still needs to be manually reattached to every new chat, and it does not give the rest of the team the same shared, always-current source the Project already provides.

INCORRECT: Create a brand-new Project for every single campaign, in addition to the one that already exists.

Building more Projects on top of one that already has the needed material adds duplication instead of fixing the actual habit of not using the Project that already exists.

What should the team do?
options: Have the team start their chats from within the existing Project instead of creating new standalone chats.
Continue as is, since pasting the details manually still gives Claude the same information each time.
Ask each team member to save the pasted details as a personal note they copy into every new chat.
Create a brand-new Project for every single campaign, in addition to the one that already exists.
html.explanation:
CORRECT: Have the team start their chats from within the existing Project instead of creating new standalone chats.

The Project already holds the guidelines and campaign history that people keep repasting, so the fix is simply working from inside it, where that material is already loaded for every chat automatically.

Domain 3: Product and Model Selection (12%)

  • Objective: Select appropriate Claude product features (Projects, research mode, chat, artifacts)

  • Objective: Understand and manage context limitations and memory considerations (when to restart, summarize, or persist)

INCORRECT: Continue as is, since pasting the details manually still gives Claude the same information each time.

Pasting the same details manually can convey the same information, but it recreates effort the Project was already built to eliminate, and it is easy to paste an outdated or incomplete version by hand.

INCORRECT: Ask each team member to save the pasted details as a personal note they copy into every new chat.

A personal copy-paste note still needs to be manually reattached to every new chat, and it does not give the rest of the team the same shared, always-current source the Project already provides.

INCORRECT: Create a brand-new Project for every single campaign, in addition to the one that already exists.

Building more Projects on top of one that already has the needed material adds duplication instead of fixing the actual habit of not using the Project that already exists.

questions.question:
An analyst uploads the company's own quarterly logistics spreadsheet and turns on Research mode before asking Claude to calculate the average shipping cost per order from that file.

What should the analyst do instead?

options.label: A
options.text: Turn off Research and ask the question directly, since the answer only requires calculating from the uploaded spreadsheet.

options.label: B
options.text: Leave Research on, since a more thorough process should only make the answer more reliable.

options.label: C
options.text: Keep Research on but tell Claude to only use the uploaded file and skip the web search step.

options.label: D
options.text: Have a colleague independently recalculate the same average afterward, regardless of which method answered it.

questions.explanation:
CORRECT: Turn off Research and ask the question directly, since the answer only requires calculating from the uploaded spreadsheet.

Research exists to gather and synthesize information across multiple sources, which this question does not need, since the answer is a direct calculation from data already sitting in the uploaded file. A regular question gets there just as accurately and faster.

Domain 3: Product and Model Selection (12%)

-
Objective: Select appropriate Claude product features (Projects, research mode, chat, artifacts)

-
Objective: Align model selection with task requirements (cost, speed, quality)

INCORRECT: Leave Research on, since a more thorough process should only make the answer more reliable.

More process is not the same as more reliability here, since the number being asked for already lives entirely in the uploaded spreadsheet. Extra steps add time without improving an answer that does not depend on outside sources.

INCORRECT: Keep Research on but tell Claude to only use the uploaded file and skip the web search step.

Research mode is built around multi-source web and integration gathering, so disabling the web portion still leaves a heavier process running for a task that never needed multi-source synthesis in the first place.

INCORRECT: Have a colleague independently recalculate the same average afterward, regardless of which method answered it.

Manually recalculating afterward addresses trust in the number, not the mismatch between a simple calculation and a research-oriented tool, and it does nothing to correct which mode was the right fit for this question.
references: [When should I use web search, extended thinking, and research?](https://support.claude.com/en/articles/11095361-when-should-i-use-web-search-extended-thinking-and-research)

questions.question:
A team uses the most capable, highest-cost model tier for routine, simple product-description tagging, reasoning that it is better to be safe. The task is high-volume and does not require complex reasoning.

What should the team do?

options.label: A
options.text: Switch this recurring, straightforward task to a faster, lower-cost model tier suited to its complexity.

options.label: B
options.text: Keep using the top-tier model, since higher-cost models are always the safer choice regardless of task.

options.label: C
options.text: Reduce how many product descriptions are tagged per batch, while keeping the same top-tier model.

options.label: D
options.text: Switch all of the team's tasks, including complex ones, to the fastest, lowest-cost tier to control costs.

questions.explanation:
CORRECT: Switch this recurring, straightforward task to a faster, lower-cost model tier suited to its complexity.

Simple, high-volume tagging does not call for the reasoning depth the top-tier model provides, so matching a faster, lower-cost tier to this specific task cuts cost and turnaround without any quality trade-off that matters here.

Domain 3: Product and Model Selection (12%)

-
Objective: Differentiate between Claude model types (Haiku, Sonnet, Opus)

-
Objective: Align model selection with task requirements (cost, speed, quality)

INCORRECT: Keep using the top-tier model, since higher-cost models are always the safer choice regardless of task.

Higher cost does not automatically mean better suited, and for a task this straightforward, the top-tier model's extra capability goes unused while its extra cost and slower turnaround still apply.

INCORRECT: Reduce how many product descriptions are tagged per batch, while keeping the same top-tier model.

Tagging fewer items per batch reduces volume, not the underlying mismatch between task complexity and model tier, so the same unnecessary cost and latency persist for every batch that is still run.

INCORRECT: Switch all of the team's tasks, including complex ones, to the fastest, lowest-cost tier to control costs.

Downshifting the complex work along with the simple work fixes this task's inefficiency by creating a new one elsewhere, since tasks that actually need deeper reasoning would now be underpowered.

questions.question:
A compliance analyst is asked to switch a multi-jurisdiction risk assessment from the top-tier model to a faster, cheaper tier to reduce costs, even though the task involves reconciling conflicting regulations.

What should the analyst do?

options.label: A
options.text: Keep the higher-tier model for this task, since its complexity and compliance stakes justify the added cost.

options.label: B
options.text: Make the switch, since a faster response would help the team meet its deadline.

options.label: C
options.text: Switch to the faster tier but ask Claude to double check its own answer afterward before finalizing it.

options.label: D
options.text: Require every future compliance task, regardless of complexity, to use the most expensive tier available.

questions.explanation:
CORRECT: Keep the higher-tier model for this task, since its complexity and compliance stakes justify the added cost.

Reconciling conflicting regulations across jurisdictions is exactly the kind of complex, high-stakes reasoning the top-tier model is suited for, and the compliance risk of missing a conflict outweighs the cost of staying on it.

Domain 3: Product and Model Selection (12%)

-
Objective: Align model selection with task requirements (cost, speed, quality)

-
Objective: Differentiate between Claude model types (Haiku, Sonnet, Opus)

INCORRECT: Make the switch, since a faster response would help the team meet its deadline.

A faster response does not help if the faster tier misses a regulatory conflict the task specifically requires catching, so meeting the deadline this way risks the quality the task actually needs.

INCORRECT: Switch to the faster tier but ask Claude to double check its own answer afterward before finalizing it.

Asking Claude to double check itself on a faster tier does not restore the deeper reasoning the original tier provided, and a self-review is not the same as the model actually being capable enough for the task.

INCORRECT: Require every future compliance task, regardless of complexity, to use the most expensive tier available.

Locking every future compliance task, however simple, into the most expensive tier overcorrects for this one high-stakes case and ignores that not every compliance task carries the same complexity.
references: [Claude Opus vs Sonnet vs Haiku: Which Tier to Use ](https://haimaker.ai/blog/claude-opus-vs-sonnet-vs-haiku/)

questions.question:
Within a single conversation, a support lead first asks Claude to quickly classify twenty tickets by category, then pivots to a detailed root-cause analysis of a recurring outage.

What should the lead do about the model tier partway through?

options.label: A
options.text: Raise the model tier partway through the conversation once the task shifts to deeper analysis.

options.label: B
options.text: Keep the same tier used for classification, since switching mid-conversation could confuse Claude.

options.label: C
options.text: End the conversation and start a brand-new one just to change the model tier for the analysis.

options.label: D
options.text: Use the higher tier for the classification step too, even though it was simple and fast.

questions.explanation:
CORRECT: Raise the model tier partway through the conversation once the task shifts to deeper analysis.

The model tier can be changed at any point in a conversation, with the change applying starting with Claude's next response, so raising it once the task shifts to deeper analysis matches the tier to the harder half of the work.

Exam Guide Mapping

Domain 3: Product and Model Selection (12%)

-
Align model selection with task requirements (cost, speed, quality)

-
Understand and manage context limitations and memory considerations (when to restart, summarize, or persist)

INCORRECT: Keep the same tier used for classification, since switching mid-conversation could confuse Claude.

Switching tiers mid-conversation does not disrupt Claude's understanding of the thread, so staying on the lighter tier only means the harder root-cause analysis gets less capability than it actually needs.

INCORRECT: End the conversation and start a brand-new one just to change the model tier for the analysis.

A new conversation is not required to change tiers, since the setting can be changed at any point without leaving the thread, so restarting here trades away the ticket-classification context for no real benefit.

INCORRECT: Use the higher tier for the classification step too, even though it was simple and fast.

Using the higher tier for simple classification spends more than that step needed, since the added reasoning capability was never the bottleneck for quickly sorting twenty tickets into categories.
references: [How to change the model version you’re chatting with in Claude.ai](https://www.guideflow.com/tutorial/how-to-change-the-model-version-youre-chatting-with-in-claudeai)

questions.question:
A long financial modeling conversation in a single chat has grown so large that Claude starts losing track of instructions given several messages earlier, and responses come out noticeably slower than before.

What should the analyst do?

options.label: A
options.text: Ask Claude to summarize the key context, then start a new conversation with that summary.

options.label: B
options.text: Continue in the same conversation, since Claude should still have access to everything said earlier.

options.label: C
options.text: Repeat the original instructions once more in the same overloaded conversation and continue as before.

options.label: D
options.text: Split the work into several new conversations that each start with no carried-over context at all.

questions.explanation:
CORRECT: Ask Claude to summarize the key context, then start a new conversation with that summary.

A conversation this large is straining its own context window, which is exactly why earlier instructions are getting lost, so summarizing the essentials and continuing in a fresh conversation gives the model a clean, focused window to work from.

Exam Guide Mapping

-
Domain 3: Product and Model Selection (12%)

-
Objective: Understand and manage context limitations and memory considerations (when to restart, summarize, or persist)

INCORRECT: Continue in the same conversation, since Claude should still have access to everything said earlier.

Assuming everything is still fully accessible ignores the symptoms already showing up, since the slowdown and dropped instructions are signs the thread has outgrown what it can reliably track.

INCORRECT: Repeat the original instructions once more in the same overloaded conversation and continue as before.

Restating the instructions adds more content to an already overloaded conversation, which is the opposite of what is needed and would likely make the slowdown and context strain worse, not better.

INCORRECT: Split the work into several new conversations that each start with no carried-over context at all.

Starting several new conversations with nothing carried over solves the overload problem by discarding the context entirely, which loses just as much continuity as staying in the overloaded thread was costing.

questions.question:
A consulting team asks Claude to draft a client proposal going through several stakeholder feedback rounds, with section edits each time. The full draft gets retyped into a new chat message every round.

Which two changes should the team make?

options.label: A
options.text: Request that Claude generate the proposal as an artifact so it becomes one persistent, editable document.

options.label: B
options.text: Highlight the specific section that needs to change and use the edit-in-place option, rather than retyping the whole document.

options.label: C
options.text: Ask Claude to always respond with shorter messages so each round of retyping takes less time.

options.label: D
options.text: Have one team member manually track every version by saving separate chat exports after each round.

options.label: E
options.text: Request the proposal in a single upfront message with every possible stakeholder edit pre-included from the start.

questions.explanation:
CORRECT: Request that Claude generate the proposal as an artifact so it becomes one persistent, editable document.

A document this substantial, headed for several rounds of edits, is exactly what an artifact is meant for, since it gives the team one persistent, editable copy instead of new chat text every round.

CORRECT: Highlight the specific section that needs to change and use the edit-in-place option, rather than retyping the whole document.

The edit-in-place option lets a specific section be changed directly within the artifact, which is what actually replaces retyping the whole draft for a change that only affects one part of it.

Exam Guide Mapping

-
Domain 3: Product and Model Selection (12%)

-
Objective: Select appropriate Claude product features (Projects, research mode, chat, artifacts)

INCORRECT: Ask Claude to always respond with shorter messages so each round of retyping takes less time.

Shorter messages would make each round of retyping faster, but retyping the whole draft is the actual problem, and that habit continues either way regardless of message length.

INCORRECT: Have one team member manually track every version by saving separate chat exports after each round.

Manually saving chat exports adds an extra tracking step on top of the same underlying habit, without giving the team the one editable, persistent copy that would remove the retyping in the first place.

INCORRECT: Request the proposal in a single upfront message with every possible stakeholder edit pre-included from the start.

Feedback that has not happened yet cannot be pre-included, and stakeholder rounds exist precisely because the specific edits are not known until each round actually happens.
references: [What are artifacts and how do I use them?](https://support.claude.com/en/articles/9487310-what-are-artifacts-and-how-do-i-use-them)

questions.question:
An operations manager is weighing two automation candidates: reformatting the same weekly inventory report every week, and resolving a one-time, highly unusual client contract dispute.

What should the manager do?

options.label: A
options.text: Treat the weekly inventory report as the well-bounded candidate, since it recurs and follows a consistent format each time.

options.label: B
options.text: Treat the contract dispute as the better candidate, since it is the more complex and valuable task to get right.

options.label: C
options.text: Treat both as equally good candidates, since Claude can attempt any task regardless of how repetitive or unique it is.

options.label: D
options.text: Treat neither as ready, since automation candidates need a dedicated developer-built tool before Claude can be involved at all.

questions.explanation:
CORRECT: Treat the weekly inventory report as the well-bounded candidate, since it recurs and follows a consistent format each time.

A well-bounded candidate is one with a stable, repeatable structure Claude can reliably work within, and the weekly report fits that description while the one-time dispute does not.

Exam Guide Mapping

-
Domain 4: Workflow Integration and Solution Design (16%)

-
Objective: Apply Claude to analyze requirements and use cases

INCORRECT: Treat the contract dispute as the better candidate, since it is the more complex and valuable task to get right.

Complexity and value are not the same thing as being well-bounded, and the dispute's highly unusual, non-repeating nature is exactly what makes it a poor fit despite how much it matters.

INCORRECT: Treat both as equally good candidates, since Claude can attempt any task regardless of how repetitive or unique it is.

Claude being willing to attempt any task says nothing about which one has the stable structure that actually makes automation reliable, so treating them as equivalent ignores the distinction the manager needs to make.

INCORRECT: Treat neither as ready, since automation candidates need a dedicated developer-built tool before Claude can be involved at all.

A recurring, structured task like the weekly report does not require a custom-built tool before Claude can help with it, since this is exactly the kind of platform-native work Claude already handles directly.

questions.question:
A hiring committee has started accepting Claude's synthesized comparison of finalist candidates as the final decision, without discussing or applying their own judgment afterward.

What should the committee do differently?

options.label: A
options.text: Use Claude's synthesis as one input, then discuss and apply the committee's own judgment before deciding.

options.label: B
options.text: Continue accepting the synthesis as the decision, since Claude weighed all the same factors the committee would consider.

options.label: C
options.text: Have the committee take a quick vote to ratify Claude's synthesis without further discussion, to save time.

options.label: D
options.text: Have a senior executive personally re-review and re-score every finalist from scratch before the committee even sees Claude's synthesis.

questions.explanation:

What should the team do?

options.label: A
options.text: Investigate whether that approval step still adds value, and remove it from the process if it does not.

options.label: B
options.text: Leave the approval step in place, since a human checkpoint is always considered good practice, regardless of the outcome it produces.

options.label: C
options.text: Automate the approval step too, having Claude generate the approval decision instead of the manager.

options.label: D
options.text: Remove every approval step from every finance process company-wide to eliminate similar inefficiencies across the organization.

questions.explanation:
CORRECT: Investigate whether that approval step still adds value, and remove it from the process if it does not.

A step that has not changed an outcome in over a year is a candidate for removal, not just automation, so checking whether it still serves a purpose is what actually addresses the inefficiency the team noticed.

questions.question:
A UX team had Claude help design a new onboarding flow, but a budget cut eliminates one of the planned interactive elements before the design ships.

What should the team do?

options.label: A
options.text: Share the updated budget constraint with Claude and have it revise the design around the new limitation.

options.label: B
options.text: Ship the original design as planned, since the budget cut can be addressed separately after launch.

options.label: C
options.text: Have the design team manually remove the interactive element from Claude's design themselves, without telling Claude about the new constraint.

options.label: D
options.text: Restart the entire onboarding flow design from a blank page, discarding all of the work completed so far.

questions.explanation:
CORRECT: Share the updated budget constraint with Claude and have it revise the design around the new limitation.

The constraint that changed is specific and known, so feeding it back to Claude lets the rest of the design get revised around it coherently, rather than leaving a gap where the cut element used to be.

Exam Guide Mapping

-
Domain 4: Workflow Integration and Solution Design (16%)

-
Objective: Use Claude to support solution design, development, and iteration

INCORRECT: Ship the original design as planned, since the budget cut can be addressed separately after launch.

Shipping a design built around an element the budget no longer supports creates a mismatch between what was designed and what can actually be built, which addressing it later does not prevent at launch.

INCORRECT: Have the design team manually remove the interactive element from Claude's design themselves, without telling Claude about the new constraint.

Manually cutting the element without updating Claude on the new constraint leaves the surrounding design built around an assumption that no longer holds, since nothing else was reconsidered in light of the change.

INCORRECT: Restart the entire onboarding flow design from a blank page, discarding all of the work completed so far.

Nearly all of the onboarding flow design remains valid after this one budget change, so discarding it entirely throws away completed, still-relevant work to address a single planned element.

questions.question:
A four-step content workflow has one slow drafting step, but the team has also routed the scheduling and publishing steps through Claude, adding review overhead without any speed benefit.

What should the team do?

options.label: A
options.text: Scope Claude back to just the drafting step, where it actually addresses the bottleneck.

options.label: B
options.text: Keep Claude across all four steps, since more automation should always make the workflow more efficient overall.

options.label: C
options.text: Simplify the review process for the scheduling and publishing steps, while keeping Claude involved in all four.

options.label: D
options.text: Add a second review layer to every step of the workflow to make sure Claude does not introduce errors.

questions.explanation:
CORRECT: Scope Claude back to just the drafting step, where it actually addresses the bottleneck.

Only the drafting step was ever the bottleneck, so scoping Claude to that one step keeps the benefit where it exists and removes the review overhead that scheduling and publishing picked up for no speed gain.

Exam Guide Mapping

-
Domain 4: Workflow Integration and Solution Design (16%)

-
Objective: Integrate Claude into existing workflows to augment or redesign them

-
Objective: Leverage Claude for research, planning, and process optimization

More automation only helps where it addresses an actual bottleneck, and scheduling and publishing were never slow to begin with, so keeping Claude there adds overhead rather than efficiency.

INCORRECT: Simplify the review process for the scheduling and publishing steps, while keeping Claude involved in all four.

A lighter review process still leaves Claude involved in two steps that were never the problem, so the underlying mismatch between where the slowdown is and where Claude was applied remains.

INCORRECT: Add a second review layer to every step of the workflow to make sure Claude does not introduce errors.

Adding a second review layer everywhere increases the overhead this workflow is already carrying without changing which steps actually needed Claude's help in the first place.
