questions.question:
An operations manager asks Claude to map a document approval workflow. Claude finds legal review, finance review, and a formatting check run one after another, though none depends on the others' output.

What should the manager do with this finding?

options.label: A
options.text: Use Claude's analysis to redesign the workflow so the three independent steps run in parallel instead of sequentially.

options.label: B
options.text: Thank Claude for the analysis, but keep running the same sequential process, since it has worked reliably so far.

options.label: C
options.text: Ask Claude to re-analyze the same workflow a second time before deciding whether the finding is worth acting on.

options.label: D
options.text: Have Claude immediately redesign every approval process company-wide based on this one workflow's finding.

questions.explanation:
CORRECT: Use Claude's analysis to redesign the workflow so the three independent steps run in parallel instead of sequentially.

Claude's analysis already identified the specific inefficiency, that three steps run in sequence despite none depending on another, so acting on that finding by redesigning this workflow to run them in parallel is what actually uses the analysis Claude was asked to produce.

Exam Guide Mapping

-
Domain 4: Workflow Integration and Solution Design (16%)

-
Objective: Leverage Claude for research, planning, and process optimization

-
Objective: Integrate Claude into existing workflows to augment or redesign them

INCORRECT: Thank Claude for the analysis, but keep running the same sequential process, since it has worked reliably so far.

Reliability so far does not mean the process is efficient, and thanking Claude for a finding while continuing the same sequence ignores the specific inefficiency the analysis was requested to surface in the first place.

INCORRECT: Ask Claude to re-analyze the same workflow a second time before deciding whether the finding is worth acting on.

Asking for the same analysis again does not add new information, since Claude already identified the independence between these three steps. Re-running it only delays acting on a finding that is already clear.

INCORRECT: Have Claude immediately redesign every approval process company-wide based on this one workflow's finding.

One workflow's finding does not establish that every other approval process shares the same pattern of independent steps running in unnecessary sequence, so extending the redesign company-wide skips the verification each process would actually need.

questions.question:
A pitch to a skeptical operations director already uses outcome-focused language like faster turnaround and consistent quality, but the director still resists, seemingly worried the team's roles will be eliminated.

Which two actions should the presenter take?

options.label: A
options.text: Directly acknowledge the concern about job security instead of assuming better outcome language will resolve it.

options.label: B
options.text: Reframe the pitch to show specific ways Claude augments the team's work rather than replacing their roles.

options.label: C
options.text: Add more statistics about turnaround time to strengthen the existing outcome-focused pitch overall.

options.label: D
options.text: Avoid discussing the topic of job impact directly, since raising it might make the concern feel more real.

options.label: E
options.text: Escalate the director's resistance to senior leadership right away to override the objection.

questions.explanation:
CORRECT: Directly acknowledge the concern about job security instead of assuming better outcome language will resolve it.

The resistance here is not about being unconvinced by outcomes, it is about a worry the pitch never actually addresses, so naming that concern directly is what the outcome-focused language alone was never going to resolve.

CORRECT: Reframe the pitch to show specific ways Claude augments the team's work rather than replacing their roles.

Showing specific ways Claude adds to the team's work, rather than stands in for it, speaks directly to the fear driving the resistance instead of repeating the same efficiency framing that already failed to land.

Exam Guide Mapping

-
Domain 4: Workflow Integration and Solution Design (16%)

-
Objective: Communicate Claude's value and limitations to stakeholders

INCORRECT: Add more statistics about turnaround time to strengthen the existing outcome-focused pitch overall.

More turnaround statistics strengthen an argument the director was never actually resisting, since the real concern is about role security, not whether the efficiency case is convincing enough.

INCORRECT: Avoid discussing the topic of job impact directly, since raising it might make the concern feel more real.

Staying silent on job impact leaves the director's actual worry unaddressed, and avoiding the topic does not make a concern this specific go away on its own.

INCORRECT: Escalate the director's resistance to senior leadership right away to override the objection.

Overriding the objection through senior leadership skips addressing the concern entirely, which risks the team's trust far more than a pitch that had simply not yet spoken to what was actually worrying the director.

questions.question:
A team requires a full manual review of every single Claude output, including routine, low-stakes summaries that have consistently checked out fine for months.

What should the team do?

options.label: A
options.text: Calibrate review requirements to actual risk level, reserving full manual review for higher-stakes outputs.

options.label: B
options.text: Continue full manual review of everything, since more oversight is always better regardless of outcome risk.

options.label: C
options.text: Apply the same shortened review checklist to every output, regardless of whether it is low-stakes or high-stakes.

options.label: D
options.text: Eliminate manual review entirely, including for the outputs that actually carry meaningful risk.

questions.explanation:
CORRECT: Calibrate review requirements to actual risk level, reserving full manual review for higher-stakes outputs.

Review effort spent on low-stakes, consistently accurate summaries is not protecting against much, so shifting full review toward higher-stakes outputs puts that effort where it can actually catch a costly mistake.

Exam Guide Mapping

-
Domain 4: Workflow Integration and Solution Design (16%)

-
Objective: Integrate Claude into existing workflows to augment or redesign them

-
Objective: Leverage Claude for research, planning, and process optimization

INCORRECT: Continue full manual review of everything, since more oversight is always better regardless of outcome risk.

More oversight only helps where an output carries enough risk to justify it, and applying that logic uniformly ignores the months of consistent accuracy already observed on the routine summaries.

INCORRECT: Apply the same shortened review checklist to every output, regardless of whether it is low-stakes or high-stakes.

A single shortened checklist for every output does not distinguish low-stakes work from high-stakes work, so it risks under-checking the outputs that actually need full review while still adding a step to the ones that do not.

INCORRECT: Eliminate manual review entirely, including for the outputs that actually carry meaningful risk.

Removing review from everything discards the oversight that higher-stakes outputs genuinely need, trading one uniform mistake, reviewing everything the same way, for another.

questions.question:
A department asks an associate to wire Claude into a proprietary internal system through a custom chain of API calls and webhooks, as part of a broader multi-system integration project.

What should the associate do?

options.label: A
options.text: Escalate this request to a Claude Architect or Developer, since it requires custom software integration work.

options.label: B
options.text: Attempt to configure the API and webhook chain directly, since Claude can generate example code for the request.

options.label: C
options.text: Break the integration into smaller pieces and try building each piece using only platform-native features.

options.label: D
options.text: Decline to support this initiative in any way, since it involves technical work outside daily Claude use.

questions.explanation:
CORRECT: Escalate this request to a Claude Architect or Developer, since it requires custom software integration work.

Custom API and webhook integration across multiple systems is exactly the kind of technical build the Associate scope is meant to escalate, so routing it to a Claude Architect or Developer matches the work to the right skill set.

Exam Guide Mapping

-
Domain 4: Workflow Integration and Solution Design (16%)

-
Objective: Communicate Claude's value and limitations to stakeholders

-
Objective: Recognize limitations and escalate more complex or technical implementations

INCORRECT: Attempt to configure the API and webhook chain directly, since Claude can generate example code for the request.

Claude generating example code does not make the associate qualified to build and maintain a production integration chain, since writing sample code and implementing a working system are very different levels of responsibility.

INCORRECT: Break the integration into smaller pieces and try building each piece using only platform-native features.

Splitting the integration into smaller pieces does not change that the work requires custom development, so attempting it with platform-native features alone still leaves the associate building something outside what those features are designed to do.

INCORRECT: Decline to support this initiative in any way, since it involves technical work outside daily Claude use.

Declining to support the initiative at all goes further than the situation calls for, since escalating the technical piece to the right specialist is different from refusing to help the department move the project forward.

questions.question:
A team has created a separate, nearly identical Project for each new client engagement, and instructions and reference material have started drifting out of sync between them.

What should the team do?

options.label: A
options.text: Consolidate the near-identical Projects into a smaller number of clearly, appropriately scoped Projects instead.

options.label: B
options.text: Continue creating a new Project per engagement, since separate Projects keep each client fully isolated.

options.label: C
options.text: Copy the most current instructions into each existing Project individually to resync them, without consolidating.

options.label: D
options.text: Merge all of the team work, across every client and every function, into a single company-wide Project.

questions.explanation:
CORRECT: Consolidate the near-identical Projects into a smaller number of clearly, appropriately scoped Projects instead.

Near-identical Projects drifting out of sync is a sign there are more of them than the actual differences between clients justify, so consolidating into fewer, well-scoped Projects removes the duplication causing the drift.

Exam Guide Mapping

-
Domain 5: Configuration and Knowledge Management (12%)

-
Objective: Inform, maintain, and update Claude configurations, knowledge sources, and instructions

-
Objective: Configure Claude Projects with instructions and knowledge sources

INCORRECT: Continue creating a new Project per engagement, since separate Projects keep each client fully isolated.

Isolation between clients does not require a fully separate Project for each one when the instructions and material are this similar, and continuing the pattern only adds another Project that can drift out of sync.

INCORRECT: Copy the most current instructions into each existing Project individually to resync them, without consolidating.

Manually resyncing every existing Project keeps the same number of near-identical copies in place, so the same drift is likely to recur the next time instructions change.

INCORRECT: Merge all of the team work, across every client and every function, into a single company-wide Project.

Combining every client and function into one Project overcorrects past the point of consolidation, mixing together work that may genuinely need separate scopes for different clients or teams.

questions.question:
A team lead connects Google Drive to Claude and asks it to update the numbers directly in an existing shared project spreadsheet. Claude cannot make the requested change to the file.

What should the team lead recognize?

options.label: A
options.text: The Drive connector can search, read, and upload files, but cannot edit an existing document's content directly.

options.label: B
options.text: Assume the connector is malfunctioning and try reconnecting Google Drive to resolve it.

options.label: C
options.text: Ask Claude to attempt the same edit again with more specific instructions about which numbers to change.

options.label: D
options.text: Have someone manually download and re-upload the entire spreadsheet every time a number needs to change.

questions.explanation:
CORRECT: The Drive connector can search, read, and upload files, but cannot edit an existing document's content directly.

Reading, searching, and uploading new files are the connector's documented capabilities, and editing an existing file's content directly is not among them, so the request was outside what the connector actually does.

Exam Guide Mapping

-
Domain 5: Configuration and Knowledge Management (12%)

-
Objective: Manage uploaded knowledge and connectors (e.g., Google Drive, Gmail)

INCORRECT: Assume the connector is malfunctioning and try reconnecting Google Drive to resolve it.

Nothing about this points to a malfunction, since the connector is working as documented. Reconnecting would not add an editing capability that was never part of it.

INCORRECT: Ask Claude to attempt the same edit again with more specific instructions about which numbers to change.

More specific instructions do not add a capability the connector does not have, so retrying the same edit request would run into the same limitation regardless of how precisely it is worded.

INCORRECT: Have someone manually download and re-upload the entire spreadsheet every time a number needs to change.

Downloading and re-uploading the whole file for every small change works around the limitation, but it recreates significant manual effort each time rather than working within what the connector already supports for reading and adding files.

questions.question:
An assistant asks Claude, connected to Google Calendar, to cancel a conflicting meeting and add a new one. Claude reports both changes are complete. The assistant then manually redoes both changes in the calendar app.

What should the assistant understand?

options.label: A
options.text: The Calendar connector creates, updates, and deletes events directly when asked, unlike Gmail's draft-only behavior.

options.label: B
options.text: Assume every connector behaves like Gmail, requiring a manual step before any change actually takes effect.

options.label: C
options.text: Ask Claude to confirm a second time that the changes were made, instead of checking the calendar directly.

options.label: D
options.text: Have a colleague independently verify every future calendar change made through the connector before trusting it going forward.

questions.explanation:
CORRECT: The Calendar connector creates, updates, and deletes events directly when asked, unlike Gmail's draft-only behavior.

The Calendar connector writes changes directly once asked within a conversation, which is a different permission level than Gmail's draft-only behavior, so Claude's report that both changes were complete reflected an action that had actually already happened.

Domain 5: Configuration and Knowledge Management (12%)

-
Objective: Manage uploaded knowledge and connectors (e.g., Google Drive, Gmail)

INCORRECT: Assume every connector behaves like Gmail, requiring a manual step before any change actually takes effect.

Treating every connector as behaving like Gmail assumes a manual step that Calendar simply does not have, which is exactly what led the assistant to redo work Claude had already completed.

INCORRECT: Ask Claude to confirm a second time that the changes were made, instead of checking the calendar directly.

Asking Claude to restate that it made the changes does not confirm anything new, since checking the calendar directly is what would show whether the changes actually took effect.

INCORRECT: Have a colleague independently verify every future calendar change made through the connector before trusting it going forward.

Requiring independent verification of every future change treats a documented, direct-write capability as though it cannot be trusted, adding an ongoing check that this connector's behavior does not call for.

questions.question:
A support team's Project instructions clearly cover routine ticket responses, but say nothing about handling a message mentioning self-harm or legal threats. Responses to those messages have been inconsistent.

What should the team do?

options.label: A
options.text: Add explicit instructions for handling those specific sensitive scenarios and when to escalate them.

options.label: B
options.text: Leave the instructions as is, since the routine guidance should generalize to any type of message.

options.label: C
options.text: Tell staff to use their best judgment on sensitive messages, without writing anything into the Project's instructions.

options.label: D
options.text: Rewrite the entire set of Project instructions from scratch to address every conceivable edge case in detail.

questions.explanation:
CORRECT: Add explicit instructions for handling those specific sensitive scenarios and when to escalate them.

Routine ticket guidance was never written with these specific, higher-stakes scenarios in mind, so adding explicit handling and escalation instructions for them is what actually closes the gap causing the inconsistency.

Exam Guide Mapping

-
Domain 5: Configuration and Knowledge Management (12%)

-
Objective: Inform, maintain, and update Claude configurations, knowledge sources, and instructions

-
Objective: Configure Claude Projects with instructions and knowledge sources

INCORRECT: Leave the instructions as is, since the routine guidance should generalize to any type of message.

Guidance built for routine tickets does not automatically extend to messages this different in stakes, and assuming it does is exactly why responses to them have been inconsistent.

INCORRECT: Tell staff to use their best judgment on sensitive messages, without writing anything into the Project's instructions.

Relying on individual judgment without updating the instructions leaves the same inconsistency in place, since nothing in the Project itself changes to guide how these messages should be handled.

INCORRECT: Rewrite the entire set of Project instructions from scratch to address every conceivable edge case in detail.

Rewriting everything to cover every conceivable scenario goes well beyond the two specific gaps identified, when targeted additions for self-harm and legal threats would close them directly.

A Project's instructions still tell Claude to route escalations to a department that was reorganized six months ago, and to reference a product line the company has since discontinued.

What should the team do?

options.label: A
options.text: Update the Project's instructions to reflect the current department structure and product lineup.

options.label: B
options.text: Leave the instructions unchanged, since the underlying guidance about how to handle escalations still applies.

options.label: C
options.text: Ask Claude to note in each response that some details might be outdated, without changing the instructions.

options.label: D
options.text: Delete all references to departments and products from the instructions so nothing can go stale again.

questions.explanation:
CORRECT: Update the Project's instructions to reflect the current department structure and product lineup.

The escalation logic itself may still be sound, but the specific department and product names it points to are six months out of date, so updating those specifics is what keeps the instructions accurate.

questions.question:
A Project's knowledge base has two current-looking documents stating conflicting versions of the same expense policy, and a file labeled draft is being cited as if it were final.

Which two actions should the team take?

options.label: A
options.text: Determine which expense policy document is accurate and remove or correct the one that conflicts with it.

options.label: B
options.text: Relabel or remove the file marked draft so it is no longer treated as an authoritative source.

options.label: C
options.text: Leave both conflicting documents in place, since Claude can be asked each time which one to use.

options.label: D
options.text: Add a third summary document that combines both versions of the policy without resolving which one is correct.

options.label: E
options.text: Rename the draft file to make it sound more official, without changing its actual approval status.

questions.explanation:
CORRECT: Determine which expense policy document is accurate and remove or correct the one that conflicts with it.

Two documents stating conflicting versions of the same policy cannot both be right, so determining which one is accurate and correcting or removing the other resolves the actual contradiction in the knowledge base.

CORRECT: Relabel or remove the file marked draft so it is no longer treated as an authoritative source.

A file still labeled draft being cited as final is a separate problem from the conflicting policy versions, and addressing its status directly stops it from being treated as authoritative until it actually is.

Exam Guide Mapping

-
Domain 5: Configuration and Knowledge Management (12%)

-
Objective: Manage uploaded knowledge and connectors (e.g., Google Drive, Gmail)

INCORRECT: Leave both conflicting documents in place, since Claude can be asked each time which one to use.

Asking each time which document to use does not resolve which version is actually correct, and it leaves the contradiction sitting in the knowledge base for the next person to run into.

INCORRECT: Add a third summary document that combines both versions of the policy without resolving which one is correct.

Combining both versions into a new document still leaves the underlying conflict unresolved, and it adds a third file that inherits the same uncertainty about which policy is accurate.

INCORRECT: Rename the draft file to make it sound more official, without changing its actual approval status.

A more official-sounding name does not change whether the file has actually been approved, so the draft would still be functioning as an authoritative source under a different label.

questions.question:
A researcher plans to share Claude-assisted session summaries that remove names, but the participant pool is small enough that job title and department alone could identify someone.

What should the researcher do before proceeding?

options.label: A
options.text: Add a further safeguard, such as generalizing job title and department, before sharing the summaries.

options.label: B
options.text: Proceed as planned, since removing names already satisfies standard anonymization practice.

options.label: C
options.text: Add a disclaimer to the summaries noting that some details could theoretically identify a participant.

options.label: D
options.text: Cancel the summary-sharing plan entirely, since any risk of re-identification makes the use inappropriate.

questions.explanation:
CORRECT: Add a further safeguard, such as generalizing job title and department, before sharing the summaries.

Removing names does not address the specific risk here, since job title and department alone can still narrow a small pool down to one person, so generalizing those fields closes the actual gap before sharing.

Exam Guide Mapping

-
Domain 6: Governance, Risk, and Responsible Use (15%)

-
Objective: Apply data sensitivity, regulatory, and privacy considerations

INCORRECT: Proceed as planned, since removing names already satisfies standard anonymization practice.

Standard anonymization practice assumes removing names is enough, but a small enough pool makes other fields just as identifying, which is exactly the risk this specific case presents.

INCORRECT: Add a disclaimer to the summaries noting that some details could theoretically identify a participant.

A disclaimer acknowledging the risk does not reduce it, since the identifying combination of job title and department would still be sitting in the shared summaries.

INCORRECT: Cancel the summary-sharing plan entirely, since any risk of re-identification makes the use inappropriate.

Canceling the plan entirely skips a safeguard that would have made the sharing appropriate, when generalizing the specific identifying fields would have resolved the risk without abandoning the project.

An analyst uploads employee data with no names attached, just job title, location, and start date, to a small ten-person team's Claude project for trend analysis.

What should the analyst recognize?

options.label: A
options.text: That combination of job title, location, and start date could still re-identify someone on this small a team.

options.label: B
options.text: That the data is already anonymized, since no names or direct identifiers are included in it.

options.label: C
options.text: That only the start date needs to be removed, since job title and location are common information.

options.label: D
options.text: That no employee data of any kind can ever be analyzed with Claude, regardless of team size or fields involved.

questions.explanation:
CORRECT: That combination of job title, location, and start date could still re-identify someone on this small a team.

On a team of only ten people, job title, location, and start date together can narrow the data down to one specific person even without a name attached, which is what makes this combination a real identifier here.

"Your organization's designated Primary Owner manages your Work account and all associated data... The use of your Claude for Work plan account is governed by the agreement between Anthropic and your organization."

-
Domain 6: Governance, Risk, and Responsible Use (15%)

-
Objective: Apply data sensitivity, regulatory, and privacy considerations

INCORRECT: That the data is already anonymized, since no names or direct identifiers are included in it.

The absence of a name field does not mean the data is anonymized, since other fields can combine to identify someone just as directly, especially on a team this small.

INCORRECT: That only the start date needs to be removed, since job title and location are common information.

Removing only the start date still leaves job title and location, which together could narrow the field enough on a ten-person team, so the re-identification risk would likely remain.

INCORRECT: That no employee data of any kind can ever be analyzed with Claude, regardless of team size or fields involved.

A blanket rule against ever analyzing employee data ignores that the actual risk here comes from this specific combination of fields on this small a team, not from employee data as a category.

questions.question:
An applicant asks Claude to draft a cover letter using their full resume, which includes a home address and date of birth that the cover letter does not need.

What should the applicant do?

options.label: A
options.text: Remove the home address and date of birth before sharing the resume, since the cover letter does not need them.

options.label: B
options.text: Share the full resume as is, since a cover letter task is low-risk and personal information is common on resumes.

options.label: C
options.text: Ask Claude not to mention the home address or date of birth in the letter, while still sharing the full resume.

options.label: D
options.text: Remove all personal information from the resume, including the applicant's name and job history, before sharing it.

questions.explanation:
CORRECT: Remove the home address and date of birth before sharing the resume, since the cover letter does not need them.

A cover letter draws on job history and skills, not a home address or date of birth, so removing those two fields before sharing keeps only what the task actually requires.

Exam Guide Mapping

-
Domain 6: Governance, Risk, and Responsible Use (15%)

-
Objective: Apply data sensitivity, regulatory, and privacy considerations

INCORRECT: Share the full resume as is, since a cover letter task is low-risk and personal information is common on resumes.

Personal information being common on resumes does not mean every field on it is needed for this specific task, and sharing fields the task has no use for adds unnecessary exposure.

INCORRECT: Ask Claude not to mention the home address or date of birth in the letter, while still sharing the full resume.

Asking Claude not to mention certain fields still means the full resume, address and birthdate included, was shared in the first place, so the unnecessary exposure already happened.

INCORRECT: Remove all personal information from the resume, including the applicant's name and job history, before sharing it.

Name and job history are exactly what a cover letter needs to reference, so removing them along with the unrelated fields strips out information the task actually depends on.

questions.question:
An employee moves from a personal Claude account to a company-provided Team plan account and prepares to manually turn off the same training toggle they used to check personally.

What should the employee do instead?

options.label: A
options.text: Recognize that Team and Enterprise accounts do not train on conversation data by default, unlike personal consumer accounts.

options.label: B
options.text: Toggle off training the same way as on the personal account, since the setting should work identically across plans.

options.label: C
options.text: Ask the administrator to enable a training opt-out toggle specifically for this employee's account.

options.label: D
options.text: Avoid using the Team account for any work conversations until an admin confirms the training policy in writing.

questions.explanation:
CORRECT: Recognize that Team and Enterprise accounts do not train on conversation data by default, unlike personal consumer accounts.

Team and Enterprise accounts operate under commercial terms that already exclude training on conversation data by default, so the personal-account toggle the employee is used to checking does not carry over the same way.

Exam Guide Mapping

-
Domain 6: Governance, Risk, and Responsible Use (15%)

-
Objective: Apply data sensitivity, regulatory, and privacy considerations

INCORRECT: Toggle off training the same way as on the personal account, since the setting should work identically across plans.

Assuming the same toggle applies equally across account types is the actual misunderstanding here, since Team and Enterprise plans already default to not training, unlike the personal account the employee is used to.

INCORRECT: Ask the administrator to enable a training opt-out toggle specifically for this employee's account.

Requesting a toggle to be enabled treats the Team plan as if it needs the same opt-out the personal account required, when the default commercial policy already covers that without any per-employee setting.

INCORRECT: Avoid using the Team account for any work conversations until an admin confirms the training policy in writing.

Avoiding work use until written confirmation adds caution beyond what the already-documented default policy calls for, since the training exclusion for Team and Enterprise accounts is already established, not something still in question."

questions.question:
A team's policy requires a supervisor to review every Claude-drafted client email before it is sent, but the supervisor has been approving them within seconds without reading the content.

What should the team do?

options.label: A
options.text: Ensure the review is substantive, confirming the supervisor is actually reading each email before approving it.

options.label: B
options.text: Consider the policy satisfied, since a supervisor is technically reviewing and approving every email.

options.label: C
options.text: Have the supervisor approve emails slightly slower, without changing what they are actually checking for.

options.label: D
options.text: Remove the supervisor review requirement entirely, since it is not preventing any actual mistakes right now.

questions.explanation:
CORRECT: Ensure the review is substantive, confirming the supervisor is actually reading each email before approving it.

A policy that requires review is meant to catch actual problems before an email goes out, and approvals happening within seconds without reading suggest that is not happening, so making the review substantive restores what the policy was for.

Exam Guide Mapping

-
Domain 6: Governance, Risk, and Responsible Use (15%)

-
Objective: Follow organizational AI policies and governance standards

INCORRECT: Consider the policy satisfied, since a supervisor is technically reviewing and approving every email.

A supervisor clicking approve satisfies the letter of the policy but not its purpose, since nothing about speed alone confirms the content was actually checked.

INCORRECT: Have the supervisor approve emails slightly slower, without changing what they are actually checking for.

Slowing down the approval without changing what is being checked does not confirm the supervisor is reading the content, so the same rubber-stamping could continue at a slightly slower pace.

INCORRECT: Remove the supervisor review requirement entirely, since it is not preventing any actual mistakes right now.

Removing the requirement assumes it was never useful, when the actual problem is that it is not being followed in substance, not that a genuine review would fail to catch anything.

questions.question:
A marketing team is unsure whether AI-content disclosure rules apply to social posts Claude drafted and a human lightly edited before publishing, given how quickly related state and federal rules are changing.

What should the team do?

options.label: A
options.text: Escalate the specific question to compliance or legal for a definitive answer before publishing.

options.label: B
options.text: Assume the rules do not apply, since a human reviewed and edited the post before it went out.

options.label: C
options.text: Add a general AI-assistance disclaimer to every post, without confirming whether the specific rules actually require it.

options.label: D
options.text: Stop using Claude for any marketing content until every advertising regulation in every jurisdiction has been reviewed.

questions.explanation:
CORRECT: Escalate the specific question to compliance or legal for a definitive answer before publishing.

Whether light human editing changes a post's disclosure obligations is exactly the kind of unsettled, jurisdiction-specific question that compliance or legal is positioned to answer, so escalating it is what resolves the actual uncertainty.

Exam Guide Mapping

-
Domain 6: Governance, Risk, and Responsible Use (15%)

-
Objective: Follow organizational AI policies and governance standards

INCORRECT: Assume the rules do not apply, since a human reviewed and edited the post before it went out.

Human editing does not automatically resolve whether disclosure is required, since several current rules turn on how much of the content was AI-generated in the first place, not just whether a human touched it afterward.

INCORRECT: Add a general AI-assistance disclaimer to every post, without confirming whether the specific rules actually require it.

A blanket disclaimer added without confirming the actual requirement might satisfy some rules and miss others, so it does not resolve the specific uncertainty the team started with.

INCORRECT: Stop using Claude for any marketing content until every advertising regulation in every jurisdiction has been reviewed.

Halting all Claude-assisted marketing work until every jurisdiction's rules are reviewed goes far beyond answering the one specific question this team actually has.

questions.question:
A resume-screening tool assisted by Claude shows a pattern of lower callback rates tied to a specific undergraduate institution rather than any stated qualification.

Which two actions should the team take?

options.label: A
options.text: Audit whether the institution-based callback pattern reflects legitimate criteria or an unlawful discriminatory proxy.

options.label: B
options.text: Route the audit findings to compliance or a fairness reviewer before continuing to use the tool.

options.label: C
options.text: Continue using the screening tool as is, since institution name was never an explicit input the team specified.

options.label: D
options.text: Remove the institution field from resumes going forward, without investigating whether the pattern reflects a deeper issue.

options.label: E
options.text: Suspend all resume screening company-wide, including manual review, until a full audit of every hiring process is complete.

questions.explanation:
CORRECT: Audit whether the institution-based callback pattern reflects legitimate criteria or an unlawful discriminatory proxy.

A callback pattern tied to one institution rather than any stated qualification is exactly the kind of proxy discrimination risk that needs investigating, so auditing whether it reflects legitimate criteria is the first step toward understanding it.

CORRECT: Route the audit findings to compliance or a fairness reviewer before continuing to use the tool.

A pattern like this carries real legal and fairness exposure, so routing the audit findings to compliance or a fairness reviewer before continuing to use the tool is what turns the finding into an actual decision.

Exam Guide Mapping

-
Domain 6: Governance, Risk, and Responsible Use (15%)

-
Objective: Identify and mitigate algorithmic bias, proxy discrimination, and fairness issues in model deployments

INCORRECT: Continue using the screening tool as is, since institution name was never an explicit input the team specified.

Institution name never being an explicit input does not mean it is not functioning as a proxy through other data the tool does use, so continuing as is leaves the pattern unexamined.

INCORRECT: Remove the institution field from resumes going forward, without investigating whether the pattern reflects a deeper issue.

Removing the field without investigating leaves open whether the same pattern is happening through some other proxy in the data, since the underlying cause was never actually identified.

INCORRECT: Suspend all resume screening company-wide, including manual review, until a full audit of every hiring process is complete.

Suspending all screening, including manual review, addresses a much broader scope than the one pattern actually identified, when a targeted audit of this tool would address the specific finding directly.

questions.question:
A company's customer chatbot discloses it is AI-powered only through a small line of text in the website's footer, similar to disclosures regulators have flagged as failing a clear and conspicuous standard.

What should the company do?

options.label: A
options.text: Make the AI disclosure clear and conspicuous within the chat interaction itself, not just present in the footer.

options.label: B
options.text: Consider the requirement already met, since a disclosure of this kind technically exists somewhere on the company website.

options.label: C
options.text: Make the footer text slightly larger, while keeping the disclosure in the same location.

options.label: D
options.text: Require customers to sign a formal AI-usage waiver before every single chat interaction.

questions.explanation:
CORRECT: Make the AI disclosure clear and conspicuous within the chat interaction itself, not just present in the footer.

Where it matters: A disclosure buried in the footer exists, but customers won't see it before they start typing. "Clear and conspicuous" means visible at the point of interaction, not just present somewhere on the page.

Fix: Put the AI disclosure directly in the chat interface itself, ideally as the first thing a customer sees when the conversation opens.

Watch out for: surface fixes like bigger footer text. Same location, same problem, regardless of font size.

Exam Guide Mapping

-
Domain 6: Governance, Risk, and Responsible Use (15%)

-
Objective: Apply data sensitivity, regulatory, and privacy considerations

"For external-facing products, disclose to your users that they are interacting with an AI system." Resource

INCORRECT: Consider the requirement already met, since a disclosure of this kind technically exists somewhere on the company website.

Existing somewhere on the website is not the same as being noticeable at the moment a customer starts the interaction, which is the actual standard the current placement fails to meet.

INCORRECT: Make the footer text slightly larger, while keeping the disclosure in the same location.

A larger footer is still a footer, so the disclosure remains in a spot customers are unlikely to see before engaging with the chatbot, leaving the core visibility problem unresolved.

INCORRECT: Require customers to sign a formal AI-usage waiver before every single chat interaction.

A signed waiver goes well beyond what a clear, conspicuous disclosure requires, adding a formal step the situation does not call for to fix what is fundamentally a visibility problem.

questions.question:
An analyst asks Claude to compare them after discussing three different vendors earlier in the conversation, and Claude compares two vendors the analyst did not actually mean.

What should the analyst do?

options.label: A
options.text: Identify the ambiguous reference as the cause and restate exactly which two vendors should be compared.

options.label: B
options.text: Accept the comparison as useful context, since it still covers two of the three vendors discussed.

options.label: C
options.text: Ask Claude to add the third vendor to the same comparison, without clarifying which two were originally intended.

options.label: D
options.text: Ask Claude to compare every possible pair among the three vendors, so the intended comparison is covered somewhere in the output.

questions.explanation:
CORRECT: Identify the ambiguous reference as the cause and restate exactly which two vendors should be compared.

The word them had three possible vendors to point back to, and Claude picked a reasonable but incorrect pair because nothing in the request narrowed it down. Naming the ambiguous reference as the actual cause, then spelling out exactly which two vendors belong in the comparison, fixes the specific thing that went wrong rather than just reacting to the output.

"Be clear and direct. Claude responds well to clear, explicit instructions. Being specific about your desired output can help enhance results... The more precisely you explain what you want, the better the result." Resource

Domain 7: Troubleshooting and Optimization (10%)

-
Objective: Identify, diagnose, and resolve issues with underperforming prompts or poor outputs

-
Objective: Adjust approach based on feedback and results

INCORRECT: Accept the comparison as useful context, since it still covers two of the three vendors discussed.

Covering two of the three vendors might look useful at a glance, but if they are not the two the analyst actually needed compared, the analysis answers a different question than the one that was asked, however coincidentally relevant it seems.

INCORRECT: Ask Claude to add the third vendor to the same comparison, without clarifying which two were originally intended.

Adding the third vendor on top of an already-wrong pairing does not tell Claude which two vendors the analyst originally meant to compare, so the comparison could easily still center on the wrong pair with an extra vendor tacked on.

INCORRECT: Ask Claude to compare every possible pair among the three vendors, so the intended comparison is covered somewhere in the output.

Generating every possible pairing produces three separate comparisons and leaves the analyst to figure out which one was actually intended, which trades one ambiguity for the extra work of sorting through redundant output to find it.

questions.question:
A summary of a 40-page strategy report covers the main findings accurately and at the right depth, but consistently leaves out the recommended next steps the executive team needs.

What should the requester do?

options.label: A
options.text: Ask specifically for the recommended next steps to be included in the summary.

options.label: B
options.text: Consider the summary complete, since the main findings are accurate and appropriately detailed.

options.label: C
options.text: Ask for a longer summary overall, without specifying that next steps need to be included.

options.label: D
options.text: Request the entire 40-page report be summarized again from a completely different starting prompt.

questions.explanation:
CORRECT: Ask specifically for the recommended next steps to be included in the summary.

The findings being accurate and well-scoped does not mean the summary covers everything the executive team actually needs from it, and the missing piece here is specific: the recommended next steps. Naming that gap directly is what gets it included, rather than hoping a general revision happens to catch it.

Exam Guide Mapping

-
Domain 7: Troubleshooting and Optimization (10%)

-
Objective: Identify, diagnose, and resolve issues with underperforming prompts or poor outputs

-
Objective: Adjust approach based on feedback and results

INCORRECT: Consider the summary complete, since the main findings are accurate and appropriately detailed.

A summary can get the findings exactly right and still miss the part of the report the audience most needs to act on, so accuracy and completeness are not the same thing here, and treating the summary as finished leaves that gap unaddressed.

INCORRECT: Ask for a longer summary overall, without specifying that next steps need to be included.

Asking for more length increases the chance the next steps might appear somewhere in the expanded text, but it does not guarantee it, since a longer summary can still elaborate on findings without ever touching recommendations if that section was never specifically requested.

INCORRECT: Request the entire 40-page report be summarized again from a completely different starting prompt.

Starting over with a different prompt discards a summary that was already accurate and well-scoped in every other respect, when the actual fix only required asking for the one specific section that was missing, not rebuilding the whole thing.

questions.question:
A standing formatting requirement was stated once early in a long project conversation, but responses have stopped following it as the thread has grown.

Which two actions should the person take?

options.label: A
options.text: Restate the requirement now so it is back in front of Claude for the current and next responses.

options.label: B
options.text: Move the requirement into a Project's persistent instructions so it does not need restating in future long threads.

options.label: C
options.text: Assume the requirement still applies automatically, since it was already stated once earlier in the thread.

options.label: D
options.text: Ask Claude to review the entire conversation history to find where the requirement was originally stated.

options.label: E
options.text: Start an entirely new conversation for every single message to keep the requirement fresh each time.

questions.explanation:
CORRECT: Restate the requirement now so it is back in front of Claude for the current and next responses.

A requirement stated once, several messages back, is competing with everything said since then for the model's attention, so restating it now puts it back in view for the response that comes next, immediately closing the gap the person actually noticed.

CORRECT: Move the requirement into a Project's persistent instructions so it does not need restating in future long threads.

Restating it now fixes the current thread, but the same decay would happen again in the next long conversation, so moving the requirement into a Project's persistent instructions gives it a standing place that does not depend on staying near the top of any one thread.

Exam Guide Mapping

-
Domain 7: Troubleshooting and Optimization (10%)

-
Objective: Identify, diagnose, and resolve issues with underperforming prompts or poor outputs

-
Objective: Adjust approach based on feedback and results

INCORRECT: Assume the requirement still applies automatically, since it was already stated once earlier in the thread.

The requirement being stated once earlier does not mean it is still shaping responses now, and the inconsistency the person already noticed is direct evidence that it is not, so assuming it still applies ignores the very symptom that prompted the question.

INCORRECT: Ask Claude to review the entire conversation history to find where the requirement was originally stated.

Having Claude locate where the requirement was originally stated confirms it exists somewhere in the history, but it does not restore the requirement's influence on the next response, which is what actually needs to happen.

INCORRECT: Start an entirely new conversation for every single message to keep the requirement fresh each time.

Restarting for every single message eliminates the very continuity a long project conversation is meant to provide, trading decay in one thread for the loss of all accumulated context in every message going forward.

questions.question:
The same prompt produces noticeably different structure and tone each time it is run, with no consistent gap in content, just unpredictable formatting from one response to the next.

What should the person do?

options.label: A
options.text: Tighten the prompt's specificity about structure and tone to reduce the run-to-run variance.

options.label: B
options.text: Treat the variation as normal, since each individual response reads fine on its own.

options.label: C
options.text: Manually reformat each response after the fact to match the previous one's structure.

options.label: D
options.text: Submit the same prompt many additional times and combine whichever elements repeat most often across all the outputs.

questions.explanation:
CORRECT: Tighten the prompt's specificity about structure and tone to reduce the run-to-run variance.

When a prompt leaves structure and tone open to interpretation, Claude has to make a fresh judgment call each time, which is exactly why the same request produces different formatting from one run to the next. Specifying the structure and tone directly closes that gap and gives every run the same target to follow.

Exam Guide Mapping

-
Domain 7: Troubleshooting and Optimization (10%)

-
Objective: Identify, diagnose, and resolve issues with underperforming prompts or poor outputs

-
Objective: Adjust approach based on feedback and results

INCORRECT: Treat the variation as normal, since each individual response reads fine on its own.

Each response reading fine in isolation does not address the actual problem, which is that the format is not staying consistent across runs, something a person relying on a predictable structure for repeated use would still notice and be affected by.

INCORRECT: Manually reformat each response after the fact to match the previous one's structure.

Fixing up each response after it comes back treats every single run as its own one-off correction, so the same inconsistency would need to be manually patched again the next time the prompt is used, since nothing about the prompt itself changed.

INCORRECT: Submit the same prompt many additional times and combine whichever elements repeat most often across all the outputs.

Running the prompt many extra times and stitching together whichever elements show up most often turns a formatting problem into a much bigger manual assembly task, without ever addressing why the outputs varied in the first place.

questions.question:
A high-stakes competitive analysis is run at the default effort level, and the resulting analysis reads shallow, missing considerations a more thorough pass would likely catch.

What should the analyst do?

options.label: A
options.text: Raise the effort level for this analysis, since higher effort suits complex, high-stakes reasoning.

options.label: B
options.text: Accept the analysis as sufficient, since the default effort level is the recommended setting for most tasks.

options.label: C
options.text: Ask Claude to double check its own analysis at the same effort level, without changing the setting.

options.label: D
options.text: Set every future task, regardless of complexity, to the maximum effort level from now on.

questions.explanation:
CORRECT: Raise the effort level for this analysis, since higher effort suits complex, high-stakes reasoning.

The default effort level is calibrated for typical, everyday requests, and this analysis is neither typical nor low-stakes, so raising the effort level gives Claude the room to reason more thoroughly through the considerations a shallow pass would otherwise miss.

Exam Guide Mapping

-
Domain 7: Troubleshooting and Optimization (10%)

-
Objective: Identify, diagnose, and resolve issues with underperforming prompts or poor outputs

INCORRECT: Accept the analysis as sufficient, since the default effort level is the recommended setting for most tasks.

Default being the right setting for most tasks does not make it the right setting for this one, since a high-stakes competitive analysis is exactly the kind of complex reasoning task that benefits from more than the default level of effort.

INCORRECT: Ask Claude to double check its own analysis at the same effort level, without changing the setting.

Reviewing the same analysis again at the same effort level asks Claude to repeat the same shallow pass rather than actually reasoning more deeply, so the missing considerations would likely still go uncaught the second time around.

INCORRECT: Set every future task, regardless of complexity, to the maximum effort level from now on.

Maxing out effort for every future task regardless of complexity spends far more time and cost than most routine work actually needs, overcorrecting for this one high-stakes case by applying it everywhere going forward.

questions.question:
Claude's output already matches the exact format the team's CRM needs, but staff continue manually reformatting every response before entering it, a habit left over from when the format used to be wrong.

What should the team do?

options.label: A
options.text: Eliminate the manual reformatting step, since the output already satisfies the format the CRM needs.

options.label: B
options.text: Keep the manual reformatting step in place indefinitely, since double-checking the format never really hurts.

options.label: C
options.text: Simplify the manual reformatting process to make it faster, without confirming it is still necessary.

options.label: D
options.text: Have staff stop checking the CRM entries altogether after they are entered, to save even more time.

questions.explanation:
CORRECT: Eliminate the manual reformatting step, since the output already satisfies the format the CRM needs.

The formatting problem this habit was built to catch no longer exists, so continuing to reformat every response manually spends effort correcting an issue that has already been resolved at the source, and removing that redundant step is what actually reflects the current, fixed state of the output.

Exam Guide Mapping

-
Domain 7: Troubleshooting and Optimization (10%)

-
Objective: Optimize workflows for efficiency and effectiveness

-
Objective: Adjust approach based on feedback and results

INCORRECT: Keep the manual reformatting step in place indefinitely, since double-checking the format never really hurts.

A check that never hurts still costs time every single time it runs, and if the thing it is checking for is no longer happening, that ongoing cost is not buying the team anything in return.

INCORRECT: Simplify the manual reformatting process to make it faster, without confirming it is still necessary.

Making the manual step faster still keeps an entire process running that the team has not actually confirmed is still needed, so the redundant effort continues, just with slightly less time spent on it each time.

INCORRECT: Have staff stop checking the CRM entries altogether after they are entered, to save even more time.

Removing the CRM entry check entirely goes well beyond the specific redundancy identified, since verifying that data landed correctly in the CRM is a different safeguard from reformatting output that no longer needs it.

questions.question:
A project coordinator gives Claude a large, multi-part request to prepare a program review, unsure how the pieces should fit together. Each attempt returns a rushed, surface-level response that blends everything at once.

What should the coordinator do?

options.label: A
options.text: Ask Claude to first break the request into an ordered task list, then work through those tasks one at a time.

options.label: B
options.text: Resend the same combined request and ask Claude to add more detail, assuming a longer single answer will cover every part well.

options.label: C
options.text: Accept the blended response, since it does touch on every part of the request in a single pass.

options.label: D
options.text: Write every section of the program review manually, without using Claude for any part of the multi-part request.

questions.explanation:
CORRECT: Ask Claude to first break the request into an ordered task list, then work through those tasks one at a time.

The coordinator is unsure how the pieces fit together, and every reply blends everything at once. When a request is large and its structure is not obvious, the most reliable move is to let Claude map it out first. Ask for an ordered list of the sub-tasks, confirm the sequence makes sense, then tackle them one by one. Each task gets full attention instead of a hurried single pass, and you get a plan you can check before any real work starts.

Exam Guide Mapping

-
Domain 1: Prompting and Task Execution (14%)

-
Objective: Apply task decomposition techniques to structure complex requests

INCORRECT: Resend the same combined request and ask Claude to add more detail, assuming a longer single answer will cover every part well.

Adding length does not fix a structural problem. A single expanded answer still makes every part compete for attention in one pass, so the depth stays uneven. This approach would only make sense if the request were simple enough for one response; here, splitting it into ordered steps is what actually restores depth.

INCORRECT: Accept the blended response, since it does touch on every part of the request in a single pass.

Touching on every part is not the same as handling each one well. The scenario already describes the combined answer as rushed and surface-level, so accepting it just locks in a shallow result. Broad coverage in a single pass is a weak signal of quality, not evidence of it.

INCORRECT: Write every section of the program review manually, without using Claude for any part of the multi-part request.

Doing it all by hand throws away a task Claude handles well once the work is sequenced. The problem was never that Claude cannot help, only that the full request arrived at once. Decomposing it keeps Claude useful, so the manual rewrite is unnecessary effort.

questions.question:
An operations analyst gives Claude a detailed request to summarize a vendor evaluation, listing every data point to include, but never states the summary will guide an executive approval decision. The result is thorough but unfocused.

What should the analyst do?

options.label: A
options.text: Tell Claude the summary is for an executive approval decision and ask it to lead with the factors that decision depends on.

options.label: B
options.text: Forward the thorough summary to the executives as is, since it already contains every data point the analyst originally asked to include.

options.label: C
options.text: Ask Claude to shorten the same summary so it reads faster, without saying what decision it needs to support.

options.label: D
options.text: Cut most of the vendor data and send only a two-line note, dropping detail the executives may still need.

questions.explanation:
CORRECT: Tell Claude the summary is for an executive approval decision and ask it to lead with the factors that decision depends on.

The request spells out every data point but never says the summary will guide an executive approval decision, so Claude cannot tell which details matter most. Supplying that purpose is the missing piece. Once Claude knows the output supports a specific decision and who will read it, it can lead with the factors that decision turns on and trim the rest. Naming the goal and the audience, not just the content to include, is what turns a thorough dump into a summary people can act on.

-
Domain 1: Prompting and Task Execution (14%)

-
Objective: Iterate prompts to improve output quality

INCORRECT: Forward the thorough summary to the executives as is, since it already contains every data point the analyst originally asked to include.

Sending it unchanged keeps the same problem: it treats completeness as the goal when the executives need focus. Covering every requested data point is a weak signal of usefulness, not proof of it. The summary reads as thorough but unfocused precisely because no decision was named to organize it around.

INCORRECT: Ask Claude to shorten the same summary so it reads faster, without saying what decision it needs to support.

Shortening makes the summary quicker to read but still never tells Claude what it is for, so it may trim the wrong parts. This would be the right move if length alone were the issue. Here the real gap is the missing purpose, which cutting words never supplies.

INCORRECT: Cut most of the vendor data and send only a two-line note, dropping detail the executives may still need.

Reducing the summary to two lines swings too far, discarding detail the executives may actually need to decide. The task was never to strip the content but to focus it around the decision. Aggressively deleting data replaces one mismatch with another instead of solving it.

questions.question:
A communications associate asks Claude to turn a long email announcement into a push notification, but the draft comes back nearly as long, with email-style greetings and paragraphs that will not fit the notification format.

What should the associate do?

options.label: A
options.text: Give Claude the notification's length limit and format conventions, then ask for a version written specifically for that channel.

options.label: B
options.text: Ask Claude to delete the greeting from the same email draft, leaving the rest of the long paragraphs unchanged.

options.label: C
options.text: Abandon the push notification channel entirely and send only the original long email to everyone instead.

options.label: D
options.text: Use the long email draft in the notification as is, since it already contains the complete and accurate announcement text.

questions.explanation:
CORRECT: Give Claude the notification's length limit and format conventions, then ask for a version written specifically for that channel.

The problem is the channel, not the wording: a push notification has a tight length limit and its own format, and Claude was told neither. Handing over the email is not enough, because Claude cannot match conventions it has never been given. Once the associate supplies the character limit and the notification's format, Claude can rewrite the message to fit that medium rather than trimming an email built for a different one. Match the output to where it will appear, and the mismatch disappears.

Exam Guide Mapping

-
Domain 1: Prompting and Task Execution (14%)

-
Objective: Adapt prompting strategies based on task type (analysis, research, drafting, brainstorming)

INCORRECT: Ask Claude to delete the greeting from the same email draft, leaving the rest of the long paragraphs unchanged.

Removing only the greeting trims one small piece but leaves long paragraphs that still will not fit a notification. This would be the right fix if the greeting were the only thing wrong. The real issue is that the whole message follows email conventions, so the channel's limits have to drive the rewrite.

INCORRECT: Abandon the push notification channel entirely and send only the original long email to everyone instead.

Dropping the notification channel throws out a useful way to reach people just because the first draft did not fit it. Nothing about the announcement makes it unsuited to notifications; it simply was not written for the format yet. Giving up avoids the task rather than adapting the message.

INCORRECT: Use the long email draft in the notification as is, since it already contains the complete and accurate announcement text.

Pushing the full email into a notification unchanged ignores the format limit the scenario describes. That it reads complete and accurate is beside the point, since it still will not display properly. Accurate content in the wrong shape for the channel is still unusable to the reader.

questions.question:
A project manager asks Claude to recommend a software tool, naming the criteria and which one matters most, and Claude recommends a strong option. The manager then notices its price exceeds the team's fixed budget cap.

What should the manager do?

options.label: A
options.text: Tell Claude the budget cap is a firm limit, then ask for recommendations only from options under it.

options.label: B
options.text: Go with Claude's recommended tool anyway, since it scored best on the criteria the manager said mattered most.

options.label: C
options.text: Drop the criteria-based comparison and just pick the cheapest tool available, regardless of how it performs.

options.label: D
options.text: Ask Claude to justify why the tool is worth exceeding the budget, without making the cap a firm limit.

questions.explanation:
CORRECT: Tell Claude the budget cap is a firm limit, then ask for recommendations only from options under it.

Naming the criteria and their priority was not enough, because a budget cap is a different kind of limit: it disqualifies an option outright, no matter how well it scores everywhere else. Claude recommended a strong tool only because nothing told it the price was non-negotiable. The fix is to state the cap as a firm boundary, so Claude weighs only options that already fit within it. Weighted preferences rank the choices; a hard constraint removes the ones that break a rule the team cannot bend.

Exam Guide Mapping

-
Domain 1: Prompting and Task Execution (14%)

-
Objective: Iterate prompts to improve output quality

INCORRECT: Go with Claude's recommended tool anyway, since it scored best on the criteria the manager said mattered most.

Choosing the tool because it scored best ignores the one limit that actually rules it out. A high score on the stated criteria is a weak reason to overspend a budget the team has fixed. The recommendation looked strong only because Claude was never told the cap could not be crossed.

INCORRECT: Drop the criteria-based comparison and just pick the cheapest tool available, regardless of how it performs.

Defaulting to the cheapest tool throws out the criteria and priorities the manager already worked out. The goal is the best option that fits the budget, not the lowest price at any quality. Swapping a careful comparison for a price-only pick trades one bad outcome for another.

INCORRECT: Ask Claude to justify why the tool is worth exceeding the budget, without making the cap a firm limit.

Asking Claude to justify the overage engages the price but still treats the budget as flexible. This would be the right approach if the cap were a soft target the team could exceed with good reason. Since the scenario calls it a fixed cap, no justification changes the fact that the option is out of bounds.

questions.question:
A business analyst asks Claude for a broad overview of remote work trends and gets a sprawling answer covering culture, real estate, and global labor law. The analyst only needs to decide whether to keep two office floors.

What should the analyst do?

options.label: A
options.text: Narrow the question to the specific decision at hand: whether to keep or cut the two office floors.

options.label: B
options.text: Ask Claude to shorten the same broad overview into a summary, without tying it to the office-floor decision.

options.label: C
options.text: Keep the sprawling overview as useful background, since it does cover the major dimensions of remote work in depth.

options.label: D
options.text: Skip Claude's input entirely and decide about the two floors based only on gut feel.

questions.explanation:
CORRECT: Narrow the question to the specific decision at hand: whether to keep or cut the two office floors.

The analyst does not need everything about remote work, only what bears on one decision: whether to keep or cut two office floors. A broad question invites a broad answer, so the fix is to scope the request to that decision. Ask Claude specifically how the two floors factor into space needs, cost, and remote work patterns. Tying the question to the decision it must support collapses the sprawl into the slice that actually matters, giving the analyst something they can act on right away.

Exam Guide Mapping

-
Domain 1: Prompting and Task Execution (14%)

-
Objective: Create effective prompts for business and technical tasks

INCORRECT: Ask Claude to shorten the same broad overview into a summary, without tying it to the office-floor decision.

Shortening the overview makes it quicker to read but keeps the same sprawling topics, none tied to the floor decision. This would be the right move if the answer were on target and merely too long. Here the content aims at the wrong question, so trimming words never focuses it.

INCORRECT: Keep the sprawling overview as useful background, since it does cover the major dimensions of remote work in depth.

Keeping the sprawling overview treats broad coverage as the goal when the analyst needs a focused answer to one question. That it covers many dimensions in depth is a weak reason to accept it. The material is thorough but pointed at everything except the decision at hand.

INCORRECT: Skip Claude's input entirely and decide about the two floors based only on gut feel.

Deciding on gut feel alone discards the useful analysis Claude can provide once the question is scoped. Nothing about the floor decision requires dropping Claude's help; the request simply needed narrowing. Abandoning the tool overcorrects for an answer that was only too broad.

questions.question:
A sales enablement lead asks Claude to draft a product one-pager. The draft is dense and detailed, but the team's one-pagers are meant to be light and skimmable for busy reps.

What should the lead do?

options.label: A
options.text: Share a past one-pager that hit the right level of detail and ask Claude to match its depth.

options.label: B
options.text: Send the dense one-pager to reps as is, since it accurately and completely describes the product's features.

options.label: C
options.text: Ask Claude to delete a few sentences from the dense draft, without showing it the depth the team expects.

options.label: D
options.text: Write the one-pager from scratch by hand, since Claude produced too much detail this time.

questions.explanation:
CORRECT: Share a past one-pager that hit the right level of detail and ask Claude to match its depth.

The draft is not wrong, it is pitched at the wrong level of detail: dense where the team's one-pagers stay light and skimmable. Describing that in words is hard, so the most reliable fix is to show Claude an example. Share a past one-pager that hit the right depth and ask Claude to match it. A concrete exemplar communicates the target density far better than adjectives like shorter or simpler, giving Claude a clear standard to calibrate against.

Exam Guide Mapping

-
Domain 1: Prompting and Task Execution (14%)

-
Objective: Iterate prompts to improve output quality

INCORRECT: Send the dense one-pager to reps as is, since it accurately and completely describes the product's features.

Sending the dense draft to reps as is ignores that it is built for a different level of detail than the team uses. That it describes the product completely is beside the point, since busy reps need something skimmable. Accurate but too dense still fails the reps it is meant for.

INCORRECT: Ask Claude to delete a few sentences from the dense draft, without showing it the depth the team expects.

Deleting a few sentences trims the draft but gives Claude no sense of the depth the team wants, so the density stays off. This would work if it only needed to be slightly shorter. The real gap is a missing example of the right level of detail, which cutting lines does not supply.

INCORRECT: Write the one-pager from scratch by hand, since Claude produced too much detail this time.

Writing the one-pager by hand throws away work Claude can do well once it has a model to follow. The draft was not unusable, only miscalibrated on detail. Starting over from scratch spends effort that a single good example would have saved.

questions.question:
A content strategist asks Claude in one message to brainstorm blog topic ideas and fully draft the best one. Claude returns a single finished draft, with no other topics to consider first.

What should the strategist do?

options.label: A
options.text: Split the task in two, first have Claude generate a range of topic ideas, then develop the chosen one.

options.label: B
options.text: Ask Claude to expand the single finished draft with more detail, without generating any other topic options first.

options.label: C
options.text: Brainstorm all the blog topics manually first, then only use Claude to polish the final wording.

options.label: D
options.text: Accept the finished draft as the final topic choice, since Claude went straight to a complete and usable blog post.

questions.explanation:
CORRECT: Split the task in two, first have Claude generate a range of topic ideas, then develop the chosen one.

Asking Claude to brainstorm and fully draft the best idea in one step pushed it straight to developing a single option, so the range of ideas never appeared. Generating breadth and building depth are different jobs, and bundling them shortchanges the first. Split the request: first have Claude produce several topic ideas to compare, then pick one and ask for a full draft. Separating idea generation from development gives the strategist real choices before committing effort to any one of them.

Exam Guide Mapping

-
Domain 1: Prompting and Task Execution (14%)

-
Objective: Apply task decomposition techniques to structure complex requests

INCORRECT: Ask Claude to expand the single finished draft with more detail, without generating any other topic options first.

Expanding the single draft adds depth to an option that was never chosen from a real set, so the strategist still sees no alternatives. This would make sense if the topic had already been selected on purpose. Here the missing step is generating a range first, which expanding one draft skips entirely.

INCORRECT: Brainstorm all the blog topics manually first, then only use Claude to polish the final wording.

Brainstorming every topic by hand and using Claude only to polish pulls Claude out of the very task it does well, generating a wide set of ideas quickly. The problem was bundling, not Claude's ideation. Doing all the brainstorming manually overcorrects for a request that just needed splitting.

INCORRECT: Accept the finished draft as the final topic choice, since Claude went straight to a complete and usable blog post.

Accepting the finished draft as the choice assumes a complete post is the same as a considered decision. A polished single draft is a weak basis for a topic choice made without seeing any alternatives. It looks done, but nothing was actually compared before landing on it.

questions.question:
A social media coordinator asks Claude to write posts for a campaign, and Claude returns one flowing paragraph combining all the messages. The scheduling tool needs each post as a separate entry under 280 characters.

What should the coordinator do?

options.label: A
options.text: Tell Claude to return each post as a separate entry, every one under the 280-character limit the tool requires.

options.label: B
options.text: Write each of the campaign posts by hand instead, since Claude combined them into one block.

options.label: C
options.text: Paste the combined paragraph directly into the scheduling tool as is, since it already contains every message the campaign needs.

options.label: D
options.text: Ask Claude to shorten the single paragraph overall, without splitting it into separate, individually capped posts.

questions.explanation:
