questions.question:
A grants associate asks Claude to draft a compliance note. The draft confidently names a specific accreditation standard and the exact title of the official who administers it, neither of which the associate recognizes.

What should the associate do?

options.label: A
options.text: Confirm the named standard and official title against the accrediting body's official records before using the note.

options.label: B
options.text: Ask Claude how confident it is in the named standard and title, and proceed if the confidence is high.

options.label: C
options.text: Include the standard and title as written, since named specifics like these are usually pulled from real sources.

options.label: D
options.text: Strip every named standard and title from the note, including ones the associate could easily confirm.

questions.explanation:
CORRECT: Confirm the named standard and official title against the accrediting body's official records before using the note.

The associate does not recognize the named accreditation standard or the official's title, and specific names like these are exactly what a language model can invent while sounding authoritative. A confident tone is not evidence they are real. The fix is to confirm both against the accrediting body's own published records before the note goes anywhere. Named specifics, a standard code, an exact title, an official body's name, carry a real fabrication risk, so checking them against the authoritative source is the diligence step here.

Exam Guide Mapping

-
Domain 2: Output Evaluation and Validation (21%)

-
Objective: Apply fact-checking and validation techniques

INCORRECT: Ask Claude how confident it is in the named standard and title, and proceed if the confidence is high.

Asking Claude to rate its own confidence engages the doubt but leans on the wrong signal. A model's self-reported confidence does not track whether a specific name is real. This would help if confidence were a reliable accuracy measure; it is not, so only an external check against the accrediting body confirms the details.

INCORRECT: Include the standard and title as written, since named specifics like these are usually pulled from real sources.

Including them because named specifics are usually real trusts a weak assumption. Specific names are among the details a model most readily fabricates, precisely because they sound authoritative. Usually is not good enough for a compliance note that other people will rely on.

INCORRECT: Strip every named standard and title from the note, including ones the associate could easily confirm.

Stripping every named standard and title, even ones easily confirmed, discards accurate content to avoid checking a couple of items. The task only needed the unfamiliar names verified, not wholesale deletion. Removing confirmable details overcorrects and leaves the note weaker than it should be.

questions.question:
An HR associate asks Claude to summarize a new tuition reimbursement benefit for a staff email. The summary says employees can be reimbursed but leaves out the eligibility conditions attached to that benefit.

What should the associate do?

options.label: A
options.text: Ask Claude to add the eligibility conditions that determine who actually qualifies for the reimbursement.

options.label: B
options.text: Send the summary as written, since it correctly states that the reimbursement benefit is available to employees.

options.label: C
options.text: Add a note saying conditions may apply, without spelling out what those conditions actually are.

options.label: D
options.text: Scrap the summary and have each employee email HR to ask whether they personally qualify.

questions.explanation:
CORRECT: Ask Claude to add the eligibility conditions that determine who actually qualifies for the reimbursement.

The summary says employees can be reimbursed but drops the conditions that decide who actually qualifies, and those conditions are exactly what readers need to act on. A rule without its attached limits can mislead people into thinking they are eligible when they are not. Ask Claude specifically to include the eligibility conditions tied to the benefit. The gap here is not a whole missing section but the fine print on a stated rule, and surfacing that fine print is what makes the summary safe to send.

Exam Guide Mapping

-
Domain 2: Output Evaluation and Validation (21%)

-
Objective: Evaluate Claude-generated outputs for accuracy and completeness

INCORRECT: Send the summary as written, since it correctly states that the reimbursement benefit is available to employees.

Sending it as written treats the benefit exists as the whole story, when the conditions decide who can actually use it. That the availability statement is accurate is a weak reason to leave out the limits. Employees acting on an unconditioned summary may assume an eligibility they do not have.

INCORRECT: Add a note saying conditions may apply, without spelling out what those conditions actually are.

Adding a vague note that conditions may apply signals they exist but never tells employees what they are, so readers still cannot tell if they qualify. This would be enough if employees only needed a heads-up. They need the actual conditions, which a general caveat does not provide.

INCORRECT: Scrap the summary and have each employee email HR to ask whether they personally qualify.

Making every employee email HR to check eligibility discards the summary's purpose and creates needless work for the whole staff. The summary only needed its conditions added, not removal. Pushing the question onto each reader overcorrects for an omission that was simple to fix.

questions.question:
A policy analyst asks Claude to draft a briefing. The draft attributes a strong conclusion to a well-known annual report, but the conclusion sounds stronger than what that report actually says.

What should the analyst do?

options.label: A
options.text: Check the actual report to confirm it supports the specific conclusion before keeping the attribution.

options.label: B
options.text: Keep the attribution as written, since it points to a real, well-known report readers can look up.

options.label: C
options.text: Send the entire briefing out for a full external fact-checking audit before it can be used at all.

options.label: D
options.text: Soften the conclusion's wording slightly, while still crediting it to the same report without checking it.

questions.explanation:
CORRECT: Check the actual report to confirm it supports the specific conclusion before keeping the attribution.

The draft points to a real report, but a real source is not the same as a source that actually says this. The conclusion sounds stronger than the report's, which is a classic sign of an overstated or misattributed claim. Confirming that the report exists proves nothing; the analyst has to open it and check that it supports this specific conclusion. Verifying the claim against the source itself, not just the source's existence, is what keeps the briefing honest.

"Users should not rely on Claude as a singular source of truth." - Resource

Exam Guide Mapping

-
Domain 2: Output Evaluation and Validation (21%)

-
Objective: Apply fact-checking and validation techniques

INCORRECT: Keep the attribution as written, since it points to a real, well-known report readers can look up.

Keeping the attribution because the report is real and lookupable trusts the wrong thing: that a genuine source must support the claim made about it. It would be fine if the report clearly stated this conclusion. Since the wording sounds stronger than the report's, only opening it settles whether the claim holds.

INCORRECT: Send the entire briefing out for a full external fact-checking audit before it can be used at all.

Sending the whole briefing for a full external audit treats one questionable attribution as a reason to gate the entire document behind a heavyweight process. Only this conclusion needed checking against its report. Routing everything through an external audit overcorrects for a discrepancy the analyst could resolve directly.

INCORRECT: Soften the conclusion's wording slightly, while still crediting it to the same report without checking it.

Softening the wording while still crediting the same report changes the tone but never checks whether the report supports the claim. This helps only if overstatement were purely a phrasing issue. The attribution itself may be wrong, which rewording cannot fix.

questions.question:
A finance associate asks Claude to pull the current headcount from a set of meeting notes. Claude returns a number that differs from the figure in the company's official HR system of record.

What should the associate do?

options.label: A
options.text: Treat the official HR system as authoritative and correct Claude's number against it.

options.label: B
options.text: Ask Claude to recalculate the headcount from the same notes, without comparing it to the HR system.

options.label: C
options.text: Use Claude's number, assuming it reflects more current information than the HR system does.

options.label: D
options.text: Discard both figures and manually recount every employee from scratch across all departments.

questions.explanation:
CORRECT: Treat the official HR system as authoritative and correct Claude's number against it.

When a Claude figure clashes with the company's official HR system of record, the system of record wins by definition: it is the authoritative source the organization maintains for exactly this number. The mistake would be assuming Claude's figure is somehow more current. Treat the HR system as the truth and correct Claude's number against it. Claude pulled from meeting notes, which can be incomplete or out of date, whereas the system of record is the sanctioned source, so it settles the discrepancy.

Exam Guide Mapping

-
Domain 2: Output Evaluation and Validation (21%)

-
Objective: Identify hallucinations, inconsistencies, and biases in responses

INCORRECT: Ask Claude to recalculate the headcount from the same notes, without comparing it to the HR system.

Asking Claude to recompute from the same notes just reruns the same limited input, so it never reconciles against the authoritative figure. It would help if the notes were the source of truth. Since the HR system is, recalculating from notes cannot resolve the conflict.

INCORRECT: Use Claude's number, assuming it reflects more current information than the HR system does.

Using Claude's number on the assumption it is more current inverts which source is authoritative. Claude drew from meeting notes, not a maintained record, so newer-sounding does not mean correct. This would hold only if the notes were the official source, which they are not; the HR system is.

INCORRECT: Discard both figures and manually recount every employee from scratch across all departments.

Manually recounting every employee from scratch discards a figure the HR system already holds authoritatively. The associate only needed to trust the system of record over the notes-derived number. A full company-wide recount overcorrects for a discrepancy the record already settles.

questions.question:
A recruiting associate asks Claude to draft a customer support job posting. The draft requires a native English speaker with no accent and someone able-bodied enough to thrive under pressure.

What should the associate do before posting it?

options.label: A
options.text: Revise the posting to focus on the actual job requirements, removing the language about accent, national origin, and physical ability.

options.label: B
options.text: Post the listing as written, since clear communication and working under pressure are fair things to expect in a support role.

options.label: C
options.text: Change native English speaker to fluent English speaker, while leaving the accent and able-bodied requirements in place.

options.label: D
options.text: Remove every skill and personal trait from the posting, leaving only the job title and the salary.

questions.explanation:
CORRECT: Revise the posting to focus on the actual job requirements, removing the language about accent, national origin, and physical ability.

The posting screens on traits that are not the job: a specific accent, native-speaker status, and physical ability. Those requirements can unlawfully exclude qualified people on the basis of national origin and disability, and they say nothing about who can do the work well. The fix is to rewrite around the actual requirements, such as clear communication and handling a busy queue, and drop the coded language. Focusing on job-relevant skills keeps the posting fair and still finds the right candidate.

Exam Guide Mapping

-
Domain 2: Output Evaluation and Validation (21%)

-
Objective: Identify hallucinations, inconsistencies, and biases in responses

INCORRECT: Post the listing as written, since clear communication and working under pressure are fair things to expect in a support role.

Posting it as written treats these traits as reasonable expectations, but an accent or being able-bodied has no bearing on support quality. Wanting good communication is legitimate; requiring a particular accent or physical status to get it is not. The listing reads acceptable only if the coded terms go unexamined.

INCORRECT: Change native English speaker to fluent English speaker, while leaving the accent and able-bodied requirements in place.

Changing native to fluent softens one phrase but leaves the accent and able-bodied requirements untouched, so the posting still screens on national origin and disability. This would be enough if a single word were the whole problem. The bias runs through several requirements, which one substitution does not remove.

INCORRECT: Remove every skill and personal trait from the posting, leaving only the job title and the salary.

Stripping every skill and trait removes the bias but also deletes the legitimate requirements a candidate needs to see. The goal was to cut the coded language, not describe the role. Leaving only a title and salary overcorrects and makes the posting useless to real applicants.

questions.question:
A compliance associate asks Claude to draft a public notice stating the deadline by which residents must renew a permit and the maximum late fee allowed. Both figures are specific.

What should the associate do before the notice is published?

options.label: A
options.text: Verify the renewal deadline and maximum late fee against the governing regulation or ordinance before the notice is published.

options.label: B
options.text: Ask Claude to reword the deadline and fee in plainer language, without confirming the figures themselves are correct.

options.label: C
options.text: Publish the notice as drafted, since Claude stated both figures precisely and they read like established public rules.

options.label: D
options.text: Publish the notice with the deadline and fee removed, telling residents to call the office for every detail.

questions.explanation:
CORRECT: Verify the renewal deadline and maximum late fee against the governing regulation or ordinance before the notice is published.

A public notice that states a legal deadline and a maximum late fee carries real consequences: residents will act on those exact figures, and getting them wrong can misinform the public or expose the office to challenge. Precise-sounding numbers are not proof they match the law. The associate should verify both against the governing regulation or ordinance, the primary source that sets them. Checking high-stakes legal figures against the authority that defines them is the step that makes the notice safe to publish.

Exam Guide Mapping

-
Domain 2: Output Evaluation and Validation (21%)

-
Objective: Apply fact-checking and validation techniques

INCORRECT: Ask Claude to reword the deadline and fee in plainer language, without confirming the figures themselves are correct.

Rewording the deadline and fee in plainer language makes the notice easier to read but never checks whether the numbers are right. This would be the correct move if the figures were already confirmed and only the wording was unclear. Here their accuracy is the open question, and clearer phrasing of a wrong figure is still wrong.

INCORRECT: Publish the notice as drafted, since Claude stated both figures precisely and they read like established public rules.

Publishing as drafted because the figures read precise and official trusts the wrong signal. A confident, specific number can still be fabricated or outdated, especially for figures set by law. That the notice reads like established public rules is exactly the impression a wrong figure would give, which is why it needs checking.

INCORRECT: Publish the notice with the deadline and fee removed, telling residents to call the office for every detail.

Removing the deadline and fee and telling residents to call for every detail defeats the notice's purpose, which is to state those figures clearly. The task was to confirm the numbers, not delete them. Pushing every resident to phone in overcorrects for figures that only needed verifying.

questions.question:
After a data breach, a communications associate has Claude draft a public statement acknowledging the incident and what the company will do for affected customers. The draft reads clear and reassuring.

What should the associate do before it is released?

options.label: A
options.text: Route the statement to legal and communications leadership for review before it is released to the public.

options.label: B
options.text: Ask Claude to confirm the statement's tone is appropriately serious, then release it on that basis.

options.label: C
options.text: Decide not to issue any public statement at all, to avoid the risk of saying the wrong thing.

options.label: D
options.text: Release the statement as drafted, since it reads clear, reassuring, and already covers what happened.

questions.explanation:
CORRECT: Route the statement to legal and communications leadership for review before it is released to the public.

A public statement about a data breach carries legal and reputational stakes far beyond a routine message: what the company admits and promises can affect its regulatory position and its customers directly. A polished draft is not the same as a cleared one. Before release, it should go to legal and communications leadership, who can weigh the wording, the commitments, and the disclosure obligations. Requiring qualified human sign-off on an externally binding statement is the safeguard that a clear, reassuring tone cannot replace.

Exam Guide Mapping

-
Domain 2: Output Evaluation and Validation (21%)

-
Objective: Determine when human review or additional verification is required

INCORRECT: Ask Claude to confirm the statement's tone is appropriately serious, then release it on that basis.

Asking Claude to confirm the tone sounds serious checks the wrong thing, since tone is not the real risk in a breach statement. This would suffice if wording were the only concern. The legal exposure in what the company admits and promises still needs qualified human review, which a tone check cannot provide.

INCORRECT: Decide not to issue any public statement at all, to avoid the risk of saying the wrong thing.

Issuing no statement at all avoids the drafting risk but creates a bigger one: staying silent after a breach can breach disclosure duties and damage trust. The task was to get the statement reviewed, not to suppress it. Refusing to communicate overcorrects for a draft that simply needed sign-off.

INCORRECT: Release the statement as drafted, since it reads clear, reassuring, and already covers what happened.

Releasing the draft because it reads clear and reassuring leans on exactly the surface quality that can mask legal problems. A statement can sound perfect and still commit the company to the wrong thing or omit a required disclosure. Reading well is not evidence it has been cleared for release.

questions.question:
A finance associate reviews a Claude-drafted budget summary. One line shows a department spent 140 percent of a category that cannot exceed its allocation, while the other figures look normal.

Which two actions should the associate take?

(choose two)

options.label: A
options.text: Recognize the 140 percent figure as internally impossible, since spending cannot exceed a capped allocation.

options.label: B
options.text: Verify that specific line against the source budget data before relying on the summary.

options.label: C
options.text: Accept the 140 percent figure as written, since every other number in the summary looks normal.

options.label: D
options.text: Re-verify all of the normal-looking figures in equal depth, rather than focusing on the impossible one.

options.label: E
options.text: Ask Claude to adjust the 140 percent down to a plausible number, without checking the source data.

questions.explanation:
CORRECT: Recognize the 140 percent figure as internally impossible, since spending cannot exceed a capped allocation.

The first skill is noticing the figure fails a basic sanity check: a capped category cannot be spent past 100 percent, so 140 percent is impossible on its face. That internal contradiction, not unfamiliarity, is what flags it. Catching numbers that cannot logically be true is a fast, powerful filter, because it lets the associate spot a likely error from the math alone before checking any external source.

CORRECT: Verify that specific line against the source budget data before relying on the summary.

Spotting the impossible figure is only half the job; the associate then has to resolve it against the source. Checking that one line against the original budget data shows whether it is a transcription slip, a miscalculation, or a deeper problem. Pairing the sanity check with a targeted source verification is what turns I noticed something wrong into a corrected, reliable summary.

Exam Guide Mapping

-
Domain 2: Output Evaluation and Validation (21%)

-
Objective: Identify hallucinations, inconsistencies, and biases in responses

-
Objective: Apply fact-checking and validation techniques

INCORRECT: Accept the 140 percent figure as written, since every other number in the summary looks normal.

Accepting it because the other numbers look normal ignores that this one is logically impossible. The surrounding figures being fine says nothing about a line that violates the cap. A number that cannot be true is not made true by good company.

INCORRECT: Re-verify all of the normal-looking figures in equal depth, rather than focusing on the impossible one.

Re-verifying every normal figure with equal effort spreads scrutiny evenly when one line clearly demands it most. This would make sense if nothing stood out, but the impossible figure is the obvious priority. Treating all numbers the same wastes effort and delays fixing the one real problem.

INCORRECT: Ask Claude to adjust the 140 percent down to a plausible number, without checking the source data.

Asking Claude to nudge the figure to something plausible replaces a wrong number with a guessed one and never consults the source. Plausible is not the same as correct. Only the original budget data reveals the true figure, which an on-the-fly adjustment skips entirely.

questions.question:
A marketing associate has Claude adapt an internal launch brief into a customer-facing announcement. The draft still names an unreleased future product, cites the internal profit margin, and mentions a competitor by name in a dismissive aside.

What should the associate do?

options.label: A
options.text: Remove the confidential internal references before publishing, keeping only information meant for customers.

options.label: B
options.text: Publish the announcement as is, since the internal details are accurate and give customers helpful extra context.

options.label: C
options.text: Ask Claude to reword the competitor aside more politely, while leaving the unreleased product and margin in the draft.

options.label: D
options.text: Cancel the customer announcement entirely, since the internal brief was never meant to be shared.

questions.explanation:
CORRECT: Remove the confidential internal references before publishing, keeping only information meant for customers.

This is a confidentiality leak, not a readability problem. The draft carries an unreleased product, an internal profit margin, and a dismissive competitor reference, all sensitive material that was never meant to leave the company. Publishing any of it could tip strategy, expose financials, or invite legal trouble. The associate should strip the internal references and keep only what customers are meant to see. The test for external content is not just is it clear, but does it reveal anything confidential, and here it does.

Exam Guide Mapping

-
Domain 6: Governance, Risk, and Responsible Use (15%)

-
Objective: Apply data sensitivity, regulatory, and privacy considerations

INCORRECT: Publish the announcement as is, since the internal details are accurate and give customers helpful extra context.

Publishing it because the details are accurate and add context misreads the risk entirely. The problem is not that the information is wrong; it is that it is confidential. Accurate internal data is often the most damaging thing to expose, which is exactly why it must be removed.

INCORRECT: Ask Claude to reword the competitor aside more politely, while leaving the unreleased product and margin in the draft.

Rewording only the competitor aside handles one leak while leaving the unreleased product and the margin figure exposed. This would be closer to enough if that aside were the sole issue. Several pieces of confidential material remain, so a single polite rewrite does not make the draft safe to publish.

INCORRECT: Cancel the customer announcement entirely, since the internal brief was never meant to be shared.

Canceling the announcement throws out a legitimate customer message because its source draft contained internal details. The announcement itself is fine once the confidential parts are removed. Abandoning it overcorrects for content that only needed cleaning up.

questions.question:
A proposal associate has Claude generate three responses to an RFP, which lists explicit scoring criteria and their point weights. Each response reads well, and the associate must submit only one.

What should the associate do before choosing?

options.label: A
options.text: Score each response against the RFP's stated criteria and point weights, then submit the highest-scoring one.

options.label: B
options.text: Submit whichever response reads the most polished, since all three are well written and clearly presented.

options.label: C
options.text: Ask Claude which of the three it thinks is strongest, and submit that one without checking it against the criteria.

options.label: D
options.text: Combine all three responses into one long submission, so every possible point is covered somewhere.

questions.explanation:
CORRECT: Score each response against the RFP's stated criteria and point weights, then submit the highest-scoring one.

The RFP does the associate a favor by naming explicit criteria and point weights, which is the exact standard the submission will be judged against. Comparing on general impression ignores that standard. The right move is to score each response against those criteria and weights and submit the one that scores highest. When the evaluation rubric is written down, measuring options against that documented spec, not against which one reads best, is what aligns the choice with how it will actually be graded.

Exam Guide Mapping

-
Domain 2: Output Evaluation and Validation (21%)

-
Objective: Edit, adapt, refine, and compare outputs for the intended audience

INCORRECT: Submit whichever response reads the most polished, since all three are well written and clearly presented.

Choosing the most polished response substitutes a gut impression for the RFP's actual scoring rubric. Reading well and scoring well on weighted criteria are not the same thing. The one that sounds best may miss the points that carry the most weight.

INCORRECT: Ask Claude which of the three it thinks is strongest, and submit that one without checking it against the criteria.

Asking Claude to pick its favorite still skips the RFP's stated criteria and their weights. This would be reasonable if there were no defined rubric to compare against. Since the RFP spells one out, the responses should be scored against it rather than chosen by preference.

INCORRECT: Combine all three responses into one long submission, so every possible point is covered somewhere.

Merging all three into one submission ignores that the RFP asks for a single, focused response and may cap length or penalize padding. The task was to choose the best fit against the criteria, not to submit everything. Bundling them overcorrects and likely scores worse, not better.

questions.question:
An operations associate asks Claude a one-time question to settle a quick internal scheduling decision and gets a clear, correct answer right in the chat. They wonder whether answers like this should always become downloadable documents.

What should the associate do?

options.label: A
options.text: Keep the answer inline, since a one-time decision does not need a downloadable, reusable document.

options.label: B
options.text: Have Claude rebuild the same answer as a formatted downloadable file, even though no one will reopen it later.

options.label: C
options.text: Make every quick Claude answer a downloadable document by default, for the sake of consistency across the team.

options.label: D
options.text: Move all quick questions like this out of Claude and into a separate documentation tool instead.

questions.explanation:
CORRECT: Keep the answer inline, since a one-time decision does not need a downloadable, reusable document.

The deciding detail is that this is a one-time decision that will not be revisited. Structured, downloadable formats earn their overhead when content will be reused, edited, or shared repeatedly, not for a throwaway answer. A clear inline reply already settles the question, so packaging it into a document only adds steps and clutter for no payoff. Choosing the format that fits how the content will actually be used, and recognizing a quick one-off does not need heavy formatting, is the judgment here.

Exam Guide Mapping

-
Domain 2: Output Evaluation and Validation (21%)

-
Objective: Organize and curate information and select appropriate output formats (artifacts, inline, structured data)

INCORRECT: Have Claude rebuild the same answer as a formatted downloadable file, even though no one will reopen it later.

Rebuilding the answer as a downloadable file dresses up a result nobody will return to, spending effort on packaging with no reuse to justify it. This would make sense if the output were meant to be revisited or shared. For a one-time decision, the file adds friction rather than value.

INCORRECT: Make every quick Claude answer a downloadable document by default, for the sake of consistency.

Defaulting every quick answer to a document treats uniformity as the goal, when the right format depends on whether the content will be reused. This would be reasonable if these answers were regularly revisited or edited. Since most are one-offs, a blanket document rule creates overhead the work does not need.

INCORRECT: Move all quick questions like this out of Claude and into a separate documentation tool instead.

Routing every quick question into a separate documentation tool abandons a fast, working answer for a heavier process. Nothing about a simple inline reply calls for another system. Relocating the whole workflow overcorrects for output that was already in the right place.
references: [What are artifacts and how do I use them?](https://support.claude.com/en/articles/9487310-what-are-artifacts-and-how-do-i-use-them)

questions.question:
A strategy associate asks Claude to synthesize several market forecasts into one outlook. The result reads as a single confident consensus, even though the associate knows the forecasts disagree sharply on growth.

What should the associate do?

options.label: A
options.text: Ask Claude to surface where the forecasts genuinely disagree and why, instead of presenting them as one consensus.

options.label: B
options.text: Add a general note that some forecasts may differ, without identifying the specific points of disagreement.

options.label: C
options.text: Use the unified outlook as written, since it reads clear and consistent across all the forecasts.

options.label: D
options.text: Drop the synthesis and paste all the raw forecasts in full for readers to compare on their own.

questions.explanation:
CORRECT: Ask Claude to surface where the forecasts genuinely disagree and why, instead of presenting them as one consensus.

A synthesis that blends conflicting forecasts into one confident outlook hides exactly what a strategist needs to see: where the sources diverge and why. Smooth agreement that papers over real disagreement is misleading, not helpful. The associate should ask Claude to call out the specific points of conflict and the reasoning behind them. Good synthesis explains where sources agree and where they part ways, so the reader can weigh the disagreement rather than inherit a false consensus that was never actually there.

Exam Guide Mapping

-
Domain 2: Output Evaluation and Validation (21%)

-
Objective: Evaluate Claude-generated outputs for accuracy and completeness

INCORRECT: Add a general note that some forecasts may differ, without identifying the specific points of disagreement.

Adding a vague note that forecasts may differ acknowledges disagreement without showing where it lies, so the reader still cannot weigh it. This would be enough if the differences were minor and immaterial. Since the forecasts disagree sharply on growth, the specific conflicts have to be named, not hinted at.

INCORRECT: Use the unified outlook as written, since it reads clear and consistent across all the forecasts.

Using the outlook because it reads clear and consistent trusts the very smoothness that is the problem. A confident, unified narrative is easy to read precisely because it erased the disagreement. Consistency on the page is not evidence the underlying sources actually agree.

INCORRECT: Drop the synthesis and paste all the raw forecasts in full for readers to compare on their own.

Dumping every raw forecast for readers to reconcile themselves throws away the synthesis entirely and pushes the hard work onto the audience. The goal was a synthesis that surfaces the disagreement, not the absence of one. Reverting to unprocessed sources overcorrects and loses the value Claude was meant to add.

questions.question:
An associate plans a recurring workflow built on uploading large reference files into a Project. Claude states with full confidence that the files are well within the size Projects accept.

What should the associate do before committing the workflow to that assumption?

options.label: A
options.text: Confirm the current Project file limits against Anthropic's official help center before building the workflow on them.

options.label: B
options.text: Ask Claude to restate how confident it is about the size limit, and proceed if the confidence stays high.

options.label: C
options.text: Proceed with the recurring workflow as planned, since Claude stated the size claim with full confidence.

options.label: D
options.text: Abandon the Project-based workflow entirely, since Claude cannot be certain about the platform's limits.

questions.explanation:
CORRECT: Confirm the current Project file limits against Anthropic's official help center before building the workflow on them.

A confident statement about a platform limit is not the same as a verified one. Product capabilities and limits change over time and can differ by context, such as chat uploads versus Project files, so a recurring workflow should not rest on the model's assurance alone. The associate should check Anthropic's official help center, the authoritative source for current limits, before committing. When a plan depends on a specific platform capability, verifying it against the official documentation is what turns a confident claim into a reliable foundation.

questions.question:
A policy analyst re-uploads the same three reference PDFs at the start of every new chat before asking Claude questions about them, repeating those uploads several times a day.

What should the analyst do?

options.label: A
options.text: Add the three reference PDFs to a Project's knowledge base once, so every chat can use them without re-uploading.

options.label: B
options.text: Keep re-uploading the three PDFs each chat, since Claude answers correctly once the files are attached.

options.label: C
options.text: Save the three PDFs in a folder on their computer for quicker access, without changing how the files actually reach Claude.

options.label: D
options.text: Paste the full text of all three PDFs into every message instead of uploading the files.

questions.explanation:
CORRECT: Add the three reference PDFs to a Project's knowledge base once, so every chat can use them without re-uploading.

The analyst is doing the same upload over and over, several times a day, which is the signal that this material belongs in a Project rather than in each separate chat. A Project's knowledge base holds reference files persistently, so every conversation in that Project can draw on them without re-uploading. Moving the three PDFs there once removes the repeated setup entirely. When the same context is needed again and again, storing it in a Project instead of re-supplying it each time is the efficient fix.

Exam Guide Mapping

-
Domain 5: Configuration and Knowledge Management (12%)

-
Objective: Configure Claude Projects with instructions and knowledge sources

INCORRECT: Keep re-uploading the three PDFs each chat, since Claude answers correctly once the files are attached.

Re-uploading each time works, but it ignores the wasted effort of repeating the same setup all day. That Claude answers well once the files are attached is not the issue; the repetition is. This would be fine for a rare, one-time need, but a recurring one calls for persistent storage.

INCORRECT: Save the three PDFs in a folder on their computer for quicker access, without changing how the files actually reach Claude.

A local folder makes the files faster to find but changes nothing about the re-uploading, since the analyst still attaches them to every new chat. This addresses the wrong step. The friction is in supplying the files to Claude each time, which only a Project's persistent knowledge base removes.

INCORRECT: Paste the full text of all three PDFs into every message instead of uploading the files.

Pasting the full text swaps one repetitive manual step for a bulkier one, filling each message with lengthy content every time. It solves nothing and crowds the conversation. The recurring supply of the same material is exactly what a Project is designed to handle once and reuse.

questions.question:
An analyst enables Research and asks Claude for a current, multi-source comparison of competitors, but the reply draws only on general background knowledge with no current sources or citations. Web search is switched off in their settings.

What should the analyst do?

options.label: A
options.text: Turn on web search, since Research depends on it to gather current sources.

options.label: B
options.text: Accept the reply as complete, since Research was switched on when the question was asked.

options.label: C
options.text: Toggle Research off and back on again, without enabling web search in the settings.

options.label: D
options.text: Give up on Research and manually visit each competitor's website one by one instead.

questions.explanation:
CORRECT: Turn on web search, since Research depends on it to gather current sources.

Research works by running many searches across the web and any connected sources, so it cannot pull current, cited information unless web search is enabled. The reply fell back on general knowledge precisely because that dependency was switched off. Turning web search on lets Research do the multi-source gathering it is built for. The lesson is that Research is not a standalone switch: it relies on web search to function, so having both enabled is what makes it actually work.

Exam Guide Mapping

-
Domain 3: Product and Model Selection (12%)

-
Objective: Select appropriate Claude product features (Projects, research mode, chat, artifacts)

INCORRECT: Accept the reply as complete, since Research was switched on when the question was asked.

Accepting the reply because Research was on trusts the toggle over the result, which clearly lacks the current sources the task needed. Research being enabled is not proof it actually searched. The missing citations are the tell that something, here the web search dependency, was not in place.

INCORRECT: Toggle Research off and back on again, without enabling web search in the settings.

Toggling Research off and on treats the problem as a glitch when the real cause is that web search, which Research requires, is disabled. This might help if it were a transient hiccup. Since the dependency itself is off, only enabling web search restores the current-source gathering.

INCORRECT: Give up on Research and manually visit each competitor's website one by one instead.

Reverting to visiting each site by hand abandons the exact multi-source synthesis Research is designed to automate. Nothing about the task made Research the wrong tool; a single setting simply was not enabled. Doing it all manually overcorrects for a one-toggle fix.

questions.question:
A support team uses Claude Opus to generate short reply suggestions that agents see live while chatting with customers, but the suggestions arrive too slowly to help mid-conversation. The task itself is simple.

What should the team do?

options.label: A
options.text: Switch to Claude Haiku, the fastest tier, since real-time suggestions need speed more than maximum capability.

options.label: B
options.text: Keep using Opus for the suggestions, since its wording is the highest quality available.

options.label: C
options.text: Ask agents to simply wait a moment longer for each Opus suggestion to appear, rather than changing the model tier at all.

options.label: D
options.text: Drop the live suggestion feature entirely and have agents write every reply unaided.

questions.explanation:
CORRECT: Switch to Claude Haiku, the fastest tier, since real-time suggestions need speed more than maximum capability.

In a live chat, a suggestion that arrives too late to use is worthless no matter how well written it is. The binding constraint here is speed, not wording quality, and the task itself is simple. Claude Haiku, the fastest tier, is built for exactly this kind of quick, high-volume work, so switching to it lets suggestions appear in time to help. Matching the tier to what the task actually demands, fast turnaround in a real-time setting, is what makes the feature usable.

Exam Guide Mapping

-
Domain 3: Product and Model Selection (12%)

-
Objective: Align model selection with task requirements (cost, speed, quality)

INCORRECT: Keep using Opus for the suggestions, since its wording is the highest quality available.

Sticking with Opus for its wording quality ignores that the suggestions arrive too late to be used at all. The best phrasing is no help if it misses the moment. This choice would make sense only if the suggestions were drafted for later review, not delivered live mid-conversation.

INCORRECT: Ask agents to simply wait a moment longer for each Opus suggestion to appear, rather than changing the model tier at all.

Telling agents to wait pushes the delay onto them during a live customer chat, where a pause is exactly what they cannot afford. It accepts the latency instead of removing it. The task is simple enough that a faster tier delivers in time, so the wait is unnecessary.

INCORRECT: Drop the live suggestion feature entirely and have agents write every reply unaided.

Scrapping the feature throws out a genuinely useful aid because one tier was too slow for it. The suggestions were valuable; they just needed to arrive faster. Abandoning the feature overcorrects for a problem a quicker tier solves.

questions.question:
An associate uses Claude Haiku to draft what looks like a routine customer email, but the reply must interpret nuanced contract terms and could create a binding commitment if it gets them wrong.

What should the associate do?

options.label: A
options.text: Switch to Claude Opus, the most capable tier, since the email's hidden legal complexity outweighs its routine look.

options.label: B
options.text: Keep drafting with Haiku, since the email looks like a simple, everyday customer message.

options.label: C
options.text: Ask Haiku to write the email more carefully and double-check itself, without moving to a higher tier.

options.label: D
options.text: Route every customer email the team sends through the most capable tier from now on, regardless of how simple the message is.

questions.explanation:
CORRECT: Switch to Claude Opus, the most capable tier, since the email's hidden legal complexity outweighs its routine look.

What makes this tricky is that the task looks routine but is not. Interpreting nuanced contract terms with a binding commitment at stake is exactly the kind of complex, high-consequence reasoning a top tier is meant for. Judging by surface appearance would send it to a fast tier that may miss the subtleties. Claude Opus, the most capable tier, suits work where getting the fine details right matters. Recognizing hidden complexity beneath a simple-looking task, and upshifting for it, is the skill here.

Exam Guide Mapping

-
Domain 3: Product and Model Selection (12%)

-
Objective: Align model selection with task requirements (cost, speed, quality)

INCORRECT: Keep drafting with Haiku, since the email looks like a simple, everyday customer message.

Sticking with Haiku because the email looks simple is the exact trap: it judges the task by its surface, not its stakes. If it truly were a routine note, Haiku would be the right, efficient choice. The hidden contract interpretation and binding-commitment risk are what change the calculus.

INCORRECT: Ask Haiku to write the email more carefully and double-check itself, without moving to a higher tier.

Asking Haiku to be more careful still relies on a tier that may not have the reasoning depth this task needs. Self-checking does not add capability the tier lacks. When the work genuinely calls for stronger reasoning, the fix is a more capable tier, not a more careful prompt on the same one.

INCORRECT: Route every customer email the team sends through the most capable tier from now on, regardless of how simple the message is.

Sending every email through the top tier overcorrects, spending capability and cost on the many messages that really are routine. Only this email's hidden complexity warranted the upshift. A blanket rule wastes resources on work a faster tier would handle perfectly well.

questions.question:
On a team running the same content-drafting workflow, each member picks a different model tier out of personal habit, so output quality and cost vary widely from person to person.

What should the team lead do?

options.label: A
options.text: Set Claude Sonnet, the balanced mid tier, as the team's shared default, overriding it only when a task clearly needs otherwise.

options.label: B
options.text: Let each member keep choosing their own tier, since everyone is getting their own work done.

options.label: C
options.text: Ask members to try to pick similar tiers on their own, without setting any agreed default for the shared workflow.

options.label: D
options.text: Mandate the most capable tier for every member on every task from now on, regardless of how simple or routine the work is.

questions.explanation:
CORRECT: Set Claude Sonnet, the balanced mid tier, as the team's shared default, overriding it only when a task clearly needs otherwise.

The inconsistency comes from each member choosing a tier by personal habit, so the fix is a shared standard, not individual preference. Setting Claude Sonnet, the balanced mid tier, as the team's default gives everyone a sensible baseline that handles most drafting well, while still allowing a step up or down when a specific task calls for it. A team-wide default steadies both quality and cost across people, which scattered individual choices cannot do.

Exam Guide Mapping

-
Domain 3: Product and Model Selection (12%)

-
Objective: Align model selection with task requirements (cost, speed, quality)

INCORRECT: Let each member keep choosing their own tier, since everyone is getting their own work done.

Leaving each member to choose accepts the very inconsistency that is causing uneven quality and cost. That everyone finishes their work misses the point, since the outputs and spend differ across people. Individual habit is exactly what a shared default is meant to replace.

INCORRECT: Ask members to try to pick similar tiers on their own, without setting any agreed default for the shared workflow.

Asking people to informally align leaves the choice to individual judgment, so the drift will continue. This might be enough if the variation were trivial. Since quality and cost vary widely, the workflow needs a defined default, not a loose suggestion.

INCORRECT: Mandate the most capable tier for every member on every task from now on, regardless of how simple or routine the work is.

Forcing the top tier on everyone for everything standardizes the team but over-provisions the routine drafting that fills most of the workflow. The goal was a sensible shared baseline, not the maximum tier everywhere. A blanket top-tier rule trades one problem for needless cost.

questions.question:
An analyst is analyzing a very large set of source documents by pasting them all into one conversation, but the chat keeps hitting its length limit before the analysis is done.

What should the analyst do?

options.label: A
options.text: Break the large document set into smaller sections and work through them in focused chunks, not all in one chat.

options.label: B
options.text: Keep adding the remaining documents to the same conversation, assuming Claude will retain everything that gets pasted in.

options.label: C
options.text: Start the same overloaded chat over from scratch and paste the entire document set back in again, without splitting it into smaller pieces first.

options.label: D
options.text: Conclude that Claude cannot analyze a document set this large and do the entire analysis by hand instead.

questions.explanation:
CORRECT: Break the large document set into smaller sections and work through them in focused chunks, not all in one chat.

The problem here is sheer volume: the document set is too large for a single chat's working memory, so loading it all at once overflows the window and the analysis stalls. Breaking the material into smaller sections and analyzing them in focused passes keeps each one within the limit, and the findings can be combined afterward. This differs from a thread that has merely grown unwieldy over many turns. When there is simply too much source material at once, the fix is to divide it.

Exam Guide Mapping

-
Domain 3: Product and Model Selection (12%)

-
Objective: Understand and manage context limitations and memory considerations (when to restart, summarize, or persist)

INCORRECT: Keep adding the remaining documents to the same conversation, assuming Claude will retain everything that gets pasted in.

Continuing to pile documents into the same chat ignores the length limit that is already being hit. Assuming Claude retains everything pasted overlooks how a context window works. More material in one overloaded conversation makes the problem worse, not better.

INCORRECT: Start the same overloaded chat over from scratch and paste the entire document set back in again, without splitting it into smaller pieces first.

Restarting and pasting the whole set back in reproduces the exact overflow, since the volume is unchanged. This would help if the thread had simply degraded over many turns and the content actually fit. Here the material itself exceeds one window, so it has to be chunked, not merely restarted.

INCORRECT: Conclude that Claude cannot analyze a document set this large and do the entire analysis by hand instead.

Deciding Claude cannot handle the set abandons a task it manages well once the input is divided. The obstacle was loading everything at once, not the analysis itself. Doing it all manually overcorrects for a limit that chunking resolves.

Restarting and pasting the whole set back in reproduces the exact overflow, since the volume is unchanged. This would help if the thread had simply degraded over many turns and the content actually fit. Here the material itself exceeds one window, so it has to be chunked, not merely restarted.

INCORRECT: Conclude that Claude cannot analyze a document set this large and do the entire analysis by hand instead.

Deciding Claude cannot handle the set abandons a task it manages well once the input is divided. The obstacle was loading everything at once, not the analysis itself. Doing it all manually overcorrects for a limit that chunking resolves.

questions.question:
A product associate keeps having Claude regenerate a full 30-row specifications table in chat every time just one or two values need updating, retyping the whole table on each small change.

What should the associate do?

options.label: A
options.text: Create the specifications table as an artifact, so small updates apply directly instead of regenerating the whole table.

options.label: B
options.text: Keep regenerating the entire table in chat for each change, since the output comes out correct every time.

options.label: C
options.text: Ask Claude to regenerate only the changed rows in chat, then paste those rows back into the full table by hand each time.

options.label: D
options.text: Move the specifications table into a separate spreadsheet program and stop using Claude to maintain it.

questions.explanation:
CORRECT: Create the specifications table as an artifact, so small updates apply directly instead of regenerating the whole table.

The associate is regenerating an entire structured table just to change a value or two, which is the signal it belongs in an artifact. Content you iterate on repeatedly, especially a self-contained deliverable like a specifications table, is exactly what artifacts are for: updates apply right in the artifact rather than forcing a full rewrite each time. Making the table an artifact means a small change touches only what changed. Recognizing that repeatedly revised, reusable content should live in an artifact is the point here.

Exam Guide Mapping

-
Domain 2: Output Evaluation and Validation (21%)

-
Objective: Organize and curate information and select appropriate output formats (artifacts, inline, structured data)

INCORRECT: Keep regenerating the entire table in chat for each change, since the output comes out correct every time.

Regenerating the whole table each time works, but it ignores the wasted effort of rebuilding 30 rows to alter one. Correct output is not the issue; the repeated full retype is. This would be acceptable for a one-off table, not one that changes again and again.

INCORRECT: Ask Claude to regenerate only the changed rows in chat, then paste those rows back into the full table by hand each time.

Regenerating just the changed rows and pasting them back reduces the retyping but leaves a manual merge step on every edit. This would be tolerable if changes were rare. Since the table is updated repeatedly, an artifact where edits apply in place removes that manual step entirely.

INCORRECT: Move the specifications table into a separate spreadsheet program and stop using Claude to maintain it.

Relocating the table to another program abandons Claude's help because of a formatting habit that an artifact would fix. The table did not need to leave Claude; it needed to stop being regenerated wholesale. Switching tools overcorrects for a problem artifacts solve directly.

questions.question:
An operations lead weighs two recurring tasks to support with Claude: sorting inbound tickets into fixed predefined categories, and resolving sensitive customer complaints that each need fresh judgment.

Which is the better-bounded use case?

options.label: A
options.text: The ticket sorting, since it follows fixed, objective categories that produce consistent results every time.

options.label: B
options.text: Either one, since both happen regularly and recur often enough to be worth automating.

options.label: C
options.text: The complaint resolution, since it takes more time and effort per case than sorting the tickets does.

options.label: D
options.text: Neither, since Claude should not be applied to any recurring customer-facing task at all.

questions.explanation:
CORRECT: The ticket sorting, since it follows fixed, objective categories that produce consistent results every time.

A well-bounded use case is defined by structure, not by how often it happens. Sorting tickets into fixed, predefined categories has clear inputs and consistent, objective outputs, which is exactly what makes a task a reliable fit for Claude. Resolving sensitive complaints recurs too, but each case turns on fresh human judgment, so it resists that kind of clean handling. Choosing the task with stable, rule-based criteria, rather than the one that merely recurs or takes effort, is the discrimination being tested.

Exam Guide Mapping

-
Domain 4: Workflow Integration and Solution Design (16%)

-
Objective: Apply Claude to analyze requirements and use cases

INCORRECT: Either one, since both happen regularly and recur often enough to be worth automating.

Treating frequency as the deciding factor misses what boundedness actually means. Both tasks recur, so recurrence cannot separate them. If both were rule-based, frequency might be a tiebreaker, but only the ticket sorting has the stable, objective structure that makes it well bounded.

INCORRECT: The complaint resolution, since it takes more time and effort per case than sorting the tickets does.

Picking the complaint task because it is more effort confuses difficulty with suitability. Effort per case says nothing about whether a task has clear, consistent criteria. The complaint work is hard precisely because it needs fresh judgment each time, which makes it less bounded, not more.

INCORRECT: Neither, since Claude should not be applied to any recurring customer-facing task at all.

Ruling out both tasks discards a genuinely strong, well-bounded candidate in the ticket sorting. Customer-facing does not make a task unsuitable; lack of structure does. Rejecting everything overcorrects and passes up a clear, reliable use case.
references: [When more complexity is warranted, workflows offer predictability and consistency for well-defined tasks...](https://www.anthropic.com/engineering/building-effective-agents#:~:text=When%2520more%2520complexity,is%2520usually%2520enough.)

questions.question:
A manager asks Claude to rank team members for a limited bonus pool, and Claude returns a clear ranked recommendation. The manager is tempted to adopt the ranking as the final allocation without further input.

What should the manager do?

options.label: A
options.text: Use Claude's ranking as input, but make and own the final decision as the accountable manager.

options.label: B
options.text: Adopt Claude's ranking as the final allocation, since it is clear, neatly ordered, and ready to use.

options.label: C
options.text: Ask Claude to double-check its own ranking, then adopt whatever revised order it returns.

options.label: D
options.text: Skip Claude entirely for the bonus decision and rank the team members from memory without any analysis.

questions.explanation:
CORRECT: Use Claude's ranking as input, but make and own the final decision as the accountable manager.

A bonus allocation directly affects people and carries real accountability, so it is not a decision to hand off to a recommendation, however clear. Claude's ranking is useful input, surfacing factors and a possible order, but the manager is the one answerable for the outcome and must make and own the final call. The point is not merely that a human decides in the abstract; a consequential, people-affecting decision needs an accountable human owning it, with the analysis serving as support.

Exam Guide Mapping

-
Domain 6: Governance, Risk, and Responsible Use (15%)

-
Objective: Understand the ethical implications of AI usage

INCORRECT: Adopt Claude's ranking as the final allocation, since it is clear, neatly ordered, and ready to use.

Adopting the ranking because it is clear and ready lets the recommendation become the decision. Clarity is not authority, especially for a call that affects people's pay. This would be reasonable only for a trivial, mechanical ordering, not an accountability-bearing allocation the manager must stand behind.

INCORRECT: Ask Claude to double-check its own ranking, then adopt whatever revised order it returns.

Having Claude recheck its own ranking still ends with the model, not the manager, effectively making the decision. A second pass does not transfer accountability to a human. The manager owning the outcome is what is required, which self-review does not provide.

INCORRECT: Skip Claude entirely for the bonus decision and rank the team members from memory without any analysis.

Dropping Claude altogether discards genuinely useful input that would inform a better decision. The problem was over-relying on the ranking, not using Claude at all. Deciding from memory alone overcorrects and throws away helpful analysis the manager could still own.

questions.question:
A team wants to speed up a workflow where documents keep bouncing between the drafting step and the review step, going back for revisions again and again.

What should the team do?

options.label: A
options.text: Map the full process to find why work loops between drafting and review, then fix the cause of the back-and-forth.

options.label: B
options.text: Add Claude to the drafting step to produce drafts faster, without looking at why the documents keep looping back for more revisions.

options.label: C
options.text: Ask reviewers to return revisions more quickly, so each pass through the loop takes less time.

options.label: D
options.text: Remove the review step entirely so documents can never be sent back for revision.

questions.explanation:
CORRECT: Map the full process to find why work loops between drafting and review, then fix the cause of the back-and-forth.

Speeding up one step will not help when the real waste is a loop: documents cycle between drafting and review over and over. Only mapping the whole process reveals why the back-and-forth happens, for instance drafts missing the review criteria, so writers can get it right the first time. Fixing the cause of the loop removes rounds of rework entirely. Looking at the end-to-end flow, rather than optimizing a single step, is what surfaces a repeating cycle no single step shows on its own.

Exam Guide Mapping

-
Domain 4: Workflow Integration and Solution Design (16%)

-
Objective: Leverage Claude for research, planning, and process optimization

INCORRECT: Add Claude to the drafting step to produce drafts faster, without looking at why the documents keep looping back for more revisions.

Speeding up drafting produces the same flawed drafts faster, so they still loop back for the same revisions. This would help if slow drafting were the bottleneck. The waste is the repeated cycle between two steps, which a faster single step does nothing to break.

INCORRECT: Ask reviewers to return revisions more quickly, so each pass through the loop takes less time.

Making each pass quicker shortens the loop but leaves it in place, so the rework keeps happening. If the loops were rare and unavoidable, faster turnaround would help. Here the repeated back-and-forth itself is the problem, so the fix is to remove its cause, not accelerate it.

INCORRECT: Remove the review step entirely so documents can never be sent back for revision.

Deleting review stops the looping by discarding a step that exists to catch problems. The goal was to end needless rework, not to abandon quality control. Cutting review overcorrects and trades one problem for worse, unreviewed output.

questions.question:
User testing of a new onboarding flow shows that most testers get stuck at one specific step, though the rest of the flow tests well. The team is tempted to scrap the whole design and start over.

What should the team do?

options.label: A
options.text: Give Claude the specific step testers got stuck on and iterate on that part, keeping the rest of the flow.

options.label: B
options.text: Scrap the entire onboarding flow and have Claude design a completely new one from scratch, ignoring the parts that tested well.

options.label: C
options.text: Ship the flow unchanged, since only one step tested poorly and the rest of it worked well.

options.label: D
options.text: Ask Claude to make the whole onboarding flow look more polished, without addressing the step testers got stuck on.

questions.explanation:
CORRECT: Give Claude the specific step testers got stuck on and iterate on that part, keeping the rest of the flow.

The testing points to one specific failure, not a broken design: most of the flow tested well, and only a single step tripped users up. The efficient fix is to give Claude that concrete finding and iterate on just that step, keeping everything that already works. Feeding specific, evidence-based feedback into a targeted revision beats discarding a mostly-successful design. Precise test data is exactly what makes focused iteration possible, so there is no reason to start over from nothing.

Exam Guide Mapping

-
Domain 4: Workflow Integration and Solution Design (16%)

-
Objective: Use Claude to support solution design, development, and iteration

INCORRECT: Scrap the entire onboarding flow and have Claude design a completely new one from scratch, ignoring the parts that tested well.

Starting over throws away the parts testing already validated because of one problem step. A full restart would only make sense if the whole design had failed. Since a single step is at fault, scrapping everything is wasteful and risks breaking what already worked.

INCORRECT: Ship the flow unchanged, since only one step tested poorly and the rest of it worked well.

Shipping as is ignores a step that most testers could not get past, a real barrier for future users. That the rest works does not excuse a known failure point. The testing surfaced a specific fix to make, not a reason to release the problem unaddressed.

INCORRECT: Ask Claude to make the whole onboarding flow look more polished, without addressing the step testers got stuck on.

Polishing the overall look leaves the one failing step exactly as it was, so users still get stuck. This treats appearance as the issue when the problem is a specific usability failure. Cosmetic changes do not fix the step the test data flagged.

questions.question:
A team applied Claude to the step they assumed was slowing a workflow, but overall turnaround barely improved. Measuring each step shows a different step is actually the main bottleneck.

What should the team do?

options.label: A
options.text: Refocus the effort on the step the measurements flag as the real bottleneck, not the one they assumed.

options.label: B
options.text: Keep Claude on the originally assumed step, since that is where they first expected the slowdown to be located.

options.label: C
options.text: Add more capacity to every single step of the workflow at once, without targeting the step the measurements flagged.

options.label: D
options.text: Conclude the workflow cannot be improved and leave it running as it currently is.

questions.explanation:
CORRECT: Refocus the effort on the step the measurements flag as the real bottleneck, not the one they assumed.

The team acted on an assumption that the measurements now contradict: the real constraint is a different step. Effort spent on the wrong step cannot move overall turnaround, which is why little changed. Refocusing on the step the data identifies as the true bottleneck is what actually speeds the process. Letting evidence, rather than an initial guess, decide where to apply Claude is the lesson here. Scoping the effort to the measured constraint puts it where it will make a real difference.

Exam Guide Mapping

-
Domain 4: Workflow Integration and Solution Design (16%)

-
Objective: Leverage Claude for research, planning, and process optimization

INCORRECT: Keep Claude on the originally assumed step, since that is where they first expected the slowdown to be located.

Staying on the assumed step keeps the effort where the data says it does not help. The original expectation has been tested and disproven by the measurements. Holding to a guess over evidence is exactly what leaves the true bottleneck untouched.

INCORRECT: Add more capacity to every single step of the workflow at once, without targeting the step the measurements flagged.

Reinforcing every step spreads effort thin and ignores the specific bottleneck the measurements pinpointed. This scattershot approach wastes resources on steps that are not constraining anything. The data already isolated where to focus, so broad, untargeted changes are unnecessary.

INCORRECT: Conclude the workflow cannot be improved and leave it running as it currently is.

Giving up treats one misplaced effort as proof nothing can help, when the measurements point directly to a fixable bottleneck. The first attempt failed only because it targeted the wrong step. Abandoning the effort overcorrects for a diagnosis the data has already corrected.

questions.question:
A team runs every purchase request, from a small supply order to a major contract, through the same long approval chain. Most requests are small and low-risk, yet all wait behind the full process.

Which two changes should the team make?

(choose two)

options.label: A
options.text: Create a fast-track path so small, low-risk requests clear with a shorter, lighter approval.

options.label: B
options.text: Route only the higher-value or higher-risk requests through the full approval chain.

options.label: C
options.text: Keep sending every request through the identical full chain, since one uniform process is simplest to administer.

options.label: D
options.text: Remove approvals altogether so that no purchase request needs any sign-off before proceeding.

options.label: E
options.text: Add an extra review stage to the existing chain, applied to small and large requests alike.

questions.explanation:
CORRECT: Create a fast-track path so small, low-risk requests clear with a shorter, lighter approval.

The rigidity is that one heavy path serves every request regardless of size, so small orders wait behind a process built for major contracts. Building a fast-track lane lets low-risk requests move through a lighter approval suited to their stakes. This is half of a two-part redesign: it fixes the many simple requests that never needed the full chain, cutting delay where the risk does not justify it.

CORRECT: Route only the higher-value or higher-risk requests through the full approval chain.

The other half is reserving the full, rigorous chain for the requests that actually warrant it. Tiering by value or risk means the heavy process still governs major contracts, where thorough sign-off matters, without slowing everything else. Paired with the fast-track lane, this splits one rigid path into a risk-based design, so scrutiny matches stakes across the whole workflow rather than applying uniformly.

Exam Guide Mapping

-
Domain 4: Workflow Integration and Solution Design (16%)

-
Objective: Integrate Claude into existing workflows to augment or redesign them

INCORRECT: Keep sending every request through the identical full chain, since one uniform process is simplest to administer.

Keeping the single chain preserves the exact rigidity causing the delay. Simplicity to administer is a weak justification when it makes every small order wait behind a heavyweight process. Ease for the approvers does not outweigh the cost of treating unlike requests alike.

Eliminating approvals entirely swings past redesign into abandoning control, exposing the organization on the very contracts that need oversight. The goal was to match scrutiny to risk, not to drop it. Removing all sign-off overcorrects and creates a far bigger problem than slow approvals.

questions.question:
An associate has already pitched a Claude workflow to a VP in clear business terms, but the VP stays hesitant and asks for proof it will actually deliver before committing budget.

What should the associate do?

options.label: A
options.text: Propose a small pilot with defined metrics, so the VP can see measurable results before committing budget.

options.label: B
options.text: Repeat the same business-outcome pitch again, since the value was already explained clearly the first time.

options.label: C
options.text: Send the VP detailed technical documentation about how the Claude workflow works under the hood.

options.label: D
options.text: Drop the proposal, since the VP did not commit immediately after the first pitch.

questions.explanation:
CORRECT: Propose a small pilot with defined metrics, so the VP can see measurable results before committing budget.

The VP is already sold on the concept and is now asking for evidence, not more explanation. What answers a request for proof is a small pilot with clear, measurable targets the VP can verify, turning claims into results they can see for themselves. A limited trial de-risks the commitment and lets the numbers make the case. Meeting a demand for proof with demonstrable outcomes, rather than repeating the pitch, is what moves a convinced-but-cautious stakeholder to commit.

Exam Guide Mapping

-
Domain 4: Workflow Integration and Solution Design (16%)

-
Objective: Communicate Claude's value and limitations to stakeholders

INCORRECT: Repeat the same business-outcome pitch again, since the value was already explained clearly the first time.

Repeating the pitch answers a question the VP is no longer asking, since they already understand the value. The block now is a lack of evidence, not a lack of clarity. Saying the same thing again offers nothing new to overcome the hesitation.

INCORRECT: Send the VP detailed technical documentation about how the Claude workflow works under the hood.

Technical documentation buries a non-technical stakeholder in detail they did not ask for and cannot easily use. The VP wants proof of results, not mechanics. This would fit a technical evaluator, but it does not give a business leader the evidence they requested.

INCORRECT: Drop the proposal, since the VP did not commit immediately after the first pitch.

Abandoning the proposal reads reasonable hesitation as rejection, when the VP actually signaled interest by asking for proof. The path forward is to supply that evidence, not to walk away. Giving up overcorrects for a request that a pilot would satisfy.

questions.question:
An associate is introducing a Claude drafting workflow to their team and wants to set expectations. Some members expect polished, perfect output on the very first try with no setup.

What should the associate tell them?

options.label: A
options.text: Explain that good results take some setup, examples, and iteration, so early drafts will improve as the workflow is tuned.

options.label: B
options.text: Assure the team that Claude will produce perfect, ready-to-use drafts from the very first prompt onward.

options.label: C
options.text: Tell the team the output quality is unpredictable, so they should not expect Claude to be much help.

options.label: D
options.text: Say nothing about expectations and let the team discover how the workflow behaves on their own.

questions.explanation:
CORRECT: Explain that good results take some setup, examples, and iteration, so early drafts will improve as the workflow is tuned.

Expecting flawless output on the first try sets the team up for disappointment and early abandonment. Accurate expectations describe the real ramp: quality climbs as the workflow is given good instructions, examples, and a few rounds of refinement. Framing it this way prepares people to invest in tuning rather than judging Claude on an unpolished first draft. Setting honest expectations about the effort-to-quality curve, neither overpromising perfection nor underselling the tool, is what sustains adoption.

INCORRECT: Assure the team that Claude will produce perfect, ready-to-use drafts from the very first prompt onward.

Promising perfect first-try drafts reinforces the exact expectation that leads to disappointment. When reality falls short of flawless, trust erodes and people give up. Overpromising sets a bar the ramp-up cannot meet at the start.

INCORRECT: Tell the team the output quality is unpredictable, so they should not expect Claude to be much help.

Underselling the tool as unreliable swings too far the other way, discouraging a team that could benefit with a little setup. It trades a false high for a false low. Accurate expectations describe steady improvement with tuning, not a warning to expect little.

INCORRECT: Say nothing about expectations and let the team discover how the workflow behaves on their own.

Leaving the team to find out themselves lets the perfect-first-try assumption stand and likely fail. Setting expectations is precisely the associate's job here. Staying silent forfeits the chance to frame the ramp so people stick with the workflow.
