questions.question:
A marketing associate wants Claude's outputs to sound more on-brand and proposes training a custom model on the company's past campaigns, building the evaluation pipeline to tune it. The associate has no machine learning background.

What should the associate do?

options.label: A
options.text: Escalate the custom model training to a Claude Architect or Developer, since it is specialized machine learning work beyond Associate scope.

options.label: B
options.text: Proceed to build and tune the custom model themselves, following online tutorials to fill the machine learning gaps.

options.label: C
options.text: Ask Claude to write all the model training and evaluation code, then run the pipeline without expert oversight.

options.label: D
options.text: Abandon the goal of more on-brand outputs entirely, since a custom model cannot be built in-house.

questions.explanation:
CORRECT: Escalate the custom model training to a Claude Architect or Developer, since it is specialized machine learning work beyond Associate scope.

Training and evaluating a custom model is specialized machine learning engineering, exactly the kind of technical build the Associate role escalates rather than attempts. The associate has no machine learning background, and the task sits squarely in Architect and Developer territory. Recognizing that boundary and routing the work to the right specialists is the correct move. The skill being tested is knowing when a goal requires expertise beyond the platform-native work an Associate handles, and escalating instead of improvising.

INCORRECT: Proceed to build and tune the custom model themselves, following online tutorials to fill the machine learning gaps.

Self-teaching model training from tutorials takes on a specialized engineering task without the expertise to do it safely or well. Good intentions do not close a real skills gap. This is precisely the kind of work an Associate should hand to a Developer or Architect, not attempt alone.

INCORRECT: Ask Claude to write all the model training and evaluation code, then run the pipeline without expert oversight.

Having Claude generate the code still leaves an untrained associate running a machine learning pipeline they cannot evaluate or debug. Generated code is not a substitute for the expertise to judge it. The build needs qualified oversight, which asking Claude to write it does not supply.

INCORRECT: Abandon the goal of more on-brand outputs entirely, since a custom model cannot be built in-house.

Dropping the goal assumes the only path to on-brand output is a custom model, which is not true. Escalating gets expert help, and simpler platform-native options like strong instructions and examples may achieve the same aim. Giving up overcorrects and forecloses approaches that do not require training a model at all.

questions.question:
A team's internal training guide, already approved and in use, now needs to serve new hires from a different department who lack the assumed background. The content is sound but pitched for the original audience.

What should the team do?

options.label: A
options.text: Have Claude adapt the approved guide for the new department's background, keeping its validated content intact.

options.label: B
options.text: Send the existing guide to the new hires unchanged, since it was already approved for the original department.

options.label: C
options.text: Write a brand-new training guide from scratch for the new department, setting the approved one aside entirely.

options.label: D
options.text: Add a short note to the front of the guide saying some sections may not apply to the new department.

questions.explanation:
CORRECT: Have Claude adapt the approved guide for the new department's background, keeping its validated content intact.

The guide's content is sound and already approved; only its framing assumes a background the new hires lack. That calls for repurposing, not replacement: have Claude adapt the existing, validated material to the new audience's starting point. Reusing the approved artifact preserves what already works while retargeting it, which is faster and lower-risk than building fresh. Recognizing that a proven deliverable can be adapted for a new purpose, rather than rewritten from nothing, is the efficient path here.

INCORRECT: Send the existing guide to the new hires unchanged, since it was already approved for the original department.

Sending it unchanged ignores that the new hires lack the background the guide assumes, so it will not land for them. Prior approval was for a different audience, not this one. The content being validated does not make it fit readers it was never written for.

INCORRECT: Write a brand-new training guide from scratch for the new department, setting the approved one aside entirely.

Starting from scratch discards a guide whose content is already sound and approved. A full rewrite would make sense only if the material itself were wrong, which it is not. Rebuilding from nothing wastes effort that adapting the existing guide would save.

INCORRECT: Add a short note to the front of the guide saying some sections may not apply to the new department.

A front-page caveat warns readers about the mismatch without fixing it, leaving new hires to struggle through content pitched over their heads. This gestures at the problem instead of resolving it. The guide needs adapting to the new audience, which a disclaimer does not accomplish.

questions.question:
A team's Project has detailed reference material and a style guide, yet Claude's monthly reports come out structured differently each time. No example of a finished report has ever been added to the Project.

What should the team do?

options.label: A
options.text: Add a couple of past finished reports as examples, so Claude has a model of the desired structure to follow.

options.label: B
options.text: Keep the current Project setup, since it already contains detailed reference material and the full style guide.

options.label: C
options.text: Add even more reference facts and background documents to the Project, without providing any example of a finished report.

options.label: D
options.text: Rebuild the Project from scratch, removing the existing reference material and style guide in the process.

questions.explanation:
CORRECT: Add a couple of past finished reports as examples, so Claude has a model of the desired structure to follow.

The Project holds plenty of facts and a style guide, but nothing showing Claude what a finished report should actually look like, which is why the structure keeps varying. The missing source is not more information; it is a model of the output. Adding a few past reports that hit the mark gives Claude a concrete target to emulate. Recognizing when the gap is a missing exemplar, rather than missing facts, and supplying example outputs is exactly what closes it.

INCORRECT: Keep the current Project setup, since it already contains detailed reference material and the full style guide.

Leaving the setup unchanged accepts the inconsistent reports, since the missing piece is still missing. Having reference material and a style guide is not the same as showing Claude a finished example. The varying structure is the signal that an output model, not more reference content, is needed.

INCORRECT: Add even more reference facts and background documents to the Project, without providing any example of a finished report.

Piling on more reference facts addresses a gap that is not the problem, since the Project is already rich in information. If the reports lacked facts, this would help. The issue is the absence of an example showing the desired structure, which more background documents do not provide.

INCORRECT: Rebuild the Project from scratch, removing the existing reference material and style guide in the process.

Starting over discards useful material that is not the cause of the problem. The reference content and style guide are fine; the Project just lacks an example report. Tearing it down overcorrects for a gap that adding one source would fill.

questions.question:
A team keeps its stable company reference material and its fast-changing, short-term campaign files in one Project. As campaign files pile up, the durable reference material is getting buried and hard to find.

What should the team do?

options.label: A
options.text: Split into two Projects, keeping stable reference material separate from the fast-changing campaign work.

options.label: B
options.text: Keep everything in the single Project, since all of the content belongs to the same team anyway.

options.label: C
options.text: Leave the one Project as it is but rename it to something broader, without separating the two kinds of content.

options.label: D
options.text: Create a brand-new Project for every individual campaign, however small or short-lived it is.

questions.explanation:
CORRECT: Split into two Projects, keeping stable reference material separate from the fast-changing campaign work.

The trouble is not how many Projects exist but what is mixed inside one: durable reference material and high-churn campaign files share a single space, so the stable content gets buried under the churn. Separating them into two Projects, one for lasting reference and one for active campaign work, keeps each clean and easy to maintain. Right-sizing structure sometimes means splitting by how long content lives, not by who owns it, so stable knowledge is not lost in the noise.

INCORRECT: Keep everything in the single Project, since all of the content belongs to the same team anyway.

Keeping it all together because it is one team's content ignores that the two kinds of material behave very differently. Shared ownership does not mean shared storage works well. Mixing stable reference with fast-changing files is precisely what is burying the durable content.

INCORRECT: Leave the one Project as it is but rename it to something broader, without separating the two kinds of content.

Renaming the Project changes its label, not its contents, so the reference material stays buried under campaign files. A broader name does nothing to reduce the clutter. The fix requires separating the content by lifecycle, which a rename does not touch.

INCORRECT: Create a brand-new Project for every individual campaign, however small or short-lived it is.

Spinning up a Project per campaign swings into fragmentation, scattering work across many thin Projects that are hard to manage. The goal was to separate durable reference from churn, not to multiply Projects endlessly. This overcorrects and trades clutter for sprawl.

questions.question:
An associate connects Google Drive and asks Claude to pull in a report a teammate created, but Claude cannot find it. The report was never shared with the associate's own Google account.

What should the associate do?

options.label: A
options.text: Recognize the connector only reaches files the connected account can access, and have the teammate share the report.

options.label: B
options.text: Assume the connector can reach any file anywhere in the company's Google Drive, and keep re-asking Claude to find it.

options.label: C
options.text: Reconnect the Google Drive connector from scratch, without changing whether the account can actually access the report.

options.label: D
options.text: Conclude the Google Drive connector is broken and stop using it to retrieve any documents at all.

questions.explanation:
CORRECT: Recognize the connector only reaches files the connected account can access, and have the teammate share the report.

A connector does not give Claude broader reach than the account it is connected to. It can only find and read files that account already has access to, so a report never shared with the associate's account is simply invisible to it. The fix is to have the teammate share the report, bringing it within the account's access. Understanding that a connector inherits the connected user's permissions, and no more, is what explains the missing file and how to resolve it.

INCORRECT: Assume the connector can reach any file anywhere in the company's Google Drive, and keep re-asking Claude to find it.

Assuming the connector can see any company file misreads how it works, so re-asking will keep failing. The connector's reach is bounded by the account's own access, not the whole organization's Drive. Repeating the request cannot retrieve a file the account was never given.

INCORRECT: Reconnect the Google Drive connector from scratch, without changing whether the account can actually access the report.

questions.question:
Using the Gmail connector, an associate asks Claude to read the figures inside a PDF attached to an email and summarize them. Claude can see the attachment's name and type but not what is inside it.

What should the associate do?

options.label: A
options.text: Download the PDF and give it to Claude directly, since the connector reads attachment metadata but not attachment content.

options.label: B
options.text: Keep asking Claude through the connector to open and read the attachment, assuming it will work if prompted clearly enough.

options.label: C
options.text: Ask Claude to summarize the attachment from its name and file type alone, without giving it the actual contents.

options.label: D
options.text: Conclude Claude cannot help with the figures at all and rekey the entire PDF by hand into a summary.

questions.explanation:
CORRECT: Download the PDF and give it to Claude directly, since the connector reads attachment metadata but not attachment content.

The Gmail connector can see an attachment's metadata, things like its name and type, but not the content inside it. No amount of rephrasing changes that, because the limit is in what the connector can access, not in how it is asked. The straightforward fix is to download the PDF and give it to Claude directly, so it can read the figures. Knowing which parts of an email a connector can and cannot reach, and supplying the rest yourself, is the practical skill here.

INCORRECT: Keep asking Claude through the connector to open and read the attachment, assuming it will work if prompted clearly enough.

Rephrasing the request cannot unlock content the connector is not able to access. The limit is a capability boundary, not a wording problem. If clearer prompts were the issue this might help, but the attachment's content is simply out of the connector's reach.

INCORRECT: Ask Claude to summarize the attachment from its name and file type alone, without giving it the actual contents.

Summarizing from the metadata alone produces guesswork, since the name and type reveal nothing about the figures inside. This treats the visible metadata as if it were the content. The actual numbers are what Claude needs, which only the file itself provides.

INCORRECT: Conclude Claude cannot help with the figures at all and rekey the entire PDF by hand into a summary.

Rekeying the whole PDF by hand abandons a task Claude handles easily once the file is supplied directly. The connector's limit was only about reaching the attachment, not about analyzing its contents. Doing it all manually overcorrects for a one-step workaround.

questions.question:
A Project's instructions tell Claude to always keep responses to a few sentences and also to always include full background and detail. Outputs swing unpredictably between very short and very long.

What should the team do?

options.label: A
options.text: Resolve the contradiction by deciding which rule wins, or when each applies, and rewrite the instructions to match.

options.label: B
options.text: Leave the instructions as they are, since each individual rule is clear and reasonable on its own.

options.label: C
options.text: Add a third instruction telling Claude to use good judgment, without resolving the direct conflict between the two existing rules.

options.label: D
options.text: Delete all length and detail instructions, leaving Claude with no guidance at all on how long responses should be.

questions.explanation:
CORRECT: Resolve the contradiction by deciding which rule wins, or when each applies, and rewrite the instructions to match.

The two rules, always be brief and always include full detail, pull in opposite directions, so Claude cannot satisfy both and the output swings unpredictably. Each rule reads fine alone; together they contradict. The fix is to decide which one takes priority, or to specify when each applies, and rewrite the instructions so they no longer clash. Instructions fail not only when they are vague but when they are contradictory, and resolving that conflict is what makes the guidance actually followable.

INCORRECT: Leave the instructions as they are, since each individual rule is clear and reasonable on its own.

Leaving them unchanged keeps the very conflict causing the swings. That each rule is clear on its own is exactly the trap, since clarity alone does not prevent two rules from contradicting. The instructions stay unfollowable until the clash is resolved.

INCORRECT: Add a third instruction telling Claude to use good judgment, without resolving the direct conflict between the two existing rules.

Adding a judgment note leaves the two contradictory rules in place, so Claude still has no consistent basis to choose between them. If the rules merely needed nuance, this might help. Because they directly conflict, one has to take precedence, which a vague third rule does not establish.

INCORRECT: Delete all length and detail instructions, leaving Claude with no guidance at all on how long responses should be.

Stripping out all length guidance removes the conflict by removing the direction entirely, so response length becomes a coin toss. The goal was consistent output, not the absence of rules. Deleting everything overcorrects and trades contradiction for no guidance.

questions.question:
A support Project's instructions tell Claude to escalate any refund over $50 to a manager, but the company raised that threshold to $200 last month. Claude keeps flagging refunds that no longer need escalation.

What should the team do?

options.label: A
options.text: Update the instruction to the current $200 threshold, so Claude escalates only refunds that now require it.

options.label: B
options.text: Leave the instruction at the old $50 threshold, since it still technically produces an escalation and nothing is outright breaking.

options.label: C
options.text: Tell agents to ignore Claude's unnecessary escalations, without changing the outdated instruction itself.

options.label: D
options.text: Remove the refund escalation instruction entirely, so that no refunds get escalated to a manager at all.

questions.explanation:
CORRECT: Update the instruction to the current $200 threshold, so Claude escalates only refunds that now require it.

The instruction still encodes the old $50 threshold, so Claude keeps escalating refunds that current policy no longer requires. This is not a wording problem but a stale rule driving the wrong action. Updating the instruction to the current $200 threshold makes Claude's behavior match the policy again. Keeping configurations current matters most when instructions tell Claude how to act, since an outdated rule does not merely mislabel something, it produces the wrong outcome every time it runs.

INCORRECT: Leave the instruction at the old $50 threshold, since it still technically produces an escalation and nothing is outright breaking.

Leaving the old threshold keeps Claude acting on a rule the company has already changed. That nothing is visibly broken ignores the steady stream of needless escalations. Producing an escalation is not the goal; producing the correct one under current policy is.

INCORRECT: Tell agents to ignore Claude's unnecessary escalations, without changing the outdated instruction itself.

Having agents ignore the extra escalations patches the symptom while the wrong rule keeps firing. This might be tolerable if the change were temporary or uncertain. Since the policy has definitively changed, the instruction itself should be updated to match.

INCORRECT: Remove the refund escalation instruction entirely, so that no refunds get escalated to a manager at all.

Deleting the instruction stops the over-escalation but also ends escalation for the large refunds that genuinely need it. The rule needed a new number, not removal. Cutting it entirely overcorrects and creates a real gap where oversight still matters.

questions.question:
A Project's knowledge file that several chats rely on has some sections that are clearly outdated and others that are still accurate. The team notices the outdated parts are skewing answers.

Which two actions should the team take?

(choose two)

options.label: A
options.text: Replace the file with an updated version that corrects the outdated sections while keeping the accurate content.

options.label: B
options.text: Check the file's remaining sections against a reliable source to confirm they are still current before relying on them.

options.label: C
options.text: Delete the entire file from the knowledge base because some of its sections are outdated.

options.label: D
options.text: Leave the file in place unchanged, since much of its content is still accurate and useful.

options.label: E
options.text: Keep both the old file and a corrected version in the knowledge base so that no information is ever lost.

questions.explanation:
CORRECT: Replace the file with an updated version that corrects the outdated sections while keeping the accurate content.

The file is not entirely wrong, only partly outdated, so deleting it outright would throw away the sections that are still accurate. The right move is to replace it with a corrected version that fixes the stale parts and preserves the good content. That keeps the knowledge base both accurate and complete, which is the goal when a source has gone partly out of date rather than wholly obsolete.

CORRECT: Check the file's remaining sections against a reliable source to confirm they are still current before relying on them.

Because part of the file has drifted out of date, the sections that look current can no longer be taken on trust either. Checking the rest against a reliable source confirms what is still accurate before the team depends on it. Pairing the fix with this verification makes the whole file trustworthy again, not just the parts that were obviously stale.

INCORRECT: Delete the entire file from the knowledge base because some of its sections are outdated.

Deleting the whole file removes the outdated sections but also discards the accurate ones, leaving a gap the team still needs filled. Wholesale deletion is the right call only when a file is entirely obsolete. Here the fix is to correct the stale parts, not erase everything.

INCORRECT: Leave the file in place unchanged, since much of its content is still accurate and useful.

Leaving the file as is keeps the outdated sections in play, and they are already skewing answers. That much of the content is still accurate does not excuse the parts that are wrong. Partial accuracy is no reason to tolerate known-stale material in a shared source.

INCORRECT: Keep both the old file and a corrected version in the knowledge base so that no information is ever lost.

Keeping the old file alongside the corrected one leaves two versions that disagree, so Claude may draw on the outdated one and reintroduce the very errors being fixed. Nothing is lost by removing the superseded file once its good content lives in the update. Retaining both creates conflicting sources, not safety.

questions.question:
A team wants to use customer feedback, originally collected only to improve product quality, to build targeted marketing profiles. Customers were never told their feedback might be used this way.

What should the team do?

options.label: A
options.text: Confirm the new marketing use is permitted and disclosed to customers before proceeding, since it exceeds the original purpose.

options.label: B
options.text: Proceed with building the profiles, since the company already holds the feedback data internally.

options.label: C
options.text: Anonymize the feedback before building the profiles, without addressing that customers were never told of this use.

options.label: D
options.text: Drop the marketing idea entirely, since customer feedback can never be used for any purpose beyond the one it was first collected for.

questions.explanation:
CORRECT: Confirm the new marketing use is permitted and disclosed to customers before proceeding, since it exceeds the original purpose.

The purpose itself, marketing analysis, is not inherently wrong, but the data was gathered only to improve product quality, and customers were never told it might be used this way. Using it for a new purpose without notice or consent is the real gap. The team should confirm the new use is permitted and disclose it before proceeding. Recognizing a purpose-limitation and consent issue, and closing it rather than assuming internal data is free to repurpose, is what makes the use appropriate.

INCORRECT: Proceed with building the profiles, since the company already holds the feedback data internally.

Proceeding because the company already holds the data treats possession as permission. Having data internally says nothing about whether it may be used for a purpose customers were never told about. The consent gap remains no matter who holds the feedback.

INCORRECT: Anonymize the feedback before building the profiles, without addressing that customers were never told of this use.

Anonymizing addresses identifiability, which is not the problem here. The concern is that the data is being repurposed beyond what customers were told, and stripping identifiers does not resolve a consent and purpose-limitation issue. This would matter if re-identification were the risk, but the missing notice is what needs closing.

INCORRECT: Drop the marketing idea entirely, since customer feedback can never be used for any purpose beyond the one it was first collected for.

Abandoning the idea assumes a new purpose is always forbidden, which is not true. With proper notice or consent, the feedback may well be usable for marketing. Giving up overcorrects for a gap that disclosure and confirmation could resolve.

questions.question:
A retail team plans to use ordinary purchase-history data to infer which customers may be pregnant, then target them with offers. The data looks routine, but the inference is highly sensitive.

What should the team do?

options.label: A
options.text: Pause and check with compliance, since inferring a sensitive condition can trigger privacy rules despite ordinary-looking data.

options.label: B
options.text: Proceed with the targeting, since purchase history is routine data the company already collects.

options.label: C
options.text: Remove customer names from the purchase data before running the inference, then proceed with the targeting as planned.

options.label: D
options.text: Abandon all use of purchase-history data for any analysis at all, since some possible uses could be sensitive.

questions.explanation:
CORRECT: Pause and check with compliance, since inferring a sensitive condition can trigger privacy rules despite ordinary-looking data.

It is tempting to treat purchase history as harmless because the company already collects it, but the concern is not the raw data, it is what the team wants to infer from it. Deducing a sensitive condition like pregnancy can bring the use under privacy rules even though the input looks ordinary. The team should pause and check with compliance before proceeding, because the processing purpose, not the data type, is what raises the risk. Judging by the use, not just the data, is the lesson.

INCORRECT: Proceed with the targeting, since purchase history is routine data the company already collects.

Proceeding because the data is routine looks only at the input, not the sensitive inference being drawn from it. Ordinary data can become a regulated matter the moment it is used to deduce something sensitive. The routine nature of purchase history does not clear the use that follows.

INCORRECT: Remove customer names from the purchase data before running the inference, then proceed with the targeting as planned.

Stripping names treats this as an identification problem, but the customers still get targeted based on a sensitive inference. Anonymizing the input does not address the sensitivity of the purpose. This would help if identifiability were the issue, yet the concern is what the inference does, not who is named.

INCORRECT: Abandon all use of purchase-history data for any analysis at all, since some possible uses could be sensitive.

Banning all purchase-history analysis discards many legitimate, low-risk uses because one specific use is sensitive. The problem is this inference, not the data as a whole. A blanket ban overcorrects for a concern that a compliance check on this use would address.

questions.question:
An associate prepares a customer feedback dataset for analysis by deleting the name and email columns, but the open-ended comment field still mentions customers by name and includes specific personal details.

What should the associate do?

options.label: A
options.text: Scrub the free-text comment field of names and personal details too, not just the structured identifier columns.

options.label: B
options.text: Proceed with the analysis, since the dedicated name and email columns have already been removed.

options.label: C
options.text: Instruct Claude to ignore any names in the comments, without actually removing them from the data.

options.label: D
options.text: Cancel the analysis entirely, since customer data can never be safely anonymized once any free-text comments are involved.

questions.explanation:
CORRECT: Scrub the free-text comment field of names and personal details too, not just the structured identifier columns.

Removing the name and email columns handles the obvious identifiers but misses the ones hiding in plain sight: the open comment field still names customers and includes personal details. Direct identifiers do not only live in labeled columns; free-text carries them too. The associate needs to scrub the comment field as well, redacting names and specifics, before the data is safe to analyze. Anonymization means finding identifiers wherever they appear, including unstructured text, not just clearing the columns meant to hold them.

INCORRECT: Proceed with the analysis, since the dedicated name and email columns have already been removed.

An HR analyst wants Claude to analyze team attendance trends and uploads the full employee dataset, which also includes salary, health status, and disciplinary records that the attendance analysis does not need.

What should the analyst do?

options.label: A
options.text: Remove the columns the analysis does not need, keeping only the attendance-related fields before uploading.

options.label: B
options.text: Upload the complete dataset as is, since Claude can simply focus on the attendance columns and ignore the rest.

options.label: C
options.text: Add an instruction telling Claude not to use the salary, health, or disciplinary columns, while still uploading them.

options.label: D
options.text: Cancel the attendance analysis entirely, since the employee dataset happens to contain some sensitive fields.

questions.explanation:
CORRECT: Remove the columns the analysis does not need, keeping only the attendance-related fields before uploading.

The attendance analysis needs only the attendance-related fields, yet the upload also carries salary, health, and disciplinary data the task never requires. Data minimization means sharing only what the job actually needs, so the fix is to strip the irrelevant sensitive columns before uploading. That removes needless exposure without affecting the analysis at all. Limiting the data to the task at hand, rather than uploading everything because it is convenient, is the safeguard being tested here.

INCORRECT: Upload the complete dataset as is, since Claude can simply focus on the attendance columns and ignore the rest.

Uploading everything because Claude can focus on the right columns still exposes salary, health, and disciplinary data that had no reason to be shared. What Claude attends to does not change what was disclosed. The unnecessary sensitive fields are exposed the moment they are uploaded.

INCORRECT: Add an instruction telling Claude not to use the salary, health, or disciplinary columns, while still uploading them.

Telling Claude to skip the sensitive columns leaves them in the uploaded data regardless, so the exposure remains. An instruction to ignore is not the same as not sharing. Minimization requires removing the unneeded fields, which an ignore instruction does not do.

INCORRECT: Cancel the attendance analysis entirely, since the employee dataset happens to contain some sensitive fields.

Canceling the analysis abandons a legitimate task because the source file included extra fields. The presence of sensitive columns is something to strip, not a reason to stop. Dropping the work overcorrects for a problem that trimming the dataset solves.

questions.question:
An employee is about to type a sensitive personal matter into their company Team-plan account, assuming those chats are completely private, since teammates cannot read one another's conversations.

What should the employee understand?

options.label: A
options.text: On a company workspace plan, the organization can access members' chats under policy, so it is not a fully private space.

options.label: B
options.text: Assume the work chats are completely private, since regular teammates cannot casually read one another's conversations.

options.label: C
options.text: Turn off the help improve Claude training setting, believing that will make the chats private from the company.

options.label: D
options.text: Conclude Claude cannot be used for any work purpose at all, since the company is able to access whatever gets typed.

questions.explanation:
CORRECT: On a company workspace plan, the organization can access members' chats under policy, so it is not a fully private space.

The mistake is treating a company workspace like a personal account. On Team and Enterprise plans, the content is not used to train models and teammates cannot casually browse each other's chats, but the organization can still access members' conversations under its policies, for example through a workspace data export. So a work account is a company asset, not a private space. Understanding this visibility model, which is separate from whether chats are used for training, is what guides handling a sensitive personal matter appropriately.

INCORRECT: Assume the work chats are completely private, since regular teammates cannot casually read one another's conversations.

Assuming full privacy because peers cannot browse chats misses that the organization itself can access workspace content under policy. Teammate-level privacy is not the same as privacy from the company. The sensitive matter would still sit in a space the employer can reach.

INCORRECT: Turn off the help improve Claude training setting, believing that will make the chats private from the company.

Turning off the training setting addresses whether chats are used to improve models, not whether the company can see them. This conflates two different things. The organization's ability to access workspace content is unaffected by the training toggle, so this does not deliver the privacy the employee assumes.

INCORRECT: Conclude Claude cannot be used for any work purpose at all, since the company is able to access whatever gets typed.

Deciding the tool is unusable swings too far, since a work account is perfectly appropriate for work content the company may access. The issue is only where a sensitive personal matter belongs. Abandoning Claude for work overcorrects for a visibility model that simply calls for judgment about what to type where.

questions.question:
A compliance-sensitive document requires review before release. The review step is being completed on every document, but the person who writes each document is also the one who reviews it.

What should the team do?

options.label: A
options.text: Assign an independent, qualified reviewer other than the author, so the review can actually catch problems.

options.label: B
options.text: Keep letting authors review their own documents, since the required review step is technically being completed each time.

options.label: C
options.text: Ask authors to review their own work more carefully, without assigning a separate reviewer to check it.

options.label: D
options.text: Remove the review step altogether, since the authors already know their own documents best.

questions.explanation:
CORRECT: Assign an independent, qualified reviewer other than the author, so the review can actually catch problems.

The review is happening in form, but an author reviewing their own work cannot provide the independent scrutiny the step exists for, since people tend to miss their own errors and assumptions. Substance requires a separate, qualified reviewer who can see what the author cannot. Assigning an independent reviewer restores the check's real purpose. A governance step is only meaningful when the right person performs it; self-review ticks the box but not the intent, which is exactly what this tests.

INCORRECT: Keep letting authors review their own documents, since the required review step is technically being completed each time.

Keeping self-review because the step is technically done treats the checkbox as the goal. A review with no independence cannot catch the author's own blind spots. Completion in name does not deliver the scrutiny the step is meant to provide.

INCORRECT: Ask authors to review their own work more carefully, without assigning a separate reviewer to check it.

Asking authors to be more careful still leaves them checking their own work, so the missing independence is never added. Care does not substitute for a second set of eyes. The problem is who reviews, not how hard they try, so a separate reviewer is required.

INCORRECT: Remove the review step altogether, since the authors already know their own documents best.

Eliminating review entirely discards an important control for compliance-sensitive documents. Authors knowing their work well is the very reason they cannot objectively review it. Dropping the step overcorrects and removes oversight precisely where it matters most.

questions.question:
A company sells to customers in several countries with different data-protection laws. An associate is unsure which country's rules govern a planned use of Claude on customer data spanning those regions.

What should the associate do?

options.label: A
options.text: Escalate the cross-border question to legal to determine which jurisdiction's rules apply before proceeding.

options.label: B
options.text: Proceed under the associate's own best guess about which country's rules most likely apply here.

options.label: C
options.text: Apply whichever country's rules seem the least restrictive, so the planned use can go ahead most easily.

options.label: D
options.text: Cancel the planned use entirely, since customers span several countries with differing data-protection laws.

questions.explanation:
CORRECT: Escalate the cross-border question to legal to determine which jurisdiction's rules apply before proceeding.

Which country's data-protection law governs a use spanning several regions is a genuine legal question, not one an associate should resolve by guessing. Getting it wrong can breach the rules of a jurisdiction the associate did not even consider. Escalating to legal for a definitive answer on which rules apply is the responsible step before proceeding. Recognizing a cross-border regulatory uncertainty as something to route to legal, rather than settle alone, is the judgment this scenario is testing.

INCORRECT: Proceed under the associate's own best guess about which country's rules most likely apply here.

Proceeding on a personal guess treats a legal determination as something an associate can decide informally. A reasonable-sounding assumption offers no protection if it is wrong in one of the jurisdictions involved. Which rules apply across borders is exactly the kind of question that needs a definitive legal answer.

INCORRECT: Apply whichever country's rules seem the least restrictive, so the planned use can go ahead most easily.

Choosing the least restrictive rules picks convenience over compliance and can violate the stricter laws that actually govern some of the customers. Ease of proceeding is not a valid basis for selecting which law applies. This invites exactly the breach the associate should be avoiding.

INCORRECT: Cancel the planned use entirely, since customers span several countries with differing data-protection laws.

Abandoning the use assumes cross-border data can never be handled compliantly, which is untrue once legal clarifies the applicable rules. The uncertainty is a question to resolve, not a dead end. Giving up overcorrects for something an escalation would settle.

questions.question:
An insurance team uses Claude to help set pricing and notices the model's suggested premiums run higher for applicants in certain neighborhoods, a pattern that may act as a proxy for a protected class.

Which two actions should the team take before deploying it?

(choose two)

options.label: A
options.text: Audit the specific criteria driving the neighborhood-based price differences for proxy discrimination.

options.label: B
options.text: Route the pricing approach to compliance or a fairness reviewer before it is deployed.

options.label: C
options.text: Deploy the pricing as suggested, since the model produced the differences from the data on its own.

options.label: D
options.text: Remove only the literal neighborhood field, assuming that alone eliminates any proxy effect.

options.label: E
options.text: Abandon AI-assisted pricing altogether, since the pattern surfaced a possible fairness concern.

questions.explanation:
CORRECT: Audit the specific criteria driving the neighborhood-based price differences for proxy discrimination.

The first action is to examine what is actually producing the skew. A neighborhood signal can stand in for a protected class, so the team needs to audit which criteria drive the higher premiums and whether they reflect legitimate risk factors or a discriminatory proxy. Investigating the specific drivers, rather than accepting the output, is what reveals whether the pattern is a genuine fairness problem.

CORRECT: Route the pricing approach to compliance or a fairness reviewer before it is deployed.

The second action is to bring in the right expertise before anything ships. Proxy discrimination in pricing carries legal and fairness stakes an associate should not adjudicate alone, so the approach should go to compliance or a fairness reviewer for sign-off. Pairing the technical audit with qualified review before deployment is what keeps a potentially discriminatory model from going live unchecked.

INCORRECT: Deploy the pricing as suggested, since the model produced the differences from the data on its own.

Deploying because the model generated the pattern itself treats an automated output as if it were automatically fair. A model learning a skew from data is how proxy discrimination arises, not a defense of it. The pattern is a reason to scrutinize, not to ship.

INCORRECT: Remove only the literal neighborhood field, assuming that alone eliminates any proxy effect.

Dropping just the neighborhood field assumes the proxy lives in one column, when other correlated variables can reproduce the same skew. This looks like a fix but leaves the underlying pattern intact. Genuine auditing, not deleting a single obvious field, is what addresses proxy effects.

INCORRECT: Abandon AI-assisted pricing altogether, since the pattern surfaced a possible fairness concern.

Scrapping AI-assisted pricing entirely overreacts to a concern that auditing and review are designed to resolve. A surfaced pattern is a prompt to investigate, not proof the whole approach is unusable. Abandoning it forgoes a workable tool that proper checks could make fair.

questions.question:
A company plans to publish AI-generated product reviews and testimonials on its site, written entirely by Claude but presented as if written by real customers, with no indication they are AI-generated.

What should the team do?

options.label: A
options.text: Disclose clearly that the reviews and testimonials are AI-generated, rather than presenting them as real customer writing.

options.label: B
options.text: Publish them as customer reviews without disclosure, since the content itself is accurate and well written.

options.label: C
options.text: Add a vague note that the site uses various content sources, without saying the reviews are AI-generated.

options.label: D
options.text: Cancel the review content entirely, since AI-generated material can never be published on the site.

questions.explanation:
CORRECT: Disclose clearly that the reviews and testimonials are AI-generated, rather than presenting them as real customer writing.

Presenting AI-written reviews as genuine customer testimonials misleads readers about who is speaking, which is the core problem regardless of how good the text is. Honest disclosure that the content is AI-generated is what the situation requires. The medium is published content rather than a live chatbot, but the duty is the same: make the AI nature clear so readers are not deceived. Recognizing that AI-authored material presented as human needs disclosure is the responsible-use principle at stake here.

INCORRECT: Publish them as customer reviews without disclosure, since the content itself is accurate and well written.

Publishing without disclosure because the writing is accurate and polished misses that the deception is about authorship, not quality. Well-crafted text presented as a real customer's words is still misleading. Accuracy does not excuse passing AI content off as human testimony.

INCORRECT: Add a vague note that the site uses various content sources, without saying the reviews are AI-generated.

A vague note about various sources gestures at transparency without actually telling readers these reviews are AI-generated. Disclosure that is too oblique to be understood does not inform anyone. To be meaningful, it has to make the AI authorship clear, which this does not.

INCORRECT: Cancel the review content entirely, since AI-generated material can never be published on the site.

Canceling assumes AI-generated content is never publishable, which is untrue when it is clearly disclosed as such. The problem was the deception, not the use of AI writing. Dropping the content overcorrects for an issue that honest disclosure resolves.

questions.question:
An analyst asks Claude to report "quarterly" revenue and gets figures that do not match the finance team's. The company uses a fiscal quarter, but Claude interpreted "quarterly" as calendar quarters.

What should the analyst do?

options.label: A
options.text: Define the term explicitly, specifying fiscal quarters, since the ambiguous word caused Claude to use the wrong definition.

options.label: B
options.text: Accept Claude's figures, since it did calculate quarterly revenue exactly as the word was written.

options.label: C
options.text: Manually adjust each of Claude's calendar-quarter figures to fiscal quarters after the fact, without fixing the prompt.

options.label: D
options.text: Stop using Claude for any revenue reporting, since it produced figures that did not match finance.

questions.explanation:
CORRECT: Define the term explicitly, specifying fiscal quarters, since the ambiguous word caused Claude to use the wrong definition.

The mismatch traces to a single ambiguous word: "quarterly" can mean fiscal or calendar quarters, and Claude picked the one the analyst did not intend. The root cause is the undefined term, not a calculation error, so the fix is to define it, telling Claude to use fiscal quarters. Diagnosing that a word with two meanings drove the wrong result, then pinning down which meaning applies, is what aligns the output with what finance expects. Naming the definition removes the ambiguity at its source.

INCORRECT: Accept Claude's figures, since it did calculate quarterly revenue exactly as the word was written.

Accepting the figures because Claude followed the word literally ignores that it used the wrong meaning of it. Technically correct on a calendar basis is still wrong for a company that reports fiscally. The literal calculation does not match the intended one, so it cannot stand.

questions.question:
A manager asks Claude to summarize a long project status report. The summary accurately covers the right topics at the right depth, but consistently leaves out the action items and next steps the team needs to act on.

What should the manager do?

options.label: A
options.text: Ask Claude to include the action items and next steps explicitly, since that is the category the summary keeps omitting.

options.label: B
options.text: Accept the summary as is, since it accurately covers the report's main topics at a reasonable level of detail.

options.label: C
options.text: Ask Claude to make the summary longer overall, without specifically requesting the action items and next steps.

options.label: D
options.text: Abandon the summaries and read the full status report each time to find the action items manually.

questions.explanation:
CORRECT: Ask Claude to include the action items and next steps explicitly, since that is the category the summary keeps omitting.

The summary is not generic or shallow; it handles the topics well but consistently drops one specific category the team depends on: action items and next steps. The fix is targeted, ask Claude to include that category explicitly, rather than reworking the whole summary. Identifying exactly what is missing and requesting it by name is what makes the output usable. When a summary is strong except for a known gap, naming the missing category is more effective than a broad instruction to do better.

INCORRECT: Accept the summary as is, since it accurately covers the report's main topics at a reasonable level of detail.

Accepting it because the topics are covered well ignores that the team cannot act without the missing next steps. Good coverage of everything except the actionable part still leaves the summary incomplete for its purpose. The known gap has to be filled, not overlooked.

INCORRECT: Ask Claude to make the summary longer overall, without specifically requesting the action items and next steps.

Asking for more length adds volume without targeting the specific missing category, so the action items may still be left out. The problem is not too little text but one absent element. A precise request for that category works where a general "make it longer" does not.

INCORRECT: Abandon the summaries and read the full status report each time to find the action items manually.

Reading the whole report by hand discards a summary that is already strong except for one fixable gap. The action items just needed to be requested. Reverting to manual reading overcorrects for a problem a single targeted instruction solves.

questions.question:
A team relies on a standing formatting requirement that one member keeps in a personal prompt. When a different teammate runs the same task, they do not know the requirement, so their output comes out wrong.

What should the team do?

options.label: A
options.text: Put the standing requirement into the Project's shared instructions, so it applies no matter who runs the task.

options.label: B
options.text: Leave the requirement in the one member's personal prompt, since it works correctly whenever that member runs the task.

options.label: C
options.text: Ask the member to remind teammates about the requirement each time someone else is about to run the task.

options.label: D
options.text: Accept that outputs will vary by teammate, since only the original member knows the formatting requirement.

questions.explanation:
CORRECT: Put the standing requirement into the Project's shared instructions, so it applies no matter who runs the task.

The requirement fails on handoff because it lives in one person's personal prompt, invisible to anyone else running the task. Moving it into the Project's shared instructions makes it apply for every member automatically, closing the gap the moment a different teammate takes over. A standing requirement that everyone must meet belongs where everyone shares it, not in an individual's private prompt. Persisting it at the team level, rather than relying on one person, is what makes the output consistent across whoever runs it.

INCORRECT: Leave the requirement in the one member's personal prompt, since it works correctly whenever that member runs the task.

Leaving it in one person's prompt keeps working only for that person, so every other teammate still produces wrong output. That it works for the original member is exactly why the failure is easy to miss. A requirement everyone needs cannot live where only one person has it.

INCORRECT: Ask the member to remind teammates about the requirement each time someone else is about to run the task.

Relying on manual reminders depends on the member being available and remembering every time, which will eventually break down. It substitutes a fragile human step for a durable shared setting. Putting the requirement in shared instructions removes the need to remind anyone.

INCORRECT: Accept that outputs will vary by teammate, since only the original member knows the formatting requirement.

Accepting inconsistent output treats a fixable configuration gap as unavoidable. The requirement can be shared so everyone meets it; there is no reason only one person should hold it. Tolerating the variation overcorrects toward giving up on a problem shared instructions solve.

questions.question:
Across many runs, Claude keeps formatting dates in the wrong format, using month/day when the company standard is day/month, the same way every single time. The associate keeps correcting them by hand.

What should the associate do?

options.label: A
options.text: Recognize the consistent date-format error and add a specific instruction for the required format, so it stops recurring.

options.label: B
options.text: Keep correcting the date format by hand each time, since every other part of the output is fine.

options.label: C
options.text: Rerun the same prompt and hope the dates come out right this time, without adding any formatting instruction at all.

options.label: D
options.text: Stop using Claude for anything involving dates, since it keeps getting the format wrong.

questions.explanation:
CORRECT: Recognize the consistent date-format error and add a specific instruction for the required format, so it stops recurring.

The same date-format mistake appearing on every run is the signal that this is a systematic error, not a random slip. Fixing it by hand each time treats a repeating cause as a series of one-off problems. The efficient fix is to recognize the pattern and add a specific instruction naming the required day/month format, so Claude gets it right from the start. Spotting a consistent error across runs and correcting it at the prompt level, rather than in each output, is the optimization here.

INCORRECT: Keep correcting the date format by hand each time, since every other part of the output is fine.

Correcting it by hand each run accepts a repeating cost that a single instruction would remove. That the rest of the output is fine does not excuse leaving a known, systematic error in place. This would be reasonable for a one-time slip, not an error that recurs identically every time.

INCORRECT: Rerun the same prompt and hope the dates come out right this time, without adding any formatting instruction at all.

Rerunning the unchanged prompt does nothing to address the cause, so the same format error is likely to appear again. Hoping for a different result from identical input is not a fix. The prompt has to specify the required format for the behavior to change.

INCORRECT: Stop using Claude for anything involving dates, since it keeps getting the format wrong.

Dropping Claude for date-related work overreacts to an error that one clear instruction resolves. The mistake is consistent and therefore easy to correct at the source. Abandoning the tool overcorrects for a problem a formatting rule fixes.

questions.question:
A team runs a daily mix of work at one fixed effort level: simple formatting jobs and deep analytical tasks alike. The routine jobs run slower than needed, while the complex analyses come out shallow.

What should the team do?

options.label: A
options.text: Set the effort level per task, raising it for the complex analyses and lowering it for the routine jobs.

options.label: B
options.text: Keep the single fixed effort level for everything, since one setting is the simplest to manage.

options.label: C
options.text: Raise the effort level for the whole mixed batch, so the complex analyses improve.

options.label: D
options.text: Stop using Claude for the complex analyses entirely, since a single effort level cannot serve every task in the mix.

questions.explanation:
CORRECT: Set the effort level per task, raising it for the complex analyses and lowering it for the routine jobs.

A mixed workload cannot be served well by one blanket effort level: the routine jobs run slower and use more than they need, while the complex analyses come out shallow. The fix is to match the effort setting to each task, raising it for the demanding analyses and lowering it for the simple jobs. Calibrating effort per task type, rather than defaulting everything to a single level, gives each task the depth it needs without spending effort on the ones that do not.

INCORRECT: Keep the single fixed effort level for everything, since one setting is the simplest to manage.

Keeping one level for the sake of simplicity is exactly what produces the mismatch, slow routine jobs and shallow analyses. Ease of management does not outweigh output that is wrong at both ends of the mix. A single setting cannot fit tasks with such different needs.

INCORRECT: Raise the effort level for the whole mixed batch, so the complex analyses improve.

Raising effort across the board does help the complex analyses, but it over-provisions the routine jobs, making them slower and more costly than necessary. This would be right if the batch were uniformly complex. Because it is mixed, each task type needs its own level, not one raised for all.

INCORRECT: Stop using Claude for the complex analyses entirely, since a single effort level cannot serve every task in the mix.

Removing the complex analyses from Claude abandons work it can do well at a higher effort level. The problem was a single blanket setting, not the tool's ability. Dropping those tasks overcorrects for something per-task effort calibration solves.

questions.question:
Each week, Claude produces a narrative summary and a separate metrics list, and an associate manually merges the two into one combined report by hand. The merge takes real time every week.

What should the associate do?

options.label: A
options.text: Have Claude produce the combined report directly, so the two parts no longer need to be merged by hand.

options.label: B
options.text: Keep merging the two outputs manually each week, since the final combined report comes out correct.

options.label: C
options.text: Ask Claude to make each of the two separate outputs shorter, without combining them into a single report at all.

options.label: D
options.text: Go back to writing the entire weekly report by hand, without using Claude for either part.

questions.explanation:
CORRECT: Have Claude produce the combined report directly, so the two parts no longer need to be merged by hand.

The weekly manual merge is a redundant step, because Claude can produce the combined report itself. Having it generate the narrative and metrics together, as one output, removes the by-hand merge entirely rather than leaving it as a standing task. The final report was never the problem; the extra manual step to assemble it was. Recognizing that Claude can deliver a single, ready-to-use output, instead of parts someone stitches together, eliminates the redundant work at its source.

INCORRECT: Keep merging the two outputs manually each week, since the final combined report comes out correct.

Continuing to merge by hand accepts a weekly task that Claude could remove. A correct final report does not justify a manual step that is entirely avoidable. This would be fine for a rare, one-time merge, not a redundant step that repeats every week.

INCORRECT: Ask Claude to make each of the two separate outputs shorter, without combining them into a single report at all.

Shortening the two outputs still leaves them as separate pieces the associate must merge, so the redundant step remains. Length was never the issue. The fix is to have Claude combine them, which trimming each part does not do.

INCORRECT: Go back to writing the entire weekly report by hand, without using Claude for either part.

Writing the whole report by hand discards Claude's useful output to avoid a merge it could simply do itself. The parts were fine; only the manual assembly was wasteful. Reverting to fully manual work overcorrects for a step Claude can absorb.

questions.question:
A farm co-op asked Claude which version of its spray safety sheet best matches the house style. That version went to print. A contractor could not tell from it which protective kit to wear.

What should the co-op do?

options.label: A
options.text: Choose again on whether a contractor can pick the right kit from the sheet.

options.label: B
options.text: Ask Claude to confirm that the printed version is safe for contractors to work from.

options.label: C
options.text: Give the versions to the contractors and let them pick one.

options.label: D
options.text: Tighten the house style guide, then have Claude choose from the versions again.

questions.explanation:
CORRECT: Choose again on whether a contractor can pick the right kit from the sheet.

House style was the only test the co-op gave, so house style is what Claude measured. Nobody told it the sheet decides what a contractor wears to spray. A version can match the house style perfectly and still leave that unanswered. The contractor has already shown which question matters. A standard comes from the job the output must do.

Exam Guide Mapping
* Domain 1: Prompting and Task Execution (14%)
* Objective: Create effective prompts for business and technical tasks

INCORRECT: Ask Claude to confirm that the printed version is safe for contractors to work from.

Asking for confirmation feels like a check, and it costs nothing. Claude judged the versions on house style, because that is the only guide it was given. A confirmation built on the same test repeats the same answer. Nobody has looked at whether a contractor could act on the words. Do not ask for reassurance in place of evidence.

INCORRECT: Give the versions to the contractors and let them pick one.

Contractors use the sheet, so letting them choose sounds fair and practical. Preference is not what the co-op needs to settle. It needs the version that tells a contractor which kit to wear. Contractors reading for style cannot answer that either. Do not hand a decision to a group when the standard is still wrong.

INCORRECT: Tighten the house style guide, then have Claude choose from the versions again.

The house style guide is the only standard in play, so improving it looks like progress. Nothing says the sheet is badly written or off style. The fault is the test itself, which measures presentation rather than whether a contractor can act. A stricter rule on the wrong measure moves nothing. Fix what you are measuring first.

questions.question:
A conference chair asks Claude to flag reviewers assigned to papers from their own institution. Claude repeats the rule correctly each time. She added a worked example, and the same twelve papers still failed, all with authors at four institutions.

What should she do?

options.label: A
options.text: Use a more capable tier where a reviewer has to be checked against four institutions.

options.label: B
options.text: Ask Claude to double-check its own conflict decisions before she reads them.

options.label: C
options.text: Check each author's institution in a separate request, then combine the answers by hand.

options.label: D
options.text: Load the full institution directory into the Project so that Claude can consult it before deciding.

questions.explanation:
CORRECT: Use a more capable tier where a reviewer has to be checked against four institutions.

Claude repeats the rule correctly, so the instruction has landed. The chair added a worked example and the same twelve papers failed again. Those papers each ask one reviewer to be checked against four institutions at once. That is more reasoning to hold, not clearer wording to supply. Capability is what a task of that shape needs.

Exam Guide Mapping
* Domain 1: Prompting and Task Execution (14%)
* Objective: Create effective prompts for business and technical tasks

INCORRECT: Ask Claude to double-check its own conflict decisions before she reads them.

A second look costs nothing and feels like a safety net. The failures sit on the papers with the most relationships to track. The same tier doing the same work a second time meets the same difficulty. Nothing in the question suggests carelessness that a review would catch. Do not ask for a recheck when capability is the limit.

INCORRECT: Check each author's institution in a separate request, then combine the answers by hand.

Splitting a hard job into small pieces is often good advice. The conflict rule compares a reviewer against every author on one paper. One author per request hides exactly the comparison that has to be made. The chair would then rebuild the whole picture herself. Split a task only where the pieces can be judged alone.

INCORRECT: Load the full institution directory into the Project so that Claude can consult it before deciding.

A Project's knowledge base holds documents Claude reads for background, so adding the directory looks helpful. Nothing here says an institution was unknown. Claude named the rule and read the papers. The twelve failures are the papers with the most affiliations to compare. Reference material fills a gap in facts, never a gap in reasoning.

questions.question:
A cricket club asked Claude how to raise its profile in the town. The committee read the reply out at its meeting. Every member agreed with it, and nobody could name a thing to do next week.

What should the club do?

options.label: A
options.text: Ask Claude to draft a letter to the town's primary schools.

options.label: B
options.text: Ask Claude to rank its suggestions by likely effect and give the top ten.

options.label: C
options.text: Send the reply to every member and ask each of them to try one thing.

options.label: D
options.text: Ask Claude to write a three year marketing strategy for the club.

questions.explanation:
CORRECT: Ask Claude to draft a letter to the town's primary schools.

Raise its profile is a result the club wants, not something Claude can hand over. That is why the reply was agreeable and empty. A letter to the schools is a thing the secretary can post on Monday. Naming the artefact turns the request into work Claude can do. Ask for the output, not the outcome.

Exam Guide Mapping
* Domain 1: Prompting and Task Execution (14%)
* Objective: Create effective prompts for business and technical tasks

INCORRECT: Ask Claude to rank its suggestions by likely effect and give the top ten.

A ranked list looks like a decision, and ranking feels like progress. Ten suggestions ordered by effect are still ten pieces of advice. Somebody still has to turn the top one into a letter, a poster or a phone call. The form changed and the type of output did not. A list of ideas is advice with numbers on it.

INCORRECT: Send the reply to every member and ask each of them to try one thing.

Members know the town, so passing the advice round sounds practical. The advice is general, which means each member now has to invent the specifics. That is the work the committee asked Claude to do. Each member inventing separately produces a different answer. Do not pass an unusable output on to other people.

INCORRECT: Ask Claude to write a three year marketing strategy for the club.

A strategy is a real document, so this does name a deliverable. Three years of marketing is a large thing for a committee that meets monthly. It also has to be agreed before anything happens, and nothing happens next week. A strategy answers a question nobody in the room asked. Match the size of the deliverable to the size of the problem.

questions.question:
A brass band must book a Christmas concert venue. The band's booking policy lists four requirements. The secretary asked Claude to compare three halls and got a recommendation praising the acoustics, which the policy never mentions.

What should she do?

options.label: A
options.text: Ask for the three halls measured against the four requirements the band's booking policy sets out.

options.label: B
options.text: Have Claude write a scoring model that weights every feature of all three halls out of a hundred.

options.label: C
options.text: Send the three halls to the committee and let members argue it out at the next meeting.

options.label: D
options.text: Upload the booking policy to a Project, so the next venue question has it.

questions.explanation:
CORRECT: Ask for the three halls measured against the four requirements the band's booking policy sets out.

The band already owns a standard. Its booking policy names four requirements, and the recommendation rests on acoustics, which is not one of them. Nothing in the request pointed at those four requirements. Handing over the four requirements gives every hall the same test, and the test is the band's own. The answer then serves the booking.

Exam Guide Mapping
* Domain 1: Prompting and Task Execution (14%)
* Objective: Create effective prompts for business and technical tasks

INCORRECT: Have Claude write a scoring model that weights every feature of all three halls out of a hundred.

A scoring model looks rigorous and produces one clear number per hall. It also invents weights nobody agreed, spread across features the policy never asked about. The band has four requirements, and a hall either meets them or does not. Machinery does not settle a question a short list already answers.

INCORRECT: Send the three halls to the committee and let members argue it out at the next meeting.

Committees do book venues, so this feels like the proper route. The members would arrive with the same recommendation and the same missing test. They would argue about acoustics because that is what the reply talks about. Give people a comparison against an agreed standard, not a debate to have.

INCORRECT: Upload the booking policy to a Project, so the next venue question has it.

A Project's knowledge base holds documents Claude reads for background, so the policy would be useful there. The band must book a hall for this Christmas. Setting a Project up leaves today's recommendation exactly as it is, still resting on acoustics. Prepare for next time after you have answered this time.

questions.question:
A volunteer asks the manager why her first aid course is not in the annual training report. Claude gathered the records as a separate step, and a colleague repeated the gathering and got the same list. The board has the report.

What should the manager do?

options.label: A
options.text: Find out where the gathering step looked, since two people can miss the same place.

options.label: B
options.text: Ask the volunteers to read the report themselves and tell the manager about any course that is missing.

options.label: C
options.text: Set up a new training database before the next report goes to the board.

options.label: D
options.text: Add the first aid course, and send the board a corrected report today.

questions.explanation:
CORRECT: Find out where the gathering step looked, since two people can miss the same place.

Two people ran the same gathering and produced the same list, so the step repeats. Repeating shows nothing about where that step looked. If both searches covered the same place, a course recorded elsewhere stays invisible to both. The volunteer found the gap the method could not reach. Check where an input came from, not only whether it repeats.

Exam Guide Mapping
* Domain 1: Prompting and Task Execution (14%)
* Objective: Apply task decomposition techniques to structure complex requests

INCORRECT: Ask the volunteers to read the report themselves and tell the manager about any course that is missing.

Volunteers know their own training, so they would catch what the report left out. It puts every volunteer to work checking a list that one gathering step produced badly. The same gap returns next year, and they check it again. Do not staff a check for an input you have not examined.

INCORRECT: Set up a new training database before the next report goes to the board.

A single training database would end the scatter, and the charity would own its records properly. Nothing yet says the records are scattered, only that one course did not reach the report. Building a system to answer a question nobody has asked is expensive guessing. Find out what went missing before you build.

INCORRECT: Add the first aid course, and send the board a corrected report today.

One course is missing and one course can be added, which settles the volunteer's question. The report is the output, and the gathering step is what produced the gap. Whatever hid that course will hide the others nobody has noticed. A correction closes one complaint and leaves the cause alone. Repair the input, not the copy that came out of it.

questions.question:
A festival's stewarding plan, ticket page and licence application were each written with Claude. A steward noticed the three name different crowd numbers. The organisers have not agreed a capacity.

What should the organisers do?

options.label: A
options.text: Fix one capacity number, and rewrite the three documents around it.

options.label: B
options.text: Copy the crowd number from the licence application into the ticket page and the stewarding plan.

options.label: C
options.text: Ask Claude to read the three documents together and list every figure that does not match.

options.label: D
options.text: Write the plan, the ticket page and the licence application in a single prompt.

questions.explanation:
CORRECT: Fix one capacity number, and rewrite the three documents around it.

Each document was written well, and each one had to name a crowd number. No capacity had been agreed, so Claude was asked for three answers to a question nobody had settled. Three reasonable guesses will not match. The licence, the stewards and the ticket buyers all depend on that one figure. Make the decision the others rest on before you write them.

Exam Guide Mapping
* Domain 1: Prompting and Task Execution (14%)
* Objective: Apply task decomposition techniques to structure complex requests

INCORRECT: Copy the crowd number from the licence application into the ticket page and the stewarding plan.

One number in three places would end the disagreement today, and the licence looks authoritative. That figure is a guess Claude produced, not a capacity anyone approved. Copying it makes the guess official across all three documents. The organisers would be licensed for a number they never chose. Spread a decision only after it has been made.

INCORRECT: Ask Claude to read the three documents together and list every figure that does not match.

A list of mismatches sounds thorough, and there may be more than the crowd number. The steward has already found the clash, and the organisers know why it happened. A longer list of symptoms does not supply the capacity nobody has set. Reasoning beats searching when the missing piece is plain. Look at what needs what.

INCORRECT: Write the plan, the ticket page and the licence application in a single prompt.

One prompt cannot contradict itself, so a single document would hold one number throughout. It would still be a number Claude picked, because no capacity exists to use. A licence application and a ticket page are different jobs for different readers. Merging them buys consistency and loses the decision. Fix the missing decision rather than merging the work.

questions.question:
A garage asks Claude to make its service reminder text clearer. The new version went out last month. The same number of customers rang the desk to ask what the text meant.

What should the garage do?

options.label: A
options.text: Ask for a text that tells a customer what to do and by when.

options.label: B
options.text: Ask Claude whether the new reminder text is clearer than the one it replaced.

options.label: C
options.text: Write the reminder text by hand, since Claude has not improved it.

options.label: D
options.text: Ask the desk staff to write down what each caller asks, then request a clearer version.

questions.explanation:
CORRECT: Ask for a text that tells a customer what to do and by when.

Clearer told Claude nothing it could aim at, so it rewrote the text and hit nothing. The calls are the evidence: customers still do not know what the reminder wants from them. What to do and by when is a target the garage can check. Read it and see whether it says both. A vague word produces a rewrite, and a named target produces progress.

Exam Guide Mapping
* Domain 1: Prompting and Task Execution (14%)
* Objective: Iterate prompts to improve output quality

INCORRECT: Ask Claude whether the new reminder text is clearer than the one it replaced.

A quick comparison sounds like a way to learn whether the rewrite worked. Claude would be grading its own text against a word nobody has defined. The customers already answered the question by ringing the desk. An opinion about clarity is not a measure of it. Judge a rewrite by what it does, not by what it is called.

INCORRECT: Write the reminder text by hand, since Claude has not improved it.

One failed rewrite makes writing it yourself look faster, and the garage knows its own customers. Nothing suggests Claude cannot write the text. The instruction it was given named no standard, and a person writing by hand would work to the same missing standard. A blank page inherits the fault. Do not change who writes when the brief is what is missing.

INCORRECT: Ask the desk staff to write down what each caller asks, then request a clearer version.

The callers know exactly what confused them, and the desk hears it every day. Collecting that is the right instinct and it is easy to do. The request then goes back with the same word, so the notes never reach the brief. Evidence you gather has to become the standard you ask for.
