questions.question:
A diving school asks Claude to write the page listing the medical forms students bring and when each expires. The page reads well. An instructor says the agency changed its medical paperwork in the spring, but not what changed.

What should the school do?

options.label: A
options.text: Have Claude find the current paperwork from the agency's published standards, then write the page.

options.label: B
options.text: Tell Claude to name only the forms that are currently in force.

options.label: C
options.text: Have Claude check the form names against the agency's standards and leave the expiry dates alone.

options.label: D
options.text: Build a Project holding all of the agency's standards documents, then write the page inside that Project.

questions.explanation:
CORRECT: Have Claude find the current paperwork from the agency's published standards, then write the page.

The page names paperwork the agency changes. Claude wrote it from what it already held, so the spring change never reached the page. The job looks like drafting, but the facts must come from outside. Have Claude gather the current standards first, then write. Ask where the facts come from before you ask for prose.

Exam Guide Mapping
* Domain 1: Prompting and Task Execution (14%)
* Objective: Adapt prompting strategies based on task type (analysis, research, drafting, brainstorming)

INCORRECT: Tell Claude to name only the forms that are currently in force.

An instruction to stay current sounds like a fix, and it costs a single line. The instruction cannot add facts Claude does not hold. The spring change is exactly what is missing here. A rule about currency does not fetch the agency's standards. Do not ask for a guarantee that the source of the answer cannot give.

INCORRECT: Have Claude check the form names against the agency's standards and leave the expiry dates alone.

Checking the names goes to the right place, which is the agency's own standards. The expiry dates came out of Claude's existing knowledge in the same pass as the names. Nobody knows what the agency changed, so nothing on the page is safe. Names and dates carry equal risk here. Check the source for the whole output, not for the part you can picture.

INCORRECT: Build a Project holding all of the agency's standards documents, then write the page inside that Project.

A Project with the standards loaded would help the school again and again. Whatever is uploaded is the version the school already downloaded, which may be as old as the page. Currency is the problem, and a stored copy does not solve it. The setup also outweighs a single page. Build a store when reuse justifies it, not to answer one question.

questions.question:
A harbour master sends boat owners a Claude summary of the new berthing charges. Three owners then phone to ask about the winter lay up discount. The charges schedule contains it and the summary never mentions it.

What should the harbour master do?

options.label: A
options.text: Ask Claude to summarise the winter lay up discount and reissue the summary.

options.label: B
options.text: Answer the three callers and leave the summary as it is.

options.label: C
options.text: Read the whole charges schedule and write a replacement summary by hand for every berth type.

options.label: D
options.text: Ask Claude whether its summary left anything else out of the schedule.

questions.explanation:
CORRECT: Ask Claude to summarise the winter lay up discount and reissue the summary.

Three owners asked about the same discount, and the schedule contains it. The summary covers the rates and drops a section owners need. Asking Claude for that section by name fills the known gap. The rest of the summary was accurate, so nothing else has to change. Name the missing part and ask for it.

Exam Guide Mapping
* Domain 2: Output Evaluation and Validation (21%)
* Objective: Evaluate Claude-generated outputs for accuracy and completeness

INCORRECT: Answer the three callers and leave the summary as it is.

The three callers get their answer, which is fair to them. Every other owner still holds a summary with the discount missing. Three phone calls are the ones that reached the harbour office, not the only people affected. The document is what went out. Fix the thing that was published, not only the people who complained.

INCORRECT: Read the whole charges schedule and write a replacement summary by hand for every berth type.

Doing it by hand guarantees nothing is left out, and the harbour master knows the schedule. The summary was accurate everywhere except one section. Rewriting all of it to add one discount spends a day on a ten minute job. Match the size of the repair to the size of the gap.

INCORRECT: Ask Claude whether its summary left anything else out of the schedule.

A completeness check sounds sensible, and it would cover future gaps too. The harbour master already knows what is missing, because three owners named it. Claude would be judging its own summary against the same schedule it just read. The known gap stays unfilled while the question runs. Ask for what you know is missing first.

questions.question:
A garden tools retailer had Claude rewrite a hundred and twenty product descriptions in a warmer tone. A customer asks why the hedge trimmer page no longer warns about the blade guard. A colleague checked five pages and found nothing missing.

What should the retailer do?

options.label: A
options.text: Check all hundred and twenty descriptions against the text each one replaced.

options.label: B
options.text: Ask Claude to confirm that the rewrite kept every safety warning in place.

options.label: C
options.text: Have the safety officer read every description again before it goes back on the site.

options.label: D
options.text: Add the safety warnings to the Project instructions so future rewrites keep them.

questions.explanation:
CORRECT: Check all hundred and twenty descriptions against the text each one replaced.

One rewrite produced all hundred and twenty descriptions. It dropped a safety warning once, so it can have dropped one anywhere else. Five clean pages out of a hundred and twenty prove very little. A customer found this fault, which tells you nothing about the rest. Recheck the whole batch a faulty pass touched.

Exam Guide Mapping
* Domain 2: Output Evaluation and Validation (21%)
* Objective: Identify hallucinations, inconsistencies, and biases in responses

INCORRECT: Ask Claude to confirm that the rewrite kept every safety warning in place.

Asking the tool that did the work is quick, and it feels like a check. A confirmation is an answer, not a comparison. Finding a missing warning means reading the new text beside the old text, page by page. Nobody has done that yet for a hundred and nineteen pages. Ask for evidence, not for reassurance.

INCORRECT: Have the safety officer read every description again before it goes back on the site.

A safety officer is the right person to judge a warning, so this sounds careful. It puts a person in front of a hundred and twenty pages with no idea what to look for. The comparison with the old text is the work, and it still has to happen. Give a reviewer a defined check, not a pile.

INCORRECT: Add the safety warnings to the Project instructions so future rewrites keep them.

Project instructions shape how Claude responds, so this does help the next rewrite. It changes nothing about the hundred and twenty descriptions already published. A customer is reading one of them today. Fixing the process and checking the output are two separate jobs. Repair what has shipped before you protect what has not.

questions.question:
A university library published plain language summaries of three hundred and fifty archive collections. A researcher reports one summary ending a collection at 1910 when the finding aid says 1930. The cataloguer finds that end date sitting in a footnote.

What should she do?

options.label: A
options.text: Treat this as one collection to correct, not as a fault running through the whole catalogue.

options.label: B
options.text: Add a catalogue notice saying collection dates are approximate and should be checked against the finding aids.

options.label: C
options.text: Ask Claude to confirm the dates in the other summaries match their finding aids.

options.label: D
options.text: Write a rule into the Project instructions telling Claude to read every footnote before it summarises a collection.

questions.explanation:
CORRECT: Treat this as one collection to correct, not as a fault running through the whole catalogue.

The researcher found one date, and the cataloguer found why. That finding aid put its end date in a footnote, which is where the fault began. Nothing points at the other collections. A response has to fit what the evidence shows, and the evidence here shows one collection. Repair on the scale of the fault.

Exam Guide Mapping
* Domain 2: Output Evaluation and Validation (21%)
* Objective: Identify hallucinations, inconsistencies, and biases in responses

INCORRECT: Add a catalogue notice saying collection dates are approximate and should be checked against the finding aids.

A public notice looks honest and covers every summary at once. It tells readers the catalogue may be wrong without making any of it right. The fault here is one collection whose end date sat in a footnote. A warning is not a correction. Never label a fault you have already found and can fix.

INCORRECT: Ask Claude to confirm the dates in the other summaries match their finding aids.

Asking the tool that wrote the summaries is quick and feels thorough. A confirmation is an answer, not a reading of three hundred and forty nine finding aids. It also spends effort on a run with one fault and one known cause. Do not buy reassurance about work you have no reason to doubt.

INCORRECT: Write a rule into the Project instructions telling Claude to read every footnote before it summarises a collection.

Project instructions tailor how Claude responds, so a footnote rule sounds sensible. It would matter only if more finding aids hid dates in footnotes, and none is known to. It also does nothing about the summary the researcher is reading today. Build a rule from a pattern, not from one traced error.

questions.question:
A scaffolding contractor asks Claude which of seven crews works most safely, from a year of near-miss reports. The summary never says how many reports each crew filed. The two that filed the fewest come top, called the most disciplined.

What should the contractor do?

options.label: A
options.text: Check whether those two crews record every near miss, since fewer reports may mean less reporting.

options.label: B
options.text: Have the safety manager read the year of reports and rank the crews herself.

options.label: C
options.text: Ask Claude to rank the crews again using recorded injuries instead of the near miss reports it used.

options.label: D
options.text: Bring in an outside safety auditor to inspect all seven crews before the contractor accepts any of the findings.

questions.explanation:
CORRECT: Check whether those two crews record every near miss, since fewer reports may mean less reporting.

The ranking rests on how many reports each crew filed. A crew that files few reports may be safe, or may be recording less than the others. Nothing in the year's data separates those two readings. The summary never names that count, so nothing in the text looks wrong. Check what a number counts before you trust the order it produces.

Exam Guide Mapping
* Domain 2: Output Evaluation and Validation (21%)
* Objective: Identify hallucinations, inconsistencies, and biases in responses

INCORRECT: Have the safety manager read the year of reports and rank the crews herself.

Reading the reports herself puts experienced judgement on the evidence, which sounds safer. She would be reading the same set of reports the ranking used. The crews that file least would still look best on paper. Her time goes into repeating the analysis rather than testing it. Redoing the work by hand does not check what the data measures.

INCORRECT: Ask Claude to rank the crews again using recorded injuries instead of the near miss reports it used.

Injuries are hard facts, so ranking on them feels safer than ranking on reports. Injuries are recorded by the same crews and are rarer still. A crew that under records near misses will under record minor injuries too. The measure changes, the reporting habit does not. Swapping one self reported count for another leaves the bias where it was.

INCORRECT: Bring in an outside safety auditor to inspect all seven crews before the contractor accepts any of the findings.

An independent auditor would produce evidence nobody disputes, and safety deserves care. The contractor already has a year of reports and one specific doubt to settle. That doubt is whether two crews record everything they should. Asking those two crews is quicker and answers it. Test the doubt you have before you buy evidence you do not need.

questions.question:
A rugby club's club-drafted plan says its card reader will take payments at the pitch, where there is no phone signal. The same reader works fine in the clubhouse. Two hundred people pay at the gate on Saturday.

What should the club do?

options.label: A
options.text: Take the reader to the pitch before Saturday and put a payment through.

options.label: B
options.text: Trust the clubhouse experience, since it is the same reader running on the same account.

options.label: C
options.text: Ask Claude to rewrite the plan without the phone signal claim.

options.label: D
options.text: Ask the volunteers who ran last season's gate whether they remember the reader working.

questions.explanation:
CORRECT: Take the reader to the pitch before Saturday and put a payment through.

The claim is about this reader, at this pitch, where there is no phone signal. The clubhouse has a signal, so it tests nothing that matters here. Carrying the reader across the ground and taking one payment settles it in ten minutes. Two hundred people arrive on Saturday and there is no second chance. Behaviour is settled by watching it happen.

Exam Guide Mapping
* Domain 2: Output Evaluation and Validation (21%)
* Objective: Apply fact-checking and validation techniques

INCORRECT: Trust the clubhouse experience, since it is the same reader running on the same account.

The reader and the account really are the same, which makes the clubhouse feel like proof. The claim turns on the phone signal, and the clubhouse is the one place that has one. Nothing about a card reader working indoors says what it does at the pitch. Evidence from a different setting is not evidence about this one.

INCORRECT: Ask Claude to rewrite the plan without the phone signal claim.

Taking a doubtful sentence out of a plan is tidy and costs nothing. The gate still has to take payments on Saturday, whatever the plan says. Removing the claim removes the question, not the risk behind it. The club would arrive with no answer and two hundred people queueing. Do not edit a plan when the thing it describes is untested.

INCORRECT: Ask the volunteers who ran last season's gate whether they remember the reader working.

Volunteers who worked the gate are the people who would have seen it fail. A season is a long time to remember which payments went through first time. They would also be recalling a different reader or a different phone network. The club can test it this week instead of asking anyone to remember. Memory of a past event cannot settle how equipment behaves.

questions.question:
A parish clerk checks a Claude summary of the new burial fees against the printed fee card, line by line. Every fee matches except one, a second interment charge that appears nowhere on the card.

What should the clerk do?

options.label: A
options.text: Check that one charge against the council's adopted fee schedule before anything is published.

options.label: B
options.text: Publish the summary, since every other fee matched the card exactly.

options.label: C
options.text: Have a second clerk check the whole summary against the fee card once more.

options.label: D
options.text: Leave the second interment charge out and publish the fees that matched the card.

questions.explanation:
CORRECT: Check that one charge against the council's adopted fee schedule before anything is published.

The clerk matched every other fee against the card by hand, so those lines are settled. One charge appears on no source the clerk holds. Nothing links it to the others, because no single pass produced them all. That makes it the only open question. Check the claim that stands alone, and leave what is confirmed.

Exam Guide Mapping
* Domain 2: Output Evaluation and Validation (21%)
* Objective: Apply fact-checking and validation techniques

INCORRECT: Publish the summary, since every other fee matched the card exactly.

Every other fee matched, so the summary looks reliable overall. The one charge that matched nothing is the one that carries risk. A fee published in error is money the parish either loses or wrongly collects. Familiar content does not vouch for the line beside it. Judge each claim by its own evidence.

INCORRECT: Have a second clerk check the whole summary against the fee card once more.

A second reader is a sound habit, and a fresh pair of eyes catches things. Every other line has already been matched against the card once. A second clerk would compare the same lines to the same card and find the same matches. Rechecking a whole set makes sense when one process produced all of it. Here each line was checked on its own.

INCORRECT: Leave the second interment charge out and publish the fees that matched the card.

Dropping the charge removes the problem from the page, and the rest is confirmed. Families would then get a fee list that may be missing a real charge. The clerk still does not know whether the fee exists. Deleting a claim answers nothing about whether it was true. Resolve an unknown, do not hide it.

questions.question:
An architecture practice sends a Claude-drafted access statement to the fire officer. He replies that he checked the escape route widths and nothing else. It also gives lift capacity, ramp gradients and door opening forces. The team logged it approved.

What should the practice do?

options.label: A
options.text: Send the lift, ramp and door figures to people qualified to check each of them.

options.label: B
options.text: Ask the fire officer to confirm the whole statement, since he has already read part of it.

options.label: C
options.text: Have the graduate who assembled the statement read it through once more.

options.label: D
options.text: Ask Claude to rewrite the statement so each figure names the standard it came from.

questions.explanation:
CORRECT: Send the lift, ramp and door figures to people qualified to check each of them.

The fire officer said what he read: the escape route widths. Lift capacity, ramp gradients and door opening forces were never in front of him. Logging the whole statement as approved turns one narrow check into a general clearance. Route each remaining figure to somebody qualified for it. An approval covers only what the reviewer actually examined.

Exam Guide Mapping
* Domain 2: Output Evaluation and Validation (21%)
* Objective: Determine when human review or additional verification is required

INCORRECT: Ask the fire officer to confirm the whole statement, since he has already read part of it.

He has the statement in front of him, so replying again costs him little. He is qualified for escape routes, not for lift capacity, ramp gradients or door forces. A wider confirmation from him would cover subjects he cannot judge. The practice would then hold an approval worth less than it looks. Ask the person whose competence matches the figure.

INCORRECT: Have the graduate who assembled the statement read it through once more.

Another read by the person closest to the statement feels like diligence, and it is quick. He assembled the figures from Claude's draft and has read them already. Reading again cannot tell him whether a ramp gradient meets the standard. The work grows and the risk stays. Repetition by an unqualified reader is not verification.

INCORRECT: Ask Claude to rewrite the statement so each figure names the standard it came from.

Naming the standard behind each figure makes the statement easier to audit later. It changes how the figures are presented, not whether they are correct. The lift, ramp and door numbers still come from a draft nobody qualified has read. A cited wrong number is still wrong. Presentation is not verification.

questions.question:
A council sends Claude drafted licence decisions to a senior officer, except renewals, which go straight out. Nobody remembers who decided that. The licensing rules changed in April. Which two actions should the council take?

(Choose two)

options.label: A
options.text: Find out what a renewal decision now involves under the April rules.

options.label: B
options.text: Look for any renewal that has been appealed or corrected since the rules changed.

options.label: C
options.text: Send every licence decision to a senior officer, since renewals were never checked.

options.label: D
options.text: Redraw the line so renewals on premises with a complaint history get an officer.

options.label: E
options.text: Add a review date to the rule, so somebody looks at it again next year.

questions.explanation:
CORRECT: Find out what a renewal decision now involves under the April rules.

The exemption says a renewal is simple enough to go out unread. That was a judgment about renewals as they were, and the rules changed in April. Nobody has looked at what a renewal decision now asks an officer to weigh. If April made renewals harder, the exempt class quietly grew teeth. An exemption is a claim about a class, and classes change.

CORRECT: Look for any renewal that has been appealed or corrected since the rules changed.

A renewal decided wrongly leaves a trace outside the council. Applicants appeal, officers reissue, and corrections get logged. That record already exists and costs an afternoon to pull. If appeals have been arriving on renewals, the line was in the wrong place before April. Look at what happened downstream before you trust an exemption.

Exam Guide Mapping
* Domain 2: Output Evaluation and Validation (21%)
* Objective: Determine when human review or additional verification is required

INCORRECT: Send every licence decision to a senior officer, since renewals were never checked.

Nobody ever tested the exemption, so reading everything feels like the safe answer. It puts a senior officer in front of every renewal before anyone has shown one is wrong. The council would spend that time whether or not renewals carry any risk. An untested rule is a reason to test it. Test the exemption before you cancel it.

INCORRECT: Redraw the line so renewals on premises with a complaint history get an officer.

Complaint history is a plausible line and sounds sharper than renewal status. It rests on the same kind of guess that produced the first line. Nobody has looked at whether either one matches where wrong decisions appear. A new untested rule replaces an old untested rule. Redraw a line from evidence, not from a second guess.

INCORRECT: Add a review date to the rule, so somebody looks at it again next year.

A dated review looks responsible and takes a minute to write down. It leaves a year of renewals going out under a rule the April change may have broken. The council can answer the question this month from records it already holds. A date in the diary is not a check. Do not postpone a question you can answer now.

Add a review date to the rule, so somebody looks at it again next year.
html.explanation:
CORRECT: Find out what a renewal decision now involves under the April rules.

The exemption says a renewal is simple enough to go out unread. That was a judgment about renewals as they were, and the rules changed in April. Nobody has looked at what a renewal decision now asks an officer to weigh. If April made renewals harder, the exempt class quietly grew teeth. An exemption is a claim about a class, and classes change.

CORRECT: Look for any renewal that has been appealed or corrected since the rules changed.

A renewal decided wrongly leaves a trace outside the council. Applicants appeal, officers reissue, and corrections get logged. That record already exists and costs an afternoon to pull. * Objective: Determine when human review or additional verification is required

questions.question:
A golf club's Claude drafted paper explains why weekday visitor rounds have fallen. The committee accepts its figures from the tee sheet. It recommends changing the booking process, because visitors find it unwelcoming. The tee sheet records bookings, cancellations and times.

What should the committee do?

options.label: A
options.text: Ask a sample of weekday visitors how the booking process felt, before the committee changes it.

options.label: B
options.text: Change the booking process now and see whether weekday visitor rounds recover.

options.label: C
options.text: Ask the club professional to work out from the tee sheet why the visitors feel unwelcome.

options.label: D
options.text: Commission a market study of weekday golf across the whole county before the committee decides anything at all.

questions.explanation:
CORRECT: Ask a sample of weekday visitors how the booking process felt, before the committee changes it.

The figures are not in dispute, so more checking of the tee sheet adds nothing. The recommendation rests on how visitors feel about booking. The tee sheet holds bookings, cancellations and times, and none of those records a feeling. Only the visitors can say. When a record cannot reach a claim, ask the people the claim is about.

Exam Guide Mapping
* Domain 2: Output Evaluation and Validation (21%)
* Objective: Determine when human review or additional verification is required

INCORRECT: Change the booking process now and see whether weekday visitor rounds recover.

Acting is decisive and the paper reads convincingly, so this feels like leadership. The club would rebuild a process on a reason nobody has tested. If rounds recover, the committee still cannot say why. If they do not, it has spent money and learned nothing. Do not treat a confident recommendation as a verified one.

INCORRECT: Ask the club professional to work out from the tee sheet why the visitors feel unwelcome.

The professional knows the members and reads the tee sheet daily, so he seems the right person. The tee sheet records bookings, cancellations and times, and nothing about how anyone felt. He would be guessing from the same three fields Claude used. His guess would then carry his authority. Do not send a person to find what the data does not hold.

INCORRECT: Commission a market study of weekday golf across the whole county before the committee decides anything at all.

A county study would produce solid evidence about weekday golf, which sounds thorough. The question is narrower: whether this club's own booking process puts visitors off. A study of the county cannot answer that. The club's own weekday visitors can, and they are reachable this month. Match the size of the check to the size of the claim.

questions.question:
A theatre has three versions of its season brochure introduction. The funding agreement requires the brochure to name the funder, list access provision, and state the ticket subsidy. The marketing lead is choosing whichever reads warmest.

What should the lead do?

options.label: A
options.text: Check each version against the three things the funding agreement requires.

options.label: B
options.text: Pick the warmest version and add the three requirements to it afterwards.

options.label: C
options.text: Send all three versions to the funder and ask which one they would prefer to see.

options.label: D
options.text: Ask a colleague outside marketing to say which version reads warmest.

questions.explanation:
CORRECT: Check each version against the three things the funding agreement requires.

The funding agreement names exactly what the brochure must contain. That is a written standard, and it is the one the theatre is held to. Warmth is a preference, and no version can be judged against it. Check each version for the funder, the access provision and the subsidy. Judge against the standard you will be measured by.

Exam Guide Mapping
* Domain 2: Output Evaluation and Validation (21%)
* Objective: Edit, adapt, refine, and compare outputs for the intended audience

INCORRECT: Pick the warmest version and add the three requirements to it afterwards.

Warmth matters for a brochure, and the requirements can be written in later. Choosing first means the choice was made on the wrong test. The version that reads warmest may be the one where three obligations sit worst. Bolting requirements onto a chosen draft can undo the warmth that won it. Apply the binding standard before the taste.

INCORRECT: Send all three versions to the funder and ask which one they would prefer to see.

The funder wrote the agreement, so asking them seems safe. The agreement already says what is required, in writing. The theatre would be asking a funder to do work it can do in ten minutes. It also invites an opinion on wording nobody asked for. Read the standard you hold before you ask its author.

INCORRECT: Ask a colleague outside marketing to say which version reads warmest.

A fresh reader gives an independent view, and warmth is a reader's judgment. The colleague would be judging on the same test the lead already chose. Nothing about that test comes from the funding agreement. A second opinion on the wrong measure is still the wrong measure. Change the standard before you change the judge.

questions.question:
A charity sent GP surgeries an accurate eight-page description of its new carers service. It wants GPs to refer carers to it. Nobody has referred anyone, and one GP said she never got past the first page.

What should the charity do?

options.label: A
options.text: Send one page that says which carers to refer, and how to do it.

options.label: B
options.text: Send the eight pages again with a covering letter asking every GP to read them properly.

options.label: C
options.text: Ask practice managers to summarise the eight pages for their GPs.

options.label: D
options.text: Ask Claude which parts of the description a GP would find most useful.

questions.explanation:
CORRECT: Send one page that says which carers to refer, and how to do it.

The description is accurate and covers the whole service, which is why it fails. A GP has minutes between patients and one thing to decide: whether this patient should be referred. Eight pages never reach that decision, and the first page did not make it. Everything a GP does not need is what stopped the referral. Select for what the reader must do.

Exam Guide Mapping
* Domain 2: Output Evaluation and Validation (21%)
* Objective: Organize and curate information and select appropriate output formats (artifacts, inline, structured data)

INCORRECT: Send the eight pages again with a covering letter asking every GP to read them properly.

A second send with a clear request feels like the way to get attention. The GP who spoke did not refuse to read it, she stopped on page one. Asking harder does not change what is on the pages. A longer envelope for the same eight pages produces the same result. Asking for attention is not the same as earning it.

INCORRECT: Ask practice managers to summarise the eight pages for their GPs.

Practice managers know their surgeries and could pull out what matters locally. It asks a busy person to do the selection the charity should have done. Each manager would choose differently, so GPs would hear different things. The charity knows its own service best. Moving the work elsewhere is not the same as selecting.

INCORRECT: Ask Claude which parts of the description a GP would find most useful.

Claude wrote the description and can rank its sections in a moment. What a GP needs depends on how referrals work in that area, and the charity knows this. A general ranking of useful sections is not a page built for one decision. The charity holds the referral route and Claude does not. Select against your own purpose, not a general one.

questions.question:
A county show's app takes its timings from a file the entries system exports. Claude wrote the printed programme separately, from the same entry list. The programme puts sheep judging at half past nine and the app says half past ten.

What should the office do?

options.label: A
options.text: Have Claude write the programme from the app's schedule file, not from the entry list.

options.label: B
options.text: Have Claude produce its own schedule file, then write the programme from it.

options.label: C
options.text: Ask the entries system's supplier to change its export so it matches what the printed programme says.

options.label: D
options.text: Ask Claude to compare every time in the programme against the app and list any differences it finds.

questions.explanation:
CORRECT: Have Claude write the programme from the app's schedule file, not from the entry list.

The app reads a file the entries system produces, so that file is what visitors follow. Claude wrote the programme from the entry list instead, which sits further back in the chain. Two readings of the same source drifted apart. Writing the programme from the file the app uses removes the second reading. Derive the human copy from the machine format people rely on.

Exam Guide Mapping
* Domain 2: Output Evaluation and Validation (21%)
* Objective: Organize and curate information and select appropriate output formats (artifacts, inline, structured data)

INCORRECT: Have Claude produce its own schedule file, then write the programme from it.

Building the human copy from a machine file is the right shape, and it fixes the drift inside the programme. The entries system already exports the file the app reads. A second schedule file made by Claude adds a third version of the timings. Visitors and stewards would then follow different files. Derive from the machine format that already exists, do not create a rival.

INCORRECT: Ask the entries system's supplier to change its export so it matches what the printed programme says.

The two do disagree, so changing one would remove the difference. The export carries the times the show actually scheduled, and the app serves them to visitors all day. The programme was written separately and has no better claim to be right. Changing the system to match a leaflet corrupts the record. Fix the copy that was derived, not the source it should follow.

INCORRECT: Ask Claude to compare every time in the programme against the app and list any differences it finds.

A comparison would catch the sheep judging clash and anything like it, before the gates open. The office must run that comparison every time either side changes. Somebody then decides which time is correct, which is the same problem again. The programme is still written independently. Checking two versions against each other is weaker than having only one.

questions.question:
A head teacher has Claude summarise parent feedback from six year groups, one summary per year group. The improvement plan needs the concerns that run across the whole school. Reading six separate summaries has not produced that.

What should the head do?

options.label: A
options.text: Ask Claude to reorganise the feedback by concern, across all six year groups.

options.label: B
options.text: Ask Claude to summarise the six summaries into one shorter document.

options.label: C
options.text: Read the six summaries again and note the repeated points by hand for the plan.

options.label: D
options.text: Ask Claude to summarise each year group again in more detail.

questions.explanation:
CORRECT: Ask Claude to reorganise the feedback by concern, across all six year groups.

Six summaries, one per year group, keep the feedback in the shape it arrived in. The improvement plan asks a question that crosses year groups, and no summary answers it. Reorganising by concern puts a worry about homework in one place, whichever year raised it. Organise by the question you have to answer, not by where the material came from.

Exam Guide Mapping
* Domain 2: Output Evaluation and Validation (21%)
* Objective: Organize and curate information and select appropriate output formats (artifacts, inline, structured data)

INCORRECT: Ask Claude to summarise the six summaries into one shorter document.

One document is easier to carry into a meeting than six. Summarising summaries keeps the year group order and shortens each part. The head would read the same six blocks, only briefer. Length is not the problem, and structure is. Compressing a wrong arrangement leaves it wrong and smaller.

INCORRECT: Read the six summaries again and note the repeated points by hand for the plan.

Reading them again would find the repeated concerns, and the head knows the school. It is the work the head asked Claude to do in the first place. Six summaries across six year groups is an evening of cross-referencing. The material is already there and can be rearranged in one request. Do not do by hand what the arrangement should give you.

INCORRECT: Ask Claude to summarise each year group again in more detail.

More detail per year group would surface concerns the first pass missed. It also produces six longer summaries in the same six-way split. The head would then have more material arranged the same unhelpful way. Depth and organisation are different problems. Adding detail to the wrong structure makes the reading longer, not clearer.

questions.question:
An auction house cataloguer describes the grading words and the way an entry is built to Claude each time she starts. Some days she explains it in full, some days in a line. Last month two entries graded the same chip differently.

What should she do?

options.label: A
options.text: Put the grading words and the entry approach into a Skill, and stop explaining them.

options.label: B
options.text: Ask Claude to check each finished entry against the grading words.

options.label: C
options.text: Add the grading words to the Project's knowledge base, so Claude can look up the house terms.

options.label: D
options.text: Ask Claude to read every catalogue entry written in the last two years before starting a new one.

questions.explanation:
CORRECT: Put the grading words and the entry approach into a Skill, and stop explaining them.

Every lot entry needs the same grading words and the same shape. Right now Claude gets them from a spoken explanation that changes with the day. That is why two entries graded one chip in two ways. A Skill gives Claude specialized knowledge and a workflow, so the terms and the method travel with the task. Stop explaining what should already be stored.

Exam Guide Mapping
* Domain 3: Product and Model Selection (12%)
* Objective: Select appropriate Claude product features (Projects, research mode, chat, artifacts)

INCORRECT: Ask Claude to check each finished entry against the grading words.

A check at the end feels careful and costs one line. Claude can only check against the grading words it was given that day. On a thin day it was given one line of them. The check would pass an entry that used the wrong term. A check is only as good as the standard behind it.

INCORRECT: Add the grading words to the Project's knowledge base, so Claude can look up the house terms.

The knowledge base holds documents Claude uses for context and background, so the terms would be there to consult. It stores the vocabulary and not the way an entry is built. The cataloguer would still describe her method afresh each time. That method is half of what keeps entries alike. Reference material answers questions, but it does not do work.

INCORRECT: Ask Claude to read every catalogue entry written in the last two years before starting a new one.

Past entries do carry the house style, so this looks like a way to learn it. Two years of catalogues contain the same drift the cataloguer is trying to fix. Reading them before every lot also costs time on every single entry. The grading words are short and settled. Do not infer a standard you can simply state.

questions.question:
A logistics coordinator asks Claude to total fuel costs per vehicle from a six-thousand-row fuel card export. Asked the same question twice, Claude returned two different totals for one van.

What should the coordinator do?

options.label: A
options.text: Have Claude write and run code over the export to produce the totals.

options.label: B
options.text: Ask the question a third time and use the total that appears twice.

options.label: C
options.text: Ask Claude to show the rows behind the van's total so it can be checked.

options.label: D
options.text: Total the fuel costs for every vehicle in a spreadsheet by hand.

questions.explanation:
CORRECT: Have Claude write and run code over the export to produce the totals.

Six thousand rows of fuel card lines is arithmetic, not reading. Two different totals for the same van show what happens when a sum is reasoned. Code runs the addition, so the same question returns the same number every time. Code execution lets Claude write and run code, so results are precise and reproducible. A number you cannot reproduce is not an answer yet.

Exam Guide Mapping
* Domain 3: Product and Model Selection (12%)
* Objective: Select appropriate Claude product features (Projects, research mode, chat, artifacts)

INCORRECT: Ask the question a third time and use the total that appears twice.

A third run and a majority sounds like a cheap tie break. Three reasoned readings of six thousand rows can all be wrong in different ways. Agreement between two guesses is not proof that either is right. The coordinator would still have no way to reproduce the number. Voting is not arithmetic.

INCORRECT: Ask Claude to show the rows behind the van's total so it can be checked.

questions.question:
A local history society is writing a display board about the closed pit, which former miners will read. The story sits across newspaper archives, a heritage page, and a museum catalogue. Claude returns one short paragraph naming no source.

What should the society do?

options.label: A
options.text: Use Research, so Claude searches the sources in turn and returns citations to check.

options.label: B
options.text: Ask Claude to write the paragraph again in much more detail.

options.label: C
options.text: Ask Claude to name a source for each fact that already appears in the short paragraph it wrote.

options.label: D
options.text: Put the board up now, and add the archive detail when a volunteer has time.

questions.explanation:
CORRECT: Use Research, so Claude searches the sources in turn and returns citations to check.

The story sits in three separate places and no single one holds it. One paragraph came back, and it points nowhere. Research keeps searching and follows what each search turns up, which is how scattered material gets pulled together. Every finding arrives with a citation, and former miners will want to check them. Match the mode to how far the answer is spread.

Exam Guide Mapping
* Domain 3: Product and Model Selection (12%)
* Objective: Select appropriate Claude product features (Projects, research mode, chat, artifacts)

INCORRECT: Ask Claude to write the paragraph again in much more detail.

More detail is the obvious answer to a paragraph that is too thin. Detail has to come from somewhere, and nothing has been gathered from the archives, the heritage page or the catalogue. A longer paragraph built on the same basis is still one paragraph. The board would say more and prove no more. Length is not the same as sourcing.

INCORRECT: Ask Claude to name a source for each fact that already appears in the short paragraph it wrote.

Citations are exactly what the board needs, so asking for them looks direct. The request would only cover the few facts the paragraph already holds. What the society is missing is everything the three places hold and the reply left out. Labelling a thin answer does not make it a full one. Gather the material first, then ask where it came from.

INCORRECT: Put the board up now, and add the archive detail when a volunteer has time.

Getting the board up is a real goal, and volunteers are stretched. The board that goes up is the one former miners will read, and it carries a thin account. Later has no date on it, so the gathering may never happen. Nothing about the work gets easier by waiting. Do the gathering before the board goes up.

questions.question:
A repairs call centre has no written guidance on choosing a model. A new adviser asks the colleague beside her, who says use the strong one whenever a letter mentions money. Three advisers picked three different models yesterday.

What should the team leader write?

options.label: A
options.text: Guidance naming each model tier the team can pick, with an example repair job for each one.

options.label: B
options.text: A rule that every adviser uses one model for all repairs work, so nobody chooses.

options.label: C
options.text: A line telling advisers to ask Claude at the start of every chat which model would suit the job.

options.label: D
options.text: A shared Project holding the team's letter templates, so every adviser starts from the same wording.

questions.explanation:
CORRECT: Guidance naming each model tier the team can pick, with an example repair job for each one.

Nothing is written down, so each adviser works from what a colleague told them. Strong and quick are relative words, and money in a letter is one person's invention. Guidance works when it names the tiers the team can pick and shows the kind of repairs work each one fits. An example turns a label into a decision.

Exam Guide Mapping
* Domain 3: Product and Model Selection (12%)
* Objective: Differentiate between Claude model types (Haiku, Sonnet, Opus)

INCORRECT: A rule that every adviser uses one model for all repairs work, so nobody chooses.

One model for everything ends the argument and is easy to remember. Repairs work runs from a two line callback text to a long disrepair history. A single tier serves one end of that range badly, whichever end it is. The team leader would trade confusion for waste. Simplify a choice, do not delete it.

INCORRECT: A line telling advisers to ask Claude at the start of every chat which model would suit the job.

Advisers already ask each other, so asking Claude looks like an improvement. The handbook would still hold no guidance of its own. The next new starter would be exactly where this one is, asking whoever is nearest. The team leader was asked to write guidance, and this writes none. Guidance must stand without its author.

INCORRECT: A shared Project holding the team's letter templates, so every adviser starts from the same wording.

A Project's knowledge base holds documents Claude reads for background, so shared templates are real and useful. Wording is not what the advisers disagree about. They disagree about which model to pick before any wording appears. Templates sit downstream of the choice the evidence names. Fix the decision the evidence points at.

questions.question:
After a near miss, an electrical contractor moved its certificates out of the general paperwork queue, and its qualified supervisor now checks them. Drafting still runs on the faster tier the general queue uses. Each certificate states the circuit's maximum load.

What should the firm do?

options.label: A
options.text: Draft the certificates on a more capable tier, so the drafting matches the new check.

options.label: B
options.text: Reclassify certificates as high-risk work, so they stop being treated as routine.

options.label: C
options.text: Add the maximum load figure to the supervisor's checklist, so he confirms it on every certificate.

options.label: D
options.text: Have the supervisor write every certificate himself, so that no Claude draft ever reaches him at all.

questions.explanation:
CORRECT: Draft the certificates on a more capable tier, so the drafting matches the new check.

Calling certificates general paperwork set two things: the tier that drafts them and the person who checks them. The firm corrected the checker and left the tier behind, because the tier came with the old queue. A certificate states a maximum load, which a weaker draft can get wrong plausibly. Move the drafting too. A correction has to reach every decision the first reading made.

Exam Guide Mapping
* Domain 3: Product and Model Selection (12%)
* Objective: Align model selection with task requirements (cost, speed, quality)

INCORRECT: Reclassify certificates as high-risk work, so they stop being treated as routine.

Reclassifying is what the firm should have done, and it names the fault exactly. It has already happened: the certificates left the general queue after the near miss. Saying it again changes nothing that is still wrong. The drafting setting is the part that did not follow. Diagnose what remains, not what has already been put right.

INCORRECT: Add the maximum load figure to the supervisor's checklist, so he confirms it on every certificate.

The supervisor is qualified and a checklist would make his check consistent. He already checks every certificate, so the review layer is the part that works. The fault sits earlier, in a draft produced at a setting chosen for routine mail. A stronger check catches errors that a better draft would not make. Fix the layer that is wrong, not the one that is working.

INCORRECT: Have the supervisor write every certificate himself, so that no Claude draft ever reaches him at all.

Removing the draft removes the risk it carries, and the supervisor is the qualified person. His time is the scarcest thing the firm has, and writing takes far longer than checking. The firm loses the help it wanted and keeps only the cost. A more capable tier gives a draft worth his check. Do not remove a tool when the setting is what is wrong.

questions.question:
A parts supplier must work out which product listings breach a new labelling rule. The chat open on the screen has run since morning on the faster tier, renaming four hundred listings.

What should the supplier do?

options.label: A
options.text: Open a new chat on a more capable tier, and leave the renaming behind.

options.label: B
options.text: Raise the tier in the chat that is already open, since the listings are all there.

options.label: C
options.text: Ask Claude to set aside the renaming work before it answers the question.

options.label: D
options.text: Have Claude summarise the whole renaming session and paste that into a new chat.

questions.explanation:
CORRECT: Open a new chat on a more capable tier, and leave the renaming behind.

Two things need to change, not one. The open chat carries four hundred renamings that have nothing to do with labelling. A long conversation has its earlier messages summarised to stay inside the context window. Judging a breach also asks for more reasoning than renaming ever did. Change the thread and the tier together.

Exam Guide Mapping
* Domain 3: Product and Model Selection (12%)
* Objective: Align model selection with task requirements (cost, speed, quality)

INCORRECT: Raise the tier in the chat that is already open, since the listings are all there.

The listings really are in that chat, which makes staying put feel efficient. A better tier would then work behind a day of renaming it does not need. The renaming carries no information about the labelling rule. A stronger model reading the wrong material is still reading the wrong material. Treat the thread and the tier as two separate choices.

INCORRECT: Ask Claude to set aside the renaming work before it answers the question.

One line asking Claude to ignore the morning seems cheaper than starting again. It leaves four hundred renamings in the conversation whatever Claude is told. The tier is also still the one chosen for renaming, so the harder half is untouched. An instruction cannot empty a chat. Start the work where you want it, rather than asking for a clean slate.

INCORRECT: Have Claude summarise the whole renaming session and paste that into a new chat.

A summary sounds like the careful way to move between chats without losing work. The labelling question needs the listings and the new rule, not an account of a morning's renaming. Carrying the summary rebuilds the clutter the new chat was opened to escape. Bring what the next task needs, not what the last one produced.

questions.question:
A customer complained that a jeweller's repair quote gave calendar days. The workshop quotes only in working days, and never quotes stone setting unseen. The jeweller writes each quote in its own chat, and types those rules in when she remembers.

What should she do?

options.label: A
options.text: Put both workshop rules into Claude's memory instead of typing them into each new chat.

options.label: B
options.text: Ask Claude to check each quote against the workshop's usual quoting rules first.

options.label: C
options.text: Correct the customer's quote and ask Claude to be more careful with all future repair quotes.

options.label: D
options.text: Put both rules into the instructions of the Project the workshop already uses for its stock questions.

questions.explanation:
CORRECT: Put both workshop rules into Claude's memory instead of typing them into each new chat.

Both rules are true of every quote she writes, whatever the repair is. Typing them by hand means each chat depends on her remembering, and this one did not. Claude's memory holds standing working details and carries them into later conversations. Saved once, the rules are there whether she thinks of them or not. Persist context that never changes, rather than retyping it.

Exam Guide Mapping
* Domain 3: Product and Model Selection (12%)
* Objective: Understand and manage context limitations and memory considerations (when to restart, summarize, or persist)

INCORRECT: Ask Claude to check each quote against the workshop's usual quoting rules first.

A check before sending sounds safer than trusting herself to type the rules. Claude has no record of what this workshop's usual rules are. In a fresh chat it would apply general practice, which is calendar days. The check would pass a wrong quote. A model cannot check work against a rule nobody has given it.

INCORRECT: Correct the customer's quote and ask Claude to be more careful with all future repair quotes.

Putting the customer right is necessary, and the request costs nothing. It treats a missing rule as carelessness on Claude's part. Claude followed what the chat gave it, and that chat gave it nothing about working days. The next quote she starts will be just as empty. Supply the context rather than asking for more care.

INCORRECT: Put both rules into the instructions of the Project the workshop already uses for its stock questions.

Project instructions do hold standing rules, so this points at a real feature. Those instructions apply to chats inside that Project, and she quotes in ordinary chats. The rules would sit where the quoting never happens. Nothing about her next quote would change. Put standing context where the work actually runs.

questions.question:
A film festival programmer pastes seventy-three entry synopses into a chat and asks for a running order by length and genre. Claude sorts the first stretch, then says the conversation has reached its length. The order is needed today.

What should the programmer do?

options.label: A
options.text: Open a fresh chat for each block of twelve synopses and merge the finished blocks afterwards.

options.label: B
options.text: Split the synopses into two halves and paste each half into this same chat.

options.label: C
options.text: Ask Claude to raise the length limit that stopped this conversation.

options.label: D
options.text: Ask Claude to write and run code that sorts the synopses by running time and genre instead.

questions.explanation:
CORRECT: Open a fresh chat for each block of twelve synopses and merge the finished blocks afterwards.

Seventy three synopses filled the conversation before the sorting finished. The task itself is simple, so no other setting will help. Split the input instead: twelve at a time in their own chat, each producing a short ordered list. Those lists then combine into the running order. Size the input to the conversation rather than hoping a chat will hold it all.

Exam Guide Mapping
* Domain 3: Product and Model Selection (12%)
* Objective: Understand and manage context limitations and memory considerations (when to restart, summarize, or persist)

INCORRECT: Split the synopses into two halves and paste each half into this same chat.

Splitting the input is the right instinct, and two halves is simpler than six blocks. Both halves would go into the chat that has already reached its length. The conversation cannot take more, whatever size the pieces are. The same stop arrives on the first half. Split the work across conversations, not inside one that is already full.

INCORRECT: Ask Claude to raise the length limit that stopped this conversation.

It sounds like a setting somebody could change, and the programmer is in a hurry. A conversation's length is not something Claude extends on request. When a chat hits its length, the move is to start a new one. Asking spends time and returns nothing. Learn the remedy a limit actually has.

INCORRECT: Ask Claude to write and run code that sorts the synopses by running time and genre instead.

Code is good at sorting, and running time is a number, so this looks efficient. The synopses still have to reach the conversation before any code can read them. That is exactly what would not fit. The length problem is untouched and the setup is heavier. Solve the input problem before choosing a cleverer method.

questions.question:
A garage owes its software team a specification for a parts ordering tool. The parts manager keeps a notebook of every counter problem this year. Asked what the tool should do, she says she would know it when she saw it.

What should the garage do?

options.label: A

options.label: B

questions.question:
A dog rescue books its home visit only after a dog is matched, and volunteers from another charity carry it out. Fourteen dogs this year were vaccinated, chipped and advertised, then failed that visit.

What should the rescue do?

options.label: A
options.text: Book the home visit when someone first applies, before any dog is matched, prepared or advertised.

options.label: B
options.text: Add a second home visit halfway through the process, so a problem appears before the dog is advertised online.

options.label: C
options.text: Ask Claude to say which applications are likely to fail the home visit.

options.label: D
options.text: Put the rehoming steps into a Project, so all staff work from the same list.

questions.explanation:
CORRECT: Book the home visit when someone first applies, before any dog is matched, prepared or advertised.

The visit can end an adoption on its own. The rescue does not run it, so the only thing it controls is when it books one. Booking after the match means the vaccination, the chip and the advert all happen before anyone knows the home passes. Fourteen dogs this year show the cost. A blocking check belongs first.

Exam Guide Mapping
* Domain 4: Workflow Integration and Solution Design (16%)
* Objective: Leverage Claude for research, planning, and process optimization

INCORRECT: Add a second home visit halfway through the process, so a problem appears before the dog is advertised online.

A midway visit does catch a failing home earlier than collection day. It also asks the other charity for two visits instead of one. The first visit still comes after the match, so the vaccination and the chip have already happened. Adding a stage is not the same as moving the stage that blocks.

INCORRECT: Ask Claude to say which applications are likely to fail the home visit.

A prediction sounds cheap and would save the volunteers some journeys. Whether a home passes is a fact about that house, and the visit is what establishes it. The rescue would go on preparing dogs against a guess and lose the same fourteen. Use a check where only a check can answer.

INCORRECT: Put the rehoming steps into a Project, so all staff work from the same list.

A Project's knowledge base holds documents Claude reads for background, so the steps would be easy to find. Staff already know the steps and follow them. The problem is the order the steps run in, and writing them down preserves that order. Record a process only once you have fixed it.

questions.question:
An athletics club has Claude plan the resurfacing of its track. The plan names every task, its owner and its date. Step six strips the old surface, after which nobody can train there. The new surface has no confirmed delivery date.

What should the club do?

options.label: A
options.text: Name the person who decides go or no go, and place that decision before the strip.

options.label: B
options.text: Add a note to the plan reminding the team that the delivery date matters.

options.label: C
options.text: Ask the surface supplier for a firm delivery date before the plan is circulated to club members.

options.label: D
options.text: Give the stripping step a named owner, so somebody is responsible.

questions.explanation:
CORRECT: Name the person who decides go or no go, and place that decision before the strip.

The plan tells everyone what to do and when, and nowhere does it ask whether to carry on. Stripping the track cannot be undone, and the club loses its training ground until the new surface arrives. A delivery date nobody has confirmed is exactly the thing to decide on. Put a named person and a stop or continue choice in front of that step.

Exam Guide Mapping
* Domain 4: Workflow Integration and Solution Design (16%)
* Objective: Leverage Claude for research, planning, and process optimization

INCORRECT: Add a note to the plan reminding the team that the delivery date matters.

A reminder is easy to add and points at the real risk. A note asks nobody to decide anything and stops nothing. On the day, the strip is still the next task with an owner and a date beside it. Everyone reads the note and carries on. A warning is not a gate.

INCORRECT: Ask the surface supplier for a firm delivery date before the plan is circulated to club members.

Getting a firm date is sensible and would settle today's uncertainty. Delivery dates slip, and the plan would still have no place where anyone stops. A date confirmed in June does not protect the club in September. The strip would go ahead on the plan's own momentum. A confirmed fact is not a substitute for a decision point.

INCORRECT: Give the stripping step a named owner, so somebody is responsible.

Named owners make plans accountable, and this step certainly deserves one. The plan already names an owner for every task, including the strip. An owner is told to do the work, not asked whether to do it. Responsibility without the authority to stop changes nothing. A decision point asks a question; an owner only carries out the answer.

questions.question:
A vineyard runs four pre-harvest checks in sequence: a soil report, a labour contract review, a bottling line service and a water test. Each takes a week, and harvest starts in sixteen days. Last year they ran in reverse order.

What should the manager do?

options.label: A
options.text: Run the four checks in the same week and set a single date for their findings.

options.label: B
options.text: Shorten each of the four checks so the sequence fits inside sixteen days.

options.label: C
options.text: Start the soil report and the contract review together, and keep the other two checks until last.

options.label: D
options.text: Ask the four leads to work evenings so each check finishes in half a week.

questions.explanation:
CORRECT: Run the four checks in the same week and set a single date for their findings.

Last year the same four checks ran in the opposite order and still worked. A check that fed another could not survive that swap. Four weeks of waiting becomes one, and the findings arrive before harvest instead of after it. A shared reporting date keeps the results together. Where steps do not depend on each other, the order is a choice, not a constraint.

Exam Guide Mapping
* Domain 4: Workflow Integration and Solution Design (16%)
* Objective: Leverage Claude for research, planning, and process optimization

INCORRECT: Shorten each of the four checks so the sequence fits inside sixteen days.

Shorter checks would fit the calendar, and the manager controls their scope. Cutting a soil report or a contract review removes work that was there for a reason. The delay comes from running them in sequence, not from their length. Four shortened checks still cost more than four full ones run together. Fix the order before you cut the content.

INCORRECT: Start the soil report and the contract review together, and keep the other two checks until last.

Running two together already saves a week, which feels like enough. Nothing makes the line service or the water test depend on the first two. Holding them back keeps a constraint that does not exist. The estate spends three weeks where one would do. Apply the finding to every independent step, not to some of them.

INCORRECT: Ask the four leads to work evenings so each check finishes in half a week.

Evening work would compress the sequence and needs no change to the plan. It asks four teams to give up their evenings to preserve an order nothing requires. The checks would still run one behind another. The saving disappears the moment somebody cannot work late. Do not spend effort defending a sequence you could simply drop.

questions.question:
A bookshop's autumn window goes up on Monday and still has no theme. A Saturday assistant asked Claude and brought back six themes. The owner has not read them, because she uses Claude only to tighten wording she has already written.

What should she do?

options.label: A
options.text: Read the six themes the assistant brought, choose one, and build the window from it.

options.label: B
options.text: Ask Claude to generate a fresh set of autumn window themes for the owner to judge herself.

options.label: C
options.text: Ask Claude which of the six themes will sell the most books.

options.label: D
options.text: Put the six themes to the shop's regular customers and let them vote on one before Monday.

questions.explanation:
CORRECT: Read the six themes the assistant brought, choose one, and build the window from it.

The blank page is already filled: six themes are sitting there unread. The owner's rule keeps Claude to editing, so she has treated the themes as not really work. Generating options from nothing is work Claude does, and the assistant proved it. Monday is close and choosing is faster than starting. Judge the options in front of you rather than the habit that produced them.

Exam Guide Mapping
* Domain 4: Workflow Integration and Solution Design (16%)
* Objective: Use Claude to support solution design, development, and iteration

INCORRECT: Ask Claude to generate a fresh set of autumn window themes for the owner to judge herself.

Asking for her own set feels more properly hers than using the assistant's. Six themes already exist and cost nothing to read. A second set delays the choice by a day she does not have. The gap is not a shortage of themes, it is that nobody has looked. Do not repeat work that is already sitting in front of you.

INCORRECT: Ask Claude which of the six themes will sell the most books.

A sales ranking would make the decision feel objective, and the owner cares about sales. Claude has never seen this shop's stock, its street or its customers. Any ranking would be a guess dressed as a forecast. She would then defend a choice on a reason that is not real. Do not ask for a prediction the model has no basis to make.

INCORRECT: Put the six themes to the shop's regular customers and let them vote on one before Monday.

Regular customers know the shop and a vote would build interest in the window. Collecting and counting votes takes days the owner does not have before Monday. The window is her decision and she has six options ready to judge. A vote also spreads a choice nobody has yet thought about. Do not move a decision you can make today to a slower group.

questions.question:
A research office put Claude into all eight steps of preparing ethics applications, cutting it from ten days to six. Applications are still only heard at the committee's monthly meeting, set when papers went by post.

Which two actions should the office take?

(Choose two)

options.label: A
options.text: Put the monthly cycle to the committee, asking what still requires it now papers are electronic.

options.label: B
options.text: Compare the date each application was ready with the date the committee actually considered it.

options.label: C
options.text: Ask Claude to take another day out of the preparation steps.

options.label: D
options.text: Ask the committee to add a second meeting each month, reserved for urgent applications only.

options.label: E
options.text: Ask researchers to submit earlier in the month, so their applications catch the meeting that follows straight away.

questions.explanation:
CORRECT: Put the monthly cycle to the committee, asking what still requires it now papers are electronic.

Claude sped up eight steps and the office still waits for one monthly meeting. That meeting is the constraint, and nobody has asked whether it must stay monthly. The reason it exists, posting papers out, no longer applies. Only the committee can answer whether a shorter cycle works. Test the constraint before spending more effort on the steps around it.

CORRECT: Compare the date each application was ready with the date the committee actually considered it.

The four days saved sit somewhere, and the gap between ready and heard is where they went. Recording both dates shows how long finished applications wait for the committee. That number tells the office what the monthly cycle costs researchers. Without it, the case for changing anything is only an opinion. Measure the wait before you argue about the schedule.

Exam Guide Mapping
* Domain 4: Workflow Integration and Solution Design (16%)
* Objective: Integrate Claude into existing workflows to augment or redesign them

INCORRECT: Ask Claude to take another day out of the preparation steps.

Another day out of preparation is a real saving, and Claude has already proved useful there. Applications then wait for a meeting that happens once a month. A day saved before that wait lands in the same queue. Researchers see no difference at all. Speeding a step that feeds a fixed gate moves nothing anybody can feel.

INCORRECT: Ask the committee to add a second meeting each month, reserved for urgent applications only.

A second meeting would halve the wait for the applications that qualify. Somebody must then decide which applications count as urgent, which is new work for the office. Nobody has yet asked whether the monthly cycle is needed at all. Most applications keep waiting exactly as long. Test the constraint before you build an exception around it.

INCORRECT: Ask researchers to submit earlier in the month, so their applications catch the meeting that follows straight away.

Submitting earlier does help an individual researcher catch a meeting, so it is not useless. It asks researchers to work around a cycle nobody has questioned. The office learns nothing about whether the meeting still needs to be monthly. The constraint keeps its grip on everything. Working around a constraint is not the same as testing it.

questions.question:
A sign making firm takes eleven days from order to delivery. Nine of those days are spent writing and revising artwork briefs. The manager plans to use Claude for the dispatch notes, which staff find tedious.

What should the manager do?

options.label: A
options.text: Use Claude on the artwork briefs, where nine of the eleven days are spent.

options.label: B
options.text: Use Claude for the dispatch notes first, then look at the artwork briefs next quarter.

options.label: C
options.text: Hire a second artworker so the artwork briefs move through the studio faster.

options.label: D
options.text: Ask Claude to shorten the dispatch note template, so the tedious step takes less time each day.

questions.explanation:
CORRECT: Use Claude on the artwork briefs, where nine of the eleven days are spent.

The firm has measured its own delay. Nine of eleven days sit in the artwork briefs, so that is the only step where time can be won. The dispatch notes are tedious and quick, and making a quick step quicker changes nothing the customer sees. Put the tool where the time is, not where the irritation is.

Exam Guide Mapping
* Domain 4: Workflow Integration and Solution Design (16%)
* Objective: Integrate Claude into existing workflows to augment or redesign them

INCORRECT: Use Claude for the dispatch notes first, then look at the artwork briefs next quarter.

Starting with the easy step gets a win on the board, and staff would welcome it. The nine day wait continues for another three months while the quick step gets quicker. Customers judge the firm on eleven days, not on how dispatch notes feel. A first step should be the one that moves the number.

INCORRECT: Hire a second artworker so the artwork briefs move through the studio faster.

A second artworker would attack the nine days, which is the right target. It costs a salary to solve a problem the firm has not yet tried a tool on. Writing and revising briefs is drafting work, which Claude can take on directly. Try the cheap change at the slow step before you buy a person.

INCORRECT: Ask Claude to shorten the dispatch note template, so the tedious step takes less time each day.

A shorter template does save the staff time, and the tedium is real. Dispatch notes sit inside the two days that are not the artwork briefs. Trimming them improves a step that was never holding the order up. Effort spent on a fast step buys comfort, not speed. Ask what the change does to the total.

A second artworker would attack the nine days, which is the right target. It costs a salary to solve a problem the firm has not yet tried a tool on. Writing and revising briefs is drafting work, which Claude can take on directly. Try the cheap change at the slow step before you buy a person.

INCORRECT: Ask Claude to shorten the dispatch note template, so the tedious step takes less time each day.

A shorter template does save the staff time, and the tedium is real. Dispatch notes sit inside the two days that are not the artwork briefs. questions.question:
A broker gives every Claude-drafted letter the same one-minute skim. Most letters confirm an address change or a renewal date. Some state a policy exclusion, which determines whether a future claim is paid.

What should the broker do?

options.label: A
options.text: Give the exclusion letters a full check by a qualified adviser, and keep the skim elsewhere.

options.label: B
options.text: Ask Claude to flag the exclusion letters, and skim those ones twice.

options.label: C
options.text: Stop using Claude for the letters that state an exclusion, and write those by hand.

options.label: D
options.text: Send a sample of ten letters each week to a senior adviser for a full check.

questions.explanation:
CORRECT: Give the exclusion letters a full check by a qualified adviser, and keep the skim elsewhere.

The letters are not alike. A renewal date is easy to check and cheap to get wrong. An exclusion decides whether a claim is paid years later, and one minute cannot test that. The same skim protects the low value letters well and the high value ones hardly at all. Set the depth of a check by what the output decides.

Exam Guide Mapping
* Domain 4: Workflow Integration and Solution Design (16%)
* Objective: Integrate Claude into existing workflows to augment or redesign them

INCORRECT: Ask Claude to flag the exclusion letters, and skim those ones twice.

A flag would separate the exclusion letters, and two skims sound better than one. A skim repeated is still a skim, and one minute twice is two minutes. The exclusion needs someone who knows the policy, not more passes by the same reader. Depth and repetition are different things.

INCORRECT: Stop using Claude for the letters that state an exclusion, and write those by hand.

Writing exclusions by hand removes the drafting risk, and those letters matter most. The one-minute skim stays the only check on every other letter, and a handwritten exclusion is still unchecked by anyone qualified. The gap is the review, not the drafting. Removing a tool does not add a reader.

INCORRECT: Send a sample of ten letters each week to a senior adviser for a full check.

Sampling is a real quality method and ten letters a week is affordable. A random sample is drawn from a population that is mostly renewal dates. Most weeks it would miss the exclusion letters entirely, which are the ones that carry the money. Sample to measure a process, and route to protect a decision.
