questions.question:
A pilot of Claude with six people in one team produced good results, so the director wants two hundred staff on it next month. The associate's slides list only the pilot's time savings.

What should the associate add?

options.label: A
options.text: Where this rollout is likely to break at two hundred people, and what would prevent it.

options.label: B
options.text: A second pilot with another six people, to confirm the first result.

options.label: C
options.text: The time savings for two hundred staff, worked out from the pilot's figures.

options.label: D
options.text: A list of the features the two hundred staff will be able to use from day one.

questions.explanation:
CORRECT: Where this rollout is likely to break at two hundred people, and what would prevent it.

Six people in one team is not two hundred across the business. The slides carry the upside and nothing else, so the director is choosing with half the picture. Scale brings problems the pilot never met: uneven training, work that does not look like the pilot's, and nobody to ask. Say where it breaks while the plan can still change.

Exam Guide Mapping
* Domain 4: Workflow Integration and Solution Design (16%)
* Objective: Communicate Claude's value and limitations to stakeholders

INCORRECT: A second pilot with another six people, to confirm the first result.

Another pilot would test the result again, and repeatable evidence is worth having. Six more people would meet the same conditions the first six met. The question is what changes at two hundred, and a second small pilot cannot answer it. Repeating a test at the same scale tells you nothing about a bigger one.

INCORRECT: The time savings for two hundred staff, worked out from the pilot's figures.

Multiplying the saving is the natural next slide and the director will want the number. It assumes two hundred people behave like the six who volunteered for a pilot. A bigger benefit figure makes the decision easier and no better informed. Do not scale the upside without scaling the questions.

INCORRECT: A list of the features the two hundred staff will be able to use from day one.

A feature list tells staff what they are getting and looks like useful detail. The director is deciding whether to commit two hundred people, not which features they will use. Features describe the tool and say nothing about how the rollout could go wrong. Tell a decision maker what could fail, not what is available.

questions.question:
A plant hire supervisor emails the director a proposal to use Claude for hire agreements. It describes Projects and knowledge sources in detail. The director asks what it is for. Agreements take two days, and four carried the wrong daily rate.

What should the supervisor do?

options.label: A
options.text: Rewrite the proposal around the two day wait for agreements and the four wrong rates.

options.label: B
options.text: Add the two day figure to the proposal and keep the feature descriptions as they are.

options.label: C
options.text: Forward the director Anthropic's help articles about Projects and knowledge sources to read.

options.label: D
options.text: Run a month long trial on hire agreements and report the results back to the director afterwards.

questions.explanation:
CORRECT: Rewrite the proposal around the two day wait for agreements and the four wrong rates.

The director asked what the proposal is for, which is a business question. The email answered a technical one. The yard already holds two facts he cares about: agreements take two days, and four went out with the wrong rate. Build the proposal on those, and say what changes. Speak to the problem the reader owns, not to the tools you would use.

Exam Guide Mapping
* Domain 4: Workflow Integration and Solution Design (16%)
* Objective: Communicate Claude's value and limitations to stakeholders

INCORRECT: Add the two day figure to the proposal and keep the feature descriptions as they are.

Adding the two day figure moves the proposal towards the business case, which is right. The feature descriptions still fill most of it and still answer a question nobody asked. The director reads the same email with one useful line buried inside. He asked what it is for, so it should say so plainly. A business case is not an appendix to a feature list.

INCORRECT: Forward the director Anthropic's help articles about Projects and knowledge sources to read.

Anthropic's articles are accurate and explain the features properly. The director would then have to work out the business case himself, from documentation. That is the supervisor's job and it is exactly what the email left out. More reading about features answers the same question again. Never send a stakeholder to research the value you were asked to state.

INCORRECT: Run a month long trial on hire agreements and report the results back to the director afterwards.

A trial produces evidence, and evidence usually persuades a cautious director. He has not agreed there is a problem worth solving, so a month's work may be wasted. The yard already knows the two day wait and the four wrong rates. Those answer his question today. Establish the problem before you spend a month proving a solution.

questions.question:
A food bank runs a Project for volunteer questions. The eligibility criteria live in a shared drive, and each volunteer pastes the part they think applies. Two volunteers asked the same question on Monday and were told different things.

What should the food bank do?

options.label: A
options.text: Upload the eligibility criteria to the Project's knowledge base, so every chat reads the same document.

options.label: B
options.text: Ask Claude to name the criteria section behind every answer it gives.

options.label: C
options.text: Tell volunteers to paste the whole eligibility document into every chat, instead of the one section they think applies.

options.label: D
options.text: Give each volunteer their own Project, so one person's pasted section cannot change what another volunteer is told.

questions.explanation:
CORRECT: Upload the eligibility criteria to the Project's knowledge base, so every chat reads the same document.

The criteria never reach the Project. Each volunteer decides which part to paste, so each chat sees a different document. That is why one question produced two answers on Monday. A Project's knowledge base holds files Claude uses for background in every chat inside that Project. Put shared reference material where it stops being a choice.

Exam Guide Mapping
* Domain 5: Configuration and Knowledge Management (12%)
* Objective: Configure Claude Projects with instructions and knowledge sources

INCORRECT: Ask Claude to name the criteria section behind every answer it gives.

A citation makes an answer easier to trace, which sounds like the fix. Claude can only name the section the volunteer pasted. If the wrong section went in, the answer names that wrong section with confidence. Both volunteers would get a source, and the two answers would still differ. Citing the input does not correct the input.

INCORRECT: Tell volunteers to paste the whole eligibility document into every chat, instead of the one section they think applies.

Pasting everything would at least give each chat the same text. It asks every volunteer to move a whole document by hand, every time. One tired volunteer pastes half of it and the split answers come back. The Project can hold that document once instead. Do not ask people to repeat what a tool can keep.

INCORRECT: Give each volunteer their own Project, so one person's pasted section cannot change what another volunteer is told.

Separate Projects would stop one volunteer affecting another, which sounds like a clean fix. The criteria would still sit outside every one of those Projects. Each volunteer would keep pasting a section of their own choosing. Two answers to one question is exactly what survives. Isolating people does not give them the same source.

questions.question:
A ski hire shop's Project answers booking emails. A customer arrived at nine and found the shop had opened at eight. Her email had told her nine. The winter timetable in the knowledge base has said eight since October.

What should the manager do?

options.label: A
options.text: Open the Project instructions, since the knowledge base has held the right opening time all winter.

options.label: B
options.text: Rebuild the Project from scratch, with new instructions and a fresh set of documents.

options.label: C
options.text: Read every booking email before it leaves the shop, so a member of staff catches the wrong time.

options.label: D
options.text: Correct the opening hours on the shop's website, in case the wrong time came from there.

questions.explanation:
CORRECT: Open the Project instructions, since the knowledge base has held the right opening time all winter.

Two things are known. The knowledge base has carried the eight o'clock time since October, and the reply still said nine. A Project holds two layers, its instructions and its knowledge. The knowledge layer is already correct, so the instructions are the layer left to explain a nine o'clock opening.

Exam Guide Mapping
* Domain 5: Configuration and Knowledge Management (12%)
* Objective: Configure Claude Projects with instructions and knowledge sources

INCORRECT: Rebuild the Project from scratch, with new instructions and a fresh set of documents.

Starting again would remove the wrong time, so it feels decisive. It also throws away a knowledge base that is already correct and a season of setup. Nobody yet knows which line produces the nine o'clock reply, so a rebuild could write it again. Find the cause before replacing the thing that holds it.

INCORRECT: Read every booking email before it leaves the shop, so a member of staff catches the wrong time.

A person reading each reply would stop the next customer arriving late. It puts staff in front of every email for the rest of the season. The wrong time stays inside the Project and keeps producing itself. Catching an error every day costs more than removing it once.

INCORRECT: Correct the opening hours on the shop's website, in case the wrong time came from there.

A website is a common home for a stale opening time, so this looks plausible. The email came from the Project, and a Project answers from its own instructions and knowledge. Nothing joins the website to that reply. Correcting it leaves the next email unchanged. Repair the source the output actually came from.

questions.question:
A bakery runs three Claude Projects: shop signs, wholesale sheets and website copy. Each holds the same allergen list and house style note, and one contact line of its own. The manager typed June's allergen change into all three.

Which setup should the bakery use?

options.label: A
options.text: Run one Project for all three jobs, with the allergen list, style note and three contact lines in it.

options.label: B
options.text: Merge the signs and wholesale Projects, and leave the website Project as it is.

options.label: C
options.text: Move the allergen list out of each knowledge base and into that Project's instructions.

options.label: D
options.text: Build a fourth Project holding the allergen list and style note, and keep the other three as they are.

questions.explanation:
CORRECT: Run one Project for all three jobs, with the allergen list, style note and three contact lines in it.

All three Projects hold the same allergen list and the same house style note. Only one contact line separates them, so a single Project can carry all three lines. One change in June went in three times, because the material sits in three places. Hold shared material once, and note the small differences inside it.

Exam Guide Mapping
* Domain 5: Configuration and Knowledge Management (12%)
* Objective: Configure Claude Projects with instructions and knowledge sources

INCORRECT: Merge the signs and wholesale Projects, and leave the website Project as it is.

Two Projects are easier to merge than three, and website copy can feel like separate work. The website Project holds the same allergen list and the same style note as the other two. The next wording change still goes in twice. Merge every copy of the material, not the easiest pair.

INCORRECT: Move the allergen list out of each knowledge base and into that Project's instructions.

Project instructions shape every chat in that Project, so the list would sit closer to the work. The bakery would still hold three allergen lists, one in each Project. June's change would still be typed three times. Moving material between layers does not reduce the number of copies.

INCORRECT: Build a fourth Project holding the allergen list and style note, and keep the other three as they are.

A single home for the shared material sounds tidy, and nothing has to be deleted. A Project's knowledge serves the chats inside that Project. Staff drafting shop signs work in the signs Project, so the list is not with them. Put shared material where the work happens, not beside it.

questions.question:
A scout district treasurer uses the Gmail connector and asks Claude which of nine campsites quoted the lowest weekend rate. Each campsite replied with its quote as an attached document. Claude lists every sender, date and subject line, and no rates.

What should the treasurer do?

options.label: A
options.text: Attach the nine quote documents to the chat, where Claude can read what is inside them.

options.label: B
options.text: Search Gmail again through the connector, using the word rate so the right messages return.

options.label: C
options.text: Upload the two cheapest looking quotes and leave the rest in Gmail.

options.label: D
options.text: Connect Google Drive as well and ask Claude to look for the campsites' quote documents in it.

questions.explanation:
CORRECT: Attach the nine quote documents to the chat, where Claude can read what is inside them.

The connector reached the nine emails and returned exactly what it can see: senders, dates and subject lines. The Gmail connector reads attachment metadata, never attachment content. The rates sit inside the attached files, which it does not open. Uploading those files into the chat gives Claude the text itself. Know what a connector can read before you ask it a question about content.

Exam Guide Mapping
* Domain 5: Configuration and Knowledge Management (12%)
* Objective: Manage uploaded knowledge and connectors (e.g., Google Drive, Gmail)

INCORRECT: Search Gmail again through the connector, using the word rate so the right messages return.

Better search terms often fix a poor result, and the word rate is specific. Claude already found all nine emails, so no message was missed. The gap is the content of the attachments, not which messages came back. Searching harder returns the same metadata again. Work out whether the fault is finding the item or reading it.

INCORRECT: Upload the two cheapest looking quotes and leave the rest in Gmail.

Uploading is the right move, and two files are quicker than nine. Nobody can tell which quotes are cheapest without reading them, which is the whole question. Choosing two by their look decides the answer before the comparison starts. Seven rates stay unread. Upload everything the comparison needs, not a guess at the shortlist.

INCORRECT: Connect Google Drive as well and ask Claude to look for the campsites' quote documents in it.

Adding a second connector feels like giving Claude more reach, and Drive does read documents. The quotes arrived as email attachments and were never saved to Drive. A connector cannot reach a file that is not there. The treasurer sets up an integration and gets the same answer. Check where a file actually lives before adding a way to reach it.

Better search terms often fix a poor result, and the word rate is specific. Claude already found all nine emails, so no message was missed. The gap is the content of the attachments, not which messages came back. Searching harder returns the same metadata again. Work out whether the fault is finding the item or reading it.

INCORRECT: Upload the two cheapest looking quotes and leave the rest in Gmail.

Uploading is the right move, and two files are quicker than nine. Nobody can tell which quotes are cheapest without reading them, which is the whole question. Choosing two by their look decides the answer before the comparison starts. Seven rates stay unread. Upload everything the comparison needs, not a guess at the shortlist.

INCORRECT: Connect Google Drive as well and ask Claude to look for the campsites' quote documents in it.

Adding a second connector feels like giving Claude more reach, and Drive does read documents. The quotes arrived as email attachments and were never saved to Drive. A connector cannot reach a file that is not there. The treasurer sets up an integration and gets the same answer. Check where a file actually lives before adding a way to reach it.

questions.question:
A courier takes weekend parcels on Saturday only. Two lines in its Project instructions cover weekend collection: a line from March offering Saturday, and an older line offering Saturday or Sunday. One customer waited in all Sunday.

Which change should the courier make?

options.label: A
options.text: Leave one weekend line in the instructions, the March one, and take the other out.

options.label: B
options.text: Write to the customer who waited, and offer a free collection.

options.label: C
options.text: Reword the older line so it reads as guidance rather than a promise.

options.label: D
options.text: Ask Claude to compare the two weekend lines against each other before it writes a reply.

questions.explanation:
CORRECT: Leave one weekend line in the instructions, the March one, and take the other out.

The courier collects on Saturday. The March line says that, and the older line still offers Sunday as well. Two lines cannot both describe one service, so the older one has stopped being true. Deleting it leaves the instructions with a single weekend answer. Adding a new rule finishes the job only when the rule it replaced comes out.

Exam Guide Mapping
* Domain 5: Configuration and Knowledge Management (12%)
* Objective: Create effective system-level instructions

INCORRECT: Write to the customer who waited, and offer a free collection.

That customer deserves an apology and a free collection, so this is worth doing. It repairs one Sunday and changes nothing in the instructions. The older line still offers Sunday to the next household that asks. The courier would be buying its way out of the same fault every week. Put the customer right, and still take the wrong line out.

INCORRECT: Reword the older line so it reads as guidance rather than a promise.

Softer wording sounds safer than a firm offer, and rewriting is quick. The line would still name Sunday, and the courier does not collect on Sunday. A customer reading guidance about Sunday will still expect a van. The instructions would hold two weekend answers, one of them hedged. A rule that no longer holds is deleted, not softened.

INCORRECT: Ask Claude to compare the two weekend lines against each other before it writes a reply.

A comparison step sounds careful, and it leaves both lines untouched. The instructions state two different weekend offers, so comparing them produces a choice, not an answer. Nothing in them says which one the courier now runs. The reply could still name Sunday. Do not ask for a rule to be resolved when it can be removed.

questions.question:
A plumbing firm's Claude Project drafts job reports. Its contract requires the fault, the work done, the parts used and any return visit. The instruction is one line: reassure the tenant. Nine reports came back missing the return visit.

What should the firm change?

options.label: A
options.text: List the four items the contract requires in the instruction, so every report names them all.

options.label: B
options.text: Have a supervisor read every report and add anything the contract requires before it goes out.

options.label: C
options.text: Move the reports to a more capable tier, so fewer items are missed.

options.label: D
options.text: Have Claude rewrite the nine returned reports and send them out again.

questions.explanation:
CORRECT: List the four items the contract requires in the instruction, so every report names them all.

The contract names four things a report must carry. The single line of instruction asks for reassurance and names none of them. Claude wrote to the instruction it was given, so the return visit was left to chance. Putting the four items into the instruction makes each one required. An instruction must say what the output must contain, not how it should feel.

Exam Guide Mapping
* Domain 5: Configuration and Knowledge Management (12%)
* Objective: Create effective system-level instructions

INCORRECT: Have a supervisor read every report and add anything the contract requires before it goes out.

A supervisor would catch the missing return visit, and a person can read a contract well. The instruction stays as it is, so every report arrives incomplete and needs the same repair. The firm buys a permanent checking job to avoid one edit. Nine reports came back in a single month. Put the requirement in the instruction, not behind a reviewer.

INCORRECT: Move the reports to a more capable tier, so fewer items are missed.

A more capable tier handles harder work, and nine returned reports look like weak output. The instruction never asks for the return visit, so no tier is asked to supply it. Anthropic's guidance is to pick the tier that fits the work, not to use capability as a repair. The fault sits in what the instruction requests. Fix the request first.

INCORRECT: Have Claude rewrite the nine returned reports and send them out again.

The association returned nine reports, so those nine plainly need fixing. Rewriting them clears today's problem and leaves the instruction untouched. The next batch is drafted from the same wording and drops the same line. The firm would be repairing reports every month. Repair the instruction that produced the fault, then repair the output.

questions.question:
A desk assistant asks where the fire steward line in the room hire replies came from. Nobody at the front desk knows. The caretaker put it into the community centre's shared Project after a safety inspection, and it is required.

Which action should the caretaker take?

options.label: A
options.text: Explain the fire steward line to the front desk, and say the inspection made it compulsory.

options.label: B
options.text: Explain the line to the assistant who asked, and leave the rest of the desk alone.

options.label: C
options.text: Ask the front desk to check any unfamiliar line with the caretaker before sending.

options.label: D
options.text: Move the fire steward line to the end of every hire reply.

questions.explanation:
CORRECT: Explain the fire steward line to the front desk, and say the inspection made it compulsory.

The caretaker changed a Project the whole desk works from, and nobody there can account for what it sends. That is not a fault in the line; it is a fault in what people know. An explanation naming the inspection turns an odd sentence into a rule the team can defend. Tell the people who work from a shared setup what you changed.

Exam Guide Mapping
* Domain 5: Configuration and Knowledge Management (12%)
* Objective: Inform, maintain, and update Claude configurations, knowledge sources, and instructions

INCORRECT: Explain the line to the assistant who asked, and leave the rest of the desk alone.

Answering the person who asked is polite and costs a minute. Nobody at the desk knows where the line came from, so the same question sits with everyone else. The next hirer who queries it meets a colleague who cannot answer. One explanation would have covered them all. A change to a shared setup is announced to everyone who uses it.

INCORRECT: Ask the front desk to check any unfamiliar line with the caretaker before sending.

A checking habit would catch this line and anything else the desk does not recognise. It makes the desk stop on every change the caretaker makes, forever. The caretaker knows today why the line is there and can say so in a minute. Staff would carry a standing cost to save one message. Announce a change once instead of leaving people to query it.

INCORRECT: Move the fire steward line to the end of every hire reply.

Position is easy to change, and a line at the end reads as a footnote. The desk did not object to where the line sits; it asked where the line came from. Moving it leaves the same unexplained sentence in the same replies. The safety inspection made the line compulsory, wherever it appears. Treat an unexplained change as a communication problem, not a layout fault.

questions.question:
A marina's Project answers berth enquiries from a charges table someone copied out of the harbour authority's tariff two years ago. A boat owner was quoted a lift out fee that rose in April.

Which two actions should the marina take?

(Choose two)

options.label: A
options.text: Check which berth enquiries since April were answered from the old figures.

options.label: B
options.text: Put the harbour authority's tariff in the Project, instead of a copy of it.

options.label: C
options.text: Add a line to the Project instructions saying the charges table may be out of date.

options.label: D
options.text: Correct the lift out fee in the table and leave the rest.

options.label: E
options.text: Ask Claude which figures in the charges table look out of date.

questions.explanation:
CORRECT: Check which berth enquiries since April were answered from the old figures.

The fee rose in April and the table still holds the old one. Every enquiry answered since then may have quoted a figure the marina cannot charge. One boat owner noticed and complained; the others simply received a wrong number. The marina can pull those replies and see. A stale source has been producing wrong answers for as long as it was stale.

CORRECT: Put the harbour authority's tariff in the Project, instead of a copy of it.

The table drifted because somebody typed it out two years ago. A copy stops matching the day the original changes, and nobody is told. The harbour authority publishes the tariff itself, so the Project can hold that document. Then a change at the authority is a change in the Project. Keep the source, not a transcription of it.

Exam Guide Mapping
* Domain 5: Configuration and Knowledge Management (12%)
* Objective: Inform, maintain, and update Claude configurations, knowledge sources, and instructions

INCORRECT: Add a line to the Project instructions saying the charges table may be out of date.

A warning is honest and takes one line to write. It leaves the wrong fee in the table and asks every reader to allow for it. Nobody can act on may be out of date, because it does not say which figures. The next enquiry gets the same number with a caveat attached. A caveat on a source is not maintenance of it.

INCORRECT: Correct the lift out fee in the table and leave the rest.

Fixing the fee that was caught stops that one wrong answer, and it takes a minute. The whole table was typed from the tariff on the same afternoon two years ago. Whatever moved the lift out fee has had two years to move the others. One stale line is a reason to doubt everything typed beside it.

INCORRECT: Ask Claude which figures in the charges table look out of date.

It sounds efficient to have the whole table reviewed in one request. Nothing in the table says when it was written, and the harbour authority's current tariff is not in the Project. There is no material available to compare the table against. The authority publishes the answer and the marina can fetch it. Compare a document with the source it came from.

questions.question:
A bakery chain's AI policy bars using Claude to produce allergen labels. A team ran Claude over two hundred past recipes and its allergen lists matched every approved label exactly. The team wants to label the new range this way.

What should the team do?

options.label: A
options.text: Keep allergen labels out of Claude's work, whatever the match on two hundred recipes showed.

options.label: B
options.text: Run the lists against another two hundred recipes before deciding anything.

options.label: C
options.text: Have Claude explain how it built each allergen list, so the method can be written down.

options.label: D
options.text: Have the label team retype Claude's lists by hand, so that a person produces the final printed label.

questions.explanation:
CORRECT: Keep allergen labels out of Claude's work, whatever the match on two hundred recipes showed.

The policy names the output and the tool together: Claude must not produce allergen labels. The two hundred recipe test measures accuracy. Accuracy is not the question the policy asks. A rule about what a tool may produce does not bend when the tool performs well. When the policy covers the work itself, the work stops.

Exam Guide Mapping
* Domain 6: Governance, Risk, and Responsible Use (15%)
* Objective: Identify appropriate and inappropriate use cases

INCORRECT: Run the lists against another two hundred recipes before deciding anything.

More testing feels responsible, and the first result was strong. The team already knows the lists match. A second test answers a question nobody is asking. The policy will read the same after four hundred recipes as it did after two hundred. Stop gathering evidence once the rule has already answered you.

INCORRECT: Have Claude explain how it built each allergen list, so the method can be written down.

A written method makes a process easier to defend, and food work needs records. The policy does not object to an unexplained list. It objects to Claude producing the label at all. A clear explanation documents a barred activity in more detail. Describing how something was done never decides whether it was allowed.

INCORRECT: Have the label team retype Claude's lists by hand, so that a person produces the final printed label.

Retyping puts a human hand on the last step, which looks like compliance. The allergen content still comes from Claude, letter for letter. The policy covers producing the label, not typing it. Retyping also adds a fresh chance to mistype an allergen. A person copying a barred output has not replaced it.

questions.question:
A car servicing chain asks Claude to group two hundred and sixty survey comments by theme. The comments name nobody. Each row carries the booking reference, which the chain's own system turns into a customer's name, phone number and registration.

What should the chain do?

options.label: A
options.text: Take the booking references out of the rows, and upload the comment text on its own.

options.label: B
options.text: Upload the comments in ten smaller batches, so that no single upload holds the whole set of references.

options.label: C
options.text: Have a service adviser read the two hundred and sixty comments and write the themes up herself.

options.label: D
options.text: Read the two hundred and sixty comments again for any customer name the survey missed.

questions.explanation:
CORRECT: Take the booking references out of the rows, and upload the comment text on its own.

The comments name nobody, so they read as anonymous. The booking reference is the identifier. The chain's own system turns it into a name, a phone number and a registration, so a reference is a customer written another way. The theme grouping needs the words, not the reference. Send only what the work needs.

Exam Guide Mapping
* Domain 6: Governance, Risk, and Responsible Use (15%)
* Objective: Apply data sensitivity, regulatory, and privacy considerations

INCORRECT: Upload the comments in ten smaller batches, so that no single upload holds the whole set of references.

Splitting the upload feels safer, because no one batch holds everything. Every row still carries a reference that points at one customer. Ten small uploads share the same identifiers as one large upload. The total is unchanged. Volume is not the risk here, and dividing it does not reduce it.

INCORRECT: Have a service adviser read the two hundred and sixty comments and write the themes up herself.

Reading by hand removes the upload and the exposure with it. It also removes the help the chain asked for, because two hundred and sixty comments is the job. The references come out in one pass, and the work then runs as planned. Keep the work and remove the risk, when both are possible.

INCORRECT: Read the two hundred and sixty comments again for any customer name the survey missed.

Cleaning free text is usually the right instinct, and surveys do collect stray names. The comments already name nobody. A second read would find nothing and would leave the references in place. The exposure sits in a field nobody thinks of as personal. Check the whole record, not the prose.

questions.question:
Label rules require the alcohol strength and an ingredients list on every can. The artwork a brewery drafted in Claude shows the beer's name, the can size and the brewery's address. The printer needs the file on Friday.

How should the brewery proceed?

options.label: A
options.text: Hold the file, put the strength and the ingredients on the can artwork, then send it.

options.label: B
options.text: Print the strength and the ingredients on the outer case instead.

options.label: C
options.text: Send the file on Friday, and add the two items to the next print run instead.

options.label: D
options.text: Ask the printer to set the strength and the ingredients into the artwork.

questions.explanation:
CORRECT: Hold the file, put the strength and the ingredients on the can artwork, then send it.

The rules bind the can, and the artwork becomes the can. It carries the beer's name, the can size and the address, and neither required item. Friday is a printing date, not a reason to send a label that breaks the rules. Adding both items is the only step that makes the can lawful. A duty sits on the thing you send out.

Exam Guide Mapping
* Domain 6: Governance, Risk, and Responsible Use (15%)
* Objective: Apply data sensitivity, regulatory, and privacy considerations

INCORRECT: Print the strength and the ingredients on the outer case instead.

The outer case is easy to change late and the trade does read it. The rules name every can, and a can leaves the case on the shelf. A shopper holding one can sees the name, the size and the address. The case satisfies nobody the rule was written for. Meet a duty on the item the rule names.

INCORRECT: Send the file on Friday, and add the two items to the next print run instead.

Friday matters to the brewery and a later run would eventually carry both items. Every can from this run reaches shops without the strength or the ingredients. The rules apply to those cans on the day they are filled, not when the next batch prints. A deadline is not an exemption. Fix an output before it goes out, not afterwards.

INCORRECT: Ask the printer to set the strength and the ingredients into the artwork.

questions.question:
A pension administrator wants Claude to find members with missing addresses. The member file holds dates of birth and national insurance numbers. Firm rules require a data protection sign off before member data enters a new tool. Nobody has asked.

What should the administrator do?

options.label: A
options.text: Get the data protection sign off before any member data is uploaded.

options.label: B
options.text: Upload only the address column, since that is the only field the task needs.

options.label: C
options.text: Run the search on ten records first, and ask for sign off if it works.

options.label: D
options.text: Ask the pensions manager whether the sign off is really needed for this file.

questions.explanation:
CORRECT: Get the data protection sign off before any member data is uploaded.

The file holds dates of birth and national insurance numbers, and the firm has a rule about where such data may go. The rule is a step before the work, not a formality after it. Nobody has run that step, so the administrator does not yet know whether the upload is allowed. Settle permission before data moves, not after.

Exam Guide Mapping
* Domain 6: Governance, Risk, and Responsible Use (15%)
* Objective: Apply data sensitivity, regulatory, and privacy considerations

INCORRECT: Upload only the address column, since that is the only field the task needs.

Sending less data is sound practice and the task really does need only addresses. An address is member data too, so the rule still applies to the upload. Minimising what you send answers how much, and the open question is whether at all. Reduce the data after you have established you may use it.

INCORRECT: Run the search on ten records first, and ask for sign off if it works.

A small test proves the method works before anyone spends time on approvals. Ten member records are member data, so the rule covers the test as much as the run. The sign off exists to decide whether the data may go at all. Do not use a pilot to get around a gate.

INCORRECT: Ask the pensions manager whether the sign off is really needed for this file.

The pensions manager runs the team and would give a quick answer. The rule is a data protection one, and the manager is not the person who owns it. An informal yes from the wrong desk protects nobody if the upload is later questioned. Take a rule to whoever is accountable for it.

questions.question:
A surveying firm's job files record who checked each calculation pack, the date, and the version issued. Its professional body asks firms to show how each pack was produced, including any AI help. Every pack this year was drafted in Claude.

What should the firm do?

options.label: A
options.text: Add a field to the job file for what Claude drafted, and fill it from now on.

options.label: B
options.text: Have the office manager ask the engineers each Friday which of that week's packs Claude helped to draft.

options.label: C
options.text: Add each engineer's qualification to the job file, since the body wants competence.

options.label: D
options.text: Draft this year's remaining packs by hand, so the firm has no AI help to show.

questions.explanation:
CORRECT: Add a field to the job file for what Claude drafted, and fill it from now on.

The files already show who checked a pack, the date and the version issued. They never show how the pack was drafted, and every pack this year came from Claude. The body asks firms to show production, including AI help. A field on the job file turns that practice into something the firm can produce. Good practice you cannot evidence does not answer an auditor.

Exam Guide Mapping
* Domain 6: Governance, Risk, and Responsible Use (15%)
* Objective: Follow organizational AI policies and governance standards

INCORRECT: Have the office manager ask the engineers each Friday which of that week's packs Claude helped to draft.

Asking every Friday captures the information while it is fresh, and costs the firm little. It creates a standing job for two people and depends on what each engineer recalls. The pack already passes through the job file, which records the checker and the date. The record belongs beside the work. Capture a fact where it happens, not in a weekly round of questions.

INCORRECT: Add each engineer's qualification to the job file, since the body wants competence.

Qualifications matter to a professional body, and the files could carry them easily. The body asked firms to show how each pack was produced, including any AI help. A qualification says who was entitled to check, not what produced the pack. The gap stays exactly where it was. Record the thing the standard asks about, not a neighbouring fact.

INCORRECT: Draft this year's remaining packs by hand, so the firm has no AI help to show.

Removing Claude removes the question, and hand drafting is what the firm used to do. Every pack this year was already drafted in Claude, and those are the packs an auditor would ask about. Stopping now leaves that history unrecorded. The firm also loses work Claude was doing well. Recording a practice costs less than abandoning it.

questions.question:
Two hundred renewal packs have gone out since January. The broker learned this week that the network's AI policy requires a named reviewer on any pack Claude drafts, and covers nothing else she sends. Today's pack names one.

Which two actions should she take?

(Choose two)

options.label: A
options.text: Work out how many packs since January went out with no reviewer named.

options.label: B
options.text: Report the gap to whoever owns the policy, so the network can decide what happens next.

options.label: C
options.text: Name a reviewer on every pack from today, and treat the earlier packs as settled business.

options.label: D
options.text: Ask each handler to remember which of their packs named a reviewer.

options.label: E
options.text: Recall the two hundred packs from customers until each one carries a named reviewer.

questions.explanation:
CORRECT: Work out how many packs since January went out with no reviewer named.

Two hundred packs went out before anyone knew the policy applied to them. Today's pack meets the rule by chance, because the handler signs her work. Nobody yet knows how many of the earlier packs carry a name. The size of the gap decides what the network has to do about it. Find out how far a late discovery reaches back.

CORRECT: Report the gap to whoever owns the policy, so the network can decide what happens next.

A policy the broker found this week has been in force the whole time. The owner of that policy, not the broker, decides what an unnoticed breach requires. Reporting early gives the network the choice while the packs are still recent. Saying nothing leaves the broker judging her own compliance. Tell the rule's owner when you find you have been outside it.

Exam Guide Mapping
* Domain 6: Governance, Risk, and Responsible Use (15%)
* Objective: Follow organizational AI policies and governance standards

INCORRECT: Name a reviewer on every pack from today, and treat the earlier packs as settled business.

Complying from today is quick and stops the gap growing, which is worth doing. The policy was in force for all two hundred earlier packs, not from the day it was found. Treating them as settled is not the broker's decision to make. The exposure does not end because the practice changed. A rule found late still applied while you did not know it.

INCORRECT: Ask each handler to remember which of their packs named a reviewer.

Handlers wrote the packs, so their memory feels like the fastest route to a number. Two hundred packs went out since January, and the packs themselves show whether a name appears. Memory would give a rough figure the network could not rely on. The evidence already exists in the documents. Count the record rather than asking people to recall it.

INCORRECT: Recall the two hundred packs from customers until each one carries a named reviewer.

A recall looks decisive and would satisfy the policy in the end. Nothing here says a pack is wrong; the policy asks for a named reviewer. Pulling two hundred customer documents back creates alarm the facts do not support. The network has not yet been told there is anything to decide. Match the response to what the rule actually requires.

questions.question:
A law firm requires a solicitor to check every Claude drafted client update, so that wrong dates never reach a client. The solicitor reads each update and fixes the tone and spelling. Dates go unchecked.

What should the firm do?

options.label: A
options.text: Have the solicitor check every date against the file before the update goes out.

options.label: B
options.text: Ask a second solicitor to read each client update before it goes out.

options.label: C
options.text: Have Claude check the dates itself before the solicitor reads the update.

options.label: D
options.text: Write the tone and spelling rules into the Project, so the solicitor has less to fix.

questions.explanation:
CORRECT: Have the solicitor check every date against the file before the update goes out.

The firm wrote the rule to stop wrong dates reaching clients. The solicitor reads every update, so the review is real, and it lands on tone and spelling. A carefully worded update with the wrong completion date is the failure the rule exists to prevent. A review is only a control when it looks at the thing that matters.

Exam Guide Mapping
* Domain 6: Governance, Risk, and Responsible Use (15%)
* Objective: Follow organizational AI policies and governance standards

INCORRECT: Ask a second solicitor to read each client update before it goes out.

Two readers catch more than one, and the firm can afford a second pair of eyes. Both solicitors would be reading for the same things, because nobody has said what to check. A wrong date would pass twice instead of once. Adding readers multiplies a review, and it does not redirect one.

INCORRECT: Have Claude check the dates itself before the solicitor reads the update.

Moving the date check earlier sounds efficient and the solicitor keeps their time. The review exists because the firm decided a person must stand behind what reaches a client. The file is the authority on the date, and the solicitor is the one accountable for it. Do not hand a control to the step it was built to check.

INCORRECT: Write the tone and spelling rules into the Project, so the solicitor has less to fix.

Better drafting rules would stop the solicitor spending time on tone and spelling. Time freed is not the same as attention redirected, and nobody has told the solicitor to check dates. The updates would read better and still carry unchecked dates. Say what a review must examine, rather than tidying what it currently sees.

questions.question:
A social landlord will close its repairs phone line and take reports online next month. Claude drew the plan from call volumes, staff costs and opening hours. The board has the plan, the costings and the supplier quotes.

Which step should the landlord take first?

options.label: A
options.text: Ask the tenants who ring what losing the phone line would mean, and weigh the answers.

options.label: B
options.text: List which groups of tenants the change affects, and put that list in the board paper.

options.label: C
options.text: Ask the repairs supervisors what the change would mean for the tenants who ring.

options.label: D
options.text: Ask the supplier to help any tenants who cannot report repairs online.

questions.explanation:
CORRECT: Ask the tenants who ring what losing the phone line would mean, and weigh the answers.

The plan was drawn from call volumes, staff costs and opening hours. The board holds the plan, the costings and the quotes. Not one of those describes a tenant who cannot report a leak online. The people who ring are the only source of that, and they have not been asked. Ask the people a decision lands on before you take it.

Exam Guide Mapping
* Domain 6: Governance, Risk, and Responsible Use (15%)
* Objective: Understand the ethical implications of AI usage

INCORRECT: List which groups of tenants the change affects, and put that list in the board paper.

Naming the affected groups is a real step, and boards should see it. The landlord can already name them: the tenants who ring the repairs line. A list tells the board who is at stake and nothing about what closing the line costs them. The paper would grow and the gap would stay. Naming a group starts the work; it does not finish it.

INCORRECT: Ask the repairs supervisors what the change would mean for the tenants who ring.

Supervisors hear the calls all day and could answer this afternoon. They would be reporting an impression of what tenants find hard, not what tenants say. A tenant with no smartphone and a broken boiler is the person with the answer. Speed here buys a second hand account of the decision. Ask the affected people, not the staff who serve them.

INCORRECT: Ask the supplier to help any tenants who cannot report repairs online.

Somebody has to catch the tenants the website will not serve, and the supplier is on hand. Nobody yet knows who those tenants are or how many there are. The landlord would be buying a remedy for a problem it has not measured. The decision would still be taken without the people in it. Understand an effect before you contract someone to absorb it.

questions.question:
A college bursary panel signs its bands tomorrow. Claude sorted four hundred applications into bands, and applicants from one school fill the lowest. School is not one of the four published criteria. The officer who noticed does not set the scoring.

What should she do?

options.label: A
options.text: Hold the bands, and give the equality lead the pattern and the applications behind it.

options.label: B
options.text: Work out herself what the sorting used the school name for, then decide.

options.label: C
options.text: Have the panel read all four hundred applications before signing tomorrow.

options.label: D
options.text: Add the school name to the published criteria, so the sorting matches the written rules.

questions.explanation:
CORRECT: Hold the bands, and give the equality lead the pattern and the applications behind it.

Applicants from one school fill the lowest band, and school is not a published criterion. The sorting is tracking something nobody agreed to score. The panel signs tomorrow, so the bands would be fixed before anyone examines it. The officer does not set the scoring, and the equality lead can reach it. Stop the decision, then hand the pattern to someone able to judge it.

Exam Guide Mapping
* Domain 6: Governance, Risk, and Responsible Use (15%)
* Objective: Understand the ethical implications of AI usage

INCORRECT: Work out herself what the sorting used the school name for, then decide.

Understanding a cause before raising an alarm is usually the careful order. The officer does not set the scoring, so the criteria are not hers to examine. The panel signs tomorrow, and the bands would be fixed while she worked. Waiting to be certain spends the one thing she does not have. Escalate with the evidence when you cannot examine the cause yourself.

INCORRECT: Have the panel read all four hundred applications before signing tomorrow.

Human reading feels safe when a sorting looks unfair, and the panel is already meeting. Four hundred applications cannot be read overnight. Reading them would show the applications, not what the sorting weighed. The pattern would stay unexplained and the bands would still be signed. Reading the inputs does not reveal what a ranking used.

INCORRECT: Add the school name to the published criteria, so the sorting matches the written rules.

Publishing a criterion does make a process transparent, and transparency is usually right. School was never agreed as a ground for awarding money, and writing it down does not make it fair. The step gives a pattern nobody understands the standing of a rule. The college would then have to defend it. Do not publish a criterion you have not justified.

questions.question:
A bike shop drafts quotes in a Claude Project. Four customers were quoted for a part their bike lacks. All four bikes came in through the new online form. The owner's usual answer to poor output is a more capable tier.

What should he do?

options.label: A
options.text: Read the four quotes and the online bookings behind them, and then choose a fix.

options.label: B

options.label: C

questions.explanation:
CORRECT: Read the four quotes and the online bookings behind them, and then choose a fix.

Four quotes name a part the bike does not have, and all four bikes arrived through the new online form. That shared route is the first thing to look at. The owner has read none of the four, so he does not know what went wrong. A fix chosen now would be chosen blind. Find the fault, then pick the remedy that treats it.

Exam Guide Mapping
* Domain 7: Troubleshooting and Optimization (10%)
* Objective: Identify, diagnose, and resolve issues with underperforming prompts or poor outputs

INCORRECT: Check every quote by hand from now on, until the wrong parts stop appearing again.

Hand checking would stop a wrong part reaching a customer, which matters this week. It would run forever, because nothing in it explains why the part appeared. The owner still would not know what the four quotes have in common. Every new quote costs the shop the same check. A guard is not a diagnosis, and it never becomes one.

INCORRECT: Rebuild the online booking form, since the four bikes used it.

The form is the one thing the four bikes share, so suspicion lands there naturally. Four bookings are a lead, not a finding, and nobody has read what the form actually sent. The fault could sit in the booking, in the Project instruction or in the quote. Rebuilding a form on a hunch is expensive. Confirm a cause before you rebuild anything.

INCORRECT: Requote the four customers correctly and apologise for the parts they never had.

The four customers deserve a corrected quote, and the shop should say sorry. Correcting them clears the visible damage and leaves the cause untouched. Nobody has looked, so the shop cannot say which other quotes carry the same fault. The next booking through the same form repeats it. Put the customer right, and still find out what happened.

questions.question:
A support team asks Claude for machine troubleshooting guides. The manual and fault logs are already in the Project. After nine rewrites, the guides still describe the machine instead of telling an engineer what to try.

Which two changes should the team make?

(Choose two)

options.label: A
options.text: Ask for the checks in the order an engineer would try them, the most common fault first.

options.label: B
options.text: Write one guide by hand and give it to Claude as the pattern to follow.

options.label: C
options.text: Move the manual out of the Project, since the guides read far too much like it.

options.label: D
options.text: Raise the tier, since nine rewrites suggest the task is too hard for it.

options.label: E
options.text: Have an engineer rewrite each of the guides after Claude produces it.

questions.explanation:
CORRECT: Ask for the checks in the order an engineer would try them, the most common fault first.

Nine rewrites have changed the words and nothing else. The guides describe the machine because nobody has said what a guide must do. An engineer needs the first thing to check, then the next, with the commonest fault at the top. That is a change to the task, not to the wording. Say what the output must be, not how the request should read.

CORRECT: Write one guide by hand and give it to Claude as the pattern to follow.

Describing a good guide in words has failed nine times. One guide written by hand shows the length, the order, and the voice at once. Claude then has a pattern to match instead of a description to interpret. An hour of writing replaces another round of rewording. Show the shape you want when saying it has stopped working.

Exam Guide Mapping
* Domain 7: Troubleshooting and Optimization (10%)
* Objective: Adjust approach based on feedback and results

INCORRECT: Move the manual out of the Project, since the guides read far too much like it.

The guides do read like the manual, so the manual looks like the source of the trouble. The manual is what the fault logs are read against, and the guides would lose their facts without it. Nothing about having a manual forces an output to copy its style. Do not remove material because the output borrowed its shape.

INCORRECT: Raise the tier, since nine rewrites suggest the task is too hard for it.

Nine failed attempts do make the task feel too hard for the setup. Writing a troubleshooting guide is ordinary work, and the material is already in the Project. Nine rewrites failed because they were all the same kind of change, not because the reasoning ran short. Read what the failures have in common before you change the tier.

INCORRECT: Have an engineer rewrite each of the guides after Claude produces it.

An engineer rewriting each guide would produce exactly what the team wants. It hands the whole job back to the person the guides were meant to save. Every future guide needs the same rewrite, because nothing about the approach has changed. Do not staff a permanent repair for a setup you have not adjusted.

questions.question:
A holiday park wins bookings on a promise of confirmation within a day. Eleven of the last ninety confirmations named the wrong caravan, and each costs a call and a reissue. In June, the park stopped having a colleague check them.

What should the manager do?

options.label: A
options.text: Put the colleague check back, and quote a confirmation time the park can keep.

options.label: B
options.text: Add someone to the phone line, so the calls about reissued confirmations are answered more quickly.

options.label: C
options.text: Print the caravan number in bold, so a wrong one is easier to spot.

options.label: D
options.text: Keep the colleague check for coach bookings, and send the rest unchecked.

questions.explanation:
CORRECT: Put the colleague check back, and quote a confirmation time the park can keep.

Eleven of ninety confirmations name the wrong caravan, and each one costs a call and a reissue. That work began when the colleague check stopped in June. A confirmation the park has to send twice is not a confirmation sent in a day. The promise the bookings were won on is not being met. Speed bought with rework is not speed.

Exam Guide Mapping
* Domain 7: Troubleshooting and Optimization (10%)
* Objective: Optimize workflows for efficiency and effectiveness

INCORRECT: Add someone to the phone line, so the calls about reissued confirmations are answered more quickly.

More phone cover would shorten the wait for guests who ring, which is a real complaint. It treats the calls as the problem when the wrong caravan is the problem. Eleven guests would still be told the wrong thing first. The park pays a person to manage a fault it could stop making. Do not staff around an error you can prevent.

INCORRECT: Print the caravan number in bold, so a wrong one is easier to spot.

Bold type helps a reader notice a detail, and the caravan is the detail going wrong. Nobody at the park reads the confirmations now, so there is no one to notice. The guest is the first reader, and by then it has been sent. The error is created before the printing. Formatting cannot replace the check that was removed.

INCORRECT: Keep the colleague check for coach bookings, and send the rest unchecked.

The coach contract is the business the park most wants to protect, so checking those first has logic. Nothing here says the eleven wrong caravans were coach bookings. Most confirmations would go out exactly as they do now. The reissues and the calls would largely continue. Scope a check by where the errors are, not by which customer feels important.

questions.question:
A charity's trustees ask how much sooner applicants now hear back. The grant team assesses an application in forty minutes instead of a full day, using Claude. It logs assessment time only. Panel dates, letters and payments are not timed.

What should the team do?

options.label: A
options.text: Take twenty recent applications and note the date on which each reached every stage.

options.label: B
options.text: Ask the panel to meet more often, since that is where the applications must be waiting longest.

options.label: C
options.text: Time the panel stage next, since it is the stage straight after assessment.

options.label: D
options.text: Use Claude on the answer letters as well, so another stage gets faster.

questions.explanation:
CORRECT: Take twenty recent applications and note the date on which each reached every stage.

The trustees asked how much sooner applicants hear back, which is a question about the whole journey. The team logs assessment time only, and panel dates, letters and payments are not timed. A forty-minute assessment says nothing about the wait an applicant feels. Following applications through every stage produces the figure the trustees asked for. Measure what the person outside experiences.

Exam Guide Mapping
* Domain 7: Troubleshooting and Optimization (10%)
* Objective: Optimize workflows for efficiency and effectiveness

INCORRECT: Ask the panel to meet more often, since that is where the applications must be waiting longest.

Panel dates are an obvious place for an application to sit, and meeting more often would help if so. Nothing has been timed except assessment, so the delay is a guess. The panel might be a day of the wait or most of it. Changing a stage on a hunch can cost money and save nothing. Measure before you move a stage.

INCORRECT: Time the panel stage next, since it is the stage straight after assessment.

Timing one more stage is closer to an answer than timing none, and the panel does come next. The team would then hold two stage times and still no total. Letters and payments stay unmeasured, and the trustees asked about the whole wait. Picking a stage by its position guesses where the time sits. Build the timeline before you choose which stage matters.

INCORRECT: Use Claude on the answer letters as well, so another stage gets faster.

Letters are the next piece of work after the panel, and speeding them up sounds like progress. Nobody knows what a letter costs in days, so the gain could be minutes. The same move already produced a saving nobody can see in the total. Another untimed stage adds another unmeasured change. Find where the time sits before you spend effort removing it.

questions.question: A regional hospital network's policy team uses Claude to draft summaries from uploaded treatment policy documents. Some drafts include cited passages, while others include claims Claude cannot connect to a supporting passage. The summaries may inform staff guidance. Which TWO actions are most appropriate before relying on the outputs?

options.label: A
options.text: Switch every prompt evaluation row to human grading instead of using automated checks.
options.feedback: This is incorrect because human grading is flexible and high quality, but it is slow and expensive. Anthropic recommends using faster, reliable, scalable grading approaches when possible and reserving human grading for cases where it is needed.

options.label: B
options.text: Route clinically significant recommendations to a qualified reviewer, even when Claude provides citations.
options.feedback: This is correct because citations and grounding techniques reduce hallucination risk but do not eliminate it. When outputs may influence high-stakes decisions, additional validation by an appropriate human reviewer is required before reliance.

options.label: C
options.text: Verify unsupported claims against the source material, and remove claims that cannot be grounded.
options.feedback: This is correct because Claude can produce confident claims that are not supported by the provided sources. A strong validation step is to require support from source text and retract or remove claims that cannot be tied to evidence.

options.label: D
options.text: Use cited passages as the only review step whenever the answer includes source locations.
options.feedback: This is incorrect because citations help locate supporting passages, but they are not a substitute for all verification. Reviewers still need to confirm that the cited passage actually supports the claim, especially for important or sensitive uses.

questions.explanation:
Claude outputs should be evaluated based on the risk of the use case and the strength of the evidence behind each claim. Anthropic recommends grounding answers in direct quotes, requiring citations, and allowing Claude to say I don’t know, but also warns that these techniques reduce hallucinations rather than eliminating them. For critical information, especially high-stakes decisions, the safest practice is to validate the output before relying on it.

Citations are useful because they connect answers to passages and locations in user-provided source documents, which makes verification easier. They do not automatically prove that the interpretation is correct, that all relevant context was considered, or that the answer is safe to use without review. See Anthropic’s guidance on reducing hallucinations and citations.

For evaluation workflows, human review is valuable when judgment, nuance, or risk requires it, but it should not be the default for every test case. Anthropic’s evaluation guidance recommends task-specific evals with edge cases and favors automated grading when it can be made reliable, reserving human grading for situations where automation is insufficient. See define success criteria for evals.

questions.question: An academic publisher's editorial operations team needs to process 12,000 chapter-review prompts overnight. Editors do not need responses during submission, but the team has previously matched some completed reviews to the wrong source chapters. Which TWO actions would best optimize this workflow?

options.label: A
options.text: Label each source chapter and review task with a reliable unique identifier.
options.feedback: This is correct because the team has already had a misattribution problem. A durable identifier gives editors a dependable way to connect each completed review back to the correct chapter.

options.label: B
options.text: Match each completed review to a chapter using submission sequence alone.
options.feedback: This is incorrect because sequence alone is a fragile tracking process. If any item is delayed, skipped, duplicated, or handled out of sequence, the same misattribution problem can happen again.

options.label: C
options.text: Use an asynchronous bulk-processing workflow for the overnight reviews.
options.feedback: This is correct because the workload does not require immediate responses while prompts are being submitted. Asynchronous bulk processing fits large overnight jobs better than making editors wait for each individual response.

options.label: D
options.text: Require editors to wait for each review before submitting the next chapter.
options.feedback: This is incorrect because it sacrifices the main efficiency advantage of an overnight workload. Waiting for each response may feel safer, but it does not scale well for thousands of prompts.

questions.explanation:
For a large job that can wait until later, asynchronous bulk processing is the better workflow pattern than handling every prompt as a live, one-at-a-time interaction. Anthropic describes batch processing as suited to non-immediate bulk work such as large-scale evaluations, bulk analysis, moderation, or generation, with cost advantages for suitable workloads. See Message Batches.

The second optimization is a workflow control, not a model-quality setting. When many similar items are processed, the team should maintain a reliable identifier or tracking process so every output can be tied back to its source. This prevents operational errors that better prompts alone would not fix. Requiring synchronous review slows the job unnecessarily, and relying on submission sequence alone is too fragile for a high-volume workflow.

questions.question: A retail bank's training team asks Claude to prepare a reusable onboarding guide that combines a branch-escalation checklist, a flowchart, and example scripts for new tellers. They expect to revise it over several rounds and share it with managers after review. Which output format should the associate request first?

options.label: A
options.text: Ask Claude to create an artifact with the guide, flowchart, and scripts as a standalone draft.
options.feedback: This is correct because the requested output is substantial, self-contained, and likely to be edited and reused. Artifacts are designed for larger standalone content such as documents, diagrams, and interactive or visual materials shown outside the main chat.

options.label: B
options.text: Ask Claude to produce separate chat replies for each section and assemble them after review.
options.feedback: This is an inefficient approach because it fragments a connected deliverable across the conversation. It also increases the chance that reviewers lose context or miss consistency issues across sections.

options.label: C
options.text: Ask Claude to answer inline with a compact summary of the guide, flowchart, and scripts.
options.feedback: This is not the best fit because an inline response is better for shorter answers or quick clarification. A compact chat response would make iterative review and reuse harder for a multi-part training guide.

options.label: D
options.text: Ask Claude to return structured JSON containing the guide sections, labels, and review owners.
options.feedback: This is not the best fit because JSON is useful when another system needs machine-readable data. The training team needs a human-reviewable guide with a checklist, flowchart, and scripts, not primarily a data payload.

questions.explanation:
For substantial, reusable work, the right mental model is to choose a format that supports the way the output will be reviewed and used. Anthropic documents that artifacts are appropriate for significant, self-contained content that users are likely to edit, iterate on, reuse, or reference later, including documents, diagrams, flowcharts, and other standalone materials: What are artifacts and how do I use them?.

An inline chat answer is still useful for brief explanations, quick summaries, or conversational refinement, but it is less suitable for a multi-section training document that needs review. Structured data, such as JSON, is most appropriate when the output needs to be consumed reliably by another system, not when the primary audience is a human team reviewing a guide. In Claude app contexts, artifacts also depend on Code execution and file creation being enabled, so users should make sure that capability is available before relying on this output surface.

questions.question: A renewable energy consultancy is configuring Claude for analysts who prepare client briefing notes. The analysts want consistent tone, source-handling expectations, and response structure across many conversations, while each client engagement uses different documents and assumptions. Which TWO practices should the team use?

options.label: A
options.text: Provide engagement-specific facts, documents, and assumptions in the current prompt or project knowledge.
options.feedback: This is correct because changing context should be supplied where it can vary by task or workspace. Keeping client-specific material outside broad reusable instructions reduces staleness and avoids applying the wrong context to unrelated work.

options.label: B
options.text: Define stable role, tone, citation, and formatting expectations in the reusable instruction layer.
options.feedback: This is correct because durable expectations belong in the instruction layer that applies across conversations. Clear role, tone, source-use, and format guidance helps Claude produce consistent outputs without analysts repeating the same directions every time.

options.label: C
options.text: Place all client examples, policy files, and edge cases into the global instruction text.
options.feedback: This is incorrect because global instructions should not become a catch-all knowledge base for every possible case. Overloading broad instructions can clutter context, make behavior less predictable, and apply irrelevant material to unrelated tasks.

options.label: D
options.text: Tell Claude to prioritize any later user request over the reusable instruction layer.

questions.explanation:
Effective system-level or reusable instructions work best when they describe stable behavior: the role Claude should take, the tone to use, the output structure to follow, and how to handle sources or uncertainty. Anthropic’s guidance on system prompts emphasizes using this layer to give Claude context and instructions that shape its behavior for the task.

The tradeoff is that reusable instructions are powerful precisely because they persist, so they should not be filled with facts that change from client to client. Variable facts, source documents, and assumptions are better supplied in the user prompt or in a scoped workspace such as project knowledge, described in What are projects?. That keeps the configuration clean while still giving Claude the context it needs for the specific briefing.

Putting every example or edge case into global instructions is a common configuration anti-pattern because it increases noise and can make irrelevant constraints appear applicable. Likewise, telling Claude to ignore the reusable instruction layer whenever a later request differs defeats the purpose of having consistent system-level guidance in the first place.

questions.question: A city transit agency's customer operations team wants Claude to help agents answer refund inquiries. Claude needs current trip records from the agency's existing case system before drafting a response, but the agency wants controlled access to customer data and human review before replies are sent. Which workflow integration approach best fits this workflow?

options.label: A
options.text: Create a Skill for refund-writing guidelines, then let Claude infer trip details while drafting each reply.
options.feedback: Skills are useful for repeatable procedures, formats, and standards. They do not replace the need to retrieve accurate trip records before drafting a refund response.

options.label: B
options.text: Store exported trip records in a Project, then use the Project as the source for every refund inquiry.
options.feedback: Projects are useful when context accumulates over time in a bounded workspace. They are not the best fit for current per-customer records that should come from a controlled business system.

options.label: C
options.text: Enable an approved connector to the case system, then require agents to review Claude's draft against policy before sending.
options.feedback: This fits a workflow where Claude can use current business data through an approved access path. Human review remains important because customer-facing refund decisions need policy checks before an agent sends the response.

options.label: D
options.text: Paste case-system credentials into each chat, then instruct Claude to sign in and retrieve the customer record.
options.feedback: Sharing credentials in a chat is not an appropriate access-control pattern for a sensitive customer workflow. Access should be governed through approved integrations and organizational controls, not ad hoc credential prompting.

questions.explanation:
For workflow integration at a foundations level, the key decision is how Claude should receive the right business context while preserving the organization’s existing controls. Connectors are designed to let Claude work with external tools and data sources, while access remains governed by authentication, permissions, and administrative enablement where applicable.

A connector-based workflow lets agents ask Claude for help drafting refund responses using current case data, but it should not remove human responsibility for customer-facing decisions. The review step matters because Claude can help summarize, draft, and organize information, while the agent still validates the answer against refund policy and the source record.

Projects and Skills can still be useful in the same environment, but for different purposes. A Project is better for accumulated context in a bounded workspace, while a Skill is better for repeatable procedures such as refund response structure or tone. Neither is a substitute for retrieving current records from an approved system of record. See Anthropic’s Connectors overview and the Skills tutorial, Teach Claude your way of working using skills.
