questions.question: A nonprofit legal clinic's operations team on a Team plan is setting up Claude to help staff summarize case-related Gmail threads and use policy documents stored in Google Drive. Which TWO actions best align with Claude's connector and knowledge-management behavior?

options.label: A
options.text: Have an Owner or Primary Owner enable Google Workspace connectors, then have each user authenticate their own Google account.
options.feedback: This is correct because Team and Enterprise plans require organization-level enablement before individual users can connect. That enablement does not by itself authenticate users or grant access to their Google Workspace data.

options.label: B
options.text: Provide Gmail attachments through a supported upload or Drive source when Claude needs their contents for analysis.
options.feedback: This is correct because the Gmail connector can access attachment metadata but not the attachment contents directly. If the contents matter, the user should supply the file through an upload or another supported source Claude can read.

options.label: C
options.text: Add Google Drive files to the shared project through the Drive connector so members see live-synced context.
options.feedback: This is incorrect because Google Drive files added to projects are available only for private projects. Although Google Docs added to chats and projects can sync from Drive, the Drive option is disabled for shared projects.

options.label: D
options.text: Use organization-level connector enablement to give every member access to all shared Google Workspace content.
options.feedback: This is incorrect because connector permissions mirror the connected user's existing Google Workspace permissions. Organization-level enablement makes the connector available, but it does not grant new access to files, email, or calendars.

questions.explanation:
Claude’s Google Workspace connectors are useful for bringing Gmail, Google Calendar, and Google Drive context into a conversation, but they follow a permission model rather than becoming a blanket organization data source. On Team and Enterprise plans, an Owner or Primary Owner must first enable the connectors, and individual users still authenticate their own Google accounts before Claude can use their accessible data. See Use Google Workspace connectors and Use connectors to extend Claude's capabilities.

A good mental model is that connectors let Claude act through the user’s existing account, with the same source-system permissions and explicit authorization flow. Enabling a connector at the organization level makes the capability available, but it does not let one person access another person’s Gmail or every shared Drive file. This design supports useful retrieval and actions while preserving the access boundaries already defined in Google Workspace.

Gmail and Google Drive also differ in what content Claude can inspect. The Gmail connector can search and read emails, create drafts, manage labels and threads, and see attachment metadata, but it cannot send email on the user’s behalf and does not directly read attachment contents. When a team needs Claude to analyze an attachment, the file should be supplied through a supported upload path or a Drive source that Claude can access.

Projects add another important boundary. Project knowledge can hold uploaded files and context for chats, but Google Drive files added to projects through the connector are only available for private projects, not shared projects. If the clinic needs shared project collaboration, it should choose a supported knowledge-management path rather than assuming Drive connector files can be attached directly to a shared project.

questions.question: An architecture studio's proposal team is creating a Claude Project for upcoming bids. They want every chat in the workspace to use the same proposal templates and background materials, and to follow a consistent tone and section structure. Which setup is most appropriate?

options.label: A
options.text: Put the templates and background details in the project name, then describe the tone in the project description.
options.feedback: This is incorrect because a project’s name and description are not used as context for Claude. They help people identify the project, but they are not the right place for reusable instructions or reference material.

options.label: B
options.text: Paste the templates into the first project chat, then tell teammates to continue from that thread.
options.feedback: This is incorrect because ordinary chat context is not automatically shared across other chats in the same project. Materials that should be reused across project chats need to be added to the project knowledge base.

options.label: C
options.text: Add the templates and background files to project knowledge, then save project instructions for tone and structure.
options.feedback: This is correct because project knowledge provides persistent source material across chats within the same project. Project instructions are the separate setting used to tell Claude how to behave or respond in all chats in that project.

options.label: D
options.text: Share the project with teammates as Can use, then ask them to update instructions as needed.
options.feedback: This is incorrect because Can use access allows members to view project contents and chat in the project, but not edit project knowledge or instructions. Members who need to change those settings require Can edit access on Team or Enterprise plans.

questions.explanation:
Claude Projects are designed as self-contained workspaces with their own chats, project knowledge, and instructions. The right mental model is to separate reusable source material from reusable behavior guidance: add proposal templates and background files to project knowledge, and use Set project instructions for tone, role, formatting, or response style that should apply across chats.

Project names and descriptions are useful for organizing the workspace, but they are not context Claude uses when generating responses. Likewise, pasting material into one chat may help that chat, but it does not make the material available to other project chats unless it is added to project knowledge. For shared projects, permissions matter: Can use is appropriate for members who only need to view and chat, while Can edit is needed for people who should modify knowledge or instructions. See Anthropic’s project overview at What are projects? and the setup guidance at How can I create and manage projects?.

questions.question: An environmental testing laboratory uses Claude to summarize regulatory guidance for field inspectors. During a pilot, reviewers notice that some fluent summaries include requirements they cannot locate in the uploaded materials. What is the most appropriate validation step before using these summaries operationally?

options.label: A
options.text: Run the same prompt again until the answer is consistent, then use the repeated claims in the report.
options.feedback: This is incorrect because repeated outputs can still repeat the same unsupported claim. Consistency across generations is useful to notice variability, but it is not proof that a claim is grounded in the source.

options.label: B
options.text: Require source citations or exact quotes for material claims, then check unsupported claims against the original guidance.
options.feedback: This is correct because factual validation should be grounded in the source material rather than in the apparent fluency of the answer. Anthropic recommends grounding and verification techniques, including citations, quotes, and retracting claims that lack support.

options.label: C
options.text: Prefer the most fluent response version in side-by-side review, then edit uncertain wording for clarity.
options.feedback: This is incorrect because fluency and polish do not establish factual correctness. Editing style may make a summary clearer, but it does not verify whether regulatory requirements are actually present in the source documents.

options.label: D
options.text: Ask Claude to assign confidence scores to material claims, then accept claims that receive high scores.
options.feedback: This is incorrect because a model's self-reported confidence is not a reliable substitute for source verification. A confident answer can still contain unsupported or fabricated details.

questions.explanation:
For factual work, the core validation habit is to tie important claims back to authoritative evidence. Anthropic recommends reducing hallucinations by allowing uncertainty, asking for word-for-word quotes where useful, requiring citations for claims, and retracting claims that lack support. These techniques reduce hallucinations, but they do not eliminate them, so critical information still needs human or process-based validation against the source.

The citations feature is designed to ground answers in provided documents and return passages that support the model's claims. That makes citations and quoted evidence useful for reviewers, because they shift evaluation from “does this sound right?” to “does this claim match the source?” See Anthropic's guidance on reducing hallucinations and the documentation for citations.

Confidence scores, fluent wording, and repeated generation can all be tempting shortcuts, but they validate surface qualities rather than factual grounding. A practical evaluation process should define what counts as an acceptable answer, such as accurate claims with traceable support, and then check outputs against that standard.

questions.question: A pharmaceutical clinical operations group plans to use Claude with regulated trial notes through Anthropic’s Claude API at api.anthropic.com. The privacy team requires documented controls for retention and approved system use before any notes are processed. Which TWO actions should the rollout team take first?

options.label: A
options.text: Rely on Claude’s privacy-focused behavior instead of reviewing service controls.
options.feedback: This is incorrect because model behavior is not a substitute for confirming data handling, retention, and approved use requirements. Privacy-aware model training can help reduce disclosure risk, but it does not establish that a workflow satisfies regulated data controls.

options.label: B
options.text: Use only an approved, documented product path for the regulated workflow.
options.feedback: This is correct because privacy controls depend on using the product path that has been reviewed and approved for the data involved. A workflow that moves sensitive notes into an unapproved interface or integration may not meet the privacy team’s requirement.

options.label: C
options.text: Submit sample trial notes and ask Claude whether the setup is compliant.
options.feedback: This is incorrect because compliance and retention controls should be verified from authoritative documentation and organizational approval, not inferred from a model response. It also risks exposing regulated data before the required review is complete.

options.label: D
options.text: Verify the applicable data retention arrangement for the planned workflow.
options.feedback: This is correct because regulated data should not be processed until the team understands the documented retention arrangement that applies to the specific service path. The appropriate control is to confirm the arrangement before sending sensitive trial notes.

questions.explanation:
When regulated or sensitive information is involved, the first governance step is to connect the proposed use to the documented service controls that actually apply. For Anthropic’s Claude API at api.anthropic.com, Anthropic documents data handling arrangements such as Zero Data Retention and HIPAA readiness, and teams should verify which arrangement applies before processing sensitive material.

The practical mental model is that privacy protection is not established by a good prompt or by asking the model to judge compliance. It comes from using an approved product path, following the organization’s policy, and confirming the relevant data handling terms before data is submitted.

Claude is designed with privacy safeguards, but those safeguards do not replace procedural controls for regulated workflows. The right actions are to verify the applicable retention arrangement and keep the work within an approved, documented path. See Anthropic’s API and data retention documentation for the relevant commercial API data handling information.

questions.question: A video game studio's tools team uses Claude Code in a shared repository. They want repository coding conventions to be available whenever Claude starts, while allowing each developer to keep personal project notes out of version control. Which action is most appropriate?

options.label: A
options.text: Use each developer's user instructions for repository conventions, and commit personal notes for the team.
options.feedback: User instructions are scoped to an individual, so they are not the right place for repository-wide conventions that should apply consistently to the team. Committing personal notes also conflicts with the requirement to keep them out of version control.

options.label: B
options.text: Use auto memory for both repository conventions and personal notes, and expect the guidance to load fully.
options.feedback: Auto memory is Claude-written persistent context, not the best mechanism for human-maintained repository instructions. It also has documented loading limits, so it should not be used when the goal is to reliably maintain shared project guidance in full.

options.label: C
options.text: Use one shared chat transcript for repository conventions, and ask developers to copy personal notes there.
options.feedback: A chat transcript is not the appropriate persistent knowledge mechanism for repository instructions that should load when Claude Code starts. Asking developers to copy personal notes into it also turns private local context into shared team context.

options.label: D
options.text: Use shared project instructions for repository conventions, and keep each developer's notes in local personal project memory.
options.feedback: This matches the collaboration need to separate team guidance from individual notes. Claude Code supports project instructions intended for shared use, while local personal project notes are meant to stay out of version control.

questions.explanation:
For Claude Code, the right knowledge location depends on who should receive the guidance. Repository conventions are shared team context, so they belong in project-level instructions that travel with the repository. Personal project notes are individual context, so they should stay in local personal project memory rather than being committed for everyone.

This separation helps teams maintain useful default context without mixing private preferences into shared standards. Claude Code memory is loaded as context at the start of conversations, but it is not a hard enforcement mechanism, so it is best used for guidance rather than policy controls. The documented memory mechanisms and scopes are described in Claude Code memory.

Auto memory can be useful, but it is not the right substitute for intentionally maintained shared project instructions. A shared chat transcript is also a poor fit because it does not serve as the repository's persistent configuration source for new Claude Code conversations.

questions.question: An auto insurer's digital claims team wants to use Claude in a web chat to assess accident descriptions and tell policyholders whether their claim is likely covered before an adjuster sees it. What is the most appropriate governance step before launch?

options.label: A
options.text: Restrict prompt wording and send likely coverage recommendations without adjuster review.
options.feedback: This is incorrect because prompt wording is not a substitute for required governance controls in high-risk use cases. Sending coverage recommendations to policyholders would still require appropriate disclosure and qualified review.

options.label: B
options.text: Use Claude confidence scores and approve only responses above an internal threshold.
options.feedback: This is incorrect because model confidence is not an adequate ethical or compliance control for insurance decisions. High-stakes recommendations need human oversight, not reliance on the model’s stated certainty.

options.label: C
options.text: Launch with a disclaimer and review only outcomes that policyholders dispute.
options.feedback: This is incorrect because a disclaimer alone does not satisfy the need for qualified review before high-risk advice or decisions are finalized. Reviewing only disputed outcomes shifts oversight until after potential harm has already occurred.

options.label: D
options.text: Require qualified review and disclose the AI interaction before users receive recommendations.
options.feedback: This is correct because insurance recommendations are a high-risk use case under Anthropic’s Usage Policy. When outputs are presented directly to people, the use also requires disclosure, and advice or recommendations need qualified human review before dissemination or finalization.

questions.explanation:
Insurance claim guidance can materially affect a person’s access to benefits, so it falls within a high-risk use case category in Anthropic’s Usage Policy. For these uses, Anthropic requires qualified professional review of advice, recommendations, or subjective decisions before they are disseminated or finalized, and it requires disclosure when outputs are presented directly to individuals or consumers.

A consumer-facing web chat also creates a transparency obligation: users should know they are interacting with AI at the beginning of each chat session. The ethical principle is not merely to avoid bad intent, but to design the workflow so that people are not misled and consequential decisions are not delegated to an automated system without appropriate oversight.

Disclaimers, prompt restrictions, or confidence scores may reduce some risk, but they do not replace required review for high-risk insurance use. For the governing requirements, see Anthropic’s Usage Policy.

questions.question: A university admissions office is piloting a service that will classify sensitive applicant appeal notes through the Claude API at api.anthropic.com. The privacy lead requires that prompts and responses not be stored at rest after each API response is returned, and the team may create a separate Claude Platform organization for production. Which TWO actions should the team take?

options.label: A
options.text: Test real applicant notes in a different Claude interface before confirming the same retention controls.
options.feedback: This is incorrect because moving sensitive data into another interface can change the applicable data-handling arrangement. Testing should use non-sensitive data or wait until the team confirms that the same required controls apply.

options.label: B
options.text: Rely on one organization’s approval for every new organization under the same account.
options.feedback: This is incorrect because the documented retention arrangement is enabled per organization rather than automatically inherited by all organizations. A new production organization needs its own confirmation before sensitive data is sent.

options.label: C
options.text: Verify the chosen Claude product surface is covered by the required retention control before using real notes.
options.feedback: This is correct because retention controls depend on the specific Claude product surface and workflow being used. Sensitive data should only be routed through surfaces that the team has confirmed meet the stated retention requirement.

options.label: D
options.text: Confirm the required retention control is enabled for the production organization before sending applicant notes.
options.feedback: This is correct because the relevant retention control is not automatic across every organization. If the team creates a separate production organization, it should confirm that the required arrangement applies there before processing sensitive applicant data.

questions.explanation:
For this scenario, the key governance step is to match the data sensitivity requirement to the exact environment where the data will be processed. Anthropic’s documentation explains that Zero Data Retention means Anthropic does not store customer prompts or responses at rest after the API response is returned, but it must be enabled for the relevant organization rather than assumed everywhere.

The same privacy posture also depends on the product surface or workflow in use. A team should not treat all Claude experiences as interchangeable for sensitive records, because a control that applies to one API workflow or organization may not apply to another interface, integration, or newly created organization.

questions.question: A museum consortium's analytics team is adopting Anthropic API use for two initiatives, one public exhibit prototype and one internal finance analysis. Its AI policy requires separate membership, separate API key access, and separate monthly cost controls for each initiative. What is the most appropriate governance action?

options.label: A
options.text: Create separate workspaces for the initiatives, assign members and API keys within each, and set spend limits for each workspace.
options.feedback: This is correct because workspaces are documented governance boundaries for API keys, members, and resource limits. Separate workspaces let the team align access and monthly cost controls with the two different initiatives.

options.label: B
options.text: Use the Claude Code workspace for both initiatives, create Console API keys there, and set per-user limits for each app.
options.feedback: This is incorrect because the Claude Code workspace has special behavior and does not allow API keys to be manually created from Console. It is designed around Claude Code sign-in and per-user keys, not as a general replacement for initiative-specific API workspaces.

options.label: C
options.text: Grant all participants the billing role, use one shared API key, and review the monthly charges after use.
options.feedback: This is incorrect because the billing role is for Workbench and billing access, not a way to isolate API usage by initiative. Reviewing charges after the fact does not enforce separate membership or cost controls before usage occurs.

options.label: D
options.text: Keep both initiatives in the Default Workspace, share one API key across teams, and separate activity by naming convention.
options.feedback: This is incorrect because a shared API key does not enforce separate access for the two initiatives. Naming conventions can help reporting discipline, but they are not a governance boundary for membership, keys, or resource limits.

questions.explanation:
When an organization needs to enforce AI governance standards for Anthropic API use, workspaces are the right organizing unit for separating API keys, members, and resource limits. The workspaces documentation explains that additional workspaces can have their own API keys, members, and resource limits, while every organization also has a Default Workspace with special restrictions. See Workspaces.

This design helps teams translate policy into controls: people only join the workspace they need, keys are scoped to that workspace's use, and spend limits can be aligned with each initiative's budget. A shared key plus a naming convention may look convenient, but it depends on behavior rather than enforcing access and cost boundaries. Role changes such as granting billing access do not separate API execution, and the Claude Code workspace is a special workspace with automatically minted per-user keys rather than manually created Console API keys. For related distinctions between monthly spend limits and request-based rate limits, see Rate limits.

questions.question: A product design consultancy has repeatable review workflow and formatting standards for one repository. Several teammates use Claude Code and want the guidance available automatically when working in that repository, while keeping it shared and maintainable rather than pasted into each prompt. Which action is most appropriate?

options.label: A
options.text: Paste the guidance into each new prompt before asking Claude Code to help.
options.feedback: Pasting the guidance can work for a one-off task, but it does not meet the goal of automatic availability. It also creates maintenance risk because teammates may paste outdated or inconsistent versions.

options.label: B
options.text: Rely on auto memory to infer the standards from future conversations.
options.feedback: Auto memory is not the right mechanism for deliberate, human-maintained project standards. The team should choose an explicit shared knowledge mechanism rather than hoping Claude will infer and preserve the rules correctly.

options.label: C
options.text: Store the guidance in Claude Code's shared project-level memory for the repository.
options.feedback: Shared project-level memory is the appropriate place for human-written repository guidance that should load when teammates work in that project. It keeps the standards tied to the repository instead of relying on repeated prompting or separate personal copies.

options.label: D
options.text: Put the guidance in each teammate's personal user instructions.
options.feedback: Personal user instructions are not the best fit for guidance that belongs to one shared repository. Separate personal copies can drift and may apply in situations where the repository standards are not relevant.

questions.explanation:
For shared project guidance, the main judgment is to match the configuration mechanism to the scope of the knowledge. Repository-specific standards should live in project-level memory, so Claude Code can load them as context when work happens in that project and teammates can maintain one shared source.

Repeated prompting is useful for one-time context, but it is a poor maintenance strategy for guidance that should be used consistently. Personal user instructions are broader and individual, so they can drift across teammates or appear in unrelated work. Auto memory is also a poor fit because it is Claude-written context rather than the team’s explicit, maintained instructions.

Claude Code memory is loaded as context, not as a hard enforcement mechanism, so it is best understood as persistent knowledge that guides behavior rather than a guaranteed policy control. See Anthropic’s Claude Code memory documentation for the distinction between human-written project guidance, user guidance, local notes, and auto memory.

questions.question: A corporate training team is preparing a series of onboarding materials over several weeks. They will repeatedly ask Claude questions that depend on the same handbook, terminology guide, and style rules, but each request will be a separate conversation. Which approach best fits this work?

options.label: A
options.text: Start a new ordinary chat, upload the materials, and restate the style rules.
options.feedback: Ordinary chat works well for one-off or single-thread work. Re-uploading and restating the same context each time adds avoidable setup for repeated work.

options.label: B
options.text: Create a Project, add the materials to project knowledge, and set project instructions.
options.feedback: This is the best fit because the team needs reusable context across separate conversations. Project knowledge and project instructions are designed to provide shared background and guidance within a project.

options.label: C
options.text: Use Research, enable web search, and ask Claude to rebuild the context each time.
options.feedback: Research is useful for multi-source investigation, especially when web search is needed. It does not replace a project knowledge base for repeatedly using the same internal materials.

options.label: D
options.text: Create an artifact, place the source materials there, and use it as the workspace.
options.feedback: An artifact can be useful for working with generated content, but it is not the documented mechanism for reusable project context. The need here is to make the same background materials available across separate conversations.

questions.explanation:
For repeated work that depends on the same documents and rules, Projects are the appropriate Claude feature. Projects are self-contained workspaces with their own chat histories and knowledge bases, and project instructions can shape Claude’s responses across chats inside that project. See What are projects? and How can I create and manage projects?.

The key mental model is that ordinary chat is best when the context lives in one conversation, while a Project is best when the same context should be reused. The usage guidance notes that Claude remembers earlier context within a single conversation, but project content is cached for repeated use when working with the same documents. See Usage limit best practices.

Research is not the right default for this scenario because the team is not asking Claude to conduct a multi-source investigation from the web. It is trying to reuse known internal materials. Research is a paid-plan feature and requires web search to function, as described in Using Research on Claude.ai.

questions.question: A maritime logistics dispatch team wants Claude to draft daily port delay summaries from vessel status notes. Early trials look useful, but stakeholders disagree about whether the responses are good enough. Before the team spends time rewriting prompts, what is the most appropriate next step?

options.label: A
options.text: Write a longer prompt with more instructions and rely on reviewers to catch misses.
options.feedback: Adding prompt detail without success criteria can make behavior harder to evaluate and may not address the real failure. Human review can be useful, but relying only on ad hoc review is slower and less scalable than a planned evaluation process.

options.label: B
options.text: Switch every summary request to the most capable model and compare informal reactions afterward.
options.feedback: Changing models may help some goals, especially latency, cost, or reasoning quality tradeoffs, but it should not be the first unmeasured move. Informal reactions do not establish whether the system meets the actual use case requirements.

options.label: C
options.text: Ask Claude to rate each draft and approve summaries with high confidence scores.
options.feedback: Claude's self-assessment is not a reliable substitute for external evaluation against defined criteria. A high confidence rating can still accompany omissions, unsupported claims, or tone mismatches.

options.label: D
options.text: Define measurable success criteria and test cases that reflect typical notes and edge cases.
options.feedback: This is correct because prompt iteration should be guided by clear requirements and empirical evaluation. A representative test set helps the team evaluate the real task, not just a few memorable examples.

questions.explanation:
For a new Claude workflow, the practical starting point is not simply making the prompt longer. Anthropic recommends starting with clear success criteria, ways to test against those criteria, and then iterating prompts or other choices based on evidence, as described in Prompt engineering overview.

Good criteria are specific and measurable across the dimensions that matter for the use case, such as task fidelity, consistency, tone, privacy preservation, context use, latency, and price. The evaluation set should mirror the real task distribution, including edge cases, so the team can see whether Claude performs well on the port delay summaries it will actually encounter. See Define success criteria for guidance on building multidimensional evaluations.

The distractors skip that requirements step. Switching models, asking Claude to judge itself, or writing a larger prompt may appear productive, but none of them creates a dependable way to decide whether the solution works for stakeholders in practice.

questions.question: A city tourism bureau is preparing to brief department leaders on using Claude to draft public-facing visitor safety updates from internal incident reports. Leaders ask how to describe Claude's role in the workflow. What message should the associate give?

options.label: A
options.text: Position Claude as an exact document retriever, with confident wording accepted as evidence.
options.feedback: Confident wording is not a reliable accuracy signal. Claude can generate plausible but incorrect or unsupported text, so the workflow should require evidence checks rather than treating fluency as proof.

options.label: B
options.text: Position Claude as drafting and synthesis support, with source grounding and human validation for public claims.
options.feedback: This accurately communicates both value and limitation. Claude can help summarize and draft from provided context, but stakeholder-facing claims should be grounded and checked because hallucinations can be reduced but not eliminated.

options.label: C
options.text: Position Claude as a source of truth, with citations requested for every public claim.
options.feedback: Citations and grounding are useful mitigations, but they do not make Claude a guaranteed source of truth. Critical claims still need validation against authoritative sources before public release.

options.label: D
options.text: Position Claude as an autonomous publisher, with the strongest model selected for each update.
options.feedback: Choosing a more capable model can improve fit for demanding tasks, but it does not remove the need for review. Model capability is specific to the selected model and task, not a blanket guarantee of publish-ready accuracy.

questions.explanation:
Claude's value is strongest when stakeholders understand it as a workflow accelerator for drafting, synthesis, and analysis, not as an unquestioned authority. Anthropic documents that Claude can produce factually incorrect or context-inconsistent text, and that techniques such as grounding, quotes, uncertainty, and citations can reduce but not eliminate hallucinations. See Reduce hallucinations.

The practical message is to set expectations around assisted work: Claude can help transform internal reports into clear public drafts, but public safety claims should be checked against the original reports or another authoritative source. It is also important not to overgeneralize from the brand name Claude, since Anthropic's models overview explains that capabilities, context windows, output limits, latency, pricing, and knowledge cutoffs vary by model. A stronger model or a request for citations may improve the workflow, but neither turns generated text into verified evidence on its own.

questions.question: A regional food bank's operations team wants Claude to turn pantry intake notes into weekly supply-request summaries for partner agencies. A few demos look promising, but the notes vary widely and leadership wants to know whether the workflow is reliable enough before expanding it. Which two actions should the team take next?

options.label: A
options.text: Use the most capable Claude model for all summaries and review cost after organization-wide rollout.
options.feedback: This is incorrect because model choice should reflect the requirements, including cost and latency, before expansion. Using the most capable model by default may waste budget if a faster or lower-cost model meets the success criteria.

options.label: B
options.text: Keep revising the prompt with polished examples until leadership approves the demo outputs.
options.feedback: This is incorrect because it overfits to selected examples and stakeholder impressions rather than testing the real task. Prompt iteration can help later, but it should be guided by measurable requirements and evaluation results.

options.label: C
options.text: Define measurable success criteria across fidelity, tone, privacy handling, latency, and cost.
options.feedback: This is correct because the team needs to know what “reliable enough” means before judging the workflow. Practical Claude use case analysis starts by translating stakeholder needs into specific criteria that can be tested, not by relying on impressions from a few demos.

options.label: D
options.text: Build a test set from common notes and edge cases, then grade outputs against the criteria.
options.feedback: This is correct because the evaluation should reflect the real distribution of work, including difficult or unusual inputs. Grading outputs against defined criteria gives the team evidence about whether Claude is suitable for the workflow.

questions.explanation:
Good workflow design with Claude begins by analyzing the use case as a product problem: what has to be true for the output to be useful, safe, and practical. Anthropic’s prompt engineering guidance emphasizes having clear success criteria, ways to test against them, and an initial prompt before deeper prompt engineering, and it notes that not every failure is best solved by prompt changes. See Prompt engineering overview.

For this food bank workflow, the team should define criteria such as whether summaries preserve the intake notes accurately, use an appropriate partner-facing tone, avoid exposing unnecessary private information, and meet latency and cost expectations. Then it should test Claude on examples that resemble the actual workload, including messy notes, missing details, contradictory requests, and other edge cases. Anthropic’s evaluation guidance recommends specific, measurable, achievable, and relevant success criteria, plus evaluation sets that mirror the real task distribution. See Define success criteria.

The tempting shortcut is to keep polishing prompts around a few impressive demos, but that does not tell the team whether the workflow will work consistently in production-like conditions. Similarly, choosing the strongest model for every case may improve some outputs, but it ignores the cost and latency dimensions that are part of the requirements. A better mental model is to treat prompting, model choice, and workflow design as tools that are selected after the requirements and evaluation method are clear.

questions.question: A renewable energy consultancy is testing Claude for drafting client-ready summaries from site inspection notes. Its evaluation results show the summaries usually meet the team's accuracy, relevance, and tone targets, but the workflow is too slow and too expensive for daily use. What should the team do next?

options.label: A
options.text: Run the prompt improver to add more instructions and examples before measuring latency and cost again.
options.feedback: The prompt improver can produce more thorough prompt templates, but that can also make prompts longer and slower. It is not the best first response when the main failures are speed and cost rather than task quality.

options.label: B
options.text: Continue changing prompt wording informally until a few sampled summaries feel acceptable to the analysts.
options.feedback: Ad hoc prompt tweaks are a weak troubleshooting method because they do not show whether changes improve the real workload. Prompt optimization should be guided by success criteria and repeatable tests.

options.label: C
options.text: Keep the successful prompt as a baseline and test model choice plus shorter inputs and outputs against the same eval suite.
options.feedback: This uses the eval results to choose an optimization lever that matches the observed problem. When quality criteria are already being met but latency and price are failing, changing model choice and token usage is more appropriate than only rewriting the prompt.

options.label: D
options.text: Replace the evaluation suite with a single reviewer score so the team can simplify future comparisons.
options.feedback: A single score hides which dimension is failing and makes it harder to choose the right fix. Real applications often need multidimensional evaluation, including quality, latency, and price.

questions.explanation:
Good troubleshooting starts by reading the evaluation results as signals about which lever to adjust. If the summaries already satisfy quality criteria but miss latency and price targets, the next experiment should preserve the working quality baseline while testing faster or cheaper configurations, shorter context, and shorter outputs against the same eval set.

Anthropic's prompt engineering guidance emphasizes starting with success criteria and empirical tests, and it notes that not every failing criterion should be solved by prompt changes. The evaluation guidance also recommends multidimensional criteria because task fidelity, tone, latency, and price can move independently. See Prompt engineering overview, Develop tests, and Reduce latency.

The prompt improver can be useful when prompt quality needs improvement, but it may create longer, more detailed templates, which is a poor fit when speed and cost are already the constraints. Informal tweaking and single-score reviews are anti-patterns because they make it difficult to connect a change to a measured outcome.

Informal tweaking and single-score reviews are anti-patterns because they make it difficult to connect a change to a measured outcome.

questions.question: A veterinary hospital network's operations team is preparing a process-improvement workshop about appointment scheduling software. The team needs a brief that reflects current vendor offerings and recent pricing changes before leaders choose which processes to redesign. Their Claude workspace has web search enabled. What is the most appropriate way to use Claude?

options.label: A
options.text: Have Claude draft the brief from its built-in knowledge and skip source review.
options.feedback: This is incorrect because built-in model knowledge may be outdated for current vendor and pricing information. Skipping source review also weakens the reliability of a brief used for planning decisions.

options.label: B
options.text: Have Claude search for current vendor information, cite sources, and synthesize a planning brief.
options.feedback: This is correct because the task depends on current and changing information, such as vendor offerings and pricing. Web search lets Claude use real-time web content and return cited sources, which supports a research brief that leaders can verify.

options.label: C
options.text: Have Claude brainstorm scheduling improvements without checking vendor information.
options.feedback: This is incorrect because brainstorming can help with process ideas, but it does not address the need for current vendor research. The team needs evidence about present offerings before using the brief in a workshop.

options.label: D
options.text: Have Claude rate its confidence in vendor claims before sharing the brief.
options.feedback: This is incorrect because self-rated confidence is not a reliable substitute for checking current sources. A confident answer can still be stale or unsupported when the topic changes over time.

questions.explanation:
For research and planning tasks that depend on current or changing information, Claude should use web search when it is available. Anthropic documents web search as a server tool that gives Claude access to real-time web content beyond its knowledge cutoff and returns cited sources, which makes it appropriate for vendor offerings, pricing, recent events, and other information that may change.

The best workflow is to let Claude gather current information, preserve citations, and then synthesize that material into the planning artifact the team needs. Claude can still help structure the workshop and identify process-improvement themes, but the factual claims about the market should be grounded in sources rather than only in the model's existing knowledge or confidence. questions.question: A health insurance claims quality team wants Claude to review several long audit notes, compare them with a checklist, identify recurring issues, and draft a concise action plan. Which two prompting approaches best decompose the request so Claude can execute it reliably?

options.label: A
options.text: Break the work into ordered steps with clear deliverables for each stage.
options.feedback: This is correct because explicit task structure helps Claude follow the intended process instead of inferring it from a broad goal. Ordered steps are especially useful when completeness or sequence matters, such as reviewing notes before drafting recommendations.

options.label: B
options.text: Separate the notes, checklist, examples, and final request with descriptive tags.
options.feedback: This is correct because tags help Claude distinguish different parts of a complex prompt. Descriptive grouping is useful when the prompt mixes source material, instructions, examples, and the final task.

options.label: C
options.text: Describe the overall goal briefly and let Claude choose any workflow it prefers.
options.feedback: This is incorrect because vague intent leaves important sequencing and completeness requirements implicit. Claude may still produce a useful answer, but the prompt gives it less guidance for a complex review task.

options.label: D
options.text: Combine all materials and instructions into one continuous paragraph for brevity.
options.feedback: This is incorrect because compressing distinct materials into one paragraph makes the prompt harder to parse. Brevity is helpful only when it does not remove the structure Claude needs to understand roles, inputs, and outputs.

questions.explanation:
Complex tasks work best when the prompt makes the work visible. Rather than asking for a broad outcome and hoping Claude infers the right path, decompose the request into ordered steps, such as review the source notes, compare against the checklist, group recurring issues, then draft the action plan.

Anthropic’s prompting guidance emphasizes clear, explicit instructions, and recommends numbered lists or bullets when order or completeness matters. It also recommends using XML-style tags to separate instructions, context, examples, and variable inputs in complex prompts, using consistent and descriptive names. See Anthropic prompt engineering guidance.

The tradeoff is that structured prompts take slightly more setup, but reduce ambiguity and make it easier for Claude to apply the right material at the right time. For long or mixed inputs, structure is not just cosmetic; it helps preserve the distinction between evidence, rules, examples, and the final requested output.

questions.question: A public library system wants Claude to tag thousands of short patron feedback comments by topic each night. The labels are straightforward, responses can be brief, and the team wants to keep both turnaround time and spending low. Which model-selection approach best fits the task?

options.label: A
options.text: Use Claude Sonnet 5 for routine tagging and maximize effort on every response.
options.feedback: Claude Sonnet 5 offers a strong balance of speed and intelligence, but the task does not indicate a need for that extra reasoning. Maximizing effort on every response also increases latency and token use, which conflicts with the goal of low turnaround time and spending.

options.label: B
options.text: Use Claude Haiku 4.5 for routine tagging and escalate only comments needing deeper review.
options.feedback: This matches a high-volume, straightforward workload where speed and cost matter. Claude Haiku 4.5 is positioned as the fastest current model with near-frontier intelligence, making it a good fit for brief classification tasks.

options.label: C
options.text: Use Claude Fable 5 for routine tagging and keep every comment on the highest-tier model.
options.feedback: This overmatches the task to a model described for next-generation intelligence and long-running agents. For simple nightly tagging, the added capability is unlikely to justify higher cost and slower comparative latency.

options.label: D
options.text: Use Claude Opus 4.8 for routine tagging and accept the added cost for consistency.
options.feedback: Claude Opus 4.8 is aimed at complex agentic coding and enterprise work, not simple short-label classification. Using it for every routine comment would spend more than needed for the stated speed and budget priorities.

questions.explanation:
Model selection should start from the work being performed, not from a habit of always choosing the most capable model. Anthropic frames model choice as a tradeoff among capability, speed, and cost, with effort as an additional lever for supported recent models when more or less reasoning is needed within the same model. See Choosing the right model.

For straightforward, high-volume categorization, a faster and lower-cost model is often the right first choice. The current model overview describes Claude Haiku 4.5 as the fastest model with near-frontier intelligence, while positioning Fable and Opus for more demanding work. The model comparison and pricing pages, Models overview and Pricing, support matching routine workloads to a model that preserves quality without unnecessary latency or cost.

questions.question: A legal aid clinic is piloting Claude to summarize eviction intake interviews into referral notes. Before staff rely on the notes, they want a lightweight but credible way to check whether the summaries are accurate and complete across routine cases and unusual situations. What should they do?

options.label: A
options.text: Create an eval set from simple intakes, score overall readability, and approve summaries above the average score.
options.feedback: This is incorrect because simple cases alone do not test whether the workflow holds up under realistic variation or edge cases. Readability is useful, but it does not directly validate whether facts are supported or important details were omitted.

options.label: B
options.text: Review a few failed examples, adjust the prompt after each one, and stop when the latest examples pass.
options.feedback: This is incorrect because a few hand-picked examples can overfit the prompt to recent failures. A reusable eval set gives a more stable way to compare prompt versions and detect regressions across the intended use cases.

options.label: C
options.text: Create an eval set that mirrors real intakes, includes edge cases, and scores factual support and missing details separately.
options.feedback: This is correct because evaluation should reflect the real task distribution and include edge cases. Scoring factual support and missing details separately makes the criteria more specific and better aligned to accuracy and completeness than a single vague judgment.

options.label: D
options.text: Ask Claude to rate its own confidence, flag low-confidence summaries, and skip checking against source interviews.
options.feedback: This is incorrect because self-reported confidence is not a reliable measure of factual correctness. Claude can produce fluent or confident text that is unsupported by the provided context, so source-based validation remains necessary for important information.

questions.explanation:
For evaluating Claude-generated outputs, the key is to turn quality into specific, measurable criteria that match the real task. Accuracy and completeness are not the same dimension: an output can avoid false claims while still omitting an important deadline, eligibility fact, or risk indicator. Treating those dimensions separately helps reviewers see where the prompt or workflow needs improvement.

Anthropic’s evaluation guidance recommends that evals mirror the real-world task distribution, include edge cases, and use multidimensional criteria where relevant. The Console Evaluation tool can support this workflow with test cases, side-by-side comparison, grading, and prompt versioning, but it is not an automatic truth oracle. See Define success criteria and Use the Evaluation tool.

For factual tasks, fluency and confidence are not enough. Anthropic’s hallucination guidance notes that Claude can generate text that is factually incorrect or inconsistent with context, and mitigation techniques reduce but do not eliminate that risk. Critical summaries should therefore be checked against the source material, using supporting evidence where possible, as described in Reduce hallucinations.

questions.question: A performing arts center's development team wants Claude to turn several donor interview notes into a board-ready briefing. The team needs consistent sections for motivations, concerns, evidence from the notes, and unresolved questions. Which prompting approach is most appropriate for this task?

options.label: A
options.text: Ask Claude to brainstorm a persuasive donor narrative and add details that make the briefing more compelling.
options.feedback: This treats an evidence-based briefing like an open-ended creative task. Adding unsupported details can undermine accuracy when the work depends on interview notes.

options.label: B
options.text: Provide the notes, define the briefing sections, and ask Claude to extract evidence before drafting recommendations.
options.feedback: This is appropriate because the task requires structured analysis before drafting a board-ready output. Clear sections and an ordered process help Claude handle the source material, preserve evidence, and produce a usable briefing.

options.label: C
options.text: Paste the notes and ask Claude to summarize them naturally without specifying format or decision criteria.
options.feedback: This may produce a fluent summary, but it leaves too much unstated for a board-ready briefing with specific sections. Vague prompting is less reliable when order, completeness, and evidence tracking matter.

options.label: D
options.text: Request a polished briefing in a formal tone and tell Claude to keep any uncertainties out of the final version.
options.feedback: A formal tone may help presentation, but it does not guide Claude through the analysis needed for this task. Hiding uncertainties is risky because unresolved questions are part of the requested output.

questions.explanation:
For an analysis-to-drafting task, the prompt should make the work process explicit: give Claude the source material, define the desired output structure, and specify the sequence of reasoning steps you want reflected in the result. Anthropic’s guidance emphasizes clear and direct instructions, including desired format, constraints, and numbered or bulleted steps when order or completeness matters, as described in Be clear and direct.

The mental model is to match the prompt to the task type. Brainstorming can invite breadth and novelty, drafting may emphasize audience and tone, while evidence-based analysis should prioritize source grounding, comparison, and explicit uncertainty. A board-ready briefing based on interview notes needs more than polish, it needs a repeatable structure that keeps claims tied to the materials.

Anthropic also frames prompt engineering as something to evaluate against success criteria, not just a matter of whether an output feels good. The Prompt engineering overview notes that effective prompting starts with clear success criteria and empirical testing, and that not every problem is best solved by prompt changes alone. In practice, this means you should design prompts around the outcome you need, then check whether outputs meet that outcome reliably.

questions.question: A museum archive team uses Claude to draft answers to researcher questions from digitized exhibit notes and donor letters. Some drafts include plausible dates and names that are hard for curators to spot quickly. Before making this workflow part of staff review, what should the team do?

options.label: A
options.text: Ask Claude to rate each draft's confidence, then route only low-confidence answers to curators for checking.
options.feedback: Self-rated confidence is not a reliable signal that the content is accurate or complete. A confident answer can still contain unsupported dates, names, or conclusions, so critical claims still need validation.

options.label: B
options.text: Test a small set of typical questions, then rely on staff edits to catch unusual missing details.
options.feedback: Testing only typical questions can miss edge cases where hallucinations or omissions are more likely to appear. Relying on later edits also makes quality control inconsistent and harder to measure.

options.label: C
options.text: Create representative and edge-case test questions, then grade answers against source-backed criteria for factual support and completeness.
options.feedback: This is the best approach because it checks the workflow against the kinds of cases staff will actually encounter, including unusual cases. Source-backed criteria make accuracy and completeness measurable instead of relying on whether an answer sounds plausible.

options.label: D
options.text: Enable citations for the source documents, then approve answers whenever every paragraph includes a citation.
options.feedback: Citations help reviewers trace claims back to provided documents, which is valuable for verification. They do not automatically prove that every inference is correct or that the answer includes all relevant information.

questions.explanation:
When evaluating Claude-generated outputs, the goal is not only to ask whether an answer sounds good, but whether it satisfies defined criteria for the real task. Anthropic recommends success criteria that are specific, measurable, achievable, and relevant, and notes that most use cases need multidimensional evaluation, such as task fidelity, context use, consistency, and privacy preservation. See Define success criteria.

For an archive workflow, that means using test questions that reflect the real distribution of researcher requests, plus edge cases involving ambiguous notes, similar names, conflicting dates, or missing evidence. Grading should check both accuracy, whether claims are supported by the source material, and completeness, whether important relevant information was omitted.

Citations and grounding techniques are useful aids, but they are not substitutes for evaluation. Anthropic’s hallucination guidance explains that Claude can produce factually incorrect or context-inconsistent text, and techniques such as requiring citations or direct quotes can reduce, but not eliminate, hallucinations. See Reduce hallucinations and Citations.

questions.question: An environmental grant review team asks Claude to summarize eligibility rules from an uploaded program guide. Claude’s response includes a requirement that applicants must have three years of operating history, but the provided guide excerpt says one year. Before the team uses the summary in reviewer training, what is the most appropriate action?

options.label: A
options.text: Ask Claude to rate its confidence and accept the requirement if the rating is high.
options.feedback: Self-reported confidence is not a reliable validation method for factual claims. A model can be confident while still producing text that is incorrect or inconsistent with the context.

options.label: B
options.text: Flag the mismatch as a possible hallucination and verify the requirement against the guide.
options.feedback: This is the best action because hallucinations can include statements that conflict with the provided context, not only invented facts. Critical eligibility information should be validated against the source before it is reused in training materials.

options.label: C
options.text: Remove the specific year count and publish the summary as a general training aid.
options.feedback: Removing the number avoids the visible contradiction but does not validate the eligibility rule. Training materials should preserve accurate requirements rather than obscure unresolved source conflicts.

options.label: D
options.text: Ask Claude to rewrite the summary more cautiously and keep the requirement if it sounds qualified.
options.feedback: Cautious wording does not resolve whether the requirement is correct. A softened claim can still mislead reviewers if it remains inconsistent with the source material.

questions.explanation:
Anthropic defines a hallucination broadly as generated text that may be factually incorrect or inconsistent with the context the user provided. In this scenario, the problem is not merely that the answer is uncertain, it directly conflicts with the program guide excerpt, so the safer response is to treat it as a possible hallucination and verify the requirement before reuse.

Hallucination-reduction techniques can reduce risk, but they do not eliminate it, especially for information that affects decisions. For document-grounded work, useful mitigations include requiring citations, asking Claude to extract supporting quotes, and retracting claims it cannot support with the source. See Anthropic’s guidance on reducing hallucinations.

For evaluation and validation, the mental model is to compare the output against an authoritative reference rather than against the model’s tone, fluency, or confidence. Polishing the answer, asking for a confidence score, or hiding the disputed detail may make the artifact look better, but none of those actions establishes that the content is correct.

questions.question: An independent audit firm's proposal team has 12 vendor questionnaires for one bid. They need Claude to compare the answers and draft a short risk memo during a single working session. They do not expect to reuse the questionnaires after this bid, and the file set is small enough to provide all at once. Which Claude feature choice best fits this work?

options.label: A
options.text: Use Research and have Claude search for supporting sources.
options.feedback: Research is intended for multi-source investigation and requires web search to function. The task is to compare provided questionnaires, not to conduct an external investigation.

options.label: B
options.text: Create a Project and add the questionnaires as Project Knowledge.
options.feedback: Projects are useful when context should persist across focused chats or be reused over time. In this scenario, the questionnaires are only needed for one bid in one working session, so a Project adds unnecessary setup.

options.label: C
options.text: Create an artifact and place the questionnaires in the artifact.
options.feedback: An artifact can be useful for working with a generated deliverable, such as a memo draft. It is not the right choice for supplying the source questionnaires as the primary analysis context.

options.label: D
options.text: Use a regular Claude chat and attach the questionnaires for that session.
options.feedback: This is the best fit because the work is one-off and contained within a single conversation. Claude can use the uploaded files as context for that session without requiring a reusable workspace.

questions.explanation:
For a single-session task, a regular Claude chat is usually the simplest product choice: provide the needed files, ask for the comparison, and iterate in the same conversation. Claude retains the earlier context within that conversation, which fits a one-time review where the source material will not be reused.

Projects are better when the same knowledge, files, or instructions should support multiple focused chats over time. The Projects documentation describes them as self-contained workspaces with their own chat histories and knowledge bases, while usage guidance distinguishes one-off chat work from reusable project context. See What are projects? and Usage limit best practices.

File upload limits also support the practical choice here: chat uploads allow multiple files in a single chat when they fit the documented limits, as described in What kinds of documents can I upload to Claude.ai?. Research is a paid-plan feature for deeper, multi-source investigation and requires web search, so it is not the best match when the needed evidence is already supplied in the questionnaires, as noted in Using Research on Claude.ai.

options.label: D
options.text: Compare each label with the rubric and responses, and remove labels that lack source support.
options.feedback: This directly checks whether Claude’s labels are supported by the provided context and stated criteria. A claim can be problematic when it is inconsistent with the source material, and an unsupported label may also introduce unfair bias into a decision workflow.

questions.explanation:
Claude can produce text that is factually incorrect or inconsistent with the given context, even when the wording sounds confident and polished. In this scenario, the risk is not only a factual mismatch with the rubric, but also a potentially biased inference from employment status to commitment.

The practical validation step is to tie each evaluative label back to the provided rubric and source responses, then remove or revise anything that lacks support. Rerunning the prompt or asking for confidence can be useful only as secondary signals. The stronger mental model is that important outputs need source-grounded validation against measurable criteria, not vague judgments about whether an answer sounds balanced, polished, or confident.

questions.question: A meal-kit retailer's merchandising team uses Claude throughout the day to draft product descriptions. Each request repeats a long approved-claims guide and category taxonomy, then adds a different product brief, and writers need responses while they work. Which action would best improve efficiency while keeping the work interactive?

options.label: A
options.text: Put the full guide and taxonomy in custom instructions, then apply those standards to every Claude task.
options.feedback: Custom instructions are better suited to broad preferences that should apply universally, such as tone or whether Claude should ask clarifying questions. A long, task-specific claims guide would be too broad for every task and is better packaged as a relevant Skill.

options.label: B
options.text: Create a reusable Skill containing the claims guide, taxonomy, and drafting procedure, then provide each product brief.
options.feedback: This uses a Skill for repeatable work that should follow the same detailed standards each time. The writers can continue working interactively while avoiding repeated setup and re-explanation.

options.label: C
options.text: Create a separate Project for each product brief, then duplicate the guide and taxonomy into every Project.
options.feedback: Projects are useful when work needs accumulated context over time, such as an ongoing campaign or research effort. Creating a separate Project for each brief and duplicating the same standards adds overhead without addressing the repeatable procedure directly.

options.label: D
options.text: Paste the guide and taxonomy into each new chat, then refine every response with the same follow-up reminders.
options.feedback: This can work for one-off prompting, but it preserves the inefficient pattern the team is trying to improve. Repeating the same long materials and reminders increases setup effort and makes consistency harder to maintain.

questions.explanation:
Skills are designed for repeatable procedures that Claude should apply automatically when the task is relevant. In this scenario, the approved-claims guide, taxonomy, and drafting procedure are stable standards, while each product brief changes. Packaging the stable materials into a Skill reduces repeated setup while preserving an interactive writing workflow.

Projects solve a different problem: they are useful when a body of work needs accumulated context over time, such as a product launch or ongoing campaign. Custom instructions are broader preferences that apply across Claude, so they are not the best place for extensive, task-specific standards. Regular prompting remains useful for one-off work, but it is less efficient when the same detailed procedure must be repeated many times.

questions.question: A regional airline's customer communications team is using Claude to draft delay-notification emails. Drafts sometimes omit required rebooking details and vary too much in tone. The team has a draft prompt and a set of past email examples. What should the team do next to improve output quality reliably?

options.label: A
options.text: Define measurable quality criteria, run representative test cases, revise the prompt, and retest.
options.feedback: This follows an evaluation-first iteration loop. Clear criteria and representative tests make it possible to tell whether prompt changes actually improve required details and tone consistency.

options.label: B
options.text: Generate a new prompt, inspect several successful examples, publish it, and monitor complaints.
options.feedback: A generated prompt can be a useful starting point, but it is not a substitute for evaluation. Looking only at successful examples can hide failures that would appear in representative or edge-case test cases.

options.label: C
options.text: Add broad quality instructions, try one recent email, accept the draft, and move on.
options.feedback: Broad instructions such as asking for quality or consistency are often too vague to measure. A single recent example is unlikely to reveal whether the revised prompt works across the team’s real task distribution.

options.label: D
options.text: Change to a stronger model, reuse the prompt, compare one output, and stop iterating.
options.feedback: Model choice can matter, but it does not replace prompt evaluation when the goal is improving prompt behavior. Comparing one output gives too little evidence to know whether omissions and tone variation have improved reliably.

questions.explanation:
Reliable prompt improvement starts with measurable success criteria, not with ad hoc rewriting. For this airline team, useful criteria might include whether required rebooking information is present, whether the tone matches approved examples, and whether the format is ready for customer review.

Anthropic describes prompt engineering as an iterative process built around testing, refining, and validating against defined criteria, as covered in Prompt engineering overview and Develop test cases. Representative test cases matter because a prompt that works on a few easy examples may still fail on unusual delays, missing context, or tone-sensitive messages.

Prompting improvements such as clearer instructions, examples, XML structure, and explicit output-format guidance can help, but they should be judged against the same evaluation set rather than accepted by intuition alone. Console tools such as the prompt generator or prompt improver can support drafting and refinement, but the mental model remains the same: use tools to propose changes, then validate whether those changes improve results in practice.

questions.question: A precision manufacturing training team is using Claude to convert technician incident reports into short safety bulletins. Early drafts are sometimes usable, but reviewers often have to fix the structure, decide whether the tone is appropriate, and add missing cautions for supervisors. Which two prompt changes would most directly improve the consistency of the drafts?

options.label: A
options.text: Remove task context and include only the incident report to keep the prompt brief.
options.feedback: Shorter prompts are not automatically better when important context is missing. Removing the task context can make Claude produce a more generic bulletin that does not fit the supervisors' needs.

options.label: B
options.text: Request a high-quality bulletin and let Claude choose the structure and tone.
options.feedback: This is too vague to reliably improve consistency. Asking for a high-quality result does not define the structure, tone, or required cautions that reviewers need.

options.label: C
options.text: State required sections, tone constraints, and supervisor cautions as a numbered checklist.
options.feedback: This makes the expected output explicit instead of leaving Claude to infer the format. Numbered requirements are especially useful when completeness and ordering matter, such as ensuring each required caution appears in the bulletin.

options.label: D
options.text: Provide 3 to 5 representative examples that match the desired bulletin style.
options.feedback: Examples are a strong way to steer tone, structure, and formatting. Providing several representative examples helps Claude imitate the desired pattern more consistently than a broad description alone.

questions.explanation:
Effective business prompts usually improve when they make the target output concrete. Anthropic’s Claude prompting best practices emphasize clear, explicit instructions, desired output formats, constraints, and bullets or numbered lists when completeness matters.

For recurring work where tone and structure matter, examples are one of the most reliable steering tools. A prompt can also use structured sections such as <instructions>, <context>, and <examples> to separate the task, background, and model outputs to imitate. Vague requests like “make it excellent” or overly stripped-down prompts leave too much for Claude to infer. Before iterating endlessly on wording, the broader prompt engineering workflow also recommends having clear success criteria so prompt changes can be judged against the actual business standard.

questions.question: A veterinary telehealth support team uses Claude to turn visit notes into owner-facing care summaries. The summaries often sound polished, but reviewers find that some omit follow-up timing or understate medication cautions. The team has been revising the prompt after each bad example, but quality is not improving reliably. What should the team do next?

options.label: A
options.text: Define task-specific success criteria and test revised prompts against representative cases.
options.feedback: This is the best next step because the team needs a repeatable way to detect whether prompt changes actually improve the outputs. Task-specific evaluations with realistic and edge-case examples make prompt iteration empirical rather than based on isolated anecdotes.

options.label: B
options.text: Rewrite the prompt after every reviewer complaint until the latest example passes.
options.feedback: This continues the team’s current ad hoc approach and can overfit the prompt to the most recent failure. Without a stable test set, the team cannot tell whether fixing one example caused regressions on others.

options.label: C
options.text: Increase the response length limit so Claude has more room for each summary.
options.feedback: More room may help only if outputs are being cut off, but the scenario does not indicate truncation. Length alone does not ensure that follow-up timing or medication cautions are included accurately.

options.label: D
options.text: Ask Claude to rate each summary and accept outputs with high confidence scores.
options.feedback: Self-rating can sound useful, but it is not a reliable substitute for checking outputs against the team’s actual requirements. The problem is missing or softened content, so the team needs criteria and tests that directly measure those failures.

questions.explanation:
When Claude outputs are underperforming, the first troubleshooting move is usually not another isolated prompt tweak. Anthropic recommends starting prompt engineering from clear success criteria and testing prompt versions against examples that reflect the real task, including edge cases. See Develop tests and Claude 4 best practices.

In this scenario, the outputs are fluent but unreliable, which is a classic case where polish can hide missing requirements. A practical evaluation might check whether every summary includes follow-up timing, medication cautions, and owner-friendly language. Once those criteria exist, the team can compare prompt revisions against the same cases instead of judging only the latest failure.

Asking Claude to self-rate does not create an independent measure of correctness. Increasing output length addresses truncation only when there is evidence that the answer is being cut off. Rewriting the prompt around each complaint is an anti-pattern because it can improve one case while making the overall workflow less consistent.

questions.question: A community bank's loan operations team is designing a Claude workflow that turns internal exception notes into manager-ready summaries. Early trials look useful, but reviewers disagree about what counts as a good output. What is the most appropriate next step before expanding the pilot?

options.label: A
options.text: Ask Claude to rate each draft, then approve outputs above an internal confidence threshold.
options.feedback: Claude's self-rating is not a reliable substitute for external quality criteria. A confidence threshold can make the process look objective while still failing to measure fidelity, tone, privacy, or context use.

options.label: B
options.text: Save reviewer preferences in a Project, then rely on context to standardize future drafts.
options.feedback: Saved context can help Claude use relevant background, but it does not by itself define success or test the workflow. The team still needs measurable criteria and representative cases to guide iteration.

options.label: C
options.text: Define measurable success criteria, then run representative cases in a Console evaluation using variables.
options.feedback: This creates a shared standard for judging output quality before the workflow is expanded. Using representative eval cases helps the team compare prompt changes against the same inputs instead of relying on ad hoc impressions.

options.label: D
options.text: Select the most capable model, then approve the workflow after several polished examples.
options.feedback: A stronger model can improve quality, but it does not resolve unclear evaluation standards. Polished examples are not enough to show that the workflow performs consistently across realistic cases.

questions.explanation:
For workflow iteration, the team should first make quality observable. Anthropic's guidance on evaluation emphasizes specific and measurable success criteria, often across multiple dimensions such as task fidelity, consistency, tone, privacy, context utilization, latency, and price. See Define success criteria.

The Claude Console Evaluation tool supports this kind of iteration by letting teams test prompts against cases that use dynamic variables, such as {{notes}} or {{audience}}. Test cases can then be added manually, generated by Claude, or imported from CSV, as described in Use the evaluation tool. Changing models, trusting self-ratings, or storing preferences may be useful in some workflows, but none replaces a repeatable evaluation process tied to agreed standards.
