questions.question: A neighborhood pharmacy chain's operations team needs Claude to draft thousands of short refill reminder messages each week. The messages follow a simple template, and the team values quick turnaround and low per-message cost while routing unusual cases to staff for separate review. Which model selection approach best fits the workload?

options.label: A
options.text: Use Claude Sonnet 5 for every draft, and optimize mainly for balanced capability.
options.feedback: Sonnet is positioned as a strong middle option for many production workloads, but this scenario emphasizes very simple, high-volume, latency-sensitive drafting. Choosing Sonnet for every message may add capability that the routine template work does not need.

options.label: B
options.text: Use Claude Haiku 4.5 for routine drafts, and handle unusual cases separately.
options.feedback: This is correct because Haiku is the recommended starting point for fast, cost-sensitive, high-volume straightforward tasks. The unusual cases can be handled separately, so the routine workload does not require a more reasoning-intensive model by default.

options.label: C
options.text: Use Claude Opus 4.8 for every draft, and prioritize deeper reasoning.
options.feedback: Opus is suited to complex reasoning and cases where accuracy outweighs cost. Routine refill reminders do not present the kind of complexity that justifies using Opus for every draft.

options.label: D
options.text: Use the model with the largest context window, and apply it to all drafts.
options.feedback: Context window size matters when a task requires a large amount of input or output context, but it is not the main deciding factor for short templated messages. This approach ignores the documented tradeoff among capability, speed, cost, and effort.

questions.explanation:
Model selection should start from the workload, not from the assumption that the most capable model is always the best fit. Anthropic’s guidance frames model choice as a tradeoff among capability, speed, cost, and effort, as described in Choosing a model.

For a high-volume stream of short, straightforward messages, Claude Haiku 4.5 is the natural starting point because it is documented for quick iteration, tight latency requirements, cost-sensitive implementations, and high-volume straightforward tasks. Claude Sonnet 5 is a strong fit for many production workloads that need a broader balance of speed and intelligence, while Claude Opus 4.8 is better reserved for complex reasoning, nuanced understanding, or cases where accuracy outweighs cost, as summarized in the models overview and pricing guidance.

questions.question: A public library innovation lab is reviewing proposed Claude pilots for patron services. Which TWO planned uses align with Anthropic’s Usage Policy requirements?

options.label: A
options.text: Use Claude responses to train a local assistant that imitates Claude’s answers without prior Anthropic authorization.
options.feedback: This use is not appropriate because Anthropic prohibits using its products to train another AI model without prior authorization. The policy describes this kind of activity as model scraping or model distillation.

options.label: B
options.text: Publish Claude-drafted tenant-rights guidance only after attorney review and an AI assistance disclosure to patrons.
options.feedback: This use can be appropriate because legal guidance is a high-risk use case rather than a blanket-prohibited use case. The required controls include review by a qualified professional before dissemination or finalization and disclosure that AI helped produce the guidance.

options.label: C
options.text: Deploy an agent to collect residents’ private social media posts for profiling without their authorization.
options.feedback: This use is not appropriate because agentic use remains subject to the Usage Policy. Anthropic’s agent guidance identifies surveillance and unauthorized data collection as examples of prohibited agent behavior.

options.label: D
options.text: Launch a public wellness chatbot that offers sleep, stress, nutrition, and exercise tips with an AI disclosure at session start.
options.feedback: This use is generally appropriate because wellness advice such as sleep, stress, nutrition, and exercise is explicitly excluded from the healthcare high-risk category. Because it is a consumer-facing chatbot, it still needs to disclose that patrons are interacting with AI at least at the beginning of each session.

questions.explanation:
Anthropic’s Usage Policy, also called the Acceptable Use Policy or AUP, does not treat every sensitive domain the same way. Some activities are prohibited outright, while others are allowed only with additional safeguards, as described in the Anthropic Usage Policy.

For high-risk consumer-facing domains such as legal services, the key mental model is controlled use, not automatic prohibition. Advice, recommendations, or subjective decisions in those areas require qualified professional review before they are shared or finalized, and users must be told that AI helped produce the advice, decision, or recommendation.

Consumer-facing chatbots have a separate disclosure requirement even when the topic is not high-risk. Wellness guidance about sleep, stress, nutrition, or exercise is specifically excluded from the healthcare high-risk category, but a public chatbot still needs to disclose that the user is interacting with AI.

By contrast, model distillation without prior authorization and unauthorized agentic collection of private information are not acceptable uses. Anthropic’s guidance on agents makes clear that agents are not exempt from policy requirements, and it lists surveillance and unauthorized data collection as prohibited examples in Using agents according to our Usage Policy.

questions.question: A marine conservation nonprofit's policy team uploads several studies about coastal restoration and asks Claude to help prepare internal notes before any public messaging is drafted. The team needs to understand what the sources collectively support and where the evidence is not aligned. Which prompting approach is most appropriate?

options.label: A
options.text: Ask Claude to generate a large set of campaign ideas, then sort them by novelty and audience appeal.
options.feedback: This approach is better suited to brainstorming, where the goal is to create many possible ideas. It does not focus Claude on source-grounded comparison or evidence alignment.

options.label: B
options.text: Ask Claude to imitate a prior press release, then produce a polished announcement in that voice.
options.feedback: This approach is better suited to drafting, especially when style and tone are the main concerns. It moves too quickly to public-facing language before the source analysis has been completed.

options.label: C
options.text: Ask Claude to provide the most persuasive conclusion first, then omit source differences to keep it concise.
options.feedback: This is an anti-pattern for research work because it encourages selective treatment of the evidence. Omitting source differences may make the output smoother, but it weakens the team's ability to evaluate reliability.

options.label: D
options.text: Ask Claude to extract key findings from each source, compare them across themes, and flag uncertain claims.
options.feedback: This fits a research synthesis task because it directs Claude to work from the provided materials and compare them systematically. It also asks Claude to surface uncertainty, which helps the team validate the notes before using them.

questions.explanation:
For a research synthesis or analysis task, the prompt should direct Claude to use the supplied materials, follow clear steps, and produce an output that supports checking the work. Anthropic’s prompting guidance emphasizes clear, explicit instructions, constraints, desired format, and sequential steps when completeness or order matters: Be clear and direct.

The best approach asks Claude to extract findings, compare them by theme, and flag uncertainty, because that matches the purpose of internal evidence review. Brainstorming prompts are useful when the goal is a wide range of ideas, while drafting prompts are useful when the goal is polished language in a specified style. A persuasive conclusion that hides disagreements may sound useful, but it works against validation and can lead the team to overlook important limits in the sources.

Prompt engineering should also be judged against success criteria rather than intuition alone. Anthropic frames prompt improvement as an empirical process, with clear criteria and testing before deciding whether the prompt is the right lever to change: Prompt engineering overview.

questions.question: A children’s museum education team uses Claude to draft activity guides for different exhibits. The team wants each guide to follow the same audience, safety, tone, and formatting expectations, while exhibit facts and source materials change from week to week. Which TWO practices should the team use when creating system-level instructions?

options.label: A
options.text: Define the persistent audience, tone, safety boundaries, and output format in the instructions.
options.feedback: This is correct because system-level or project-level instructions are best used for stable behavioral guidance that should apply across many conversations. Audience, tone, safety expectations, and formatting rules are persistent preferences rather than changing source content.

options.label: B
options.text: Keep exhibit-specific facts in project knowledge or attached files instead of embedding them in the instructions.
options.feedback: This is correct because changing source material belongs in the knowledge or file context where Claude can use it for the current work. Putting volatile facts into standing instructions can make the configuration harder to maintain and can cause outdated guidance to persist.

options.label: C
options.text: Place every current exhibit note inside the instructions so Claude always sees the full archive.
options.feedback: This is incorrect because instructions should not become a dumping ground for large or frequently changing reference material. Large archives are better handled as project knowledge, files, or connector-provided context, depending on the workflow.

options.label: D
options.text: Leave the instructions minimal and restate all standards manually in each new chat.
options.feedback: This is incorrect because it increases inconsistency and relies on users remembering the same guidance every time. Persistent standards are a good fit for system-level or project-level instructions, while one-off prompts are better for task-specific requests.

questions.explanation:
Effective system-level instructions should capture the stable rules of the work: who the output is for, what tone to use, what safety or compliance boundaries matter, and what structure the response should follow. This gives Claude durable guidance without requiring users to restate the same expectations in every chat.

Changing exhibit facts, source notes, and weekly materials should live in knowledge context, such as project knowledge or attached files, rather than in the standing instructions. Claude Projects are designed for focused workspaces with their own instructions and knowledge bases, so the mental model is to separate how Claude should work from what facts Claude should use for this task. See Anthropic’s help page on What are projects?.

Overloading instructions with an archive of changing material makes them harder to review and can leave obsolete details in a place that continues to steer future outputs. At the other extreme, relying only on manual prompting wastes the configuration layer and often leads to inconsistent results across team members.

questions.question: A performing arts center's marketing team uses Claude to turn event blurbs into social posts for teen audiences. The first drafts are accurate but read like formal brochures, and managers disagree about whether a revised prompt is better. What is the most appropriate next step?

options.label: A
options.text: Add explicit tone, format, and audience guidance, include representative examples, then compare prompt versions against measurable criteria.
options.feedback: This addresses both the output adaptation problem and the validation problem. Clear instructions and representative examples help steer tone, format, and structure, while measurable criteria make comparison less subjective.

options.label: B
options.text: Ask Claude to make posts less formal, then approve whichever draft receives the highest self-rated confidence.
options.feedback: This gives Claude a vague direction but does not define the desired audience fit or format. Self-rated confidence is not a reliable substitute for evaluating outputs against observable success criteria.

options.label: C
options.text: Switch to longer posts for all events, then judge improvement mainly by the amount of detail included.
options.feedback: More detail does not necessarily make a post better for a teen audience or a social channel. Evaluation should reflect relevant dimensions such as tone, clarity, task fidelity, and audience appropriateness.

options.label: D
options.text: Remove audience examples from the prompt, then choose the most polished single output after one review.
options.feedback: Removing examples makes it harder to steer the intended tone, format, and structure. Choosing from one output after one review does not provide a dependable comparison between prompt versions.

questions.explanation:
When refining Claude outputs for a specific audience, start by making the target behavior concrete. Anthropic’s prompting guidance emphasizes clear, explicit instructions, useful context, specific format constraints, and examples, with 3 to 5 examples recommended as a reliable way to steer format, tone, and structure. See Claude 4 best practices.

Validation should then move beyond personal preference. Anthropic’s evaluation guidance recommends success criteria that are specific, measurable, achievable, and relevant, often across multiple dimensions such as task fidelity, tone and style, relevance, privacy, latency, and price. The Console Evaluation tool also supports comparing prompt versions, side-by-side output review, and quality grading on a 5-point scale, which helps teams decide whether a prompt change is actually improving the output. See Define success criteria and Claude Console Evaluation tool.

questions.question: An urban planning consultancy's grant-writing team has used one Claude chat for weeks to draft proposals, compare funder rules, and revise budgets. The chat now contains obsolete drafts, side discussions, and several uploaded documents, and recent answers are slower and sometimes focus on old assumptions. Which two actions are most appropriate?

options.label: A
options.text: Keep extending the same chat so Claude can use the entire history as permanent memory.
options.feedback: This is incorrect because the context window is active working memory, not permanent model memory. Long histories can consume context with stale details and make the current request harder to answer cleanly.

options.label: B
options.text: Start a new chat with a concise summary of current decisions, open questions, and relevant sources.
options.feedback: This is correct because a shorter, curated handoff gives Claude the information needed for the next phase without carrying obsolete context. Restarting can improve focus when a long conversation has accumulated irrelevant or outdated material.

options.label: C
options.text: Reupload all previous drafts and documents into each prompt so no earlier material can be missed.
options.feedback: This is incorrect because adding everything back increases the amount of context Claude must process. It can make the prompt less focused and may push the conversation closer to the context limit.

options.label: D
options.text: Save the stable proposal brief and reusable funder rules separately, then add only relevant items to future chats.
options.feedback: This is correct because stable context should be persisted somewhere the team controls, rather than depending on a long chat to remain useful forever. Reintroducing only the relevant materials keeps the working context focused on the current task.

questions.explanation:
Claude’s context window is the active working memory available for a response, not a guarantee that every past detail remains equally useful forever. The official context window documentation explains that prior messages, documents, tool results, and the current output all draw from this limited space.

When a conversation has accumulated obsolete drafts and side discussions, the practical move is to curate the context: summarize the current state, restart when needed, and bring forward only the materials that still matter. Persisting stable briefs, rules, or source references outside the running chat also helps the team avoid treating a long conversation as permanent memory. The anti-pattern is to keep adding everything because it feels safer; in practice, excess context can crowd out the relevant signal and make responses less focused.

questions.question: A disaster response nonprofit is using Claude to turn dense field reports into one-page briefings for local volunteers. The facts are mostly accurate, but reviewers disagree about which prompt produces the clearest, most usable version for that audience. What is the most appropriate next step?

options.label: A
options.text: Add explicit style and format guidance with examples, then compare prompt versions using measurable criteria.
options.feedback: This is the best approach because audience adaptation improves when prompts specify the desired tone, structure, constraints, and examples. Comparing versions against clear criteria helps the team evaluate clarity and usefulness rather than relying on vague preferences.

options.label: B
options.text: Use only a grammar check on each draft, then select the version with the fewest edits.
options.feedback: Grammar quality is only one dimension of a usable volunteer briefing. A grammatically clean draft can still fail on relevance, tone, structure, or context use for the intended audience.

options.label: C
options.text: Choose the most polished-sounding draft, then ask Claude to make future outputs match it.
options.feedback: A polished draft may still be poorly matched to volunteers if the evaluation criteria are unclear. Using a single preferred example without measurable criteria can make the process subjective and hard to reproduce.

options.label: D
options.text: Remove detailed instructions from the prompt, then let Claude infer the best audience style.
options.feedback: This is an anti-pattern for audience-specific output because it makes the desired tone and format implicit. Claude performs better when the prompt clearly states what the output should do and provides relevant constraints or examples.

questions.explanation:
For adapting outputs to a specific audience, the prompt should give Claude clear, explicit instructions about the intended readers, desired tone, structure, and formatting constraints. Anthropic’s prompting guidance also recommends examples as a reliable way to steer format, tone, and structure, typically using several examples when quality matters: Claude 4 prompt engineering best practices.

When reviewers disagree, the next step is not just to pick the draft that sounds best. A stronger evaluation process defines specific, measurable criteria such as clarity for volunteers, completeness of key actions, appropriate tone, and consistency of structure, then compares candidate outputs against those criteria. Anthropic’s evaluation guidance emphasizes that “good performance” is too vague and that most use cases benefit from multidimensional evaluation: Define success criteria.

The Claude Console Evaluation tool supports practical refinement through side-by-side comparison, grading, and prompt versioning, which lets teams rerun a test set after edits instead of relying on one-off impressions. That workflow helps separate factual correctness from audience fit, so the final briefing can be both accurate and useful for the people who will act on it: Use the Evaluation tool.

questions.question: A national fitness app team is reviewing proposals for a Claude-powered feature in its mobile app. The feature would answer members’ questions about sleep routines, stress management, nutrition, and exercise plans. Which approach is most appropriate under Anthropic’s Usage Policy?

options.label: A
options.text: Disclose the AI interaction at session start and keep responses focused on general wellness guidance.
options.feedback: This approach fits the documented distinction between general wellness guidance and healthcare high-risk use cases. It also satisfies the separate requirement that consumer-facing chatbots disclose that users are interacting with AI at least at the beginning of each session.

options.label: B
options.text: Skip the AI disclosure because wellness guidance is excluded from the healthcare high-risk category.
options.feedback: Wellness guidance such as sleep, stress, nutrition, and exercise advice is excluded from the healthcare high-risk category. That exclusion does not remove the separate disclosure requirement for all consumer-facing chatbots.

options.label: C
options.text: Let Claude provide treatment recommendations without review when users describe medical symptoms.
options.feedback: Medical treatment recommendations are not the same as general wellness guidance. Healthcare high-risk uses require appropriate extra controls, including qualified professional review before advice or recommendations are disseminated or finalized.

options.label: D
options.text: Present the feature as a human coach and rely on Claude safeguards to block risky answers.
options.feedback: Presenting the feature as a human coach conflicts with the requirement to disclose AI interaction in consumer-facing chatbots. Anthropic also describes safety as a shared responsibility, so product teams should not rely only on model safeguards.

questions.explanation:
Anthropic’s Usage Policy distinguishes between prohibited conduct, high-risk use cases that require extra controls, and additional guidelines for areas such as consumer-facing chatbots. General wellness advice, including sleep, stress, nutrition, and exercise guidance, is explicitly excluded from the healthcare high-risk category, so the fitness app is not automatically barred from offering that type of help.

The important governance point is that a use case can be lower risk in one respect and still carry other obligations. A consumer-facing chatbot must tell users they are interacting with AI at least at the beginning of each chat session, regardless of whether the topic is high-risk. If the conversation shifts into medical diagnosis or treatment, the product team should avoid unreviewed healthcare recommendations and use appropriate escalation or qualified professional review.

This is why the best approach combines AI disclosure with clear scope control. Anthropic’s deployment guidance also emphasizes shared responsibility: safeguards are not failsafe, so teams should add practical controls such as disclosure, moderation, and human review where the use case becomes sensitive. See the Anthropic Usage Policy and the launch guidance in I’m planning to launch a product using the Claude API.

questions.question: A specialty food importer uses Claude to turn long inspection reports into short incident summaries for operations managers. The team wants to decide whether the summaries are accurate and complete enough for routine use. Which two actions should the team take?

options.label: A
options.text: Tune the prompt on one typical inspection report, then accept the workflow once that single case passes.
options.feedback: This is incorrect because one typical case does not show whether the workflow handles the range of real inputs. A useful eval suite should cover the actual task distribution, including unusual or difficult cases.

options.label: B
options.text: Build an eval set from representative inspections and edge cases, then score summaries against measurable accuracy and completeness criteria.
options.feedback: This is correct because evaluation should reflect the real-world task distribution and include edge cases. Specific, measurable criteria make accuracy and completeness review more consistent than ad hoc judgment.

options.label: C
options.text: Approve summaries that sound confident and coherent, then rely on reviewers to notice any missing facts later.
options.feedback: This is incorrect because confident or polished language is not a reliable signal of factual accuracy. Claude can produce plausible text that is inconsistent with the source context, so evaluation should check evidence and completeness directly.

options.label: D
options.text: Require cited source passages for factual claims, then verify critical or unsupported statements against the original inspection materials.
options.feedback: This is correct because citations and direct supporting passages help ground outputs in the provided source material. They improve traceability, but critical information still needs validation because grounding techniques reduce, not eliminate, hallucinations.

questions.explanation:
For output evaluation, the useful mental model is that Claude’s response is a draft that must be tested against the task’s required evidence and coverage. Anthropic’s evaluation guidance recommends specific, measurable, achievable, and relevant success criteria, and it emphasizes evals that mirror real-world task distribution, including edge cases. For a summarization workflow, that means checking whether important facts from the inspection report are included, whether unsupported facts are avoided, and whether the summary remains useful for the intended reader.

Grounding techniques such as citations or direct quotes can make factual review much easier because they connect claims to source material. However, Anthropic’s hallucination guidance is clear that these techniques reduce hallucinations rather than eliminating them, so critical information still needs validation. The Citations feature similarly provides source traceability, not a guarantee that every inference is correct. See Define success criteria, Reduce hallucinations, and Citations.

questions.question: An independent insurance brokerage's training team is refining a Claude prompt that turns sales call transcripts into coaching notes. Results are inconsistent, and a manager suggests rewriting the prompt until one recent transcript produces a strong note. The team has a draft prompt and dozens of representative transcripts. What should they do next?

options.label: A
options.text: Define measurable note-quality criteria, build a representative transcript test set, and compare prompt versions.
options.feedback: This is correct because prompt iteration should be grounded in measurable success criteria and empirical evaluation. A representative test set lets the team check whether changes improve the task broadly, not just on one appealing example.

options.label: B
options.text: Keep editing the prompt around one transcript, then deploy when that sample reads well.
options.feedback: This is incorrect because optimizing for a single example can hide failures on other realistic cases. It may produce a prompt that looks better in one instance but performs worse across the real task distribution.

options.label: C
options.text: Use the prompt generator to replace the draft, then deploy the generated prompt immediately.
options.feedback: This is incorrect because the prompt generator is useful for producing a starting point, not for proving quality. Generated prompts still need testing and iteration against success criteria before being relied on.

options.label: D
options.text: Use the prompt improver to lengthen the prompt, then accept the more detailed output.
options.feedback: This is incorrect because a longer or more detailed prompt is not automatically better for the task. The prompt improver can help with complex accuracy-critical tasks, but its output should still be validated and may increase response length or latency.

questions.explanation:
Effective prompt iteration starts with an evaluation loop, not with repeated ad hoc rewriting. Anthropic’s prompt engineering guidance assumes you have clear success criteria, a way to test against them, and a draft prompt before making changes, as described in Prompt engineering overview.

For this training-team task, measurable criteria might include whether the coaching note identifies the main objection, gives one concrete coaching recommendation, preserves the transcript’s facts, and follows the team’s required format. A representative set of transcripts, including ordinary calls and edge cases, makes it possible to see whether a revised prompt improves performance across the work the team actually needs Claude to do. Anthropic’s evaluation guidance emphasizes specific, measurable success criteria and tests that mirror the real-world task distribution, covered in Develop tests.

Console tools such as the prompt generator and prompt improver can support drafting and refinement, but they do not replace validation. If the team uses the Claude Console Evaluation tool, features such as side-by-side comparison, quality grading, and prompt versioning can help compare revisions across the same test cases, as documented in Evaluation tool.

questions.question: A patent litigation firm's research team needs Claude to compare several dense expert reports, trace subtle disagreements across them, and prepare a cautious issue map for attorneys. The task volume is low, response time is flexible, and the team cares more about careful analysis than minimizing token cost. Which model selection approach best fits this workload?

options.label: A
options.text: Use Claude Sonnet for the analysis, treating it as the default for all legal work.
options.feedback: Sonnet is appropriate for many production workloads because it balances speed and intelligence. However, the scenario states that the team is handling low-volume, high-stakes analysis where accuracy matters more than cost.

options.label: B
options.text: Use the lowest-cost model for the analysis, then ask Claude to rate confidence.
options.feedback: Choosing primarily by lowest cost does not match the stated priority of careful reasoning. Asking Claude to rate its own confidence is not a reliable substitute for selecting an appropriate model and validating outputs.

options.label: C
options.text: Use Claude Opus for the analysis, accepting higher cost for stronger reasoning.
options.feedback: This is the best fit because the work requires nuanced understanding and careful reasoning, while cost and speed are secondary. Anthropic positions Opus for the most complex reasoning and high-accuracy workloads.

options.label: D
options.text: Use Claude Haiku for the analysis, prioritizing fastest turnaround for each report.
options.feedback: Haiku is a strong choice for fast, cost-sensitive, and straightforward workloads. In this scenario, the main need is careful analysis of dense and conflicting material, not the fastest response.

questions.explanation:
Claude model selection is a practical tradeoff among capability, speed, cost, and effort, rather than a rule that one model is always best. For low-volume work involving dense materials, subtle disagreements, and a high cost of analytical mistakes, Opus is the best starting point because Anthropic recommends it for complex reasoning and cases where accuracy outweighs cost.

Haiku is optimized for speed and cost-sensitive tasks, so it is often a good fit for quick iteration, tight latency needs, or high-volume straightforward work. Sonnet is the balanced option for many production workloads, but the scenario gives reasons to favor the more capable model instead of the middle option. Self-rated confidence is also not a dependable control, since model choice and external review should be based on the task's risk and complexity.

For more on these tradeoffs, see Anthropic's Choosing a model guide and the Claude models overview.

options.label: D
options.text: Add a broad reminder that old ideas are obsolete without removing or summarizing the chat.
options.feedback: This is weaker because the obsolete material still remains in the working context. A reminder can help, but it does not reduce the amount of irrelevant context or create a reliable source of current requirements.

questions.explanation:
Claude works from the information available in its context window, which is best understood as active working memory for the current request, not as model training memory. The official Context windows documentation explains that the context window includes the prompt, prior messages, documents and other included inputs, and the current output being generated.

When a conversation becomes cluttered with rejected ideas, outdated assumptions, or long excerpts, the practical move is often to restart with a compact handoff. That preserves the decisions and open questions that matter while removing stale material that can distract from the current task.

Persisting a short source-of-truth note outside the chat also supports good context management. It gives the team a stable, reusable summary they can paste into a new chat or update as decisions change, instead of treating a long conversation transcript as the only record of the project.

Simply continuing the same chat or adding a broad reminder may feel convenient, but it leaves the irrelevant material in Claude's working context. The tradeoff is control: summarizing and restarting requires a little setup, but it usually gives Claude a cleaner signal and makes future work easier to manage.

questions.question: A community credit union's compliance team asks Claude to summarize uploaded anti-money-laundering guidance and draft a recommendation about whether a flagged account should be escalated. Claude includes citations to the uploaded documents and a confident conclusion. What should the analyst do before using the recommendation?

options.label: A
options.text: Ask Claude for a confidence score before acting on the recommendation.
options.feedback: This is incorrect because Claude's self-reported confidence is not a dependable validation method. A confidence score does not replace checking the source material or applying compliance judgment.

options.label: B
options.text: Use the conclusion once citations appear in the response.
options.feedback: This is incorrect because citations reduce uncertainty but do not make the conclusion automatically reliable. The analyst still needs to confirm that the cited passages actually support the recommendation, especially for compliance action.

options.label: C
options.text: Rerun the prompt in the Evaluation tool and use the highest-scoring output.
options.feedback: This is incorrect because the Evaluation tool is designed for testing prompts across scenarios, not for approving an individual production decision. A high-scoring prompt test does not validate that this account-specific recommendation is correct.

options.label: D
options.text: Review the cited passages and get compliance approval before acting on the recommendation.
options.feedback: This is correct because the output may affect a high-stakes compliance decision. Citations can help verify what Claude used, but a qualified human should confirm that the cited support and recommendation are appropriate before action is taken.

questions.explanation:
For decisions that may affect regulated financial action, the right mental model is evidence plus review. Claude can summarize documents and provide citations, but Anthropic notes that hallucination-reduction techniques reduce risk rather than eliminate it, and that critical information, especially high-stakes decisions, should be validated. See Reduce hallucinations.

Citations are useful because they ground answers in user-provided source documents and give passages or locations to inspect. They are not a substitute for human judgment about whether the cited material actually supports the conclusion or whether organizational policy requires escalation. See Citations.

The Evaluation tool is valuable for comparing prompt behavior across test cases, versioning prompts, and grading outputs, but it is not an automatic production validator for a live compliance recommendation. For evaluation design, Anthropic emphasizes task-specific tests and scalable grading, while recognizing that human grading is sometimes needed when quality and flexibility matter. See Use the Evaluation tool and Define success criteria.

questions.question: A municipal water utility’s customer communications team uses Claude to turn outage reports into resident notifications. Recent drafts vary in quality: some miss important service details, some use overly technical wording, and some do not follow the required notification format. Which two actions should the team take to improve the prompt reliably?

options.label: A
options.text: Create task-specific evaluation cases with success criteria and rerun them after prompt changes.
options.feedback: This is correct because prompt improvement should be guided by measurable success criteria and empirical testing. A task-specific evaluation set helps the team see whether changes improve performance across normal cases and edge cases, rather than only fixing the latest failed draft.

options.label: B
options.text: Revise the prompt with explicit instructions, context, examples, and separated format guidance.
options.feedback: This is correct because unclear or inconsistent outputs often improve when the prompt states the task more directly and provides the structure Claude should follow. Relevant examples and separated sections help Claude distinguish source information, instructions, and the desired output format.

options.label: C
options.text: Keep editing the prompt after each poor draft until the next draft looks acceptable.
options.feedback: This is incorrect because ad hoc edits can make the prompt better for one example while making it worse for others. Without a repeatable evaluation process, the team cannot tell whether quality is improving reliably.

options.label: D
options.text: Increase the response length limit so Claude has more room to include every detail.
options.feedback: This is incorrect because the symptoms are inconsistent content, wording, and format, not clearly truncated responses. A larger output limit may help when a response is being cut off, but it does not by itself teach Claude what details, style, or structure to use.

questions.explanation:
When a prompt underperforms, the most reliable path is to treat improvement as an evaluation-driven iteration problem. Anthropic recommends defining success criteria and testing prompts against representative examples, including edge cases, rather than making isolated edits based only on the most recent failure. The Console evaluation workflow is designed for this kind of comparison and re-running of prompt versions, as described in develop tests and the Evaluation tool.

The prompt itself should also be made clearer. For current Claude models, strong prompts use explicit instructions, useful context, examples, and structure that separates instructions from inputs and formatting requirements. Anthropic’s prompting guidance emphasizes telling Claude what to do, giving detailed formatting guidance, and using structure such as XML-style sections where helpful, as covered in Claude 4 best practices.

The weaker approaches either optimize the wrong thing or lack a way to measure improvement. Editing after each poor draft is a common anti-pattern because it can overfit the prompt to one failure. Increasing output length is only a good diagnosis when responses are being cut off, but the described problem is about missing requirements and inconsistent formatting, so clearer instructions and systematic tests are the better first steps.

questions.question: A subscription news platform is rolling out a Claude API pilot for automated article tagging. Its AI governance policy requires the pilot team to have its own API keys, limited members, and a lower resource limit than the rest of the organization. Leadership does not want other teams' access or limits changed. What is the most appropriate action?

options.label: A
options.text: Lower the organization-level limit so every team follows the pilot cap.
options.feedback: This would enforce a lower cap, but it would also affect teams that are not part of the pilot. The scenario says leadership does not want other teams' limits changed, so an organization-wide change is too broad.

options.label: B
options.text: Keep the pilot in the shared workspace and track compliance manually.
options.feedback: Manual tracking may help with oversight, but it does not provide the separate governance boundary required by the policy. It also leaves the pilot sharing the same workspace-level controls as other users.

options.label: C
options.text: Create a separate workspace for the pilot and configure its keys, members, and limits there.
options.feedback: This follows the documented governance purpose of workspaces. Additional workspaces can have their own API keys, members, and resource limits, so the pilot can be managed without changing other teams.

options.label: D
options.text: Assign billing roles to pilot users and leave the workspace unchanged.
options.feedback: Role assignment does not replace workspace-level separation for API keys, members, and resource limits. A billing role is intended for billing access, not for isolating a pilot team's API governance controls.

questions.explanation:
Workspaces are the appropriate governance boundary when different teams or projects need separate API keys, membership, and resource limits. Anthropic documents that additional workspaces can be used to manage these controls independently, which fits a pilot that should not change access or limits for the rest of the organization. See Workspaces.

The practical governance principle is to scope controls to the group that needs them. Lowering organization-level limits applies broadly, while relying only on manual tracking leaves the control outside the product boundary designed for this purpose.

Roles and workspaces solve different governance problems. Roles define what a person can do in the organization, while workspaces help separate API keys, members, and resource limits for teams or projects. See Organization management overview.

questions.question: A botanical garden's education team is creating a Claude Project for school lesson materials. They want each new chat in the workspace to use the same curriculum references and follow the same reading-level and formatting rules. Which setup is most appropriate?

options.label: A
options.text: Add the reference files to project knowledge and save the rules using Set project instructions.
options.feedback: This is correct because project knowledge persists across chats within the project, so the curriculum references can inform future conversations. Project instructions are the right place for behavior and response guidance that should apply to all chats in the project.

options.label: B
options.text: Put the reference details in the project description and include the rules in the project name.
options.feedback: This is incorrect because a project's name and description are not provided to Claude as working context. They may help people organize the workspace, but they should not be used as the source of instructions or knowledge for Claude.

options.label: C
options.text: Paste the reference files into the first project chat and rely on later chats to reuse them.
options.feedback: This is incorrect because ordinary chat context is not automatically shared across separate chats in the same project. Information that should carry across project chats needs to be added to the project's knowledge base.

options.label: D
options.text: Repeat the reference files and rules manually at the start of every new project chat.
options.feedback: This is not the most appropriate configuration because it creates avoidable repetition and increases the chance of inconsistent setup. Projects are designed to provide persistent knowledge and shared instructions for related work.

questions.explanation:
Claude Projects are self-contained workspaces with their own chat histories, knowledge bases, and project-level instructions. For repeated work, place durable source material in project knowledge and put stable behavior guidance, such as tone, format, and reading level, in Set project instructions. See What are projects? and How can I create and manage projects?.

The important mental model is that knowledge and instructions solve different configuration problems. Knowledge supplies reusable background content for chats in that project, while instructions tell Claude how to behave or respond whenever work is done inside that project.

Project names and descriptions help humans manage the workspace, but they are not context Claude uses to answer. Similarly, content pasted into one chat stays in that chat unless it is added to project knowledge, so relying on a starter chat is a common configuration mistake.

questions.question: A marine logistics firm's operations team uses Claude to turn vessel delay notes into customer-facing status updates. The drafts are often readable, but they vary in structure, sometimes omit the expected next step, and sometimes include internal port terminology customers may not understand. Which prompt change would most directly improve the consistency of the updates?

options.label: A
options.text: Ask Claude to write a better update and decide which details matter most.
options.feedback: This keeps the prompt vague and leaves important business standards implicit. Claude may produce a polished answer, but it has little guidance on required sections or customer-safe wording.

options.label: B
options.text: Ask Claude to rate each draft before sending it to the customer.
options.feedback: Self-rating does not reliably enforce the team's required format or terminology standards. The prompt should guide the first draft more explicitly rather than relying on Claude to judge its own output afterward.

options.label: C
options.text: Wrap the same short request in XML-style tags without adding requirements.
options.feedback: XML-style tags can help organize complex prompts, but they do not replace clear instructions. If the underlying request remains underspecified, tagging alone will not define the audience, format, or content requirements.

options.label: D
options.text: Specify the audience, required sections, wording constraints, and a few representative examples.
options.feedback: This option gives Claude clear instructions about the expected output and constraints, which directly addresses inconsistent structure and inappropriate terminology. Relevant examples are also a reliable way to steer format, tone, and content.

questions.explanation:
Effective business prompts make the task’s standards visible to Claude. When outputs vary in structure or include the wrong level of detail, the best improvement is usually to state the audience, required output sections, constraints, and desired style directly, then reinforce those expectations with relevant examples.

Anthropic’s prompting guidance emphasizes clear, explicit instructions, including desired format and constraints, and notes that examples are a strong way to steer tone, structure, and output format. XML-style tags such as <instructions> and <examples> can make a complex prompt easier to parse, but they are a structure aid rather than a substitute for specifying what good output looks like. See Claude prompting best practices and Prompt engineering overview.

The main tradeoff is between relying on Claude’s general writing ability and giving it the business context needed to behave like a trained teammate. A vague request may produce fluent text, but clear requirements and examples make the output more repeatable and easier to evaluate.

questions.question: A public health nonprofit's research team is piloting Claude to draft donor briefing answers from a packet of study summaries. In the first review, some answers read well but add unsupported details, and reviewers disagree about which outputs should pass. Which two actions should the team take next?

options.label: A
options.text: Run the prompt improver once, adopt the longer template, and pause evaluation until the pilot is live.
options.feedback: This is incorrect because the prompt improver can help refine prompts, but it is not a replacement for testing against success criteria. Pausing evaluation until deployment prevents the team from learning whether the revised prompt actually fixes the observed failures.

options.label: B
options.text: Use Claude’s confidence ratings, accept answers above a threshold, and defer source checks to later reviews.
options.feedback: This is incorrect because it substitutes a model-generated confidence signal for evaluation against defined criteria and source evidence. It also delays the factual validation needed for a workflow where unsupported details have already appeared.

options.label: C
options.text: Define measurable success criteria, build a representative eval set, and compare prompt versions against the results.
options.feedback: This is correct because prompt optimization should be guided by specific criteria and empirical evaluation, not by informal reactions. A representative test set helps the team see whether changes improve the kinds of cases the workflow will actually face.

options.label: D
options.text: Revise the prompt to use only supplied materials, allow uncertainty, and request support for factual claims.
options.feedback: This is correct because unsupported details are a factuality problem, and Anthropic documents techniques such as restricting answers to provided documents, allowing “I don’t know,” and requiring citations or supporting evidence. These steps reduce hallucinations, although they do not guarantee perfect factuality.

questions.explanation:
When early results expose quality problems, the best next step is to turn the feedback into measurable success criteria and test changes against a realistic eval set. Anthropic’s evaluation guidance emphasizes criteria that are specific, measurable, achievable, and relevant, and recommends evals that reflect the real task distribution and include edge cases. See Define success criteria and develop tests.

The unsupported details call for factuality-focused prompt changes, not just a more polished writing style. Anthropic’s hallucination guidance recommends approaches such as allowing uncertainty, grounding responses in provided documents, using direct quotes or citations, and iterative verification. These methods reduce hallucinations but do not eliminate the need for review in sensitive outputs. See Reduce hallucinations.

Tools like the Console evaluation workflow and prompt improver are useful when used inside an evaluation loop. The key mental model is: define what success means, test representative cases, adjust the prompt or model choice based on the observed failure mode, then re-run the eval. The Console supports comparing prompt versions across test cases, while the prompt improver should not be treated as a one-time substitute for validation. See Claude Console Evaluation tool and Prompting tools.

questions.question: An environmental engineering consultancy is introducing Claude to help analysts turn site notes, uploaded photos, and research excerpts into first drafts of client remediation briefs. Senior partners ask for the rollout message to set expectations without overselling. What message should the associate give?

options.label: A
options.text: Position Claude as a final-decision system that reliably produces complete recommendations from minimal context.
options.feedback: This frames Claude as a replacement for professional judgment rather than a tool that supports it. Brief or incomplete context can produce incomplete or inaccurate outputs, especially for consequential client recommendations.

options.label: B
options.text: Position Claude as a model-dependent assistant that speeds drafting and analysis while requiring source checks for important claims.
options.feedback: This message communicates value without overstating reliability. Claude can accelerate drafting and analysis, but model capabilities vary and important factual claims still need validation against trusted sources.

options.label: C
options.text: Position Claude as a standalone expert that can replace review when its answers include detailed citations.
options.feedback: This overstates Claude's reliability and treats citations as proof of accuracy. Claude can generate factually incorrect or unsupported details, so stakeholder-facing work still requires verification.

options.label: D
options.text: Position Claude as a uniform product where all models provide equivalent speed, cost, context, and outputs.
options.feedback: This incorrectly treats Claude models as interchangeable. Anthropic documents that models differ in characteristics such as context windows, output limits, latency, pricing, and knowledge cutoffs.

questions.explanation:
Stakeholders need a practical mental model: Claude is an assistant for accelerating knowledge work, not an authority that removes the need for review. Its usefulness depends on the selected model, the quality of the provided context, and the workflow around the output.

Anthropic documents that Claude models vary in capabilities and operational characteristics, including context windows, maximum outputs, latency, pricing, and knowledge cutoffs, so teams should avoid describing Claude as one undifferentiated capability. See the Claude models overview.

Claude can also produce hallucinations, meaning text that is factually incorrect or inconsistent with the provided context. Grounding, citations, quotes, and uncertainty can reduce this risk, but they do not eliminate it, so client-facing or high-stakes claims should be validated against reliable sources. Anthropic discusses these mitigations in reduce hallucinations.

questions.question: A specialty pharmacy's benefits team is adding Claude to its prior authorization workflow. Before drafting each status update, Claude must use the current authorization status from the team's internal case system, while the existing application must keep control of database access and audit logging. Which integration approach best fits this workflow?

options.label: A
options.text: Use a controlled workflow that retrieves the authorized case status before Claude drafts the update.
options.feedback: This fits a workflow where the existing application keeps control of internal system access and auditing. Claude can use the retrieved status to help draft the update without becoming the uncontrolled source of database access.

options.label: B
options.text: Use web search for each lookup, rely on public results to find the case, and draft from returned pages.
options.feedback: Public web search is not a substitute for controlled access to a private internal case system. It also does not satisfy the need for the existing application to control database access and audit logging.

options.label: C
options.text: Make the case-status lookup optional, describe it loosely, and expect Claude to retrieve status when needed.
options.feedback: An optional and loosely described lookup step does not reliably ensure that current status is checked before drafting. For a required workflow control, the process should make retrieval explicit before Claude generates the update.

options.label: D
options.text: Place the case-system URL in the prompt, ask Claude to infer the needed record, and draft the update directly.
options.feedback: A prompt does not give Claude direct access to an internal case system. This approach also risks drafting from incomplete or guessed information instead of using the current record.

questions.explanation:
For workflow integration, the key judgment is to keep Claude in the part of the process where it adds value, while preserving the controls already required by the business system. In this scenario, Claude should help turn verified case information into a useful status update, but the application should remain responsible for authorized data retrieval, access control, and audit logging.

The safer workflow pattern is to retrieve the current case status through the controlled internal process first, then provide that verified context to Claude for drafting. That design reduces the risk of hallucinated or stale information and keeps sensitive workflow steps inside the system that already governs them.

Anthropic's tool-use documentation distinguishes between Claude requesting access to external information and the surrounding system handling how that information is actually obtained. See the tool use overview and define tools for the general model of connecting Claude to external sources. At a foundations level, the practical takeaway is not an API detail: do not ask Claude to guess, search public pages, or rely on vague optional steps when the workflow requires current, authorized internal data.

Place the case-system URL in the prompt, ask Claude to infer the needed record, and draft the update directly.

For workflow integration, the key judgment is to keep Claude in the part of the process where it adds value, while preserving the controls already required by the business system. In this scenario, Claude should help turn verified case information into a useful status update, but the application should remain responsible for authorized data retrieval, access control, and audit logging.

The safer workflow pattern is to retrieve the current case status through the controlled internal process first, then provide that verified context to Claude for drafting. That design reduces the risk of hallucinated or stale information and keeps sensitive workflow steps inside the system that already governs them.

Anthropic's tool-use documentation distinguishes between Claude requesting access to external information and the surrounding system handling how that information is actually obtained. questions.question: A performing arts festival's programming team has Code execution and file creation enabled in Claude. They need two outputs from the same planning notes: a reusable sponsor packet with venue maps, schedules, and bios that coordinators will revise over time, and a compact machine-readable list of performer names, dates, stages, and review flags for an existing scheduling import. Which two output-format choices are most appropriate?

options.label: A
options.text: Request schema-constrained JSON for the scheduling list and validate it before importing.
options.feedback: This is correct because machine-readable records for another system are a good fit for structured output. Validation is still needed because structured outputs can fail to match the schema in cases such as refusals or incomplete outputs.

options.label: B
options.text: Request strict tool use for the scheduling list and let Claude perform the import directly.
options.feedback: This is incorrect because strict tool use constrains tool inputs, not the execution of outside operations by Claude. For client tools, the application still executes the operation and handles the results.

options.label: C
options.text: Request an artifact for the sponsor packet and iterate on it in the separate workspace.
options.feedback: This is correct because the sponsor packet is substantial, self-contained, and likely to be edited and reused later. Those are the kinds of outputs Claude is documented to place in an artifact when the required capability is enabled.

options.label: D
options.text: Request one inline chat response for both outputs and manually separate the sections afterward.
options.feedback: This is incorrect because it treats a reusable, revisable packet the same as a short conversational answer. Inline chat can be useful for brief responses, but it is less suitable for substantial standalone content that the team expects to revise and reference later.

questions.explanation:
Choose the output surface based on how the result will be used. Artifacts are intended for substantial, standalone content that users are likely to edit, iterate on, reuse, or refer back to, such as documents, diagrams, web pages, and interactive components. They are a Claude app, Claude Desktop, and Claude Code output surface, and the documented prerequisite is that Code execution and file creation is enabled. See What are artifacts and how do I use them?.

For the scheduling import, the important property is not presentation but predictable structure. Anthropic documents structured outputs as API features, including JSON outputs via output_config.format and strict tool use via strict: true. JSON outputs constrain what Claude says, while strict tool use constrains tool-call inputs, so they solve different problems and can be used independently or together. See Structured outputs.

A good mental model is to use artifacts when humans need a durable working object, inline chat when the answer is short and conversational, and structured data when another system needs to consume the result. Even with structured outputs, downstream validation remains part of responsible use because documented stop conditions such as refusal or max_tokens can produce output that does not match the schema.

questions.question: A museum's visitor services team is iterating on a Claude workflow that turns free-text guest complaints into routing recommendations. They want a repeatable way to compare prompt changes across many realistic complaint examples before staff start using it. What is the most appropriate next step?

options.label: A
options.text: Ask Claude to self-rate each prompt version, then select the version with the highest score.
options.feedback: Claude's self-rating can be a weak signal, but it is not a substitute for defined success criteria and representative cases. The team still needs an evaluation process that checks the actual outputs against the routing goals.

options.label: B
options.text: Deploy the prompt after a few successful examples, then collect staff feedback during daily use.
options.feedback: A few successful examples are not enough evidence that the workflow will handle varied real complaints. Collecting feedback after rollout can help improvement, but it should not replace pre-use evaluation.

options.label: C
options.text: Run several informal chats with sample complaints, then choose the version that seems most helpful.
options.feedback: Informal chats can be useful for early exploration, but they do not create a consistent basis for comparing prompt changes. Relying on what seems helpful makes it harder to detect regressions or align reviewers.

options.label: D
options.text: Create an evaluation prompt with dynamic variables, representative test cases, and measurable success criteria.
options.feedback: This is the best next step because it turns prompt iteration into a repeatable evaluation process. Dynamic variables let the team test many complaint examples, while measurable criteria help reviewers compare outputs consistently.

questions.explanation:
For solution design and iteration, the practical move is to make evaluation systematic rather than relying on a few promising demonstrations. Anthropic's evaluation guidance emphasizes specific and measurable success criteria, often across multiple dimensions such as task fidelity, consistency, relevance, tone, privacy, latency, and price. The Claude Console Evaluation tool supports this workflow by using prompt variables such as {{complaint}} and building test sets manually, with Claude, or from CSV, as described in Test and evaluate prompts with the Evaluation tool and Define success criteria.

The weaker approaches skip an important design tradeoff: early exploration is useful, but production readiness needs consistent examples and consistent judgment standards. Deploying after only a few good cases risks discovering failures in front of staff rather than during testing. Asking Claude to rate its own outputs can help prompt reflection, but it should not replace measurable criteria applied across representative cases.

questions.question: An architecture studio wants Claude to use a client interview transcript, zoning notes, and a preferred proposal sample to prepare a renovation proposal outline with risks and next steps. Which two prompting approaches best decompose the work for reliable execution?

options.label: A
options.text: Paste the sample proposal first and tell Claude to imitate it without naming the intermediate analysis steps.
options.feedback: This is incorrect because a sample can steer format and tone, but it does not by itself decompose the work. Without explicit steps, Claude may copy the style while missing constraint checks or risk identification.

options.label: B
options.text: Separate the transcript, notes, sample, instructions, and output request with descriptive XML-style tags.
options.feedback: This is correct because tags help Claude distinguish different parts of a complex prompt. Descriptive tags are especially useful when context, examples, and task instructions all appear in the same request.

options.label: C
options.text: Give Claude an ordered checklist for extracting needs, checking constraints, drafting sections, and listing next steps.
options.feedback: This is correct because an ordered checklist makes the intended workflow explicit. It reduces the chance that Claude skips a step or blends analysis, drafting, and review into one undifferentiated response.

options.label: D
options.text: Ask Claude to infer the best workflow from the materials and produce the final outline immediately.
options.feedback: This is incorrect because it leaves the task structure implicit. Claude may still produce something useful, but it is less reliable when the desired sequence and completeness requirements matter.

questions.explanation:
For complex work, a good prompt acts like a lightweight project plan. Anthropic’s prompting guidance emphasizes clear, explicit instructions, including numbered lists or bullets when order and completeness matter. In this scenario, separating the work into extraction, constraint checking, drafting, and next-step planning helps Claude execute each part rather than jumping straight to prose.

XML-style tags are another practical decomposition tool. Tags such as <transcript>, <zoning_notes>, <sample_proposal>, and <instructions> make the prompt easier to parse because Claude can tell which text is source material, which text is an example, and which text is the actual task. Anthropic documents both explicit task structure and XML-style prompt organization in its prompt engineering guidance: Claude prompt engineering documentation.

Examples are useful, but they are not a replacement for a decomposed request. A preferred proposal sample can steer the output’s structure and voice, while the ordered steps tell Claude what reasoning and transformations to perform before producing that output. Asking Claude to infer the whole workflow is a common anti-pattern for complex tasks because it hides important requirements inside vague intent.

questions.question: A trade school's admissions office plans to use Claude to score candidate essays, suggest interview invitations, and show the resulting recommendations in an applicant portal. What is the most appropriate governance approach before using this workflow?

options.label: A
options.text: Let Claude rank applicants automatically after validating the rubric and publish the rankings in the portal.
options.feedback: This is incorrect because a rubric does not replace qualified human review for subjective decisions in admissions. Automated publication also fails to address the disclosure requirement for AI-presented outputs.

options.label: B
options.text: Remove applicant names before scoring essays and publish the recommendations without additional review.
options.feedback: This is incorrect because de-identification can reduce some privacy and bias concerns, but it does not satisfy the required review step. The workflow still involves admissions recommendations that need qualified human oversight before finalization or dissemination.

options.label: C
options.text: Have qualified admissions staff review the recommendations before final decisions and disclose the AI involvement in the portal.
options.feedback: This is correct because admissions decisions are a high-risk context under Anthropic’s Usage Policy. Human review by qualified staff preserves accountability, and disclosure is required when outputs are presented directly to individuals or consumers.

options.label: D
options.text: Ask Claude to provide confidence scores for each recommendation and publish only high-confidence results.
options.feedback: This is incorrect because self-reported confidence is not a substitute for human review in high-risk decisions. It also does not ensure applicants are told that they are seeing AI-assisted recommendations.

questions.explanation:
Admissions workflows raise ethical concerns because they can materially affect a person's educational opportunities. Anthropic’s Usage Policy treats areas such as academic testing, accreditation, and admissions as high-risk use cases, requiring qualified professional review of advice, recommendations, or subjective decisions before they are disseminated or finalized.

Disclosure is also part of responsible use when AI outputs are presented directly to individuals or consumers. In practice, this means the school should not simply publish model-generated rankings or recommendations, even if the prompt uses a carefully designed rubric or asks Claude for confidence scores.

The right mental model is that Claude can assist the admissions process, but it should not become the accountable decision-maker. Human review helps check for errors, unfair reasoning, missing context, and policy compliance, while disclosure helps applicants understand the role AI played in what they are seeing. See Anthropic’s Usage Policy for the documented requirements that apply to these kinds of high-risk and consumer-facing uses.

questions.question: A regional transit authority's maintenance team wants Claude to help plan improvements to its bus parts ordering process. The team needs to combine internal reorder logs with up-to-date public information about supplier availability and replacement-part guidance. Which two actions are most appropriate?

options.label: A
options.text: Ask Claude to rely on its pretrained knowledge and summarize supplier status without source citations.
options.feedback: This is incorrect because pretrained knowledge may be outdated for changing supplier or product information. Omitting citations also makes it harder to validate the facts behind a process improvement plan.

options.label: B
options.text: Ask Claude to search for current supplier information and include citations for the sources it used.
options.feedback: This is correct because supplier availability and replacement-part guidance can change over time. Web search is appropriate when a request depends on current or changing information, and cited sources help the team verify the findings before using them in a plan.

options.label: C
options.text: Ask Claude to keep searching until it is confident and select one workflow change without review.
options.feedback: This is incorrect because confidence alone is not a reliable substitute for reviewing cited evidence and operational fit. Search should support a bounded research process, not replace human judgment about process changes.

options.label: D
options.text: Provide the reorder logs and ask Claude to distinguish sourced findings from process recommendations.
options.feedback: This is correct because Claude can analyze provided content such as internal logs while using current sources for outside facts. Separating evidence from recommendations makes the planning output easier to review and reduces the risk of treating suggestions as verified facts.

questions.explanation:
For research and planning tasks, Claude is strongest when the workflow separates current external facts, provided internal context, and recommendations. Supplier availability and replacement guidance are examples of information that can change, so web search is a good fit because it gives Claude access to real-time web content beyond its knowledge cutoff and returns cited sources.

The internal reorder logs should be supplied directly as context, since they are not something web search can infer. Claude can then help identify patterns, bottlenecks, and planning options, but the team should keep sourced market findings distinct from suggested workflow changes so stakeholders can verify facts and evaluate tradeoffs.

Relying only on pretrained knowledge is a poor fit for current vendor or product status, and asking Claude to search until it feels confident is an anti-pattern. A better mental model is to use search as a bounded evidence-gathering step, then use Claude for synthesis and planning. See Anthropic's documentation on the web search tool for when Claude searches and how cited web results support current-information tasks.

questions.question: A renewable energy lender's credit team is piloting Claude to answer due diligence questions from project memos, permits, and site reports. The demos are persuasive, but the team needs a defensible way to decide whether the workflow is ready for routine analyst use. What is the most appropriate next step?

options.label: A
options.text: Define measurable review criteria, test representative cases with edge cases, and check key claims against the source materials.
options.feedback: This is correct because a reliable evaluation starts with specific success criteria and test cases that reflect the real task distribution. Verifying key claims against the provided materials helps catch fluent but unsupported statements before analysts rely on them.

options.label: B
options.text: Use an LLM grader for every response, skip manual source checks, and scale once scores improve.
options.feedback: LLM-based grading can be useful, but it should be tested for reliability before being scaled. It also does not remove the need to validate critical factual claims against authoritative source material.

options.label: C
options.text: Select the prompt from the most polished demo, expand usage gradually, and collect complaints from analysts.
options.feedback: This relies on informal inspection rather than a measurable evaluation process. Polished examples can miss edge cases and may not reveal whether the workflow performs consistently on realistic inputs.

options.label: D
options.text: Ask Claude to rate each answer's confidence, approve high scores, and review only low-scoring responses.
options.feedback: Self-reported confidence is not a dependable substitute for checking factual support. A confident answer can still contain unsupported or incorrect claims, especially in high-stakes due diligence work.

questions.explanation:
Strong validation begins with measurable success criteria, not with a general impression that outputs sound good. Anthropic's evaluation guidance recommends defining criteria that fit the task, then testing against a distribution that mirrors real use, including edge cases, as described in Define success criteria.

For fact-heavy workflows, evaluation should also include direct evidence checks. Techniques such as allowing Claude to say I don't know, asking for citations, and grounding analysis in source documents can reduce hallucinations, but they do not eliminate them, so critical claims still need validation, as covered in Reduce hallucinations.

The distractors reflect common anti-patterns: relying on polished demos, trusting the model's own confidence, or scaling an automated judge without confirming that it matches the team's factual standards. A defensible readiness decision combines task-relevant eval design with source-based verification of the claims people will act on.

questions.question: A boutique hotel group's guest experience team is working in Claude.ai to turn 12 guest review excerpts into a tracker with columns for issue, sentiment, urgency, and suggested owner. The tracker will be pasted into a spreadsheet for a one-time weekly review. Which output request is most appropriate?

options.label: A
options.text: Ask Claude to return a compact table or CSV with one row per excerpt.
options.feedback: This matches the need for a short, structured, one-time output that can be reviewed and pasted into another tool. A table or CSV keeps the information organized without creating an unnecessary reusable artifact.

options.label: B
options.text: Ask Claude to write a narrative memo summarizing the overall complaint themes.
options.feedback: A memo can be useful for qualitative synthesis, but it does not preserve one row per excerpt or the requested tracking fields. It would make spreadsheet transfer and validation harder.

options.label: C
options.text: Ask Claude to use API structured JSON outputs for the Claude.ai response.
options.feedback: Structured JSON outputs are an API feature, not a Claude.ai output surface like chat or artifacts. They are appropriate when an application needs schema-constrained API responses, not when a user is manually preparing a small tracker in Claude.ai.

options.label: D
options.text: Ask Claude to create an artifact containing an interactive review dashboard.
options.feedback: Artifacts are best for substantial, standalone content that users are likely to edit, reuse, or reference later. An interactive dashboard adds unnecessary complexity for a small, one-time tracker.

questions.explanation:
Good output selection starts with the work product, not with the most advanced feature. For a small extraction task that will be pasted into a spreadsheet, a compact table or CSV is easy to scan, validate, and transfer. It also keeps each review excerpt aligned with the same fields, which helps the team catch missing or inconsistent entries.

Artifacts are intended for substantial, standalone content displayed in a dedicated window, such as documents, diagrams, single-page apps, or interactive components. Anthropic documents that artifacts are typically useful when the content is self-contained, reusable, editable, and likely to be referenced later, see What are artifacts and how do I use them?. A small one-time tracker does not benefit enough from that extra surface.

Anthropic's structured outputs features, including JSON outputs through output_config.format, are for API workflows where software needs schema-constrained responses. They can be useful when an application must parse model output reliably, but they are not the same thing as asking Claude.ai to format an answer for a person. For details, see Structured outputs.
