questions.question: A maritime insurance claims unit is creating a Claude Project to help adjusters draft loss summaries. They want every new chat in the project to use the same policy wording, escalation checklist, and response format, without relying on information from one chat appearing in another. Which TWO actions should they take?

options.label: A
options.text: Explain the policy wording in the first chat and continue work in new chats.
options.feedback: This is incorrect because ordinary chat context is not shared across separate chats in a project. Information that should persist across project chats needs to be added to project knowledge.

options.label: B
options.text: Add the policy wording and escalation checklist to the project knowledge base.
options.feedback: This is correct because project knowledge is persistent across chats inside the same project. Adding stable reference materials to the knowledge base makes them available for future chats in that project.

options.label: C
options.text: Set project instructions that describe the required loss-summary response format.
options.feedback: This is correct because project instructions are a separate project configuration that applies to all chats in the project. Format, tone, and response behavior belong in instructions rather than in a one-time prompt.

options.label: D
options.text: Put the checklist and response rules in the project name and description.
options.feedback: This is incorrect because a project’s name and description are not context that Claude can use. They may help humans identify the project, but they do not configure Claude’s behavior or provide usable knowledge.

questions.explanation:
Claude Projects are workspaces with their own chats, knowledge base, and instructions. For reusable source material such as policy wording, templates, checklists, or reference documents, the right place is project knowledge, because content added there is available across chats within that project. See What are projects? and How can I create and manage projects?.

Project instructions serve a different purpose: they tell Claude how to behave or respond in every chat in that project. A required summary structure, writing style, or review approach should be saved through Set project instructions, while the underlying reference documents should be stored as knowledge.

The common anti-pattern is treating a first chat, project title, or project description as durable configuration. Separate chats do not automatically inherit ordinary chat context, and Claude does not use the project name or description as working context. Separating what Claude should know from how Claude should respond makes the project more reliable for repeated work.

questions.question: A university alumni office is refining a Claude Console prompt that turns donor meeting notes into follow-up email drafts. The drafts are sometimes too generic and miss promised next steps. The team has a first-draft prompt and many past notes with approved emails, and wants to improve the prompt reliably. Which two actions should they take?

options.label: A
options.text: Tune the prompt on one recent donor note, accept the best-looking draft, and reuse that wording broadly.
options.feedback: This is incorrect because a single example can hide failures that appear across the real distribution of work. It encourages overfitting the prompt to one case rather than validating performance across varied inputs.

options.label: B
options.text: Template the changing inputs as variables, create prompt versions, and compare each version on the same test cases.
options.feedback: This is correct because the Console Evaluation tool uses prompt variables for test sets, and prompt versioning supports controlled comparison. Re-running the same cases helps the team see whether a prompt change actually improves quality.

options.label: C
options.text: Define measurable criteria for tone, next-step coverage, and format, then test with representative donor-note cases.
options.feedback: This is correct because prompt iteration should begin with clear success criteria and evaluations that reflect the real task. Testing representative cases makes improvements more reliable than judging a single output informally.

options.label: D
options.text: Run the prompt improver once, keep the longer template, and deploy it without retesting the suite.
options.feedback: This is incorrect because the prompt improver can help refine a template, but it does not replace evaluation. A longer, more detailed prompt may improve some outputs, but it still needs to be tested against the team’s success criteria.

questions.explanation:
Effective prompt iteration follows a test, refine, validate loop. Before rewriting the prompt repeatedly, the team should define what a good donor follow-up email must do, such as preserve promised next steps, match the desired tone, and follow the required format. Anthropic’s guidance on prompt engineering emphasizes starting from success criteria and empirical tests, not from subjective impressions of a single output: Prompt engineering overview.

For this kind of repeatable task, evaluations should resemble the real workload and include enough varied examples to reveal patterns. The Console Evaluation tool supports this workflow through prompt variables such as {{meeting_notes}}, test cases, side-by-side comparison, quality grading, and prompt versioning: Evaluation tool. Prompting tools such as the prompt improver can be useful, but they are best treated as aids within an evaluation loop rather than as proof that the new prompt is better: Prompting tools. The practical tradeoff is that structured prompts, examples, and XML-style organization can improve consistency, but quality still depends on testing against the criteria that matter for the task.

questions.question: An airline catering provider uses Claude to review uploaded supplier incident reports and draft a recommendation about whether a batch of meals should be held or released. Claude returns a concise answer with citations to the reports and notes that one detail is uncertain. The decision affects food safety and flight operations. What is the most appropriate next step before using the recommendation?

options.label: A
options.text: Ask Claude to assign a five-point quality score to its response before making the recall decision.
options.feedback: This is incorrect because a model's own rating is not a dependable validation method for a critical operational decision. Quality scoring can support evaluation workflows, but it does not replace checking the sources and decision criteria.

options.label: B
options.text: Have a qualified reviewer verify the cited passages and source documents before making the recall decision.
options.feedback: This is correct because citations and uncertainty handling can help ground Claude's response, but they do not make a consequential recommendation automatically reliable. A qualified reviewer should check the cited source material and apply the organization's food safety procedures before acting.

options.label: C
options.text: Treat Claude's citations and cautious wording as sufficient validation before making the recall decision.
options.feedback: This is incorrect because citations reduce the risk of unsupported claims, but they are not a complete substitute for verification. Cautious wording is useful, but it is not a guarantee that the recommendation is accurate or appropriate.

options.label: D
options.text: Rerun the prompt in the Console Evaluation tool and use the best output before making the recall decision.
options.feedback: This is incorrect because the Console Evaluation tool is designed to test prompts across scenarios, compare outputs, and support prompt iteration. Rerunning a prompt may reveal variation, but it does not verify the underlying facts or approve a safety-related decision.

questions.explanation:
Claude can be made more reliable by grounding answers in sources, allowing I don't know, requiring citations, and retracting unsupported claims, but Anthropic states that these techniques reduce rather than eliminate hallucinations and that critical information, especially high-stakes decisions, should be validated. See Reduce hallucinations.

Citations help because they point to passages and locations in user-provided documents, so a reviewer can trace a claim back to the material Claude used. They are not a substitute for all external verification, and their scope matters, for example citations work over supported text content when enabled with citations.enabled=true, as described in Citations.

The Claude Console Evaluation tool is useful for testing prompts across scenarios, comparing versions, and grading outputs, but it is not an automatic validator for a particular production decision. In practice, the right tradeoff is to use automated and prompt-level evaluation to improve the workflow, then add human review when the output will drive a safety, legal, financial, or other consequential action.

questions.question: A public health hotline's training team uses Claude to turn caller notes into referral categories with a short rationale. The prompt seems unreliable, but each revision is judged on whichever recent transcript is easiest to find, and reviewers disagree about whether the output improved. What should the team do next?

options.label: A
options.text: Define measurable success criteria and test revisions on representative edge cases.
options.feedback: This is the best next step because prompt improvement should be evaluated against clear, task-specific criteria rather than informal impressions. Representative and edge-case examples make it easier to see whether a prompt is actually improving reliability.

options.label: B
options.text: Rewrite the prompt after each failure and judge the next transcript manually.
options.feedback: This continues the ad hoc pattern that is already producing inconsistent judgments. Testing one convenient transcript at a time does not show whether the prompt generalizes across the task.

options.label: C
options.text: Increase the prompt length and add broader background context to every request.
options.feedback: More context can help when the missing information is relevant, but it is not a systematic way to diagnose whether revisions improve performance. Longer prompts can also add noise if they are not guided by measured failures.

options.label: D
options.text: Ask Claude to rate its confidence and accept outputs above a fixed threshold.
options.feedback: Claude's self-rated confidence is not a reliable substitute for evaluating output quality against the team's requirements. The team needs external criteria and test cases, not another model-generated assertion.

questions.explanation:
When a prompt is underperforming, the first troubleshooting move is to make quality observable. Anthropic recommends starting prompt engineering from success criteria, ways to test those criteria, and a first-draft prompt, then iterating empirically rather than relying on ad hoc edits. See Develop tests for guidance on task-specific evaluations and measurable success metrics.

For this hotline workflow, a useful evaluation set would include common caller notes plus difficult cases, such as ambiguous symptoms, missing details, or notes that could fit multiple referral categories. Once the team agrees on what counts as a correct category and an acceptable rationale, prompt revisions can be compared consistently. Techniques like adding context, changing wording, or using examples may help later, but without a stable test set the team cannot tell whether those changes are real improvements or just lucky results on the latest transcript.

questions.question: An independent video game studio plans to launch a Claude-powered support chat for players on its website. The chat will answer account and gameplay questions directly, and the product lead argues that no extra governance step is needed because the chat will not provide legal, medical, or financial advice. What is the most appropriate action before release?

options.label: A
options.text: Add disclosure only when a player asks whether AI is involved.
options.feedback: This is incorrect because waiting for the user to ask does not satisfy the documented minimum timing. The disclosure should happen at the beginning of each chat session, not only after a direct question.

options.label: B
options.text: Skip disclosure unless the chat gives high-risk advice to a player.
options.feedback: This is incorrect because the disclosure requirement for consumer-facing chatbots is not limited to high-risk advice. Treating only legal, medical, or financial uses as needing transparency misses a broader user-facing AI disclosure obligation.

options.label: C
options.text: Disclose at the beginning of each chat that users are interacting with AI.
options.feedback: This is correct because consumer-facing chatbots must disclose that the user is interacting with AI, at minimum at the beginning of each chat session. The requirement applies even when the chatbot is not otherwise a high-risk use case.

options.label: D
options.text: Present the chat as a human agent to reduce player confusion.
options.feedback: This is incorrect because representing an AI system as a human undermines transparency and can create deceptive user expectations. Anthropic’s Usage Policy also includes restrictions related to impersonation and consumer-facing disclosure.

questions.explanation:
Ethical AI use includes transparency, not only avoiding obviously high-risk domains. Anthropic’s Usage Policy requires consumer-facing chatbots to disclose that the user is interacting with AI, at minimum at the beginning of each chat session.

The product lead’s reasoning is incomplete because the absence of legal, healthcare, finance, or similar high-risk advice does not remove the disclosure requirement. Users should understand whether they are interacting with an automated system so they can set appropriate expectations about reliability, accountability, and escalation to human support.

Presenting the chatbot as human, delaying disclosure until asked, or treating disclosure as optional are poor governance choices. The practical mental model is that responsible deployment combines use-case review with user notice, and the AUP is an enforceable product-use constraint rather than informal best practice.

questions.question: A wildlife conservation nonprofit has used one Claude chat for a seasonal fundraising campaign. The conversation now includes early message drafts, rejected donor segments, old budget assumptions, and the final approved campaign brief. Claude has begun blending old and current details when drafting the launch email. What is the most appropriate next step?

options.label: A
options.text: Continue in the same chat and tell Claude to disregard every rejected draft.
options.feedback: This may help somewhat, but the old content still remains in the active conversation context. When obsolete information is extensive, instructions to ignore it are less reliable than providing a clean, current summary.

options.label: B
options.text: Increase the effort setting and ask Claude to reconcile all campaign versions.
options.feedback: Higher effort can improve thoroughness, but it does not remove outdated details from the conversation. Reconciling all versions also invites Claude to spend attention on material that the team already rejected.

options.label: C
options.text: Paste the full chat history into a new chat to preserve every campaign detail.
options.feedback: This preserves the same clutter that caused the problem. Moving all old material into a new chat does not create a clearer working context for the launch email.

options.label: D
options.text: Create a concise summary of the approved brief, then start a focused new chat.
options.feedback: This keeps the relevant current context while reducing interference from outdated material. A fresh chat with a concise summary gives Claude a cleaner working set for the next task.

questions.explanation:
The context window is Claude's active working memory for the current request, not a permanent model memory or training store. When a conversation contains obsolete drafts and current decisions together, Claude may use details that are technically present but no longer useful. A practical response is to extract the approved facts, constraints, and decisions into a concise summary, then continue from that cleaner context.

This approach trades completeness for focus. Keeping every past message can be useful for audit or exploration, but it is often a poor input for final production work because rejected alternatives compete with the latest instructions. Starting a focused new chat, or using a Project when ongoing accumulated context is needed, helps separate current working context from historical clutter.

Anthropic's documentation explains that a request's context window includes the prompt, messages, documents, tool results, and generated output, so large or messy histories can affect what Claude has available to consider. See Context windows for the mental model behind context limits and why managing what enters the working context matters.

questions.question: A city museum's acquisitions team asks Claude to review uploaded provenance notes and draft a recommendation about whether a donated sculpture can be accepted under the museum's acquisition policy. Claude returns a confident recommendation with citations to several documents. The result will be used in a board packet. What should the curator do before relying on the recommendation?

options.label: A
options.text: Run the prompt in the Claude Console Evaluation tool and accept the output if it scores well.
options.feedback: This is incorrect because the evaluation tool helps test prompts across scenarios, not validate a specific production decision automatically. A good evaluation score can improve trust in a prompt pattern, but it does not replace review of the actual recommendation.

options.label: B
options.text: Check the cited source passages and route the recommendation to a qualified provenance reviewer.
options.feedback: This is correct because citations help locate supporting passages, but they do not make the conclusion automatically reliable. A decision that affects acquisition approval should receive additional verification and appropriate human review before it is used.

options.label: C
options.text: Ask Claude to rate its confidence and include the rating beside the board recommendation.
options.feedback: This is incorrect because a self-reported confidence rating is not a reliable substitute for source verification. It may make the output look more rigorous without addressing whether the cited passages actually support the conclusion.

options.label: D
options.text: Use the recommendation as written after confirming that each paragraph contains a citation.
options.feedback: This is incorrect because the presence of citations is not the same as validating the reasoning or the policy conclusion. Citations can support review, but high-stakes or critical information should still be checked.

questions.explanation:
Citations are useful because they ground Claude's answer in user-provided source documents and provide passages or locations that a reviewer can inspect. However, Anthropic's documentation is clear that hallucination-reduction techniques, including citations and grounding in quotes, reduce but do not eliminate errors, and that critical information should be validated before use. See Reduce hallucinations and Citations.

The practical mental model is that Claude can accelerate review by finding relevant text, summarizing it, and drafting a recommendation, but the human remains responsible for deciding whether the evidence supports the conclusion. For a board packet about an acquisition decision, the safer workflow is to inspect the cited passages and involve a qualified reviewer who understands the policy and provenance risks. The Claude Console Evaluation tool can help compare prompts and test behavior across examples, but it is not an automatic validator for a specific real-world decision, as described in Claude Console Evaluation tool.

questions.question: An agricultural cooperative's procurement desk wants Claude to help prepare vendor follow-up notes. Some requests require checking the cooperative's existing inventory system, while others are only wording edits. The inventory lookup must stay under the cooperative's approved workflow. Which workflow practice best fits this need?

options.label: A
options.text: Create a Skill for the follow-up note format, verify inventory details in the approved system, and send only after review.
options.feedback: This keeps Claude focused on repeatable drafting and formatting while preserving the inventory system as the source of truth. It also adds a review step before vendor-facing notes are sent, which is appropriate when operational facts may be included.

options.label: B
options.text: Paste style instructions into each prompt, ask Claude to infer missing stock levels, and correct mistakes after vendors reply.
options.feedback: Repeating the same guidance in every prompt is inefficient for a recurring workflow. Asking Claude to infer missing stock levels is a hallucination-prone anti-pattern because the answer depends on current internal data.

options.label: C
options.text: Use public web searches for stock questions, let Claude estimate available inventory, and send notes after light editing.
options.feedback: Public web searches are not an authoritative way to check a cooperative's private inventory. Letting Claude estimate stock levels risks inserting unsupported operational facts into vendor communications.

options.label: D
options.text: Require an inventory review for every request, route simple wording edits through that check, and draft notes afterward.
options.feedback: This adds unnecessary friction when the request is only a wording edit and does not involve inventory facts. A good workflow distinguishes between low-risk drafting tasks and tasks that require validation against an authoritative system.

questions.explanation:
Claude should augment the procurement workflow without replacing the cooperative's authoritative inventory process. A Skill is appropriate for repeatable procedures such as a vendor follow-up format, standard tone, and review checklist, while the inventory system remains the source of truth for stock facts.

Skills are designed to package proven ways of working so Claude can apply them automatically when the task matches, instead of having users repeat the same standards in every prompt. Anthropic describes this product-level use of Skills in Teach Claude your way of working using skills.

The tradeoff is practical: Claude can save time on drafting, structuring, and applying standards, but factual operational details still need validation against the approved internal system. Public searches, guessing missing stock levels, or forcing unnecessary checks for wording-only tasks either reduce reliability or add avoidable friction.

questions.question: A language learning platform is screening several Claude-based ideas before approving them. Which TWO proposed uses should the platform reject as inappropriate under Anthropic’s Usage Policy?

options.label: A
options.text: Offer a wellness chatbot that discloses AI at session start and gives general lifestyle tips.
options.feedback: This is not automatically prohibited because wellness advice such as sleep, stress, nutrition, and exercise is excluded from the healthcare high-risk category. The chatbot still needs to disclose that the user is interacting with AI at the start of the session.

options.label: B
options.text: Release a general career-planning chatbot that discloses AI at session start and uses qualified professional review.
options.feedback: This is not automatically prohibited, because general career-planning advice is not the same as an employability decision, resume screening, hiring tool, or other employment determination. The disclosure also supports the separate rule that consumer-facing chatbots must tell users they are interacting with AI.

options.label: C
options.text: Use Claude outputs at scale to create training data for a new tutoring model without Anthropic authorization.
options.feedback: This is inappropriate because Anthropic prohibits using its products to train another AI model without prior authorization. The policy describes this as model scraping or model distillation, even if the intended downstream model is educational.

options.label: D
options.text: Design prompts that bypass Claude’s safeguards to obtain harmful content for a launch demo without authorization.
options.feedback: This is inappropriate because intentionally bypassing product restrictions or guardrails to obtain harmful outputs is prohibited without prior authorization. A public demo or testing goal does not make jailbreaking acceptable under the Usage Policy.

questions.explanation:
Anthropic’s Usage Policy, also called the Acceptable Use Policy or AUP, distinguishes between prohibited activity and allowed uses that require extra safeguards. Some uses, such as model scraping or intentionally bypassing safeguards to obtain harmful outputs, are not appropriate without prior authorization.

High-risk does not mean automatically banned, but the category should be read carefully. Employment-related high-risk uses cover areas such as employability decisions, resume screening, hiring tools, and other employment determinations, rather than every form of general career-planning advice.

Wellness guidance is another useful boundary case. General sleep, stress, nutrition, and exercise advice is explicitly excluded from the healthcare high-risk category, although a consumer-facing chatbot must still disclose that the user is interacting with AI. The practical mental model is to separate forbidden methods, such as unauthorized model distillation or jailbreaking, from sensitive domains that may proceed only with appropriate human review and transparency safeguards.

See Anthropic’s official Usage Policy and the deployment guidance on launching a product using Claude while following the Usage Policy.

questions.question: A shopping center security contractor wants to use Claude to combine incident reports, public social media posts, and camera-derived notes to identify named visitors who are likely to shoplift, then share a watchlist with guards and local police. What is the most appropriate governance response?

options.label: A
options.text: Add entrance signage and require a guard to approve each watchlist entry.
options.feedback: Disclosure and human review are important in some high-risk use cases, but they do not authorize a prohibited use. A human-in-the-loop process can reduce some harms, but it does not change the nature of a predictive watchlist used for policing or security action.

options.label: B
options.text: Stop the workflow and redesign it around aggregate, non-identifying safety trends.
options.feedback: This is the appropriate response because the proposed use involves identifying people as likely future offenders and sharing a watchlist for security action. Anthropic’s Usage Policy prohibits certain surveillance and law-enforcement-adjacent uses, including predictive policing, so disclosure or review alone would not make this workflow acceptable.

options.label: C
options.text: Limit the inputs to public social media posts and run a short pilot.
options.feedback: Using publicly available information does not automatically make the use ethical or policy-compliant. The core issue is the intended use of the system to identify named people as likely offenders, not only the source of the data.

options.label: D
options.text: Tell Claude to avoid protected traits and continue using named watchlists.
options.feedback: Avoiding protected traits is not enough to address the ethical and policy problem. Named watchlists for predicted misconduct can still create surveillance and enforcement harms even if the prompt excludes explicit demographic attributes.

questions.explanation:
Responsible AI governance starts by asking whether a proposed use is allowed at all, not just whether it can be made more accurate or better documented. Anthropic’s Usage Policy is an enforceable product-use constraint and prohibits certain privacy, surveillance, identity, and law-enforcement-adjacent uses, including predictive policing and some uses that make criminal-justice-related determinations.

In this scenario, the risk is not merely that Claude might hallucinate or classify someone incorrectly. The larger ethical issue is using AI to convert mixed evidence into a named watchlist of people predicted to commit misconduct, then using that list for security or police action. Measures such as human review, signage, or removing protected-trait language may be good controls in other settings, but they cannot convert a prohibited use into an acceptable one.

A safer direction is to redesign the work toward aggregate, non-identifying analysis, such as summarizing incident patterns by time, location, or procedure so staff can improve lighting, staffing, or store policies without targeting named individuals. For the governing policy, see Anthropic’s Usage Policy.

questions.question: A regional food bank's operations team wants Claude to turn warehouse inventory notes, volunteer shift constraints, and recipient agency requests into a weekly allocation plan with assumptions and follow-up questions. The team has been sending one long paragraph and getting inconsistent plans. What is the best way to restructure the prompt?

options.label: A
options.text: Ask Claude to think harder about the full problem, then request a polished allocation plan without specifying intermediate analysis steps.
options.feedback: Thinking settings can help with complex reasoning, but they are not a substitute for a well-structured prompt. Without explicit steps and separated inputs, Claude still has to infer the workflow and output structure.

options.label: B
options.text: Combine the materials into one narrative prompt, then ask Claude to use its judgment to decide the order of analysis and the final sections.
options.feedback: This keeps the work largely implicit, which is what caused inconsistent results. Claude can often handle natural language prompts, but complex tasks benefit from clear structure rather than relying on unstated ordering.

options.label: C
options.text: Start with the requested final allocation plan, then paste the supporting notes afterward and ask Claude to revise anything that seems inconsistent.
options.feedback: This puts the output request ahead of the source material and does not decompose the work into manageable steps. For complex or long-input tasks, it is usually better to provide the relevant materials clearly and then give the task instructions.

options.label: D
options.text: Separate the materials with descriptive XML-style tags, then give Claude a numbered sequence for extracting constraints, comparing requests, drafting the plan, and listing open questions.
options.feedback: This is the best approach because it makes the prompt structure explicit and separates different kinds of information. Numbered steps help Claude follow the intended workflow, while descriptive tags help distinguish context, inputs, and requested outputs.

questions.explanation:
For complex requests, a strong prompt reduces ambiguity by making the task structure visible. Anthropic’s prompting guidance emphasizes using clear, explicit instructions, especially numbered lists or bullets when order and completeness matter, and using XML-style tags to separate instructions, context, examples, and inputs.

In this scenario, the food bank is asking Claude to combine several different inputs and produce several different outputs. A decomposed prompt might use tags such as <inventory_notes>, <shift_constraints>, and <agency_requests>, followed by numbered instructions to identify constraints, compare requests, draft allocations, state assumptions, and list follow-up questions.

Simply asking Claude to “use judgment” or “think harder” leaves too much of the workflow implied. Thinking features can support difficult multistep reasoning, but prompt structure still matters because it tells Claude what information belongs where and what sequence of work to perform. See Anthropic’s prompt engineering guidance on clear instructions and structured prompts at Anthropic prompt engineering documentation.

questions.question: A boutique architecture firm's planning team needs a one-time briefing on recent zoning proposals in three cities. They have not gathered the source documents yet, and they expect Claude to investigate several public sources before synthesizing the findings. Which Claude feature choice best fits this work?

options.label: A
options.text: Create an artifact to present findings before gathering external sources.
options.feedback: Artifacts are useful when the output should be a separate document, visualization, or interactive object. Creating one first does not address the main need to locate and synthesize information from multiple public sources.

options.label: B
options.text: Use ordinary chat and ask Claude to rely on general background knowledge.
options.feedback: Ordinary chat is appropriate for one-off work when the necessary context can be supplied in the conversation. It is a weaker fit here because the team needs current, multi-source investigation rather than only general model knowledge.

options.label: C
options.text: Use Research with web search enabled to investigate and synthesize the sources.
options.feedback: This is the best fit because the task calls for a one-time, multi-source investigation where the team has not already assembled the materials. Research is designed for that kind of agentic investigation and requires web search to be turned on.

options.label: D
options.text: Create a Project and leave the source collection to each new chat.
options.feedback: Projects are best when reusable context, files, instructions, or ongoing work need to persist across related chats. Starting a project without adding relevant knowledge does not solve the need to gather current public sources.

questions.explanation:
Research is the best product feature when the work is an investigation rather than a simple prompt response. In this scenario, the team does not already have the documents and wants Claude to investigate multiple public sources before summarizing them. The Research documentation states that Research is available on paid plans and requires web search to be turned on, which matches the need to gather outside information rather than only analyze uploaded files. See Using Research on Claude.ai.

Projects serve a different purpose: they are self-contained workspaces with their own chat histories, knowledge bases, and project instructions. They are strongest when the same context will be reused over time, especially when documents or instructions should be available across multiple chats in that project. For a one-time investigation where the sources have not yet been gathered, a Project can be useful later for organizing work, but it is not the feature that performs the investigation. See What are projects?.

Ordinary chat is still valuable for one-off tasks when the user can provide the needed context directly, and artifacts can help package or refine an output once the content exists. Neither replaces the need to search across current sources. The practical selection principle is to match the feature to the workflow: use chat for contained prompts, Projects for reusable context, Research for multi-source investigation, and artifacts for working with substantial outputs.

questions.question: A home fitness equipment startup's marketing team is using Claude at the beginning of a campaign to explore possible themes for a new rowing machine. They are not ready for final copy yet and want a range of directions to discuss. Which prompting approach is most appropriate?

options.label: A
options.text: Ask Claude to follow a legal-review checklist, identifying risks and required approvals for each concept.
options.feedback: This applies an analysis or compliance workflow before the team has developed enough ideas to assess. Risk review can be useful later, but it does not match the immediate brainstorming goal.

options.label: B
options.text: Ask Claude to summarize market research sources first, with citations, before allowing any concepts to be proposed.
options.feedback: This would be more appropriate if the task were primarily research synthesis or source evaluation. The team may use research later, but the stated need is to generate a range of campaign directions.

options.label: C
options.text: Ask Claude for a varied idea list, with audience, constraints, and a simple format for comparing concepts.
options.feedback: This fits an early brainstorming task because it encourages variety while still giving Claude useful boundaries. Stating the audience, constraints, and output format helps make the ideas easier to review and compare.

options.label: D
options.text: Ask Claude to produce one polished campaign immediately, without context, so creative direction stays unconstrained.
options.feedback: This skips the exploration phase the team needs and is likely to narrow the output too soon. Removing context is not a good way to improve creativity because Claude still benefits from clear goals and constraints.

questions.explanation:
Prompting should match the task type. For brainstorming, the goal is usually to create a useful range of possibilities, so the prompt should invite multiple directions while still naming the audience, goal, constraints, and desired response format.

Clear instructions do not make Claude less creative. They reduce wasted output by telling Claude what kind of ideas are useful, how many to produce, and how to organize them for discussion. Anthropic’s guidance emphasizes clear, explicit instructions, desired formats, constraints, and ordered steps when needed: Be clear and direct.

A research-style prompt, a compliance checklist, or a request for one final polished campaign can all be valid in other phases of work, but they are mismatched here. Anthropic also frames prompt improvement as something to connect to success criteria and empirical evaluation rather than intuition alone: Prompt engineering overview.

They have not gathered the source documents, expect the work to require checking several public sources, and want a draft briefing they can revise during the same session. options.feedback: Ordinary chat can work well for one-off tasks when the necessary context is already in the conversation. For a newly proposed rule that requires several public sources, relying only on existing model knowledge is not the best fit.

options.label: B
options.text: Create an artifact for the draft briefing so reviewers can iterate on it.
options.feedback: Artifacts are appropriate when Claude is creating a standalone deliverable that the user will review and refine. A member-facing briefing is a draft output, not primarily a reusable knowledge base.

options.label: C
options.text: Use Research with web search enabled to investigate the public sources.
options.feedback: Research is designed for multi-source investigation where Claude conducts searches that build on one another. It requires web search to be turned on, so enabling it is necessary for this type of current public-source research.

options.label: D
options.text: Create a Project for the one-session task before collecting any sources.
options.feedback: Projects are most useful when reusable context, project instructions, or accumulated workspaces are needed across chats. Creating one before sources exist does not solve the need for public multi-source investigation.

questions.explanation:

questions.question: A specialty insurance review team wants Claude to help screen claim files for items that need adjuster attention. Early trials show useful results, but the team sees different kinds of mistakes across routine claims, unusual exclusions, and high-value files. Before choosing a final prompt or model, what is the most appropriate next step?

options.label: A
options.text: Ask Claude to rate confidence and route low-confidence files to adjusters.
options.feedback: This is incorrect because Claude's self-reported confidence is not a dependable substitute for evaluation against known criteria. It may sound plausible, but it does not establish whether the screening workflow meets accuracy, consistency, privacy, latency, or cost needs.

options.label: B
options.text: Rewrite the prompt and judge several new responses using informal review.
options.feedback: This is incorrect because informal review of a few outputs can miss important failure patterns. Prompt changes are useful only after the team has a clear way to measure whether the changes improve the use case.

options.label: C
options.text: Define measurable criteria and evaluate representative claims, including edge cases.
options.feedback: This is correct because the team needs to know what good performance means before optimizing the workflow. A representative evaluation set, including edge cases, helps reveal whether Claude is reliable across the actual claim types the team expects to handle.

options.label: D
options.text: Choose the most capable model and skip separate evaluation before launch.
options.feedback: This is incorrect because a stronger model does not remove the need to test the workflow against the team's requirements. It may also increase cost or latency, which are part of the requirements tradeoff rather than issues to ignore.

questions.explanation:
Good workflow design starts with the use case, not with prompt wording alone. Anthropic's prompt engineering guidance says teams should have clear success criteria, a way to empirically test against those criteria, and a first-draft prompt before serious prompt engineering. It also notes that some problems, such as latency and cost, may be better addressed through model selection rather than more prompt edits. See Prompt engineering overview.

For a claim-screening workflow, the team should define measurable criteria such as task fidelity, consistency, privacy preservation, context use, latency, and price, then test on examples that mirror real work. The evaluation set should include routine cases and edge cases, because unusual exclusions and high-value files may reveal different failure modes than easy examples. Anthropic's evaluation guidance emphasizes specific, measurable, achievable, and relevant criteria, plus multidimensional evaluation across the factors that matter for the use case. See Define success criteria.

questions.question: A pharmaceutical medical writing group on a Team plan wants Claude to use protocol documents stored in Google Drive while drafting study summaries. The Owner has enabled Google Workspace connectors, but one writer cannot retrieve a protocol that lives in another department's Drive folder. What should the workspace admin advise?

options.label: A
options.text: Make the Claude project shared organization-wide so the connector can read all department Drive folders for project members.
options.feedback: This is incorrect because sharing a Claude project does not grant new Google Drive permissions. Connector access remains tied to the connected Google account and the permissions that account already has in Google Workspace.

options.label: B
options.text: Have the writer connect their own Google account and obtain Drive access to the protocol before asking Claude to retrieve it.
options.feedback: This is correct because organization-level enablement makes the connector available, but each user still needs to authenticate unless a managed enterprise authentication flow applies. Claude also mirrors the connected account's Google Workspace permissions, so it cannot retrieve a Drive file the writer cannot access.

options.label: C
options.text: Paste the protocol's Drive URL into the chat so Claude can access it without the writer's Drive permission.
options.feedback: This is incorrect because a URL does not bypass source-system permissions. Claude can only access Google Drive data available to the connected account, so the writer still needs permission to view the file.

options.label: D
options.text: Set the Google Drive connector to Always available so Claude loads the connector before the writer asks about the protocol.
options.feedback: This is incorrect because tool access mode affects when connectors are loaded, not what Google Drive data a user is allowed to access. Loading the connector earlier does not authenticate the writer or expand their Drive permissions.

questions.explanation:
Google Workspace connectors separate availability from access. On Team and Enterprise plans, an Owner or Primary Owner can enable the connectors at the organization level, but that does not automatically mean every user is authenticated to Google or allowed to read every Drive file. See Use Google Workspace connectors and Use connectors to extend Claude's capabilities.

The practical mental model is that Claude acts through the connected user's account and mirrors that account's existing Google Workspace permissions. If the writer cannot open the protocol in Drive, Claude should not be expected to retrieve it through the connector, even if the connector is enabled for the organization.

Changing tool access mode, such as using Always available, can affect connector loading behavior, but it does not grant authentication or new source-system access. Sharing a Claude project or pasting a Drive URL likewise does not override Google Drive permissions. For connector loading behavior, see Manage Claude's tool access.

questions.question: A nonprofit legal aid clinic's intake team uses Claude to draft appointment-preparation emails for many different clients. Client facts, documents, and deadlines change daily, but the clinic's voice, boundaries, and response format should stay consistent. Which approach is most appropriate for the system-level instructions?

options.label: A
options.text: Use a broad instruction to write helpful legal-aid emails, then correct tone, format, and legal boundaries after each draft.
options.feedback: A vague instruction gives Claude too little guidance about the clinic's repeatable standards. Relying on manual correction each time increases inconsistency and defeats the purpose of reusable configuration.

options.label: B
options.text: Define durable role, tone, boundaries, format, source use, and missing-information behavior, then provide case facts in the relevant chat or project.
options.feedback: This separates stable guidance from changing context, which makes the instructions reusable across many client matters. It also tells Claude how to behave when information is incomplete rather than encouraging it to fill gaps.

options.label: C
options.text: Add client histories, deadlines, exhibits, and preferred conclusions to global instructions, then let every new chat inherit that context.
options.feedback: Global or system-level instructions are a poor place for changing client-specific facts because they can become stale and apply to the wrong matter. Case materials should be supplied only where they are relevant.

options.label: D
options.text: Direct Claude to follow the latest uploaded case note first, then ignore standing instructions when personalization creates conflicts.
options.feedback: Case notes are useful context, but they should not override stable clinic boundaries or safety expectations. Standing instructions should define how Claude handles conflicts, uncertainty, and missing information.

questions.explanation:
Effective system-level instructions should capture durable behavior: Claude's role, audience, tone, output structure, source-handling expectations, and what to do when needed information is missing. The changing facts of a client matter belong in the current chat or project knowledge, not in a broad instruction that applies across unrelated work.

This division reduces instruction clutter and avoids stale context leaking into future tasks. It also gives Claude a clear operating frame while still allowing each case's documents and facts to guide the specific draft.

Claude features are designed around this distinction: Custom Instructions express broad preferences, Projects support accumulated context for a focused workspace, and Skills support repeatable procedures that activate when relevant. The comparison in Anthropic's Skills overview is a useful mental model for deciding where persistent instructions, reusable workflows, and project knowledge should live.

questions.question: An independent film distributor's acquisitions team needs Claude to compare several festival deal memos and draft a recommendation for executives. The work requires nuanced reasoning and polished writing, but the team needs same-day turnaround and wants to avoid unnecessary model cost. Which model-selection approach best fits the task?

options.label: A
options.text: Use Claude Sonnet 5 as the default model for these executive recommendation drafts.
options.feedback: This is the best fit because the task needs stronger reasoning and writing quality than the simplest high-volume work, while still valuing speed and cost control. Claude Sonnet 5 is positioned as a strong balance of speed and intelligence, making it a practical default for this scenario.

options.label: B
options.text: Use Claude Opus 4.8 as the default model for these executive recommendation drafts.
options.feedback: Claude Opus 4.8 is aimed at more complex agentic coding and enterprise work, so it may be more capability than this drafting task needs by default. Using it for every pass would likely add cost without clearly matching the stated cost-control goal.

options.label: C
options.text: Use Claude Haiku 4.5 as the default model for these executive recommendation drafts.
options.feedback: Claude Haiku 4.5 is well suited when the priority is the fastest response and low cost for simpler tasks. In this scenario, the executive recommendation requires enough nuance and polish that choosing only the fastest model risks underweighting quality.

options.label: D
options.text: Use Claude Fable 5 as the default model for these executive recommendation drafts.
options.feedback: Claude Fable 5 is described for next-generation intelligence for long-running agents, which is not the main shape of this task. Making it the default would not align well with the need for same-day turnaround and avoiding unnecessary model cost.

questions.explanation:
Good model selection is a tradeoff among capability, speed, and cost, not a rule that always picks either the cheapest model or the most capable model. The Choosing the right model guide frames selection in exactly those terms, and also notes that effort can be a separate lever for some recent models.

For this scenario, Claude Sonnet 5 is the best default because the work needs nuanced analysis and polished communication, but it is not described as a long-running agentic task or the deepest possible reasoning task. Anthropic’s models overview describes Claude Sonnet 5 as offering the best combination of speed and intelligence, while Claude Haiku 4.5 is the fastest model with near-frontier intelligence, Claude Opus 4.8 is positioned for complex agentic coding and enterprise work, and Claude Fable 5 is positioned for long-running agents.

questions.question: A science museum's education team uses Claude to rewrite exhibit descriptions into a worksheet for middle school visitors. The drafts are factually accurate, but some sound too formal and others sound too childish. The team needs a dependable way to choose and refine the best version for that audience. What is the most appropriate action?

options.label: A
options.text: Choose the shortest draft and manually restore any exhibit facts that were omitted.
options.feedback: Shorter text may be easier to read, but length alone does not determine suitability for middle school visitors. This approach also treats factual completeness separately from tone and clarity rather than evaluating the output as a whole.

options.label: B
options.text: Add grade-level examples and score prompt versions against measurable tone and clarity criteria.
options.feedback: This directly addresses the audience mismatch by showing Claude the desired tone, structure, and level. Scoring versions against measurable criteria gives the team a repeatable basis for comparison instead of relying on impressions.

options.label: C
options.text: Ask Claude to select the most engaging draft and adopt the version it recommends.
options.feedback: Claude can help compare drafts, but its preference alone is not a reliable evaluation method. The team still needs audience-relevant success criteria and a way to validate whether the output meets them.

options.label: D
options.text: Tell Claude to avoid formal language and rerun drafts until reviewers agree.
options.feedback: Negative instructions such as avoiding a style are usually less effective than clearly specifying the desired style. Rerunning until reviewers agree is inconsistent and does not create a reusable evaluation process.

questions.explanation:
When refining outputs for a specific audience, the strongest approach combines explicit guidance with evaluation criteria. Anthropic's prompting guidance emphasizes telling Claude what to do, providing useful context, setting format or style constraints, and using examples to steer tone, format, and structure. For an audience such as middle school visitors, examples of acceptable wording are more useful than a vague instruction like do not sound formal.

Comparison should also be tied to defined success criteria. Anthropic's evaluation guidance recommends criteria that are specific, measurable, achievable, and relevant, and notes that many use cases benefit from multidimensional evaluation such as tone, relevance, consistency, and task fidelity. The Console Evaluation tool supports side-by-side comparison, quality grading, and prompt versioning, which are practical ways to compare refinements rather than relying on a single subjective reaction.

As a mental model, prompting shapes the output, while evaluation checks whether that shaping worked. Asking Claude to choose its own favorite draft, picking the shortest version, or rerunning prompts until people agree can all produce a usable answer occasionally, but they do not create a dependable refinement process. For more detail, see Anthropic's Claude 4 best practices, Define success criteria, and Evaluation tool documentation.

questions.question: A wildlife rehabilitation center's outreach coordinator is using Claude.ai with Code execution and file creation enabled. They have notes from a release event and need a short volunteer email to send today, a public information sheet that staff will revise and reuse during the week, and a small animal-release schedule to paste into a tracking spreadsheet. Which output-format request best fits these needs?

options.label: A
options.text: Ask Claude to format the volunteer email, information sheet, and schedule as one structured JSON-style list.
options.feedback: Structured data is useful for the schedule, but it is a poor primary format for a readable email and public-facing sheet. This choice optimizes for machine-like structure at the expense of human review and reuse.

options.label: B
options.text: Ask Claude to draft the volunteer email inline, create the information sheet as an artifact, and provide the schedule as CSV.
options.feedback: This matches each output to its intended use. A short message belongs inline, reusable standalone material is a good fit for an artifact, and a spreadsheet-bound schedule is easiest to validate and paste as structured data.

options.label: C
options.text: Ask Claude to combine the volunteer email, information sheet, and schedule into a single reusable artifact.
options.feedback: An artifact is appropriate for the reusable information sheet, but it is unnecessary for the short same-day email. It also does not make the schedule as convenient for spreadsheet transfer as a structured CSV output.

options.label: D
options.text: Ask Claude to place the volunteer email, information sheet, and schedule in one continuous inline chat response.
options.feedback: This may work for quick review, but it is not the best format for material that will be revised and reused. Keeping the public information sheet only in chat makes later editing and reference less convenient than using an artifact.

questions.explanation:
Good output evaluation includes choosing the format that makes the result easy to review, reuse, and transfer. Claude's artifacts are designed for substantial, self-contained content that users are likely to edit, iterate on, or reference later, displayed in a dedicated window separate from the chat. Anthropic's documentation lists examples such as documents, diagrams, websites, and interactive components, and notes that artifacts require Code execution and file creation to be enabled in Claude settings: What are artifacts and how do I use them?.

The most practical plan separates the deliverables by use case. A short volunteer email can stay inline because it is immediate and easy to copy. The public information sheet should be an artifact because staff will revise and reuse it. The animal-release schedule should be structured data, such as CSV, because it is destined for a spreadsheet and should be easy to validate row by row.

questions.question: An online tutoring service's curriculum team is piloting Claude to convert lesson notes into parent updates. After an initial trial, reviewers say the output is "not ready" because some drafts miss required next-step recommendations and some sound too formal, especially for accommodation-related cases. The team wants to improve the workflow without guessing. What is the most appropriate next step?

options.label: A
options.text: Ask Claude to score each draft's quality, and accept drafts with high self-ratings.
options.feedback: Claude-generated grading can be useful only when the grading approach has been tested for reliability. Treating high self-ratings as the decision rule does not address the missing recommendations or tone mismatch in a verifiable way.

options.label: B
options.text: Define measurable pass criteria, add representative edge-case tests, and rerun the prompt.
options.feedback: This is correct because the team has feedback, but it is not yet structured enough to guide reliable improvement. Specific success criteria and realistic eval cases let the team compare prompt changes against the actual failures they care about.

options.label: C
options.text: Rewrite the prompt repeatedly using the same examples, and keep the version that feels strongest.
options.feedback: This is an ad hoc optimization loop that can overfit to a small set of examples. Without measurable criteria and broader tests, the team cannot tell whether the new prompt actually improves the workflow.

options.label: D
options.text: Remove the accommodation-related cases from testing, and optimize the prompt for typical lessons.
options.feedback: Removing difficult but realistic cases makes the evaluation look better without improving the real workflow. Edge cases should be included when they are part of the task distribution and matter to users.

questions.explanation:
When feedback shows uneven results, the next step is to turn that feedback into specific, measurable success criteria and test cases that reflect the real work. Anthropic’s guidance emphasizes starting prompt optimization with defined success criteria, a way to test them, and a first draft prompt, rather than making informal prompt tweaks until something looks better. See Prompt engineering overview and Develop tests.

In this scenario, the failures span more than one dimension: task fidelity, because required recommendations are missing, and tone or style, because some drafts sound too formal. A useful eval set should include ordinary lesson notes and accommodation-related edge cases, since optimizing only for easy examples can hide failures that will appear in production. Tools such as the Console Evaluation workflow can support this iteration by comparing prompt versions across test cases, as described in Evaluation tool. The key mental model is to treat feedback as evidence for a testable improvement loop: define what success means, test against realistic examples, change one approach, and compare results.

questions.question: A renewable energy operations team uses Claude Code to help with maintenance scripts. They keep runbook guidance in CLAUDE.md, but a safety policy requires preventing one specific command from being used even if a future conversation omits the reminder. Which action is most appropriate?

options.label: A
options.text: Implement the restriction with an approved enforcement control outside Claude Code memory.
options.feedback: This is correct because Claude Code memory is loaded as context, not as an enforcement boundary. A separate enforcement control is the appropriate place for a rule that must block behavior rather than merely guide it.

options.label: B
options.text: Add the restriction to CLAUDE.md and rely on startup memory loading.
options.feedback: This is incorrect because CLAUDE.md helps provide persistent context, but it does not force Claude to obey a rule in all circumstances. It is useful for guidance, conventions, and reminders, not for hard safety controls.

options.label: C
options.text: Ask Claude to save the restriction in auto memory for later sessions.
options.feedback: This is incorrect because auto memory is also contextual knowledge rather than an enforcement mechanism. It may help Claude remember preferences, but it is not the right control for blocking a prohibited tool action.

options.label: D
options.text: Place the restriction in the opening prompt for every maintenance chat.
options.feedback: This is incorrect because repeated prompting depends on users remembering to include the instruction. It can reduce mistakes, but it does not meet a requirement that the behavior be blocked even when the reminder is missing.

questions.explanation:
Claude Code memory, including CLAUDE.md and auto memory, is designed to supply persistent context at the start of conversations. That makes it well suited for runbooks, coding conventions, project notes, and preferred workflows, but it is still information that Claude considers while deciding what to do.

When a rule must be enforced regardless of whether Claude follows or even sees a reminder, the control should live outside ordinary memory text. Anthropic documents that behavior which must be blocked regardless of Claude’s decision should use an enforcement mechanism rather than relying on memory. See the official Claude Code memory documentation.

The tradeoff is between guidance and control. Memory keeps helpful knowledge available with low friction, while enforcement controls are better suited to safety-critical restrictions that cannot depend on a reminder being present in the conversation.

questions.question: A regional food bank's operations team asks Claude to analyze a 60-page grant agreement and list reporting obligations. Claude returns a polished checklist with dates, thresholds, and section labels. Before program managers rely on the checklist, what should the reviewer do?

options.label: A
options.text: Request a shorter checklist and treat clearer wording as sufficient validation for managers.
options.feedback: Improving clarity can make the artifact easier to use, but it does not establish that the obligations are correct. Validation requires checking the claims against the grant agreement, not just making the language more concise.

options.label: B
options.text: Approve the checklist after asking Claude to rate its confidence in the listed obligations.
options.feedback: Claude's self-reported confidence is not a reliable substitute for evidence from the source document. A confident answer can still contain fabricated or unsupported details, especially when the output includes specific dates or section labels.

options.label: C
options.text: Regenerate the checklist twice and accept items that appear consistently across the responses.
options.feedback: Consistency across multiple model outputs can be useful as a weak signal, but it does not prove the claims are grounded in the document. The same unsupported obligation could appear repeatedly if the model is relying on a plausible pattern rather than the source.

options.label: D
options.text: Check each obligation against the source agreement, using cited or quoted passages to confirm key details.
options.feedback: This directly validates the factual claims that matter most, such as dates, thresholds, and section references. Citations and quoted evidence help reduce hallucinations, but the reviewer still needs to confirm that the cited source actually supports the checklist item.

questions.explanation:
When Claude produces source-based work with specific obligations, the safest validation step is to compare the claims back to the authoritative material. Anthropic recommends grounding and verification techniques such as requiring citations, asking for word-for-word quotes before analysis for long documents, and retracting claims that lack supporting evidence. These practices reduce hallucinations, but they do not eliminate them, so critical information still needs human review against the source. See Reduce hallucinations.

A good reviewer should treat fluency, confidence, and repeated answers as insufficient evidence. For a repeated workflow, the same principle can be extended into measurable evaluation criteria, such as accuracy of extracted obligations, correct use of context, and privacy preservation, then tested on examples that reflect the real task distribution. Anthropic describes this broader evaluation approach in Define success criteria.

questions.question: A port authority's digital services group is assigning Claude Console access for a governed API pilot. Internal policy says project engineers may create API keys for approved work, finance reviewers may inspect billing only, and access should avoid unnecessary privileges. Which TWO actions align with documented governance controls?

options.label: A
options.text: Keep pilot resources in an existing workspace regardless of membership.
options.feedback: This ignores the role of workspace membership as a governance control. If membership is not reviewed, pilot access may not match the internal least-privilege policy.

options.label: B
options.text: Create a dedicated workspace for pilot API keys, members, and limits.
options.feedback: Workspaces are documented governance boundaries for API keys, members, and resource limits. Using a dedicated workspace supports clearer separation for a governed pilot without relying only on informal tracking.

options.label: C
options.text: Assign the admin role to finance reviewers who only need billing visibility.
options.feedback: The admin role includes broader permissions, including user management. Finance reviewers who only need billing visibility should not receive unnecessary administrative access.

options.label: D
options.text: Assign the developer role to project engineers who need API key access.
options.feedback: The documented developer role includes Workbench access and API key capabilities. This fits engineers who need to work with approved API keys without giving them broader administrative permissions.

questions.explanation:
Governed AI access should follow least privilege: give people the permissions needed for their role, and avoid permissions that create unnecessary risk. In Claude Console, the documented developer role includes Workbench access and API key capabilities, while the admin role includes broader administrative permissions such as user management. That makes developer access a better fit for project engineers than overbroad admin access.

Governance is also about how resources are grouped and reviewed. Workspaces provide boundaries for API keys, members, and resource limits, so a dedicated workspace can help keep a pilot's access and limits distinct from unrelated work. Finance reviewers who only need billing visibility should not be given admin access just to inspect costs. See Anthropic's documentation on organization roles and workspaces.

questions.question: An urban water utility's communications team is using Claude.ai with Code execution and file creation enabled. They have notes from a service interruption. They need a three-sentence update for call-center supervisors today and a more substantial public response kit, including a timeline, FAQ, service-area diagram, and response templates, that staff will revise over several meetings. Which two output requests are most appropriate?

options.label: A
options.text: Request the supervisor update as an artifact for separate-window editing.
options.feedback: This is incorrect because a three-sentence operational update is not substantial standalone content. Using an artifact for very short text adds overhead without improving validation or reuse.

options.label: B
options.text: Request the public response kit as an artifact for iterative review and later reuse.
options.feedback: This is correct because the response kit is substantial, self-contained, and likely to be edited and reused. Those qualities match when Claude should use an artifact in the Claude app or Claude Desktop.

options.label: C
options.text: Request the supervisor update as a concise inline message in the chat.
options.feedback: This is correct because a short same-day update does not need a separate artifact window. Keeping it inline makes it easy to review, copy, and send without adding unnecessary structure.

options.label: D
options.text: Request the public response kit as inline chat text only for later reuse.
options.feedback: This is incorrect because a multi-part kit with a diagram, FAQ, and templates is likely to benefit from a dedicated editable surface. Keeping it only in the chat transcript makes iteration and later reference less convenient.

questions.explanation:
Artifacts are best suited for substantial standalone content that users are likely to edit, iterate on, reuse, or reference later. In this scenario, the public response kit has multiple components and will be revised across meetings, so an artifact is a practical output surface.

Short operational text usually belongs inline in the chat. A three-sentence supervisor update can be reviewed and copied directly, while making it an artifact would add unnecessary workflow friction.

The key judgment is to match the output surface to the job. Claude artifacts are a product experience in Claude, Claude Desktop, and Claude Code, not a universal answer format for every response. Anthropic documents artifact criteria and examples in What are artifacts and how do I use them?, including that artifacts currently require Code execution and file creation to be enabled.

questions.question: A specialty insurance claims analytics team wants to analyze claim notes that include medical details and customer identifiers. The privacy review requires an approved deployment where prompts and responses are not stored at rest after the response is returned, subject to documented exceptions such as legal requirements and automated trust-and-safety flagging. Which TWO actions should the team take before processing the notes?

options.label: A
options.text: Enter the notes first and request deletion in the prompt text.
options.feedback: This is incorrect because prompt instructions are not a substitute for documented retention controls. Sensitive data governance depends on product settings, contractual arrangements, and approved workflows, not on asking the model to apply a retention policy.

options.label: B
options.text: Use only the product surface approved for the required data controls.
options.feedback: This is correct because retention arrangements depend on the specific deployment and supported product surface. A governance review should ensure the team does not move sensitive data into an interface or integration that has not been approved for the required controls.

options.label: C
options.text: Verify the required retention arrangement for the intended Claude deployment.
options.feedback: This is correct because sensitive or regulated data should be handled only after confirming the applicable retention and processing controls. For the Claude API, Zero Data Retention is a documented arrangement, but it must be enabled rather than assumed and remains subject to documented exceptions.

options.label: D
options.text: Assume the retention setting applies to every Claude product automatically.
options.feedback: This is incorrect because documented retention arrangements are not automatically universal across all Claude products and surfaces. Treating one approval as account-wide can create a privacy gap if the team uses a different interface than the one reviewed.

questions.explanation:
For sensitive records, the practical governance move is to confirm the actual deployment controls before any data is entered. Anthropic documents that for the Claude API at api.anthropic.com, Zero Data Retention means customer prompts and responses are not stored at rest after the API response is returned, but it is an enabled arrangement rather than a default assumption.

That retention statement should not be treated as exception-free. Anthropic documents that data may still be retained where required by law or when flagged by automated trust-and-safety systems, so governance reviews should account for those boundaries rather than describing ZDR as an absolute deletion guarantee.

The same privacy requirement can be satisfied or missed depending on where the data is sent. The documented controls for the Claude API do not mean every Claude product surface, third-party integration, or cloud-provider deployment has the same Anthropic-managed retention behavior, so teams should use only the reviewed and approved path.

Asking Claude not to store information in the prompt is an anti-pattern because it confuses model instructions with platform governance. The right mental model is that privacy controls are enforced through the service arrangement and approved workflow, while prompts guide model behavior within that workflow. See Anthropic’s API and data retention documentation for the relevant retention arrangements, scope, and exceptions.

The documented controls for the Claude API do not mean every Claude product surface, third-party integration, or cloud-provider deployment has the same Anthropic-managed retention behavior, so teams should use only the reviewed and approved path.

Asking Claude not to store information in the prompt is an anti-pattern because it confuses model instructions with platform governance. The right mental model is that privacy controls are enforced through the service arrangement and approved workflow, while prompts guide model behavior within that workflow. See Anthropic’s API and data retention documentation for the relevant retention arrangements, scope, and exceptions.

questions.question: A university admissions office is piloting Claude to condense scholarship applications into eligibility notes for committee review. Reviewers find most notes readable, but they worry that omitted constraints or misread achievements could affect decisions. What is the most appropriate next step before using the notes routinely?

options.label: A
options.text: Define measurable review criteria, then test representative and edge-case notes against the source applications.
options.feedback: This is the best way to evaluate whether the notes are accurate and complete for the real workflow. It uses measurable criteria and checks both common cases and edge cases against the materials Claude was asked to summarize.

options.label: B
options.text: Accept notes that include citations, then review only the applications chosen for final awards.
options.feedback: Citations can help reviewers trace claims to source passages, but they do not automatically prove that every inference is correct or that nothing important was omitted. Reviewing only final-award applications also misses failures in rejected or borderline cases.

options.label: C
options.text: Review several typical applications manually, then defer unusual cases until errors appear.
options.feedback: Checking only typical examples can make the workflow look safer than it is. Evaluation should mirror the real task distribution and include edge cases before the output is relied on routinely.

options.label: D
options.text: Ask Claude to score each note’s reliability, then approve notes above a chosen threshold.
options.feedback: A self-assigned reliability score is not enough to validate factual accuracy or completeness. LLM-based grading can be useful, but it needs a clear rubric and should be tested for reliability before being used at scale.

questions.explanation:
For evaluating Claude-generated summaries, the core practice is to turn quality concerns into specific and measurable criteria, then test outputs against the original source material. Anthropic’s evaluation guidance emphasizes success criteria that are specific, measurable, achievable, and relevant, and it recommends eval sets that reflect the real-world task distribution rather than only easy or typical examples. See Define success criteria.

Readable or polished text is not the same as verified accuracy. Claude can produce text that is factually incorrect or inconsistent with the provided context, so critical information should still be validated against authoritative sources. Anthropic’s hallucination guidance describes techniques such as grounding in quotes and requiring citations, but notes that these reduce rather than eliminate hallucinations. See Reduce hallucinations.

Citations are useful for traceability, because they point back to supporting passages in provided documents, but they are not an automatic truth oracle for completeness or reasoning quality. A practical admissions review should therefore combine source-based checking with representative and edge-case examples, especially where omissions or misread details could change a decision.
