questions.question: A renewable energy cooperative's support team wants Claude to turn technician visit notes into customer-facing outage explanations. Early demos vary: some are clear, some omit safety caveats, and some take too long. The lead wants to know whether the workflow is ready and whether to adjust the prompt or model. Which two actions should the team take next?

options.label: A
options.text: Use the most capable model for all notes and treat remaining failures mainly as prompt wording issues.
options.feedback: This is incorrect because the most capable model is not automatically the right fit for every workflow. Latency and cost concerns may require model selection tradeoffs, and not every failure is best addressed through prompting.

options.label: B
options.text: Define measurable acceptance criteria covering factual fidelity, required safety caveats, customer tone, privacy handling, latency, and cost.
options.feedback: This is correct because the team needs clear success criteria before deciding whether the workflow is ready. The criteria should cover multiple dimensions, not just whether a sample explanation sounds polished.

options.label: C
options.text: Test the draft workflow on representative technician notes, including routine outages, ambiguous causes, and unusual safety-sensitive cases.
options.feedback: This is correct because evaluation should reflect the real distribution of tasks the workflow will handle. Including edge cases helps reveal failures that a small set of favorable demos could miss.

options.label: D
options.text: Rewrite the prompt around the best demo outputs and approve the workflow after stakeholders prefer the new wording.
options.feedback: This is incorrect because preferred wording from a few demos is not an empirical readiness test. It also risks optimizing for surface style while missing factual, safety, privacy, latency, or cost requirements.

questions.explanation:
For a workflow like customer-facing outage explanations, the first design step is to translate the use case into measurable success criteria. Anthropic's Prompt engineering overview emphasizes starting with clear criteria, ways to test against them, and a first-draft prompt before spending time on prompt engineering.

Good evaluation is usually multidimensional: task fidelity, consistency, tone, privacy preservation, context use, latency, and price can all matter at the same time. The Define success criteria guidance also recommends test cases that mirror the real task distribution, including edge cases, rather than relying on a few impressive demos.

In practice, this means the cooperative should test routine notes, ambiguous notes, and safety-sensitive notes against stated acceptance criteria. Prompt edits may still be useful, but they should be driven by measured failures. If the issue is response time or cost, choosing a different model may be a better lever than repeatedly rewriting the prompt.

questions.question: A performing arts venue's operations team wants to use Claude to draft nightly incident summaries from usher notes, maintenance photos, and manager updates. The executive director asks how to describe the rollout to department heads. What message should the associate give?

options.label: A
options.text: Present Claude as a task-support tool, choose the model and capabilities for the workflow, and review important facts before distribution.
options.feedback: This sets realistic expectations by framing Claude as support for drafting and synthesis rather than an authority that guarantees correctness. It also reflects that Claude capabilities vary by model and that stakeholder-facing outputs should be checked for factual accuracy.

options.label: B
options.text: Present Claude as an autonomous operator, let it resolve incident details, and treat generated summaries as final reports.
options.feedback: This incorrectly suggests Claude can independently determine operational truth and finalize reports without oversight. Claude can assist with synthesis, but it can still generate inaccurate or unsupported content.

options.label: C
options.text: Present Claude as a records system, rely on it to preserve every update, and skip separate review when notes are complete.
options.feedback: This mischaracterizes Claude as a system of record rather than a tool that works from the context and inputs provided. Complete notes can improve the task, but they do not remove the need to validate important facts.

options.label: D
options.text: Present Claude as a universal expert, use the same model for all work, and publish summaries when the tone sounds confident.
options.feedback: This overstates Claude's role and ignores differences among models, such as latency, context windows, pricing, and supported capabilities. A confident style is not a reliable signal that the summary is accurate.

questions.explanation:
Claude is most valuable when stakeholders understand it as a workflow assistant that can draft, summarize, analyze, and transform information, not as a replacement for judgment or authoritative records. Anthropic’s models differ in capabilities and tradeoffs, so the rollout message should connect the selected model and enabled capabilities to the venue’s actual work rather than treating “Claude” as one undifferentiated capability. See the official models overview.

The key limitation to communicate is that Claude can produce fluent but incorrect or unsupported statements. Anthropic’s guidance on reducing hallucinations explains that grounding, uncertainty, quotes, and citations can reduce hallucinations, but they do not eliminate them. For operational summaries that may affect staffing, safety follow-up, or executive decisions, important claims should be checked against source notes, photos, logs, or responsible staff before being shared.

questions.question: A regional architecture studio is configuring Claude for proposal coordinators who draft responses to many different bid opportunities. The studio wants consistent voice, fixed proposal sections, and a rule that Claude must not claim experience unless it appears in provided materials. Each bid has different RFP requirements, deadlines, and client priorities. How should the studio write the system-level instructions?

options.label: A
options.text: Use a brief instruction to write persuasive proposals; let Claude infer missing qualifications from context.
options.feedback: This instruction is too vague to reliably enforce the studio’s voice, structure, or evidence boundary. Letting Claude infer missing qualifications creates a risk of unsupported claims.

options.label: B
options.text: Prioritize the strongest marketing claims in the instructions; check source support only after drafting.
options.feedback: This encourages Claude to optimize for persuasion before grounding claims in provided materials. For proposal work, source boundaries should guide drafting from the start, not be treated as a later cleanup step.

options.label: C
options.text: Paste all current RFP details into the standing instructions; replace them whenever a new bid starts.
options.feedback: This treats system-level instructions as a storage place for changing task data. It increases maintenance burden and makes it easier for outdated bid details to influence later work.

options.label: D
options.text: Define the studio voice, evidence boundary, and standard section headings; provide each RFP’s facts separately.
options.feedback: This keeps stable behavioral guidance in the system-level instructions while leaving changing bid details in the prompt or supporting materials. It also gives Claude clear constraints for style, structure, and evidence use across many conversations.

questions.explanation:
Effective system-level instructions should describe durable operating behavior: role, tone, boundaries, formatting expectations, and source-use rules. They are not the best place for facts that change from task to task, such as a specific RFP’s deadlines, scoring criteria, or client priorities.

Anthropic’s guidance on system prompts emphasizes using them to give Claude a clear role and context that improves performance across a task pattern, while the user prompt supplies the immediate request and materials. See Use system prompts.

The practical tradeoff is maintainability and reliability. Stable instructions help Claude behave consistently, but variable facts should remain close to the current task so they can be updated, cited, and checked without contaminating future work.

questions.question: A wildlife conservation nonprofit is planning two Claude workflows: daily triage of thousands of short ranger notes, and a monthly synthesis of ambiguous ecological, policy, and donor documents for leadership. The team has a limited budget, but the monthly synthesis matters more for quality than speed. Which two choices best align model selection with the task requirements?

options.label: A
options.text: Start the monthly synthesis on Claude Sonnet 5, then adjust effort upward if quality is insufficient.
options.feedback: This fits a task that needs stronger reasoning while still respecting budget and turnaround. Sonnet 5 is documented as the best combination of speed and intelligence, and effort can be used as a separate lever on recent Sonnet and Opus models before switching models.

options.label: B
options.text: Select Claude Fable 5 for both workflows so the same advanced model handles every request.
options.feedback: This overuses a model positioned for next-generation intelligence in long-running agents. It ignores the daily triage workload’s speed and cost priorities, where a faster, lower-cost model is the better fit.

options.label: C
options.text: Select Claude Opus 4.8 for the daily triage to maximize reasoning quality on every note.
options.feedback: This overprioritizes reasoning quality for a short, high-volume task where speed and cost matter most. Opus 4.8 is positioned for complex agentic coding and enterprise work, so it is not the best default for simple triage.

options.label: D
options.text: Select Claude Haiku 4.5 for the short daily triage where speed and low cost matter most.
options.feedback: This matches the routine, high-volume part of the workload. Claude Haiku 4.5 is documented as the fastest current model with near-frontier intelligence, and it has substantially lower listed pricing than the larger models.

questions.explanation:
Good model selection starts by matching the workload to the tradeoff among capability, latency, and cost. The daily ranger-note triage is short, repetitive, and high volume, so a fast, lower-cost model is a better fit than defaulting to a more capable model for every request.

For the monthly synthesis, the task has more ambiguity and higher quality expectations, but the team still has a budget constraint. Claude Sonnet 5 is documented as offering the best combination of speed and intelligence, and Anthropic’s model-selection guidance treats effort as a separate control that can trade more reasoning for additional latency and cost within supported recent models.

The anti-pattern is treating model choice as a single “always use the strongest model” decision. That can waste budget and slow down simple work without producing meaningful quality gains, while also missing the practical middle ground of choosing a balanced model and raising effort only when the task warrants it. See Anthropic’s Choosing the right model, Models overview, and Pricing documentation for the underlying model-positioning and cost tradeoffs.

questions.question: A university advancement office on a Claude Team plan is coordinating grant reviews over several weeks. Staff will ask separate questions about the same funder guidelines and budget template, and most reviewers should be able to use the materials without changing them. Which feature choice best fits this work?

options.label: A
options.text: Use a regular chat and upload the funder files again whenever each reviewer starts a new thread.
options.feedback: A regular chat can work for one-off or single-thread work, but it does not provide reusable context across separate conversations. Re-uploading the same files creates avoidable setup work and does not address shared access control.

options.label: B
options.text: Create an artifact containing the guidelines and ask each reviewer to refer to it manually.
options.feedback: An artifact may be useful for drafting or presenting content, but it is not the persistent workspace mechanism for shared project context. It also does not provide the documented Project permission model for using versus editing shared materials.

options.label: C
options.text: Start Research so Claude can investigate public sources before every reviewer asks questions.
options.feedback: Research is meant for multi-source investigation, especially when Claude needs to search and build on findings. Here the relevant materials are already known internal files, so repeated investigation is not the main need.

options.label: D
options.text: Create a shared Project with the materials in Project Knowledge and grant most reviewers Can use access.
options.feedback: This is the best fit because the work spans multiple chats and depends on reusable source materials. On Team and Enterprise plans, shared Projects can give members access to project contents while limiting editing through permission levels.

questions.explanation:
Use a Project when work depends on the same background materials across multiple separate chats. Project Knowledge is designed for reusable context inside a self-contained workspace, while project instructions and uploaded knowledge apply to chats in that project. See What are projects? and How can I create and manage projects?.

Research is also not the right default here because the key need is not agentic public-source investigation, it is consistent use of known documents.

questions.question: A heritage museum's collections team is planning a Claude pilot to create bilingual draft exhibit labels from curator notes, object images, and archival excerpts. The museum director asks which two points should be included in the stakeholder briefing so curators understand Claude's value and limitations. Which two points should the associate include?

options.label: A
options.text: Require curator review of factual claims, translations, and source references before publication.
options.feedback: This is correct because Claude can generate fluent text that is factually incorrect or inconsistent with supplied context. Review is especially important for public-facing museum content where dates, attributions, translations, and citations matter.

options.label: B
options.text: Describe Claude as an assistant whose results depend on the selected model and available capabilities.
options.feedback: This is correct because Claude's value is not a single uniform capability across every use case. Different current models and capabilities can affect suitability for multilingual work, image input, latency, output length, and cost.

options.label: C
options.text: Present Claude as a single capability that performs the same regardless of model choice.
options.feedback: This is incorrect because model choice matters for practical workflow expectations. Treating Claude as one undifferentiated capability can lead stakeholders to misunderstand tradeoffs such as cost, latency, context window, and supported capabilities.

options.label: D
options.text: Promise that citations and source excerpts make curator review unnecessary before publication.
options.feedback: This is incorrect because grounding and citations can reduce hallucinations but do not eliminate them. Public-facing or high-stakes factual content still needs validation against authoritative sources.

questions.explanation:
When communicating Claude's role to stakeholders, frame it as a workflow accelerator, not as an automatic authority. Claude can help transform notes, images, and excerpts into useful drafts, and current Claude models support capabilities such as text and image input, text output, multilingual capabilities, and vision, but those capabilities vary by model and practical tradeoffs such as latency, cost, context window, and output length. See Anthropic's models overview for the model-specific framing.

The limitation message is equally important: Claude can hallucinate. Grounding outputs in provided sources, asking for uncertainty, and using quotes or citations can reduce factual errors, but they do not make review optional. Anthropic's guidance on reducing hallucinations emphasizes validation for critical information, which applies to exhibit labels that may include dates, attributions, provenance, translations, or cultural context.

The strongest stakeholder message balances enthusiasm with boundaries: use Claude to speed up drafting, synthesis, and iteration, then keep human review in the publication workflow. Overpromising that one generic version of Claude always behaves the same, or that citations remove the need for review, creates operational risk and undermines trust when the system's real design is probabilistic and model-dependent.

questions.question: A regional veterinary network's clinical education team is setting up a Claude Project on a Team plan. They want staff veterinarians to draft client-facing discharge notes using the same clinical protocol files and the same response rules, but only the education leads should be able to change those files or rules. Which setup is most appropriate?

options.label: A
options.text: Add the protocol files to project knowledge, save the response rules as project instructions, and share the project with staff as Can edit.
options.feedback: This would make the common knowledge and instructions available, but it gives staff more permission than the scenario requires. Can edit allows members to modify project instructions and knowledge, which conflicts with keeping those changes limited to education leads.

options.label: B
options.text: Add the protocol files to project knowledge, save the response rules as project instructions, and share the project with staff as Can use.
options.feedback: This uses the project features for their intended roles: knowledge sources provide persistent reference material, and project instructions guide behavior across chats. Sharing with Can use lets staff view and chat in the project without editing the knowledge or instructions.

options.label: C
options.text: Attach the protocol files in the first project chat, write the response rules in that chat, and share the project with staff as Can use.
options.feedback: Ordinary chat context is not shared across separate chats in a project unless the information is added to project knowledge. This setup may help one chat, but it does not reliably configure the project for every staff member's future chats.

options.label: D
options.text: Put the protocol summary in the project description, save the response rules in the project name, and share the project with staff as Can use.
options.feedback: A project's name and description help people manage the workspace, but they are not context that Claude uses in chats. This would not reliably provide the clinical protocols or response rules to Claude when staff draft discharge notes.

questions.explanation:
For this scenario, the clean separation is to put reusable source material in project knowledge and put persistent behavior guidance in project instructions. Project knowledge is designed to carry files and reference content across chats inside the same project, while project instructions tell Claude how to behave or respond throughout that project. See What are projects? and How can I create and manage projects?.

The permission choice matters because the team wants broad use without broad editing. On Team and Enterprise plans, Can use lets members see project contents, knowledge, and instructions and chat within the project, while Can edit lets members modify the project knowledge and instructions. Putting important guidance in a normal chat or in the project name or description is a common configuration mistake, since chat context is not automatically shared across project chats and the name and description are not context for Claude.

questions.question: A municipal transit planning team wants Claude to turn a large rider survey export, service disruption notes, and three sample board memo excerpts into a concise memo with themes, evidence, contradictions, and recommended next steps. Which two prompting approaches best decompose the request for reliable execution?

options.label: A
options.text: Place the source materials first, then give a numbered workflow for extracting themes, checking contradictions, drafting recommendations, and writing the memo.
options.feedback: This is correct because complex tasks work better when the materials and execution steps are clearly separated and ordered. A numbered workflow makes completeness and sequence explicit instead of relying on Claude to infer the intended process.

options.label: B
options.text: Separate the context, instructions, examples, and final request with descriptive XML-style tags, and wrap the memo samples as structured examples.
options.feedback: This is correct because XML-style tags help Claude parse complex prompts that mix different kinds of information. Structured examples can steer the memo format, tone, and organization more reliably than informal references to samples.

options.label: C
options.text: Combine all documents into one continuous block, then ask Claude to infer the analysis steps and memo format from the content.
options.feedback: This is incorrect because it leaves the task structure implied rather than explicit. Claude may still produce a useful answer, but the approach increases the chance of missed steps, weak formatting, or inconsistent treatment of evidence.

options.label: D
options.text: Request a polished memo immediately, then use follow-up prompts only if themes, evidence, or contradictions are missing.
options.feedback: This is incorrect because it treats decomposition as an after-the-fact repair process. Follow-up refinement can help, but it is less reliable than structuring the initial request so Claude knows the required subtasks before drafting.

questions.explanation:
For complex work, Claude performs best when the prompt makes the work plan visible. Breaking the request into ordered subtasks, such as extract themes, compare against disruption notes, identify contradictions, then draft recommendations, helps Claude execute the full assignment rather than optimizing only for a polished final memo.

Structure also matters when a prompt contains several types of material. Anthropic documents using descriptive XML-style tags to separate instructions, context, examples, and inputs, and recommends structured examples when steering format, tone, or organization. See Anthropic prompt engineering guidance.

Putting source material before the query is especially useful for large inputs because Claude can process the evidence before receiving the specific task. By contrast, asking Claude to infer the process from one pasted block or fixing omissions through follow-up prompts can work sometimes, but it makes the initial result less predictable and puts more review burden on the user.

questions.question: A telehealth scheduling team wants Claude to classify incoming appointment messages by request type and draft one-sentence replies while patients are waiting. The task is repetitive, inputs are short, and unusual cases will be escalated to staff. Which model-selection approach best fits this workload?

options.label: A
options.text: Use Claude Sonnet 5 with maximum effort for all messages to deepen every response.
options.feedback: Sonnet 5 is a strong balance of speed and intelligence, but maximum effort increases thoroughness at the expense of latency and token use. The task calls for brief, fast, routine responses, not deeper analysis on every message.

options.label: B
options.text: Use Claude Fable 5 for all messages to support long-running agent work.
options.feedback: Fable 5 is positioned for next-generation intelligence in long-running agents, which is not the stated need here. Using it for simple, short scheduling replies would add unnecessary cost and latency for this workload.

options.label: C
options.text: Use Claude Opus 4.8 for all messages to maximize complex enterprise reasoning.
options.feedback: Opus 4.8 is better aligned with complex agentic coding and enterprise work than with routine message classification. Choosing it for every short reply would overfit the model to a level of reasoning the task does not require.

options.label: D
options.text: Use Claude Haiku 4.5 for the routine classifications and short drafts.
options.feedback: This matches a high-volume, time-sensitive workload where speed and cost matter more than deep reasoning. Haiku 4.5 is positioned as the fastest current Claude model with near-frontier intelligence, making it a good fit for straightforward short outputs.

questions.explanation:
Good model selection starts by matching the workload to the tradeoff among capability, speed, and cost. For repetitive classification and one-sentence drafting, the value comes from fast turnaround and economical scaling, not from the deepest available reasoning.

Anthropic’s model overview describes Claude Haiku 4.5 as the fastest model with near-frontier intelligence, while positioning models such as Fable 5 and Opus 4.8 for more demanding long-running or complex work. See the official models overview and Choosing the right model guidance.

Effort is also a useful lever on supported models, but higher effort trades more thoroughness for higher latency and token use. In this scenario, escalating unusual cases to staff allows the routine path to prioritize a faster, lower-cost model while reserving heavier reasoning for work that actually needs it.

questions.question: A public radio newsroom's production team is using Claude Desktop with Code execution and file creation enabled. They have interview notes, sponsor-read requirements, segment ideas, and a production checklist for a new series. The output will be revised during planning meetings and reused as a standing reference. Which output request is most appropriate?

options.label: A
options.text: Request a compact spreadsheet-style table, such as rows for each interview note.
options.feedback: A table can be useful when the main goal is to extract structured fields for sorting or pasting elsewhere. The scenario calls for a reusable planning resource with narrative sections and checklists, not just a compact data grid.

options.label: B
options.text: Request a brief inline chat response, such as a paragraph summary of the notes.
options.feedback: An inline response is better for short, one-time answers or quick summaries. It does not fit as well when the team needs a substantial reference document that will be revised during meetings.

options.label: C
options.text: Request a substantial editable artifact, such as a Markdown episode-planning board.
options.feedback: This fits content that is self-contained, reusable, and likely to be edited over multiple rounds. An artifact gives the team a dedicated workspace separate from the chat for a planning asset they will reference later.

options.label: D
options.text: Request a compact JSON block, such as fields for quotes and segment names.
options.feedback: JSON is useful when downstream systems need machine-readable structured data. It is not the best primary format for a collaborative planning document that people will revise and read as a standing reference.

questions.explanation:
Claude uses artifacts for substantial, standalone content that is likely to be edited, reused, or referenced later. Anthropic describes artifacts as a dedicated window separate from the main chat, with common examples including Markdown documents, diagrams, single-page HTML, and interactive components. See What are artifacts and how do I use them?.

The practical judgment is to match the output surface to the job. A short inline answer is efficient for a quick summary, and tables or JSON are useful when the primary need is compact structured data. For a multi-part planning resource that humans will revise and reuse, an artifact gives a better working surface than a transient chat message or machine-oriented data block.

The scenario also states that Code execution and file creation is enabled, which matters because artifacts currently require that capability in Claude app and Claude Desktop. That prerequisite does not make every output an artifact, but it removes a setup blocker when the content otherwise meets the artifact criteria.

questions.question: An employment law firm's case intake team wants to test Claude on confidential witness interview excerpts. Their privacy requirement is that prompts and responses not be stored at rest after each response is returned. The team plans to use a faster testing interface that has not been reviewed for this requirement. What should they do before using the excerpts?

options.label: A
options.text: Paste the excerpts after instructing Claude not to retain the content.
options.feedback: This is incorrect because prompt instructions do not change service-level data-handling controls. The team still needs an approved workflow that satisfies the privacy requirement before processing the excerpts.

options.label: B
options.text: Proceed with short excerpts because the activity is only a preliminary test.
options.feedback: This is incorrect because confidentiality and retention requirements can apply even during testing. Using smaller samples may reduce exposure, but it does not address whether the workflow meets the stated privacy requirement.

options.label: C
options.text: Use the faster testing interface after deleting the visible conversation history.
options.feedback: This is incorrect because removing a conversation from a visible history does not prove that the required data-handling arrangement applies. It also does not substitute for confirming whether the tool is approved for confidential material.

options.label: D
options.text: Verify the approved data-handling arrangement and use only an approved workflow.
options.feedback: This is correct because confidential excerpts should be processed only through a workflow that has been reviewed against the team's privacy requirement. Different Claude offerings and deployment paths can have different data-handling controls, so the team should confirm the arrangement before entering the data.

questions.explanation:
For sensitive legal material, the governance decision should start with the data requirement, not convenience. If the requirement is that prompts and responses are not stored at rest after each response is returned, the team should confirm that the selected Claude workflow is covered by an appropriate data-handling arrangement before entering the excerpts.

Anthropic documents data-handling arrangements for the Claude API, including Zero Data Retention, and explains that controls vary by offering and deployment path. The practical point for a foundation-level user is not to memorize every boundary, but to recognize that an unreviewed interface should not be assumed to meet a confidential-data requirement. See API and data retention.

Deleting visible history, using a short sample, or adding a prompt such as do not retain this may feel safer, but none of those actions verifies the underlying retention control. For regulated or confidential content, the safest approach is to use the organization’s approved workflow or get the workflow reviewed before processing the data.

questions.question: A regional food bank's volunteer coordination team asks Claude to summarize shift feedback and identify causes of cancellations. Claude says student volunteers are unreliable because several notes mention exam week, but the uploaded notes also show full-time workers canceling for scheduling conflicts and do not ask for volunteer age or student status. Before using the summary to adjust recruitment, what is the most appropriate action?

options.label: A
options.text: Choose the most detailed rerun, keep its group findings, and use it for planning.
options.feedback: Running the prompt again can reveal inconsistent outputs, but detail is not evidence of accuracy. Anthropic describes inconsistent outputs as possible hallucination signals, not as a reason to accept the most polished answer.

options.label: B
options.text: Add an AI-generated disclaimer, keep the cancellation analysis, and proceed with recruitment changes.
options.feedback: A disclaimer does not correct an unsupported conclusion or make it appropriate for decision-making. The team still needs to validate the claim against the source notes before acting on it.

options.label: C
options.text: Check the notes for quoted support, remove unsupported group claims, and revise the summary.
options.feedback: This addresses both the inconsistency with the source material and the unsupported generalization about a group. Requiring support from the provided notes helps distinguish grounded findings from claims Claude may have inferred or fabricated.

options.label: D
options.text: Ask Claude to soften the language, keep the same group claims, and share the summary.
options.feedback: Softer wording may reduce how biased the summary sounds, but it does not validate whether the claim is supported. Keeping the same group claim preserves the underlying factual and fairness problem.

questions.explanation:
Claude can produce content that is factually incorrect or inconsistent with the given context, even when the response sounds plausible. In this scenario, the conclusion about student volunteers is not grounded in the provided feedback because the notes do not establish student status as a measured category and similar cancellation reasons appear across other groups.

A practical validation step is to require source-grounded evidence, such as word-for-word quotes or citations for the claim, and to retract or revise statements that cannot be supported. Anthropic specifically recommends allowing Claude to say I don’t know, requiring citations for claims, and instructing Claude to retract claims it cannot support with a quote as hallucination-reduction techniques.

Rephrasing the claim, choosing a more detailed rerun, or adding a disclaimer all fall short because they do not test whether the output matches the evidence. For guidance on hallucination reduction and inconsistency checks, see Anthropic’s documentation on Reduce hallucinations.

questions.question: An actuarial consulting team uses Claude during live pricing reviews. Analysts often bring hundreds of routine policy-description classifications to the meeting, even though most are not needed immediately. The volume crowds out discussion of edge cases and makes the review run long. Which action would best optimize this workflow?

options.label: A
options.text: Use the most capable model for every routine classification by default.
options.feedback: This is incorrect because routine classifications do not necessarily require the highest-capability option. Choosing the most capable model for all work can increase cost and latency without addressing the meeting workflow problem.

options.label: B
options.text: Ask Claude to skip documenting uncertainty to finish the review faster.
options.feedback: This is incorrect because removing uncertainty notes may make the workflow faster at the expense of review quality. For actuarial classification work, uncertainty is often exactly what should be surfaced for human attention.

options.label: C
options.text: Process routine classifications offline and reserve the live review for edge cases.
options.feedback: This is correct because routine work that does not require an immediate answer is a good candidate for an offline workflow. Keeping the live session focused on edge cases improves efficiency without removing human review where it matters most.

options.label: D
options.text: Run every classification live so reviewers can see each response immediately.
options.feedback: This is incorrect because the scenario states that most routine classifications are not needed immediately. Keeping all work in the live meeting preserves the bottleneck and leaves less time for judgment-heavy discussion.

questions.explanation:
Workflow optimization with Claude often starts by separating work that needs interactive judgment from work that can be completed outside the live session. In this scenario, the routine classifications are high volume and mostly not needed immediately, while the edge cases benefit from discussion and human review. Moving the routine work offline reduces meeting load and lets analysts use Claude where it adds the most value during the review.

questions.question: A specialty pharmacy's operations team is redesigning its prior authorization handoff process. The team has denial logs and staff notes, and leaders want the plan to account for payer policy bulletins that may have changed recently. Claude has web search enabled. What is the most appropriate way to use Claude?

options.label: A
options.text: Ask Claude to draft the workflow from general knowledge, then add citations after approval.
options.feedback: General model knowledge may be outdated for changing payer policies. Adding citations after the plan is approved does not validate that the recommendations were based on current, relevant sources.

options.label: B
options.text: Ask Claude to search payer sources first, then ignore the logs to avoid conflicting signals.
options.feedback: Current web sources can help with changing external requirements, but they do not replace the team's own evidence about where handoffs fail. Ignoring the logs would weaken the process optimization work by dropping the most relevant operational context.

options.label: C
options.text: Ask Claude to analyze only the logs, then infer recent payer changes from denial patterns.
options.feedback: Internal logs can reveal process pain points, but they are not a reliable source for current payer policy details. Inferring recent changes without checking sources increases the risk of building the workflow around mistaken assumptions.

options.label: D
options.text: Ask Claude to analyze the logs, search current payer sources with citations, and draft workflow changes.
options.feedback: This uses Claude for both internal process analysis and current research. Because payer policy bulletins may have changed recently, web search with cited sources is the right way to ground those parts of the plan.

questions.explanation:
For planning and process optimization, Claude is most useful when you give it the local evidence that explains the current workflow and ask it to research only the parts that depend on current information. In this scenario, denial logs and staff notes help Claude identify bottlenecks, while recent payer policy bulletins are the kind of changing information that should be checked against current sources.

Anthropic documents that web search gives Claude access to real-time web content beyond its knowledge cutoff and returns cited sources, and that Claude should search when a request depends on current, changing, or out-of-training-data information. See the official Web search tool documentation. The practical tradeoff is that search grounds volatile facts, but the user's own documents still provide the organization-specific context needed to make the redesigned workflow useful.

questions.question: An architecture studio's research team uses a Team plan and has an Owner-enabled Google Workspace connector setup. A researcher can add the same Google Doc in a private chat, but the Drive option is unavailable when the team tries to add it to a shared Claude Project for everyone to use. What is the most appropriate next step?

options.label: A
options.text: Ask the Owner to re-enable Google Workspace connectors for the organization.
options.feedback: The scenario already shows the connector works in a private chat, so organization-level enablement is not the likely issue. Re-enabling the connector would not make Google Drive additions available in shared projects.

options.label: B
options.text: Upload an exported copy of the document to the shared project knowledge.
options.feedback: This works around the project sharing limitation while still making the content available in the shared project. It gives up live Google Drive syncing, so the team should refresh the uploaded copy when the source changes.

options.label: C
options.text: Change Claude's tool access mode from Auto to Always available.
options.feedback: Tool access mode controls when connector tools are loaded into a conversation. It does not change whether Google Drive files can be added to a shared project's knowledge area.

options.label: D
options.text: Have each team member authenticate to Google Drive before reopening the project.
options.feedback: Individual authentication is required for connector use, but it does not override project-level availability. The disabled Drive option is tied to the shared project context, not simply missing user authentication.

questions.explanation:
Google Workspace connectors can make Google Drive content available to Claude, but connector capabilities still depend on where they are being used. The Google Workspace connector documentation states that Google Drive files can be added to projects only for private projects, and the option is disabled for shared projects. See Use Google Workspace connectors.

For a shared Claude Project, the practical choice is to place the material into project knowledge through supported uploads or pasted content, accepting that this is not the same as a live synced Google Doc. The team should manage version updates deliberately, because Google Docs added through Drive sync stay current only in supported contexts. Changing tool loading behavior or repeating organization-level connector setup does not alter this project sharing constraint. The mental model is that Projects manage persistent workspace knowledge, while connectors provide permissioned access to external sources within the boundaries Claude supports.

questions.question: A community college financial aid office uses Claude to rewrite scholarship eligibility rules into email responses for first-generation applicants. The drafts are factually accurate, but some use policy jargon and others miss the supportive tone advisors want. The team needs to choose a prompt revision before using it broadly. What is the most appropriate action?

options.label: A
options.text: Make the prompt less specific, let Claude choose the tone each time, and edit awkward replies afterward.
options.feedback: Removing specificity usually makes audience adaptation less consistent, especially when tone and formatting matter. Manual cleanup after the fact can catch some issues, but it does not create a dependable process for choosing the better prompt.

options.label: B
options.text: Define measurable audience criteria, add a few model replies as examples, and compare prompt versions on representative cases.
options.feedback: This is the best approach because it evaluates the outputs against the audience needs, not just general writing quality. Specific criteria, examples, and side-by-side prompt comparison help the team refine tone, clarity, and structure in a repeatable way.

options.label: C
options.text: Ask Claude to identify the best prompt, accept its overall preference, and avoid separate reviewer criteria.
options.feedback: Claude’s preference can be useful as input, but an undefined “best” judgment is too vague for reliable validation. The team still needs explicit success criteria tied to clarity, tone, and usefulness for the audience.

options.label: D
options.text: Choose the most polished single draft, reuse its wording as a template, and skip broader comparison cases.
options.feedback: A single polished draft may not represent the range of applicant questions the office will receive. Skipping broader comparison makes it harder to know whether the prompt works consistently for the intended audience.

questions.explanation:
For audience adaptation, the useful mental model is that a prompt revision should be judged against explicit success criteria, not against a general impression that one version “sounds better.” Criteria such as plain-language clarity, supportive tone, policy accuracy, and next-step usefulness are more actionable than a vague goal like “good emails.” Anthropic’s eval guidance emphasizes making success criteria specific, measurable, achievable, and relevant, and it notes that many use cases need multidimensional evaluation: Define your success criteria.

Examples are especially helpful when adapting style for an intended audience. Providing several representative examples can steer format, tone, and structure more reliably than simply telling Claude to “be supportive” or “avoid jargon.” Anthropic’s prompting guidance recommends clear instructions, useful context, format constraints, and examples, often 3 to 5 examples for best results: Claude 4 best practices.

When the team has multiple prompt revisions, comparing them on representative cases is stronger than choosing from one favorite output. The Claude Console Evaluation tool supports side-by-side comparison, quality grading, and prompt versioning so teams can rerun a test suite after edits: Use the Evaluation tool. This workflow makes refinement practical because it turns subjective disagreement into a structured review of how well each version serves the actual readers.

questions.question: An animal welfare nonprofit's adoption team uses Claude to turn veterinary intake notes into public pet profiles. The profiles are factually accurate, but some sound too clinical while others make overly confident claims about an animal's future behavior. The team needs to refine the prompt before publishing profiles. What is the most appropriate action?

options.label: A
options.text: Keep the current prompt unchanged, then ask reviewers to manually soften any clinical wording before publication.
options.feedback: Manual cleanup may catch some issues, but it does not improve the prompt or create a repeatable standard. It also leaves reviewers without clear criteria for handling tone and behavioral claims consistently.

options.label: B
options.text: Select the profile draft that sounds most engaging, then use that wording pattern for all future profiles.
options.feedback: Choosing a single appealing draft can overlook accuracy, consistency, and audience fit across varied cases. A one-off example is not enough evidence that the prompt will behave reliably.

options.label: C
options.text: Add instructions that tell Claude not to sound clinical and not to exaggerate, then publish the next outputs.
options.feedback: Negative instructions alone are a weaker way to steer style than explicit guidance about what the output should do. Publishing without comparing revised outputs against criteria does not validate that the change solved the problem.

options.label: D
options.text: Define audience-specific success criteria, add clear tone guidance and examples, then compare prompt versions on representative cases.
options.feedback: This approach addresses both adaptation and validation. It gives Claude explicit guidance for tone and structure, then tests whether revisions work for the intended audience across realistic inputs.

questions.explanation:
When the issue is not factual accuracy alone but audience fit, the refinement process should make the desired reader experience explicit. Useful success criteria might include warmth, plain language, careful uncertainty around behavior, and preservation of the medical facts that adopters need.

Anthropic's prompting guidance emphasizes clear instructions, concrete format constraints, relevant context, and examples, with examples being a reliable way to steer format, tone, and structure. See Prompting best practices.

For validation, Anthropic's evaluation guidance recommends specific, measurable, relevant criteria rather than vague goals such as "good writing." The Console Evaluation tool can support this kind of refinement through prompt versioning, side-by-side comparison, and quality grading, as described in Using the Evaluation Tool and Define success criteria and build evaluations.

questions.question: A maritime insurance broker's claims analytics team wants Claude to review adjuster notes, summarize coverage issues, and draft internal negotiation briefs each day. The work is recurring and business-critical, but it is not advanced scientific analysis or deep autonomy work. The team needs a strong balance of reasoning quality, latency, and cost. Which model selection approach best fits the workload?

options.label: A
options.text: Use any current Claude model interchangeably for the claims workflow.
options.feedback: Current Claude models share core capabilities such as text and image input and text output, but they are not interchangeable for workload planning. Model selection still involves tradeoffs among capability, speed, cost, and effort.

options.label: B
options.text: Use Claude Haiku 4.5 as the default model for every claims workflow.
options.feedback: Claude Haiku 4.5 is well suited to quick iteration, tight latency, cost-sensitive use, and high-volume straightforward tasks. This scenario needs stronger reasoning for business-critical summaries and briefs, so making Haiku the default for every part of the workflow underfits the stated need.

options.label: C
options.text: Use Claude Sonnet 5 as the default model for the daily claims workflow.
options.feedback: Claude Sonnet 5 is the best fit for a production workload that needs a balance of speed and intelligence. It avoids treating the task as either a simple lowest-cost batch job or a highest-complexity reasoning task.

options.label: D
options.text: Use Claude Opus 4.8 as the default model for every claims workflow.
options.feedback: Claude Opus 4.8 is recommended for the most complex reasoning, nuanced high-accuracy work, and advanced agentic or coding workloads. Using it for all daily production claims work would likely add cost and latency where the scenario asks for a balanced choice.

questions.explanation:
For this scenario, Claude Sonnet 5 is the best default because the task is a recurring production workflow that needs solid reasoning without treating every request as a maximum-complexity problem. Anthropic positions Sonnet as offering a strong combination of speed and intelligence, and its pricing guidance frames Sonnet as the choice for most production workloads.

Claude Haiku 4.5 is often the right starting point for fast, lower-cost, high-volume, straightforward tasks. Claude Opus 4.8 is better reserved for the most complex reasoning or cases where accuracy outweighs cost and latency. The practical judgment is to match the model to the workload rather than assume the fastest or most capable model is always best.

The official guidance emphasizes evaluating capabilities, speed, cost, and effort together when selecting among Claude models. See Anthropic's Choosing a model, Models overview, and Pricing documentation for the model positioning and tradeoff guidance.

questions.question: A museum exhibition team wants Claude to turn curator notes, donor requirements, visitor research, and a sample wall-label format into a draft exhibit brief. Their current prompt pastes everything together and asks for “a polished brief,” but Claude sometimes misses constraints or blends source types. What is the best way to structure the request?

options.label: A
options.text: Separate the materials with descriptive tags, then give Claude a numbered workflow and output sections.
options.feedback: This decomposes the task into clear inputs, ordered steps, and expected deliverables. Descriptive tags help Claude distinguish context, constraints, examples, and the final request instead of treating the prompt as one undifferentiated block.

options.label: B
options.text: Ask Claude to write the brief first, then provide the notes only if revisions are needed.
options.feedback: This withholds the information Claude needs to execute the task well on the first pass. It can create extra revision cycles and may lead to a generic draft that does not reflect the team’s actual constraints.

options.label: C
options.text: Start with the final format request, then append the source materials without labels.
options.feedback: This gives Claude an output goal but does not clearly separate the inputs it must use. For complex prompts, unlabeled materials make it harder to distinguish evidence, constraints, examples, and instructions.

options.label: D
options.text: Paste the materials in one block, then ask Claude to infer the best workflow and format.
options.feedback: This leaves the task structure implied, which increases the chance that Claude will miss requirements or combine unlike materials. Asking Claude to infer the workflow can work for simple tasks, but it is less reliable for complex requests with multiple source types.

questions.explanation:
Complex requests work better when the prompt makes the task structure explicit rather than leaving Claude to infer it. A strong prompt separates inputs, instructions, examples, and output requirements, then breaks the work into a clear sequence such as review constraints, identify themes, draft sections, and note unresolved questions.

Anthropic’s prompting guidance recommends clear instructions, numbered lists or bullets when order and completeness matter, and XML-style tags such as <curator_notes> or <sample_format> to separate parts of complex prompts. See Anthropic prompt engineering documentation for guidance on structuring complex prompts.

The less reliable approaches all keep some important structure hidden: they rely on Claude to infer the workflow, omit labels for distinct sources, or delay providing necessary context. Those approaches may still produce fluent text, but fluency is not the same as faithful execution against multiple constraints.

questions.question: A regional transit authority's service quality team uses Claude to classify rider comments for a monthly report. Reviewers disagree about whether the drafts are useful because some focus on category accuracy, others focus on tone, and others focus on concise explanations. What should the team do before continuing to tune the prompt?

options.label: A
options.text: Wrap the comments in XML-style tags and request a cleaner report format.
options.feedback: XML-style structure can help Claude parse complex prompts, especially when separating inputs, context, and instructions. It does not by itself define whether category labels, tone, or explanation length should determine success.

options.label: B
options.text: Add a senior analyst role and ask Claude to be more accurate each time.
options.feedback: Role prompting can help frame Claude's behavior, but it does not resolve disagreement about what the output should optimize. Asking for more accuracy is still too vague without criteria that reviewers can apply consistently.

options.label: C
options.text: Switch to a stronger model and accept outputs that sound more polished.
options.feedback: A more capable model may help some tasks, but model choice does not replace clear evaluation criteria. Polished wording can hide classification errors or inconsistent explanations.

options.label: D
options.text: Define measurable success criteria and test draft prompts on representative rider comments.
options.feedback: This is the best next action because prompt tuning works best when the team knows what success means. Specific criteria and representative tests make it possible to compare prompt revisions instead of relying on subjective impressions.

questions.explanation:
Effective prompting starts with knowing what the prompt is supposed to achieve. Anthropic's prompt engineering workflow assumes you already have clear success criteria and empirical tests before you iterate heavily on wording, as described in Prompt engineering overview.

In this scenario, the team is not just missing better phrasing, it is missing an agreed target. A useful evaluation might specify acceptable category accuracy, required tone, and a concise explanation format, then test several prompt versions on the same representative rider comments.

Prompt techniques such as role prompting, XML-style organization, and clearer formatting can be valuable once the target is known. Anthropic also recommends clear, explicit instructions and structured prompts in Claude prompting best practices, but those techniques work best when they are tied to measurable goals rather than vague preferences like better or more polished.

When a governance policy requires a pilot to be managed separately, moving it into its own workspace gives the administrator a concrete boundary for access and limits rather than depending on users to self-police.

Rate limits and spend limits address different risks. A rate limit controls API requests over a defined period, while a spend limit controls maximum monthly API cost. Choosing the wrong control can leave the actual policy requirement unmet, even if it improves governance in another way. See Anthropic's documentation on Workspaces and Rate limits.

questions.question: A public radio network's audience insights team is choosing a Claude model for a weekday production workflow that reviews listener survey comments, summarizes recurring themes, and drafts notes for producers. The work needs more reasoning than simple templated classification, but the team has steady volume and cannot optimize only for the deepest possible analysis. Which model selection approach best fits the workload?

options.label: A
options.text: Select Claude Haiku for the main workflow and optimize primarily for lowest latency.
options.feedback: Claude Haiku is a strong starting point for fast, cost-sensitive, straightforward tasks. The scenario calls for stronger reasoning over survey comments and producer notes, so Haiku is less aligned than Sonnet as the main production model.

options.label: B
options.text: Select Claude Opus for every run and prioritize maximum reasoning depth over throughput.
options.feedback: Claude Opus is best suited for the most complex reasoning and cases where accuracy outweighs cost. Using it for every routine production run would likely overspend on capability the scenario does not require.

options.label: C
options.text: Select Claude Sonnet for the main workflow and reserve deeper review for exceptional cases.
options.feedback: Claude Sonnet is positioned as the strong middle choice for most production workloads, balancing speed and intelligence. This fits a recurring workflow that needs solid reasoning without treating cost and latency as secondary concerns.

options.label: D
options.text: Select the model mainly by image support and use the highest tier for compatibility.
options.feedback: Current Claude models share core support for text and image input, text output, multilingual capabilities, and vision. Choosing primarily by image compatibility would miss the relevant tradeoff among capability, speed, and cost.

questions.explanation:
Model selection should match the work to the right capability, speed, and cost profile rather than defaulting to the largest model. Anthropic positions Haiku as the fast, cost-conscious option for straightforward workloads, Sonnet as the best combination of speed and intelligence for most production workloads, and Opus as the strongest fit for the most complex reasoning where accuracy is worth higher cost.

For this audience-insights workflow, the task is recurring and production-oriented, but it is not described as advanced scientific analysis, deep autonomy, or unusually high-stakes reasoning. Claude Sonnet is therefore the best fit because it provides a stronger reasoning balance than Haiku without the cost and latency tradeoff of using Opus for every run.

See Anthropic's Choosing a model, Models overview, and Pricing documentation for the official guidance on matching Haiku, Sonnet, and Opus to workload needs.

questions.question: A hotel group's revenue management team uses Claude during recurring live pricing reviews. Each review uses the same rate-policy manual, market-segmentation guide, and required analysis format, then adds a different hotel's current occupancy notes. Analysts spend time re-explaining the same standards and want more consistent outputs during meetings. Which action would best optimize the workflow?

options.label: A
options.text: Create a new Project for each hotel's review and paste the same standards into every Project.
options.feedback: This is incorrect because Projects are most useful for accumulated context around an ongoing body of work. Creating separate Projects and duplicating the same standards adds setup work rather than reducing it.

options.label: B
options.text: Create a Skill for the pricing-review procedure and use it when analyzing each hotel's notes.
options.feedback: This is correct because Skills are designed for repeatable procedures that Claude should apply consistently when relevant. Packaging the shared standards and analysis format into a Skill reduces repeated setup while leaving room to provide each hotel's current notes.

options.label: C
options.text: Put the full pricing manual into universal custom instructions for every Claude conversation.
options.feedback: This is incorrect because custom instructions are best for broad preferences that should apply generally. A detailed pricing manual and specialized review format are task-specific, so placing them in universal instructions can clutter unrelated work.

options.label: D
options.text: Continue using regular prompts and ask Claude to follow the format at the start of each review.
options.feedback: This is incorrect because regular prompting works well for one-time or exploratory tasks. Here the team has a repeated workflow with known standards, so re-explaining the same procedure each time is less efficient.

questions.explanation:
For a recurring workflow with stable standards and a known output structure, a Skill is the best fit. Skills are meant for task-specific procedures that Claude can load when relevant, such as a review framework, brand rules, or a report format. See Skills overview.

Projects are better when Claude needs accumulated context for a particular initiative, while custom instructions are better for broad preferences that should apply across all conversations. Regular prompting remains useful for one-time work, but it is inefficient when the same procedure has already been refined and needs to be repeated consistently.

The practical optimization is to package the stable rate-review method once, then provide the variable hotel notes during each meeting. This improves consistency and reduces setup without forcing unrelated Claude conversations to carry specialized pricing instructions.

questions.question: A coastal food bank's logistics team is improving its emergency meal distribution process before storm season. Staff have internal delivery-delay notes, and the plan must reflect current county shelter locations and recently announced road closures. Claude has web search enabled. What is the most appropriate way to use Claude?

options.label: A
options.text: Use only the internal notes to draft the distribution workflow, then add a reminder that conditions may have changed.
options.feedback: This is incorrect because the stated plan needs current shelter and road information, not just historical internal observations. A general caveat does not supply the up-to-date evidence needed for planning.

options.label: B
options.text: Combine the internal notes with a web-searched brief on current shelter locations and road closures, then draft a cited distribution workflow.
options.feedback: This is correct because the task depends on current, changing information that may not be in Claude's training data. Using web search with citations helps the team connect internal process evidence with up-to-date external constraints.

options.label: C
options.text: Have Claude create the workflow first, then ask it to rate whether the shelter and road details sound current.
options.feedback: This is incorrect because Claude's self-assessment is not a dependable way to validate time-sensitive facts. The team should ground those details in cited current sources rather than in a confidence rating.

options.label: D
options.text: Ask Claude to estimate likely shelter locations and road closures from prior seasons, then draft the distribution workflow.
options.feedback: This is incorrect because estimates from prior seasons are not a reliable substitute for current emergency information. Claude should not infer changing public-safety details when a current source can be searched.

questions.explanation:
For workflow improvement, Claude is most useful when it combines provided internal context with the right external information for the decision. In this scenario, delivery-delay notes explain the team's existing bottlenecks, while shelter locations and road closures are current facts that may change quickly.

Anthropic documents web search as a server tool that gives Claude access to real-time web content beyond its knowledge cutoff and returns cited sources. The documented guidance is that Claude should search when a request depends on current, changing, or out-of-training-data information, while stable knowledge and provided-content analysis can often be answered directly. See Web search tool.

The practical judgment is to use Claude for a grounded planning workflow: synthesize the internal notes, search for the current external constraints, and produce a process recommendation with citations that staff can verify. Relying on old patterns, caveats, or Claude's self-rated confidence leaves the plan vulnerable to stale or fabricated operational details.

questions.question: A medical device manufacturer's regulatory affairs team wants Claude to draft first-pass comparison memos from supplier documentation. Pilot outputs are promising, but some miss required evidence, some use the wrong tone for reviewers, and the preferred model is slow for high-volume review weeks. What is the most appropriate next step?

options.label: A
options.text: Use the most capable model for every memo and accept slower review cycles.
options.feedback: This is incorrect because model selection should reflect the use case requirements, including latency and cost. A more capable model may improve some outputs, but it does not automatically satisfy operational constraints.

options.label: B
options.text: Rewrite the prompt with stricter instructions and approve it after several strong examples.
options.feedback: This is incorrect because a few strong examples do not show whether the workflow works across the real task distribution. Prompt changes may help, but they should be guided by success criteria and evaluation results.

options.label: C
options.text: Ask Claude to score each memo and keep drafts that receive high self-ratings.
options.feedback: This is incorrect because self-ratings are not a reliable substitute for a tested evaluation process. LLM-based grading can be useful, but its reliability should be checked before relying on it at scale.

options.label: D
options.text: Define measurable success criteria and test representative cases before changing prompts or models.
options.feedback: This is correct because the team has multiple requirements, including evidence coverage, tone, and speed. Defining measurable criteria and testing representative cases helps determine whether the issue is prompting, model choice, or workflow fit.

questions.explanation:
When applying Claude to a new workflow, start by translating the use case into specific success criteria rather than immediately tuning the prompt. In this scenario, quality is multidimensional: the team cares about evidence coverage, reviewer-appropriate tone, and operational speed, so evaluation should measure more than a single subjective impression.

Anthropic guidance recommends having clear success criteria, empirical tests, and a first-draft prompt before doing prompt engineering, and it notes that not every failure is best fixed by prompting. Latency and cost concerns may point toward model selection rather than prompt wording, which is why the best next step is to evaluate the workflow against representative examples before deciding what to change. See Prompt engineering overview and Define your success criteria.

A sound evaluation set should mirror the real task distribution, including edge cases such as incomplete supplier documentation or unusual regulatory evidence. Relying on a few polished demos, always choosing the most capable model, or accepting Claude's own self-scores can all hide failure modes that will appear in production use.

questions.question: A film post-production studio's contracts team uses Claude with the Gmail connector to find vendor emails about licensing invoices. Claude can locate the relevant email threads, but the team needs Claude to summarize terms inside PDF attachments to those messages. What is the most appropriate next step?

options.label: A
options.text: Add the PDF attachments as uploaded files or Drive files before requesting the clause summary.
options.feedback: This provides Claude with access to the document content it needs to analyze. The Gmail connector can find and read email content, but it does not directly access attachment contents.

options.label: B
options.text: Narrow the Gmail search by vendor and date before requesting the clause summary.
options.feedback: Narrowing the search can help locate the right email thread, but it does not expose the text inside attached PDFs. The missing input is the attachment content, not the email search criteria.

options.label: C
options.text: Have the Owner enable Google Workspace connectors before requesting the clause summary.
options.feedback: The scenario already shows the Gmail connector is available because Claude can locate the relevant threads. Organization-level enablement does not change the documented limitation that Gmail attachment content is not directly accessible through the connector.

options.label: D
options.text: Ask Claude to use attachment metadata from Gmail before requesting the clause summary.
options.feedback: Attachment metadata can indicate that an attachment exists and may include details such as its name. It is not a substitute for the attachment's actual text when summarizing contractual terms.

questions.explanation:
The practical distinction is between finding messages and reading attached documents. The Google Workspace connector documentation explains that Gmail can search and read emails and access attachment metadata, but attachment content is not directly accessible through Gmail: Use Google Workspace connectors.

When the task depends on the contents of a PDF attachment, the team should provide that file as accessible knowledge, for example by uploading it or adding it from Google Drive. Claude supports uploaded PDFs as documents, and uploaded files become context for the conversation or project within the applicable limits: What kinds of documents can I upload to Claude.ai?.

A good mental model is that connectors mirror the capabilities and boundaries of the connected service integration. Re-running a Gmail search or relying on metadata may retrieve better email references, but it still leaves Claude without the source text needed for a reliable clause summary.

questions.question: A community newspaper's investigations desk uses Claude to draft an article from interview notes and public records, then plans to publish the text on its website under a staff byline. What is the most appropriate governance step before publication?

options.label: A
options.text: Publish the draft after asking Claude to confirm that the article is accurate and balanced.
options.feedback: This is not sufficient because Claude's self-assessment is not a reliable substitute for editorial accountability. It also does not satisfy the disclosure expectation for AI output presented to readers.

options.label: B
options.text: Publish the draft without labeling it if the source notes came from human reporters.
options.feedback: Human-provided source material does not remove the governance obligations for AI-assisted journalistic content. The ethical issue is how the generated output is reviewed and presented to the public.

options.label: C
options.text: Review reader complaints after publication and correct only the claims that are challenged.
options.feedback: Post-publication correction processes are useful, but they do not replace review before dissemination. Waiting for readers to find problems increases the risk of publishing inaccurate or misleading content.

options.label: D
options.text: Have a qualified editorial professional review the draft and disclose the AI involvement to readers.
options.feedback: This is the correct action because externally published media or journalistic content is treated as a high-risk use case under Anthropic's Usage Policy. The workflow needs qualified human review before publication, and readers should be told when AI output is presented to them.

questions.explanation:
Anthropic's Usage Policy treats externally published media and journalistic content as a high-risk use case, which means AI-generated advice, recommendations, or subjective decisions should be reviewed by a qualified professional before dissemination. It also requires disclosure when outputs are presented directly to individuals or consumers, so readers should not be misled about AI involvement in the published content. See the official Anthropic Usage Policy.

The ethical principle is not that AI can never assist journalism. The practical requirement is that human editorial responsibility remains in place, especially where public trust, reputation, and factual accuracy are at stake. Asking Claude to validate itself, relying on human source notes alone, or correcting only after complaints all fall short because they shift accountability away from the people publishing the work.

questions.question: A specialty pharmacy's training team is iterating a Claude workflow that turns de-identified medication counseling transcripts into follow-up message drafts. So far, they test each prompt revision with one pasted transcript and fixed patient details, but they want to compare prompt revisions across many realistic transcript variations and edge cases. What is the most appropriate next step?

options.label: A
options.text: Increase the selected model’s effort level, then compare revisions on one transcript.
options.feedback: Higher effort can help Claude spend more reasoning budget on a response, but it does not show how the workflow performs across varied cases. Testing on one transcript gives weak evidence about reliability across realistic inputs.

options.label: B
options.text: Move the examples into custom instructions, then test in separate conversations.
options.feedback: Custom instructions are better suited to broad preferences than to evaluating a workflow across cases. Separate conversations can make comparison less consistent and do not address the need for measurable success criteria.

options.label: C
options.text: Create a structured evaluation set with varied examples and measurable success criteria.
options.feedback: This is correct because prompt revisions should be compared against a representative set of cases, not a single fixed example. Specific criteria help the team judge whether outputs meet the workflow’s needs consistently.

options.label: D
options.text: Ask Claude to rate each output, then choose the highest self-score.
options.feedback: Claude’s self-rating is not a reliable substitute for external evaluation against defined criteria. This approach also does not create coverage for different transcript patterns or edge cases.

questions.explanation:
For prompt iteration, the team should build a structured evaluation set that represents the kinds of inputs the workflow will face in practice. A single transcript can be useful for early exploration, but it cannot reveal whether a revised prompt handles edge cases, different counseling patterns, tone requirements, privacy constraints, or unsupported claims consistently.

Good evaluation starts with specific and measurable success criteria. For this pharmacy workflow, useful criteria might include factual fidelity to the transcript, appropriate tone, no unsupported medical claims, privacy-safe handling, and clarity for the intended recipient. Anthropic’s guidance on defining success criteria emphasizes evaluating across multiple dimensions because real workflows usually fail in more than one way.

The Claude Console Evaluation workflow supports comparing prompts across test cases, but the foundation-level principle is broader than any specific tool syntax: vary the examples, define what success means, and compare outputs systematically. The official guide to creating and running evals describes how evaluation sets support prompt iteration in practice.

questions.explanation:

Anthropic documents that ZDR means customer prompts and responses are not stored at rest after the API response is returned, but it must be enabled by Anthropic for each organization and applies only to covered uses.

Instead, they should route the work through an eligible Claude API workflow in the organization where ZDR is enabled.

This tradeoff exists because different product surfaces support different user experiences, persistence models, and operational controls.
