questions.question: An online tutoring provider's curriculum team uses Claude to turn lesson transcripts into short practice questions. After several prompt edits, some outputs still miss learning objectives or include questions that are too easy, and the team is unsure whether the latest prompt is actually better. What should the team do next?

options.label: A
options.text: Define task-specific success criteria, build an eval set with edge cases, and compare prompt versions against it.
options.feedback: This is correct because prompt improvement should be measured against defined goals rather than judged from a few recent examples. A task-specific eval set with normal and difficult cases helps reveal whether the new prompt improves the failure modes that matter.

options.label: B
options.text: Run the prompt improver on the current template, accept the revised prompt, and monitor complaints after release.
options.feedback: The prompt improver can help strengthen an existing prompt, but it is not a substitute for measuring whether the result works. Deploying the revised prompt without evaluation leaves the team unable to tell whether quality actually improved.

options.label: C
options.text: Ask reviewers to choose the better prompt from memory, update the template, and revisit defects later.
options.feedback: Reviewer judgment can be useful, but relying on memory makes the comparison inconsistent and hard to reproduce. The team needs explicit criteria and repeatable tests, not another informal prompt edit cycle.

options.label: D
options.text: Increase the response length limit, retry the latest transcript, and use that output as the deciding test.
options.feedback: A longer output limit may help when responses are being cut off, but the stated problems are missed objectives and weak question difficulty. Testing only the latest transcript is too narrow and can hide regressions on other cases.

questions.explanation:
When a prompt underperforms in inconsistent ways, the practical troubleshooting move is to turn vague dissatisfaction into measurable success criteria and test against representative examples. For this tutoring task, criteria might include covering the intended learning objective, matching the expected difficulty level, and producing the required number and format of questions.

Anthropic’s guidance emphasizes developing tests with task-specific success criteria, edge cases, and automated grading where feasible, as described in Develop tests. If the team uses the Claude Console Evaluation tool, it can compare prompt versions and rerun test suites after edits, with test cases built around variables such as {{transcript}}, as documented in Use the Evaluation tool.

The prompt improver and manual review are useful inputs to an iteration process, but they do not replace evaluation. The mental model is: first define what good output means, then test prompts against a stable set of cases, then revise based on observed failures. This prevents the anti-pattern of chasing the last bad example and makes prompt optimization more reliable.

questions.question: A food safety consultancy is prototyping a Claude-assisted process that reviews many restaurant inspection notes against the same long audit rubric. The rubric changes rarely, while each review has different inspection observations. Before sharing the process with consultants, the team wants confidence that the outputs are useful and consistent. What is the most appropriate next step?

options.label: A
options.text: Ask Claude to score its own reliability before sharing the process.
options.feedback: This is incorrect because Claude’s self-assessment is not a substitute for validating outputs against external criteria. A high self-rated score does not reliably demonstrate accuracy, consistency, or suitability for the intended use.

options.label: B
options.text: Approve the process after one review that matches the rubric closely.
options.feedback: This is incorrect because one good example does not show that the process will work across the range of inspection notes consultants will encounter. A single case can miss edge cases, inconsistent reasoning, or tone problems.

options.label: C
options.text: Compare Claude’s reviews across varied notes using measurable success criteria.
options.feedback: This is correct because iteration should test actual outputs against specific, measurable criteria, not just whether a prompt seems reasonable. Varied realistic examples reveal consistency, rubric fidelity, and failure patterns before the process is used more broadly.

options.label: D
options.text: Focus on making the prompt shorter before checking review quality.
options.feedback: This is incorrect because prompt brevity alone does not establish whether the reviews meet the consultancy’s standards. Shortening the prompt too early could also remove rubric detail that is needed for quality.

questions.explanation:
When using Claude to support a repeatable work process, the practical design question is not only whether Claude can produce one good answer. The team should define specific and measurable success criteria, then compare outputs across realistic examples that represent the work consultants will actually do.

Anthropic’s evaluation guidance emphasizes that most use cases benefit from multidimensional criteria such as task fidelity, consistency, relevance, tone, privacy, context use, latency, and price. See Define success.

This approach supports iteration because failures become actionable: the team can revise the rubric, prompt, examples, or review checklist based on observed gaps. The alternatives rely on weak signals, such as one promising output, Claude’s own confidence, or prompt length, none of which directly validates whether the process is ready for broader use.

questions.question: A commercial real estate research group uploads several market reports and broker memos to Claude before preparing a client-facing outlook. The team is still trying to understand the material, including where the sources agree or conflict. Which prompting approach is most appropriate?

options.label: A
options.text: Ask Claude to summarize each document separately in the order uploaded.
options.feedback: Separate summaries may be useful as a first pass, but they do not directly ask Claude to synthesize across sources. The team needs a prompt that helps reveal themes and conflicts, not just document-by-document condensation.

options.label: B
options.text: Ask Claude to write a polished outlook using the strongest positive claims first.
options.feedback: This moves too quickly into drafting before the team has understood the source material. It may also bias the result toward favorable claims instead of revealing agreement, uncertainty, or contradictions.

options.label: C
options.text: Ask Claude to extract key claims, note source conflicts, and organize findings by theme.
options.feedback: This fits a research and analysis task because it asks Claude to work from the provided materials, surface patterns, and identify disagreements. It also gives a clear structure for the output, which helps make the response easier to verify before client-facing drafting begins.

options.label: D
options.text: Ask Claude to brainstorm taglines and campaign angles for the final outlook.
options.feedback: This is better suited to an ideation task where the goal is a range of creative directions. It does not address the team’s need to understand evidence across multiple uploaded sources.

questions.explanation:
Different task types call for different prompting strategies. For a research synthesis or analysis task, the prompt should direct Claude to work from the supplied materials, identify important claims, organize patterns, and flag tensions or gaps. That is different from a drafting prompt, which would emphasize voice, audience, and final format, or a brainstorming prompt, which would prioritize variety and exploration.

Anthropic’s guidance emphasizes being clear and direct about the desired output, constraints, and steps when order or completeness matters. In practice, asking for themes, source conflicts, and key findings gives Claude a useful structure while keeping the task focused on understanding before persuasion. See Anthropic’s guidance on being clear and direct and the broader prompt engineering overview.

questions.question: A specialty coffee roaster's customer experience team asks Claude to draft a subscriber notice about a packaging defect. The notice must match the roaster's warm, concise voice and avoid making promises the operations team has not approved. Which prompting approach is most appropriate?

options.label: A
options.text: Ask for a broad list of campaign themes, then choose the most creative direction.
options.feedback: This approach fits early brainstorming better than a controlled customer notice. It prioritizes idea generation rather than producing a constrained draft that matches an approved voice.

options.label: B
options.text: Upload background materials and ask Claude to identify contradictions across all sources.
options.feedback: This approach is better suited to research synthesis or analysis of source material. It does not directly guide Claude toward the required customer-facing draft, tone, and approved boundaries.

options.label: C
options.text: Ask Claude to write the notice in its best style and self-rate the result.
options.feedback: This is an anti-pattern because it relies on vague style guidance and Claude's own judgment rather than explicit criteria. A self-rating is not a substitute for providing examples, constraints, and a target format.

options.label: D
options.text: Provide approved sample notices, define the audience, specify constraints, and request the final format.
options.feedback: This is a drafting task where tone, format, and constraints matter. Supplying examples and clear instructions gives Claude concrete guidance for matching the desired voice while avoiding unsupported commitments.

questions.explanation:
Prompting strategy should match the task type. For drafting, especially customer-facing writing, Claude benefits from clear instructions about audience, tone, constraints, and output format, plus examples when a specific voice or format must be followed.

Anthropic’s guidance emphasizes being clear and direct, including explicit instructions, constraints, and structured steps when they matter: Be clear and direct. In this scenario, approved sample notices and specific boundaries help Claude draft within the organization’s standards rather than inventing wording or commitments.

Brainstorming prompts are useful when the goal is to explore many possibilities, while research synthesis prompts are useful when the goal is to compare sources and surface contradictions. A customer notice is different: the goal is controlled drafting, so the prompt should narrow the space rather than expand it. Anthropic also frames prompt improvement around clear success criteria and empirical testing, not intuition alone, in its prompt engineering overview.

questions.question: A university admissions office is planning a Claude-powered applicant portal that answers questions about degree requirements and prepares preliminary scholarship eligibility notes for admissions staff. Which launch plan best aligns with Anthropic’s Usage Policy?

options.label: A
options.text: Let Claude rank applicants, finalize scholarship awards, and send decisions without staff review.
options.feedback: This removes the qualified professional review required for high-risk consumer-facing decisions such as admissions or financial recommendations. It also places final decision authority on the model rather than using it as an assistive tool.

options.label: B
options.text: Present Claude as a human admissions counselor and disclose AI use only when applicants ask.
options.feedback: Consumer-facing chatbots must disclose that the user is interacting with AI at least at the beginning of each chat session. Waiting until applicants ask does not satisfy the disclosure expectation and can mislead users about who is advising them.

options.label: C
options.text: Use Claude to draft guidance and notes, disclose AI involvement, and require qualified staff review.
options.feedback: This approach treats admissions and scholarship recommendations as a sensitive, high-risk context rather than as fully automated decisions. It pairs AI assistance with disclosure to users and review by qualified staff before recommendations are finalized or shared.

options.label: D
options.text: Collect portal conversations and Claude outputs to train a separate admissions model without authorization.
options.feedback: Anthropic prohibits using its products to train another AI model without prior authorization. This kind of model scraping or distillation is not made acceptable by the educational purpose of the portal.

questions.explanation:
Admissions, scholarship eligibility, and similar education decisions can be high-risk use cases when they affect people in a consumer-facing setting. Anthropic’s Usage Policy does not treat every high-risk use case as banned, but it requires controls such as qualified professional review before advice, recommendations, or subjective decisions are disseminated or finalized.

A good mental model is to use Claude as an assistive drafting and analysis tool, while humans remain accountable for sensitive decisions that affect access, opportunity, or benefits. The same policy also requires consumer-facing chatbots to disclose that the user is interacting with AI at least at the beginning of each session, regardless of whether the use case is high-risk. The official deployment guidance reinforces that safety is a shared responsibility, since model safeguards are not failsafe and product teams should add review and disclosure controls before launch, as described in Anthropic’s API launch guidance.

The incorrect plans fail for different reasons: they automate final admissions-related decisions, hide the AI nature of the interaction, or use Claude outputs to train another model without authorization. These are not merely quality issues, they are governance failures because they bypass the controls that make an otherwise sensitive use case appropriate.

questions.question: A regional wildlife rescue center is testing Claude to turn veterinary treatment logs into short release-readiness summaries for animal-care staff. The drafts are easy to read, but staff need to know whether they preserve critical facts such as medications, restrictions, and unresolved observations. What is the most appropriate way to evaluate the outputs before routine use?

options.label: A
options.text: Ask Claude to rate its confidence for each summary, then route low-confidence summaries for review.
options.feedback: A model's self-reported confidence is not a reliable substitute for checking claims against the source material. This approach can leave confident but incorrect or incomplete summaries unchallenged.

options.label: B
options.text: Have reviewers score only readability and tone, then adjust the prompt until scores are consistently high.
options.feedback: Readability and tone may matter, but they do not establish whether the summaries preserve critical facts. This approach could approve fluent outputs that omit key details or include unsupported claims.

options.label: C
options.text: Create a representative eval set with edge cases, then compare summaries against source logs using specific criteria for factual support and omissions.
options.feedback: This directly tests whether the summaries are accurate and complete for the workflow that staff will actually use. A representative set with edge cases helps reveal both common failures and uncommon but important omissions.

options.label: D
options.text: Ask Claude to attach citations to each summary, then accept summaries with at least one citation per paragraph.
options.feedback: Citations help trace claims back to provided source documents, but they are not an automatic guarantee that every inference is correct or complete. A citation requirement alone can miss omitted medications, restrictions, or unresolved observations.

questions.explanation:
For output evaluation, the central question is not whether Claude's response is polished, but whether it satisfies the task's real success criteria. Anthropic's evaluation guidance recommends defining specific, measurable, achievable, and relevant criteria and using multidimensional evaluation where appropriate, such as task fidelity, consistency, context utilization, and other dimensions that matter for the workflow. See Define success criteria.

A good eval set should reflect the real-world task distribution and include edge cases, because routine examples alone often hide failures that matter in production. In this scenario, that means checking summaries against the original treatment logs for supported facts and missing critical details, not just asking whether they sound clear.

Citations can be useful because they provide source traceability, but they do not make the model an automatic truth oracle. Anthropic's hallucination guidance notes that Claude can produce factually incorrect or context-inconsistent text, and techniques such as grounding, quotes, and citations reduce but do not eliminate the need to validate critical information. See Reduce hallucinations and Citations.

options.feedback: This is incorrect because model-generated grading should not be trusted blindly as the sole readiness signal. If LLM-based grading is used, its reliability should be tested before scaling it.

options.label: C
options.text: Define measurable success criteria and evaluate representative examples before revising the prompt or model.
options.feedback: This is correct because a readiness decision should start from the use case requirements, not from prompt tinkering. Specific criteria and representative evaluations make it possible to decide whether Claude is meeting the workflow's needs.

options.label: D
options.text: Move the workflow to a faster model and review quality after curators begin using it.
options.feedback: This is incorrect because the scenario asks for a defensible readiness decision, not only faster operation. Model selection can address latency or cost, but quality and task fitness still need empirical evaluation.

questions.question: A nonprofit grants office is drafting a public donor briefing in a Claude Project. Claude produces a polished summary of this year's grant eligibility rules, including exact quoted wording and application dates. The team discussed some current materials in earlier chats, but the only file uploaded to Project knowledge is last year's grant PDF. Which two actions should the grants associate take to evaluate the output for accuracy and completeness?

options.label: A
options.text: Rely on earlier Project chats to supply the grant materials Claude did not upload.
options.feedback: This is incorrect because Project chats do not automatically share context with one another. Unless information is added to Project knowledge, Claude should not be assumed to have access to materials merely discussed in another chat.

options.label: B
options.text: Use web search, if available, to locate current grant sources and review Claude's citations.
options.feedback: This is correct because web search is intended for current, straightforward factual information when it is enabled. Reviewing the cited sources remains necessary because Claude's synthesis may omit important context or depend on imperfect source material.

options.label: C
options.text: Compare each quoted rule and date with the official grant page or current source document.
options.feedback: This is correct because Claude can produce convincing but incorrect quotes, citations, and factual details. Checking the claims against an authoritative current source is the safest way to evaluate both accuracy and whether the summary reflects the right materials.

options.label: D
options.text: Accept the briefing because quotation marks and specific dates indicate reliable sourcing.
options.feedback: This is incorrect because a confident tone, quotation marks, and specific dates do not prove accuracy. Claude can generate authoritative-looking but false details, so the output still needs source review.

questions.explanation:
When evaluating Claude's work, treat polished writing and specific-looking details as signals to verify, not proof. Anthropic notes that Claude can produce incorrect or misleading responses, including convincing but false quotes or citations, so users should not rely on Claude as a singular source of truth: Claude is providing incorrect or misleading responses, what's going on?.

Completeness depends on the materials Claude can actually use. In a Project, Project knowledge is shared across chats, but context from one chat is not automatically available in another unless it has been added to the knowledge base: How can I create and manage Projects?.

For current facts such as this year's deadlines or eligibility language, web search can help Claude use live web content and provide citations, but the user should still open and review the cited sources. Anthropic's web search guidance emphasizes cross-referencing sources and using authoritative sources for critical decisions: Enabling and using web search.

questions.question: An urban planning consultancy uses Claude to draft a city council memo from meeting notes and a zoning ordinance PDF. The draft includes parcel numbers, vote counts, and ordinance section references that will be sent to elected officials. Which TWO actions are most appropriate before sending the memo?

options.label: A
options.text: Ask Claude to create a claim-by-claim source checklist, then manually review high-impact items.
options.feedback: This is correct because having Claude list the factual claims can make validation more systematic. The key is that the final check still happens against source material, especially for details that could affect decisions or public trust.

options.label: B
options.text: Compare the specific numbers and section references against the source documents and official meeting record.
options.feedback: This is correct because exact factual details should be verified against authoritative sources before being used in an official memo. Claude can help draft and organize, but the source documents and official records are the basis for accuracy.

options.label: C
options.text: Ask Claude whether it is confident in the memo, then send it if the confidence rating is high.
options.feedback: This is incorrect because Claude's self-reported confidence is not a reliable measure of factual accuracy. A confident answer can still contain fabricated or unsupported details, especially precise citations and numbers.

options.label: D
options.text: Revise the memo to use cautious wording, then send it without checking the cited details.
options.feedback: This is incorrect because cautious wording does not verify whether the facts are true. It may reduce the tone of certainty, but it does not address incorrect parcel numbers, vote counts, or section references.

questions.explanation:
For public or official communications, treat Claude's draft as work product that must be checked against authoritative records. Language models can produce fluent, plausible details that are not actually supported, especially exact numbers, names, dates, and citations.

A practical validation workflow is to separate the prose from the facts: identify discrete claims, map them to source passages, and manually compare the important ones with the ordinance, minutes, or other official record. Claude can help organize this checklist, but the human review against trusted sources is the accuracy control.

Asking for a confidence score or making language cautious does not prove correctness. Anthropic's guidance on reducing hallucinations emphasizes grounding responses in documents and checking uncertain claims; see Reduce hallucinations and the user-oriented Getting started with Claude.ai.

questions.question: A regional healthcare training department keeps a Claude Project for onboarding materials. In one chat, a coordinator pasted a revised FAQ and told Claude to use a new tone rule for trainee communications. The department now wants future chats in that same Project to use the updated FAQ and tone rule. What should the coordinator do?

options.label: A
options.text: Put the tone rule in Instructions for Claude and leave the FAQ in the chat.
options.feedback: Instructions for Claude apply broadly across conversations, so they are not the best fit for a rule that is specific to one onboarding Project. Leaving the FAQ in one chat also fails to make it persistent Project knowledge.

options.label: B
options.text: Keep using the same chat and ask Claude to remember the FAQ and tone rule.
options.feedback: Continuing one chat may preserve context inside that conversation, but it does not make the information available to other chats in the Project. Future chats need the information added to the Project knowledge base or project instructions.

options.label: C
options.text: Add the FAQ to Project knowledge and put the tone rule in Set project instructions.
options.feedback: This makes the updated source material available across chats in the Project and applies the tone rule to all chats in that Project. Project knowledge is the right place for persistent reference content, while project instructions are the right place for project-specific requirements.

options.label: D
options.text: Rename the Project with the tone rule and summarize the FAQ in the description.
options.feedback: Project name and description help people identify the Project, but they are not accessible to Claude as working instructions or knowledge. Putting important guidance there would not reliably change future responses.

questions.explanation:
For work that should carry across chats inside a single workspace, use Project knowledge for reference materials and project instructions for project-specific requirements. Anthropic documents that Projects are self-contained workspaces with their own chat histories and knowledge bases, and that context is not shared across chats unless it is added to the Project knowledge base. See What are projects? and How can I create and manage projects?.

The important distinction is scope. Instructions for Claude apply account-wide, while Project instructions apply only to chats in that Project. That makes project instructions a better fit for an onboarding tone rule, while the updated FAQ belongs in Project knowledge so Claude can use it as a source in future Project chats. Anthropic’s personalization guidance explains these differences in Understanding Claude's personalization features.

questions.question: A talent acquisition team at a retail chain wants to use Claude during a hiring cycle. Which planned use best fits responsible use expectations?

options.label: A
options.text: Send Claude-generated rejection explanations directly to applicants without human review.
options.feedback: Rejection explanations affect applicants in an employment context, so they require careful review before being shared. Sending them directly also risks relying on inaccurate or inappropriate output without independent confirmation.

options.label: B
options.text: Rank applicants from resumes and advance only the highest-scored candidates automatically.
options.feedback: Employment decisions are listed as high-risk use cases when recommendations or decisions directly affect individuals. Using Claude to automatically advance candidates removes the qualified human review expected before finalizing such a decision.

options.label: C
options.text: Use Claude's salary recommendation as the final compensation decision without checking.
options.feedback: Compensation decisions affect individuals in an employment context and should not be finalized solely from Claude's output. Claude outputs can be inaccurate, so responsible use requires independent review before relying on them.

options.label: D
options.text: Draft neutral interview-question ideas from the job description for a recruiter to review.
options.feedback: This is an appropriate productivity use because Claude is helping draft content that a human recruiter can review and adapt. It does not make the hiring decision or replace required human judgment for an employment outcome.

questions.explanation:
Claude is well suited for general productivity tasks such as drafting, summarizing, brainstorming, and organizing ideas, especially when a person remains responsible for reviewing the result. In this scenario, generating interview-question ideas is a drafting aid, not an automated hiring decision. Anthropic's examples of appropriate uses include writing, summarizing, brainstorming, translation, and image analysis, as described in What are some things I can use Claude for?.

By contrast, employment decisions are included in Anthropic's High-Risk Use Cases. The Usage Policy does not treat every high-risk use as automatically banned, but it requires extra safeguards when advice, recommendations, or subjective decisions directly affect people. A qualified professional must review the content or decision before it is finalized, and direct AI-generated advice or recommendations to individuals may require disclosure.

A useful mental model is to separate assistive drafting from delegated decision-making. Claude can help prepare materials for a hiring team, but it should not be the unchecked authority that ranks applicants, explains rejections, or determines compensation. The Consumer Terms also note that outputs may be inaccurate, so users should independently confirm accuracy before relying on them.

questions.question: A sustainability consulting team is using Claude to design and refine a client implementation playbook over several weeks. They plan to run separate chats for risk review, stakeholder messaging, and timeline planning, while keeping Claude aligned to the latest approved requirements. Which two actions should they take?

options.label: A
options.text: Rely on the project name and description to carry the implementation context.
options.feedback: This is incorrect because Claude does not see a project’s name and description. Important context must be placed in project knowledge or project instructions if Claude should use it.

options.label: B
options.text: Add approved source documents and evolving decisions to the project knowledge base.
options.feedback: This is correct because project knowledge is available across chats inside the same project. Adding approved materials there helps Claude use the shared context during future iterations, rather than depending on a prior chat.

options.label: C
options.text: Put durable tone, scope, and review criteria in the project instructions.
options.feedback: This is correct because project instructions apply to chats within that project. Stable guidance belongs there when the team wants Claude to follow the same expectations across multiple workstreams.

options.label: D
options.text: Leave finalized decisions only in earlier chats within the same project.
options.feedback: This is incorrect because ordinary chat context is not automatically shared with other chats. If a decision should guide later work, the team should add it to project knowledge or restate it in the relevant chat.

questions.explanation:
When using Claude to support iterative solution design, a Project is useful because it gives related work a shared workspace. The key distinction is that project knowledge and project instructions persist across chats in that project, while the conversation history from one ordinary chat does not automatically become context for another chat.

For this team, approved source documents, constraints, and decisions should be maintained in project knowledge so future chats can refer to the same working materials. Durable guidance such as tone, scope boundaries, and review criteria belongs in project instructions because it tells Claude how to approach work inside that project.

Project names and descriptions are helpful for human organization, but they are not visible to Claude, so they should not be used as the place to store working context. Likewise, leaving decisions buried in earlier chats creates a weak handoff between workstreams because a new chat will not automatically inherit that content.

See Anthropic’s guidance on how to create and manage Projects and Claude’s personalization features for how project knowledge and project instructions are scoped.

questions.question: A museum education team asks Claude, "Make this family workshop description more exciting." Claude returns a polished but generic paragraph that does not match the museum's playful tone or include the required age range and registration details. The team has an approved example and a short style guide. What should they do next?

options.label: A
options.text: Provide the style guide, approved example, required details, and ask Claude to rewrite the description.
options.feedback: This is the best next step because it gives Claude clearer context, an example of the desired output, and specific constraints to satisfy. Iterating with targeted feedback is more effective than repeating a vague request.

options.label: B
options.text: Start a new chat with the same prompt and expect a different response to better match the tone.
options.feedback: Starting over with the same vague prompt does not address why the first answer was generic. Claude needs clearer instructions, context, and feedback, not simply another chance with the same limited input.

options.label: C
options.text: Ask Claude to rate whether its paragraph follows the museum tone before using it in the brochure.
options.feedback: Self-rating can sound useful, but it does not supply the style guide, example, or required facts Claude needs to revise well. The team should guide the output directly rather than relying on Claude's assessment of its own draft.

options.label: D
options.text: Ask Claude to try again with more creativity and decide later whether to add the missing details.
options.feedback: This may improve the wording, but it does not give Claude the missing information or show what the museum's tone should look like. Asking for more creativity alone is still too vague for a reliable revision.

questions.explanation:
When an output is close but not useful enough, the strongest move is to iterate the prompt with clearer context, examples, constraints, and feedback. Claude responds to the information you provide in the chat, so a vague request like make this more exciting often produces a generic improvement rather than a version that matches a specific organization’s standards.

Anthropic’s guidance recommends refining prompts and asking follow-up questions, and it specifically suggests explaining the ask clearly, giving enough background context, breaking down complex requests, and asking Claude to rewrite when needed. See Get started with Claude and My prompt isn't giving me a helpful answer.

In practice, the team should treat the first answer as a draft and provide the missing ingredients for a better second draft: the approved example, style guide, age range, registration details, and a direct rewrite instruction. Asking Claude to simply be more creative, restarting with the same prompt, or asking Claude to judge itself does not add the concrete guidance needed to improve the output.

questions.question: A publishing team is using a Claude Project to draft newsletter blurbs. Claude keeps missing the publication’s required disclosure sentence and uses a tone that feels too academic. The team had placed the disclosure requirement and tone note in the Project description, but the drafts still do not reflect them. What should the team do next?

options.label: A
options.text: Create a style for the disclosure language, leave instructions blank, and ask Claude to make the draft shorter.
options.feedback: Styles are useful for how Claude formats and delivers responses, but they are not a substitute for project instructions or knowledge. Shortening the draft does not address the missing disclosure requirement.

options.label: B
options.text: Keep the Project description unchanged, start a new chat, and ask Claude to infer the missing requirements.
options.feedback: Starting a new chat does not make the Project description usable as context for Claude. Asking Claude to infer requirements is unreliable when the missing information has not been placed where Claude can use it.

options.label: C
options.text: Update the account-wide profile instructions, keep the Project materials unchanged, and ask Claude to regenerate.
options.feedback: Profile instructions are account wide, so they are not the best place for a requirement tied to one publication workflow. This also leaves the Project knowledge and project instructions unchanged, which misses the Project-specific fix.

options.label: D
options.text: Add the disclosure to project knowledge, set the tone guidance in project instructions, and ask Claude to revise.
options.feedback: This uses parts of the Project that Claude can apply to the work. Project knowledge can supply recurring context across chats, while project instructions can guide how Claude should behave within that Project.

questions.explanation:
When Claude’s output is not useful, the recommended response is to iterate: make the request clearer, add missing context, break complex work into parts, or give follow-up feedback asking Claude to revise. Anthropic’s Help Center describes this approach in My prompt isn't giving me a helpful answer.

In a Claude Project, the placement of information matters. Project knowledge is available as context across chats in that Project, and project instructions apply to all chats within that Project, but the Project name and description are not accessible to Claude. For Project behavior and knowledge, see How can I create and manage Projects?.

The right adjustment is to put the recurring disclosure where Claude can use it, then place the recurring tone guidance in the Project’s instructions and ask for a revision. Profile instructions are broader than this use case, and styles mainly affect response presentation, so they should not be treated as interchangeable with Project-specific context and requirements. Anthropic explains these distinctions in Understanding Claude's personalization features.

questions.question: A legal operations team uses Claude for two recurring tasks: quick rewrites of internal status notes and detailed reviews of long vendor policies against an internal checklist. They are close to usage limits, routine rewrites feel slower than needed, and policy reviews sometimes miss important details. Which adjustment best optimizes their workflow?

options.label: A
options.text: Use standard settings for rewrites and increase effort or thinking for policy reviews.
options.feedback: This matches Claude's settings to the complexity of each task. Routine rewrites usually do not need extra effort, while long, multi-step reviews can benefit from higher effort or thinking.

options.label: B
options.text: Use longer prompts for both tasks without changing effort or thinking settings.
options.feedback: Clearer prompts can help, but longer prompts alone do not address the team's different task needs. For complex reviews, adjusting effort or thinking can be a better fit than simply adding more text.

options.label: C
options.text: Use the fastest settings for both tasks to preserve usage across the team.
options.feedback: This may help routine rewrites, but it is likely to under-serve the detailed policy review task. Optimization means balancing efficiency with the level of reasoning the task requires.

options.label: D
options.text: Use maximum effort and thinking for every request to keep the process uniform.
options.feedback: This may improve some difficult tasks, but it wastes usage and time on simple rewrites. A uniform setting is less efficient when the team's tasks vary in complexity.

questions.explanation:
Claude settings should be matched to the work being done. For simple, repetitive tasks such as quick rewrites, standard or lower-effort settings can save time and usage. For complex, multi-step tasks such as reviewing a long policy against a checklist, increasing effort or enabling thinking can help Claude spend more attention on the reasoning process.

The tradeoff is that more effort can improve performance on harder tasks, but it can also make responses slower and use more of the team's available capacity. Treat effort and thinking as task-specific controls, not as settings that should always be maximized. Anthropic's guidance on changing the model, effort, and thinking settings describes using defaults for everyday tasks and higher effort or thinking for complex work.

Claude settings should be matched to the work being done. For simple, repetitive tasks such as quick rewrites, standard or lower-effort settings can save time and usage. For complex, multi-step tasks such as reviewing a long policy against a checklist, increasing effort or enabling thinking can help Claude spend more attention on the reasoning process.

The tradeoff is that more effort can improve performance on harder tasks, but it can also make responses slower and use more of the team's available capacity. Treat effort and thinking as task-specific controls, not as settings that should always be maximized. Anthropic's guidance on changing the model, effort, and thinking settings describes using defaults for everyday tasks and higher effort or thinking for complex work.

questions.question: A boutique accounting firm keeps a Claude Project for drafting recurring client meeting recaps. New recaps often need the same style: plain English, a short risks section, and a clear list of owner/date follow-ups. The team also wants Claude to avoid adding tax advice that is not present in the notes. Which setup is most appropriate?

options.label: A
options.text: Ask Claude at the end of each chat to remember these preferences for later project recaps.
options.feedback: A request inside one conversation is not the most reliable way to set guidance for future Project work. Persistent preferences for that workspace should be captured in the Project setup rather than repeated or assumed after each chat.

options.label: B
options.text: Write project instructions that define the style, required sections, and limits on unsupported advice.
options.feedback: This is correct because project instructions are designed for stable guidance within a Project. They help Claude apply consistent tone, structure, and boundaries across chats without requiring the team to restate them every time.

options.label: C
options.text: Upload one example recap as project knowledge and rely on Claude to infer all future rules.
options.feedback: Examples can be useful project knowledge, but relying only on inference is less dependable than stating the recurring rules directly. Claude may imitate the example unevenly or miss important constraints such as not adding unsupported advice.

options.label: D
options.text: Put all prior client notes into instructions so Claude can reuse those details in every recap.
options.feedback: Project instructions should not become a storage place for source material or client history. Prior notes belong in the relevant chat or project knowledge when needed, while instructions should describe how Claude should handle the work.

questions.explanation:
In a Claude Project, project instructions are the right place for stable rules about how Claude should work in that workspace: role, tone, formatting expectations, recurring constraints, and when to ask for clarification. They work best when they are clear and specific, but not overloaded with every piece of background information.

Project knowledge is better for source material, templates, or reference documents, while instructions tell Claude how to use that material. In this scenario, the useful guidance is procedural: use plain English, include the required sections, and flag missing support rather than inventing advice. That separation makes the Project easier to maintain because the team can update notes and examples without burying them inside the rules Claude should follow. For more on how Projects combine knowledge and instructions, see What are Projects?.

questions.question: An event production team uses Claude with Google Workspace connectors to review vendor communications. Claude finds the relevant Gmail thread and shows the attached contract's filename, but the summary does not include the contract terms. What is the most appropriate next step?

options.label: A
options.text: Ask Claude to read the attachment through the Gmail thread.
options.feedback: This is incorrect because Gmail access does not include direct access to attachment content. Repeating the request through the thread does not change what the connector can retrieve.

options.label: B
options.text: Approve the Gmail search again to include the attachment text.
options.feedback: This is incorrect because explicit approval is required for connector actions, but approval does not expand the Gmail connector beyond its documented scope. Gmail attachment content remains unavailable through that connector.

options.label: C
options.text: Add the contract as a separate file rather than relying on Gmail.
options.feedback: This is correct because the Gmail connector can access attachment metadata, not the contents of attachments. Providing the contract as its own file gives Claude the document content needed for a meaningful summary.

options.label: D
options.text: Ask Claude to summarize the contract from the attachment metadata.
options.feedback: This is incorrect because metadata such as a filename is not enough to reliably summarize legal or commercial terms. Asking Claude to infer missing document content increases the risk of unsupported details.

questions.explanation:
Google Workspace connectors let Claude work with connected services, but each connector has a specific scope. For Gmail, Claude can search and read emails, access email metadata including attachment metadata, create drafts, manage labels and threads, and list saved drafts, but it does not directly read attachment contents through Gmail.

The practical workflow is to give Claude the actual document content another way, such as adding the contract as a separate file or using a supported Drive workflow if the file is available there. This keeps the task grounded in source material rather than asking Claude to guess from a filename or surrounding email conversation.

Connector use is also request-driven and approval-based: Claude uses the relevant tool when asked and requires explicit approval for actions. Approval is important for control, but it does not turn Gmail into full attachment processing. See Anthropic's documentation on Google Workspace connectors for the documented Gmail and Google Drive capabilities.

questions.question: An independent film festival's programming team asks Claude to create a weekend schedule, sponsor announcement, and volunteer briefing using filmmaker bios, venue limits, sponsor commitments, and audience survey notes. The first response is generic and misses several constraints. What is the most appropriate next step?

options.label: A
options.text: Ask Claude to choose the best constraints itself, then generate the schedule and materials without intermediate review.
options.feedback: This skips the user's judgment about which constraints matter most for the festival. It also increases the chance that an early misunderstanding carries into every final deliverable.

options.label: B
options.text: Ask for all deliverables again in one prompt, adding that the answer should be more detailed and polished.
options.feedback: This keeps the request broad and does not help Claude prioritize the many source materials. Asking for more detail may improve tone or length, but it does not address the missed constraints.

options.label: C
options.text: Start a new chat for each file, asking Claude to summarize everything before producing the same final package.
options.feedback: Separate chats can make it harder to combine related constraints across the whole task. Summaries may be useful, but isolating each file does not structure the final work effectively.

options.label: D
options.text: Break the work into stages: extract constraints, review them, draft the schedule, then create supporting materials.
options.feedback: This is the best choice because it turns a large, multi-part request into a sequence of smaller tasks. Having Claude identify constraints first creates a shared foundation before asking for polished deliverables.

questions.explanation:
Complex requests work better when they are decomposed into clear stages, especially when several source materials and deliverables are involved. In this scenario, Claude first needs to understand the operating constraints, such as venue limits and sponsor commitments, before it can produce a useful schedule or accurate supporting communications.

A practical workflow is to ask Claude to identify requirements, organize them, and surface any conflicts before drafting final outputs. This gives the user a chance to verify the foundation and correct misunderstandings early, instead of discovering them after Claude has generated several polished but flawed documents.

Claude's own getting started guidance emphasizes being specific about the problem and using clear prompts for more complex requests. See Getting started with Claude.ai for user-facing guidance on prompting, uploads, and choosing the right settings for a task.

questions.question: A community arts nonprofit is preparing its spring donor campaign. The team has audience notes, past campaign examples, and a few constraints, but has not chosen the campaign theme yet. Which prompt strategy is most appropriate?

options.label: A
options.text: Ask Claude for varied campaign themes, share audience notes and constraints, then have it group and compare strong ideas.
options.feedback: This fits an early-stage idea generation task because the team needs breadth before choosing a direction. Providing audience notes, examples, and constraints helps Claude generate useful options rather than generic ideas.

options.label: B
options.text: Ask Claude to find external donor campaign examples for similar audiences, then copy the first relevant structure.
options.feedback: This treats the task mainly as research and relies too heavily on one outside example. Research can provide inspiration, but copying the first relevant structure is less useful than generating and comparing options for the nonprofit's own audience.

options.label: C
options.text: Ask Claude to draft the final donor email for review, then revise the wording after the campaign theme becomes clear.
options.feedback: This treats the task as drafting even though the main decision has not been made yet. Drafting a final message too early can lock the team into one direction before exploring better alternatives.

options.label: D
options.text: Ask Claude to summarize recent station performance metrics and past results, then use the summary as the campaign theme.
options.feedback: This treats the task as analysis, which may be useful later but does not directly solve the need to explore campaign directions. Metrics can inform constraints or priorities, but they should not automatically become the creative theme.

questions.explanation:
Different task types call for different prompting strategies. For brainstorming, Claude is most useful when you ask for multiple possibilities, provide context such as audience and constraints, and then narrow or compare the results. That pattern creates room for variety before the team commits to a direction.

For drafting, a stronger prompt would usually specify the intended format, tone, audience, and source material for a polished output. For analysis, you would ask Claude to identify patterns, explain tradeoffs, or compare evidence. For research synthesis, you would focus on sources, key findings, contradictions, and themes. The practical skill is matching the prompt to the kind of work you need at that moment.

Claude's getting started guidance recommends speaking naturally, being specific about the task, and adding helpful context or documents when needed. See Anthropic's Getting started with Claude.ai tutorial for user-facing guidance on prompting, uploads, and choosing settings for different work.

questions.question: A city university's continuing education office is deciding which Claude tasks to allow for staff. Which two planned uses best fit responsible use expectations?

options.label: A
options.text: Draft multilingual orientation emails, then have staff verify dates and links before sending.
options.feedback: This is a general productivity use involving drafting and translation, which are appropriate uses for Claude. Staff verification is important because Claude outputs can be inaccurate even when they sound polished.

options.label: B
options.text: Give individualized tuition appeal advice, then deliver it to students without disclosure.
options.feedback: Personalized advice that affects a student's financial situation can fall within high-risk decision support. Directly showing such advice without qualified review or AI disclosure does not meet the safeguards expected for high-risk uses.

options.label: C
options.text: Score admissions essays, then send acceptance decisions based only on Claude's ranking.
options.feedback: Admissions decisions are a listed high-risk use case when recommendations or decisions directly affect individuals. Using Claude's ranking as the sole basis for final decisions skips the required qualified human review.

options.label: D
options.text: Brainstorm general sleep and stress tips, then review the handout before publishing it.
options.feedback: General wellness topics such as sleep and stress are not treated as healthcare high-risk use cases in the Usage Policy. Reviewing the handout before publication is still responsible because users should not treat outputs as automatically reliable.

questions.explanation:
Claude is well suited to general productivity work such as drafting, summarizing, brainstorming, translation, and image or document analysis, as described in Anthropic's help article on what you can use Claude for. These uses still call for human judgment, especially before publishing or sending information to others.

The key distinction is not whether a topic is important, but whether Claude is being used to make or deliver advice, recommendations, or decisions that directly affect individuals. Anthropic's Usage Policy treats areas such as academic admissions, finance, legal, healthcare, employment, housing, insurance, and journalism as high-risk when they affect people in this way. High-risk uses are not automatically forbidden, but they require safeguards such as qualified professional review and, when outputs are shown directly to people, disclosure that AI helped produce the advice, decision, or recommendation.

General wellness content is a useful edge case: the policy states that sleep, stress, nutrition, and exercise advice does not fall under the healthcare high-risk category. Even so, Claude's Consumer Terms warn that outputs and actions may be inaccurate, so a responsible user should verify facts and avoid presenting Claude's output as guaranteed correct.

questions.question: A regional water utility's operations coordinator wants Claude to help prepare a one-page field crew checklist for switching to a new work-order process. Earlier, the coordinator typed, "Help with the new process," and received a generic response. What is the best next prompt?

options.label: A
options.text: Provide the field crew audience, process goal, key background, required sections, and one-page checklist format.
options.feedback: This gives Claude the context and constraints needed to produce a useful business deliverable. It also makes the desired output format clear, which helps avoid another generic response.

options.label: B
options.text: Add a stronger instruction like “be very thorough,” keep the original request, and ask for a polished checklist.
options.feedback: This relies on a vague intensifier instead of explaining the task. Claude is more likely to improve when the user supplies concrete context, format, and constraints.

options.label: C
options.text: Ask for a finished checklist immediately, avoid extra context, and handle missing details in later revisions.
options.feedback: Iterating can be helpful, but starting without relevant context makes the first draft less useful. For a practical checklist, Claude needs enough background to understand the audience and purpose.

options.label: D
options.text: Paste the full policy notes at once, skip organizing them, and ask Claude to infer the best format.
options.feedback: Providing materials can help, but unstructured material without a clear ask often leads to uneven results. Claude should be told what to do with the information and what the final output should look like.

questions.explanation:
Effective prompting is a clear instruction skill, not a search for a special wording trick. Claude can follow natural-language directions, but it needs the kind of context a new collaborator would need: who the output is for, what the task is meant to accomplish, and what constraints the result must follow.

In this scenario, the better prompt would turn Help with the new process into a specific request for a one-page checklist for field crews, with relevant background and required sections. Anthropic's Introduction to prompt design explains that prompts should state exactly what you want Claude to do, and the troubleshooting guidance in My prompt isn't giving me a helpful answer recommends being clear, contextual, stepwise, and iterative.

The distractors all leave Claude guessing in different ways. Asking it to be “very thorough” does not define what thorough means, delaying all context makes the first answer weaker, and dumping notes without structure shifts too much interpretation onto Claude. A strong prompt gives Claude enough information to act, then uses follow-up feedback to refine the result.

questions.question: A retail merchandising team on a Claude for Work Team plan prepares weekly category briefs. Several analysts need Claude to follow the same brief format and use the same approved product notes, pricing guidance, and past campaign summaries. Analysts also want their exploratory chats to remain private unless they choose to share them. What is the most appropriate way to integrate Claude into this workflow?

options.label: A
options.text: Use an Artifact as the shared workspace, store the source materials there, and update it each week.
options.feedback: Artifacts are best for substantial, self-contained outputs that users want to edit or reuse, such as documents or diagrams. They are not the right substitute for Project Knowledge and project instructions in an ongoing shared workflow.

options.label: B
options.text: Create a shared Project and rely on earlier project chats to provide context for each new brief.
options.feedback: Projects organize related work, but prior chat context is not automatically shared across chats inside a project. Information that should be available across chats needs to be added to the Project Knowledge base or included in project instructions.

options.label: C
options.text: Create a shared Project with approved materials in Project Knowledge and instructions for the brief format.
options.feedback: This uses Projects for a related, ongoing body of work with shared knowledge and consistent instructions. On Team and Enterprise plans, project sharing can give colleagues access to the project while individual chats remain private unless explicitly shared.

options.label: D
options.text: Keep separate chats, paste approved materials each week, and have analysts reuse the same prompt.
options.feedback: This can work for occasional one-off requests, but it creates repeated setup work and increases the chance that analysts use different source materials or wording. It does not centralize the approved knowledge or instructions for the recurring workflow.

questions.explanation:
Projects are designed for related work that benefits from a shared workspace, reusable knowledge, and consistent instructions. In this scenario, the team needs Claude to work from the same approved materials and follow the same brief format, so adding those materials to Project Knowledge and setting project instructions is the best fit. The Projects documentation describes Projects as self-contained workspaces with chat history, knowledge, and instructions: What are Projects?

A key mental model is that a Project is not just a folder of chats. Claude does not automatically treat every prior chat in a Project as reusable context for every future chat, so durable reference material should be placed in Project Knowledge, as described in How can I create and manage Projects? For a Claude for Work Team plan, sharing can give colleagues access to project contents, knowledge, and instructions while individual chats stay private unless someone shares a chat snapshot, as covered in Project visibility and sharing.

Repeatedly pasting materials into separate chats may be acceptable for a short one-time task, but it does not redesign the workflow to reduce setup and inconsistency. Artifacts are useful for reusable outputs, not for managing a team's ongoing source knowledge and standing instructions.

questions.question: A renewable energy installer’s training team uses a Claude for Work Team plan and wants Claude to help coordinators draft role-specific onboarding checklists. The coordinators need the same safety handbook, benefits FAQ, and tone guidelines, but they also want to run separate working chats without automatically exposing draft conversations to the whole team. Which workflow best integrates Claude into this process?

options.label: A
options.text: Create one kickoff chat with the reference files, ask everyone to continue from it, and put the tone guidance in the project description.
options.feedback: A single chat is not the right shared operating space for multiple private workstreams. Also, project names and descriptions are not available to Claude as context, so behavior guidance belongs in project instructions instead.

options.label: B
options.text: Have each coordinator start regular chats, upload the reference files when needed, and paste the tone guidelines into every new conversation.
options.feedback: This can work for isolated one-off tasks, but it does not redesign the workflow around reusable shared context. It increases repeated setup and makes consistency depend on each coordinator remembering the same uploads and instructions.

options.label: C
options.text: Link the Google Docs in a shared project, rely on live sync for all files, and treat prior project chats as shared knowledge.
options.feedback: The Google Drive integration for Projects is available only in private projects, not shared projects. In addition, chat context is not shared across chats within a project unless the information is added to Project Knowledge.

options.label: D
options.text: Create a shared Claude Project, add the reference files to Project Knowledge, set project instructions, and invite coordinators with suitable access.
options.feedback: This uses a Project as a shared workspace for common materials and response guidance. Project sharing can give teammates access to project contents, knowledge, and instructions while individual chats remain private unless explicitly shared.

questions.explanation:
Projects are designed for organizing related work in Claude around a shared set of materials, instructions, and conversations. For a team workflow where several people need consistent reference material and consistent style guidance, adding files to Project Knowledge and placing tone rules in project instructions gives Claude reusable context without requiring every person to rebuild the setup each time.

The important boundary is that a Project is not simply one giant shared chat history. Anthropic documents that context from one chat is not shared across other chats in the project unless that information is added to the project knowledge base, and shared project chats remain private unless a user explicitly shares a chat snapshot. See How can I create and manage Projects? and Project visibility and sharing.

This design supports a practical tradeoff: shared standards and source documents can be centralized, while exploratory drafts and individual working conversations can remain separate. Repeated uploads or pasted prompts may be acceptable for occasional tasks, but they are less reliable for an ongoing team process. The general role of Projects as self-contained workspaces is described in What are Projects?.

questions.question: A hospital foundation's hiring team wants to use Claude to draft short explanations for apprenticeship applicants about why they were or were not selected. The drafts would be sent directly to applicants after a recruiter checks them quickly for tone. The team's AI policy says staff must follow Anthropic's public usage rules. What should the team do before adopting this workflow?

options.label: A
options.text: Send the drafts after tone review and mention AI only if asked.

options.label: B
options.text: Ask Claude to include confidence scores and send high-scoring drafts.
options.feedback: This is incorrect because Claude's confidence wording or scoring is not a substitute for human responsibility. Automated confidence thresholds do not address the policy requirements for high-risk use cases.

options.label: C
options.text: Use Claude only for negative decisions and keep the process internal.
options.feedback: This is incorrect because limiting use to negative decisions does not reduce the governance concern. The workflow still involves employment-related outputs that affect individuals, so review and disclosure safeguards remain relevant.

options.label: D
options.text: Require qualified human review and disclose AI involvement to applicants.
options.feedback: This is correct because employment is a high-risk domain under Anthropic's Usage Policy. When outputs in high-risk use cases are presented directly to individuals or consumers, the policy calls for qualified human review and disclosure.

questions.explanation:

For high-risk use cases, the documented safeguards include qualified human review and disclosure when outputs are presented directly to individuals or consumers. A quick tone review may improve style, but it does not necessarily verify fairness, accuracy, policy compliance, or the basis for an employment-related explanation.

questions.question: A regional food bank's volunteer coordination team wants Claude to help improve how it plans monthly pantry staffing. The team has past rosters, shift-feedback notes, and delivery calendars, and the constraints will change as partners confirm dates. Which approach best uses Claude for research, planning, and process optimization?

options.label: A
options.text: Ask Claude for a final staffing plan from general knowledge, then adjust only the names and dates.
options.feedback: This skips the evidence needed to understand the food bank's real constraints, past issues, and volunteer patterns. Claude may produce a plausible plan, but it would not be grounded in the team's actual materials.

options.label: B
options.text: Create a Project with the relevant materials, ask Claude to find bottlenecks, and have staff review the proposed workflow.
options.feedback: This approach gives Claude the changing context it needs to compare past plans, feedback, and future constraints in one organized workspace. Human review remains important because Claude can suggest process improvements, but staff must confirm feasibility and operational accuracy.

options.label: C
options.text: Create a Skill immediately, ask Claude to enforce it, and use the same staffing method for every month.
options.feedback: Skills are best for repeatable procedures after the team has figured out a proven approach. Creating one before researching the current process may preserve assumptions instead of helping the team discover improvements.

options.label: D
options.text: Paste a few recent notes into a new chat each month, ask for improvements, and discard the conversation afterward.
options.feedback: This can help with a small one-time question, but it does not support accumulated context across changing plans and lessons learned. The team would repeatedly recreate context instead of building an organized planning workspace.

questions.explanation:
For work like staffing process improvement, Claude is most useful when it can combine research, planning context, and prior feedback rather than responding to a vague request in isolation. A Project is a good fit because the team’s materials and constraints accumulate over time, and Claude can use that workspace to analyze patterns, identify bottlenecks, and draft a revised process for people to evaluate.

Skills serve a different purpose: they package a known, repeatable way of working so Claude can apply it automatically when relevant. The guidance in Teach Claude your way of working using skills distinguishes this from Projects, which are better for work that needs ongoing context such as an evolving campaign, launch, or research effort.

A good mental model is: use a Project while discovering and refining the process, then consider a Skill later if the team settles on a standard monthly staffing method. Claude can accelerate the analysis, but the final workflow should still be reviewed by staff who understand volunteer availability, delivery realities, and service obligations.

questions.question: A museum collections team is introducing Claude to curators who worry that it will either replace expert review or be too limited to help. Which message best communicates Claude's practical value and limitations for their exhibit planning workflow?

options.label: A
options.text: Present Claude as a drafting and synthesis partner that uses provided or connected materials, with curator review before final decisions.
options.feedback: This accurately balances value and limitations. Claude can help summarize, draft, compare, and organize work, but expert review remains important for factual accuracy, judgment, and final accountability.

options.label: B
options.text: Present Claude as useful only for brainstorming exhibit ideas, and avoid using any project documents or connected sources.
options.feedback: This understates Claude's usefulness for workflow integration. Claude can work with uploaded or connected materials when access, permissions, and data-sensitivity requirements are appropriate.

options.label: C
options.text: Present Claude as a system that can automatically access all museum files and finalize exhibit content without staff involvement.
options.feedback: This misrepresents how Claude access works and removes necessary human oversight. Connected data depends on enabled connectors, authentication, and existing permissions, and final content should still be reviewed.

options.label: D
options.text: Present Claude as a replacement for curator review whenever it provides confident summaries and source-style references.
options.feedback: This overstates Claude's reliability and creates risk around factual claims. Confident language and citation-like details should not be treated as a substitute for checking authoritative sources.

questions.explanation:
When explaining Claude to stakeholders, the strongest message is usually a balanced one: Claude is valuable as a work accelerator for drafting, synthesis, comparison, and organization, but it does not remove the need for professional judgment. In a workflow such as exhibit planning, Claude can help curators turn notes, source materials, and prior examples into useful drafts more quickly.

Claude's reach depends on what the user provides or connects. Connectors overview explains that connectors can give Claude access to external tools and data sources, but that access is not automatic or unlimited. It depends on the connector, authentication, and the user's permissions.

The practical mental model is: use Claude to reduce setup work and generate a strong first pass, then have the accountable expert validate the result. This avoids two common anti-patterns, treating Claude as an authority because it sounds confident, and dismissing it as useful only for vague brainstorming. Good workflow design keeps Claude close to the work while keeping humans responsible for sensitive, factual, or final decisions.

questions.question: A professional certification board is using Claude to turn several meeting notes into a candidate handbook update. The team needs a clear draft with sections, a policy-change table, and an action checklist that reviewers can revise and reuse later. Which request would best match the output format to the task?

options.label: A
options.text: Ask Claude to answer with one paragraph that combines all changes into a single narrative.
options.feedback: This would make the information harder to review because it removes the requested structure. A single paragraph is not ideal when the task calls for sections, a table, and a checklist.

options.label: B
options.text: Ask Claude to keep the handbook details in the chat and update them only through follow-up messages.
options.feedback: This is less effective because the draft needs to be easy to reference, edit, and reuse outside the flow of chat. Keeping the work only in follow-up messages can make curation and review harder.

options.label: C
options.text: Ask Claude to provide a short inline response with only the three most important takeaways.
options.feedback: This is not the best fit because the team needs a full handbook update, not just a brief summary. Inline chat is useful for quick answers, but it is less suitable for a substantial draft that reviewers will iterate on.

options.label: D
options.text: Ask Claude to create a self-contained artifact with organized sections, a change table, and a checklist.
options.feedback: This is correct because the team needs a substantial, reusable draft that can stand on its own and be revised later. An artifact is well suited for significant content such as a document with structured sections and tables.

questions.explanation:
Claude Artifacts are designed for substantial, self-contained outputs that a user is likely to edit, iterate on, reuse, or reference later. The documented guidance says Claude creates artifacts for significant standalone content, typically over 15 lines, such as documents, websites, diagrams, and other reusable materials. See What are artifacts and how do I use them?.

In this scenario, the useful output is not merely a quick answer. The team needs curated information organized into sections, a policy-change table, and an action checklist, so a self-contained artifact gives reviewers a clearer workspace for revision than an ordinary chat response. This matches the broader Claude for Work framing of using Claude to create, manage, and collaborate on files and content, described at Claude for Work.

Inline responses are still valuable for brief answers, quick summaries, or exploratory follow-ups. However, when the output has enough structure and staying power to become a working document, asking for an artifact helps keep the work organized and reusable.

questions.question: A tax advisory firm's operations team uses Claude for Work Team plan to summarize patterns across client onboarding surveys. The spreadsheet includes client names, tax identification numbers, and account balances. The firm's policy allows AI-assisted analysis only when regulated personal data is minimized. What should the associate do before asking Claude to analyze the file?

options.label: A
options.text: Remove or mask direct identifiers and upload only the fields needed for the trend summary.
options.feedback: This applies data minimization before sharing the file with Claude. It lets the analysis proceed while reducing exposure of regulated personal data and staying aligned with the firm's policy.

options.label: B
options.text: Place the spreadsheet in a new Project and ask Claude not to reveal identifiers.
options.feedback: A Project can organize ongoing work, but it is not a substitute for removing unnecessary sensitive data. Asking Claude not to reveal identifiers does not reduce the identifiers present in the uploaded file.

options.label: C
options.text: Submit the full file through feedback if Claude needs more context after analysis.
options.feedback: Feedback is not the right channel for providing sensitive task context. Explicitly reported materials, such as feedback, may be used under Anthropic's stated data-use terms.

options.label: D
options.text: Upload the full spreadsheet because Team plan data is not used for training by default.
options.feedback: Commercial data-use practices do not override the firm's data-minimization policy. Even if data is not used for model training by default, the associate should still limit sensitive information shared for the task.

questions.explanation:
For privacy-sensitive work, the safest practical approach is to share the minimum necessary data for the business task. Removing or masking names, tax identification numbers, and other direct identifiers reduces the risk while still allowing Claude to analyze patterns in the remaining fields.

Claude for Work documentation explains that, for Team and Enterprise plans, the customer organization is the Controller of user-submitted data and Anthropic acts as the Processor to provide Claude. It also states that Anthropic does not use data from commercial products to train models unless the customer opts into certain programs or explicitly reports materials, such as feedback. See Anthropic's privacy explanation at Does Anthropic act as a data processor or controller?.

That data-use protection is important, but it is not permission to upload every sensitive field. Good governance separates two questions: how the service handles data and whether the employee should share that data for this task. If policy requires minimizing regulated personal data, the associate should reduce the file first rather than relying on a Project, a prompt instruction, or feedback after the fact.
