questions.question: A neighborhood credit union's member services team wants to use Claude to draft individualized explanations for applicants who were not approved for personal loans. The drafts would be sent to applicants with only minor edits by the support team. What is the most appropriate action?

options.label: A
options.text: Have a qualified loan officer review each draft and disclose AI assistance before sending.
options.feedback: This is the appropriate action because loan explanations are in a finance context and can directly affect individuals. Human review by a qualified professional and disclosure of AI assistance help reduce ethical risk before the content reaches applicants.

options.label: B
options.text: Ask Claude to make each draft sound empathetic and send after checking grammar.
options.feedback: Improving tone and grammar does not address whether the explanation is accurate, fair, or appropriate for a financial decision. A polished message can still contain misleading reasoning or unsupported details.

options.label: C
options.text: Remove references to AI assistance and send the drafts under a staff member’s name.
options.feedback: Hiding AI involvement is inappropriate when AI-produced output is presented directly to consumers in a high-risk setting. It also risks making applicants believe the content was generated solely by a human when that is not true.

options.label: D
options.text: Ask Claude to rate each draft’s accuracy and use drafts with high confidence scores.
options.feedback: Claude’s self-assessment is not a reliable substitute for qualified review. Claude can produce confident but incorrect or misleading information, including content that sounds authoritative.

questions.explanation:
Financial decisions are part of Anthropic’s listed high-risk use cases when Claude is used to provide advice, recommendations, or subjective decisions that directly affect people. In that setting, the ethical issue is not only whether the draft sounds professional, but whether it is accurate, fair, reviewed by someone qualified, and transparent about AI assistance.

Anthropic’s Usage Policy says high-risk outputs that directly affect individuals or consumers require review by a qualified professional before dissemination or finalization, and AI assistance must be disclosed when outputs are presented directly to individuals or consumers. See the Anthropic Usage Policy.

Claude can help draft clearer language, but its output should not be treated as authoritative by default. Anthropic notes that Claude can produce incorrect or misleading responses, including authoritative-looking content, so high-stakes communications need scrutiny rather than relying on Claude’s confidence or tone. See Claude is providing incorrect or misleading responses, what’s going on?.

questions.question: An independent film festival's communications coordinator asks Claude to draft a sponsor thank-you note for local restaurants. The draft is accurate but sounds like a formal grant report, while the note needs to feel warm, brief, and suitable for social media captions. What is the most appropriate next step?

options.label: A
options.text: Change account-wide instructions to always use a warm social media tone, then rerun the same prompt.
options.feedback: Account-wide instructions are broad preferences and should not be changed for one sponsor note unless that tone should apply generally. The immediate issue is better handled by refining this task with specific audience and format guidance.

options.label: B
options.text: Give Claude the audience, channel, tone, and length goals, then ask for two revised versions to compare.
options.feedback: This uses Claude conversationally by adding the missing context and giving clearer instructions for the intended audience. Asking for more than one revised version supports comparison and refinement before using the output.

options.label: C
options.text: Publish the draft after removing a few formal phrases, since the facts are already accurate.
options.feedback: Accuracy alone does not make an output fit for its audience or channel. Light manual cleanup may miss the larger tone and format problem that Claude can help revise with better guidance.

options.label: D
options.text: Create a new project with a friendly name and description, then submit the same request again.
options.feedback: A project can help organize reusable context, but the project name and description are not themselves available to Claude as instructions. Rerunning the same under-specified request is unlikely to fix the audience mismatch.

questions.explanation:
Claude is designed for conversational refinement: if a draft is accurate but poorly matched to the audience, the best next move is to tell Claude what was off and provide clearer constraints. Anthropic guidance recommends speaking naturally, being specific, and iterating with follow-up prompts, as described in Get started with Claude and My prompt isn't giving me a helpful answer.

For audience adaptation, useful refinement details include who will read the output, where it will appear, the desired tone, the length, and any examples of language that should be avoided or imitated. Asking Claude for two versions gives the coordinator something concrete to compare, which is often more effective than trying to perfect a first draft in one step.

Account-wide instructions, project instructions, and project knowledge serve different purposes. Broad personalization should not be changed just to fix one social post, and a project name or description should not be relied on to guide Claude's writing, as explained in Understanding Claude's personalization features and How can I create and manage projects?.

questions.question: An urban planning consultancy's proposal lead asks Claude, "Draft our response to this RFP," and attaches the RFP plus several notes. Claude's draft is generic, skips required questions, and adds claims not supported by the notes. Which troubleshooting step is most appropriate before relying on the next draft?

options.label: A
options.text: Repeat the same prompt in fresh chats until Claude produces stronger tone, coverage, and detail.
options.feedback: Repeating the same unclear request is an inefficient way to troubleshoot. It may produce a different answer, but it does not address why the original draft missed required sections and invented details.

options.label: B
options.text: Ask Claude to make the response more polished, persuasive, concise, accurate, and complete.
options.feedback: This may improve tone, but it does not tell Claude which RFP questions must be answered or which notes support each claim. Broad quality words are often too vague to fix missing content or unsupported statements.

options.label: C
options.text: Revise the prompt to specify the audience, sources, required sections, constraints, and quality checklist.
options.feedback: This is the best troubleshooting step because the poor output points to missing structure and unclear success criteria. Giving Claude explicit requirements and asking it to stay grounded in the provided sources makes the next draft easier to evaluate and improve.

options.label: D
options.text: Switch to a more capable model before changing the prompt, examples, context, or requested structure.
options.feedback: A more capable model can help with harder work, but it is not a substitute for clear instructions and grounded source material. If the prompt remains vague, the next output can still miss requirements or include unsupported claims.

questions.explanation:
When Claude produces a weak draft, the first optimization step is usually to improve the prompt, not to keep retrying the same request. A stronger prompt should define the audience, the source material Claude should rely on, the required output structure, and the criteria for a usable answer.

In this scenario, the problems are practical signs of under-specification: generic language, skipped RFP questions, and unsupported claims. Asking Claude to use only the attached notes, follow the RFP's section order, flag gaps, and apply a checklist gives it a clearer target and gives the user a clearer way to review the result.

Model and effort settings can matter for complex tasks, but they do not replace good task framing. Anthropic's user guidance emphasizes being specific about the problem because clear prompts help Claude use its effort effectively: Changing model, effort, and thinking settings.

questions.question: A public health nonprofit’s communications lead asks Claude to summarize recent community feedback about a vaccination campaign. Claude produces a polished brief saying, “young parents are the main source of misinformation,” citing two comments from one focus group and a web article. The brief will be used in a board packet. What should the lead do before sharing it?

options.label: A
options.text: Use the brief as written because it includes citations and a clear explanation.
options.feedback: Citations and fluent writing do not guarantee factual accuracy. Claude can produce incorrect or misleading statements, so polished wording should not replace source review.

options.label: B
options.text: Remove the quoted comments and keep the main conclusion in neutral wording.
options.feedback: Changing the tone does not fix a possibly unsupported conclusion. The lead still needs to compare the claim against the underlying feedback and cited sources.

options.label: C
options.text: Check the cited sources and feedback records, then revise claims to match the evidence.
options.feedback: This is the best action because the conclusion may be broader than the evidence supports. Reviewing the original materials helps identify hallucinated details, missing context, or biased generalizations before the brief is used for a high-stakes audience.

options.label: D
options.text: Ask Claude to state its confidence, then keep claims with a high confidence rating.
options.feedback: Claude’s stated confidence is not a reliable substitute for checking evidence. A confident response can still contain hallucinations, unsupported claims, or misleading framing.

questions.explanation:
Claude can be a useful drafting and synthesis partner, but its output still needs human review, especially when a summary may influence leadership decisions. Anthropic describes cases where Claude can produce incorrect or misleading responses, sometimes called hallucinations, and warns users not to treat Claude as a singular source of truth: Claude is providing incorrect or misleading responses. What’s going on?

In this scenario, the risk is not only a fabricated fact. The phrase young parents are the main source of misinformation may be a biased or overbroad generalization if it rests on only a few comments and a single article. questions.question: A botanical garden's membership team uses a Claude Project to plan seasonal member emails. In one chat, the coordinator corrected the event timeline, but in a later chat in the same Project Claude drafts an email with the old timeline again. What should the coordinator do next?

options.label: A
options.text: Start another chat in the same Project, then ask Claude to remember the correction from the earlier chat.
options.feedback: This is incorrect because it relies on prior-chat information instead of making the corrected timeline durable Project context. Some eligible Claude features may help reference prior conversations, but adding important project facts to knowledge or instructions is the more reliable workflow.

options.label: B
options.text: Add the corrected timeline to the Project knowledge or project instructions, then ask Claude to revise the email.
options.feedback: This is correct because the corrected timeline needs to be placed where Claude can use it as durable Project context. Project knowledge and project instructions are appropriate places for project-specific facts, requirements, and workflow guidance.

options.label: C
options.text: Switch Claude to a more polished writing style, then ask Claude to rewrite the email with the same request.
options.feedback: This is incorrect because styles affect how Claude formats and delivers responses, not whether Claude has the corrected event facts. A style change may improve tone or presentation, but it does not fix outdated timeline context.

options.label: D
options.text: Put the corrected timeline in the Project name and description, then ask Claude to regenerate the email.
options.feedback: This is incorrect because the Project name and description are not accessible to Claude for generating responses. They may help humans organize the workspace, but they do not provide usable context to Claude.

questions.explanation:
When Claude repeats an outdated detail, treat the result as feedback that the needed context should be placed somewhere more reliable. In a Project, project knowledge and project instructions are designed for context, requirements, and guidance that should apply across work in that Project. questions.question: A university alumni relations team has used one long Claude chat for several months of reunion planning. The chat is now slow, usage is being consumed quickly, and Claude warns that the conversation may be too long. The team wants future chats to retain only current decisions, deadlines, and tone guidance, not every draft. What should they do next?

options.label: A
options.text: Create a new Project with a descriptive name, rely on its description, and keep the planning files in the old chats.
options.feedback: A Project can be useful, but its name and description are not the durable context Claude uses for future work. The important information should be added to Project knowledge or Project instructions, not left only in earlier chats.

options.label: B
options.text: Paste the full prior conversation into each new chat, attach every draft again, and continue from the combined record.
options.feedback: This preserves too much information and can recreate the same length-limit problem in the new chat. It also makes Claude work through irrelevant drafts instead of focusing on the current decisions and reusable guidance.

options.label: C
options.text: Keep using the same chat, rely on automatic context management for the history, and skip summaries of earlier decisions.
options.feedback: Automatic context management can help in some situations, but it is not a reason to keep an overgrown conversation forever. Long conversations can consume more usage, and summarizing or restarting is often the cleaner approach when only selected context needs to continue.

options.label: D
options.text: Ask Claude for a handoff summary, start a fresh chat, and store durable context in Project knowledge or Project instructions.
options.feedback: This is the best choice because it reduces the amount of active context while preserving the parts the team needs later. A fresh chat helps avoid carrying months of unnecessary conversation, and Project knowledge or instructions are the right places for reusable context across chats in a Project.

questions.explanation:
Claude has a finite context window, which is the amount of information it can work with in a single chat. This is different from usage limits, which govern how much you can interact with Claude over time. When a conversation grows too long, a practical workflow is to ask Claude for a concise handoff summary, then continue in a fresh chat with only the still-relevant decisions and guidance.

For ongoing work, Projects are useful because they provide a workspace with chat history and a knowledge base. However, context is not automatically shared across separate chats in a Project unless the information is added to the Project knowledge base, and Project names or descriptions are not the right place to store working context. Tone rules and reusable ways of working often belong in Project instructions, while decisions, reference files, and background documents belong in Project knowledge.

Automatic context management can help as a chat approaches the length limit, but it is conditional and can still consume more usage in long conversations. The better mental model is to keep active chats focused, summarize when the thread becomes unwieldy, and persist only the context that future work actually needs. See Anthropic’s guidance on how usage and length limits work, what Projects are, and creating and managing Projects.

questions.question: A regional theater's marketing coordinator uses Claude to turn approved event details into short performance reminders for email and social media. The work is high volume, repetitive, and does not require complex reasoning. Which model choice best fits this task?

options.label: A
options.text: Use Haiku for quick routine drafts, then review samples before publishing.
options.feedback: This is the best fit because Haiku is designed for faster, more cost-effective work on simpler tasks. Human review still matters because even routine drafts can contain wording, date, or tone issues.

options.label: B
options.text: Use Sonnet for all routine drafts, then shorten anything that feels slow.
options.feedback: Sonnet is a strong general-purpose choice when the task needs a balance of capability and speed. For very high-volume, simple drafting, it may be more capability than the work requires.

options.label: C
options.text: Use Opus for every reminder, then reduce detail after each response.
options.feedback: Opus is best reserved for the most demanding tasks that need deeper reasoning or higher capability. Using it for simple, repetitive reminders is usually an inefficient match.

options.label: D
options.text: Use the same model randomly, then compare outputs only if problems appear.
options.feedback: Random selection does not align the model with the task's speed, cost, and capability needs. Waiting for problems before comparing outputs is a weak quality process for public communications.

questions.explanation:
Claude model families are best chosen by matching the task to the tradeoff you need. Haiku is appropriate for fast, lightweight work such as routine drafting, classification, or summarization where speed and efficiency matter more than deep analysis. Sonnet is a strong balanced choice for many everyday knowledge-work tasks, while Opus is better saved for work that benefits from the highest capability and deeper reasoning.

In this scenario, the event details are already approved and the task is repetitive, so choosing the most capable model for every message would likely waste time or usage without adding much value. The practical approach is to use a faster model family first and keep a human review step before publishing. Claude’s help article on model settings explains that users can change the model from the model menu: Change the model, effort, and thinking settings.

questions.question: A specialty coffee roaster's training manager pastes a 12-page barista guide into Claude and asks, "Make this guide better." Claude returns a smooth rewrite, but it drops safety steps, changes drink ratios, and sounds unlike the company’s usual training materials. What is the best next troubleshooting step?

options.label: A
options.text: Switch to a higher effort setting, rerun the same prompt, and compare which version reads better.
options.feedback: Higher effort can help with complex tasks, but it does not replace clear task instructions and source constraints. If the prompt stays vague, Claude still may optimize for a fluent rewrite rather than preserving required procedures.

options.label: B
options.text: Use the revised guide as a draft, add a broad disclaimer, and correct issues after staff feedback.
options.feedback: This leaves known quality problems in a training document and pushes review onto staff later. A better troubleshooting step is to improve the prompt before relying on the next output.

options.label: C
options.text: Rewrite the prompt with the desired outcome, fixed facts, tone guidance, and a request to show material changes.
options.feedback: This directly addresses the likely cause of the poor output: the original request was too broad for a document where factual accuracy, brand voice, and preservation of procedures matter. Asking Claude to show material changes also makes it easier to review whether important content was altered.

options.label: D
options.text: Ask Claude for a cleaner rewrite with stronger wording, shorter sections, and a more polished training style.
options.feedback: This may improve readability, but it does not tell Claude which details must remain unchanged or what the company’s tone should be. It risks producing another polished answer that still changes important facts.

questions.explanation:
When Claude produces a fluent but unreliable result, the first troubleshooting move is usually to improve the prompt, not to assume the model simply needs to try again. A vague request such as Make this guide better gives Claude room to decide what “better” means, which can lead to unwanted rewrites, changed facts, or a mismatched tone.

For work documents, effective prompts should name the goal, audience, required format, and boundaries. In this case, the user should specify which facts must not change, describe the desired voice, and ask Claude to surface meaningful edits so the human reviewer can check them. Claude’s user guidance emphasizes communicating naturally and providing clear context, as described in Claude Help Center.

Settings such as effort and thinking can be useful for complex tasks, but they are not a substitute for defining success criteria. Anthropic’s guidance on changing the model, effort, and thinking settings notes that clear prompts help Claude use its effort effectively. The practical pattern is to diagnose whether the failure is due to missing instructions, missing source material, or a task that needs verification, then revise the prompt accordingly.

questions.question: A logistics provider's safety coordinator asks Claude to summarize recent workplace safety guidance and suggest updates to an internal warehouse checklist. Claude returns a polished answer with several quoted passages and web search citations. What is the most appropriate next step before using the draft as internal guidance?

options.label: A
options.text: Ask Claude to rate its confidence and use the draft if it reports a high score.
options.feedback: Claude's self-reported confidence is not a reliable substitute for checking important facts. A high confidence rating can still accompany hallucinated quotes, incorrect interpretations, or incomplete source use.

options.label: B
options.text: Ask Claude to rewrite the draft in cautious language before sharing it internally.
options.feedback: Cautious wording can make uncertainty clearer, but it does not validate the substance of the guidance. A polished or more careful tone can still contain incorrect or unsupported information.

options.label: C
options.text: Have the safety owner verify the cited claims against authoritative sources before use.
options.feedback: This is the best action because the draft may affect workplace safety decisions, and Claude can produce convincing but incorrect claims. Human review and source verification reduce the risk of relying on unsupported quotes or misleading guidance.

options.label: D
options.text: Share the draft with warehouse managers after adding a note that Claude used web search.
options.feedback: Web search can help Claude find relevant information, but citations do not remove the need to verify important claims. A note about using web search does not confirm that the quotes or recommendations are accurate.

questions.explanation:
Claude is useful for drafting, summarizing, and organizing information, but it should not be treated as a single source of truth for important operational guidance. Anthropic notes that Claude can produce incorrect or misleading responses, including authoritative-looking quotes or claims that are not grounded in fact, as described in Claude is providing incorrect or misleading responses, what's going on?.

When a draft will influence safety, compliance, legal, financial, medical, or similarly high-stakes decisions, the practical standard is to verify the important claims against authoritative sources and involve the responsible human reviewer. Web search and citations can help identify where to look, but they do not guarantee that Claude selected the right source, quoted it accurately, or applied it correctly.

Rewriting the output, adding a disclaimer, or asking Claude for a confidence score may improve presentation, but those actions do not establish factual accuracy. The safer workflow is to use Claude for a first draft, then have a qualified person confirm the cited facts before the content is relied on or shared.

questions.question: A corporate learning team uses a Claude Project to build onboarding materials. In one chat, the lead finalized the tone rules, terminology choices, and review criteria. She now wants to start separate chats for each course module and have Claude use those approved decisions without copying the whole earlier chat each time. What is the most appropriate action?

options.label: A
options.text: Store approved decisions in Project knowledge or instructions before opening separate module chats.
options.feedback: This preserves the reusable context in the Project area where Claude can use it across chats in that Project. A concise summary is usually better than carrying forward an entire long conversation because it keeps the useful decisions without unnecessary context.

options.label: B
options.text: Continue all module work in the original long chat for continuity before opening separate chats.
options.feedback: Continuing one long chat can make the conversation harder to manage and may run into length or usage considerations over time. Starting new chats is reasonable when the reusable context has been summarized and stored where Claude can access it.

options.label: C
options.text: Save approved decisions in the Project name and description before opening separate module chats.
options.feedback: A Project name and description help the human user organize the workspace, but Claude will not have access to those details. Durable guidance should be placed in Project knowledge or Project instructions instead.

options.label: D
options.text: Attach approved decisions only to the first module chat before opening separate module chats.
options.feedback: A file or summary attached only to one chat does not automatically become available to other chats. If the decisions should guide multiple chats in the Project, they need to be added to the Project’s persistent context.

questions.explanation:
For repeated work inside a Claude Project, the key distinction is between conversation context and Project-level context. A useful decision made in one chat is not automatically shared with every other chat in the Project unless it is added to the Project knowledge base, and durable behavioral guidance can also belong in Project instructions. Anthropic documents this in How can I create and manage Projects? and explains the broader Project model in What are Projects?.

The practical move is to summarize the finalized decisions, tone rules, and review criteria, then place that reusable material in Project knowledge or Project instructions before starting the module-specific chats. This keeps each new chat focused while still giving Claude the shared background it needs. It also avoids the anti-pattern of keeping all work in one ever-growing conversation, which can become inefficient and eventually run into length or usage issues described in How do usage and length limits work?.

questions.question: A regional architecture studio uses a Claude Project to draft client-facing design briefs. The studio coordinator updated the Project description with new wording standards and links to revised template files, but new chats in the Project still do not reliably follow those standards. What should the coordinator do so future Project chats use the updated guidance?

options.label: A
options.text: Add the guidance with Set project instructions, and place source materials in Project knowledge.
options.feedback: This is correct because project instructions are the place for requirements Claude should follow across all chats in that Project. Project knowledge is the place for source materials that should persist across chats in the same Project.

options.label: B
options.text: Revise the Project name and description, and continue drafting in the same Project.
options.feedback: This is incorrect because Claude does not use the Project name or description as chat context. Those fields help people organize Projects, but they are not a substitute for project instructions or project knowledge.

options.label: C
options.text: Move the guidance to account-wide Instructions for Claude, and apply it to every conversation.
options.feedback: This is incorrect because account-wide instructions affect all Claude conversations, not just this client-facing Project. They are useful for general preferences, but project-specific standards belong in the Project.

options.label: D
options.text: Paste the guidance into one chat, and ask Claude to remember it for later chats.
options.feedback: This is incorrect because chats inside a Project do not automatically share context with each other. Information pasted into one chat should be added to the Project knowledge base if future chats need it.

questions.explanation:
For recurring work inside a single Project, use project instructions for standing requirements and Project knowledge for documents Claude should reference across chats. Anthropic documents that users can add project instructions through Set project instructions, and that Claude uses those instructions for chats within that Project.

A useful mental model is that a Project is a workspace with persistent resources, but individual chats inside it are still separate conversations. If a standard, template, or source document should carry forward, put it in the Project configuration rather than relying on one chat’s history. The Project name and description are for human organization, not for telling Claude how to respond.

Account-wide Instructions for Claude are better for preferences that should apply everywhere, such as a general writing style or collaboration preference. For guidance limited to one client, campaign, department, or workflow, project instructions and Project knowledge keep the configuration targeted and easier to maintain. questions.question: A wildlife rehabilitation center's grant team uses Claude to draft applications several times a month. Each application should follow the same approved boilerplate, funder-response template, tone guide, and impact metrics, but each grant should have its own focused conversation. What should the team do?

options.label: A
options.text: Create an artifact for the standards and reuse that artifact in new chats.
options.feedback: Artifacts are useful for creating and iterating on visible outputs, such as drafts or documents. They are not the best choice for making shared reference materials automatically available across multiple focused conversations.

options.label: B
options.text: Create a Project and add the shared grant materials to project knowledge.
options.feedback: This is the best fit because Projects provide a self-contained workspace with a knowledge base that can be used across chats in that project. The team can keep separate grant conversations while reusing the same approved materials and instructions.

options.label: C
options.text: Use Research mode and ask Claude to rediscover the standards each time.
options.feedback: Research mode is intended for deeper investigation and source-grounded research, not for maintaining a reusable internal reference set. Asking Claude to rediscover known standards adds unnecessary work and may not reflect the team's approved materials.

options.label: D
options.text: Use one long regular chat and keep adding each grant request there.
options.feedback: A single long chat can preserve earlier context, but it becomes harder to keep separate workstreams organized. It also does not use the documented Project feature designed for recurring work with the same reference material.

questions.explanation:
Projects are designed for recurring work that depends on the same background materials. A Project is a self-contained workspace with its own chat histories and knowledge base, so a team can keep separate conversations for separate grant applications while still giving Claude access to shared templates, examples, and instructions. See Anthropic's Help Center page on What are projects?.

For repeated use of the same documents, Anthropic also recommends Projects because reused project content can support more efficient ongoing work. The usage-limit guidance specifically recommends using Projects for anything you will reference multiple times, with core working documents uploaded to project knowledge at the start. See Usage limit best practices.

A regular chat is often fine for a one-time task, and an artifact can be valuable when Claude is producing a standalone draft or document. Research mode is better suited to deeper investigation, not to preserving an approved internal work pattern. The practical product-selection judgment is to match the feature to the work pattern: use Project knowledge when the same reference material should guide many related chats.

questions.question: A travel insurance claims team uses Claude to draft many brief status-update emails from approved templates. Most requests are routine, but a smaller set involves disputed claims that require careful wording and deeper review. The team wants fast turnaround while preserving quality where the work is more complex. Which choice best fits the task?

options.label: A
options.text: Use extended thinking for every draft and keep the same model for all claim types.
options.feedback: Extended thinking can help when deeper reasoning is needed, but applying it to every routine template draft can slow the workflow and use more tokens. It does not separate simple work from complex work.

options.label: B
options.text: Use the most capable model for every draft and review only the disputed cases afterward.
options.feedback: This may preserve quality, but it does not align well with the speed and usage goals for routine drafts. It spends higher-capability model effort on work that is mostly straightforward.

options.label: C
options.text: Use the fastest available model for all drafts and ask reviewers to fix complex cases.
options.feedback: This favors speed too heavily and risks lower-quality first drafts for disputed claims. Human review is important, but model choice should still reflect the complexity of the work.

options.label: D
options.text: Use a faster model for routine drafts and switch to a more capable model for disputed cases.
options.feedback: This matches the model to the level of work instead of treating every task the same. Routine template-based drafts benefit from speed, while disputed cases justify a more capable model because quality and reasoning matter more.

questions.explanation:
Good model selection is a practical tradeoff among speed, usage, and quality. Routine, template-driven work usually does not require the most capable model or the highest effort setting, while work involving ambiguity, risk, or careful reasoning can justify a more capable choice.

Claude lets users change the model during a conversation, and changes apply starting with Claude's next response. The model and effort controls are described in Anthropic's help article on changing the model, effort, and thinking settings.

The useful mental model is to avoid a single default for every task. Use lower-cost, faster settings where the task is repetitive and well constrained, then move to a stronger model or higher effort when the task needs deeper analysis, careful wording, or more nuanced judgment.

questions.question: A community bank's HR coordinator uses the bank's Claude for Work Team plan and wants help drafting a response about an employee's medical accommodation request. The coordinator knows commercial chats are not used for model training unless the organization explicitly opts in. What should the coordinator do before using Claude?

options.label: A
options.text: Submit the request through feedback so Anthropic can handle it as a reported item.
options.feedback: This is incorrect because feedback is not a privacy safeguard for sensitive workplace material. Explicitly reported materials, such as thumbs up or thumbs down feedback, may be used under separate rules, so it is not a way to reduce exposure.

options.label: B
options.text: Paste the full request because commercial chats are not used for training by default.
options.feedback: This is incorrect because the default training policy does not make all sensitive data appropriate to share. Medical accommodation details can still be sensitive, and the organization may control or access submitted workplace data.

options.label: C
options.text: Remove unnecessary personal details and use only approved workplace information.
options.feedback: This is correct because model training is only one privacy consideration. Sensitive employee information should still be minimized and handled according to the organization’s policies, especially because Team plan data is controlled by the customer organization.

options.label: D
options.text: Move the request into a personal Claude account to separate it from the bank workspace.
options.feedback: This is incorrect because moving regulated workplace information into a personal account can create a larger governance problem. The safer action is to follow the employer’s approved process and minimize sensitive details before using Claude.

questions.explanation:
For sensitive workplace data, the key judgment is not only whether a chat may be used for model training. In Claude for Work Team and Enterprise plans, Anthropic states that the customer organization is the Controller of user-submitted data and Anthropic acts as the Processor to provide Claude, as described in Does Anthropic act as a data processor or controller?.

That means an employee should treat Claude use as part of the organization’s governed work environment, not as a private substitute for HR systems or policy controls. Anthropic also states that commercial product data is not used to train models unless the customer chooses to participate in the Development Partner Program, but that does not remove the need to minimize medical, financial, legal, or other sensitive information.

A good practical habit is to share only what Claude needs for the task, such as a de-identified summary or policy language, and avoid unnecessary names, diagnoses, account numbers, or other regulated details. Sending sensitive content as feedback or moving it to a personal account does not solve the governance issue and can increase risk.

questions.question: An environmental policy institute uses a Claude Project to prepare recurring two-page briefing notes for city council staff. The team wants each brief to follow the same structure, separate confirmed facts from uncertainties, and avoid adding policy claims that are not supported by the Project materials. Which setup is most appropriate?

options.label: A
options.text: Store source files in Project Knowledge and let Claude infer the format and source rules.
options.feedback: Project Knowledge gives Claude background materials, but it does not replace explicit instructions about how to use them. Relying on inference is a common anti-pattern when the team needs consistent structure and boundaries.

options.label: B
options.text: Add Project instructions for brief format, source boundaries, and uncertainty handling.
options.feedback: This is correct because Project instructions are meant to guide Claude's behavior across chats within that Project. Clear, specific instructions about format, allowed sources, and uncertainty handling make the recurring workflow more consistent.

options.label: C
options.text: Use Custom Instructions to make all Claude responses accurate, concise, and helpful.
options.feedback: Custom Instructions apply broadly across Claude, so they are not the best place for detailed rules tied to one recurring Project. The wording is also too vague to enforce the institute's specific structure and source-use expectations.

options.label: D
options.text: Paste a sample brief into each chat and ask Claude to imitate its format and tone.
options.feedback: A sample can help for a single conversation, but it is less reliable as a repeatable setup. It also depends on the user remembering to provide the same guidance every time.

questions.explanation:
Project instructions are best for persistent guidance that should apply inside a particular Claude Project, such as audience, tone, response structure, and how Claude should treat the Project's knowledge. In this scenario, the team needs a repeatable briefing workflow, so the instruction should be specific enough to tell Claude how to format the brief, how to distinguish supported facts from uncertainty, and how to avoid unsupported policy claims.

Project Knowledge and instructions play different roles. Knowledge supplies the background materials Claude can draw from, while instructions tell Claude how to use those materials and what standards to follow. A sample brief or a vague global preference can be useful, but neither is as reliable as well-scoped Project instructions for recurring work. See Anthropic's help article on What are Projects? for how Projects combine knowledge, chat histories, and instructions.

questions.question: A city history museum's exhibits coordinator uses Claude with web search to draft a short label for a newly donated photograph. Claude gives a polished paragraph with exact dates, names, and a quotation attributed to a local newspaper. The label will be printed for a public exhibit. What should the coordinator do next?

options.label: A
options.text: Ask Claude to rate its certainty about the dates and quotation before approving the label.
options.feedback: A self-rated confidence score is not a substitute for checking the underlying evidence. The key issue is whether the dates and quotation are supported by reliable records, not whether Claude sounds certain about them.

options.label: B
options.text: Verify the dates, names, and quotation against the cited newspaper and museum records.
options.feedback: This is the best action because the label contains specific factual claims and an attributed quotation that will be presented publicly. Claude's citations and confident wording are useful starting points, but important claims should be checked against authoritative sources before publication.

options.label: C
options.text: Remove the citations and publish the label as general interpretive copy for visitors.
options.feedback: Removing citations reduces transparency without addressing whether the content is accurate. Public exhibit text should still be grounded in reliable records, especially when it includes names, dates, and quotations.

options.label: D
options.text: Approve the label because Claude included web citations for the names, dates, and quotation.
options.feedback: Citations do not make an output automatically correct. Claude can still misunderstand a source, cite something that does not fully support the claim, or produce authoritative-looking details that need human review.

questions.explanation:
Claude is helpful for drafting and synthesis, but it should not be treated as a single source of truth for factual material that others will rely on. Anthropic's guidance notes that Claude can produce incorrect or misleading responses, including authoritative-looking claims or quotes that are not grounded in fact, so important information should be scrutinized before use: Claude is providing incorrect or misleading responses, what's going on?

Web search citations can make review easier because they point to possible source material, but they do not remove the need for human judgment. In this scenario, the coordinator should compare the dates, names, and quoted language with the cited newspaper item and the museum's own records before approving the label.

The practical mental model is to use Claude as a drafting assistant and research accelerator, then use authoritative sources and subject-matter review for claims that affect public accuracy, compliance, safety, finances, or reputation. Asking Claude how confident it is, improving the wording, or removing citations changes the presentation, but none of those actions establishes that the underlying claims are true.

questions.question: A professional certification board wants to use Claude to draft individualized explanations of exam-accommodation decisions for candidates to read in an online portal. The board's AI policy says staff must follow Anthropic's Usage Policy. What should the board do before using this workflow?

options.label: A
options.text: Publish the explanations after checking that each draft is polite and easy to understand.
options.feedback: Tone review can improve clarity, but it does not satisfy the governance requirement for high-risk use cases. The issue is not only whether the explanation sounds appropriate, but whether qualified review and disclosure occur before candidates rely on it.

options.label: B
options.text: Use an incognito chat so the explanations are not saved in the user's chat history.
options.feedback: Incognito mode may affect chat history and retention behavior, but it does not replace policy compliance steps for high-risk use cases. The workflow still needs appropriate human review and disclosure before candidates see the output.

options.label: C
options.text: Require qualified human review and disclose the AI-assisted output before candidates see it.
options.feedback: This is the best-aligned action because academic testing, accreditation, and admissions are listed among high-risk domains in Anthropic's Usage Policy. When outputs in high-risk use cases are presented directly to individuals or consumers, the policy requires qualified human review and disclosure.

options.label: D
options.text: Ask Claude to add a short disclaimer and then post the explanations automatically.
options.feedback: A disclaimer alone is not enough for this type of workflow. The policy also requires qualified human review when high-risk outputs are presented directly to individuals or consumers.

questions.explanation:
Anthropic's Usage Policy applies to people who submit inputs to Anthropic products and services, and it includes extra requirements for high-risk use cases. The policy lists areas such as academic testing, accreditation, and admissions among high-risk domains, which fits an exam-accommodation decision workflow.

For these cases, the practical governance lesson is that Claude can help draft or organize language, but it should not become the unchecked decision communicator. When outputs are shown directly to individuals or consumers, the organization needs qualified human review and disclosure of the AI-assisted output. Politeness checks, automatic posting, or relying on a chat mode do not address the core risk, which is that people may rely on the output for an important decision affecting their opportunities or rights.

questions.question: A food bank's volunteer coordinator asks Claude for a complete volunteer orientation outline with sections for safety, client dignity, pantry workflow, and end-of-shift reporting. Claude gives a useful but too-short outline that covers safety and workflow only. The coordinator wants to improve the output without starting the task over. What should the coordinator do next?

options.label: A
options.text: Send a follow-up that only says “make it more complete” and lets Claude infer the missing sections.
options.feedback: A vague request gives Claude little guidance about what was missing or what standard to meet. It may produce more text, but it does not reliably target the omitted sections.

options.label: B
options.text: Open a new chat with the same request and compare drafts, then choose the one that happens to be longer.
options.feedback: Repeating the same prompt does not address why the first output was too short. Iteration is more effective when the user adds clarifications, constraints, or feedback.

options.label: C
options.text: Ask Claude whether the outline is complete, then use the draft if it answers with strong confidence.
options.feedback: Claude’s self-assessment is not a substitute for checking the output against the requested sections. This action does not provide the missing information needed to improve the draft.

options.label: D
options.text: Send a follow-up naming the missing sections, with the earlier prompt and draft, and ask for expansion.
options.feedback: This gives Claude clear feedback and missing context instead of asking it to guess. Including the prior prompt and draft helps Claude pick up from the incomplete answer and revise toward the requested structure.

questions.explanation:
When Claude gives an incomplete answer, the best next step is usually to iterate the prompt, not abandon the task or repeat the same request. A useful follow-up names what is missing, supplies the relevant context, and asks for a targeted revision.

Anthropic’s guidance on unhelpful prompts emphasizes clarity, context, task decomposition, and feedback, as described in My prompt isn't giving me a helpful answer. For responses that are too brief, Anthropic also recommends giving Claude the previous prompt and response when asking it to continue, as covered in Claude's response to my prompt is too brief.

The mental model is to treat Claude like a capable collaborator who improves with clearer direction. Short feedback such as make it better often leaves too much unstated, while a specific follow-up turns the first draft into useful working context.

questions.question: A performing arts center's education team is preparing next season's student matinee program. They have teacher survey comments, past attendance summaries, accessibility notes, and budget limits. They want Claude to help them improve the planning process, not simply draft promotional copy. Which approach best fits the goal?

options.label: A
options.text: Ask Claude to create a full season plan from general knowledge, then revise only the wording and layout afterward.
options.feedback: This skips the team's actual evidence and constraints, so Claude may produce a polished but poorly grounded plan. Rewording the output does not fix missing context or unreliable assumptions.

options.label: B
options.text: Have Claude write the teacher brochure first and infer planning steps from the final promotional language afterward.
options.feedback: Starting with promotional copy puts the deliverable ahead of the process analysis. It may be useful later, but it does not directly help identify bottlenecks, tradeoffs, or operational improvements.

options.label: C
options.text: Share the relevant materials and ask Claude to identify patterns, constraints, bottlenecks, and workflow priorities.
options.feedback: This uses Claude for synthesis and planning, not just content generation. Giving Claude the source materials helps it reason from the team's actual context and propose a process that can be reviewed and refined.

options.label: D
options.text: Use Claude only to format attendance summaries and keep survey, access, and budget planning outside the conversation.
options.feedback: Formatting can help prepare materials, but it underuses Claude for research, synthesis, and process optimization. The team still misses the opportunity to compare evidence, surface constraints, and draft a better workflow.

questions.explanation:
For research, planning, and process optimization, Claude is most useful when it can work from relevant context and be asked to reason across it. In this scenario, teacher feedback, attendance history, accessibility requirements, and budget limits are the inputs Claude needs to identify patterns and tradeoffs before recommending a workflow.

The strongest approach treats Claude as a planning partner: ask it to extract themes, note assumptions, surface conflicts, and propose prioritized next steps that humans can validate. This is different from asking for a polished final artifact first, which can hide weak assumptions behind fluent writing.

If the planning work will continue over time, a Claude Project can help keep the materials and conversation organized; if the team later develops a repeatable method for every season, a Skill may be appropriate for packaging that approach. Anthropic's guidance explains that Projects fit work where context accumulates, while Skills fit repeatable procedures Claude should apply across conversations: Teach Claude your way of working using skills.

questions.question: An independent publishing house's editorial operations manager has refined a reliable way to use Claude for turning manuscript feedback into one-page author memos. The approach uses the same tone guide, memo structure, examples, and quality checklist each time, but the books and conversations change. What is the most appropriate way to make this workflow easier to reuse?

options.label: A
options.text: Create a separate Claude Project for each book and store the workflow there.
options.feedback: Projects are useful when context accumulates over time within a bounded workspace, such as one book's evolving notes. They are less suitable for a reusable procedure that should be available across unrelated conversations and projects.

options.label: B
options.text: Add the full memo workflow to custom instructions for all Claude conversations.
options.feedback: Custom instructions are better for broad preferences that should affect most or all interactions with Claude. A detailed author-memo workflow is specific to one type of work and could clutter or misdirect unrelated tasks.

options.label: C
options.text: Paste the complete workflow into every new chat before drafting each memo.
options.feedback: This can work for occasional one-off use, but it preserves the repetitive setup burden the manager wants to avoid. It also increases the chance that steps, examples, or quality checks are omitted across repeated uses.

options.label: D
options.text: Package the memo workflow as a Claude Skill with its guide, examples, and checklist.
options.feedback: This is correct because the team has a repeatable procedure that should apply across different conversations and materials. A Skill is well suited for packaging task-specific instructions, examples, and standards so Claude can load them when relevant.

questions.explanation:
Claude is most useful when the way you set it up matches the nature of the work. A Project is best when a bounded effort needs accumulated context, such as notes, drafts, and decisions for a specific manuscript. A Skill is better when the team has a proven, repeatable way of doing a task that should be applied whenever that task appears, even in different chats or projects.

In this scenario, the stable requirement is not one book's background knowledge, it is the publishing house's reusable method for producing author memos. Packaging the tone guide, examples, structure, and checklist into a Skill lets Claude apply that method without the user pasting the same instructions each time. Custom instructions would be too broad because they apply generally, while repeated prompting is workable but inefficient and easier to apply inconsistently.

For more on when Skills are appropriate, see Anthropic's Teach Claude your way of working using skills tutorial and the Skills overview.

questions.question: A private language school's admissions team plans to use Claude to score applicant essays, recommend who should receive a limited scholarship, and email each applicant a personalized explanation of the decision. Which action best addresses the ethical and policy concerns?

options.label: A
options.text: Use Claude for drafting, have qualified admissions staff review before final decisions, and disclose AI assistance to applicants.
options.feedback: This is correct because scholarship and admissions decisions can directly affect individuals, so Claude should not be the sole final decision maker. A qualified human review before finalization and disclosure for applicant-facing output address the main ethical concerns.

options.label: B
options.text: Use Claude's scholarship recommendations as final unless applicants complain, then have staff reconsider decisions after the deadline.
options.feedback: This makes AI-generated recommendations the default final decision, which is not appropriate for a high-risk academic admissions context. A complaint process does not replace qualified review before the decision is finalized.

options.label: C
options.text: Anonymize applicant names, let Claude assign final scholarship rankings, and omit disclosure because essays are anonymized.
options.feedback: Anonymizing names can help reduce some privacy risks, but it does not make Claude suitable as the final decision maker. It also does not remove the need to disclose AI assistance when outputs are presented directly to applicants.

options.label: D
options.text: Ask Claude to provide confidence scores, send explanations above a chosen threshold, and review only disputed scholarship cases.
options.feedback: Claude's self-reported confidence is not a reliable safeguard for decisions that affect people. Reviewing only after a dispute comes too late, because the decision and explanation have already been delivered.

questions.explanation:
Academic admissions and scholarship allocation are examples of decisions that can materially affect an individual, so using Claude ethically means treating it as an assistant rather than an authority. Anthropic's Usage Policy identifies academic testing, accreditation, and admissions as High-Risk Use Cases, and requires qualified professional review before advice, recommendations, or subjective decisions are disseminated or finalized in such domains.

Disclosure also matters when AI-generated output is presented directly to individuals or consumers. questions.question: A regional dental network's operations manager is using Claude to design and iterate an internal patient-referral workflow over several weeks. She wants separate chats for process map revisions, staff FAQ drafts, and pilot-feedback summaries, while keeping each chat aligned to the same approved assumptions and formatting standards. What should she do?

options.label: A
options.text: Use regular chats, paste the assumptions each time, and rely on Claude to infer the formatting standards.
options.feedback: This can work for one-off tasks, but it adds repeated setup effort and increases the chance of drift. It also leaves formatting standards implicit, which makes iteration less reliable.

options.label: B
options.text: Start one detailed chat, upload the assumptions there, and ask Claude to remember them in later chats.
options.feedback: Ordinary chat context does not automatically carry into other chats. This approach risks inconsistent outputs when the manager opens separate chats for different parts of the workflow.

options.label: C
options.text: Create a project, put the assumptions in the project description, and start a new chat for each workstream.
options.feedback: A project can organize the work, but Claude does not use the project name or description as working context. Important assumptions need to be placed where Claude can actually use them, such as project knowledge or project instructions.

options.label: D
options.text: Create a project, add approved assumptions to project knowledge, and place formatting standards in project instructions.
options.feedback: This keeps reusable context available across chats in the same project. Project knowledge and project instructions are the right places for shared background and recurring requirements.

questions.explanation:
For ongoing solution design work, a Claude Project is useful when several related chats need the same background. Project knowledge is shared across chats in that project, and project instructions apply to all chats in that project, so they are well suited for approved assumptions, recurring standards, and stable requirements. Ordinary chat history is not shared from one chat to another unless the information is added to project knowledge.

The project name and description are mainly for organization and are not visible to Claude as working context, so they should not be used as the only place for requirements. The better mental model is: use project knowledge for reference material Claude should draw from, use project instructions for how Claude should behave within that project, and use individual chats for separate design, review, and iteration tasks. See Anthropic's help articles on creating and managing projects and Claude's personalization features.

questions.question: A university grants office asks Claude to draft eligibility guidance for a new federal funding program. Claude returns a clear memo with exact deadline dates and a quoted sentence from the program notice. The memo will be sent to department administrators who will use it to decide whether to apply. What should the grants officer do next?

options.label: A
options.text: Ask Claude to rewrite the key dates, eligibility rules, and quote more cautiously.
options.feedback: A more cautious tone may reduce overconfidence, but it does not establish whether the facts are correct. The risk is factual accuracy, not just wording or style.

options.label: B
options.text: Share the key dates, eligibility rules, and quote because they are specific.
options.feedback: Specific details can make an output look credible, but specificity does not prove accuracy. Sending the memo without checking could spread incorrect deadlines or eligibility guidance.

options.label: C
options.text: Compare the key dates, eligibility rules, and quote with the official notice.
options.feedback: This is the safest next step because the memo contains specific factual claims that will guide funding decisions. Claude can produce authoritative-looking details that are wrong, so important claims should be checked against the official source before use.

options.label: D
options.text: Ask Claude to score the key dates, eligibility rules, and quote for confidence.
options.feedback: Claude's self-reported confidence is not a reliable substitute for checking the source material. A confident answer can still contain hallucinated or misleading details.

questions.explanation:
Human review or additional verification is required when Claude's output contains high-impact factual claims, especially dates, eligibility requirements, quotations, citations, or instructions that other people will rely on. In this scenario, the memo affects whether departments pursue funding, so the grants officer should compare the important details with the official program notice before distributing it.

Claude is useful for drafting and organizing information, but it should not be treated as a single source of truth. Anthropic notes that Claude can produce incorrect or misleading responses, including authoritative-looking claims that are not grounded in fact, as described in Claude is providing incorrect or misleading responses, what's going on?. The right mental model is to use Claude to accelerate the first draft, then use authoritative sources and human judgment to validate anything consequential.

Rewriting, confidence scoring, or polished formatting can improve presentation, but none of those actions confirms that the quoted language or deadline is real. Verification is most important when an error would cause compliance, financial, safety, legal, or reputational harm.

questions.question: A pharmaceutical market access team is using Claude to synthesize a one-time executive memo from several conflicting payer interview summaries. The memo will guide a pricing recommendation, and the team can tolerate a slower response and higher usage if the reasoning is more careful. Which choice best fits the task?

options.label: A
options.text: Use a faster, lower-cost model with a low effort setting for the synthesis.
options.feedback: This prioritizes speed and usage savings over the reasoning quality the team needs. Faster, lower-cost choices are better suited to routine or high-volume tasks where deep analysis is less important.

options.label: B
options.text: Use the current default model and prioritize the shortest possible response.
options.feedback: This may save time, but it does not intentionally align the model choice with the task's quality needs. Asking for the shortest response can also reduce the space Claude has to explain tradeoffs and uncertainty.

options.label: C
options.text: Use separate new chats for each source and combine the first outputs.
options.feedback: This can make the work faster in pieces, but it risks losing the cross-source context needed to reconcile conflicts. Combining first outputs without deeper synthesis is not a good fit for a recommendation with significant consequences.

options.label: D
options.text: Use a more capable model with a higher effort setting for the synthesis.
options.feedback: This matches the task because the team values careful reasoning and quality over speed and usage. A more capable model and higher effort setting are appropriate when the work involves nuanced synthesis and important judgment.

questions.explanation:
Model selection is a practical tradeoff among speed, usage, and quality. For a nuanced executive memo that must reconcile conflicting inputs, it is reasonable to spend more time and usage on a more capable model and a higher Effort setting.

Claude’s model menu lets users change the model and, for supported models, choose how much effort Claude applies to a response. Anthropic notes that higher effort can produce more thorough responses, but takes longer and uses more tokens, so it should be reserved for tasks where that extra reasoning is worth the cost. See Change the model, effort, and thinking settings.

The incorrect choices all optimize the wrong thing for this situation. Lower effort, shortest-possible answers, or splitting context across separate chats may be useful for some simple drafting or speed-sensitive work, but they do not fit a task where the main risk is poor synthesis of conflicting information.

questions.question: A logistics company's operations lead asks Claude to turn a detailed incident report into a short update for warehouse shift supervisors. Claude's draft is accurate, but it reads like an executive summary and does not make the immediate next-shift actions easy to find. What is the most appropriate next step?

options.label: A
options.text: Ask Claude to improve the response without giving more audience direction.
options.feedback: A vague improvement request may lead to changes, but it does not tell Claude what better means for this audience. Clearer feedback about tone, format, and reader needs is more likely to produce a useful revision.

options.label: B
options.text: Give Claude targeted feedback on audience, tone, length, and action format.
options.feedback: This is the best next step because the output is factually useful but poorly matched to its audience and purpose. Claude works best when the user refines the prompt with clearer instructions, added context, and specific feedback.

options.label: C
options.text: Share the draft as written because the incident details are already accurate.
options.feedback: Accuracy alone does not make an output fit for purpose. The intended readers need a usable shift update, so the user should adapt the style and structure before sharing it.

options.label: D
options.text: Change the project name to describe the warehouse shift-supervisor audience.
options.feedback: Changing a project name is not a reliable way to guide Claude's output. Project names and descriptions are not the place to provide the reusable working context Claude should apply inside project chats.

questions.explanation:
When an output is accurate but not useful for the intended readers, the best move is to iterate with clearer direction rather than accept it as final. Claude is designed for conversational refinement, so a user can say what audience the draft is for, what tone it should use, how long it should be, and what format would help the reader act on it.

Anthropic's guidance emphasizes speaking naturally, being specific, and refining through follow-up prompts when the first answer misses the mark. In this scenario, asking for a concise supervisor update with visible next-shift actions gives Claude concrete criteria to revise against, while a vague request such as make this better leaves too much unspecified. See Get started with Claude and My prompt isn't giving me a helpful answer.

Account, project, and skill features can help with recurring patterns, but they do not replace evaluating whether a specific output fits its audience. Project guidance should be supplied through project instructions or project knowledge, not inferred from a project name. For more on those distinctions, see Understanding Claude's personalization features and How can I create and manage projects?.

questions.question: A renewable energy cooperative's member services team is using Claude to create a launch packet for a new home-battery program. The packet needs a member FAQ, staff call script, enrollment checklist, and manager briefing, based on a tariff summary, eligibility notes, installation timeline, and brand voice guide. Which TWO prompting approaches best apply task decomposition to this request?

options.label: A
options.text: Ask Claude to draft the FAQ, script, checklist, and briefing in one response, then refine only sections that seem weak afterward.
options.feedback: This is a plausible shortcut, but it does not decompose the task before drafting. Waiting until the end to find weak sections makes it easier for important constraints to be missed across the packet.

options.label: B
options.text: Ask Claude to list needed inputs, constraints, and deliverables first, then draft one deliverable at a time from the uploaded materials.
options.feedback: This breaks the complex request into manageable pieces before asking for final content. Listing inputs and constraints first helps catch missing or conflicting information before Claude drafts multiple deliverables.

options.label: C
options.text: Ask Claude to create a brief plan that separates source review, outline approval, drafting, and final consistency checks before generating final copy.
options.feedback: This structures the work into clear stages and gives the team a chance to review the approach early. Separating review, drafting, and checking reduces the risk that Claude will overlook source materials or mix requirements across deliverables.

options.label: D
options.text: Ask Claude to use general knowledge for any missing tariff, eligibility, or timeline details so the packet can be completed without follow-up.
options.feedback: This encourages Claude to fill gaps instead of identifying what is unknown. For a program launch packet, missing eligibility, tariff, or timeline details should be clarified or verified against provided materials.

questions.explanation:
For complex workplace requests, a strong prompt often starts by turning one large assignment into smaller steps: identify the needed inputs, confirm constraints, outline the deliverables, draft in sections, and then check for consistency. This gives Claude a clearer path and gives the human user natural review points before the work becomes a polished final answer.

The useful mental model is to treat Claude like a capable coworker who still needs a well-scoped assignment. A prompt such as first list the inputs, constraints, and deliverables helps reveal gaps before Claude writes member-facing material. The official Getting started with Claude.ai tutorial emphasizes providing clear prompts and relevant context, which is especially important when several source documents and audiences are involved.

Asking for everything at once can work for simple tasks, but it is riskier when a single request spans FAQs, scripts, checklists, and briefings. Asking Claude to invent missing program details is also an anti-pattern because it can turn uncertainty into confident but unsupported content.

questions.question: A city museum's exhibits team asks Claude with web search enabled to draft a wall label for a new photography exhibit. Claude returns a polished paragraph with a direct quote attributed to the photographer and a claim that “critics widely view the series as a rejection of her community’s traditions,” citing two arts blogs. The label will be printed for visitors. What should the team do before approving it?

options.label: A
options.text: Ask Claude to restate the label in more neutral language before relying on the quote or interpretation.
options.feedback: Changing tone can reduce apparent bias, but it does not establish whether the quote exists or whether the interpretation is supported. It may preserve a false claim in more careful wording.

options.label: B
options.text: Remove the source links and publish the paragraph as an unattributed exhibit summary.
options.feedback: Removing citations makes the claim harder to audit. It does not address whether Claude invented a quote or overstated a pattern from limited sources.

options.label: C
options.text: Ask Claude to confirm the cited quote and interpretation before approving the exhibit label.
options.feedback: Claude can repeat or reinforce its own mistake when asked to check itself. Self-checking can help with drafting, but it is not a substitute for reviewing source material.

options.label: D
options.text: Review original sources and authoritative materials before relying on the quote or interpretation.
options.feedback: This checks both factual accuracy and possible bias in Claude’s framing. Direct quotes and broad interpretive claims should be verified against original sources or authoritative materials before public use.

questions.explanation:
Claude can produce incorrect or misleading responses, including authoritative-sounding quotes or interpretations that are not grounded in the cited material. Anthropic describes this as hallucination and cautions users not to rely on Claude as a singular source of truth, especially when the output will guide important decisions or public communication: Claude is providing incorrect or misleading responses. What’s going on?

Web search can make an answer more grounded by adding citations and links, but citations are not a guarantee that Claude’s synthesis captured the source accurately or completely. For a public exhibit label, the practical validation step is to check the cited pages, compare them with authoritative materials such as the artist’s own statements or museum records, and look for whether the interpretation fairly represents the evidence.

This is also a bias check. A claim about a photographer’s relationship to a community can oversimplify or stereotype if it rests on limited sources, so the team should examine source quality and context before adopting the framing. Anthropic’s web search guidance similarly advises reviewing cited sources and using authoritative sources for critical decisions: Enable and use web search.

questions.question: A regional insurance agency is piloting Claude with account managers who prepare renewal summaries from policy notes, claim histories, and standard templates. Several executives want a simple rollout message for staff. Which message best communicates Claude's value and limitations for this workflow?

options.label: A
options.text: Use Claude to replace account manager expertise, then rely on its confidence level to decide which summaries need review.
options.feedback: This frames Claude as a replacement for human expertise rather than an assistant. A confident tone or self-reported confidence is not a dependable accuracy signal, especially for business facts and client-facing work.

options.label: B
options.text: Use Claude only for spelling and grammar edits, then keep all summary organization and comparison work outside Claude.
options.feedback: This understates Claude's practical value for knowledge work. Claude can help organize notes, compare materials, and produce draft summaries, as long as users provide appropriate context and review the results.

options.label: C
options.text: Use Claude to draft and organize summaries from approved materials, then have account managers verify details and apply final judgment.
options.feedback: This message sets a realistic expectation: Claude can speed up drafting, structuring, and synthesis when given relevant context. It also makes clear that humans remain responsible for checking accuracy and making professional decisions.

options.label: D
options.text: Use Claude to complete renewal summaries independently, then send the outputs directly once the formatting matches the template.
options.feedback: This overstates Claude's reliability and treats formatting as a substitute for factual review. Claude can produce polished text that still contains incorrect or unsupported details.

questions.explanation:
The strongest stakeholder message positions Claude as a productivity assistant, not an autonomous decision maker. In this workflow, Claude can help turn approved notes, templates, and histories into a clearer first draft, which can reduce repetitive writing and improve consistency. The tradeoff is that Claude may still misunderstand context, omit important qualifications, or generate statements that sound plausible but need verification.

A good rollout message should explain both the value and the operating model: staff provide the right materials, Claude drafts or organizes the work, and accountable employees review the output before it is used. Features such as Projects and Skills can help standardize repeatable procedures, but they do not remove the need for human review. Anthropic's Skills guidance describes Skills as a way to package repeatable approaches so Claude can apply them when relevant, which is useful for consistency rather than a guarantee of correctness: Teach Claude your way of working using skills.

Stakeholders also need clear expectations about data handling. Teams should follow their organization's rules about client or regulated information and avoid pasting sensitive data unless they are authorized to do so. Anthropic's privacy guidance for commercial products explains how data use and feedback work, which is relevant when communicating responsible use to staff: Is my data used for model training?.
