questions.question: A language school’s admissions coordinator asks Claude, “Make this email sound better,” then pastes a rough reply to a prospective student. Claude’s draft is polished, but it promises scholarship deadlines the school has not confirmed and uses a tone that feels too sales-focused. What is the best troubleshooting step before asking Claude for another draft?

options.label: A
options.text: Tell Claude to make the next message more persuasive and fill any missing school details.
options.feedback: This encourages Claude to prioritize persuasion over accuracy. Letting Claude fill gaps is especially risky when the message could imply commitments about scholarships or deadlines.

options.label: B
options.text: Ask Claude to generate several versions and choose the one with the most polished wording.
options.feedback: Generating more drafts can help with style, but it does not fix missing constraints or unverified claims. A polished version can still contain invented or inappropriate details if the prompt remains vague.

options.label: C
options.text: Revise the prompt with confirmed facts, audience, tone, and a rule to flag unknowns.
options.feedback: This addresses the likely cause of the poor output: the prompt left too much for Claude to infer. Giving Claude the confirmed facts, audience, tone guidance, and a rule for uncertain details makes the next draft more likely to stay accurate and useful.

options.label: D
options.text: Switch to the most capable model and keep the original prompt unchanged for the next draft.
options.feedback: A stronger model can help with complex tasks, but it cannot reliably infer school-specific facts that were not provided. Troubleshooting should first improve the task instructions and source information.

questions.explanation:
When Claude gives a polished but unreliable answer, the issue is often not fluency, it is underspecified prompting. A request like Make this email sound better leaves Claude to infer the audience, voice, allowed claims, and what to do when facts are missing.

The practical fix is to tighten the prompt: provide the confirmed facts, describe the reader, state the desired tone, and ask Claude to mark or ask about unknown details instead of inventing them. This matches Anthropic’s guidance to be clear and direct when giving Claude a task, including context and constraints that shape a useful response: Be clear and direct.

Regenerating several drafts or choosing a more capable model may improve wording, but neither directly corrects the missing guardrails. Asking for more persuasion can make the problem worse because it rewards confident-sounding language even when the underlying facts are not established.

questions.question: A community food bank’s volunteer coordination team uses Claude for Work to prepare monthly distribution plans. Coordinators need Claude to use the same safety procedures, partner-site rules, and planning checklist, while keeping each coordinator’s exploratory planning chat private unless they choose to share it. Which two actions best integrate Claude into this workflow?

options.label: A
options.text: Put the planning checklist in the Project name and description so Claude uses it as ongoing context.
options.feedback: This is incorrect because the project name and description are not available to Claude as context. Reusable instructions should be placed in project instructions, and reusable reference content should be placed in Project Knowledge.

options.label: B
options.text: Set project instructions that tell Claude how to structure each monthly distribution plan and checklist review.
options.feedback: This is correct because project instructions apply across chats within the Project and help tailor Claude’s behavior and response format. They are appropriate for reusable workflow guidance, such as how to organize plans or apply a planning checklist.

options.label: C
options.text: Rely on previous planning chats in the Project to automatically inform every coordinator’s future chats.
options.feedback: This is incorrect because ordinary Project chat context is not automatically shared across all chats in a Project. Reusable workflow context should be placed in Project Knowledge or project instructions rather than depending on prior chats to carry the team’s standards forward.

options.label: D
options.text: Create a shared Project for the team and add the procedures, site rules, and checklist to Project Knowledge.
options.feedback: This is correct because Projects are designed as organized workspaces for related work, and Project Knowledge is the place to make shared reference materials available across chats in that Project. On Claude for Work, a Project can be shared with organization members while individual chats remain private unless explicitly shared.

questions.explanation:
Projects are a practical way for a non-technical team to make Claude part of an ongoing workflow without building an integration or redesigning systems. A Project gives the team a workspace for related work, while Project Knowledge holds the shared materials Claude should use across chats, such as procedures, templates, and reference documents. See Anthropic’s overview of What are Projects?.

A useful mental model is to separate stable workflow context from individual working conversations. Stable items belong in Project Knowledge or project instructions, while exploratory chats can remain separate. Anthropic notes in How can I create and manage Projects? that ordinary context from one Project chat is not automatically shared across all other chats in the Project, so teams should put reusable workflow context in Project Knowledge or project instructions rather than relying on prior chats.

For collaboration, sharing the Project does not mean every draft conversation becomes visible to everyone. On Claude for Work, Project sharing can provide access to project contents, knowledge, and instructions, while chats inside a shared Project remain private unless a user explicitly shares a chat snapshot. This distinction is covered in Project visibility and sharing.

questions.question: A city library system's adult learning team asks Claude to prepare a public workshop package for a new digital-literacy series. The package must include a one-page flyer, instructor agenda, registration reminder email, and post-session survey, using a grant requirement summary, branch schedule, accessibility guidelines, and tone guide. The first prompt, “Make the workshop materials from these files,” produces uneven drafts and misses several source details. What is the most effective next prompt?

options.label: A
options.text: Ask Claude to identify the required inputs and outputs first, then draft each material in sequence for review.
options.feedback: This approach breaks the complex request into smaller steps before producing the final materials. It helps Claude use the provided sources more deliberately and gives the user chances to catch missing constraints before errors spread across multiple deliverables.

options.label: B
options.text: Ask Claude to rewrite the entire package in a warmer tone and keep the response shorter.
options.feedback: This may improve style, but it does not address the missed details from the source materials. A shorter, warmer rewrite can still omit grant, schedule, or accessibility requirements.

options.label: C
options.text: Ask Claude to make reasonable assumptions about any missing details and produce a polished final version.
options.feedback: This encourages Claude to fill gaps rather than checking the supplied materials or asking for clarification. For work tied to grant requirements and accessibility guidelines, assumptions can create inaccurate or noncompliant output.

options.label: D
options.text: Ask Claude to combine all four materials into one document so the package is easier to edit.
options.feedback: Combining the outputs may make editing convenient, but it does not improve how Claude reasons through the task. The main issue is that the request needs clearer stages, source checking, and review points.

questions.explanation:
For a complex request with several deliverables and several source documents, a strong prompt should help Claude work through the task in manageable stages. Asking Claude to first identify the needed inputs and outputs creates a shared plan before drafting begins, which reduces the chance that important constraints are skipped.

This is a practical form of task decomposition: separate planning, source review, drafting, and review rather than asking for everything at once. Claude can still produce the final materials, but the user remains responsible for checking that grant requirements, schedules, accessibility guidance, and tone standards are correctly reflected.

Style-focused rewrites, assumptions, or document merging may be useful later, but they do not solve the core problem of an overly broad prompt. Anthropic’s guidance for getting started with Claude emphasizes being specific about the task and providing useful context, which is especially important when a request has multiple parts: Getting started with Claude.ai.

questions.question: A medical device manufacturer’s training team uses a Claude Project to create internal lesson plans from approved procedure documents. The team wants every chat in the Project to use the same lesson format, flag missing source information, and avoid adding steps not found in the approved materials. Which setup is most appropriate?

options.label: A
options.text: Put the workflow in global custom instructions so every Claude task uses the same role, sections, and source-use rules.
options.feedback: Global custom instructions are better for broad preferences that should apply everywhere. A specialized lesson-plan workflow is more appropriate inside the relevant Project so it does not affect unrelated Claude tasks.

options.label: B
options.text: Add project instructions that define Claude’s role, required sections, source-use rules, and when to ask clarifying questions.
options.feedback: This is correct because stable guidance that should apply across chats belongs in the Project’s instructions. Clear role, structure, source-use, and clarification rules help Claude follow the team’s workflow consistently without requiring the user to restate it every time.

options.label: C
options.text: Create a new chat each time and include only the latest source files, without persistent project instructions.
options.feedback: Starting fresh chats can help keep context focused, but it does not preserve the team’s recurring standards by itself. Without persistent instructions, each user must remember to restate the same rules and may do so inconsistently.

options.label: D
options.text: Upload a sample lesson and rely on Claude to infer the role, required sections, source-use rules, and clarification triggers.
options.feedback: A sample can be useful context, but relying on inference is less reliable than writing explicit instructions. Claude may imitate visible formatting while missing rules such as when to flag gaps or avoid unsupported additions.

questions.explanation:
Project instructions are the right place for recurring, project-specific rules such as Claude’s role, output format, source-grounding expectations, and when to ask clarifying questions. They guide chats within that Project while the Project knowledge provides the approved materials Claude should use as context.

Effective system-level instructions should be specific and operational: tell Claude what to do, what to avoid, how to structure the answer, and how to handle missing information. This is different from simply uploading examples, because examples may show a pattern but do not reliably communicate rules such as do not invent unsupported procedure steps.

Custom instructions are useful for broad personal preferences, while Projects are designed as focused workspaces with their own knowledge and instructions. See Anthropic’s help article on What are Projects? for how Projects combine chat history, knowledge, and project-level instructions.

questions.question: A university career services office is setting up a Claude Project for employer outreach. Staff will open new chats throughout the semester, and they want Claude to consistently follow the office’s email style while using current sponsor tiers, event dates, and an approval checklist. Which setup best supports this work?

options.label: A
options.text: Put the email style and source materials in the first chat and ask staff to refer back to it.
options.feedback: Ordinary chat context is not shared across new chats in a project. Information that should be reused across project chats needs to be added to project knowledge or project instructions.

options.label: B
options.text: Add the office preferences to account-wide profile settings and paste source materials only as needed.
options.feedback: Account-wide preferences are broader than this project and are not the best place for project-specific style rules. Pasting materials repeatedly can work for one-off chats, but it does not create a consistent shared knowledge base for the project.

options.label: C
options.text: Place the background details in the project name and description and leave the knowledge base empty.
options.feedback: A project’s name and description are for organizing the project, not for giving Claude working context. If Claude needs to use the details, they should be placed where Claude can use them, such as project instructions or project knowledge.

options.label: D
options.text: Set the email style in project instructions and add the tiers, dates, and checklist to project knowledge.
options.feedback: This separates behavior guidance from reusable reference material. Project instructions apply across chats in the project, while project knowledge gives Claude shared context for chats in that workspace.

questions.explanation:
Project instructions and project knowledge serve different purposes. Instructions tell Claude how to behave or respond in every chat inside that project, while knowledge supplies reusable source material that Claude can draw on for chats in the project. In this scenario, the email style is a behavior rule, while sponsor tiers, dates, and approval steps are reference materials.

A useful mental model is that a Project is a focused workspace, not just a folder name. Details placed only in a project’s name, description, or a prior chat should not be treated as reliable context for future chats. To make reusable information available across project chats, add it to the project knowledge base, and to make Claude follow a recurring working style, use Set project instructions. questions.question: A regional aquarium's visitor experience coordinator gives Claude a folder of exhibit notes and asks, "Make a school handout for tomorrow." The draft is attractive, but it mixes facts from several exhibits, invents a feeding schedule, and lacks a clear activity flow for teachers. Which two troubleshooting actions should the coordinator take before asking for the next draft?

options.label: A
options.text: Switch to the most capable available model and keep the same request unchanged.
options.feedback: This is incorrect because a stronger model can still produce poor output when the task is vague. Model choice may help complex tasks, but it does not replace clear instructions, relevant context, and verification.

options.label: B
options.text: Rewrite the prompt with the audience, exhibit scope, required sections, and source-only constraint.
options.feedback: This is correct because the original request is too broad for a reliable handout. Adding audience, scope, structure, and source boundaries gives Claude clearer criteria for what to include and what to avoid.

options.label: C
options.text: Ask Claude to extract the relevant facts and outline the handout before drafting it.
options.feedback: This is correct because separating fact selection from writing makes errors easier to catch early. An outline step also helps ensure the activity flow fits the teacher-facing purpose before Claude polishes the final handout.

options.label: D
options.text: Resubmit the same request with "be accurate" added at the end.
options.feedback: This is incorrect because a general accuracy reminder does not define which facts are allowed or how the handout should be organized. It is a weak fix for a prompt that needs clearer source boundaries and task structure.

questions.explanation:
When Claude gives a polished but unreliable result, the best troubleshooting move is usually to improve the task definition, not just ask for a nicer rewrite. The coordinator should specify who the handout is for, which exhibit notes are in scope, what sections are required, and whether Claude should use only the provided material or flag gaps instead of filling them in.

Breaking the work into stages is also useful. Asking Claude to extract relevant facts and propose an outline first creates a checkpoint before the final draft, which helps catch mixed sources, missing flow, or unsupported claims while they are still easy to fix.

Changing model, effort, or thinking settings can be helpful for harder work, but those settings do not compensate for unclear instructions or unverified source use. Anthropic's guidance emphasizes communicating with Claude through prompts and being specific about the problem or question, as described in changing the model, effort, and thinking settings and the general Claude help documentation at Claude Support.

questions.question: A regional insurance brokerage's HR team has pasted anonymized employee survey comments into Claude. The HR director needs a compact comparison of top themes for tomorrow's leadership meeting, plus a longer manager discussion guide with agenda, talking points, and a follow-up checklist that will be revised before rollout. Which TWO requests best match the output format to these needs?

options.label: A
options.text: Return the manager discussion guide as a short inline paragraph and handle revisions in later chat replies.
options.feedback: This is incorrect because the guide needs an agenda, talking points, and a checklist, which are easier to review as a structured document. Keeping it as a short paragraph would sacrifice the organization and reusability the team needs.

options.label: B
options.text: Return the theme comparison as a concise table in chat with columns for theme, evidence, and owner.
options.feedback: This is correct because the leadership need is a compact comparison, not a substantial standalone deliverable. A structured table in the chat organizes the information clearly without adding unnecessary artifact overhead.

options.label: C
options.text: Create the theme comparison as a standalone artifact because any table should be kept outside the chat.
options.feedback: This is incorrect because artifacts are not required for every structured table. A small comparison table can be effective directly in the chat when the output is brief and mainly for immediate reference.

options.label: D
options.text: Create the manager discussion guide as a Markdown artifact with sections the team can revise before rollout.
options.feedback: This is correct because the manager guide is longer, self-contained, and likely to be edited and reused. Those qualities match when Claude should create an artifact rather than keep everything inline.

questions.explanation:
Good output evaluation includes choosing a format that fits how people will use the result. For a quick leadership comparison, structured data such as a concise table can make themes, evidence, and ownership easy to scan directly in the conversation.

Artifacts are better reserved for substantial, self-contained work that someone is likely to edit, iterate on, reuse, or refer back to later. The Claude Help Center describes artifacts as appropriate for significant content, typically over 15 lines, that can stand on its own, such as Markdown documents and other reusable outputs: What are artifacts and how do I use them?.

The common anti-pattern is treating artifacts as the default for every output, or avoiding them when the work is clearly becoming a reusable document. Claude for Work frames tools such as Artifacts and Projects around organizing work and collaborating on content, so the practical question is not whether a format is impressive, but whether it helps the team review and use the output effectively: Claude for Work.

questions.question: An urban planning consultancy is using Claude to prepare a client proposal. A coordinator tries to paste a very large set of interview notes into one chat and receives a length-limit error, but the team still wants future proposal chats to use the final themes, client constraints, and agreed writing style. What should the coordinator do next?

options.label: A
options.text: Break notes into smaller relevant sections and store summaries in Project knowledge.
options.feedback: This addresses the immediate length-limit problem by reducing or restructuring what Claude needs to process at once. Saving durable summaries in Project knowledge also makes the key context available across future chats in that Project.

options.label: B
options.text: Put the client constraints in the Project name and continue in new chats.
options.feedback: Project names and descriptions help users organize work, but they are not available to Claude as working context. Important constraints should be placed in Project knowledge or Project instructions instead.

options.label: C
options.text: Start an incognito chat and paste the full notes again for a fresh context.
options.feedback: A new chat may help when an existing conversation has grown too long, but incognito does not make an oversized input fit. Incognito chats also are not saved to chat history or memory, so they are a poor place to preserve reusable proposal context.

options.label: D
options.text: Increase the usage limit and resend the entire notes file in the same chat.
options.feedback: Usage limits and length limits are different. More usage over time does not necessarily let one oversized message fit into a single chat context.

questions.explanation:
Length limits are about how much information Claude can work with in a single chat, not how much you are allowed to use Claude over time. When a message is too large, the practical move is to reduce or restructure the input, for example by breaking it into smaller chunks, summarizing key sections, or starting a new conversation with only the relevant material.

For work that should carry forward across related conversations, a Project is the better persistence mechanism. Project knowledge lets you store documents, summaries, and other context for use in chats within that Project, while ordinary chat context is tied to the specific conversation. The important caveat is that context from one Project chat is not automatically shared with another unless it is added to the Project knowledge base.

Putting facts in a Project name is not enough because Claude does not use the Project name or description as working context. Incognito is also the wrong fit for reusable work because it is designed for temporary conversations, not for building a persistent workspace. See Anthropic’s guidance on usage and length limits, troubleshooting Claude error messages, and creating and managing Projects.

questions.question: A performing arts venue's operations manager wants Claude to draft a quick troubleshooting guide for volunteer ushers using new ticket-scanner tablets during events. The operations manager has the venue’s ticket-scanner SOP and scanner FAQ available. The first prompt, “Write tablet instructions,” produced a broad answer that was not useful during a live shift. What is the best next prompt?

options.label: A
options.text: Ask Claude to write perfect tablet instructions for event staff, using a friendlier tone and adding anything it thinks is useful.
options.feedback: This still relies on vague wording and a broad quality goal instead of supplying the context Claude needs. Asking for a “perfect” answer is not a substitute for explaining the audience, materials, format, and constraints.

options.label: B
options.text: Upload the SOP and FAQ, then request a complete summary of the documents without naming the user group.
options.feedback: Providing materials helps, but asking for a general summary does not match the practical troubleshooting task. Without naming the audience and desired format, Claude may produce a document that is accurate but not usable for ushers during events.

options.label: C
options.text: Use the SOP and scanner FAQ to create a one-page usher guide with setup steps, common errors, escalation, and a checklist.
options.feedback: This prompt gives Claude the source materials, audience, format, and the specific content needed for the task. It makes the desired output concrete enough for Claude to produce something usable rather than a generic set of instructions.

options.label: D
options.text: Have Claude draft the guide from general tablet knowledge, then replace any inaccurate venue details after volunteers test it.
options.feedback: This approach invites Claude to fill gaps from general knowledge, which is risky for venue-specific procedures. Testing with volunteers can be useful later, but the first improvement should be giving Claude the right context and instructions.

questions.explanation:
Effective prompting is less about finding a special phrase and more about giving Claude the same kind of context you would give a capable new coworker. Anthropic’s prompt design guidance explains that Claude can follow natural-language instructions, but you should state clearly what you want it to do and provide the background it would not otherwise know: Introduction to prompt design.

For this task, the useful prompt names the source materials, the audience, the output format, and the required sections. That combination turns a broad request into an executable assignment, so Claude can shape the answer for volunteers using tablets during an event rather than producing generic device advice.

When a first response is weak, Anthropic recommends being clearer, adding context, breaking complex requests into steps, and iterating with feedback rather than relying on a magic phrase: My prompt isn’t giving me a helpful answer. Prompting best practices also emphasize being specific about format and constraints, especially when order or completeness matters: Use XML tags.

questions.question: A bicycle repair cooperative's training lead has a one-time workshop outline and wants Claude to turn it into a polished participant handout. The lead wants to review the handout beside the conversation, ask for revisions, and download the final version, but does not need an ongoing workspace for future chats. Which Claude feature choice best fits this task?

options.label: A
options.text: Use a regular chat and ask Claude to create the handout as an artifact.
options.feedback: This is the best fit because the task is a one-time deliverable that benefits from a separate, editable work area. Artifacts are designed for working with generated content beside the chat, iterating on it, and exporting it for use elsewhere.

options.label: B
options.text: Use a regular chat and track revisions only through chat replies.
options.feedback: A regular chat can work for simple drafting, but it is less convenient when the user wants a standalone handout to revise and download. Keeping every version only in chat replies does not use the product feature built for visible deliverables.

options.label: C
options.text: Create a new Project and use only its name to steer the handout.
options.feedback: A Project is useful when chats need shared project knowledge or instructions over time. The project name and description are not working context for Claude, so naming a Project would not by itself guide the handout.

options.label: D
options.text: Start Research mode and ask Claude to investigate the topic from scratch.
options.feedback: Research mode is better suited to deeper, source-grounded investigation when the task requires gathering and synthesizing information. This scenario already has the workshop outline and mainly needs a polished deliverable.

questions.explanation:
When the goal is a single polished deliverable, a regular chat plus an artifact is usually the right product choice. Artifacts give Claude a dedicated space for content such as documents, allowing the user to review and iterate on the work without treating the task as an ongoing knowledge workspace.

Projects are better for recurring or sustained work where project knowledge and project instructions should apply across multiple chats. The Help Center explains that Projects are self-contained workspaces with their own chat histories and knowledge bases, and that project knowledge and instructions apply within the project, see What are projects? and How can I create and manage projects?. Creating a Project just for a one-time handout adds structure the scenario does not need, and relying on the Project name would be especially ineffective because Claude does not use the name and description as working context.

Research is useful when the user needs Claude to perform deeper source-grounded investigation. Here, the material already exists, so the main need is presentation and revision, not investigation. For a handout that needs to be revised beside the conversation and downloaded, the documented artifact workflow is the better match, see publishing and sharing artifacts.

questions.question: An independent film studio’s payroll coordinator uses Claude with web search to summarize state payroll rules for hiring temporary crew members. Claude returns a clear table with state-specific thresholds, dates, and source links. The coordinator plans to send the table to producers who will use it when budgeting shoots. What is the most appropriate next step?

options.label: A
options.text: Remove the state-specific citations and share only plain-language recommendations.
options.feedback: Removing citations makes the output harder to verify and does not improve accuracy. For compliance-related information, keeping traceable sources and checking them is more appropriate than simplifying away the evidence.

options.label: B
options.text: Check the state-specific rules with official agency sources or a payroll specialist before sharing.
options.feedback: This is the safest next step because the output contains specific rules, dates, and thresholds that could affect compliance and budgeting. Claude’s citations are useful starting points, but important claims should still be checked against authoritative sources or reviewed by a qualified person.

options.label: C
options.text: Ask Claude to soften the state-specific payroll guidance before sharing the table.
options.feedback: Changing the tone may reduce overconfidence, but it does not establish whether the payroll rules are correct. The main risk is factual accuracy, not just how confidently the answer is worded.

options.label: D
options.text: Share the state-specific summary as final because Claude included web search citations.
options.feedback: Web search citations do not guarantee that every claim is accurate, current, or interpreted correctly. Important information should be cross-checked rather than treated as final because it appears with links.

questions.explanation:
Claude is useful for drafting and organizing information, but it should not be treated as a single source of truth for high-impact decisions. Anthropic notes that Claude can produce incorrect or misleading responses, including authoritative-looking claims that are not grounded in fact, as described in Claude is providing incorrect or misleading responses, what’s going on?.

Payroll rules with exact thresholds and dates are the kind of output that requires additional verification before people rely on it. Web search citations can help identify where to check, but they do not prove that Claude selected the right source, read it correctly, or captured the latest applicable rule.

The practical workflow is to use Claude’s table as a draft or research aid, then compare the important claims with official agency materials or ask a qualified payroll specialist to review them. Asking Claude to sound less certain or removing citations changes presentation, not reliability.

questions.question: A specialty coffee roaster's membership team asks Claude to draft a renewal email for lapsed subscribers using a detailed benefits sheet. Claude's first draft is factually accurate, but it reads like an internal policy memo rather than a short customer-facing message. What is the most appropriate next step?

options.label: A
options.text: Rename the project to describe lapsed subscribers and rerun the original prompt unchanged.
options.feedback: Changing a project name is not a reliable way to guide Claude's response. Project names and descriptions are not available to Claude, so the needed audience and style guidance should be placed in the prompt, project instructions, or reusable project knowledge as appropriate.

options.label: B
options.text: Send the email after adding a subject line that sounds more promotional to subscribers.
options.feedback: A better subject line may help, but it does not fix the body of the message if the main draft is still too dense and internal. The output should be refined before it is treated as ready for the audience.

options.label: C
options.text: Ask Claude to rewrite the email with the target audience, desired tone, length, and call to action.
options.feedback: This uses Claude's conversational refinement process to improve a usable but poorly fitted output. Giving clearer audience, tone, length, and action guidance helps Claude adapt the draft for the intended readers without discarding the accurate source content.

options.label: D
options.text: Turn the first draft into a skill so Claude uses the same structure for future emails.
options.feedback: A skill is useful for repeatable procedures or style workflows, not for preserving a weak draft that has not been adapted successfully. Creating a reusable process should come after the team has identified the approach that actually works for the audience.

questions.explanation:
When an output is factually usable but poorly matched to its readers, the best move is iterative refinement: tell Claude what needs to change and provide concrete criteria such as audience, tone, length, format, and desired next action. Anthropic's guidance emphasizes being specific, giving enough context, breaking down complex requests, and using follow-up instructions when the first response is not helpful, as described in My prompt isn't giving me a helpful answer.

For audience adaptation, the user remains responsible for judging whether Claude's draft fits the communication goal. Claude can write in different formats and styles, but a professional should still evaluate whether the draft is suitable before sharing it, as reflected in What are some things I can use Claude for. Project and skill features can support repeatable work, but they do not replace the immediate need to revise an unsuitable draft with clear feedback.

questions.question: A renewable energy nonprofit's grant operations team wants Claude to help improve its quarterly proposal-planning process. They have anonymized reviewer comments, funder guidelines, past timeline slips, and staff availability notes. Which approach best uses Claude for research, planning, and process optimization?

options.label: A
options.text: Ask Claude to write a polished proposal calendar from general best practices, then adopt it as the team’s new planning process.
options.feedback: General best practices may be useful background, but they do not reflect this team’s actual constraints or history. Adopting the result without review is risky because Claude can miss operational realities.

options.label: B
options.text: Ask Claude to rewrite last quarter’s proposal in a clearer style, then keep the current proposal-planning process unchanged.
options.feedback: Rewriting a proposal may improve a document, but it does not address the planning workflow. The stated goal is process optimization, so Claude should help analyze patterns and redesign the steps.

options.label: C
options.text: Give Claude only the funder guidelines, ask it to rank staff performance, then assign proposal owners based on the ranking.
options.feedback: Funder guidelines alone are not enough to evaluate process problems or staff capacity. Ranking staff performance from incomplete materials would be an unreliable and inappropriate use of Claude.

options.feedback: Projects are useful when work needs accumulated context over time, such as an ongoing initiative with evolving materials. The question asks for the best first step in exploratory requirements analysis, not for a persistent workspace that will necessarily be reused.

options.label: D

options.feedback: Custom instructions are meant for broad preferences about how Claude should work with the user in general. Intake-process details are too specific to apply across all conversations and could interfere with unrelated work.

questions.explanation:

questions.question: A museum conservation lead maintains a Google Doc with handling guidelines that staff update weekly. They want Claude to help draft recurring exhibit labels, training notes, and grant summaries using the current guidelines and the same plain-language style, without re-pasting the material each time. What workflow best integrates Claude into this work?

options.label: A
options.text: Export the Google Doc as DOCX, upload it once to Project Knowledge, and depend on that file for updates.
options.feedback: A one-time exported file can provide context, but it does not use the Google Docs integration’s live syncing behavior. This would make it easier for Claude to rely on an outdated copy as staff continue updating the source document.

options.label: B
options.text: Rename the Project with the guideline summary, add a description, and restate style guidance in each chat.
options.feedback: Project instructions can guide Claude across chats, but the project name and description are not available to Claude as working context. Repeating the style guidance in each chat also fails the goal of reducing setup effort.

options.label: C
options.text: Create a private Project, add the Google Doc to Project Knowledge, and add project instructions for the style guide.
options.feedback: This workflow gives Claude a reusable workspace for related conservation writing and places the changing Google Doc where Claude can use it across project chats. Project instructions are the right place for the recurring plain-language style guidance.

options.label: D
options.text: Create a private Project, paste the Google Doc into one chat, and rely on later chats to reuse that discussion.
options.feedback: Chats inside a Project do not automatically share context with other chats. Information must be added to Project Knowledge if it should be available across project conversations.

questions.explanation:
Projects are useful when recurring work needs a stable workspace with shared materials and instructions. For this scenario, the handling guidelines belong in Project Knowledge, while the plain-language requirements belong in project instructions. Claude does not automatically carry the contents of one project chat into another, so pasting important material into a single chat is a common workflow anti-pattern.

The Google Docs integration is especially relevant when the source document changes over time. Added Google Docs stay synced to the latest Drive version, subject to the documented limits and permissions, and the integration works in Projects only for private projects. That makes a private Project with the Google Doc added as knowledge a better fit than exporting and uploading a static copy.

Use the workspace feature for ongoing related work, use Project Knowledge for reusable source material, and use project instructions for how Claude should respond. See How can I create and manage Projects?, What are Projects?, and Using the Google Docs integration.

questions.question: A legal aid clinic’s intake team is creating a private Claude Project on a paid plan. They maintain their intake guidance in a 6 MB Google Doc that changes weekly, and they want every new chat in the project to use a standard plain-language response format. Which setup best supports this?

options.label: A
options.text: Put the response format in the project description, then rely on the project name to preserve the Google Doc context.
options.feedback: A project’s name and description are useful for humans managing projects, but they are not available to Claude as working context. Background that Claude must use should be placed in project instructions or project knowledge instead.

options.label: B
options.text: Set the response format with Set project instructions, then add the Google Doc from Drive to the private project’s knowledge.
options.feedback: Project instructions apply to all chats within that project, so they are the right place for a repeated response style or format. Adding the Google Doc from Drive to a private project’s knowledge lets Claude use that document as project context, and Drive-added Google Docs remain synced to the latest version.

options.label: C
options.text: Add a Google Slides copy from Drive, then ask Claude to use embedded images as the source.
options.feedback: The documented Google Drive integration for Projects supports adding Google Docs, not Google Slides. It also uses text extraction, so relying on embedded images would not be a sound way to provide the guidance.

options.label: D
options.text: Paste the Google Doc text into the first chat, then have staff begin later chats in the same project.
options.feedback: Ordinary chat context is not shared across new chats in a project. If later chats need the intake guidance, the content should be added to the project knowledge base rather than only pasted into one conversation.

questions.explanation:
Project instructions are the right place for behavior that should repeat across every chat in a specific project, such as tone, format, or role-specific response expectations. The intake guidance itself belongs in project knowledge, because Claude can use project knowledge as context across chats in that same project.

The project name and description help people organize their work, but they are not available to Claude as context. Similarly, content pasted into one chat does not automatically become available in later chats unless it is added to the project knowledge base.

For a private project, the Google Drive integration can add a supported Google Doc directly to project knowledge, and the document remains synced to the latest version in Google Drive. That makes it a better fit for a weekly changing source than repeatedly pasting copied text into individual chats. See How can I create and manage Projects? and Using the Google Docs integration.

questions.question: A pharmaceutical distributor's procurement analyst uses the organization's Claude for Work Team plan to compare vendor proposals. The proposals include pricing tables, supplier bank account details, and personal mobile numbers for several vendor contacts. The analyst knows the plan is a commercial product and wants to use Claude responsibly. What is the most appropriate action before asking Claude to compare the proposals?

options.label: A
options.text: Remove unnecessary bank details and personal contact data before uploading the proposals.
options.feedback: This is the best action because it applies data minimization while still allowing Claude to help with the pricing comparison. Commercial product data handling does not remove the need to follow privacy, confidentiality, and regulatory expectations for sensitive information.

options.label: B
options.text: Paste the proposals into a new chat and ask Claude not to remember the sensitive fields.
options.feedback: A prompt instruction is not a substitute for removing sensitive information that is not needed for the task. The safer practice is to avoid sharing unnecessary regulated, confidential, or personal data in the first place.

options.label: C
options.text: Upload the proposals unchanged because commercial chats are not used for training by default.
options.feedback: Not using chats for model training by default does not mean all sensitive information is appropriate to submit. Bank details and personal contact data may still be unnecessary for the task and should be minimized before use.

options.label: D
options.text: Send the proposals through feedback controls so Anthropic can handle them securely.
options.feedback: Feedback mechanisms are not the right way to process sensitive business documents. Explicitly reported materials, such as feedback, may be used under separate data handling rules, so this creates additional privacy risk rather than reducing it.

questions.explanation:
Responsible use of Claude starts with data minimization: provide the information needed for the task, and avoid including sensitive fields that do not help the analysis. In this scenario, Claude can compare pricing and proposal terms without supplier bank account details or personal mobile numbers.

For Claude for Work Team and Enterprise plans, Anthropic documents that the customer organization is the Controller of user-submitted data and Anthropic acts as the Processor to provide Claude. Anthropic also states that commercial product data is not used to train models unless the customer opts into specific programs or explicitly reports materials, but that protection is not a license to upload unnecessary sensitive data. See Does Anthropic act as a data processor or controller?.

The practical judgment is to keep the useful business context, such as prices, dates, and service terms, while removing fields that increase privacy or confidentiality exposure. Telling Claude not to remember information or relying on default training settings does not replace the employee's responsibility to follow organizational policy and handle sensitive data carefully.

questions.question: A marine insurance association’s communications coordinator uses Claude with web search enabled to draft a same-day member alert about a newly announced federal reporting requirement. Claude returns a clear summary with citations, a quotation, and a short list of what changed. The alert will be emailed to members who may rely on it for compliance planning. What should the coordinator do to evaluate the output before sending it?

options.label: A
options.text: Review the cited sources and official agency materials before sending the alert.
options.feedback: This is the best action because web search results and citations are aids, not proof that the synthesis is complete or accurate. For a compliance-related alert, the coordinator should check Claude’s claims, quotation, and omissions against authoritative sources.

options.label: B
options.text: Send the alert after confirming that each paragraph includes a citation.
options.feedback: Citations are useful for tracing information, but their presence does not guarantee that Claude interpreted the source correctly. Claude may omit context or produce convincing but incorrect details, so the cited material still needs review.

options.label: C
options.text: Turn on extended thinking and resend the same prompt before using the alert.
options.feedback: Extended thinking can help with complex reasoning, but it is not a substitute for checking current source material. The alert depends on a newly announced requirement, so validation should focus on authoritative sources rather than extra reasoning alone.

options.label: D
options.text: Ask Claude to rate its confidence and send the alert if confidence is high.
options.feedback: A model’s self-reported confidence is not a reliable measure of factual accuracy or completeness. The issue is whether the output matches authoritative sources, not whether Claude sounds certain.

questions.explanation:
Claude can be highly useful for quickly synthesizing current information, especially when web search is enabled, but the user still owns the final validation step. Anthropic notes that Claude can produce incorrect or misleading responses, including authoritative-looking citations or quotations, so users should not treat it as a singular source of truth for important decisions: Claude is providing incorrect or misleading responses, what’s going on?.

For web-search-based answers, citations should be treated as a path back to the source, not as an automatic quality seal. The practical evaluation workflow is to open the cited sources, prefer official or authoritative materials for critical claims, and check whether Claude’s summary left out important conditions, dates, exceptions, or limits. Anthropic’s web search guidance similarly advises cross-referencing cited sources and using authoritative sources for critical decisions: Enabling and using web search.

Extended thinking changes how Claude reasons through a task, but it does not make stale or incomplete source material fresh. For current, source-grounded validation, the stronger practice is to verify against live or authoritative materials rather than relying on tone, confidence, or the mere presence of citations.

questions.question: A veterinary hospital's client education coordinator uses Claude with web search to draft a pet owner handout about a newly prescribed medication. Claude returns a polished handout with source links, exact dosage timing, and a list of possible side effects. The handout will be distributed after appointments. Which TWO actions are most appropriate before using it?

options.label: A
options.text: Distribute the handout after confirming that the source links open.
options.feedback: This is incorrect because a working link does not prove that Claude used the source accurately. The content may still contain unsupported wording, outdated details, or claims that do not match the referenced material.

options.label: B
options.text: Check the medication details against authoritative veterinary references.
options.feedback: This is correct because exact dosing timing and side effect claims need verification against trusted sources. Web search citations can help locate information, but important claims still require cross-checking.

options.label: C
options.text: Ask Claude to add a disclaimer and make the tone more cautious.
options.feedback: This is incorrect because cautious wording does not validate clinical accuracy. A disclaimer may be useful, but it cannot replace expert review or verification against authoritative references.

options.label: D
options.text: Have a licensed veterinarian review the handout for clinical accuracy.
options.feedback: This is correct because medication guidance affects health decisions and should be reviewed by a qualified human expert. Claude's polished wording and source links do not make the medical details reliable enough for distribution.

questions.explanation:
Claude can be very useful for drafting clear materials, but it should not be treated as a single source of truth for important or high-stakes information. Anthropic notes that Claude can produce incorrect or misleading outputs, including confident claims or authoritative-looking details that are not grounded in fact, as described in Claude is providing incorrect or misleading responses, what's going on?.

In this scenario, the handout includes exact medication timing and side effect information that pet owners may rely on. That combination calls for both human review by a qualified veterinarian and additional verification against authoritative veterinary references. Web search citations and polished formatting are helpful starting points, but they do not guarantee that the claims are current, complete, or correctly interpreted.

Opening source links or adding a disclaimer can improve presentation, but neither action checks whether the content is true. The practical habit to build is to match the review process to the risk of the output: the more an answer affects health, safety, legal, financial, or compliance decisions, the more it needs independent verification before use.

questions.question: A city transit authority’s rider communications team uses Claude on a paid plan with web search enabled and its policy notes connected in Google Docs. It asks for a complete, current comparison of reduced-fare eligibility rules across several transit agencies. Claude returns a polished table with citations and a few exact quotes from agency pages. Which two actions should the communications lead take before publishing the comparison?

options.label: A
options.text: Turn on extended thinking and ask Claude to verify the table without opening source pages.
options.feedback: This is not sufficient because extended thinking is for deeper reasoning, not for obtaining fresh or source-grounded information. For current public rules, the lead should use current sources and inspect them directly rather than relying only on Claude's self-check.

options.label: B
options.text: Use Research or a broader source-gathering pass when coverage must span several agencies.
options.feedback: This is appropriate because a complete comparison across multiple agencies may need more than a quick web-search synthesis. Research is designed for more comprehensive information gathering across the web and connected context when available, while still requiring the user to review important sources.

options.label: C
options.text: Accept the table once each row includes at least one citation link to an agency source.
options.feedback: This is not sufficient because the presence of citations does not prove that the cited sources support every claim. Claude's synthesis can omit context, misstate details, or include citations that do not fully support the wording.

options.label: D
options.text: Check the cited agency pages against Claude's thresholds, dates, and quoted language before sharing.
options.feedback: This is appropriate because Claude can produce convincing but incorrect citations, quotes, or details. Reviewing the original sources helps confirm that the table reflects the actual agency guidance and has not omitted important context from the cited pages.

questions.explanation:
When Claude provides current factual information, especially with quotes, dates, or eligibility thresholds, the safest evaluation step is to treat the output as a draft synthesis, not as the final authority. Anthropic notes that Claude can produce incorrect or misleading responses, including authoritative-looking citations or quotes, so users should not rely on Claude as a singular source of truth for important decisions, see Claude is providing incorrect or misleading responses, what's going on?.

Web search can help Claude use live web content and provide citations, but those citations are starting points for validation. Anthropic's web search guidance emphasizes reviewing and cross-referencing sources, particularly for critical uses, see Enabling and using web search. For a broader task such as comparing many agencies, Research is a better fit than a quick one-off search because it performs multi-step searches across the web and connected context when available, as described in Using Research on Claude.ai. Extended thinking can improve reasoning through complex material, but it does not replace fresh sources or direct source review for current, source-grounded validation.

questions.question: A community theater's fundraising manager creates a Claude Project for its annual donor campaign. She names the Project “2026 Gala, use warm donor tone” and adds the latest donor-segment notes only inside one planning chat. New chats in the Project do not consistently use that tone or those notes. What should she do to maintain the Project configuration for future chats?

options.label: A
options.text: Upload the donor-segment notes into each new chat and repeat the tone guidance in every prompt.
options.feedback: This can provide context for a single conversation, but it does not maintain the Project configuration for future chats. It also creates avoidable repetition and increases the chance that one chat uses outdated guidance.

options.label: B
options.text: Put the donor-segment notes and tone guidance in Instructions for Claude for the whole account.
options.feedback: This is incorrect because account-wide instructions apply across conversations, not just this donor campaign Project. It could unnecessarily affect unrelated work, and it does not make the chat-only notes persistent project knowledge.

options.label: C
options.text: Keep the donor-segment notes in the original chat and rename the Project with the full tone guidance.
options.feedback: This is incorrect because chats in a Project do not automatically share context with other chats. The Project name and description are not accessible to Claude as working instructions.

options.label: D
options.text: Add the donor-segment notes to project knowledge and enter the tone guidance through Set project instructions.

questions.question: An architecture studio's proposals coordinator has a regular Claude chat containing weeks of brainstorming, rejected drafts, and final client preferences. The chat is becoming hard to work in, and she needs several upcoming proposal chats to use only the finalized preferences and approved source files. What is the most appropriate next step?

options.label: A
options.text: Keep using the same chat and ask Claude to ignore the rejected drafts when preparing future proposals.
options.feedback: Continuing the same long chat keeps unnecessary material in the working context and can make length or usage issues worse. Asking Claude to ignore older content is less reliable than moving the approved context into a durable workspace.

options.label: B
options.text: Rename the Project with the final preferences and rely on Claude to apply them in each chat.
options.feedback: Claude does not use a Project name or description as working context for responses. Durable instructions or source material should be placed in Project instructions or Project knowledge instead.

options.label: C
options.text: Start an incognito chat and paste the final preferences before each new proposal request.
options.feedback: Incognito chats are not saved to chat history or memory, so they are a poor fit for reusable proposal context. Re-pasting the same material also adds avoidable setup work for each new chat.

options.label: D
options.text: Create a Project, add the finalized brief and approved files to Project knowledge, then start new chats there.
options.feedback: This preserves the durable context that future proposal chats need while avoiding reliance on a long, cluttered conversation. Project knowledge is designed to provide shared context across chats within that Project.

questions.explanation:
When a conversation gets long or cluttered, the practical issue is usually the context window, Claude's working space for the current chat, not simply how many messages the user is allowed to send over time. Anthropic explains that length limits govern how much information Claude can work with in a single chat, and recommends starting a new conversation or using features like Projects when a chat is becoming too large. See How do usage and length limits work?.

Projects are the better choice when context should persist across related work. A Project can contain its own knowledge base and chat history, so the coordinator can store the finalized brief and approved files once, then use them in new, cleaner chats. Anthropic also notes that context is not shared across chats within a Project unless it is added to the Project knowledge base, so relying on an earlier chat alone would miss the point. See What are projects? and How can I create and manage Projects?.

The distractors reflect common anti-patterns: stretching one chat indefinitely, pasting the same context repeatedly, or assuming a Project name carries instructions into Claude's work. A concise, curated handoff into Project knowledge gives Claude the relevant context without bringing along weeks of rejected material.

questions.question: A university alumni relations team uses Claude to plan three unrelated events: a reunion weekend, a mentoring launch, and a donor briefing. They have been keeping all planning in one long chat, but Claude increasingly blends audience details and action items across events. What change would best optimize the workflow?

options.label: A
options.text: Create one Skill that contains all event goals, timelines, and attendee profiles.
options.feedback: This is incorrect because Skills are best for repeatable procedures or standards, not for storing unrelated ongoing project context. A single Skill containing all event details would not solve the need to keep each event's information separate.

options.label: B
options.text: Add every event detail to custom instructions so Claude applies them in all chats.
options.feedback: This is incorrect because custom instructions apply broadly across Claude interactions. Putting event-specific details there would likely make cross-event confusion worse rather than isolate the work.

options.label: C
options.text: Create a separate Project for each event and add only the relevant planning materials.
options.feedback: This is correct because each event needs its own accumulated context without mixing details from unrelated work. Projects are well suited for ongoing work where Claude should use a specific set of background materials and conversation history.

options.label: D
options.text: Continue in the same chat and ask Claude to ignore earlier event information.
options.feedback: This is incorrect because repeatedly asking Claude to ignore old context is a fragile workaround. It does not create a cleaner workspace or reduce the risk of details from prior planning influencing later outputs.

questions.explanation:
When a workflow involves several ongoing but unrelated efforts, the optimization problem is often context separation. A Project is useful when Claude should keep using a particular body of background knowledge and conversation history for one stream of work, such as one event, campaign, or research effort.

Skills solve a different problem: they package repeatable procedures, standards, or workflows that should activate when relevant. For example, a team might create a Skill for its standard event-brief format, then use that Skill across several Projects. Custom instructions are broader still, and are better for general preferences such as concise answers or asking clarifying questions before starting.

The practical mental model is to put stable, event-specific context in the relevant Project, put reusable methods in Skills, and reserve ordinary prompting for one-time needs. Anthropic's documentation describes Skills as task-specific procedures and Projects as static background knowledge for specific chats: Skills overview.

questions.question: A retail merchandising team uses Claude throughout the day for simple product-description rewrites, but once a week they also ask Claude to compare supplier notes, sales feedback, and margin concerns to recommend assortment changes. The team wants faster everyday work without reducing the care used for the weekly analysis. Which adjustment best optimizes the workflow?

options.label: A
options.text: Use default settings for routine rewrites and increase effort or thinking for the weekly analysis.
options.feedback: This matches the level of Claude’s settings to the complexity of the task. Simple rewrites usually do not benefit much from extra thinking, while multi-step analysis can benefit from more effort and a more deliberate approach.

options.label: B
options.text: Keep one long conversation for all merchandising tasks so Claude can reuse prior context.
options.feedback: A single long conversation can mix unrelated context and make everyday tasks less focused. Reusing context is helpful when it is relevant, but it is not the best fix for matching effort to different task types.

options.label: C
options.text: Ask Claude to self-check every product description before producing each final rewrite.
options.feedback: Self-checking can be useful for important or risky outputs, but requiring it for every simple rewrite adds friction. It does not directly address the difference between routine drafting and weekly multi-step analysis.

options.label: D
options.text: Use the highest effort setting for every request so all outputs receive equal attention.
options.feedback: This may slow down routine work and use more of the team’s allowance without a proportional quality benefit. Optimization means reserving heavier settings for work that actually needs deeper reasoning.

questions.explanation:
Efficient Claude workflows come from matching the amount of assistance to the job. For everyday drafting, the default settings are often enough, especially when the task is short, familiar, and low risk. For work that requires comparing sources, weighing tradeoffs, and making recommendations, increasing effort or using thinking can improve the quality of reasoning, although responses may take longer.

This is a practical optimization tradeoff: do not make every task heavier just to feel safer, and do not force complex analysis through the lightest workflow if accuracy and completeness matter. Claude’s help guidance on changing the model, effort, and thinking settings describes using lower effort for simple everyday work and higher effort or thinking for more complex tasks. The goal is not one universal setting, but a workflow that fits the task’s complexity and business value.

questions.question: A disaster-relief nonprofit’s grants director asks Claude to compare several conflicting funding opportunities, weigh tradeoffs across mission fit, reporting burden, timing risk, and long-term partnership value, then recommend which proposals to pursue. Depth and judgment matter more than speed. Which model choice best fits the first-pass analysis?

options.label: A
options.text: Use the fastest available model and ask Claude to state high confidence before deciding.
options.feedback: Speed is not the main requirement in this situation, and self-reported confidence is not a reliable quality control. A confident response can still miss tradeoffs or overstate its reasoning.

options.label: B
options.text: Use Sonnet for every part of the task to keep quality and speed balanced.
options.feedback: Sonnet is a strong general-purpose choice when a balance of capability and speed is needed. In this scenario, the stated priority is deeper judgment for the first-pass analysis, so Opus is a better fit among Haiku, Sonnet, and Opus.

options.label: C
options.text: Use Opus for the analysis, then use faster models for simpler follow-up drafting.
options.feedback: This is the best fit because the task requires nuanced reasoning across multiple competing criteria. Among Haiku, Sonnet, and Opus, Opus is the best model type to choose when depth and capability matter more than speed or efficiency.

options.label: D
options.text: Use Haiku for the analysis, then rely on repeated follow-up prompts to add depth.
options.feedback: Haiku is better suited to fast, lightweight, or high-volume tasks. Using it for a complex strategic recommendation may save time initially, but repeated follow-ups are an inefficient substitute for choosing a more capable option among these three model types.

questions.explanation:
Claude model selection is a practical tradeoff among speed, cost or usage efficiency, and capability. For lightweight drafting or repetitive transformations, a faster model such as Haiku is often appropriate. For broad day-to-day work, Sonnet is commonly the balanced choice. Among Haiku, Sonnet, and Opus, Opus is the better fit for more complex reasoning, synthesis, and high-judgment work when speed is less important.

In this scenario, the grants director is not simply rewriting text or summarizing a single document. The task requires comparing competing priorities, identifying risks, and making a recommendation under uncertainty, so starting with Opus is justified among the three named model types. After the strategic direction is set, simpler follow-up work such as email drafts, checklists, or summaries could move to a faster model to conserve usage.

The model menu in Claude lets users change the model during a conversation, and changes apply starting with Claude’s next response. Claude’s help article on changing the model, effort, and thinking settings explains that users can adjust model and effort choices to match the task. The key mental model is not to use one model for everything, but to match the model to the work: simple and fast, balanced, or deep and capable.

questions.question: A regional history museum's collections registrar asks Claude to draft exhibit labels from scanned donor forms, old newspaper clippings, and a curator's notes. The draft includes dates, quote attributions, and object provenance that will be printed for visitors. What is the most appropriate next step?

options.label: A
options.text: Check each date, attribution, and provenance claim against museum records before approval.
options.feedback: This is the best validation step because it compares specific factual claims with authoritative source material. Public-facing labels require accuracy, especially for details like dates, quotes, and provenance.

options.label: B
options.text: Ask Claude to make each date, attribution, and provenance claim sound less certain before approval.
options.feedback: Softer wording can signal uncertainty, but it does not establish whether the claims are true. A cautious tone can still contain incorrect facts.

options.label: C
options.text: Ask Claude to score each date, attribution, and provenance claim for confidence before approval.
options.feedback: Claude's self-reported confidence is not a reliable substitute for verification. A model can sound confident about details that are incomplete, misread, or fabricated.

options.label: D
options.text: Ask Claude in a new chat to recreate each date, attribution, and provenance claim before approval.
options.feedback: A second Claude response is not the same as checking an independent authoritative source. Matching outputs can repeat the same error if the underlying evidence was misunderstood.

questions.explanation:
Claude is useful for turning messy source materials into readable drafts, but factual details in generated text should be treated as claims to verify, not as finished evidence. Dates, quotations, and provenance statements are the kinds of details that can look precise even when they are wrong, incomplete, or based on a misread source.

The strongest validation technique is to compare the output with authoritative records, such as the museum's catalog system, accession files, donor forms, or original clippings. Asking Claude to sound cautious, rate its confidence, or regenerate the same content may help with wording or review workflow, but those actions do not prove the facts. Anthropic's guidance on reducing hallucinations emphasizes grounding outputs in reliable sources and verifying important claims, especially before sharing them externally: Reduce hallucinations.

questions.question: A credit union’s member experience team asks Claude with web search enabled to draft a briefing on why applicants are abandoning online loan forms. Claude returns a confident memo with a direct quote attributed to a financial regulator, a claim about a rule that changed last week, and a recommendation to focus outreach on older members because they are “typically less comfortable with digital forms.” The cited links include a trade newsletter and a government page. The memo will guide a leadership discussion. Which two actions should the team take before relying on the memo?

options.label: A
options.text: Ask Claude for a confidence rating and use the memo for leadership if the rating is high.
options.feedback: This is incorrect because Claude’s self-reported confidence is not a reliable substitute for checking important claims. A high confidence rating would not validate the quote, the recent rule change, or the member-segmentation recommendation.

options.label: B
options.text: Challenge the age-based recommendation and ask Claude to ground any member segmentation in evidence.
options.feedback: This is correct because the recommendation may reflect an unsupported stereotype rather than evidence from the credit union’s data or cited sources. Asking Claude to ground segmentation in evidence helps identify bias and separates useful analysis from an unverified generalization.

options.label: C
options.text: Accept the memo when web search citations are present and the writing is internally consistent.
options.feedback: This is incorrect because citations and polished wording do not guarantee accuracy. Anthropic warns that users should still review cited original sources, since Claude’s synthesis can miss context or contain mistakes.

options.label: D
options.text: Verify the quote and recent rule change against the cited sources or official regulator page.
options.feedback: This is correct because Claude can produce convincing but incorrect quotes, citations, and current-event claims. Reviewing the original cited sources, especially an official regulator page for a recent rule change, is the appropriate validation step before using the memo.

questions.explanation:
Claude can be useful for quickly synthesizing information, but its output still needs evaluation for hallucinations, inconsistencies, and unsupported assumptions. Anthropic notes that Claude can provide incorrect or misleading responses, including convincing quotes or claims that are not grounded in fact, especially when current information is involved: Claude is providing incorrect or misleading responses. What’s going on?

Web search helps ground answers in live web content, but it does not remove the need for human review. Anthropic’s web search guidance says users should cross-reference cited sources and use authoritative sources for critical decisions: Enable and use web search. In this scenario, the regulator quote and recent rule claim should be checked in the original source, preferably the official government page.

The age-based outreach recommendation is a separate evaluation issue. Even if the factual claims are verified, the team should look for evidence that supports the segmentation rather than accepting a broad demographic assumption. Good output validation means checking both whether the facts are true and whether the reasoning is fair and evidence-based.

questions.question: A public health outreach team drafts weekly partner updates in Claude, but staff spend most of their time copying background notes, recent messages, and source documents from approved work tools into each chat. The team wants Claude to help with the same drafting workflow while reducing manual copying and preserving each user’s existing access boundaries. What is the most appropriate way to integrate Claude into this workflow?

options.label: A
options.text: Enable the relevant connectors, authenticate the approved tools, and ask Claude to retrieve the needed work context.
options.feedback: This is the best fit because connectors are designed to let Claude access relevant information from connected work tools with permission. They reduce the need to manually copy context into each chat while still depending on the user’s access to the connected source.

options.label: B
options.text: Paste complete message threads into every chat, then ask Claude to ignore unrelated material while drafting.
options.feedback: This can work for an occasional one-off request, but it does not redesign the workflow to reduce repeated manual copying. It also increases the chance of adding unnecessary or sensitive information that Claude does not need for the task.

options.label: C
options.text: Add the names of key partners to custom instructions, then ask Claude to draft updates from memory.
options.feedback: Custom instructions can guide Claude’s general behavior, but they are not a source of current work data. Asking Claude to draft from memory risks missing recent information or inventing details that should come from approved sources.

options.label: D
options.text: Create a reusable artifact for the update format, then use it as the source for all future partner updates.
options.feedback: Artifacts are useful for substantial, reusable outputs that users want to edit or reference later. An artifact template may help with presentation, but it does not connect Claude to the team’s current work context or source materials.

questions.explanation:
Connectors are the right workflow tool when the friction is repeatedly moving context from existing tools into Claude. They let Claude retrieve relevant work context from connected services, with permission, so the user can spend more time asking useful questions and less time copying background material. See Anthropic’s overview of connectors at Connect your tools to unlock a smarter, more capable AI companion.

This does not mean every workflow needs a connector. For a one-time task, pasting a short document into a chat may be enough. For an ongoing process where the same people repeatedly need current information from approved tools, connecting those tools is a better fit because it augments the existing workflow rather than replacing it with manual copy-and-paste.

Artifacts and custom instructions solve different problems. Artifacts are best for substantial standalone outputs such as documents, diagrams, or reusable content, while custom instructions shape Claude’s general response style. Neither one supplies fresh context from work systems, so they do not address the team’s main bottleneck.

options.feedback: This is incorrect because vague instructions such as “best possible” do not give Claude a reliable standard to follow. Asking for minimal follow-up questions can also discourage Claude from surfacing missing information that matters for accuracy.

questions.explanation:
Project instructions are best for guidance that should consistently shape Claude’s behavior inside a particular Project, such as the desired voice, recurring format, and rules for handling missing or unsupported information. In this scenario, the newsletter standards are stable, while the facts for each issue change, so the facts should come from the uploaded notes or the current prompt.

Effective system-level guidance is specific, durable, and scoped to the work. A useful instruction tells Claude what pattern to follow and what boundaries to respect, for example, to use only provided sources for factual claims and to ask when required details are missing. Vague goals, issue-by-issue details, or broad personal preferences are weaker fits because they either fail to guide Claude reliably or apply in the wrong places.
