questions.question: A regional hotel group's guest experience team is using a Claude Project to design and refine a lost-and-found workflow. After one chat produces approved escalation rules, the manager opens a separate chat in the same Project to draft staff scripts, but Claude does not use those rules unless she pastes them again. What is the most appropriate next step?

options.label: A
options.text: Ask Claude to retrieve the rules from the earlier project chat automatically.
options.feedback: This is incorrect because ordinary chat context is not automatically shared between separate chats in a project. Claude can use project knowledge and project instructions across chats, but it should not be expected to rely on a previous chat unless the needed information is added to shared project context.

options.label: B
options.text: Add the approved escalation rules to project knowledge or project instructions.
options.feedback: This is correct because project knowledge and project instructions are available across chats within the same project. Moving approved working context there lets later chats use it without relying on the conversation history from a different chat.

options.label: C
options.text: Move the approved escalation rules into the project name and description.
options.feedback: This is incorrect because Claude does not use the project name or description as working context. Those fields may help humans organize projects, but they are not the right place for instructions Claude must follow.

options.label: D
options.text: Make the project public so all project chats share their full context.
options.feedback: This is incorrect because project sharing is about collaboration visibility, not merging every chat's context. Even in a shared or public project, chats remain private unless manually shared, and their contents are not automatically treated as project knowledge.

questions.explanation:
When using Claude to support solution design over time, a Project is useful because it gives related work a shared workspace. The key distinction is that project knowledge and project instructions are shared across chats in that project, while the contents of one ordinary chat are not automatically carried into another.

For an iterative workflow, the practical pattern is to promote stable decisions, approved requirements, reusable templates, and operating rules into project knowledge or project instructions. Then separate chats can focus on different parts of the work, such as staff scripts, checklists, or pilot feedback, while staying aligned to the same approved context.

Project names and descriptions are not a substitute for working context because Claude does not see them as instructions to follow. Sharing a project also does not merge private chat histories into shared knowledge. For more detail, see Anthropic's help articles on creating and managing projects and Claude's personalization features.

questions.question: An insurance brokerage's customer care manager asks Claude to draft a response explaining why a claim may not be covered. Claude produces a clear paragraph quoting a clause number from the customer's policy and recommends wording for the email. The email could affect the customer's next steps and will be sent externally. What should the manager do before sending it?

options.label: A
options.text: Ask Claude to rate its confidence and send it after it reports high confidence.
options.feedback: Claude's self-reported confidence is not a reliable substitute for verification. The issue is not how confident the answer sounds, but whether the cited clause and interpretation match the official policy.

options.label: B
options.text: Ask Claude to add more citations and send it after the source list looks complete.
options.feedback: More citations do not automatically make the content correct or relevant. Important claims still need to be checked against authoritative records, especially when the output affects a customer's decisions.

options.label: C
options.text: Verify the cited policy language with official files and get claims reviewer approval.
options.feedback: This is correct because the draft includes a specific policy citation and will be used in a high-impact customer communication. Claude can produce authoritative-looking but incorrect details, so the manager should verify the source material and involve the appropriate human reviewer.

options.label: D
options.text: Ask Claude to make the explanation more cautious and send it after the tone sounds balanced.
options.feedback: Improving tone may make the message more appropriate, but it does not confirm whether the policy clause or coverage interpretation is accurate. A cautious style can still contain incorrect or unsupported information.

questions.explanation:
Claude is useful for drafting and organizing language, but it should not be treated as a single source of truth for consequential claims. The official guidance on incorrect or misleading responses explains that Claude can hallucinate, including producing authoritative-looking quotes or claims that are not grounded in fact: Claude is providing incorrect or misleading responses. What's going on?

In this scenario, the risk is not just a poorly worded email. The draft includes a specific policy reference and could influence a customer's financial or procedural choices, so the right workflow is to verify the cited language against the official policy files and get the appropriate human review before sending. Rewriting the tone, adding more citations, or asking Claude for confidence may improve the appearance of reliability, but none of those actions confirms the underlying facts.

questions.question: An independent bookstore chain's purchasing manager asks Claude to turn an inventory export and several supplier catalog PDFs into a reorder plan. Claude recommends quantities and includes ISBNs, discount rates, and expected ship dates for each title. What is the most appropriate action before using the plan to place an order?

options.label: A
options.text: Ask Claude to add a confidence rating for each line item before placing the order.
options.feedback: A confidence rating from Claude is not a reliable substitute for checking source data. It may make the output easier to review, but it does not prove that the ISBNs, discounts, dates, or totals are correct.

options.label: B
options.text: Approve only the rows where Claude included exact ISBNs and ship dates before placing the order.
options.feedback: Specific-looking details can still be wrong, especially when they involve identifiers or dates. The presence of exact values should trigger verification, not replace it.

options.label: C
options.text: Reformat the recommendations into a spreadsheet before placing the order.
options.feedback: A spreadsheet may make the plan easier to read or sort, but formatting does not validate the facts. Incorrect ISBNs, prices, or dates can look authoritative when presented in a clean table.

options.label: D
options.text: Check the ISBNs, discounts, ship dates, and totals against the supplier records before placing the order.
options.feedback: This validates the specific factual and numerical claims that would affect a real purchase. Claude can help organize and draft the plan, but source records remain the authority for identifiers, prices, dates, and calculations.

questions.explanation:
Claude is useful for transforming messy inputs into a structured draft, but its output should be treated as a working version when money, inventory, deadlines, or customer commitments are involved. The safest validation step is to compare important claims against authoritative source records, such as the supplier catalog, ordering portal, or original export.

This is especially important for details that look precise, such as ISBNs, discount percentages, dates, and calculated totals. A polished table or a confident tone can make an error harder to notice, so verification should focus on the facts that would drive action. Anthropic's guidance on using Claude emphasizes being specific and iterating on outputs, and its guidance on hallucinations explains why factual claims should be checked when accuracy matters: Getting started with Claude.ai and Reduce hallucinations.

questions.question: A children’s science museum’s education team is using Claude to plan a new weekend program. The team has the target age range, staffing limits, safety rules, and past attendance notes. They first want a range of possible program concepts, then they will turn the selected concept into a parent-facing event description. Which TWO prompt strategies best fit these tasks?

options.label: A
options.text: Give Claude the chosen concept, audience, tone, length, and required details for the event description.
options.feedback: This fits a drafting task because Claude needs the purpose, audience, style, and required facts to produce a usable first version. Supplying these details reduces generic language and makes the output easier to edit.

options.label: B
options.text: Ask Claude for varied program concepts that follow the constraints and include brief pros and cons.
options.feedback: This is appropriate when the team is still exploring possibilities. Giving Claude constraints and asking for varied concepts helps generate useful options rather than one premature recommendation.

options.label: C
options.text: Ask Claude to produce the final event page before choosing a program concept or audience angle.
options.feedback: This skips the decision point the team has not yet completed. Claude may produce polished text, but it will be anchored to assumptions rather than a selected direction.

options.label: D
options.text: Ask Claude to research current museum attendance trends without supplying sources or checking the results.
options.feedback: This does not match the immediate task, which uses known internal constraints and past notes to create and describe a program. If outside research is needed later, factual claims should be checked against reliable sources rather than accepted unverified.

questions.explanation:
Different task types call for different prompts. For an early idea-generation task, a strong prompt gives Claude the boundaries and asks for multiple distinct options, often with tradeoffs, so the team can compare directions instead of receiving a single polished answer too soon.

For a drafting task, the better prompt is more specific about audience, tone, format, and required facts. Claude’s getting-started guidance emphasizes communicating naturally but clearly, and using prompts to provide enough context for the request, as described in Getting started with Claude.ai.

The less effective choices either collapse exploration and drafting into one step or introduce unverified research that the team did not need for the immediate work. A useful mental model is to match Claude’s role to the stage of work: ask for breadth when deciding, ask for structure when analyzing, ask for source-aware synthesis when researching, and ask for audience-specific language when drafting.

A useful mental model is to match Claude’s role to the stage of work: ask for breadth when deciding, ask for structure when analyzing, ask for source-aware synthesis when researching, and ask for audience-specific language when drafting.

questions.question: A city transit agency’s service-design lead is using Claude to refine a rider-complaint triage process over a month. She expects to open separate chats for intake forms, supervisor scripts, and pilot-review summaries. The source pack contains many policy excerpts and sample cases, each well under 30 MB, and may grow beyond what Claude can consider all at once. Which two actions should she take?

options.label: A
options.text: Add the approved source materials to the Project knowledge so later chats can use them.
options.feedback: Project knowledge is shared across chats within the same Project. Adding approved materials there gives Claude a stable source base for separate workstreams such as forms, scripts, and summaries.

options.label: B
options.text: Keep separate chats in the Project and rely on automatic project retrieval as materials grow.
options.feedback: Projects can use automatic retrieval when project knowledge approaches or exceeds the context window. The user does not need to design or manually control a retrieval setup for this workflow.

options.label: C
options.text: Put the workflow rules in the Project name and description so Claude applies them.
options.feedback: A Project’s name and description are for organizing the workspace, not for instructing Claude. If Claude must use rules or background context, place them in Project instructions or Project knowledge.

options.label: D
options.text: Upload the source pack to the first chat and expect later Project chats to inherit it.
options.feedback: Ordinary chat context is not shared with other chats, even inside the same Project. Materials needed across chats should be added to Project knowledge instead.

questions.explanation:
For an iterative design effort, a Project is useful because it gives related chats a shared workspace without forcing every conversation into one long thread. The important distinction is that Project knowledge and Project instructions apply across chats in that Project, while ordinary chat context stays inside the chat where it was provided. Anthropic’s project documentation explains this behavior and also notes that the Project name and description are not visible to Claude as working context: How can I create and manage Projects?.

When the shared materials become large, the right mental model is not to build a separate search system. Claude’s retrieval augmented generation for Projects is automatic and can retrieve relevant uploaded project content when the knowledge base approaches or exceeds the context window, as described in Retrieval augmented generation (RAG) for Projects. The user still needs to place the approved source materials where Claude can use them, but Claude handles the project retrieval behavior without a manual setup step.

The file detail matters because Project uploads have their own limits and behavior. If a team is preparing a source pack, it should be organized so files fit the Project knowledge requirements rather than relying on a one-time chat upload, which is documented in What kinds of documents can I upload to Claude.ai?. This keeps the workflow practical for ongoing solution design and iteration.

questions.question: A university alumni relations office is introducing Claude to staff who prepare donor briefing notes from approved messaging documents, event notes, and connected Google Docs. Some leaders expect Claude to produce final, source-perfect briefings without review, while others think it is only useful for rewriting sentences. Which message best communicates Claude's value and limitations for this workflow?

options.label: A
options.text: Present Claude as a drafting and synthesis partner that can use approved context and formats, while staff verify facts, source coverage, and donor-sensitive judgments.
options.feedback: This sets realistic expectations by describing Claude as useful for synthesis, drafting, and applying reusable guidance. It also preserves human responsibility for checking facts, confirming that the right sources were used, and making judgment calls involving donor relationships.

options.label: B
options.text: Present Claude as a safe place for complete donor records, then rely on instructions in the chat to satisfy any privacy or consent concerns.
options.feedback: This is a poor privacy practice because a chat instruction is not a substitute for organizational data-handling rules. Staff should avoid sharing unnecessary sensitive information and follow policy before pasting, attaching, or connecting data.

options.label: C
options.text: Present Claude as an automated briefing owner that can replace staff review once approved documents are connected and the prompt names the desired audience.
options.feedback: This overstates what Claude should be trusted to do in a stakeholder-facing workflow. Connected documents can improve context, but they do not remove the need for human review of accuracy, completeness, tone, and appropriate use.

options.label: D
options.text: Present Claude as a basic wording assistant that should not use Projects, Skills, or connected documents for recurring briefing workflows.
options.feedback: This understates Claude's practical value for recurring knowledge work. Projects, Skills, and connected documents can help Claude reuse relevant context and procedures, as long as users still validate the output.

questions.explanation:
The strongest rollout message frames Claude as a productivity partner, not as either a fully autonomous decision-maker or a simple spellchecker. In this kind of workflow, Claude can help synthesize notes, draft briefing language, and apply reusable standards, especially when staff use approved documents, Projects, or Skills to provide consistent context.

The limitation to communicate is just as important: Claude's output still needs human review before it informs donor strategy or external communication. Connected sources and reusable instructions can improve relevance, but they do not guarantee that every fact is complete, current, or appropriate for the relationship context.

Claude Skills are designed for repeatable procedures and standards, such as preferred formats or review frameworks, while connected documents can provide task-specific context when users have access to them. See Anthropic's guidance on teaching Claude your way of working using Skills and the Google Drive integration for how these features support recurring work. A good stakeholder message should emphasize the value of faster synthesis and more consistent drafts, while making clear that staff remain accountable for verification, privacy, and final judgment.

questions.question: A veterinary clinic's client education manager asks Claude to create a discharge handout for pet owners after routine surgery. Claude returns three versions: one is concise, one is warm, and one includes the most complete warning signs and follow-up steps. The handout will be given to anxious first-time pet owners at checkout. What is the most appropriate next step before using it?

options.label: A
options.text: Ask Claude to polish all three versions for checkout without changing their structure or content.
options.feedback: General polishing does not directly address the gap between the drafts and the handout's purpose. Claude works better when the user gives specific feedback about audience, tone, content, and desired outcome.

options.label: B
options.text: Use the warmest version for checkout because emotional fit matters most for anxious pet owners.
options.feedback: A warm tone is helpful, but it cannot replace complete warning signs, follow-up steps, and appropriate review in a care handout. Choosing tone alone risks leaving out information the audience needs to act safely.

options.label: C
options.text: Ask Claude to revise the handout in plain, reassuring language, then have qualified veterinary staff verify it.
options.feedback: This is the best next step because it evaluates the drafts against the real audience and purpose, then adds qualified human review before client use. It preserves important safety information while adapting tone and wording for anxious pet owners.

options.label: D
options.text: Use the most complete version because accuracy matters more than adapting it for first-time pet owners.
options.feedback: Completeness is important, but a discharge handout must also be understandable to the intended readers. If the wording is not clear for first-time pet owners, the output still needs refinement and review before use.

questions.explanation:
Claude is strongest as a collaborative drafting and revision tool, not as a source whose first output should automatically be treated as final. When several drafts have different strengths, the user should compare them against the intended audience and ask for a focused revision that combines what works.

In this case, the handout needs both usable care guidance and an accessible tone. A good refinement prompt would identify the audience, such as anxious first-time pet owners, and specify the desired result, such as plain language, reassuring wording, and retained warning signs. Because the content affects how clients care for pets after surgery, qualified veterinary staff should verify the medical instructions, warning signs, and follow-up steps before distribution.

Anthropic's guidance emphasizes being specific, giving enough context, and iterating with follow-up instructions when an answer is not yet helpful. See Get started with Claude and My prompt isn't giving me a helpful answer. Claude can draft across formats and styles, but the human user still needs to judge fit for purpose before sharing an output with others.

questions.question: A regional fitness chain’s marketing coordinator uses Claude to create hundreds of short promotional text-message variations for upcoming class discounts. The messages follow a simple approved style guide, and a human reviewer will select and edit the best drafts before sending. The coordinator wants to conserve usage while getting drafts quickly. Which choice best fits the task?

options.label: A
options.text: Use the most capable model with max effort for every message draft.
options.feedback: This may improve some outputs, but it is inefficient for simple, repetitive drafting. Higher effort takes longer and uses more tokens, which works against the stated need to conserve usage.

options.label: B
options.text: Use a shared Project as the main way to reduce response time.
options.feedback: A Project can help organize context such as the style guide, but it is not the primary control for model speed or effort. It does not replace choosing a model and effort level that fit the task.

options.label: C
options.text: Use a faster model with low or medium effort for the initial message drafts.
options.feedback: This fits a high-volume, low-complexity drafting task where speed and usage efficiency matter. Human review is still needed, but the task does not require the deepest reasoning for every variation.

options.label: D
options.text: Use extended thinking for each draft before comparing message options.
options.feedback: Extended thinking is better suited to tasks that benefit from extra planning or deeper reasoning. Applying it to every short marketing variation would likely slow the workflow without matching the task’s needs.

questions.explanation:
For routine, high-volume drafting, the practical choice is usually a faster model and a lower or medium effort setting, especially when a person will review the drafts before use. This matches the work to the required quality level without spending extra time and usage on reasoning that the task does not need.

Claude’s model menu lets users change the model and effort level, and higher effort generally produces more thorough responses but takes longer and uses more tokens. The right mental model is a tradeoff: reserve the most capable model, higher effort, or extended thinking for tasks with complex reasoning, high ambiguity, or high stakes, not for every simple variation. See Anthropic’s help article on Change the model, effort, and thinking settings.

A Project may still be useful for storing the style guide or campaign background, but it is not a substitute for model selection. Extended thinking and max effort can be valuable when the problem requires deeper analysis, but using them by default for simple promotional copy is an inefficient pattern.

questions.question: A public radio station's membership team has asked Claude to review anonymized listener feedback from a recent pledge drive. The team needs two outputs: a same-day recap that can be pasted into a Slack update, and a more polished pledge-drive messaging guide that staff will revise and reuse for future campaigns. Which TWO requests best match the output format to the work?

options.label: A
options.text: Ask Claude to create an artifact for the messaging guide with sections, examples, and revision notes.
options.feedback: This is correct because the messaging guide is substantial, self-contained, and likely to be edited and reused. An artifact gives the team a separate workspace for iterating on a durable deliverable.

options.label: B
options.text: Ask Claude to create an artifact for the Slack recap with only three bullets and no supporting detail.
options.feedback: This is incorrect because a very short recap is usually better handled directly in the chat. Using an artifact for a few bullets adds unnecessary structure without improving review or reuse.

options.label: C
options.text: Ask Claude for a concise inline recap with themes, examples, and next steps for the Slack update.
options.feedback: This is correct because the same-day recap is short-lived and meant to be pasted into another communication tool. An inline response is appropriate when the output is compact and does not need its own reusable workspace.

options.label: D
options.text: Ask Claude to keep the full messaging guide inline so it stays tied to the chat context.
options.feedback: This is incorrect because a reusable guide should stand on its own as a working document. Keeping it only inline makes it harder to revise, reference, and reuse outside the immediate conversation.

questions.explanation:
Choosing the right output format is part of evaluating whether Claude's work will be useful in the real workflow. A brief update intended for Slack or email is often best as an inline response, because the user can quickly review, copy, and send it without managing a separate document.

An artifact is better when the output is substantial, self-contained, and likely to be edited, iterated on, reused, or referenced later. Anthropic's Help Center describes artifacts as appropriate for significant standalone content, typically over 15 lines, such as documents, websites, diagrams, and other reusable materials: What are artifacts and how do I use them?.

The practical tradeoff is simplicity versus durability. Inline output keeps small answers fast and lightweight, while artifacts create a dedicated space for larger deliverables that need review and refinement. Claude for Work also frames artifacts as a way to create, manage, and collaborate on files and other content, while Projects help organize more complex work: Claude for Work.

questions.question: A nonprofit wildlife rescue’s development manager asks Claude to “summarize these donor survey results for leadership” and attaches a spreadsheet export plus several open-ended comments. Claude’s summary is well written, but it highlights a few emotional comments as if they represent the whole group, overlooks the strongest numeric trend, and suggests campaign changes not supported by the survey. What is the best next troubleshooting step?

options.label: A
options.text: Switch to the most capable available model and rerun the original prompt with the same attachments and instructions.
options.feedback: A stronger model can help with complex work, but it cannot reliably infer unstated requirements. When the prompt lacks criteria, structure, or grounding instructions, changing models alone is not the best first fix.

options.label: B
options.text: Ask Claude to make the same summary more executive-ready, persuasive, and emotionally compelling for leadership.
options.feedback: This may improve the tone, but it does not fix the missing trend or unsupported conclusions. Making the output more persuasive can make weak or unverified claims harder to notice.

options.label: C
options.text: Rewrite the prompt with the audience, required sections, grounding rules, and a findings versus recommendations split.
options.feedback: This directly addresses the likely cause of the poor output: the task was underspecified for the kind of analysis needed. Giving Claude a clearer audience, structure, and grounding rules helps it focus on the evidence and avoid blending observations with unsupported suggestions.

options.label: D
options.text: Remove the spreadsheet export and provide only the open-ended comments that seem most memorable to leadership.
options.feedback: This would make the evidence base less representative and could worsen the overemphasis on anecdotes. If numeric trends matter, Claude needs access to those data and clear instructions for how to use them.

questions.explanation:
When Claude produces a polished but unreliable output, the first troubleshooting step is often to improve the task framing, not just the style. A prompt like summarize these results leaves important choices unstated: who the summary is for, which evidence matters most, what sections to include, and whether recommendations must be tied to the supplied data.

A better revision gives Claude a clear role and output shape, asks it to prioritize quantitative trends alongside comments, and tells it to label recommendations separately from findings. This helps reduce hallucinated or overgeneralized claims because Claude has explicit constraints for how to use the source material. Anthropic’s user guidance emphasizes being specific about what you want and providing context when using Claude, as described in Get started with Claude.

Model choice and effort settings can matter for difficult analysis, but they are not a substitute for a clear prompt. The practical optimization habit is to diagnose whether the failure is about capability, missing context, vague instructions, or insufficient verification, then fix the prompt or inputs before relying on the next draft.

questions.question: A specialty food importer’s category manager asks Claude to review a proposed expansion into three new countries, compare supplier reliability, labeling constraints, retailer expectations, margin pressure, and reputational risk, then draft questions for the executive team. The deadline allows for a slower response if the analysis is stronger. Which model choice best fits this task?

options.label: A
options.text: Use Opus for the review and executive-question draft.
options.feedback: Opus is the best fit when the task calls for the strongest reasoning across many competing factors. The scenario values depth and judgment more than speed, which matches where Opus is typically preferred.

options.label: B
options.text: Use the same model for every Claude task.
options.feedback: Using one model for all work ignores the tradeoffs among speed, cost, and reasoning capability. Model choice should vary based on whether the task is lightweight, balanced, or highly complex.

options.label: C
options.text: Use Haiku for the review and executive-question draft.
options.feedback: Haiku is a good choice for fast, lightweight, high-volume tasks, but this scenario requires more complex tradeoff analysis. Choosing it primarily for a nuanced strategic review would under-prioritize reasoning depth.

options.label: D
options.text: Use Sonnet only to minimize the response time.
options.feedback: Sonnet is often a strong balanced choice, but the stated priority is the strongest analysis rather than speed. If the task is unusually complex and time allows, Opus is the better fit.

questions.explanation:
Claude model selection is about matching the model to the work, not always choosing the fastest or always choosing the most capable. A useful mental model is that Haiku is best suited to fast, lightweight tasks, Sonnet is a balanced choice for many everyday knowledge-work tasks, and Opus is the strongest fit when a task needs deeper reasoning across complex tradeoffs.

In this scenario, the manager is asking Claude to compare several business risks and constraints, then produce questions for executives. Since the task values depth over speed, Opus is the best match. Haiku would be more appropriate for short summaries or simple classification, while Sonnet would be reasonable for many mid-complexity tasks but is not the strongest choice when maximum reasoning quality is the priority.

You can change models from the model menu in Claude, and changes apply starting with Claude’s next response. For more on where model and effort choices appear in the Claude interface, see Change the model, effort, and thinking settings. Anthropic also describes Claude on the official Claude page.

questions.question: A boutique hotel group's guest experience lead asks Claude to create a service recovery toolkit from four uploaded files: a refund policy, brand voice guide, common complaint themes, and property amenities list. The toolkit needs a front desk script, supervisor escalation checklist, training quiz, and guest follow-up email templates. Claude's first draft is uneven, and the quiz mentions policy details that do not appear in the checklist. What is the most effective next prompt?

options.label: A
options.text: Ask Claude to map sources to deliverables, flag assumptions, then draft each toolkit piece in sequence.
options.feedback: This option breaks the complex request into smaller parts before asking for final output. Mapping sources to deliverables helps Claude use the right materials for each piece, and sequencing the drafts makes review easier.

options.label: B
options.text: Ask Claude to handle each toolkit piece in separate chats, without carrying prior context between them.
options.feedback: Separate chats can reduce complexity, but removing shared context can create inconsistent outputs. In this scenario, the pieces need to align with the same policy, brand voice, and complaint themes.

options.label: C
options.text: Ask Claude to start with the final guest emails, then adapt the other materials from that tone.
options.feedback: This prioritizes one output type, but it does not address how policy details, escalation steps, and training content should connect. Tone alone is not enough to organize a multi-part toolkit.

options.label: D
options.text: Ask Claude to regenerate the full toolkit in one response, emphasizing that every file must be used.
options.feedback: This may sound stricter, but it keeps the task as one large undivided request. It does not create checkpoints for catching mismatches between the checklist, quiz, and templates.

questions.explanation:
For a complex request, a strong prompt often asks Claude to plan before drafting. A source-to-deliverable plan gives Claude a simple structure: which uploaded materials matter for the script, which matter for the escalation checklist, which should feed the quiz, and which should shape the follow-up emails.

This approach also creates useful checkpoints. If Claude flags assumptions or missing details before writing, the user can correct the direction early instead of reviewing a large, inconsistent final draft. Drafting each piece in sequence keeps the work manageable while still preserving shared context across the toolkit.

The less effective prompts either keep the work as one broad request, over-focus on tone, or split the work so much that consistency may suffer. Claude can handle multi-step work well, but the user improves results by being specific about the task, materials, and process, as emphasized in Anthropic's Getting started with Claude.ai guidance.

html.explanation:

This approach also creates useful checkpoints. If Claude flags assumptions or missing details before writing, the user can correct the direction early instead of reviewing a large, inconsistent final draft. Drafting each piece in sequence keeps the work manageable while still preserving shared context across the toolkit.

The less effective prompts either keep the work as one broad request, over-focus on tone, or split the work so much that consistency may suffer. questions.question: An environmental consulting firm’s grants coordinator creates a Claude Project for a year-long grant portfolio. She puts the naming convention, funder priorities, and review checklist in the Project name and description, then opens separate chats for each proposal. Claude’s drafts do not consistently apply those standards. What is the most appropriate next step?

options.label: A
options.text: Start each proposal in an incognito chat to keep unrelated history out of drafts.
options.feedback: This is incorrect because incognito chats are designed not to save chat history or memory, so they are not a persistence tool. They can reduce carryover from prior conversations, but they do not help Claude reuse the grant standards across proposal work.

options.label: B
options.text: Move the standards into Project instructions or Project knowledge before drafting proposals.
options.feedback: This is correct because durable working context should be placed where Claude can use it, such as Project instructions or the Project knowledge base. Project names and descriptions help the user organize work, but they are not the right place to store instructions Claude must apply.

options.label: C
options.text: Paste the full prior proposal conversation into each new chat before drafting proposals.
options.feedback: This is incorrect because pasting a full prior conversation is inefficient and can consume the available context window. A concise summary or persistent Project knowledge is a better fit for standards that need to guide multiple chats.

options.label: D
options.text: Expand the Project name and description with more detailed standards before drafting proposals.
options.feedback: This is incorrect because adding more detail to the Project name or description does not make those details available as working context for Claude. It may improve human organization, but it does not solve the problem of Claude applying the standards in chats.

questions.explanation:
Projects are useful when work needs an ongoing workspace, but the durable context must be stored in the right place. Anthropic documents that Project knowledge and Project instructions are the places to put background material and guidance Claude should use, while Project names and descriptions are not available to Claude. See How can I create and manage projects?.

The mental model is that a Project is not a magic memory of everything a user meant by its title. If the coordinator wants each proposal chat to follow the same naming convention, funder priorities, and review checklist, those standards should be added as Project instructions or as files or text in Project knowledge.

Pasting full old conversations is a common anti-pattern because it fills the context window with drafts, dead ends, and irrelevant details. Claude’s length limits govern how much information it can work with in a single chat, so summarizing or restructuring context is usually better than repeatedly pasting everything. Anthropic’s length-limit guidance is described in How do usage and length limits work?.

Incognito is also the wrong tool for this need. It is useful when a user does not want a chat saved to history or memory, but it does not create shared context for future chats. For details on memory and incognito behavior, see Use Claude’s chat search and memory to build on previous context.

questions.question: A medical device distributor’s customer success lead needs Claude to turn warranty terms, sample customer emails, and service-level rules into a guide for new representatives. The first prompt, “Make a support escalation guide,” produced a generic guide that missed key policy details. What is the best next prompt?

options.label: A
options.text: Ask Claude to make the guide as complete as possible from general knowledge, avoiding follow-up questions so the team can use it immediately.
options.feedback: This is incorrect because completeness from general knowledge is not a substitute for the team’s actual materials. Preventing follow-up questions can also hide gaps that should be clarified before the guide is used.

options.label: B
options.text: Ask Claude to rewrite the generic guide in a more polished style, keeping the same scope and adding a few practical examples.
options.feedback: This is incorrect because polishing the previous answer does not address the missing context. Better wording may make the guide easier to read, but it will not reliably incorporate the warranty and service-level details.

options.label: C
options.text: Ask Claude to act as a senior support strategist and create an impressive escalation checklist using industry best practices and confident recommendations.
options.feedback: This is incorrect because a role label and industry best practices do not provide the organization-specific rules Claude needs. It may produce plausible guidance that conflicts with the distributor’s actual policies.

options.label: D
options.text: Ask Claude to use the attached warranty terms, email examples, and service rules to create a numbered escalation checklist for new reps, flagging unclear cases.
options.feedback: This is correct because it gives Claude the source materials, audience, desired format, and relevant constraints. It also asks Claude to flag unclear cases instead of inventing policy details.

questions.explanation:
Effective prompting is less about finding a special phrase and more about giving Claude the information a capable coworker would need. Anthropic’s prompt design guidance recommends treating Claude like someone with no prior context about your organization or task, then stating clearly what you want it to do: Introduction to prompt design.

In this scenario, the useful prompt names the source materials, the intended audience, the output format, and the need to flag uncertainty. Those details help Claude produce a practical work product instead of a generic support article. If the first response is weak, the best next step is to add context, break the request into clearer parts, and iterate with feedback, not rely on vague instructions such as make it better or be an expert; see My prompt isn’t giving me a helpful answer. For business materials that must follow policy, asking Claude to identify unclear cases is also important because it reduces the chance that a polished answer will quietly fill gaps with unsupported assumptions.

questions.question: A neighborhood credit union’s financial wellness team is redesigning its first-time homebuyer workshop workflow. They have anonymized participant survey themes, branch event calendars, staff availability notes, and lender-partner requirements. They want Claude to help identify bottlenecks and create a repeatable planning process for future workshops. Which TWO actions best use Claude for research, planning, and process optimization?

options.label: A
options.text: Ask Claude to compare the inputs, surface recurring constraints, and propose a staged planning checklist.
options.feedback: This uses Claude to synthesize several planning inputs rather than treating the task as simple drafting. It also asks for an actionable process output, which fits planning and process optimization.

options.label: B
options.text: Have Claude write only the promotional email before reviewing the survey and scheduling inputs.
options.feedback: Writing promotional copy may be useful later, but it does not address the stated goal of improving the planning workflow. Skipping the underlying inputs prevents Claude from helping identify bottlenecks or constraints.

options.label: C
options.text: Ask Claude to pick final workshop dates and announce them without confirming staff availability.
options.feedback: Claude can help analyze constraints and draft a plan, but it should not replace confirmation with the people and partners involved. Publishing dates without checking availability creates an avoidable operational risk.

options.label: D
options.text: Have Claude turn the improved workflow into a reusable template with roles, timing, and review points.
options.feedback: This helps the team convert a one-time planning effort into a repeatable operating process. A reusable template captures what the team learned and makes future workshop planning more consistent.

questions.explanation:
Claude is most useful for research, planning, and process optimization when it is given the relevant materials and asked to find patterns, constraints, risks, and next steps. In this scenario, the strongest use is to synthesize survey themes, calendars, staffing notes, and partner requirements into a structured planning process rather than jumping straight to an outward-facing deliverable.

For work that repeats, the team should also capture the improved process as a template or checklist. Anthropic describes Skills as a way to package proven work approaches so Claude can apply them across conversations, while Projects are useful when context accumulates around a specific ongoing effort. See Teach Claude your way of working using skills and Skills overview.

The weaker choices skip the process-improvement step. Asking Claude to announce dates without human confirmation overstates what Claude should do in an operational workflow, and asking only for promotional copy turns a planning problem into a writing task.

questions.question: A museum education director uses Claude for exhibit labels, school outreach emails, and internal planning notes in separate chats and Projects. For her own Claude account, she wants Claude to consistently ask one clarifying question before drafting and keep first drafts concise, no matter where she starts the work. What should she update?

options.label: A
options.text: Create a Skill for the exhibit-label workflow.
options.feedback: Skills are better for specific repeatable workflows or capabilities that should activate when relevant. A general habit such as asking a clarifying question across all work belongs in account-wide instructions instead.

options.label: B
options.text: Update one Project's instructions with the preference.
options.feedback: Project instructions apply only to chats inside that specific Project. They would not guide regular chats or other Projects where the director starts similar work.

options.label: C
options.text: Update each Project description with the preference.
options.feedback: Project descriptions help people identify and organize Projects, but they are not a reliable way to instruct Claude. Claude does not use the Project name or description as working context.

options.label: D
options.text: Update Instructions for Claude with the preference.
options.feedback: This is correct because the preference is meant to apply across the director's conversations, not just within one workspace. Instructions for Claude are the appropriate place for broad, account-wide working preferences.

questions.explanation:
Claude offers several personalization surfaces, and the right one depends on scope. A broad preference for how Claude should collaborate across all conversations is best placed in Instructions for Claude, while Project instructions are for requirements that apply only within a specific Project. Anthropic describes this distinction in Understanding Claude's personalization features.

Projects are useful when work needs persistent context, such as a campaign brief, source documents, or project-specific rules. However, Project configuration should not be used for account-wide behavior, and the Project name or description is not the same as knowledge or instructions that Claude can use. The Projects documentation explains how Projects work as self-contained workspaces in What are projects?.

The practical mental model is: use Instructions for Claude for general working preferences, use Project instructions for a workspace's local requirements, use Project knowledge for reusable source material, and use Skills for repeatable task-specific procedures. Choosing the narrowest feature that matches the need keeps Claude's behavior predictable without making unrelated work inherit the wrong context.

questions.question: A corporate training provider's program coordinator uses Claude with Google Workspace connectors to prepare client communications. She asks Claude to review a recent Gmail thread about a workshop and draft a reply, but the thread includes an attached venue policy PDF whose contents affect the answer. Which two actions are most appropriate? Select two.

options.label: A
options.text: Approve Claude to send the completed Gmail message directly from the conversation.
options.feedback: This is incorrect because the Gmail connector does not allow Claude to send Gmail messages for the user. Even if permissions screens mention sending, Gmail messages must still be sent manually.

options.label: B
options.text: Add the venue policy PDF separately as a file or Drive item before drafting.
options.feedback: This is correct because Gmail attachment content is not directly accessible through the Gmail connector. If the PDF's contents matter, the user should provide that content through a supported file or Google Drive workflow.

options.label: C
options.text: Use Claude to create a Gmail draft, then review and send it manually in Gmail.
options.feedback: This is correct because Claude can create drafts in Gmail, but it cannot send Gmail messages on the user's behalf. The user should review the draft for accuracy and send it manually from Gmail.

options.label: D
options.text: Rely on the Gmail connector to read the PDF attachment content from the thread.
options.feedback: This is incorrect because Claude can access Gmail attachment metadata, not the attachment contents, through the Gmail connector. The attachment's filename or other metadata is not enough when the content affects the reply.

questions.explanation:
Google Workspace connectors let Claude work with Gmail, Google Calendar, and Google Drive from a conversation, but each connector has a defined scope. For Gmail, Claude can search and read emails, create drafts, manage labels and threads, and access attachment metadata, but it cannot send Gmail messages for the user.

Attachment handling is the key judgment point in this scenario. If the content of a PDF attachment matters, the user should add that PDF separately, such as through an upload or a supported Google Drive workflow, rather than assuming the Gmail connector can inspect the attachment body. Google Drive support is broader than just Google Docs, and the documented connector can read PDFs when provided through Drive.

Connectors are designed to keep the user in control: Claude uses them when the user makes a relevant request, actions require explicit approval, and responses include citations to source emails, events, or documents when available. This makes connector use powerful for retrieving context, while still requiring human review before external communication is sent. See Use Google Workspace connectors for the documented Gmail and Google Drive capabilities and limits.

questions.question: A regional transit agency's rider outreach team uses a Claude Project for service-change announcements. The team has updated route-change source documents and a new rule that every summary must name affected neighborhoods first. They want future chats in that Project, but not unrelated Claude work, to use the updated material and rule. Which two actions should the team take?

options.label: A
options.text: Paste the new rule into one active chat and ask Claude to remember it later.
options.feedback: Pasting the rule into one chat is not the right way to maintain a Project-scoped configuration. Even if memory or prior-chat search is available, a rule that should consistently guide future Project chats belongs in Project instructions.

options.label: B
options.text: Add the rule to account-wide Instructions for Claude so every conversation follows it.
options.feedback: Account-wide Instructions for Claude apply broadly across conversations, not just this Project. That would be too broad because the team only wants the neighborhood-first rule for service-change announcement work.

options.label: C
options.text: Use Set project instructions to record the neighborhood-first summary rule for the Project.
options.feedback: Project instructions are scoped to all chats within that Project, which fits a rule that should not affect unrelated Claude work. This keeps the behavior tied to the service-change workspace rather than the whole account.

options.label: D
options.text: Add the updated source documents to the Project knowledge and remove outdated copies.
options.feedback: Project knowledge is the persistent source material Claude can use across chats within that Project. Replacing outdated materials helps future Project chats use the current source set instead of conflicting older information.

questions.explanation:
Project knowledge and Project instructions solve different maintenance problems. Source documents belong in the Project knowledge base because Claude can use that content across chats in the Project. Behavioral rules, such as how to structure summaries, belong in Set project instructions when they should apply to every chat in that Project.

A key mental model is that a Project is a focused workspace for related work, but each chat is still its own conversation. Features such as memory or prior-chat search may make earlier conversation details available when enabled, but they are not the clearest maintenance mechanism for a rule or source set that the team wants to manage deliberately. For durable Project-scoped context, put source material in Project knowledge and behavioral requirements in Project instructions.

Account-wide instructions are useful for general preferences that should follow you everywhere, such as asking clarifying questions or keeping answers concise. They are not the right place for a route-announcement rule that should affect only one Project. See Anthropic’s guidance on Projects and project knowledge in What are projects?, project management in How can I create and manage projects?, and personalization choices in Understanding Claude’s personalization features.

questions.question: An architecture studio's operations manager asks Claude to prepare a client onboarding packet from uploaded materials: a scope template, billing policy, project milestone notes, and brand voice guide. The packet needs a welcome email, kickoff agenda, client responsibilities checklist, and internal handoff note. The first prompt, “Create everything we need for onboarding,” returns polished text, but some source details are misplaced across the materials. What is the most effective next prompt?

options.label: A
options.text: Ask Claude to create a plan that separates audiences, maps source files to deliverables, then drafts and reviews the pieces in sequence.
options.feedback: This approach breaks a complex request into smaller, checkable parts before asking for final content. It helps Claude use the right source material for each deliverable and reduces the chance that details meant for one audience appear in another document.

options.label: B
options.text: Ask Claude to expand every section with additional examples, keep the same combined format, then ask for a quick final proofread.
options.feedback: Adding more examples can make an already mixed output harder to review. A final proofread is useful only after the materials have been organized correctly and checked against their sources.

options.label: C
options.text: Ask Claude to rewrite the packet in a warmer voice, remove obvious internal notes, then produce a single polished version for approval.
options.feedback: This focuses on tone and cleanup rather than on how the work should be structured. It may improve style, but it does not address the underlying issue of matching each deliverable to the right source details.

options.label: D
options.text: Ask Claude to use the billing policy as the main source, draft all materials together, then adjust the tone afterward.
options.feedback: Prioritizing one source does not fit a packet that depends on several different uploaded materials. Drafting everything together again repeats the same broad approach that caused misplaced details.

questions.explanation:
For a complex request with several outputs, a strong prompt gives Claude a workable process instead of asking for everything at once. The practical pattern is to ask for a short plan, connect each deliverable to the relevant source material, and then draft the pieces in a sequence that can be reviewed.

This is a form of task decomposition: it reduces the number of decisions Claude has to make at the same time and gives the user natural checkpoints. In this scenario, the welcome email, kickoff agenda, checklist, and handoff note have different audiences and should not all draw from the same details in the same way.

Claude's user-facing guidance emphasizes being specific about the task and providing the materials needed for better results. See Anthropic's Getting started with Claude.ai tutorial, which explains how clear prompts and relevant documents help Claude handle more complex work.

questions.question: A university library's outreach coordinator has approved event details, a target audience, a sample newsletter that matches the library's voice, and a word-count limit. She wants Claude to help create the next version of an announcement for students. Which prompt strategy is most appropriate?

options.label: A
options.text: Ask Claude to generate several fresh creative angles before giving it the approved announcement details.
options.feedback: This fits brainstorming more than drafting. It may be useful earlier in planning, but it is less helpful when the event details and message direction are already approved.

options.label: B
options.text: Share the source details, audience, voice sample, and limits, then ask Claude to draft the announcement.
options.feedback: This fits a drafting task because the facts, audience, and desired form are already known. Giving Claude the source material and constraints helps it produce useful copy without guessing about the message or style.

options.label: C
options.text: Ask Claude to analyze possible attendance barriers and recommend messaging priorities.
options.feedback: This fits an analysis task focused on understanding a pattern or problem. It could inform future outreach, but it does not directly create the student-facing announcement the coordinator needs next.

options.label: D
options.text: Ask Claude to research current student interests before sharing the library's source materials.
options.feedback: This fits a research task, not the immediate need to create copy from known materials. Research may add context, but it should not replace the approved details and voice guidance.

questions.explanation:
Prompting works best when the request matches the type of task. For drafting, Claude needs the ingredients for the communication: source facts, audience, tone or style examples, length, format, and any must-include or avoid language.

questions.question: A veterinary clinic network's operations manager has been using a Claude Project to redesign appointment reminder scripts. After several exploratory chats, the team has agreed on approved wording, escalation rules, and a preferred tone. They want future chats in the same Project to use those decisions without manually copying them each time. What is the most appropriate next step?

options.label: A
options.text: Paste the entire earlier discussion into each new chat, skip Project Knowledge, and rely on manual repetition.
options.feedback: This is a weak workflow because it recreates the copying burden the team is trying to avoid. It can also bring in irrelevant exploratory discussion instead of the approved decisions Claude should consistently follow.

options.label: B
options.text: Put the decisions in the project name and description, open new Project chats, and rely on those fields.
options.feedback: This is incorrect because the project name and description are not available to Claude as working context. They help humans identify and manage the Project, but they are not a substitute for Project Knowledge or project instructions.

options.label: C
options.text: Keep the decisions in the earlier chat, open new Project chats, and expect Claude to reuse that history.
options.feedback: This is incorrect because chat context is not automatically shared across chats inside a Project. Earlier exploratory conversations may be useful to the person who had them, but their contents do not become shared Project context unless the relevant information is added to Project Knowledge.

options.label: D
options.text: Create an approved decisions note, add it to Project Knowledge, and update project instructions for the workflow.
options.feedback: This is correct because future chats in a Project can use content that has been added to the Project Knowledge base. Project instructions are also the right place to set consistent behavior, such as tone and response style, across chats in that Project.

questions.explanation:
Projects are designed as organized workspaces for related work, with their own chats, Project Knowledge, and project instructions. They are useful when a workflow needs stable background material and consistent guidance across multiple related conversations, such as approved wording, policies, or tone standards.

The important workflow detail is that a Project does not make every prior chat automatically available to every future chat. Anthropic's documentation explains that context is not shared across chats within a Project unless the information is added to the Project Knowledge base, so the team should capture the approved decisions in a concise source note and add that note to Project Knowledge. Project instructions can then tell Claude how to use that material, for example to follow the approved tone and escalation rules.

Relying on the project name, project description, or an earlier conversation is an anti-pattern for reusable workflow context. Those approaches may feel organized to the human user, but they do not give Claude the durable, explicit context it needs in later chats. See What are Projects? and How can I create and manage Projects? for the documented behavior of Project Knowledge and project instructions.

questions.question: A regional theater's production office uses a Claude for Work Team plan to revise its seasonal operations handbook. Editors need a shared Claude workspace with the same handbook text and response guidelines, while the source handbook lives in a Google Doc that changes after legal review. They also want to avoid assuming that every past chat automatically becomes shared context. What is the most appropriate way to integrate Claude into this workflow?

options.label: A
options.text: Create private Projects for each editor, add the handbook through Google Drive, and merge the team’s drafts outside Claude.
options.feedback: This could allow each editor to use the synced Google Doc in a private Project. It does not provide one shared workspace with common Project Knowledge and instructions for the team.

options.label: B
options.text: Use one continuing chat for the season, paste policy updates into replies, and ask Claude to remember the team’s decisions.
options.feedback: A long chat can work for a narrow one-off task, but it is a poor fit for an ongoing team workflow. It also creates a fragile process where reusable guidance and source material are not managed as Project Knowledge and project instructions.

options.label: C
options.text: Create a shared Project, add the handbook to Project Knowledge, set instructions, and refresh it after policy changes.
options.feedback: This uses Projects for a shared, organized workspace and uses Project Knowledge for information that should be available across chats. It also accounts for the fact that Google Docs in Projects are only supported in private projects, so a shared workflow may require adding or refreshing the handbook content in Project Knowledge.

options.label: D
options.text: Create a shared Project, add the handbook through Google Drive, set instructions, and rely on live syncing.
options.feedback: This is plausible because Google Docs added through the Google Drive integration can stay synced. However, the Google Drive integration in Projects is available only in private projects, so this does not fit a shared Project workflow.

questions.explanation:
Projects are designed for organizing related work in Claude.ai, with their own project knowledge bases, instructions, and chat histories. For a team workflow, the durable material that future chats should use belongs in Project Knowledge, while the recurring response style or working rules belong in project instructions.

A key mental model is that a Project is not a single shared memory of every conversation. Anthropic notes that context is not shared across chats within a project unless the information is added to the project knowledge base, so important decisions and source content should be promoted into Project Knowledge rather than left buried in prior chats.

The Google Docs integration is useful when a user wants to add a supported Google Doc and keep it synced, but the documented Project use is limited to private projects. In a shared Team plan Project, the safer workflow is to add the handbook content to Project Knowledge, set the instructions, and refresh the knowledge when the approved source changes.

For more detail, see Anthropic's documentation on What are Projects?, How can I create and manage Projects?, Project visibility and sharing, and Using the Google Docs integration.

questions.question: A specialty coffee roaster’s operations team is setting internal guidelines for how staff may use Claude. Which planned use best fits routine productivity support without requiring the extra safeguards associated with high-risk recommendations about individuals?

options.label: A
options.text: Recommend disciplinary action based on employee performance notes.
options.feedback: This asks Claude to advise on an employment decision affecting a specific worker. That makes it a high-risk use case rather than routine productivity support, even if a manager ultimately considers the recommendation.

options.label: B
options.text: Summarize supplier sustainability reports for an internal planning memo.
options.feedback: This is a general productivity use involving summarization for internal business planning. It does not ask Claude to make a recommendation or subjective decision that directly affects an individual’s access to employment, housing, finance, healthcare, or another listed high-risk area.

options.label: C
options.text: Rank job applicants and recommend which candidates to interview.
options.feedback: This uses Claude for employment-related recommendations about individuals. Employment is listed as a high-risk use case when advice or decisions directly affect people, so it requires safeguards such as qualified professional review before finalization.

options.label: D
options.text: Rank staff housing applicants based on submitted applications.
options.feedback: This asks Claude to support housing-related decisions about individuals. Housing is included in the high-risk use cases, so it should not be treated like ordinary summarization or drafting.

questions.explanation:
Claude is well suited for many general productivity tasks, including drafting, summarizing, brainstorming, translation, learning support, and analyzing image or chart content. A supplier-report summary for an internal planning memo fits that pattern, provided the user still reviews the output for accuracy before relying on it.

The key distinction is whether Claude is being used to make or shape advice, recommendations, or subjective decisions that directly affect people in sensitive areas. Anthropic’s Usage Policy identifies areas such as employment and housing as high-risk use cases, which are not treated the same as routine productivity tasks. High-risk uses may require safeguards such as qualified professional review before dissemination or finalization.

The employment and housing options fall short because they ask Claude to rank, recommend, or guide decisions about specific people. Those uses are not automatically banned simply because they are high risk, but they cannot be treated as ordinary low-risk productivity support. The safer mental model is to use Claude for assistance with information work while keeping sensitive decisions, especially those affecting individuals’ opportunities or rights, under appropriate human oversight.

Anthropic also reminds users that Claude’s outputs may be inaccurate, even when they sound detailed or confident. The Consumer Terms emphasize independently confirming accuracy before relying on outputs or actions, and the Help Center lists common appropriate uses at What are some things I can use Claude for?.

questions.question: A city food bank's donor relations manager is using a Claude Project to prepare an email for first-time pantry volunteers. Claude returns two drafts: one includes all required arrival and safety details but sounds bureaucratic, while the other feels welcoming but omits several required steps. The manager also has a short audience guide and a checklist of required details. What is the most appropriate next step?

options.label: A
options.text: Add the audience guide to the project description, then ask Claude to rewrite the email in a new chat.
options.feedback: This is incorrect because a project’s name and description are not available to Claude as working context. Reusable context should be provided in the chat or added to project knowledge, not placed only in the description.

options.label: B
options.text: Ask Claude to compare the drafts against the guide and checklist, then produce a concise combined revision.
options.feedback: This is correct because it uses iteration to refine the output for both audience fit and required content. It gives Claude clear criteria for comparison instead of treating either imperfect draft as final.

options.label: C
options.text: Ask Claude which draft it prefers, then use that version after making minor style edits.
options.feedback: This is incorrect because Claude's preference is not the same as evaluation against the manager's audience and content requirements. The user should supply concrete criteria and verify the result against those criteria.

options.label: D
options.text: Send the welcoming draft after proofreading it, since tone matters most for first-time volunteers.
options.feedback: This is incorrect because the draft omits required steps that volunteers need before arrival. A friendly tone is valuable, but it does not replace validating that essential instructions are included.

questions.explanation:
When Claude produces partial or mismatched drafts, the strongest next move is to iterate with clearer criteria. Anthropic’s guidance emphasizes being specific, providing enough context, breaking complex requests into substeps, and using follow-up instructions when an answer is not helpful, as described in My prompt isn't giving me a helpful answer.

Here, the manager needs both audience adaptation and content completeness. Asking Claude to compare the drafts against the audience guide and checklist turns refinement into an evaluative task: preserve the accurate operational details, adapt the language for first-time volunteers, and produce a usable revision. This reflects Claude’s conversational workflow, where users can naturally refine prompts and ask follow-up questions, as noted in Get started with Claude.

It is risky to choose the warmer draft just because it sounds better, since missing safety or arrival steps could create confusion. It is also not enough to ask Claude which version it prefers, because the standard is the intended audience and required checklist, not Claude’s subjective preference. If the team wants reusable context across project chats, they should understand how project knowledge works and avoid relying on fields Claude cannot see, as explained in How can I create and manage Projects?.

questions.question: A renewable energy installer’s people operations team wants to use Claude to compare technician job applications, recommend which applicants should advance, and draft rejection messages that would be sent directly to candidates. What is the most appropriate action?

options.label: A
options.text: Remove candidate names from the application files and let Claude make advancement decisions automatically.
options.feedback: Reducing identifying details may help with privacy, but it does not make automated hiring decisions appropriate. Employment-related recommendations still require qualified human review before finalization.

options.label: B
options.text: Send Claude’s ranked list to candidates immediately and invite them to appeal after receiving the message.
options.feedback: An appeal process does not replace qualified human review before a decision is finalized. Sending Claude’s recommendations directly would rely too heavily on an output that may be incomplete, biased, or incorrect.

options.label: C
options.text: Require qualified hiring review before final decisions and disclose AI assistance in candidate-facing messages.
options.feedback: Employment decisions are a high-risk use case because they can directly affect individuals’ opportunities. A qualified professional should review Claude-assisted recommendations before finalization, and candidates should be told when AI helped produce outputs presented to them.

options.label: D
options.text: Ask Claude to explain its confidence in each ranking and advance the candidates with the highest scores.
options.feedback: Claude’s self-reported confidence is not a reliable safeguard for decisions affecting job applicants. The ethical issue is not only explanation quality, but whether a qualified human reviews the recommendation before it is used.

questions.explanation:
Using Claude in an employment context requires extra care because hiring decisions can materially affect a person’s opportunities. Anthropic’s Usage Policy identifies employment as a High-Risk Use Case when AI is used to provide recommendations or subjective decisions that directly affect individuals, and it requires review by a qualified professional before dissemination or finalization.

The right mental model is that Claude can assist with drafting, summarizing, and organizing information, but it should not become the sole decision-maker for consequential outcomes. Anthropic also warns that Claude can produce incorrect or misleading responses, so users should not treat it as a single source of truth, especially in high-stakes settings; see Claude is providing incorrect or misleading responses, what’s going on?. Disclosure matters when AI-generated outputs are presented directly to individuals, because people should not be led to believe a message or decision was produced entirely by a human when AI materially helped create it.

questions.question: An independent book publisher's rights team uploads a long PDF of a licensing agreement to a Claude Project and asks Claude to identify every payment obligation. The agreement includes narrative clauses and scanned fee tables near the end. Claude returns a polished checklist and states that it found no additional obligations outside the main royalty section. Before using the checklist in a negotiation, what is the most appropriate way to evaluate the output?

options.label: A
options.text: Ask Claude to confirm that the checklist is complete before using it in the negotiation.
options.feedback: This is incorrect because Claude’s self-assessment is not a reliable substitute for checking the source. A confident confirmation can still be wrong or incomplete.

options.label: B
options.text: Accept the checklist because the uploaded agreement gives Claude the source context it needs.
options.feedback: This is incorrect because source context improves grounding but does not guarantee that every relevant detail was extracted or interpreted correctly. Claude can still omit, misunderstand, or overstate information, especially in complex documents.

options.label: C
options.text: Enable extended thinking and regenerate the checklist without checking the agreement.
options.feedback: This is incorrect because extended thinking is useful for reasoning, not for proving that all source details were captured. It does not replace source verification for contract terms or scanned content.

options.label: D
options.text: Check the checklist against the agreement, including tables and later sections, before using it.
options.feedback: This is correct because Claude’s output should be checked against the source material before it is used for a high impact business decision. Long documents and nonstandard content such as scanned tables can create completeness risks, so reviewing the original agreement is the appropriate validation step.

questions.explanation:
When Claude summarizes or extracts obligations from a source document, the safest mental model is assisted review, not automatic certification. Claude can produce incorrect or misleading responses, and Anthropic advises users not to rely on Claude as a singular source of truth, especially for important decisions: Claude is providing incorrect or misleading responses, what's going on?.

Project knowledge can help Claude use uploaded materials across chats, but it does not remove the need to validate outputs against the underlying source. Anthropic’s Projects documentation explains that project files provide context and that retrieval may be used when project knowledge is large, which is helpful for relevance but not a guarantee of completeness: How can I create and manage Projects?.

In practice, polished formatting and complete-sounding wording should be treated as signals to verify, not as proof. For a negotiation, the rights team should compare the checklist with the original agreement, paying particular attention to tables, later sections, definitions, exhibits, and any content that may not be easy for Claude to extract.

options.feedback: This is appropriate for information the team wants Claude to use repeatedly in a Project. Project context does not automatically carry across chats unless the information is made available through the Project's shared materials or instructions.

options.label: C
