questions.question: In a planning conversation, Claude begins developing a communications plan even though the team has returned to budget prioritization. Earlier messages discussed both topics. Which action is BEST?

options.label: A
options.text: Allow Claude to finish the communications plan because changing direction during a response is always harmful.

options.label: B
options.text: Delete the entire Project immediately because one off-track response proves the configuration is unusable.

options.label: C
options.text: Redirect Claude explicitly to budget prioritization, restate the current objective, and exclude communications planning from this step.

options.label: D
options.text: Ask Claude to combine budget prioritization and communications planning into one answer without changing the objective.

questions.explanation:
Correct option:

Redirect Claude explicitly to budget prioritization, restate the current objective, and exclude communications planning from this step.

The instruction identifies the active workstream and the topic that should no longer guide the response. It provides enough context for Claude to recover without discarding all useful conversation history.

Course correction should be precise when the model follows an earlier but now inactive branch. The current objective and exclusions remove ambiguity.

This action is efficient when the chat remains otherwise usable. A clean restart is available later if conflicting context continues to dominate.

Incorrect options:

Allow Claude to finish the communications plan because changing direction during a response is always harmful.

The response is addressing the wrong workstream. Finishing it consumes time and may create irrelevant deliverables.

Users can steer Claude when priorities change. The manager should correct course as soon as the drift is clear.

Delete the entire Project immediately because one off-track response proves the configuration is unusable.

A single drift event does not establish that the whole Project is defective. The earlier conversation included both topics, making the cause understandable.

A targeted redirection is the proportional first response. Broader repair is appropriate only if the problem persists.

Ask Claude to combine budget prioritization and communications planning into one answer without changing the objective.

Combining the topics preserves the confusion rather than resolving it. The team has specifically returned to budget prioritization.

The model needs one current task and clear exclusions. Unnecessary synthesis can dilute the decision process.

questions.question: An education professional wants fresh ideas for increasing seminar participation, then plans to evaluate the strongest ideas against course constraints. Which prompting strategy is MOST appropriate?

options.label: A
options.text: Begin with broad brainstorming, then apply explicit feasibility criteria to shortlist and refine the ideas.

options.label: B
options.text: Require Claude to produce one final recommendation immediately without considering alternative approaches.

options.label: C
options.text: Ask Claude to research current participation statistics without first defining the seminar's actual participation problem.

options.label: D
options.text: Give Claude all constraints before allowing any divergent thinking and reject every idea not immediately implementable.

questions.explanation:
Correct option:

Begin with broad brainstorming, then apply explicit feasibility criteria to shortlist and refine the ideas.

The first phase encourages a useful range of possibilities before practical constraints narrow them. The second phase turns creative output into a decision-ready shortlist.

Brainstorming and evaluation require different instructions and success criteria. Separating them prevents early constraints from suppressing potentially valuable ideas.

The strategy supports exploration without treating every generated idea as equally workable. It gives the professional a transparent basis for selecting final interventions.

Incorrect options:

Require Claude to produce one final recommendation immediately without considering alternative approaches.

A single immediate recommendation limits exploration for a task whose first goal is idea generation. The professional cannot compare alternatives or understand trade-offs.

The output may reflect the first plausible pattern rather than the best course fit. A staged strategy better matches the creative and evaluative parts of the task.

Ask Claude to research current participation statistics without first defining the seminar's actual participation problem.

External statistics may provide context but do not replace understanding the specific seminar. The task is to generate and evaluate interventions for a known local setting.

Research could consume effort without clarifying what success means for the course. The professional should first use a strategy aligned to brainstorming and feasibility.

Give Claude all constraints before allowing any divergent thinking and reject every idea not immediately implementable.

Applying every constraint at the outset can make the brainstorming phase unnecessarily narrow. Ideas that require modest adaptation may be discarded too early.

The process should distinguish generating possibilities from testing them. Immediate rejection reduces creativity without improving the later evaluation method.

References:

Prompting best practices

Web search, extended thinking, and Research

Begin with broad brainstorming, then apply explicit feasibility criteria to shortlist and refine the ideas.

The strategy supports exploration without treating every generated idea as equally workable. It gives the professional a transparent basis for selecting final interventions.

Require Claude to produce one final recommendation immediately without considering alternative approaches.

A single immediate recommendation limits exploration for a task whose first goal is idea generation. The professional cannot compare alternatives or understand trade-offs.

The output may reflect the first plausible pattern rather than the best course fit. A staged strategy better matches the creative and evaluative parts of the task.

Ask Claude to research current participation statistics without first defining the seminar's actual participation problem.

External statistics may provide context but do not replace understanding the specific seminar. The task is to generate and evaluate interventions for a known local setting.

Research could consume effort without clarifying what success means for the course. The professional should first use a strategy aligned to brainstorming and feasibility.

Give Claude all constraints before allowing any divergent thinking and reject every idea not immediately implementable.

Applying every constraint at the outset can make the brainstorming phase unnecessarily narrow. Ideas that require modest adaptation may be discarded too early.

The process should distinguish generating possibilities from testing them. Immediate rejection reduces creativity without improving the later evaluation method.

options.label: A
options.text: Use Haiku exclusively because every recurring task should prioritize speed over synthesis quality.

options.label: B
options.text: Use Opus for every summary because professional readers expect the highest possible model tier.

options.label: C
options.text: Use Sonnet as the balanced default for strong synthesis, responsive performance, and practical cost.

options.label: D
options.text: Alternate models randomly each week so the team does not develop a preference for one model.

questions.explanation:
Correct option:

Use Sonnet as the balanced default for strong synthesis, responsive performance, and practical cost.

The task requires dependable reasoning and writing but does not demonstrate a need for the most demanding model tier. Moderate turnaround time and recurring use also make efficiency relevant.

Sonnet is positioned as a balance of intelligence and speed for broad professional workloads. That profile fits regular policy synthesis better than a speed-only or maximum-capability default.

The team can validate the summaries against source documents and monitor edge cases. A different model should be selected only when benchmarks show a material benefit.

Use Haiku exclusively because every recurring task should prioritize speed over synthesis quality.

Recurrence does not eliminate the need for careful interpretation and writing. The policy summaries are more complex than straightforward extraction.

Speed is one criterion rather than the only requirement. The team needs a model that balances quality with efficiency.

Use Opus for every summary because professional readers expect the highest possible model tier.

Reader expectations do not by themselves justify maximum model capability and cost. The task description does not identify unusually difficult reasoning.

Alternate models randomly each week so the team does not develop a preference for one model.

Random selection prevents consistent measurement and makes output differences harder to diagnose. It does not connect the model choice to task requirements.

The team should establish a suitable default and benchmark alternatives deliberately. Model diversity is not a goal unless it improves defined outcomes.

questions.domain: Domain 6: Governance, Risk, and Responsible Use
questions.question: A communications team uses Claude to draft a public report from internal analysis. Leaders want readers to understand the evidence and know who remains responsible for the conclusions. Which TWO practices are MOST appropriate?

options.label: A
options.text: Preserve source attribution for material claims and disclose important uncertainty or evidence limitations.

options.label: B
options.text: Describe Claude as the author so the organization does not need to accept responsibility for all published conclusions in the report.

options.label: C
options.text: Assign named human owners to review, approve, and stand behind the final conclusions.

options.label: D
options.text: Remove citations to make the report easier to read and ask readers to trust the summarized analysis.

options.label: E
options.text: Present every conclusion with equal certainty so the report appears consistent and decisive.

questions.explanation:
Correct options:

Preserve source attribution for material claims and disclose important uncertainty or evidence limitations.

Attribution lets readers trace consequential statements to their underlying evidence. Limitations prevent the report from presenting uncertain analysis as settled fact.

Transparency is especially important when Claude has synthesized multiple sources or interpretations. Readers should be able to distinguish evidence from inference.

This practice improves credibility and supports independent scrutiny. It also makes later corrections easier.

Assign named human owners to review, approve, and stand behind the final conclusions.

Human ownership makes clear that the organization, not Claude, is accountable for publication. Reviewers can challenge unsupported claims and confirm that the report reflects organizational judgment.

Using Claude for drafting does not transfer responsibility for what is communicated. Approval should be performed by people with the relevant authority and expertise.

This practice preserves accountability while retaining the efficiency of AI assistance. It also establishes a clear escalation path for disputed conclusions.

Incorrect options:

Describe Claude as the author so the organization does not need to accept responsibility for all published conclusions in the report.

Attributing authorship to Claude does not transfer legal, ethical, or organizational accountability. The organization chooses to publish and use the content.

Human owners must remain responsible for review and conclusions. The model cannot serve as an accountable institutional decision maker.

Remove citations to make the report easier to read and ask readers to trust the summarized analysis.

Removing citations reduces traceability and prevents readers from inspecting material evidence. Ease of reading should not require loss of transparency.

The report can use clear presentation while retaining source references. Trust should be supported by evidence and review.

Present every conclusion with equal certainty so the report appears consistent and decisive.

Uniform certainty can misrepresent differences in evidence strength. Some findings may depend on assumptions or incomplete data.

Responsible communication should disclose material uncertainty. Decisive tone cannot replace accurate calibration.

References:

Incorrect or misleading responses

Use Research on Claude

questions.question: A user wants Claude to convert approved procedure notes into a draft checklist that a supervisor will review before use. Is this an appropriate use case?

options.label: A
options.text: Yes, because Claude can draft the checklist from approved sources while a supervisor validates the final procedure.

options.label: B
options.text: No, because Claude should never transform any internal document into structured content without formal specialist and compliance approval.

options.label: C
options.text: Yes, because any output based on approved sources can be used operationally without human review or local procedure testing.

options.label: D
options.text: No, because only a Claude Architect may create any workflow that produces a checklist.

questions.explanation:
Correct option:

Yes, because Claude can draft the checklist from approved sources while a supervisor validates the final procedure.

The task is bounded, source-based, and designed to produce a reviewable draft. It does not transfer operational authority to Claude.

Using approved procedure notes provides a clear grounding source. Supervisor review can check completeness, sequence, and local requirements before adoption.

This is an appropriate augmentation of routine knowledge work. The controls match the consequence and uncertainty of the output.

Incorrect options:

No, because Claude should never transform any internal document into structured content without formal specialist and compliance approval.

The absolute restriction is broader than the risk described. Claude can appropriately organize approved internal material when access and review are authorized.

The key considerations are source quality, sensitivity, and human validation. The scenario already includes a supervisor review.

Yes, because any output based on approved sources can be used operationally without human review or local procedure testing.

Approved sources reduce uncertainty but do not guarantee a complete or correctly sequenced checklist. Claude can omit or misinterpret details.

The supervisor review is an important part of the appropriate workflow. Grounding does not eliminate validation.

No, because only a Claude Architect may create any workflow that produces a checklist.

A simple reviewed productivity workflow is within Associate-level use. It does not require architecture or API implementation.

Escalation is appropriate for complex technical integration, not every structured business task. The associate can complete this use case with ordinary Claude features.

questions.question: An education professional creates a Project for a new curriculum. The available files include final standards, draft notes, unrelated older courses, and copyrighted articles that are not needed. What should be uploaded?

options.label: A
options.text: Upload only relevant, authorized, current sources and label drafts or reference materials according to their status within the Project.

options.label: B
options.text: Upload every available file so Claude can independently decide what is relevant and legally usable.

options.label: C
options.text: Upload only the draft notes because unfinished sources encourage Claude to produce more creative curriculum ideas.

options.label: D
options.text: Exclude the final standards because Claude may already know the curriculum requirements from training data.

questions.explanation:
Correct option:

Upload only relevant, authorized, current sources and label drafts or reference materials according to their status within the Project.

The Project should contain information that is necessary and appropriate for the curriculum task. Irrelevant or unauthorized material increases risk without improving the output.

Source status matters because Claude may otherwise treat a draft and an approved standard as equally authoritative. Clear labels help preserve that distinction.

A curated knowledge base improves relevance, maintainability, and responsible use. The professional can add new material later when a defined need arises.

Incorrect options:

Upload every available file so Claude can independently decide what is relevant and legally usable.

More content is not automatically better context. Claude cannot assume responsibility for authorization or organizational source selection.

Unrelated and unnecessary material can distract retrieval and increase data risk. The professional must curate the knowledge base.

Upload only the draft notes because unfinished sources encourage Claude to produce more creative curriculum ideas.

Draft notes alone omit the final standards that should govern the curriculum. Creativity cannot replace required alignment.

The Project needs authoritative sources and clearly identified drafts. Source selection should match the task rather than maximize novelty.

Exclude the final standards because Claude may already know the curriculum requirements from training data.

Existing model knowledge may be incomplete, outdated, or different from the approved local standards. The task has a clear authoritative source available.

Providing the final standards grounds the work in the required framework. The professional should not rely on unverified background knowledge.

questions.question: An organization uses Claude to recommend advanced-course candidates using teacher comments. The shortlist favors students described as confident speakers, although the course criteria focus on analytical work and many quieter students have stronger results. What is the PRIMARY concern?

options.label: A
options.text: The only concern is that the shortlist should include longer descriptions of every student's speaking style.

options.label: B
options.text: There is no concern because teacher comments are human-authored and therefore free from bias.

options.label: C
options.text: The output may encode biased proxy criteria that disadvantage students whose communication style is unrelated to course success.

options.label: D
options.text: The shortlist is valid because confidence is always necessary for success in any advanced course.

questions.explanation:
Correct option:

The output may encode biased proxy criteria that disadvantage students whose communication style is unrelated to course success.

Confidence in speaking is being treated as evidence for suitability without alignment to the stated analytical criteria. That proxy can systematically disadvantage quieter students.

Bias evaluation should examine whether generated reasoning substitutes stereotypes or convenient signals for job-related or task-related evidence. Strong analytical results provide a more relevant basis here.

The team should review the criteria, source comments, and shortlist before any decision. Claude should support consistent evidence use rather than amplify subjective impressions.

Incorrect options:

The only concern is that the shortlist should include longer descriptions of every student's speaking style.

More detail about the same irrelevant proxy would not improve fairness. It could reinforce the biased basis for selection.

The issue is criterion relevance rather than descriptive depth. The team should return to analytical evidence.

There is no concern because teacher comments are human-authored and therefore free from bias.

Human-authored sources can contain inconsistent standards and subjective assumptions. Claude may reproduce or amplify those patterns.

Source origin does not guarantee fairness. The team must evaluate both the evidence and the generated reasoning.

The shortlist is valid because confidence is always necessary for success in any advanced course.

The universal claim is unsupported and contradicts the stated course criteria. Different courses require different capabilities.

Using an assumed trait instead of approved criteria creates unfair selection risk. The decision should be grounded in relevant analytical performance.

questions.question: A knowledge worker has made many revisions, and a planning chat contains conflicting deadlines, two abandoned scopes, and obsolete stakeholder instructions. Claude repeatedly mixes old requirements into the latest plan. Which action is BEST?

options.label: A
options.text: Continue in the same chat and repeat the latest deadline at the end of every new message.

options.label: B
options.text: Ask Claude to preserve every prior instruction and reconcile the contradictions without identifying which ones are obsolete.

options.label: C
options.text: Move the conversation into a Project and assume the move automatically removes outdated chat context.

options.label: D
options.text: Start a clean conversation with a concise current-state summary, approved requirements, and superseded items explicitly excluded from future planning.

questions.explanation:
Correct option:

Start a clean conversation with a concise current-state summary, approved requirements, and superseded items explicitly excluded from future planning.

A clean conversation removes the accumulated conflicting context that is degrading the plan. The current-state summary gives Claude one authoritative set of requirements.

Explicitly naming superseded items prevents them from being treated as unresolved alternatives. The latest deadline and stakeholder priorities can be presented in one controlled brief.

This approach restores clarity without asking Claude to guess which historical instructions still apply. It should improve consistency and make later revisions easier to govern.

Incorrect options:

Continue in the same chat and repeat the latest deadline at the end of every new message.

Repeating one fact does not remove obsolete scopes and stakeholder instructions from the conversation. Claude can still draw on conflicting context elsewhere in the chat.

The workaround makes every future prompt more cumbersome without resolving the root cause. The manager needs a cleaner source of current requirements.

Ask Claude to preserve every prior instruction and reconcile the contradictions without identifying which ones are obsolete.

Claude cannot reliably determine the authoritative requirement when the manager has not identified it. Preserving all instructions guarantees that conflicts remain active.

A reconciliation may invent compromises that stakeholders never approved. The manager must establish a current source of truth.

Move the conversation into a Project and assume the move automatically removes outdated chat context.

A Project can provide persistent instructions and knowledge, but moving a chat does not sanitize its contents. The conflicting conversation history would still need deliberate handling.

Using a new workspace without cleaning requirements could reproduce the same confusion. The key action is to reset the operative context.

References:

Usage and length limits

Create and manage projects

questions.question: A project manager will run recurring planning conversations using the same approved charter, terminology, decision rules, and reference documents over several months. Which Claude feature is BEST suited?

options.label: A
options.text: Create a Project with the approved knowledge and project-specific instructions for the recurring work.

options.label: B
options.text: Use a new standalone Chat for every planning session each month and rely on Claude to reconstruct the charter.

options.label: C
options.text: Use Research to search the public web for the internal charter during every planning session.

options.label: D
options.text: Create an Artifact containing only the latest plan and treat it as the complete project knowledge base.

questions.explanation:
Correct option:

Create a Project with the approved knowledge and project-specific instructions for the recurring work.

A Project provides a persistent workspace for the shared documents and guidance used across related chats. It avoids reattaching the same charter and rewriting the same rules each time.

Project knowledge supplies reusable source context while project instructions define how Claude should handle the work. Both apply to conversations conducted within that project.

This choice supports consistency, maintainability, and collaboration over a continuing initiative. The manager should update the Project when the charter or decision rules change.

Incorrect options:

Use a new standalone Chat for every planning session each month and rely on Claude to reconstruct the charter.

Separate standalone chats do not automatically receive the approved project knowledge and instructions. Claude would have to infer or be retold the context each time.

This increases inconsistency and repeated setup effort. A persistent Project better matches recurring work with stable sources.

Use Research to search the public web for the internal charter during every planning session.

Research is designed for gathering and synthesizing information, not for storing a private recurring work context. The internal charter may not be available publicly.

Repeated web research would be inefficient and could introduce irrelevant external material. The team needs maintained project knowledge.

Create an Artifact containing only the latest plan and treat it as the complete project knowledge base.

An Artifact is useful for substantial standalone content but does not replace a managed Project workspace. A single plan cannot represent all approved sources and instructions.

The manager needs persistent context across multiple conversations and documents. Artifacts can be outputs within the workflow rather than the workspace itself.

Correct option:

Use Claude to summarize account evidence and policy indicators, then require authorized finance and legal reviewers to decide.

Claude can reduce preparation time by organizing payment history, communications, and applicable policy factors. The final recovery decision remains consequential and context-dependent.

Authorized reviewers must assess disputed facts, contractual terms, commercial relationships, and exceptions. Those judgments cannot be delegated solely to generated reasoning.

This design keeps Claude in a decision-support role while preserving accountable authority. It balances operational efficiency with legal and relationship risk.

Incorrect options:

Let Claude send accounts to legal recovery automatically whenever the overdue balance exceeds a fixed threshold.

A balance threshold may be relevant but cannot capture disputes, payment plans, contractual terms, or strategic relationships. Automatic escalation could create avoidable harm.

The action requires authorized judgment under policy. Claude may flag cases but should not own the final decision.

Avoid using Claude for any account review because financial information makes every supporting task prohibited.

Sensitive financial information requires approved handling and access controls, but it does not automatically prohibit all assistance. Claude can support authorized summarization within policy.

The workflow boundary should focus on data governance and final authority. A controlled support use may be appropriate.

Ask Claude to rewrite the recovery policy so its recommendations become automatically compliant.

Claude cannot unilaterally change organizational or contractual policy. A generated rewrite would still require governance and legal approval.

Changing policy to fit automation reverses the proper control relationship. The workflow must follow approved policy and escalation.

questions.question: A business analyst asks Claude to summarize a quarterly report. The summary states that revenue increased, but the source table shows a decline. What should the analyst do FIRST?

options.label: A
options.text: Keep the summary because Claude probably identified a trend that the source table does not display.

options.label: B
options.text: Ask Claude whether it is confident that revenue increased and accept the answer if confidence is high.

options.label: C
options.text: Compare the summary claim with the source table, correct the error, and inspect other material figures.

options.label: D
options.text: Rewrite the summary in a more cautious tone without changing the direction of the revenue claim.

questions.explanation:
Correct option:

Compare the summary claim with the source table, correct the error, and inspect other material figures.

The source table directly contradicts the generated claim, so the discrepancy must be resolved before use. Checking related figures determines whether the problem is isolated or systematic.

Claude can produce fluent statements that are not grounded in the supplied evidence. Material numerical claims therefore require direct comparison with the original report.

This action restores factual accuracy while preserving any portions of the summary that remain valid. It also creates a defensible review process for the final deliverable.

Incorrect options:

Keep the summary because Claude probably identified a trend that the source table does not display.

The option assumes hidden evidence without establishing that any exists. The provided source explicitly shows the opposite result.

Retaining the statement would knowingly preserve a material factual error. The analyst must treat the source report as the controlling evidence.

Ask Claude whether it is confident that revenue increased and accept the answer if confidence is high.

Claude's stated confidence is not independent evidence of correctness. A confident response can still repeat the same unsupported claim.

The source table already provides a direct validation method. The analyst should inspect evidence rather than ask the model to evaluate itself.

Rewrite the summary in a more cautious tone without changing the direction of the revenue claim.

Cautious wording changes presentation but not the underlying factual contradiction. A decline cannot be represented as an increase merely by adding qualifiers.

The material claim must be corrected before tone is refined. Stylistic editing cannot substitute for factual validation.

questions.question: A recurring report was previously reliable until the source spreadsheet changed column names and added a new region. Claude now omits that region and mislabels two metrics. Which diagnosis is BEST?

options.label: A
options.text: The workflow and instructions no longer match the changed source structure and must be updated and retested before the next report.

options.label: B
options.text: The model has become less capable, so the team should switch immediately without checking the source change.

options.label: C
options.text: The report should be shortened because omissions usually occur when an output contains too many words.

options.label: D
options.text: The new region should be excluded permanently because reliable workflows cannot adapt to changed inputs.

questions.explanation:
Correct option:

The workflow and instructions no longer match the changed source structure and must be updated and retested before the next report.

The failures began after a specific source-schema change. The omitted region and mislabeled metrics are consistent with stale field assumptions.

Troubleshooting should connect the observed defects to changes in inputs, configuration, model, or process. Here the source and workflow alignment is the strongest causal signal.

Updating mappings and representative tests addresses the root cause rather than editing each report manually. The team should also add change ownership for future source updates.

Incorrect options:

The model has become less capable, so the team should switch immediately without checking the source change.

The timing points directly to a changed spreadsheet rather than unexplained model degradation. Switching models would leave stale mappings in place.

A more capable model may still misinterpret renamed columns. The team should inspect source-workflow alignment first.

The report should be shortened because omissions usually occur when an output contains too many words.

The missing region and metric labels relate to source interpretation rather than output length. Shortening the report would not restore the absent data.

The diagnosis should explain the pattern of errors. Stale schema assumptions provide that explanation.

The new region should be excluded permanently because reliable workflows cannot adapt to changed inputs.

Input changes require maintenance, not automatic exclusion of valid data. The region is part of the updated source and likely belongs in the report.

A maintainable workflow should update mappings and tests. Removing data would hide rather than solve the defect.

References:

Create and manage projects

Prompting best practices

questions.question: A team receives a weekly project summary covering completed work and upcoming milestones. The summary omits unresolved risks and decisions awaiting sponsors. Which evaluation method is BEST?

options.label: A
options.text: Approve the summary because all included statements are accurate and no sentence contains an obvious error.

options.label: B
options.text: Ask Claude to increase the word count until the summary appears detailed enough for senior stakeholders.

options.label: C
options.text: Compare the summary only with last week's generated summary and retain any sections that look similar.

options.label: D
options.text: Check the summary against a required-content checklist that includes progress, milestones, risks, decisions, and owners before approval.

questions.explanation:
Correct option:

Check the summary against a required-content checklist that includes progress, milestones, risks, decisions, and owners before approval.

The checklist converts completeness into observable criteria rather than a general impression. It exposes the missing risks and sponsor decisions immediately.

A generated summary can be factually accurate while still omitting information necessary for action. Comparing it with defined sections verifies whether the full request was satisfied.

This method is reusable across weekly reporting cycles and supports consistent review by different team members. It improves accountability without requiring the manager to rewrite every summary manually.

Incorrect options:

Approve the summary because all included statements are accurate and no sentence contains an obvious error.

Accuracy of included statements does not establish completeness. The omitted risks and decisions are essential to stakeholder action.

An incomplete report can mislead by presenting progress without unresolved constraints. The manager must evaluate coverage as well as correctness.

Ask Claude to increase the word count until the summary appears detailed enough for senior stakeholders.

More words do not guarantee that the omitted categories will be covered. Claude may expand completed-work descriptions while still ignoring risks and decisions.

Completeness should be tested against requirements rather than document length. The manager needs a content checklist, not a verbosity target.

Compare the summary only with last week's generated summary and retain any sections that look similar.

A previous generated output may contain the same omission or follow outdated reporting needs. Similarity does not demonstrate that current risks and decisions are represented.

The controlling standard should be the present reporting requirements and source information. Past wording can support consistency but cannot replace completeness validation.

References:

Prompting best practices

questions.question: An HR specialist needs Claude to convert job descriptions into standardized internal summaries. Early outputs vary in headings, detail, and terminology. Which action will BEST improve consistency?

options.label: A
options.text: Tell Claude to summarize each description naturally and decide which details are most important.

options.label: B
options.text: Provide the required headings, terminology rules, length limit, and one representative input-output example for every summary.

options.label: C
options.text: Ask Claude to produce a longer explanation of every job description before creating the summary.

options.label: D
options.text: Remove all terminology guidance so Claude can mirror the wording used in each source document.

questions.explanation:
Correct option:

Provide the required headings, terminology rules, length limit, and one representative input-output example for every summary.

The option defines the expected structure and demonstrates what a successful transformation looks like. It addresses both formatting variation and inconsistent terminology.

Examples complement written rules by showing how the requirements apply to realistic source content. The fixed heading sequence and length limit also make summaries easier to compare.

This design supports reuse across many job descriptions without repeated manual reformatting. The specialist can still review exceptional roles that do not fit the standard pattern.

Incorrect options:

Tell Claude to summarize each description naturally and decide which details are most important.

This instruction leaves format and selection criteria to Claude for every document. The summaries can continue to vary in headings, emphasis, and terminology.

Natural variation conflicts with a standardized internal process. The specialist needs repeatable requirements rather than unrestricted discretion.

Ask Claude to produce a longer explanation of every job description before creating the summary.

A longer intermediate explanation adds work without defining the desired final structure. It does not resolve inconsistent headings or terminology.

Extra analysis can consume time that the workflow does not require. The underlying problem is missing output specifications, not insufficient verbosity.

Remove all terminology guidance so Claude can mirror the wording used in each source document.

Mirroring every source preserves the variation the specialist is trying to eliminate. Different job descriptions may use inconsistent labels for similar responsibilities.

The internal summaries need normalized language for comparison and downstream use. Removing guidance would make the process less standardized.

References:

Prompting best practices

Create and manage projects

questions.question: A shared Project still uses last year's policy documents and review checklist. Claude produces internally consistent answers that conflict with a newly approved process. Which action is BEST?

options.label: A
options.text: Keep the old documents and add a prompt asking Claude to remember that a newer process exists.

options.label: B
options.text: Correct each answer manually while leaving the Project unchanged for future users.

options.label: C
options.text: Delete the entire Project and stop using maintained knowledge for compliance work.

options.label: D
options.text: Replace outdated sources, update the Project instructions and checklist, then test representative questions against the new process before future use.

questions.explanation:
Correct option:

Replace outdated sources, update the Project instructions and checklist, then test representative questions against the new process before future use.

The Project is behaving consistently with obsolete configuration rather than failing randomly. The authoritative knowledge and review criteria must therefore be updated together.

Testing representative questions confirms that retrieval and instructions now reflect the approved process. It also identifies remnants of old guidance.

This maintenance cycle addresses source freshness, configuration alignment, and validation. It is more reliable than correcting each generated answer individually.

Incorrect options:

Keep the old documents and add a prompt asking Claude to remember that a newer process exists.

The prompt supplies no complete authoritative description of the new process. Old sources remain available to influence answers.

A reminder cannot replace maintained knowledge and instructions. The team should update the configuration at its source.

Correct each answer manually while leaving the Project unchanged for future users.

Manual correction treats symptoms one response at a time. Other users will continue receiving the same obsolete guidance.

A recurring configuration defect requires a shared maintenance fix. The Project should be updated and retested.

Delete the entire Project and stop using maintained knowledge for compliance work.

The issue is outdated content, not the concept of a maintained Project. Rebuilding from nothing creates unnecessary disruption.

A curated Project can still support compliance workflows when sources and instructions are current. The team should repair and govern the configuration.

References:

Create and manage projects

Retrieval augmented generation for projects

questions.question: An organization's policy permits approved AI analysis of exit-interview themes only with data minimization and accountable HR review. The notes include employee names, health details, and unresolved allegations. Which TWO actions should the team take?

options.label: A
options.text: Keep the records unchanged but tell Claude to ignore names and health-related information.

options.label: B
options.text: Distribute the generated themes automatically to all managers because the records have been collected internally.

options.label: C
options.text: Replace employee names but retain every allegation and health detail because pseudonyms make the data anonymous.

options.label: D
options.text: Remove direct identifiers and sensitive details that are unnecessary for identifying aggregate themes.

options.label: E
options.text: Require an accountable HR reviewer to validate the findings and approve any resulting organizational action.

questions.explanation:
Correct options:

Remove direct identifiers and sensitive details that are unnecessary for identifying aggregate themes.

The action limits the data supplied to what the approved analytical purpose actually requires. Names and unrelated health details do not need to be present for aggregate theme analysis.

Data minimization reduces exposure and the chance of inappropriate inference about individuals. The team should also consider indirect identifiers in contextual details.

This safeguard addresses the input before Claude receives it. It is stronger than merely instructing Claude not to mention sensitive fields.

Require an accountable HR reviewer to validate the findings and approve any resulting organizational action.

Theme extraction can still misinterpret ambiguous comments or overstate patterns. Unresolved allegations require careful professional handling.

HR review preserves accountability for interpretation, fairness, and policy response. The model should not determine consequences for employees.

This checkpoint complements data minimization by governing how the output is used. Together the controls address both input risk and decision risk.

Incorrect options:

Keep the records unchanged but tell Claude to ignore names and health-related information.

An instruction to ignore data does not remove that data from the input. Claude still receives the sensitive fields.

The policy explicitly requires minimization before analysis. The team should remove unnecessary content rather than rely on prompt wording.

Distribute the generated themes automatically to all managers because the records have been collected internally.

Internal collection does not grant every manager a need to know. Automatic distribution can expose sensitive interpretations and unverified allegations.

Access and review should remain limited to the approved purpose. HR must validate findings before broader use.

Replace employee names but retain every allegation and health detail because pseudonyms make the data anonymous.

Replacing names alone may not prevent reidentification through context. It also retains sensitive details that may be unnecessary for aggregate analysis.

Pseudonymization is not equivalent to complete anonymization or minimization. The team must assess all fields against the approved purpose.

References:

Be mindful with sensitive data

Incorrect or misleading responses

questions.question: A team receives a recommendation for Vendor A after listing Vendor B as stronger on cost, implementation time, security, and support. The conclusion provides no weighting or exception. What is the MOST important evaluation finding?

options.label: A
options.text: The recommendation is not traceable to the stated evidence or an explicit decision framework.

options.label: B
options.text: The recommendation is acceptable because vendor selection always involves subjective judgment that cannot be explained.

options.label: C
options.text: The only problem is that the comparison needs stronger descriptive adjectives.

options.label: D
options.text: Vendor A should remain selected because Claude may possess private market knowledge not shown in the response.

questions.explanation:
Correct option:

The recommendation is not traceable to the stated evidence or an explicit decision framework.

The conclusion conflicts with the comparison presented immediately before it. No criterion weighting or additional requirement explains why Vendor A should prevail.

Reasoning quality requires a visible connection between evidence, evaluation criteria, and the final recommendation. Without that connection, the reader cannot test whether the decision is coherent.

The consultant should require explicit criteria and recalculate the comparison before presenting the recommendation. This protects stakeholders from a polished conclusion that the supporting analysis does not justify.

Incorrect options:

The recommendation is acceptable because vendor selection always involves subjective judgment that cannot be explained.

Professional judgment can influence a decision, but material reasoning should still be articulated. The scenario provides no stated judgment factor favoring Vendor A.

Treating the inconsistency as inherently subjective prevents meaningful review. The consultant needs a transparent basis for the recommendation.

The only problem is that the comparison needs stronger descriptive adjectives.

Additional adjectives would change style rather than resolve the logical conflict. The evidence already favors Vendor B across the listed criteria.

The missing element is a defensible decision framework or qualifying requirement. More expressive language could make the unsupported conclusion appear stronger without making it valid.

Vendor A should remain selected because Claude may possess private market knowledge not shown in the response.

The consultant cannot rely on unreferenced or inaccessible information as the basis for a client recommendation. The decision must be grounded in approved evidence and stated criteria.

Assuming hidden knowledge prevents verification and creates accountability risk. Any additional evidence must be identified, validated, and incorporated explicitly.

References:

Incorrect or misleading responses

questions.question: A team is unsure whether Haiku or Sonnet should handle a recurring report workflow. Both can produce plausible samples, but operating cost differs significantly. What should the team do?

options.label: A
options.text: Benchmark both models on representative reports using accuracy, completeness, latency, and cost criteria before full deployment.

options.label: B
options.text: Select Sonnet because the higher-cost option must be more appropriate for every recurring report.

options.label: C
options.text: Select Haiku because lower cost is the only objective that can be measured consistently.

options.label: D
options.text: Alternate models without recording results until users informally decide which outputs they prefer.

questions.explanation:
Correct option:

Benchmark both models on representative reports using accuracy, completeness, latency, and cost criteria before full deployment.

Representative testing converts a general model preference into evidence about the actual workflow. The selected criteria capture both output quality and operating constraints.

Plausible samples are not enough because edge cases and omissions may appear across a broader evaluation set. The analyst should compare the same inputs and scoring rules for both models.

This method supports the lowest-cost model that reliably meets the required standard. It also provides a baseline for future model or workflow changes.

Incorrect options:

Select Sonnet because the higher-cost option must be more appropriate for every recurring report.

Price alone does not establish that Sonnet creates necessary value for this workflow. Haiku may already meet the defined quality standard.

The analyst should compare measured performance rather than assume a universal hierarchy. Recurring cost makes evidence-based selection especially important.

Select Haiku because lower cost is the only objective that can be measured consistently.

Accuracy, completeness, and latency can also be measured with a defined evaluation set. Cost is not the only requirement for a usable report.

A cheaper model that misses material information may create greater downstream cost. The decision must balance all stated criteria.

Alternate models without recording results until users informally decide which outputs they prefer.

Unrecorded informal preference does not identify why one model performs better. It also makes cost and error patterns difficult to compare.

questions.question: An organization wants Claude to help prepare interview packs. Recruiters must retain judgment over candidate evaluation, and approved competency criteria cannot change. Which workflow is MOST appropriate?

options.label: A
options.text: Use Claude to draft role-specific questions and organize evidence under approved competencies, with recruiters reviewing every pack and evaluation.

options.label: B
options.text: Let Claude rank candidates automatically from interview notes and send rejection decisions without recruiter review.

options.label: C
options.text: Ask Claude to invent new competency criteria for every candidate so each interview is fully personalized.

options.label: D
options.text: Avoid Claude entirely because any assistance in recruitment automatically removes human accountability.

questions.explanation:
Correct option:

Use Claude to draft role-specific questions and organize evidence under approved competencies, with recruiters reviewing every pack and evaluation.

The workflow uses Claude for preparation and organization without delegating candidate judgment. Approved competencies remain the controlling framework.

Recruiters can verify that questions are relevant, lawful, and consistent before interviews. They also retain responsibility for interpreting candidate evidence.

This design augments repeatable work while preserving human expertise in a consequential process. It improves efficiency without allowing generated content to redefine selection criteria.

Incorrect options:

Let Claude rank candidates automatically from interview notes and send rejection decisions without recruiter review.

Automatic ranking and rejection transfer a high-impact employment decision to the model. Interview notes may also contain incomplete or biased observations.

The stated requirement is that recruiters retain judgment. Claude should support preparation and evidence organization rather than final selection.

Ask Claude to invent new competency criteria for every candidate so each interview is fully personalized.

Changing criteria by candidate undermines consistency and fairness. It also violates the requirement to preserve approved competencies.

Personalization should occur within a stable job-related framework. The team must not allow generated criteria to govern evaluation.

Avoid Claude entirely because any assistance in recruitment automatically removes human accountability.

Claude can support bounded drafting and organization while recruiters remain accountable. The risk depends on the task delegated and the controls applied.

Rejecting all assistance overlooks appropriate low-risk uses. The workflow should preserve judgment rather than eliminate useful support.

questions.question: A business analyst is asked to use Claude to improve monthly management reporting. Stakeholders only say that the current report takes too long and is not useful. What should the analyst do FIRST?

options.label: A
options.text: Choose the most capable Claude model immediately and let it determine the reporting requirements.

options.label: B
options.text: Automate the existing report exactly as written so no stakeholder interviews are necessary.

options.label: C
options.text: Define users, decisions, source inputs, current pain points, success measures, and nonnegotiable review requirements.

options.label: D
options.text: Ask Claude to create a new report from public information without reviewing internal data sources.

questions.explanation:
Correct option:

Define users, decisions, source inputs, current pain points, success measures, and nonnegotiable review requirements.

The request is too broad to design a reliable Claude-assisted workflow immediately. The analyst first needs to understand what decisions the report must support and why the current process fails.

Requirements should cover inputs, outputs, users, constraints, and measurable outcomes. Review requirements also identify where human accountability must remain.

This discovery step creates a basis for selecting features and redesigning the workflow. It prevents the team from automating an unclear process that may not solve the real problem.

Incorrect options:

Choose the most capable Claude model immediately and let it determine the reporting requirements.

Model capability does not resolve missing business requirements. Claude cannot decide stakeholder priorities without grounded input.

Starting with a model choice risks optimizing the wrong workflow. The analyst should define the use case before selecting the solution.

Automate the existing report exactly as written so no stakeholder interviews are necessary.

The existing report is already described as slow and not useful. Automating it unchanged could make an ineffective process run faster.

The analyst should understand which content and steps create value. Workflow redesign should precede automation when the current design is deficient.

Ask Claude to create a new report from public information without reviewing internal data sources.

Public information cannot replace the internal inputs required for management reporting. The option also ignores user decisions and review requirements.

A report design must be grounded in the organization's actual data and needs. External sources may supplement but cannot define the core workflow.

questions.question: A communications specialist asks Claude to simplify a policy notice. The revision remains dense, uses unexplained acronyms, and keeps sentences that are too long for the intended audience. What should the specialist do NEXT?

options.label: A
options.text: Repeat the word simplify several times without identifying what remains difficult to understand.

options.label: B
options.text: Give targeted feedback on acronyms, sentence length, reading level, and one example of the desired rewrite.

options.label: C
options.text: Ask Claude to add more policy terminology so readers become familiar with the official language.

options.label: D
options.text: Accept the notice because any accurate policy wording is suitable for every audience.

questions.explanation:
Correct option:

Give targeted feedback on acronyms, sentence length, reading level, and one example of the desired rewrite.

The feedback identifies observable defects rather than repeating a general request to simplify. An example demonstrates how the requested standard should look in practice.

Targeted iteration is more effective when Claude can connect each criticism to a concrete revision rule. Reading level and sentence length provide testable constraints.

This action preserves useful policy content while directing a focused second revision. The specialist can then compare the result with the stated audience criteria.

Incorrect options:

Repeat the word simplify several times without identifying what remains difficult to understand.

Repetition increases emphasis but supplies no new instruction. Claude still lacks a concrete standard for acronyms, syntax, and reading level.

The next output may differ without improving the identified problems. Feedback should be specific and actionable.

Ask Claude to add more policy terminology so readers become familiar with the official language.

Additional terminology would increase the density the specialist is trying to reduce. The audience already struggles with unexplained acronyms.

Necessary terms should be explained in plain language rather than multiplied. The revision should prioritize comprehension.

Accept the notice because any accurate policy wording is suitable for every audience.

Accuracy is necessary but does not establish accessibility or usefulness. Dense wording can prevent readers from understanding their obligations.

The specialist has clear audience requirements that remain unmet. The output should be revised and validated.

questions.question: An operations team asks Claude to analyze 240 customer comments, create an issue taxonomy, calculate frequencies, and recommend process changes. One-pass results contain overlapping categories and unreliable counts. Which TWO actions should the team take?

options.label: A
options.text: Define and review the taxonomy before asking Claude to classify the complete comment set.

options.label: B
options.text: Validate the classifications and frequency totals before asking Claude to propose process changes.

options.label: C
options.text: Repeat the complete one-pass request and add a sentence telling Claude that every result must be accurate.

options.label: D
options.text: Analyze a convenient sample and assume its category frequencies represent every remaining customer comment.

options.label: E
options.text: Create the management presentation first, then revise the underlying analysis only if leaders raise objections.

questions.explanation:
Correct options:

Define and review the taxonomy before asking Claude to classify the complete comment set.

This action establishes stable category definitions before those categories are applied at scale. It prevents classification from shifting while frequency analysis is already underway.

A reviewed taxonomy creates a checkpoint where overlapping or ambiguous categories can be corrected. The team can also add examples that distinguish similar themes.

Separating definition from classification reduces error propagation into later calculations. It makes the process easier to audit and repeat.

Validate the classifications and frequency totals before asking Claude to propose process changes.

Recommendations should be based on categories and counts that the team has already checked. This action keeps analytical errors from becoming operational conclusions.

Validation can include spot checks, reconciliation of totals, and review of borderline comments. Those checks reveal whether the taxonomy was applied consistently.

The sequence preserves the complete evidence set while adding quality controls between stages. It balances efficiency with the human oversight needed for dependable recommendations.

Incorrect options:

Repeat the complete one-pass request and add a sentence telling Claude that every result must be accurate.

The stronger accuracy instruction does not change the structure that produced the errors. Claude still performs taxonomy design, classification, counting, and recommendation in one combined step.

Without checkpoints, category mistakes can remain hidden until the final output. The team needs a verifiable process rather than a more emphatic outcome request.

Analyze a convenient sample and assume its category frequencies represent every remaining customer comment.

A sample may omit themes that occur elsewhere in the full dataset. The scenario provides no evidence that the selected comments are representative.

The resulting frequencies and recommendations could be materially distorted. Task decomposition should improve control without discarding relevant data.

Create the management presentation first, then revise the underlying analysis only if leaders raise objections.

This sequence prioritizes presentation before the analytical foundation has been checked. A polished deliverable cannot correct overlapping categories or incorrect totals.

Leaders could act on unsupported findings before the errors are discovered. Validation belongs before recommendation and presentation.

References:

Prompting best practices

Incorrect or misleading responses

questions.question: An organization receives a public briefing from Claude that includes three quotations with precise page numbers. Two quotations cannot be found in the linked reports. Which action is MOST appropriate?

options.label: A
options.text: Keep the quotations but remove the page numbers so readers cannot focus on minor citation discrepancies.

options.label: B
options.text: Remove or replace the unverified quotations after checking the original reports and documenting the valid evidence before publication.

options.label: C
options.text: Ask Claude to generate new page numbers that better match the apparent length of each report.

options.label: D
options.text: Retain the quotations because precise wording and page numbers indicate that Claude probably accessed reliable evidence.

questions.explanation:
Correct option:

Remove or replace the unverified quotations after checking the original reports and documenting the valid evidence before publication.

The missing quotations cannot remain as attributed evidence when the source reports do not contain them. Direct source inspection is the appropriate way to distinguish valid citations from fabricated details.

Claude can produce convincing quotations, titles, or page references that are not grounded in fact. The specialist must verify exact wording and context before public use.

Removing or replacing unsupported material preserves transparency and protects the credibility of the briefing. Documenting the verified evidence also supports later review.

Incorrect options:

Keep the quotations but remove the page numbers so readers cannot focus on minor citation discrepancies.

Removing page numbers hides the verification problem rather than correcting it. The quotations themselves remain unsupported.

Readers could still be misled by statements falsely presented as direct source language. The specialist must resolve the evidence defect, not make it less visible.

Ask Claude to generate new page numbers that better match the apparent length of each report.

Inventing replacement page numbers compounds the original problem. Pagination must come from the actual source, not an estimate.

The briefing would contain deliberately fabricated attribution. The correct response is source verification and removal of unsupported claims.

Retain the quotations because precise wording and page numbers indicate that Claude probably accessed reliable evidence.

Specificity can make a hallucinated citation look authoritative without making it genuine. The reports have already failed the direct verification check.

Assuming reliability from presentation style reverses the proper evidence standard. The original documents must control the decision.

questions.question: A consultant identifies a useful workflow but the client wants a custom application that calls the Claude API, manages authentication, and integrates with production systems. What should the Associate do?

options.label: C
options.text: Document the business requirements and escalate the implementation design to qualified Claude Developer or Architect resources.

options.label: D
options.text: Promise a delivery date before technical reviewers assess authentication, integration, and operational constraints.

questions.explanation:
Correct option:

Document the business requirements and escalate the implementation design to qualified Claude Developer or Architect resources.

The Associate can clarify the use case, success criteria, data needs, and workflow boundaries. The requested build includes software integration and production architecture beyond the Associate scope.

Authentication, API implementation, reliability, and production-system integration require specialized technical expertise. Those decisions should be handled by the appropriate credentialed roles.

This escalation preserves the Associate's valuable business analysis while avoiding unsupported technical commitments. It also gives the technical team a grounded requirements package.

Incorrect options:

Build the production application independently because regular use of Claude provides enough API expertise.

Productivity experience does not establish competence in secure application development or production integration. The requested work includes technical responsibilities outside the certification scope.

Attempting it without qualified support could create security and reliability defects. The Associate should escalate rather than overextend.

Reject the use case completely because any custom implementation is inappropriate for an organization.

questions.question: An education team pilots Claude-generated lesson briefs. Teachers report that objectives are clear, but activities do not fit available class time and often assume unavailable materials. What should the team do NEXT?

options.label: A
options.text: Abandon the pilot because any teacher criticism proves Claude cannot support lesson planning.

options.label: B
options.text: Ask Claude to make the activities more creative without mentioning class time or available materials.

options.label: C
options.text: Approve the existing briefs because teachers can shorten activities and find materials themselves.

options.label: D
options.text: Add time and resource constraints, test revised briefs on representative lessons, and compare results with teacher feedback.

Correct option:

Add time and resource constraints, test revised briefs on representative lessons, and compare results with teacher feedback.

The teacher feedback identifies two specific design gaps rather than a general failure. Adding the missing constraints targets those gaps directly.

Representative retesting shows whether the revised instructions work across different lesson types. Teacher comparison provides evidence beyond Claude's own assessment.

This iteration preserves the successful objectives while improving feasibility. It demonstrates a controlled build, test, feedback, and refine cycle.

Abandon the pilot because any teacher criticism proves Claude cannot support lesson planning.

The criticism concerns correctable constraints rather than the entire use case. The clear objectives show that part of the workflow already works.

Ending the pilot would discard evidence and learning prematurely. The team should refine the known weaknesses and test again.

Ask Claude to make the activities more creative without mentioning class time or available materials.

Creativity does not address the feasibility problems reported by teachers. The same time and resource assumptions may continue.

The next prompt should reflect the specific operational feedback. Broad stylistic improvement is not a substitute for targeted iteration.

Approve the existing briefs because teachers can shorten activities and find materials themselves.

This transfers the workflow defect back to the users the solution is intended to help. It also makes outputs inconsistent across teachers.

The pilot should reduce avoidable rework through better instructions. Known feasibility gaps should be corrected before broader adoption.

questions.domain: Domain 6: Governance, Risk, and Responsible Use
questions.question: A marketing team finds a useful Claude feature, but the organization's AI policy has not approved it for customer data. What should the team do?

options.label: A
options.text: Pause customer-data use and follow the organization's approval process before adopting the feature.

options.label: B
options.text: Use the feature quietly for a small campaign because limited scale removes the policy requirement.

options.label: C
options.text: Ask Claude whether the feature is compliant and proceed if the response is affirmative.

options.label: D
options.text: Move the customer data into a private Project for this campaign because privacy settings automatically satisfy every policy.

questions.explanation:
Correct option:

Pause customer-data use and follow the organization's approval process before adopting the feature.

The organizational policy establishes the permitted boundary for customer information. A useful capability does not override governance requirements.

The team can document the use case, data involved, expected value, and proposed controls for review. Approvers can then determine whether the feature is suitable.

This action supports responsible innovation without creating an unauthorized exception. It also protects the team from inconsistent handling of customer data.

Incorrect options:

Use the feature quietly for a small campaign because limited scale removes the policy requirement.

A smaller deployment can reduce impact but does not create authorization. Customer data remains within the policy boundary.

Unapproved testing may still expose information or create precedent. The team should use the established review process.

Ask Claude whether the feature is compliant and proceed if the response is affirmative.

Claude cannot grant organizational approval or interpret internal governance authoritatively. It may not know the complete policy context.

Compliance decisions belong to designated human owners. The team should consult the approved process and reviewers.

Move the customer data into a private Project for this campaign because privacy settings automatically satisfy every policy.

Project privacy is one control and does not replace organizational authorization. The feature itself may have different data handling or access implications.

The team must follow the policy's approval conditions. A technical setting cannot unilaterally resolve governance.

questions.domain: Domain 4: Workflow Integration and Solution Design
questions.question: A project manager is introducing Claude-generated status reports to sponsors. Sponsors want faster updates, but source systems are inconsistent and some milestones require owner confirmation. Which TWO expectations should the manager set?

options.label: A
options.text: Every generated report will be final because using Claude removes the need for source-system reconciliation.

options.label: B
options.text: Sponsors should ignore missing owner confirmations because Claude can estimate milestone completion from writing tone.

options.label: C
options.text: Claude can accelerate drafting, but source inconsistencies must be resolved before the report is treated as authoritative.

options.label: D
options.text: Milestone claims requiring accountable owner confirmation will remain subject to a human approval checkpoint.

options.label: E
options.text: The team will measure success only by how many minutes the drafting step takes.

questions.explanation:
Correct options:

Claude can accelerate drafting, but source inconsistencies must be resolved before the report is treated as authoritative.

The statement separates drafting efficiency from evidence quality. Faster generation does not reconcile conflicting source systems automatically.

Sponsors should understand that the report's authority depends on validated inputs. The team must define how conflicts are surfaced and resolved.

This expectation preserves the value of automation without overstating reliability. It also clarifies where process improvement is still needed.

Milestone claims requiring accountable owner confirmation will remain subject to a human approval checkpoint.

Owner confirmation represents organizational accountability that Claude cannot assume. The checkpoint protects sponsors from acting on unverified milestone status.

The workflow can still prepare the report and identify items awaiting confirmation. Human review is focused on the statements that require authority.

This expectation balances faster reporting with appropriate governance. It gives sponsors a clear interpretation of draft and approved status.

Incorrect options:

Every generated report will be final because using Claude removes the need for source-system reconciliation.

Claude cannot make inconsistent source systems authoritative merely by summarizing them. The report may conceal rather than resolve discrepancies.

Presenting drafts as final creates avoidable decision risk. The manager must preserve reconciliation and confirmation controls.

Sponsors should ignore missing owner confirmations because Claude can estimate milestone completion from writing tone.

Writing tone is not reliable evidence of milestone completion. An estimate cannot replace the accountable owner's confirmation.

This expectation would weaken the reporting control the scenario explicitly requires. The workflow should flag rather than infer unconfirmed status.

The team will measure success only by how many minutes the drafting step takes.

Drafting time captures one efficiency metric but not accuracy, completeness, or decision usefulness. A fast report can still be unreliable.

Sponsors need a balanced view of workflow outcomes. Success measures should include quality and review performance.

questions.question: A team has 80 meeting notes containing decisions, owners, deadlines, open questions, and repeated background discussion. Which instruction will BEST produce an actionable summary?

options.label: A
options.text: Summarize every note in its original order so no repeated discussion is omitted.

options.label: B
options.text: Write one narrative paragraph that blends decisions, deadlines, questions, and background into a continuous story.

options.label: C
options.text: Group verified decisions, owners, deadlines, and open questions into separate sections while removing duplicate background for follow-up.

options.label: D
options.text: List only final decisions and discard open questions, owners, and deadlines as unfinished information.

questions.explanation:
Correct option:

Group verified decisions, owners, deadlines, and open questions into separate sections while removing duplicate background for follow-up.

The instruction prioritizes information that drives follow-up and separates it by operational purpose. Removing repeated background reduces noise without discarding action items.

Organization should reflect how the team will use the output rather than the order of the original notes. Distinct sections make missing owners or deadlines easier to detect.

This format supports rapid review, assignment, and tracking after the meetings. The team can still retain source links for traceability.

Incorrect options:

Summarize every note in its original order so no repeated discussion is omitted.

Preserving the original order reproduces fragmentation and duplication. It makes actions harder to locate across 80 notes.

Completeness does not require repeating nonessential discussion. The output should curate information according to operational use.

Write one narrative paragraph that blends decisions, deadlines, questions, and background into a continuous story.

A continuous narrative obscures the categories needed for execution. Owners and deadlines can be difficult to scan or compare.

The team needs structured information rather than literary continuity. Separate sections better support accountability.

List only final decisions and discard open questions, owners, and deadlines as unfinished information.

Open questions, owners, and deadlines are essential to future work. Discarding them creates an incomplete operational record.

The summary must support both completed and pending actions. The instruction should prioritize rather than eliminate unresolved items.
