questions.domain: Domain 4: Workflow Integration and Solution Design
questions.question: An HR team manually converts approved policy changes into manager FAQs, training notes, and intranet drafts. Specialists must interpret policy and approve final wording. Which redesign is MOST appropriate?

options.label: A
options.text: Have Claude interpret the policy independently and publish all materials without specialist involvement.

options.label: B
options.text: Keep every drafting step manual because any use of Claude would eliminate human accountability.

options.label: C
options.text: Use Claude to generate channel-specific drafts from approved interpretations, then require specialist validation and approval.

options.label: D
options.text: Ask managers to choose whichever Claude draft they prefer without a shared policy review.

questions.explanation:
Correct option:

Use Claude to generate channel-specific drafts from approved interpretations, then require specialist validation and approval.

This option automates repetitive adaptation while keeping policy meaning and publication decisions with qualified people. That is the most direct way to augment repetitive drafting while preserving expert policy interpretation and approval.

Claude can assist with transformation and drafting even when accountable professionals retain consequential judgment. The scenario applies that principle by requiring the team to provide approved interpretations as input and keep specialist review before any material is published.

The team can improve speed without weakening accountability. The result is more dependable and maintainable than a response that addresses only part of the problem.

Incorrect options:

Have Claude interpret the policy independently and publish all materials without specialist involvement.

This option assigns policy interpretation and publication authority to Claude. The option does not meet the scenario’s requirement to augment repetitive drafting while preserving expert policy interpretation and approval.

Incorrect wording could be distributed across several employee channels. The workflow instead needs to provide approved interpretations as input and keep specialist review before any material is published.

Keep every drafting step manual because any use of Claude would eliminate human accountability.

This option treats assistance and decision authority as the same thing. This leaves the core need to augment repetitive drafting while preserving expert policy interpretation and approval unresolved.

The team would miss an opportunity to reduce repetitive drafting while retaining expert review. The better direction is to provide approved interpretations as input and keep specialist review before any material is published.

Ask managers to choose whichever Claude draft they prefer without a shared policy review.

This option distributes interpretation responsibility to users who may apply inconsistent standards. It addresses a secondary concern while failing to augment repetitive drafting while preserving expert policy interpretation and approval.

Employees could receive conflicting guidance across teams. The required corrective action is to provide approved interpretations as input and keep specialist review before any material is published.

Use Claude for Word

Use Claude Cowork safely

questions.question: A benefits Project still contains last year’s eligibility rules and provider list. New guidance has been approved, but Claude continues returning outdated answers. What should the Project owner do?

options.label: A
options.text: Add a message telling users that some answers may be old while leaving the obsolete files unchanged.

options.label: B
options.text: Replace superseded sources, update the instructions and labels, then test representative benefits questions.

options.label: C
options.text: Upload the new guidance alongside every older version and let Claude determine which rules should prevail.

options.label: D
options.text: Require users to correct Claude manually whenever they independently recognize an outdated rule in practice.

questions.explanation:
Correct option:

Replace superseded sources, update the instructions and labels, then test representative benefits questions.

This option refreshes the governing knowledge and verifies that the maintained configuration now behaves correctly. It responds to the decisive requirement to update stale knowledge and confirm that the Project uses the new authoritative guidance.

The governing idea is that configuration maintenance requires replacing superseded sources and testing the updated behavior. Here, that means the user should refresh the knowledge base and instructions, then validate common and edge-case questions.

The owner can detect residual retrieval problems before employees rely on the Project. This preserves the intended benefit while controlling the failure mode highlighted in the stem.

Incorrect options:

Add a message telling users that some answers may be old while leaving the obsolete files unchanged.

This option acknowledges the maintenance problem without correcting the knowledge base. As a result, the approach cannot reliably update stale knowledge and confirm that the Project uses the new authoritative guidance.

Claude may continue retrieving and presenting outdated benefits information. The scenario calls for the team to refresh the knowledge base and instructions, then validate common and edge-case questions.

Upload the new guidance alongside every older version and let Claude determine which rules should prevail.

This option creates conflicting sources without establishing authority or removing superseded material. That choice is inconsistent with the requirement to update stale knowledge and confirm that the Project uses the new authoritative guidance.

Users may receive blended or inconsistent answers. An appropriate solution must refresh the knowledge base and instructions, then validate common and edge-case questions.

Require users to correct Claude manually whenever they independently recognize an outdated rule in practice.

This option moves responsibility to individual users and makes correction reactive. It therefore fails to update stale knowledge and confirm that the Project uses the new authoritative guidance.

Unrecognized errors can continue affecting employee decisions. A suitable response must refresh the knowledge base and instructions, then validate common and edge-case questions.

options.label: B
options.text: Turn on memory and rely on it to remove abandoned alternatives from the active conversation automatically.

options.label: C
options.text: Delete every previous decision and restart without carrying forward any verified constraints or conclusions.

Claude receives a cleaner working set without forcing the team to reconstruct the project from nothing. The approach improves the result without introducing an avoidable control or quality gap.

Incorrect options:

Continue adding corrective messages because all previous context remains equally useful to the model.

This option assumes more context always improves performance despite the accumulated irrelevant and conflicting material. It addresses a secondary concern while failing to reduce context clutter while preserving the verified current state of the plan.

Claude may continue retrieving obsolete assumptions while the conversation becomes harder to manage. The required corrective action is to carry forward a curated current-state summary into a new task-focused conversation.

Turn on memory and rely on it to remove abandoned alternatives from the active conversation automatically.

This option uses memory as a substitute for actively curating the current task context. That choice is inconsistent with the requirement to reduce context clutter while preserving the verified current state of the plan.

Delete every previous decision and restart without carrying forward any verified constraints or conclusions.

This option removes useful current state together with the irrelevant history. It therefore fails to reduce context clutter while preserving the verified current state of the plan.

questions.question: A team lead asks Claude to explain a newly revised safety standard. The response cites an old training manual and a current discussion forum but not the issuing authority. What should the lead do?

options.label: A
options.text: Check the issuing authority’s current standard and implementation guidance, then revise the explanation against those sources.

options.label: B
options.text: Use the discussion forum because recent practitioner comments are more useful than formal source documents.

options.label: C
options.text: Keep the old manual and add a disclaimer that safety standards occasionally change over time.

options.label: D
options.text: Ask Claude to combine the manual and forum into one confident summary without listing disagreements.

questions.explanation:
Correct option:

Check the issuing authority’s current standard and implementation guidance, then revise the explanation against those sources.

This option uses the authoritative and current material that defines the actual requirement. That is the most direct way to base the explanation on the current authoritative safety requirements.

High-consequence factual guidance should be checked against the primary source that governs the issue. The scenario applies that principle by requiring the team to retrieve the current standard, compare it with the draft, and correct any outdated statements.

The lead can distinguish binding changes from outdated training content and informal interpretation. The result is more dependable and maintainable than a response that addresses only part of the problem.

Incorrect options:

Use the discussion forum because recent practitioner comments are more useful than formal source documents.

This option substitutes informal opinion for the authority that issued the standard. It addresses a secondary concern while failing to base the explanation on the current authoritative safety requirements.

Practitioner comments may be incomplete, inaccurate, or based on different circumstances. The required corrective action is to retrieve the current standard, compare it with the draft, and correct any outdated statements.

Keep the old manual and add a disclaimer that safety standards occasionally change over time.

This option acknowledges possible staleness without correcting the explanation. That choice is inconsistent with the requirement to base the explanation on the current authoritative safety requirements.

Employees could still follow requirements that are no longer current. An appropriate solution must retrieve the current standard, compare it with the draft, and correct any outdated statements.

Ask Claude to combine the manual and forum into one confident summary without listing disagreements.

This option blends weak sources and suppresses uncertainty instead of resolving it. It therefore fails to base the explanation on the current authoritative safety requirements.

The resulting guidance may appear authoritative while remaining unsupported. A suitable response must retrieve the current standard, compare it with the draft, and correct any outdated statements.

questions.question: Claude proposes which students should receive emergency financial assistance using application essays, attendance, and teacher comments. The recommendation could determine access to essential support. Which review approach is MOST appropriate?

options.label: A
options.text: Approve the ranking automatically if Claude provides a detailed explanation for each student.

options.label: B
options.text: Have one administrator review only the students that Claude ranks near the funding cutoff.

options.label: C
options.text: Require qualified reviewers to verify the evidence, approved criteria, fairness, and final decisions for every award.

options.label: D
options.text: Remove teacher comments and use Claude’s general understanding of student hardship instead.

questions.explanation:
Correct option:

Require qualified reviewers to verify the evidence, approved criteria, fairness, and final decisions for every award.

This option preserves human accountability for a consequential decision affecting essential support. The action therefore satisfies the scenario’s need to retain accountable human decision-making for a high-impact allocation of essential assistance.

Consequential decisions require qualified review of evidence, criteria, fairness, and the final action. In this case, the team should use Claude only as analytical support while authorized people verify every recommendation and decide the awards.

Reviewers can correct factual errors and ensure the ranking follows the institution’s authorized criteria. The approach improves the result without introducing an avoidable control or quality gap.

Incorrect options:

Approve the ranking automatically if Claude provides a detailed explanation for each student.

This option treats generated reasoning as sufficient authority for a high-impact allocation decision. That choice is inconsistent with the requirement to retain accountable human decision-making for a high-impact allocation of essential assistance.

A persuasive explanation can still contain bias, factual error, or an inappropriate criterion. An appropriate solution must use Claude only as analytical support while authorized people verify every recommendation and decide the awards.

Have one administrator review only the students that Claude ranks near the funding cutoff.

This option limits oversight to borderline cases even though errors could affect any applicant. It therefore fails to retain accountable human decision-making for a high-impact allocation of essential assistance.

Systematic bias or incorrect source interpretation may remain throughout the ranking. A suitable response must use Claude only as analytical support while authorized people verify every recommendation and decide the awards.

Remove teacher comments and use Claude’s general understanding of student hardship instead.

This option replaces imperfect evidence with unsupported general knowledge rather than improving the process. This leaves the core need to retain accountable human decision-making for a high-impact allocation of essential assistance unresolved.

The ranking would become less traceable and more vulnerable to assumptions. The better direction is to use Claude only as analytical support while authorized people verify every recommendation and decide the awards.

questions.question: A school uses Claude to draft descriptions of students selected for an advanced program. The drafts repeatedly praise assertiveness and leadership visibility while overlooking strong analytical work by quieter students. Which TWO concerns should reviewers raise?

options.label: A
options.text: The descriptions are too short to celebrate every selected student equally.

options.label: B
options.text: The program should select only students whose communication style Claude can describe most easily in polished language.

options.label: C
options.text: The drafts may encode a biased view of merit that disadvantages students with different communication styles.

options.label: D
options.text: Claude should be allowed to define the program criteria because automated standards are more objective.

options.label: E
options.text: Using these drafts without correction could reinforce exclusion and distort future judgments about student potential.

questions.explanation:
Correct options:

The drafts may encode a biased view of merit that disadvantages students with different communication styles.

This option identifies the unfair association between visible assertiveness and program suitability. It is aligned with the stated requirement to identify biased framing and prevent its downstream influence on student opportunity.

This reflects the principle that ethical review should examine both the immediate representation and the harms created by repeated reliance on it. For this task, the appropriate direction is to compare the drafts with approved criteria and correct language that privileges an irrelevant communication style.

Reviewers can compare descriptions with the actual approved selection criteria. The option balances the operational objective with the review and evidence needs described in the scenario.

Using these drafts without correction could reinforce exclusion and distort future judgments about student potential.

This option recognizes the downstream harm of repeatedly presenting one behavioral style as superior. It responds to the decisive requirement to identify biased framing and prevent its downstream influence on student opportunity.

The governing idea is that ethical review should examine both the immediate representation and the harms created by repeated reliance on it. Here, that means the user should compare the drafts with approved criteria and correct language that privileges an irrelevant communication style.

Reviewers can prevent generated language from shaping decisions beyond the evidence. This preserves the intended benefit while controlling the failure mode highlighted in the stem.

Incorrect options:

The descriptions are too short to celebrate every selected student equally.

This option focuses on length rather than the potentially unfair criteria embedded in the drafts. It therefore fails to identify biased framing and prevent its downstream influence on student opportunity.

Longer text would not correct the representational imbalance. A suitable response must compare the drafts with approved criteria and correct language that privileges an irrelevant communication style.

The program should select only students whose communication style Claude can describe most easily in polished language.

This option adapts the decision criteria to the model’s output tendencies. The option does not meet the scenario’s requirement to identify biased framing and prevent its downstream influence on student opportunity.

Qualified students could be excluded for irrelevant presentation characteristics. The workflow instead needs to compare the drafts with approved criteria and correct language that privileges an irrelevant communication style.

Claude should be allowed to define the program criteria because automated standards are more objective.

This option transfers institutional judgment to a generated standard and assumes automation removes bias. As a result, the approach cannot reliably identify biased framing and prevent its downstream influence on student opportunity.

The new criteria may reproduce hidden assumptions without accountable approval. The scenario calls for the team to compare the drafts with approved criteria and correct language that privileges an irrelevant communication style.

options.text: Use Research to gather and synthesize current external evidence with citations that can be inspected.

options.label: B
options.text: Use memory as the primary source for current regulations because it persists information from earlier conversations.

options.label: C
options.text: Use a general chat without web research and ask Claude to provide citations from its existing knowledge.

options.label: D
options.text: Use an Artifact for the impact matrix so the client can independently review and refine the structured deliverable.

options.label: E
options.text: Use the fastest available model and skip source inspection because workshop discussion will reveal any errors.

questions.explanation:

Use Research to gather and synthesize current external evidence with citations that can be inspected.

This option selects the feature suited to current, multi-source investigation and traceability. This directly addresses the requirement to combine current sourced research with an editable client deliverable.

The consultant can review the original evidence before presenting regulatory conclusions. This makes the option stronger than alternatives that leave the same requirement unresolved.

Use an Artifact for the impact matrix so the client can independently review and refine the structured deliverable.

This option selects an editable output surface appropriate for a workshop matrix. That is the most direct way to combine current sourced research with an editable client deliverable.

Product features should be selected separately for evidence gathering and for presenting a reusable work product. The scenario applies that principle by requiring the team to use Research for current sources and an Artifact for the structured workshop matrix.

The findings can be organized and revised without rebuilding the content from chat text. The result is more dependable and maintainable than a response that addresses only part of the problem.

Use memory as the primary source for current regulations because it persists information from earlier conversations.

Human reviewers can assess credibility, context, and procedural requirements. This preserves the intended benefit while controlling the failure mode highlighted in the stem.

Authorized decision-makers must retain final responsibility and apply policy, fairness, and due-process safeguards.

This option preserves accountability for a consequential employment action. The option fully supports the goal to use Claude only for bounded analytical support while preserving qualified investigation and accountable decisions.

questions.question: A project office receives a concise portfolio update from Claude. It lists completed milestones and current dates but omits cross-project dependencies, unresolved risks, and decisions awaiting sponsors. Which evaluation is MOST appropriate?

options.label: A
options.text: Approve the update because concise reporting should exclude issues that have not yet produced a delay.

options.label: B
options.text: Evaluate only whether the dates are accurate because completeness is less important than factual correctness.

options.label: C
options.text: Add more milestone descriptions without checking whether the missing dependencies and decisions are included.

options.label: D
options.text: Independently compare the update with reporting requirements and source records, then add all material omitted management information.

questions.explanation:
Correct option:

Independently compare the update with reporting requirements and source records, then add all material omitted management information.

This option evaluates both accuracy and completeness against the intended use of the report. The action therefore satisfies the scenario’s need to confirm that the update contains every decision-relevant category required by sponsors.

Output quality includes completeness relative to the requested purpose, not accuracy alone. In this case, the team should use a requirements checklist and source records to identify and repair material omissions.

The final update can support sponsor decisions rather than merely describe finished work. The approach improves the result without introducing an avoidable control or quality gap.

Incorrect options:

Approve the update because concise reporting should exclude issues that have not yet produced a delay.

This option treats brevity as permission to omit information required for management action. It addresses a secondary concern while failing to confirm that the update contains every decision-relevant category required by sponsors.

Sponsors may miss emerging risks and decisions until they become more costly. The required corrective action is to use a requirements checklist and source records to identify and repair material omissions.

Evaluate only whether the dates are accurate because completeness is less important than factual correctness.

This option checks one quality dimension while ignoring required sections of the requested update. That choice is inconsistent with the requirement to confirm that the update contains every decision-relevant category required by sponsors.

A factually accurate but incomplete report can still be unfit for its purpose. An appropriate solution must use a requirements checklist and source records to identify and repair material omissions.

Add more milestone descriptions without checking whether the missing dependencies and decisions are included.

This option increases detail in the wrong area and leaves the identified omissions unresolved. It therefore fails to confirm that the update contains every decision-relevant category required by sponsors.

The longer report could remain operationally incomplete. A suitable response must use a requirements checklist and source records to identify and repair material omissions.

questions.question: Claude produces a detailed network-outage analysis for engineers. A communications specialist needs a customer update explaining impact, restoration status, and next steps without exposing internal security details. What should the specialist request?

options.label: A
options.text: Rewrite the analysis for customers using plain language, confirmed impact, current status, and approved next steps.

options.label: B
options.text: Publish the engineering analysis unchanged so customers can see every technical action the team performed.

options.label: C
options.text: Remove all outage details and send only a general apology to prevent customers from asking technical questions.

options.label: D
options.text: Ask Claude to make the incident sound minor even if the confirmed impact was significant.

questions.explanation:
Correct option:

Rewrite the analysis for customers using plain language, confirmed impact, current status, and approved next steps.

This option adapts the technical content to the audience while preserving the facts customers need. This directly addresses the requirement to adapt verified technical information into a clear and appropriately bounded customer communication.

The relevant principle is that audience adaptation changes language and structure without changing confirmed facts or disclosing unnecessary information. Applied here, the workflow should retain customer-relevant impact and status while removing internal technical detail that is not appropriate to share.

The update can remain clear and useful without disclosing unnecessary internal details. This makes the option stronger than alternatives that leave the same requirement unresolved.

Incorrect options:

Publish the engineering analysis unchanged so customers can see every technical action the team performed.

This option ignores the customer audience and the need to limit internal security information. The option does not meet the scenario’s requirement to adapt verified technical information into a clear and appropriately bounded customer communication.

The message may confuse readers and reveal details that should remain internal. The workflow instead needs to retain customer-relevant impact and status while removing internal technical detail that is not appropriate to share.

Remove all outage details and send only a general apology to prevent customers from asking technical questions.

This option eliminates essential impact and restoration information rather than adapting it. This leaves the core need to adapt verified technical information into a clear and appropriately bounded customer communication unresolved.

Customers would lack the facts needed to plan around the disruption. The better direction is to retain customer-relevant impact and status while removing internal technical detail that is not appropriate to share.

Ask Claude to make the incident sound minor even if the confirmed impact was significant.

This option changes the substance to manage perception instead of communicating accurately. As a result, the approach cannot reliably adapt verified technical information into a clear and appropriately bounded customer communication.

Misleading reassurance can damage trust and create additional support issues. The scenario calls for the team to retain customer-relevant impact and status while removing internal technical detail that is not appropriate to share.

questions.question: A marketing team is planning entry into a new region using internal brand guidance and current competitor, customer, and regulatory information. Which Claude workflow BEST supports the work?

options.label: A
options.text: Use a Project for approved internal guidance, use Research for current external evidence, and independently validate material claims.

options.label: B
options.text: Place all internal and external assumptions in memory and reuse them without checking whether market conditions change.

options.label: C
options.text: Ask Claude to create the final launch plan from general knowledge before sharing any internal brand requirements.

options.label: D
options.text: Use only internal documents because external research could introduce information that challenges the preferred strategy.

questions.explanation:
Correct option:

Use a Project for approved internal guidance, use Research for current external evidence, and independently validate material claims.

This option separates stable internal context from current sourced investigation while retaining review. It is aligned with the stated requirement to combine maintained internal guidance with current external research and source validation.

This reflects the principle that research and planning workflows should distinguish stable organizational context from time-sensitive external evidence. For this task, the appropriate direction is to use a Project and Research together, then verify claims before the plan is approved.

The plan can remain brand-consistent, current, and traceable. The option balances the operational objective with the review and evidence needs described in the scenario.

Incorrect options:

Place all internal and external assumptions in memory and reuse them without checking whether market conditions change.

This option treats persistent context as a substitute for current evidence and source maintenance. As a result, the approach cannot reliably combine maintained internal guidance with current external research and source validation.

The plan may rely on outdated regulations or competitor information. The scenario calls for the team to use a Project and Research together, then verify claims before the plan is approved.

Ask Claude to create the final launch plan from general knowledge before sharing any internal brand requirements.

This option withholds essential organizational context and current evidence from the planning task. It addresses a secondary concern while failing to combine maintained internal guidance with current external research and source validation.

The output may conflict with brand rules and misrepresent the regional market. The required corrective action is to use a Project and Research together, then verify claims before the plan is approved.

Use only internal documents because external research could introduce information that challenges the preferred strategy.

This option excludes current market evidence to protect a predetermined direction. That choice is inconsistent with the requirement to combine maintained internal guidance with current external research and source validation.

The team may miss regulatory constraints, customer needs, or competitor changes. An appropriate solution must use a Project and Research together, then verify claims before the plan is approved.

References:

What are Projects

Use Research on Claude

Incorrect or misleading responses

questions.domain: Domain 4: Workflow Integration and Solution Design
questions.question: A team lead presents a Claude-assisted content workflow to executives. The pilot reduced drafting time, but editors still corrected factual and brand issues. Which message BEST communicates the workflow’s value?

options.label: A
options.text: The workflow accelerates first drafts, while editorial review remains necessary for facts, brand alignment, and publication decisions.

options.label: B
options.text: The pilot proves Claude can replace editors because most drafts required only limited correction.

options.label: C
options.text: The workflow has no value because any human correction means the automation failed.

options.label: D
options.text: The workflow guarantees faster publication and error-free content once users become familiar with it.

questions.explanation:
Correct option:

The workflow accelerates first drafts, while editorial review remains necessary for facts, brand alignment, and publication decisions.

This option states the demonstrated benefit without hiding the observed limitations or review requirement. It is aligned with the stated requirement to explain measured productivity gains together with the continuing limits and human responsibilities.

This reflects the principle that stakeholder communication should distinguish augmentation benefits from unsupported claims of autonomy or perfection. For this task, the appropriate direction is to present the pilot evidence honestly and describe the review controls required for safe use.

Executives receive a realistic basis for deciding where the workflow can create value. The option balances the operational objective with the review and evidence needs described in the scenario.

Incorrect options:

The pilot proves Claude can replace editors because most drafts required only limited correction.

This option converts partial productivity improvement into an unsupported replacement claim. As a result, the approach cannot reliably explain measured productivity gains together with the continuing limits and human responsibilities.

The organization may remove controls that caught factual and brand errors. The scenario calls for the team to present the pilot evidence honestly and describe the review controls required for safe use.

The workflow has no value because any human correction means the automation failed.

This option uses an unrealistic standard that ignores time saved during assisted drafting. It addresses a secondary concern while failing to explain measured productivity gains together with the continuing limits and human responsibilities.

Leaders may reject a useful augmentation opportunity. The required corrective action is to present the pilot evidence honestly and describe the review controls required for safe use.

The workflow guarantees faster publication and error-free content once users become familiar with it.

This option promises outcomes that the pilot did not demonstrate. That choice is inconsistent with the requirement to explain measured productivity gains together with the continuing limits and human responsibilities.

Unrealistic expectations can lead to unsafe scaling and loss of trust. An appropriate solution must present the pilot evidence honestly and describe the review controls required for safe use.

References:

Define success criteria and build evaluations

Incorrect or misleading responses

Use Claude Cowork safely

questions.question: Claude summarizes employee-engagement comments by stating that younger staff resist accountability. The source comments use inconsistent age labels, contain opposing examples, and mostly discuss unclear role expectations. What should the review team identify?

options.label: A
options.text: The summary introduces an unsupported age-based generalization and ignores contradictory evidence about the actual workplace issue.

options.label: B
options.text: The summary is acceptable because broad demographic patterns are more useful than reviewing individual comments.

options.label: C
options.text: The main concern is Claude's missing percentage calculation for every age group mentioned in the source comments.

options.label: D
options.text: The team should remove comments that disagree with the summary so the final report presents one clear message.

questions.explanation:
Correct option:

The summary introduces an unsupported age-based generalization and ignores contradictory evidence about the actual workplace issue.

This option recognizes both the biased framing and the inconsistency between the conclusion and the source comments. The action therefore satisfies the scenario’s need to identify bias and inconsistency rather than accepting a demographic conclusion unsupported by the comments.

Evaluation must test whether group claims are supported, consistently defined, and balanced against counterevidence. In this case, the team should reject the age-based inference and reanalyze the comments around the documented role-expectation themes.

The team can reframe the analysis around role clarity and report uncertainty honestly. The approach improves the result without introducing an avoidable control or quality gap.

Incorrect options:

The summary is acceptable because broad demographic patterns are more useful than reviewing individual comments.

This option assumes a demographic conclusion is valuable despite weak and inconsistent evidence. This leaves the core need to identify bias and inconsistency rather than accepting a demographic conclusion unsupported by the comments unresolved.

The organization could reinforce stereotypes and overlook the operational problem employees described. The better direction is to reject the age-based inference and reanalyze the comments around the documented role-expectation themes.

The main concern is Claude's missing percentage calculation for every age group mentioned in the source comments.

This option treats missing quantification as the primary issue even though the categories and conclusion are unreliable. As a result, the approach cannot reliably identify bias and inconsistency rather than accepting a demographic conclusion unsupported by the comments.

Adding percentages would not correct the biased inference or contradictory examples. The scenario calls for the team to reject the age-based inference and reanalyze the comments around the documented role-expectation themes.

The team should remove comments that disagree with the summary so the final report presents one clear message.

This option proposes deleting counterevidence to preserve the generated conclusion. It addresses a secondary concern while failing to identify bias and inconsistency rather than accepting a demographic conclusion unsupported by the comments.

The resulting report would be misleading and could distort people decisions. The required corrective action is to reject the age-based inference and reanalyze the comments around the documented role-expectation themes.

References:

Evaluate and mitigate discrimination

Reduce hallucinations

Challenges in evaluating AI systems

questions.question: A user prepares a weekly planning pack by copying the same approved priorities into a checklist, calendar, and status note, then manually updates each version. Which optimization is BEST?

options.label: A
options.text: Continue maintaining every copy separately because repeated entry provides the strongest possible quality control.

options.label: B
options.text: Remove the checklist and calendar so only one format remains, regardless of how stakeholders use the information.

options.label: C
options.text: Ask Claude to invent new priorities for each format so the three outputs no longer need to match.

options.label: D
options.text: Maintain one verified priority source, then generate the checklist, calendar, and status note from it after each approved update.

questions.explanation:
Correct option:

Maintain one verified priority source, then generate the checklist, calendar, and status note from it after each approved update.

This option eliminates repeated entry while preserving the different deliverables stakeholders need. It is aligned with the stated requirement to remove duplicate maintenance while preserving consistent stakeholder-specific outputs.

This reflects the principle that optimization should create a verified source of truth and reuse it across required deliverables. For this task, the appropriate direction is to maintain the approved priorities once and derive each planning format from the same controlled source.

Updates can be made once and propagated consistently after review. The option balances the operational objective with the review and evidence needs described in the scenario.

Incorrect options:

Continue maintaining every copy separately because repeated entry provides the strongest possible quality control.

This option treats duplicate manual work as a control even though the copies can diverge. That choice is inconsistent with the requirement to remove duplicate maintenance while preserving consistent stakeholder-specific outputs.

The user spends more time and may introduce inconsistent priorities across outputs. An appropriate solution must maintain the approved priorities once and derive each planning format from the same controlled source.

Remove the checklist and calendar so only one format remains, regardless of how stakeholders use the information.

This option reduces duplication by discarding outputs that may serve distinct operational purposes. It therefore fails to remove duplicate maintenance while preserving consistent stakeholder-specific outputs.

Stakeholders could lose useful planning views rather than gaining an efficient workflow. A suitable response must maintain the approved priorities once and derive each planning format from the same controlled source.

Ask Claude to invent new priorities for each format so the three outputs no longer need to match.

This option avoids consistency by changing the underlying information across deliverables. The option does not meet the scenario’s requirement to remove duplicate maintenance while preserving consistent stakeholder-specific outputs.

The planning pack would become contradictory and no longer reflect approved priorities. The workflow instead needs to maintain the approved priorities once and derive each planning format from the same controlled source.

References:

What are Artifacts

Create and edit files with Claude

Schedule recurring tasks in Claude Cowork

questions.question: A support team uses Claude to draft routine account instructions and responses to disputed contract charges. Routine instructions follow approved scripts, while disputed charges can create legal obligations. Which workflow is BEST?

options.label: A
options.text: Allow Claude-assisted routine drafts, but route disputed-charge responses to an authorized reviewer before sending any message.

options.label: B
options.text: Require legal review for every routine password-reset instruction and every disputed charge response.

options.label: C
options.text: Send both categories automatically because approved scripts make every customer response equally low risk.

options.label: D
options.text: Ask Claude to label uncertain disputed responses but send them unless the customer objects afterward.

questions.explanation:
Correct option:

Allow Claude-assisted routine drafts, but route disputed-charge responses to an authorized reviewer before sending any message.

This option matches review intensity to the consequence and authority required for each type of response. It responds to the decisive requirement to apply human review where the response carries contractual consequence or requires authority.

The governing idea is that review thresholds should reflect risk, uncertainty, and decision authority rather than treating every task identically. Here, that means the user should automate bounded routine drafting while preserving authorized review for disputed contractual matters.

The team gains efficiency on standard work without delegating contractual judgment to Claude. This preserves the intended benefit while controlling the failure mode highlighted in the stem.

Incorrect options:

Require legal review for every routine password-reset instruction and every disputed charge response.

This option applies the highest review burden even to low-risk standardized communication. That choice is inconsistent with the requirement to apply human review where the response carries contractual consequence or requires authority.

The workflow would create avoidable delay without improving control over routine tasks. An appropriate solution must automate bounded routine drafting while preserving authorized review for disputed contractual matters.

Send both categories automatically because approved scripts make every customer response equally low risk.

This option treats a contractual dispute as equivalent to a routine instruction. It therefore fails to apply human review where the response carries contractual consequence or requires authority.

The organization could communicate an unauthorized position or create unintended obligations. A suitable response must automate bounded routine drafting while preserving authorized review for disputed contractual matters.

Ask Claude to label uncertain disputed responses but send them unless the customer objects afterward.

This option moves review to after a potentially consequential message has already been delivered. The option does not meet the scenario’s requirement to apply human review where the response carries contractual consequence or requires authority.

The organization may be unable to reverse the legal or relationship impact. The workflow instead needs to automate bounded routine drafting while preserving authorized review for disputed contractual matters.

References:

Anthropic Usage Policy

Use Claude Cowork safely

Use Claude for Word

questions.question: An organization publishes a community-impact report developed with Claude. Leaders want the report to remain transparent about evidence, uncertainty, and responsibility without distracting readers with internal workflow detail. Which approach is BEST?

options.label: A
options.text: State that Claude produced the findings and therefore bears responsibility for any errors in the report.

options.label: B
options.text: Remove source references and uncertainty language so the report presents one confident institutional position.

options.label: C
options.text: Carefully describe every prompt and intermediate draft even when those details do not help readers evaluate the evidence.

options.label: D
options.text: Cite material evidence, label important uncertainty, and identify the organization as responsible for the conclusions and follow-up.

questions.explanation:
Correct option:

Cite material evidence, label important uncertainty, and identify the organization as responsible for the conclusions and follow-up.

This option provides readers with traceability and limits while preserving clear human accountability. It responds to the decisive requirement to communicate evidence, uncertainty, and accountable human ownership clearly.

The governing idea is that responsible transparency focuses on what supports the conclusion, what remains uncertain, and who owns the decision. Here, that means the user should cite the evidence and limitations while keeping responsibility with the publishing organization.

The report can be concise without hiding the basis or ownership of its claims. This preserves the intended benefit while controlling the failure mode highlighted in the stem.

Incorrect options:

State that Claude produced the findings and therefore bears responsibility for any errors in the report.

This option assigns accountability to a tool rather than the organization publishing the conclusions. The option does not meet the scenario’s requirement to communicate evidence, uncertainty, and accountable human ownership clearly.

Readers receive no clear human owner for correction or decision-making. The workflow instead needs to cite the evidence and limitations while keeping responsibility with the publishing organization.

Remove source references and uncertainty language so the report presents one confident institutional position.

This option reduces transparency to create a stronger appearance of certainty. This leaves the core need to communicate evidence, uncertainty, and accountable human ownership clearly unresolved.

Readers cannot trace claims or understand important limitations. The better direction is to cite the evidence and limitations while keeping responsibility with the publishing organization.

Carefully describe every prompt and intermediate draft even when those details do not help readers evaluate the evidence.

This option confuses transparency with disclosing irrelevant process detail. As a result, the approach cannot reliably communicate evidence, uncertainty, and accountable human ownership clearly.

The report may become harder to understand without improving accountability. The scenario calls for the team to cite the evidence and limitations while keeping responsibility with the publishing organization.

References:

Anthropic Usage Policy

Use Research on Claude

Citations for source verification

questions.question: A communications specialist needs Claude to rewrite technical service notices into plain-language customer updates. Previous outputs vary widely in tone and omit required safety wording. Which instruction is MOST effective?

options.label: A
options.text: Tell Claude to sound friendly and assume it will preserve every required statement from the source.

options.label: B
options.text: Ask Claude to shorten each notice as much as possible before checking whether essential warnings remain.

options.label: C
options.text: Upload unrelated examples from other brands so Claude can choose whichever style appears most engaging.

options.label: D
options.text: Provide an approved example, mandatory safety statements, audience guidance, tone rules, maximum length, and explicit review criteria.

questions.explanation:
Correct option:

Provide an approved example, mandatory safety statements, audience guidance, tone rules, maximum length, and explicit review criteria.

This option combines a representative example with explicit content and style constraints for the rewrite. The option fully supports the goal to create consistent customer notices that retain mandatory safety information.

Examples work best when they are paired with clear rules and success criteria. A sound application in this scenario is to show Claude the desired pattern while identifying content that cannot be removed.

The specialist gains a stable standard for checking consistency, readability, and required wording. The choice is preferable because it solves the root requirement rather than merely changing presentation or speed.

Incorrect options:

Tell Claude to sound friendly and assume it will preserve every required statement from the source.

This option uses a broad tone request without identifying the mandatory language or showing the expected transformation. This leaves the core need to create consistent customer notices that retain mandatory safety information unresolved.

Claude may simplify away safety information while producing superficially friendly prose. The better direction is to show Claude the desired pattern while identifying content that cannot be removed.

Ask Claude to shorten each notice as much as possible before checking whether essential warnings remain.

This option optimizes brevity before defining the information that must be preserved. As a result, the approach cannot reliably create consistent customer notices that retain mandatory safety information.

Critical safety wording could disappear and require costly rework. The scenario calls for the team to show Claude the desired pattern while identifying content that cannot be removed.

Upload unrelated examples from other brands so Claude can choose whichever style appears most engaging.

This option introduces examples that do not represent the organization’s required voice or compliance needs. It addresses a secondary concern while failing to create consistent customer notices that retain mandatory safety information.

The resulting notices may imitate unsuitable wording and remain inconsistent. The required corrective action is to show Claude the desired pattern while identifying content that cannot be removed.

Claude Console prompting tools

options.text: Choose the concise summary because executives generally prefer shorter documents regardless of omitted dependencies.

options.label: B
options.text: Score each summary against accuracy, completeness, source currency, audience clarity, and decision usefulness.

options.label: C
options.text: Repair the strongest candidate by validating sources and clearly separating verified facts from assumptions.

options.label: D
options.text: Merge all three summaries automatically so every useful sentence appears in the final version.

options.label: E
options.text: Select the most polished summary and ask sponsors to identify any factual issues during the meeting.

Score each summary against accuracy, completeness, source currency, audience clarity, and decision usefulness.

This option applies explicit criteria that reflect the actual purpose and known failure modes of the summaries. It is aligned with the stated requirement to select and refine an output using explicit quality criteria rather than presentation alone.

This reflects the principle that comparative evaluation should measure the dimensions required for the intended decision and then repair the best candidate. For this task, the appropriate direction is to score the drafts systematically and validate the evidence and reasoning in the strongest one before use.

The office can compare alternatives consistently rather than favoring one superficial strength. The option balances the operational objective with the review and evidence needs described in the scenario.

Repair the strongest candidate by validating sources and clearly separating verified facts from assumptions.

This option combines comparative evaluation with targeted correction of the most suitable draft. That is the most direct way to select and refine an output using explicit quality criteria rather than presentation alone.

Comparative evaluation should measure the dimensions required for the intended decision and then repair the best candidate. The scenario applies that principle by requiring the team to score the drafts systematically and validate the evidence and reasoning in the strongest one before use.

The final summary can preserve useful structure while removing material evidence and reasoning defects. The result is more dependable and maintainable than a response that addresses only part of the problem.

Choose the concise summary because executives generally prefer shorter documents regardless of omitted dependencies.

This option uses length as the decisive criterion even though the document omits management-critical information. The option does not meet the scenario’s requirement to select and refine an output using explicit quality criteria rather than presentation alone.

The selected summary could conceal risks that require sponsor action. The workflow instead needs to score the drafts systematically and validate the evidence and reasoning in the strongest one before use.

Merge all three summaries automatically so every useful sentence appears in the final version.

This option combines outputs without resolving contradictions, duplication, or outdated evidence. It addresses a secondary concern while failing to select and refine an output using explicit quality criteria rather than presentation alone.

Select the most polished summary and ask sponsors to identify any factual issues during the meeting.

This option defers validation until the document is already influencing a consequential discussion. That choice is inconsistent with the requirement to select and refine an output using explicit quality criteria rather than presentation alone.

options.text: The project should avoid measuring quality because productivity is the only relevant success indicator.

Claude’s value and limitations vary with task complexity, source quality, consequence, and workflow design. A sound application in this scenario is to measure each use case before scaling instead of promising uniform immediate savings.

Leaders can compare real outcomes and expand only where the balance is favorable. The choice is preferable because it solves the root requirement rather than merely changing presentation or speed.

Incorrect options:

Every department should directly adopt the same workflow immediately so savings can be compared on a common schedule.

This option ignores differences in task suitability, evidence, and control requirements. As a result, the approach cannot reliably set realistic adoption expectations based on use-case evidence and multiple success dimensions.

questions.question: A shared Project can access procurement files and draft supplier messages. Some users can approve contracts, while others may only prepare analysis. Which control design BEST supports organizational governance?

options.label: A
options.text: Align Project access and approvals with job authority, restrict sources, and log consequential review decisions for auditability and accountability.

options.label: B
options.text: Give every Project user the same broad access so collaboration remains simple and no one waits for approvals.

options.label: C
options.text: Rely on a general instruction telling Claude to behave responsibly instead of configuring access and approvals.

options.label: D
options.text: Allow the most experienced user to approve all actions informally without documenting decisions or role assignments.

questions.explanation:
Correct option:

Align Project access and approvals with job authority, restrict sources, and log consequential review decisions for auditability and accountability.

This option connects permissions and workflow checkpoints to the organization’s actual roles and responsibilities. The option fully supports the goal to align access, sources, approvals, and records with organizational authority.

Governance controls should translate policy into role-appropriate permissions and accountable checkpoints. A sound application in this scenario is to restrict the Project and its consequential actions according to approved responsibilities.

Users can prepare work efficiently without gaining authority they do not possess. The choice is preferable because it solves the root requirement rather than merely changing presentation or speed.

Incorrect options:

Give every Project user the same broad access so collaboration remains simple and no one waits for approvals.

This option removes role-based limits and treats speed as more important than authorization. It therefore fails to align access, sources, approvals, and records with organizational authority.

Users may access restricted files or communicate commitments beyond their authority. A suitable response must restrict the Project and its consequential actions according to approved responsibilities.

Rely on a general instruction telling Claude to behave responsibly instead of configuring access and approvals.

This option uses wording as a substitute for enforceable governance controls. The option does not meet the scenario’s requirement to align access, sources, approvals, and records with organizational authority.

The Project may still expose sources or enable actions that users are not authorized to perform. The workflow instead needs to restrict the Project and its consequential actions according to approved responsibilities.

Allow the most experienced user to approve all actions informally without documenting decisions or role assignments.

This option creates a person-dependent process without transparent authority or records. This leaves the core need to align access, sources, approvals, and records with organizational authority unresolved.

The workflow becomes difficult to audit and may fail when personnel change. The better direction is to restrict the Project and its consequential actions according to approved responsibilities.

options.label: A
options.text: Keep the statement because Claude may have considered contextual information that is not visible in the workbook.

options.label: B
options.text: Carefully compare the statement with the relevant workbook cells and correct the summary before using it.

options.label: C
options.text: Ask Claude to make the summary sound less certain while leaving the travel-cost conclusion unchanged.

options.label: D
options.text: Remove every financial figure and provide only a general narrative about spending priorities.

questions.explanation:
Correct option:

Carefully compare the statement with the relevant workbook cells and correct the summary before using it.

This option checks the disputed claim against the authoritative data supplied for the task. It responds to the decisive requirement to ensure the summary agrees with the authoritative budget data.

The governing idea is that Claude output should be checked against source material when a factual discrepancy appears. Here, that means the user should verify the specific claim in the workbook and correct the output before distribution.

The analyst can correct the error and review related calculations for similar problems. This preserves the intended benefit while controlling the failure mode highlighted in the stem.

Incorrect options:

Keep the statement because Claude may have considered contextual information that is not visible in the workbook.

This option accepts a claim that directly conflicts with the supplied source without identifying supporting evidence. As a result, the approach cannot reliably ensure the summary agrees with the authoritative budget data.

The summary could misinform budget owners and weaken confidence in the remaining analysis. The scenario calls for the team to verify the specific claim in the workbook and correct the output before distribution.

Ask Claude to make the summary sound less certain while leaving the travel-cost conclusion unchanged.

This option changes tone instead of resolving the factual contradiction. That choice is inconsistent with the requirement to ensure the summary agrees with the authoritative budget data.

A qualified but incorrect conclusion can still lead readers to the wrong decision. An appropriate solution must verify the specific claim in the workbook and correct the output before distribution.

Remove every financial figure and provide only a general narrative about spending priorities.

This option avoids the detected error by discarding useful quantitative evidence. It therefore fails to ensure the summary agrees with the authoritative budget data.

Leaders would lose the budget information needed to understand the variance. A suitable response must verify the specific claim in the workbook and correct the output before distribution.

options.text: Use Haiku because the work is simple, repetitive, time-sensitive, and supported by planned sampling and review.

options.label: C
options.text: Use Sonnet because balanced general-purpose reasoning is always preferable to optimizing for speed and cost.

options.label: D
options.text: Select a model only by context-window size, even though each message is short and independent.

questions.explanation:

Use Haiku because the work is simple, repetitive, time-sensitive, and supported by planned sampling and review.

This option matches a fast and economical model to a bounded extraction task with planned quality checks. It is aligned with the stated requirement to select an efficient model for straightforward high-volume extraction with human spot checks.

This reflects the principle that model choice should reflect task complexity, required quality, latency, and cost rather than prestige. For this task, the appropriate direction is to start with Haiku and use sampling to confirm that the bounded extraction remains reliable.

The team can process volume efficiently and escalate only cases that fail validation. The option balances the operational objective with the review and evidence needs described in the scenario.

Use Opus because the highest reasoning capability is necessary whenever the dataset contains many records.

questions.question: A consultant must compare onboarding procedures across four regions, identify policy differences, calculate operational impacts, and recommend a common process. The work involves separate source sets and regional reviewers. Which TWO planning actions are MOST appropriate?

options.label: A
options.text: Create a standard comparison framework, then analyze each region against the same criteria and evidence fields.

options.label: B
options.text: Ask one reviewer to summarize all regions from memory so the source differences do not slow the project.

options.label: C
options.text: Assign regional workstreams, record uncertainties, and reconcile findings at a shared cross-region review checkpoint.

options.label: D
options.text: Generate the global recommendation first, then search the regional procedures for statements that support it.

options.label: E
options.text: Merge every source into one undifferentiated prompt and ask Claude to resolve all conflicts automatically.

questions.explanation:
Correct options:

Create a standard comparison framework, then analyze each region against the same criteria and evidence fields.

This option establishes a consistent structure before the regional analyses begin. It responds to the decisive requirement to compare regional procedures consistently while preserving source traceability and expert reconciliation.

The governing idea is that parallel workstreams need common criteria, documented uncertainties, and an explicit integration checkpoint. Here, that means the user should separate the regional analyses and reconcile them against one shared comparison framework.

The final comparison can distinguish genuine policy differences from inconsistent analyst treatment. This preserves the intended benefit while controlling the failure mode highlighted in the stem.

Assign regional workstreams, record uncertainties, and reconcile findings at a shared cross-region review checkpoint.

This option separates the source-heavy work while preserving a deliberate integration and validation stage. This directly addresses the requirement to compare regional procedures consistently while preserving source traceability and expert reconciliation.

The relevant principle is that parallel workstreams need common criteria, documented uncertainties, and an explicit integration checkpoint. Applied here, the workflow should separate the regional analyses and reconcile them against one shared comparison framework.

Specialists can resolve conflicting interpretations before a common process is recommended. This makes the option stronger than alternatives that leave the same requirement unresolved.

Incorrect options:

Ask one reviewer to summarize all regions from memory so the source differences do not slow the project.

This option replaces source-based analysis with recollection and removes regional accountability. That choice is inconsistent with the requirement to compare regional procedures consistently while preserving source traceability and expert reconciliation.

Important local requirements could be missed or represented inaccurately. An appropriate solution must separate the regional analyses and reconcile them against one shared comparison framework.

Generate the global recommendation first, then search the regional procedures for statements that support it.

This option starts with a preferred conclusion and uses the evidence selectively afterward. The option does not meet the scenario’s requirement to compare regional procedures consistently while preserving source traceability and expert reconciliation.

The process encourages confirmation bias and can conceal material regional exceptions. The workflow instead needs to separate the regional analyses and reconcile them against one shared comparison framework.

Merge every source into one undifferentiated prompt and ask Claude to resolve all conflicts automatically.

This option removes the regional structure and assumes Claude can determine authoritative interpretations without reviewers. This leaves the core need to compare regional procedures consistently while preserving source traceability and expert reconciliation unresolved.

Conflicting policies may be blended into an unsupported compromise. The better direction is to separate the regional analyses and reconcile them against one shared comparison framework.

Prompting best practices

Define success criteria and build evaluations

What are Projects

questions.question: Claude produces a technically accurate incident explanation for engineers. The communications specialist must adapt it for customers without hiding impact or uncertainty. Which approach is BEST?

options.label: A
options.text: Add reassuring claims that are not in the incident record to reduce customer concern.

options.label: B
options.text: Remove every uncertain statement so the customer message appears fully resolved.

options.label: C
options.text: Keep the engineering language unchanged because technical accuracy is the only quality criterion.

options.label: D
options.text: Preserve verified facts and uncertainty, replace internal jargon, explain customer impact, and separate confirmed details from pending findings.

questions.explanation:
Correct option:

Preserve verified facts and uncertainty, replace internal jargon, explain customer impact, and separate confirmed details from pending findings.

Readers understand impact, confirmed facts, and what remains under investigation. The adaptation changes the presentation while retaining the substance that customers need.

Plain language and explicit status labels make the same evidence accessible. Audience adaptation should not erase uncertainty or introduce unsupported reassurance.

Future findings can be added without contradicting an earlier claim of certainty. The message becomes useful to customers without weakening transparency.

Incorrect options:

Add reassuring claims that are not in the incident record to reduce customer concern.

Unsupported reassurance changes factual content rather than adapting it. That approach cannot reliably adapt a verified technical output for customers without distorting facts or uncertainty.

The organization may make promises that the incident record cannot support. The task calls for the team to change language and structure while preserving evidence, impact, and unresolved points.

Remove every uncertain statement so the customer message appears fully resolved.

Deleting uncertainty creates a false impression that the incident is fully understood. It therefore fails to adapt a verified technical output for customers without distorting facts or uncertainty.

Later corrections can damage trust and confuse affected customers. The appropriate alternative is to change language and structure while preserving evidence, impact, and unresolved points.

Keep the engineering language unchanged because technical accuracy is the only quality criterion.

Engineering terminology can be accurate but inaccessible to the intended audience. This does not provide a sound way to adapt a verified technical output for customers without distorting facts or uncertainty.

Customers may not understand the practical impact or required action. A controlled workflow should change language and structure while preserving evidence, impact, and unresolved points.

questions.question: A project team must create a recovery plan using internal incident records and current external supplier information. Which TWO workflow choices BEST support a reliable plan?

options.label: A
options.text: Maintain approved internal records and recovery assumptions in a Project with clear instructions.

options.label: B
options.text: Use Research for current supplier developments, inspect citations, and reconcile findings with internal evidence during plan preparation.

options.label: C
options.text: Merge all sources automatically and accept the first plan without checking contradictions.

options.label: D
options.text: Rely solely on the Project knowledge because external supplier conditions cannot change after upload.

options.label: E
options.text: Use only public web information because internal records may complicate the analysis.

questions.explanation:
Correct options:

Maintain approved internal records and recovery assumptions in a Project with clear instructions.

The Project provides a controlled home for the incident records, assumptions, and recovery requirements. Repeated planning conversations begin from the same approved internal context.

Project instructions can define the recovery format, priorities, and decision boundaries. Stable organizational knowledge belongs in a maintained workspace.

The team reduces repeated setup while preserving governance over internal evidence. Outdated assumptions can be reviewed and updated before reuse.

Use Research for current supplier developments, inspect citations, and reconcile findings with internal evidence during plan preparation.

Research adds current supplier information that the internal records cannot provide. The team can identify recent disruptions, announcements, or capacity changes.

Current external claims require traceable sources and human inspection. Citation review and reconciliation expose conflicts between public developments and internal assumptions.

The plan gains current awareness without treating public sources as automatically authoritative. The final recovery action rests on verified evidence from both source categories.

Incorrect options:

Merge all sources automatically and accept the first plan without checking contradictions.

Automatic merging does not resolve contradictory dates, definitions, or evidence quality. The underlying requirement remains to combine stable internal context with current external evidence and validation.

The first plan can combine incompatible facts into a confident but unreliable recommendation. The stronger course is to use a Project for maintained internal knowledge and Research for current external developments.

Rely solely on the Project knowledge because external supplier conditions cannot change after upload.

Uploaded Project knowledge can become stale as supplier conditions change. That approach cannot reliably combine stable internal context with current external evidence and validation.

The plan may rely on outdated capacity or availability assumptions. The task calls for the team to use a Project for maintained internal knowledge and Research for current external developments.

Use only public web information because internal records may complicate the analysis.

Public information cannot replace organization-specific incident records and operational constraints. It therefore fails to combine stable internal context with current external evidence and validation.

The plan may ignore the actual failure history and internal dependencies. The appropriate alternative is to use a Project for maintained internal knowledge and Research for current external developments.

questions.question: A Project supports a quarterly reporting workflow used by several teams, but policies, owners, and data definitions change throughout the year. Which TWO maintenance practices are MOST appropriate?

options.label: A
options.text: Keep every prior policy active so Claude can choose the most relevant version.

options.label: B
options.text: Schedule quarterly reviews of Project instructions, knowledge files, connector scope, reporting assumptions, and policy changes.

options.label: C
options.text: Record ownership and version changes, then test representative outputs after each material update.

options.label: D
options.text: Update files silently without documenting what changed or who approved the revision.

options.label: E
options.text: Review the configuration only after a stakeholder reports an incorrect quarterly result.

questions.explanation:
Correct options:

Schedule quarterly reviews of Project instructions, knowledge files, connector scope, reporting assumptions, and policy changes.

Scheduled reviews prevent configuration from drifting away from current policies and definitions. Instructions, sources, connector scope, and assumptions are examined before the next reporting cycle.

A periodic cadence catches gradual changes that individual users may not notice. Reusable workflows require maintenance rather than one-time setup.

The team invests predictable effort instead of responding to avoidable failures. Outdated rules are removed before they affect stakeholder reports.

Record ownership and version changes, then test representative outputs after each material update.

Ownership and version records establish who changed the configuration and why. Representative testing confirms that the update produces the intended behavior.

Material changes should be traceable and validated. Post-change tests identify conflicts, retrieval problems, or formatting regressions.

The workflow can evolve without sacrificing reliability. Unapproved or ineffective revisions can be rolled back or corrected.

Incorrect options:

Keep every prior policy active so Claude can choose the most relevant version.

Keeping every old policy active makes authority ambiguous. This leaves the workflow unable to keep recurring configuration, sources, permissions, and assumptions current and accountable.

Claude can combine incompatible versions in a single report. The scenario instead requires the team to perform scheduled reviews and documented testing after material changes.

Update files silently without documenting what changed or who approved the revision.

Undocumented changes remove accountability and make later troubleshooting difficult. That approach cannot reliably keep recurring configuration, sources, permissions, and assumptions current and accountable.

The team cannot determine which revision caused a defect. The task calls for the team to perform scheduled reviews and documented testing after material changes.

Review the configuration only after a stakeholder reports an incorrect quarterly result.

Reactive review allows configuration problems to reach stakeholders before detection. It therefore fails to keep recurring configuration, sources, permissions, and assumptions current and accountable.

The quarterly report may already have influenced decisions. The appropriate alternative is to perform scheduled reviews and documented testing after material changes.

https://support.claude.com/en/articles/11176164-use-connectors-to-extend-claude-s-capabilities
