questions.question: A project manager asks Claude to compare six vendor proposals, score mandatory requirements, analyze trade-offs, and recommend finalists. Claude mixes eligibility failures with preference scores. What should the manager do?

options.label: A
options.text: Ask Claude to recommend finalists first, then create criteria that support the selected vendors afterward.

options.label: B
options.text: Combine all requirements into one overall score and accept the highest total even when mandatory eligibility failures remain unresolved.

options.label: C
options.text: Increase the score range so Claude can distinguish every proposal without changing the evaluation sequence.

options.label: D
options.text: Separate the work into eligibility screening, scored comparison, trade-off review, and a documented final recommendation checkpoint.

questions.explanation:
Correct option:

Separate the work into eligibility screening, scored comparison, trade-off review, and a documented final recommendation checkpoint.

The staged process checks mandatory eligibility before applying preference scores. Ineligible proposals cannot be rescued by strengths in optional categories.

Each checkpoint produces an inspectable intermediate result before the next analysis. Complex tasks become more reliable when dependencies are expressed as ordered steps.

The manager gains both efficiency and a defensible evaluation trail. The final recommendation remains tied to approved criteria rather than a blended score.

Incorrect options:

Ask Claude to recommend finalists first, then create criteria that support the selected vendors afterward.

Choosing finalists before evaluating them reverses the required decision sequence. That approach cannot reliably preserve the dependency between mandatory eligibility and comparative scoring.

The later criteria can become a justification exercise instead of an objective assessment. The task calls for the team to run ordered stages with checkpoints before recommending finalists.

Combine all requirements into one overall score and accept the highest total even when mandatory eligibility failures remain unresolved.

One overall score hides whether a vendor failed a mandatory condition. It therefore fails to preserve the dependency between mandatory eligibility and comparative scoring.

The recommendation may be mathematically convenient but procedurally invalid. The appropriate alternative is to run ordered stages with checkpoints before recommending finalists.

Increase the score range so Claude can distinguish every proposal without changing the evaluation sequence.

A larger numerical range does not separate pass-fail requirements from comparative preferences. This does not provide a sound way to preserve the dependency between mandatory eligibility and comparative scoring.

An ineligible vendor could still rank highly because optional strengths outweigh a mandatory failure. A controlled workflow should run ordered stages with checkpoints before recommending finalists.

https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/test-and-evaluate/strengthen-guardrails/increase-consistency

questions.question: A communications specialist uses Claude to draft a public apology. The draft accepts responsibility for facts that the investigation has not confirmed. Which action is MOST appropriate?

options.label: A
options.text: Remove every reference to impact so the organization avoids implying responsibility.

options.label: B
options.text: Publish the draft because accepting broad responsibility is always the most ethical response.

options.label: C
options.text: Ask Claude to make the unconfirmed facts sound less specific while preserving them as unsupported admissions.

options.label: D
options.text: Revise the message to distinguish confirmed facts, acknowledged impact, commitments, and unresolved investigation findings.

questions.explanation:
Correct option:

Revise the message to distinguish confirmed facts, acknowledged impact, commitments, and unresolved investigation findings.

The revision preserves accountability for known impact while remaining accurate about unresolved facts. The public receives a clear statement of what is known, what is being investigated, and what the organization will do.

Ethical communication requires both transparency and factual discipline. Explicit categories prevent uncertainty from being converted into an unsupported admission.

The message can be sincere without prejudging the investigation. Later findings are less likely to contradict the public statement.

Incorrect options:

Remove every reference to impact so the organization avoids implying responsibility.

Removing acknowledged impact avoids meaningful accountability. This leaves the workflow unable to communicate transparently without making unsupported admissions or hiding acknowledged impact.

The apology can appear evasive and fail to address harm already known. The scenario instead requires the team to separate confirmed facts, impact, commitments, and unresolved findings.

Publish the draft because accepting broad responsibility is always the most ethical response.

Broad responsibility for unconfirmed facts can create a false public record. As a result, the option does not communicate transparently without making unsupported admissions or hiding acknowledged impact.

The message may mislead affected people and complicate the investigation. A dependable response would separate confirmed facts, impact, commitments, and unresolved findings.

Ask Claude to make the unconfirmed facts sound less specific while preserving them as unsupported admissions.

Vaguer wording does not make an unsupported admission accurate. The underlying requirement remains to communicate transparently without making unsupported admissions or hiding acknowledged impact.

The organization still accepts facts that have not been established. The stronger course is to separate confirmed facts, impact, commitments, and unresolved findings.

questions.question: A long policy-analysis chat contains several superseded drafts, unrelated questions, and contradictory assumptions. Claude begins blending old and current rules. Which context-management decision is BEST?

options.label: A
options.text: Continue in the same chat because more historical context always improves reasoning.

options.label: B
options.text: Summarize the approved rules and open issues, start a focused conversation, and include only relevant source material.

options.label: C
options.text: Enable personalization preferences and assume they will resolve task-specific policy contradictions.

options.label: D
options.text: Delete all source documents and rely on Claude's recollection instead of preserving the approved evidence and decisions for review.

questions.explanation:
Correct option:

Summarize the approved rules and open issues, start a focused conversation, and include only relevant source material.

The focused conversation removes superseded drafts and unrelated material from the active task context. Claude can reason from the approved rules and clearly identified open issues.

A current-state summary establishes which decisions and sources are authoritative. More context is not always better when it contains contradictions or irrelevant history.

The user preserves useful conclusions without carrying the entire noisy conversation forward. Relevant documents remain available for verification.

Incorrect options:

Continue in the same chat because more historical context always improves reasoning.

Additional conflicting history increases rather than reduces the ambiguity Claude must resolve. That approach cannot reliably reduce conflicting context while preserving the current policy state and evidence.

Old rules can continue appearing in supposedly current analysis. The task calls for the team to move to focused context containing an approved summary and relevant sources.

Enable personalization preferences and assume they will resolve task-specific policy contradictions.

Personalization controls general preferences and does not adjudicate contradictory policy content. This does not provide a sound way to reduce conflicting context while preserving the current policy state and evidence.

The task remains confused even if tone or style preferences are remembered. A controlled workflow should move to focused context containing an approved summary and relevant sources.

Delete all source documents and rely on Claude's recollection instead of preserving the approved evidence and decisions for review.

Removing the source documents eliminates the evidence needed to verify the approved rules. This leaves the workflow unable to reduce conflicting context while preserving the current policy state and evidence.

Claude may reconstruct details inaccurately from conversational context. The scenario instead requires the team to move to focused context containing an approved summary and relevant sources.

questions.question: A project manager has three Claude-generated status summaries with different emphasis and wording. Which TWO actions BEST support an objective selection for the steering committee?

options.label: A
options.text: Score each summary against agreed criteria for accuracy, decision relevance, clarity, and unresolved risks.

options.label: B
options.text: Select the version that sounds most confident, even if its claims and risks remain unverified.

options.label: C
options.text: Choose the longest summary because it is most likely to contain all important information.

options.label: D
options.text: Combine all three drafts automatically, even when they contain conflicting facts or priorities.

options.label: E
options.text: Compare every material statement with the underlying project records before selecting or combining drafts.

questions.explanation:
Correct options:

Score each summary against agreed criteria for accuracy, decision relevance, clarity, and unresolved risks.

The scoring method turns subjective preference into a transparent comparison. Each draft is judged on the qualities the steering committee actually needs.

Accuracy, relevance, clarity, and risk coverage expose different strengths and defects. Multiple outputs should be compared against defined success criteria.

The manager can select or combine content without relying on style alone. The final summary reflects the committee's decision needs rather than the writer's personal preference.

Compare every material statement with the underlying project records before selecting or combining drafts.

Record-level validation establishes which statements are factually dependable. Conflicts between drafts can be resolved before any wording is selected.

Comparison does not remove the need to verify consequential content. The project records provide an independent reference for status, dates, and risks.

The manager retains useful phrasing while rejecting unsupported claims. The steering committee receives a coherent summary built from verified information.

Incorrect options:

Select the version that sounds most confident, even if its claims and risks remain unverified.

Confidence is a presentation characteristic rather than evidence quality. As a result, the option does not select or combine outputs using explicit quality criteria and verified facts.

A decisive tone can make incorrect status information more persuasive. A dependable response would evaluate drafts against agreed criteria and validate material statements.

Choose the longest summary because it is most likely to contain all important information.

Length is not a reliable measure of completeness, relevance, or accuracy. The underlying requirement remains to select or combine outputs using explicit quality criteria and verified facts.

The longest version may include unnecessary detail while missing a critical risk. The stronger course is to evaluate drafts against agreed criteria and validate material statements.

Combine all three drafts automatically, even when they contain conflicting facts or priorities.

Automatic combination can preserve contradictions and duplicate low-value content. That approach cannot reliably select or combine outputs using explicit quality criteria and verified facts.

The committee may receive a longer document with unresolved factual conflicts. The task calls for the team to evaluate drafts against agreed criteria and validate material statements.

questions.question: A Cowork workflow can edit shared files and send draft updates through connected organizational tools during monthly operations. Which TWO controls BEST support responsible organizational use?

options.label: A
options.text: Require explicit approval before Claude sends, deletes, shares, or makes any other consequential change externally.

options.label: B
options.text: Grant unrestricted tool access so Claude can recover from missing context independently.

options.label: C
options.text: Allow instructions found inside connected documents to override the approved workflow plan.

options.label: D
options.text: Disable the activity review because detailed logs can slow operational decisions.

options.label: E
options.text: Scope tools and folders to the task, then test the workflow on copies before using live records.

questions.explanation:
Correct options:

Require explicit approval before Claude sends, deletes, shares, or makes any other consequential change externally.

Claude can prepare work without silently completing a consequential step. Approval keeps accountable users in control of actions that affect people, data, or external communications.

Users can inspect the proposed change and stop or revise it before execution. Delegated workflows should preserve confirmation boundaries for meaningful actions.

Mistakes do not automatically become sent messages, deletions, or shared files. The workflow remains productive while retaining organizational accountability.

Scope tools and folders to the task, then test the workflow on copies before using live records.

Scoped access and copy-based testing reduce both exposure and operational impact. The workflow proves its behavior on representative material before touching live records.

Limited folders constrain what Claude can access if the workflow behaves unexpectedly. Permissions and testing should be proportional to the task.

The team gains confidence without granting broad standing access. Irreplaceable files and unrelated systems remain protected.

Incorrect options:

Grant unrestricted tool access so Claude can recover from missing context independently.

Unrestricted access exceeds the task need and increases the potential impact of error or malicious content. As a result, the option does not control consequential actions, permissions, and untrusted workflow behavior.

The workflow can reach unrelated tools and sensitive information. A dependable response would require approval, least-needed access, and safe testing before live use.

Allow instructions found inside connected documents to override the approved workflow plan.

Connected documents can contain untrusted or conflicting instructions. The underlying requirement remains to control consequential actions, permissions, and untrusted workflow behavior.

Allowing them to override the approved plan can redirect the workflow toward unsafe actions. The stronger course is to require approval, least-needed access, and safe testing before live use.

Disable the activity review because detailed logs can slow operational decisions.

Activity review supports accountability and troubleshooting rather than being an unnecessary delay. That approach cannot reliably control consequential actions, permissions, and untrusted workflow behavior.

Removing it makes actions harder to explain or investigate. The task calls for the team to require approval, least-needed access, and safe testing before live use.

References:

https://support.claude.com/en/articles/11176164-use-connectors-to-extend-claude-s-capabilities

questions.question: An education professional asks Claude to create beginner exercises for new adult learners, but the output assumes advanced terminology and prior experience. Which revision is MOST appropriate?

options.label: A
options.text: Request twice as many exercises so some examples will probably match the intended difficulty.

options.label: B
options.text: Ask Claude to make the exercises easier without identifying what beginners already know.

options.label: C
options.text: Keep the exercises unchanged and add a glossary containing every advanced term afterward.

options.label: D
options.text: Define the learner prerequisites, prohibited jargon, target difficulty, and a sample exercise at the expected level.

questions.explanation:
Correct option:

Define the learner prerequisites, prohibited jargon, target difficulty, and a sample exercise at the expected level.

The revision identifies the instructional gap that caused Claude to overestimate learner knowledge. Claude can design tasks that begin from the stated prerequisites rather than inferred expertise.

The sample gives Claude a concrete reference for acceptable challenge and terminology. Specific constraints and representative examples improve control over difficulty and style.

The educator corrects the cause instead of editing every exercise afterward. The resulting activities remain accessible without oversimplifying the learning objective.

Incorrect options:

Request twice as many exercises so some examples will probably match the intended difficulty.

Increasing volume does not improve alignment with the learner profile. That approach cannot reliably align exercises with the learners' actual starting knowledge and target difficulty.

The educator receives more material to review without a reliable increase in suitability. The task calls for the team to revise the prompt with explicit prerequisites, language limits, difficulty, and an example.

Ask Claude to make the exercises easier without identifying what beginners already know.

The word easier does not define prerequisite knowledge, acceptable terminology, or target challenge. It therefore fails to align exercises with the learners' actual starting knowledge and target difficulty.

Claude may simplify surface wording while preserving advanced concepts. The appropriate alternative is to revise the prompt with explicit prerequisites, language limits, difficulty, and an example.

Keep the exercises unchanged and add a glossary containing every advanced term afterward.

A glossary explains jargon but does not redesign exercises that require advanced prior knowledge. This does not provide a sound way to align exercises with the learners' actual starting knowledge and target difficulty.

Beginners can still face tasks they are not prepared to complete. A controlled workflow should revise the prompt with explicit prerequisites, language limits, difficulty, and an example.

References:

https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/prompt-engineering/claude-prompting-best-practices

https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/test-and-evaluate/strengthen-guardrails/increase-consistency

questions.question: A consultant must investigate a recent regulatory development across official notices, industry responses, and current reporting, then provide traceable findings. Which Claude capability is MOST appropriate?

options.label: A
options.text: Use a Project containing last year's regulatory files and assume they remain accurate for the new development.

options.label: B
options.text: Use an Artifact because a standalone deliverable automatically gathers current evidence.

options.label: C
options.text: Use memory to retrieve public developments that were never discussed in previous conversations.

options.label: D
options.text: Use Research to investigate multiple current sources and return findings with citations for inspection.

questions.explanation:
Correct option:

Use Research to investigate multiple current sources and return findings with citations for inspection.

Research is designed to investigate a question across multiple current sources. The consultant receives a synthesized view with citations that can be inspected.

Feature selection should reflect whether the task requires current external evidence. Research can gather official notices, industry material, and reporting within one investigation.

The consultant gains breadth and traceability without manually assembling every source. Citations allow the findings to be validated before client use.

Incorrect options:

Use a Project containing last year's regulatory files and assume they remain accurate for the new development.

Last year's files cannot establish what changed in a recent regulatory development. This leaves the workflow unable to perform current multi-source external investigation with traceable evidence.

The consultant may provide outdated requirements or miss the current effective date. The scenario instead requires the team to use Research and inspect its cited sources.

Use an Artifact because a standalone deliverable automatically gathers current evidence.

An Artifact is an output surface and does not automatically perform external investigation. As a result, the option does not perform current multi-source external investigation with traceable evidence.

The deliverable may be well presented but unsupported by current evidence. A dependable response would use Research and inspect its cited sources.

Use memory to retrieve public developments that were never discussed in previous conversations.

Memory builds on prior context rather than discovering public information that was never provided. The underlying requirement remains to perform current multi-source external investigation with traceable evidence.

The resulting answer can be incomplete or based on stale general knowledge. The stronger course is to use Research and inspect its cited sources.

References:

https://support.claude.com/en/articles/11088861-use-research-on-claude

https://support.claude.com/en/articles/11095361-when-should-i-use-web-search-extended-thinking-and-research

questions.question: A Project instructs Claude to be concise, include full evidence, never exceed one page, and explain every uncertainty in detail. Outputs are inconsistent. What should the owner do?

options.label: A
options.text: Keep the rules unchanged and switch models whenever an output misses a requirement.

options.label: B
options.text: Delete all Project instructions and rely on users to communicate every requirement independently.

options.label: C
options.text: Prioritize the instructions, resolve conflicts, and define when evidence depth or the one-page limit takes precedence.

options.label: D
options.text: Add more conflicting instructions and let Claude decide which requirements to prioritize in each response without owner guidance.

questions.explanation:
Correct option:

Prioritize the instructions, resolve conflicts, and define when evidence depth or the one-page limit takes precedence.

The revision acknowledges that full evidence, detailed uncertainty, concision, and a fixed page limit can conflict. Claude receives a clear rule for handling trade-offs instead of guessing.

Instructions should be internally consistent and prioritized. Conditional guidance defines when completeness outweighs brevity or when a summary should link to detail.

The Project retains useful standards while reducing unpredictable compromises. Users can review whether each output followed the intended priority.

Incorrect options:

Keep the rules unchanged and switch models whenever an output misses a requirement.

A model change does not repair contradictory Project instructions. That approach cannot reliably resolve contradictory durable instructions that cannot always be satisfied together.

The same impossible trade-off can reappear with a different model. The task calls for the team to clarify priorities and conditional rules within the Project.

Delete all Project instructions and rely on users to communicate every requirement independently.

Removing all shared guidance transfers consistency problems to individual users. It therefore fails to resolve contradictory durable instructions that cannot always be satisfied together.

Each conversation can interpret the workflow differently. The appropriate alternative is to clarify priorities and conditional rules within the Project.

Add more conflicting instructions and let Claude decide which requirements to prioritize in each response without owner guidance.

Additional conflicting rules increase ambiguity rather than resolving it. This leaves the workflow unable to resolve contradictory durable instructions that cannot always be satisfied together.

Outputs can become even less predictable across similar requests. The scenario instead requires the team to clarify priorities and conditional rules within the Project.

https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/prompt-engineering/claude-prompting-best-practices

https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/test-and-evaluate/strengthen-guardrails/increase-consistency

questions.question: A business analyst asks Claude to summarize quarterly performance from an uploaded spreadsheet. The narrative cites several percentages that do not match the source cells. What should the analyst do FIRST?

options.label: A
options.text: Keep the narrative because the overall business direction appears reasonable despite calculation differences.

options.label: B
options.text: Ask Claude to make the percentages internally consistent without reopening the uploaded spreadsheet.

options.label: C
options.text: Trace each material percentage to the relevant spreadsheet values and recalculate the figures before using the narrative.

options.label: D
options.text: Round every percentage to a whole number so small discrepancies become less visible.

questions.explanation:
Correct option:

Trace each material percentage to the relevant spreadsheet values and recalculate the figures before using the narrative.

Calculation or interpretation errors can be identified before the summary is distributed. The analyst checks the disputed percentages against the evidence that is supposed to support them.

Recalculation distinguishes a source-data issue from a generation error. Claude's output should be treated as a draft that requires verification for material facts.

Decision makers receive figures that can be reproduced from the spreadsheet. This targeted review focuses effort on claims that could change the business interpretation.

Incorrect options:

Keep the narrative because the overall business direction appears reasonable despite calculation differences.

A plausible direction is not sufficient when the stated figures are wrong. This leaves the workflow unable to verify that material numerical claims match the underlying source data.

Stakeholders may make decisions based on unsupported magnitudes or trends. The scenario instead requires the team to trace claims to source cells and independently recalculate them.

Ask Claude to make the percentages internally consistent without reopening the uploaded spreadsheet.

Internal consistency does not prove that the percentages match the spreadsheet. As a result, the option does not verify that material numerical claims match the underlying source data.

Claude could produce a coherent set of incorrect numbers. A dependable response would trace claims to source cells and independently recalculate them.

Round every percentage to a whole number so small discrepancies become less visible.

Rounding changes presentation rather than validating the calculations. That approach cannot reliably verify that material numerical claims match the underlying source data.

A material error can remain hidden behind simplified formatting. The task calls for the team to trace claims to source cells and independently recalculate them.

questions.question: A business analysis workflow suddenly produces outdated competitor profiles. Prompts are unchanged, but the Project contains old reports and no current research step. What should the team diagnose FIRST?

options.label: A
options.text: Whether stale Project knowledge and the missing current-research step are driving the outdated profiles.

options.label: B
options.text: Whether the response font and heading hierarchy changed during the last month.

options.label: C
options.text: Whether Claude should be instructed to sound more confident about the existing profiles.

options.label: D
options.text: Whether adding more historical reports will increase the chance of retrieving current information.

questions.explanation:
Correct option:

Whether stale Project knowledge and the missing current-research step are driving the outdated profiles.

The source configuration explains why unchanged prompts now return outdated competitor information. The team can separate stale internal knowledge from the need for current external evidence.

Workflow quality depends on source freshness as well as prompt wording. Project review and current research address both stable and changing information needs.

The team fixes the evidence path rather than rewriting a prompt that already worked. Future profiles include a defined currency check.

Incorrect options:

Whether the response font and heading hierarchy changed during the last month.

Formatting changes do not explain why competitor facts are outdated. It therefore fails to identify a source-freshness and workflow-design cause rather than a language problem.

The team may restyle the same stale content. The appropriate alternative is to review stale knowledge and add an appropriate current research step.

Whether Claude should be instructed to sound more confident about the existing profiles.

Confidence affects tone and can make outdated claims more persuasive. This does not provide a sound way to identify a source-freshness and workflow-design cause rather than a language problem.

The evidence problem remains unresolved. A controlled workflow should review stale knowledge and add an appropriate current research step.

Whether adding more historical reports will increase the chance of retrieving current information.

Additional historical reports increase stale material rather than providing current developments. This leaves the workflow unable to identify a source-freshness and workflow-design cause rather than a language problem.

Retrieval can become noisier and less authoritative. The scenario instead requires the team to review stale knowledge and add an appropriate current research step.

options.label: C
options.text: Follow the policy and keep the unreleased results out of Claude until an approved workflow or exception is authorized.

options.label: D
options.text: Proceed in a private Project because privacy settings automatically override organizational policy.

Follow the policy and keep the unreleased results out of Claude until an approved workflow or exception is authorized.

Use the results because internal presentations are exempt from every organizational data restriction under the policy.

questions.question: An educator uses Claude Research to prepare guidance on a recently changed admissions policy. Which TWO validation actions are MOST appropriate before sharing the guidance with students?

options.label: A
options.text: Compare consequential claims with another authoritative source and document any remaining uncertainty.

options.label: B
options.text: Ask Claude to rewrite uncertain claims in more definitive language for student clarity.

options.label: C
options.text: Rely on the most detailed secondary article because longer explanations are usually more accurate.

options.label: D
options.text: Confirm the effective date and requirements in the institution's current official policy materials before sharing the guidance.

options.label: E
options.text: Publish the draft immediately because Research already provides citations and a polished synthesis.

questions.explanation:
Correct options:

Compare consequential claims with another authoritative source and document any remaining uncertainty.

Independent authoritative corroboration tests whether the material claims are consistently supported. Conflicts or gaps become visible before the guidance influences student choices.

Consequential claims deserve stronger evidence than a single synthesis path. Documented uncertainty distinguishes verified requirements from issues still needing confirmation.

The guidance remains useful while avoiding false certainty. Students and advisers know which points require further checking.

Confirm the effective date and requirements in the institution's current official policy materials before sharing the guidance.

The institution's current official materials are the primary authority for its own admissions policy. The educator can confirm dates, eligibility rules, and exceptions at the source.

Fast-changing guidance should be checked for currency and authority. The effective date prevents an older rule from being presented as current.

The action provides strong validation without relying on secondary interpretation. Students receive requirements that match the institution's published policy.

Incorrect options:

Ask Claude to rewrite uncertain claims in more definitive language for student clarity.

Definitive wording changes tone rather than resolving uncertainty. As a result, the option does not confirm that fast-changing policy claims are current, authoritative, and sufficiently supported.

Students may act confidently on a claim that remains unverified. A dependable response would verify official materials, corroborate material claims, and disclose unresolved uncertainty.

Rely on the most detailed secondary article because longer explanations are usually more accurate.

Length and detail do not establish authority or currency. The underlying requirement remains to confirm that fast-changing policy claims are current, authoritative, and sufficiently supported.

A comprehensive secondary article can still describe an outdated policy. The stronger course is to verify official materials, corroborate material claims, and disclose unresolved uncertainty.

Publish the draft immediately because Research already provides citations and a polished synthesis.

Research citations support inspection but do not complete the educator's validation responsibility. It therefore fails to confirm that fast-changing policy claims are current, authoritative, and sufficiently supported.

An outdated or misinterpreted source can pass directly to students. The appropriate alternative is to verify official materials, corroborate material claims, and disclose unresolved uncertainty.

questions.question: A marketing associate needs fresh campaign concepts during an ideation session and evidence-backed market claims for the final brief. Which prompting strategy BEST matches the two task types?

options.label: A
options.text: Use broad divergent brainstorming for concepts, then switch to sourced research and explicit validation for factual claims.

options.label: B
options.text: Generate market claims from Claude's existing knowledge and add sources only after the campaign has already launched publicly worldwide.

options.label: C
options.text: Require citations during the first idea-generation step and reject every concept lacking published evidence.

options.label: D
options.text: Use a single highly constrained prompt so creativity and factual validation occur simultaneously.

questions.explanation:
Correct option:

Use broad divergent brainstorming for concepts, then switch to sourced research and explicit validation for factual claims.

The associate can generate varied concepts without treating imaginative ideas as verified market facts. The strategy gives creative exploration and factual research different objectives and constraints.

The later research stage introduces sources and validation when factual claims become consequential. Prompting should reflect whether a task requires divergence, evidence, or both.

Unsupported claims are identified before they enter campaign materials. This preserves creativity while maintaining accuracy before external use.

Incorrect options:

Generate market claims from Claude's existing knowledge and add sources only after the campaign has already launched publicly worldwide.

Claude's existing knowledge cannot establish that fast-changing market claims are current and accurate. It therefore fails to use different interaction strategies for creative exploration and factual validation.

Adding sources after launch leaves the campaign exposed to avoidable misinformation. The appropriate alternative is to separate divergent ideation from sourced research and claim verification.

Require citations during the first idea-generation step and reject every concept lacking published evidence.

Requiring evidence for every early concept constrains brainstorming before ideas have been developed. This does not provide a sound way to use different interaction strategies for creative exploration and factual validation.

Potentially useful creative directions may be discarded for lacking immediate published support. A controlled workflow should separate divergent ideation from sourced research and claim verification.

Use a single highly constrained prompt so creativity and factual validation occur simultaneously.

One tightly constrained prompt combines objectives that benefit from different evaluation standards. This leaves the workflow unable to use different interaction strategies for creative exploration and factual validation.

The result may be neither genuinely creative nor adequately verified. The scenario instead requires the team to separate divergent ideation from sourced research and claim verification.

questions.question: A marketing team creates a Project for campaign work, but outputs vary by user and sometimes violate brand rules. Which configuration improvement is MOST appropriate?

options.label: A
options.text: Ask each user to remember the brand rules and correct Claude after every violation.

options.label: B
options.text: Add clear Project instructions covering audience, brand voice, prohibited claims, source priorities, review steps, and output formats.

options.label: C
options.text: Place the brand rules only in one old chat and assume every Project conversation will automatically inherit them.

options.label: D
options.text: Upload more unrelated campaign files so Claude has a larger knowledge base.

questions.explanation:
Correct option:

Add clear Project instructions covering audience, brand voice, prohibited claims, source priorities, review steps, and output formats.

The Project instructions create a shared behavioral standard for recurring campaign work. Users receive outputs shaped by the same audience, voice, claim, source, and review requirements.

Durable instructions are appropriate for guidance that should apply across Project conversations. Explicit formats and prohibited claims reduce reliance on individual user memory.

The team improves consistency without repeating the full brand brief in every prompt. Review steps remain part of the workflow rather than an informal afterthought.

Incorrect options:

Ask each user to remember the brand rules and correct Claude after every violation.

Individual correction makes consistency depend on each user's memory and diligence. This leaves the workflow unable to make recurring campaign behavior consistent across Project conversations and users.

The same violations can recur across conversations and team members. The scenario instead requires the team to define durable Project instructions that state the operating rules.

Place the brand rules only in one old chat and assume every Project conversation will automatically inherit them.

A single chat is not a reliable Project-wide instruction source. The underlying requirement remains to make recurring campaign behavior consistent across Project conversations and users.

New conversations may not receive the intended brand constraints. The stronger course is to define durable Project instructions that state the operating rules.

Upload more unrelated campaign files so Claude has a larger knowledge base.

Additional files do not resolve missing or unclear behavioral instructions. That approach cannot reliably make recurring campaign behavior consistent across Project conversations and users.

Irrelevant material can increase retrieval noise and create conflicting examples. The task calls for the team to define durable Project instructions that state the operating rules.

questions.question: A company processes routine summaries daily but occasionally receives complex strategic analyses with ambiguous evidence and significant consequences. Which TWO model-selection practices BEST balance quality, speed, and cost?

options.label: A
options.text: Route routine, well-tested summaries to a faster lower-cost model that satisfies the team's defined quality criteria.

options.label: B
options.text: Use the fastest model for every task and accept reduced analysis quality on consequential work.

options.label: C
options.text: Use a stronger reasoning model for complex high-consequence analyses and retain human review.

options.label: D
options.text: Use the strongest model for every task so the workflow never needs routing criteria.

options.label: E
options.text: Change models randomly so each business unit experiences an equal mix of capabilities.

questions.explanation:
Correct options:

Route routine, well-tested summaries to a faster lower-cost model that satisfies the team's defined quality criteria.

The routing rule aligns routine work with a model that has already met explicit quality criteria. Daily summaries can be produced quickly and economically without assuming that lower cost means acceptable quality.

Model selection should be based on demonstrated task requirements. Testing defines when the faster model is sufficient and when escalation is needed.

The company reduces recurring cost while preserving consistent service. Quality monitoring can detect when the routine workload changes.

Use a stronger reasoning model for complex high-consequence analyses and retain human review.

Complex and consequential analyses justify stronger reasoning capability and deeper oversight. Ambiguous evidence receives more careful synthesis before it influences important decisions.

The model supports analysis while accountable reviewers challenge assumptions and conclusions. Capability and human review should increase with task complexity and consequence.

Higher cost is concentrated where it can materially improve decision quality. The workflow does not delegate final judgment to the model.

Incorrect options:

Use the fastest model for every task and accept reduced analysis quality on consequential work.

Uniform use of the fastest model prioritizes efficiency over the stated quality needs of consequential analysis. It therefore fails to match different task classes to appropriate capability and review levels.

Important decisions may be based on shallow or incomplete reasoning. The appropriate alternative is to route routine work efficiently and reserve stronger reasoning for complex consequential analysis.

Use the strongest model for every task so the workflow never needs routing criteria.

Using the strongest model everywhere ignores meaningful differences between routine and complex work. This leaves the workflow unable to match different task classes to appropriate capability and review levels.

The company pays higher cost and latency even when a tested faster model is sufficient. The scenario instead requires the team to route routine work efficiently and reserve stronger reasoning for complex consequential analysis.

Change models randomly so each business unit experiences an equal mix of capabilities.

Random assignment is unrelated to task complexity, quality, or cost objectives. As a result, the option does not match different task classes to appropriate capability and review levels.

Performance becomes inconsistent and difficult to evaluate or govern. A dependable response would route routine work efficiently and reserve stronger reasoning for complex consequential analysis.

questions.question: An operations team spends hours copying status updates between systems, reconciling duplicate fields, and chasing missing approvals. Which Claude-assisted analysis should the team perform before redesigning the workflow?

options.label: A
options.text: Automate the final email first because visible outputs create the fastest impression of progress.

options.label: B
options.text: Map each step, handoff, delay, duplicate entry, decision, and approval to identify the highest-value improvement opportunities.

options.label: C
options.text: Remove every approval step before determining which controls are mandatory.

options.label: D
options.text: Ask Claude to invent a completely new process without examining current users or failure points.

questions.explanation:
Correct option:

Map each step, handoff, delay, duplicate entry, decision, and approval to identify the highest-value improvement opportunities.

The process map reveals where effort, delay, and errors accumulate across the workflow. The team can distinguish necessary controls from avoidable manual steps.

Claude can help structure the map and analyze patterns across the documented process. Workflow improvement should be based on observed handoffs and failure points.

The team focuses redesign effort where it can produce measurable value. Mandatory approvals remain visible rather than being removed accidentally.

Incorrect options:

Automate the final email first because visible outputs create the fastest impression of progress.

Automating the final email addresses presentation rather than the underlying delays and duplication. This leaves the workflow unable to identify where delay, duplication, and control needs occur in the existing workflow.

The workflow may look faster while retaining most of its manual burden. The scenario instead requires the team to map the current process and prioritize redesign opportunities.

Remove every approval step before determining which controls are mandatory.

Approvals may protect financial, compliance, or operational decisions. The underlying requirement remains to identify where delay, duplication, and control needs occur in the existing workflow.

Removing them before analysis can create unacceptable control gaps. The stronger course is to map the current process and prioritize redesign opportunities.

Ask Claude to invent a completely new process without examining current users or failure points.

A design created without current users and failure points may solve the wrong problem. That approach cannot reliably identify where delay, duplication, and control needs occur in the existing workflow.

The new process can introduce different bottlenecks or omit required work. The task calls for the team to map the current process and prioritize redesign opportunities.

questions.question: A user wants to iteratively edit a process map, preserve versions, and share the finished visual with colleagues. Which Claude output approach is MOST appropriate?

options.label: A
options.text: Keep the entire process map embedded in a long conversational paragraph.

options.label: B
options.text: Create the process map as an Artifact so it can be viewed, refined, and shared separately from the chat.

options.label: C
options.text: Use Research because every editable visual deliverable requires external web sources.

options.label: D
options.text: Store only the final map description in memory and recreate the visual from scratch whenever colleagues need it.

questions.explanation:
Correct option:

Create the process map as an Artifact so it can be viewed, refined, and shared separately from the chat.

An Artifact gives the process map a dedicated workspace separate from the conversational discussion. The user can inspect, refine, and share the visual as a coherent deliverable.

Output format should match how the result will be used after generation. The Artifact surface supports iterative work on content intended to stand on its own.

The chat remains available for instructions while the map stays easy to review. Colleagues receive the intended deliverable rather than a transcript they must reconstruct.

Incorrect options:

Keep the entire process map embedded in a long conversational paragraph.

A conversational paragraph is a poor surface for an editable visual process map. That approach cannot reliably choose an editable and shareable output surface for a standalone visual deliverable.

Reviewers must interpret prose instead of working with the actual deliverable. The task calls for the team to use an Artifact rather than burying the deliverable in conversation.

Use Research because every editable visual deliverable requires external web sources.

Research addresses sourced investigation rather than the need for an editable output surface. This does not provide a sound way to choose an editable and shareable output surface for a standalone visual deliverable.

It adds unnecessary workflow complexity without improving the visual deliverable. A controlled workflow should use an Artifact rather than burying the deliverable in conversation.

Store only the final map description in memory and recreate the visual from scratch whenever colleagues need it.

Memory is intended for persistent context and preferences, not as storage for a versioned visual. This leaves the workflow unable to choose an editable and shareable output surface for a standalone visual deliverable.

Recreation can produce a different map and lose prior edits. The scenario instead requires the team to use an Artifact rather than burying the deliverable in conversation.

questions.question: Claude creates lesson summaries that are accurate but too abstract for students preparing for an introductory assessment. The educator can identify specific confusing passages. Which feedback method is BEST?

options.label: A
options.text: Add more source chapters without explaining the level or style students need.

options.label: B
options.text: Say only that the summaries are bad and ask Claude to try harder without identifying the abstract passages or desired style.

options.label: C
options.text: Point to the confusing passages, explain why they are difficult, and provide an example of the desired concrete explanation.

options.label: D
options.text: Request a completely different subject so Claude forgets the previous abstraction problem.

questions.explanation:
Correct option:

Point to the confusing passages, explain why they are difficult, and provide an example of the desired concrete explanation.

The feedback connects a specific defect with a concrete replacement pattern. Claude can revise the exact passages and generalize the preferred level to similar sections.

The example defines what concrete explanation means for this learner group. Actionable feedback is more effective than a broad quality complaint.

The educator preserves accurate content while improving accessibility. Later revisions can be checked against the same example.

Incorrect options:

Add more source chapters without explaining the level or style students need.

Additional content does not define the students' required explanation level. This leaves the workflow unable to correct a known output defect through targeted, actionable feedback.

The summaries may become longer without becoming more concrete. The scenario instead requires the team to identify examples of the problem and demonstrate the desired explanation style.

Say only that the summaries are bad and ask Claude to try harder without identifying the abstract passages or desired style.

The word bad does not identify what should change or what success looks like. As a result, the option does not correct a known output defect through targeted, actionable feedback.

Claude may alter tone, length, or structure while remaining abstract. A dependable response would identify examples of the problem and demonstrate the desired explanation style.

Request a completely different subject so Claude forgets the previous abstraction problem.

Changing subjects avoids rather than solves the feedback problem. That approach cannot reliably correct a known output defect through targeted, actionable feedback.

The next lesson can reproduce the same abstraction defect. The task calls for the team to identify examples of the problem and demonstrate the desired explanation style.

questions.domain: Domain 6: Governance, Risk, and Responsible Use
questions.question: A communications team wants Claude to generate routine internal event reminders from approved details. The messages contain no sensitive data and follow an existing approval process. Which use is MOST appropriate?

options.label: A
options.text: Send every generated reminder externally because the source details were approved, without applying the normal communication review process.

options.label: B
options.text: Prohibit the use because every AI-assisted message is automatically a high-risk activity.

options.label: C
options.text: Use Claude to draft the reminders within approved templates, then follow the normal communication review process.

options.label: D
options.text: Allow Claude to invent event details whenever the approved information appears incomplete.

questions.explanation:
Correct option:

Use Claude to draft the reminders within approved templates, then follow the normal communication review process.

The task is bounded, repetitive, and based on approved non-sensitive information. Claude can reduce drafting effort without changing the underlying event decisions.

Appropriate use depends on task risk, data sensitivity, and retained oversight. Approved templates and normal review define the acceptable operating boundary.

The team gains efficiency without weakening communication controls. Incorrect dates or wording can be corrected before distribution.

Incorrect options:

Send every generated reminder externally because the source details were approved, without applying the normal communication review process.

Approved source facts do not guarantee that every generated message is correct or appropriate. That approach cannot reliably identify a suitable low-risk productivity use while preserving normal controls.

Errors can be distributed without the normal checkpoint. The task calls for the team to use Claude for bounded drafting from approved facts with routine review.

Prohibit the use because every AI-assisted message is automatically a high-risk activity.

The scenario does not make every AI-assisted reminder inherently high risk. It therefore fails to identify a suitable low-risk productivity use while preserving normal controls.

A blanket ban removes a suitable productivity use without addressing any specific harm. The appropriate alternative is to use Claude for bounded drafting from approved facts with routine review.

Allow Claude to invent event details whenever the approved information appears incomplete.

Invented details exceed the approved source information. This leaves the workflow unable to identify a suitable low-risk productivity use while preserving normal controls.

Recipients may receive incorrect dates, locations, or requirements. The scenario instead requires the team to use Claude for bounded drafting from approved facts with routine review.

questions.question: A team asks Claude to create onboarding guidance from several policy files, but each draft emphasizes different rules and omits required sections. Which prompt change is MOST appropriate?

options.label: A
options.text: State the audience, required sections, approved policy sources, exclusions, and final format before requesting the guide.

options.label: B
options.text: Tell Claude that accuracy is essential while leaving the required content and evidence unspecified.

options.label: C
options.text: Ask Claude to make the next draft more professional without adding any further task details.

options.label: D
options.text: Request several unrelated versions and select whichever one appears most complete at first glance.

questions.explanation:
Correct option:

State the audience, required sections, approved policy sources, exclusions, and final format before requesting the guide.

The revised prompt gives Claude the missing operational context and a concrete definition of the deliverable. It makes the required policies, sections, and exclusions visible before generation begins.

Claude can check each section against the same stated requirements. Clear instructions and explicit output constraints improve consistency.

The action improves reliability without multiplying unnecessary drafts. It also keeps unsupported policies outside the final guide.

Incorrect options:

Tell Claude that accuracy is essential while leaving the required content and evidence unspecified.

An accuracy reminder does not identify which sources, sections, or exclusions control the task. As a result, the option does not define the intended content, evidence, and output structure.

Claude must still infer the requirements and may repeat the same omissions. A dependable response would provide explicit context, requirements, and constraints before drafting.

Ask Claude to make the next draft more professional without adding any further task details.

This changes tone rather than supplying the missing content requirements. The underlying requirement remains to define the intended content, evidence, and output structure.

Another polished draft could still omit mandatory sections or introduce unsupported policies. The stronger course is to provide explicit context, requirements, and constraints before drafting.

Request several unrelated versions and select whichever one appears most complete at first glance.

Generating unrelated versions does not establish a shared standard for completeness. That approach cannot reliably define the intended content, evidence, and output structure.

Selection by appearance can reward fluent wording instead of policy accuracy. The task calls for the team to provide explicit context, requirements, and constraints before drafting.

questions.question: Claude drafts a routine internal announcement and also recommends disciplinary action against an employee based on incomplete notes. Which output requires accountable human review before use?

options.label: A
options.text: The disciplinary recommendation, because it is high impact, uncertain, and dependent on professional judgment.

options.label: B
options.text: Review only the announcement because internal communications always require more scrutiny than personnel recommendations in every organization.

options.label: C
options.text: Both outputs require identical legal review regardless of their different consequences and uncertainty.

options.label: D
options.text: Neither output, because Claude used the same source notes for both tasks.

questions.explanation:
Correct option:

The disciplinary recommendation, because it is high impact, uncertain, and dependent on professional judgment.

The recommendation could materially affect an employee and rests on incomplete information. A qualified human must evaluate evidence, policy, fairness, and due process before action.

Review intensity should increase with consequence and uncertainty. Human judgment can seek missing context and reject unsupported inferences.

Routine drafting can remain efficient while high-impact decisions retain oversight. Claude does not become the accountable decision maker for disciplinary action.

Incorrect options:

Review only the announcement because internal communications always require more scrutiny than personnel recommendations in every organization.

The announcement may need normal communication review, but it is not the higher-risk output described. It therefore fails to match the level of human review to consequence, uncertainty, and required expertise.

Prioritizing it leaves the consequential personnel recommendation insufficiently examined. The appropriate alternative is to require accountable review for the high-impact personnel recommendation.

Both outputs require identical legal review regardless of their different consequences and uncertainty.

The outputs do not necessarily require the same type or intensity of review. This does not provide a sound way to match the level of human review to consequence, uncertainty, and required expertise.

A blanket process can waste effort on routine work while obscuring the specialized review needed for discipline. A controlled workflow should require accountable review for the high-impact personnel recommendation.

Neither output, because Claude used the same source notes for both tasks.

Using the same notes does not make the two outputs equally safe or reliable. This leaves the workflow unable to match the level of human review to consequence, uncertainty, and required expertise.

The disciplinary recommendation can exceed what incomplete evidence supports. The scenario instead requires the team to require accountable review for the high-impact personnel recommendation.

questions.domain: Domain 4: Workflow Integration and Solution Design
questions.question: A Claude-assisted proposal workflow passes basic tests but fails when source documents disagree or stakeholders request exceptions during review. What should the team do NEXT before expanding access?

options.label: A
options.text: Increase output length so Claude has more space to hide source disagreements.

options.label: B
options.text: Ignore the failures because normal cases already produce acceptable drafts.

options.label: C
options.text: Add representative conflict and exception cases, define expected handling, and retest before expanding the workflow.

options.label: D
options.text: Expand access immediately and rely on live users to discover unresolved problems during production work after launch.

questions.explanation:
Correct option:

Add representative conflict and exception cases, define expected handling, and retest before expanding the workflow.

The new tests target the conditions that exposed the workflow's current weakness. The team can determine whether Claude should reconcile, flag, or escalate each case.

Iteration should be driven by observed failures and measurable expectations. Representative exceptions turn vague concerns into repeatable evaluation cases.

The team improves robustness before investing in wider adoption. Users are not forced to discover known defects in live consequential work.

Incorrect options:

Increase output length so Claude has more space to hide source disagreements.

Longer output does not resolve contradictory evidence or unclear exception rules. This leaves the workflow unable to refine the solution against realistic failure modes before scale.

The problem can become harder to detect inside additional prose. The scenario instead requires the team to add conflict and exception tests with explicit expected behavior.

Ignore the failures because normal cases already produce acceptable drafts.

Success on normal cases does not make known conflict and exception failures acceptable. As a result, the option does not refine the solution against realistic failure modes before scale.

The workflow will break precisely when users need more careful handling. A dependable response would add conflict and exception tests with explicit expected behavior.

Expand access immediately and rely on live users to discover unresolved problems during production work after launch.

Live expansion transfers unresolved testing work to users and increases exposure. That approach cannot reliably refine the solution against realistic failure modes before scale.

options.label: B
options.text: Use the same fastest model for both outputs because deadlines are the only model-selection criterion.

options.label: C
options.text: Use the strongest model for the preliminary scan and skip review of the board recommendation.

options.label: D

Stronger reasoning and accountable review are applied when evidence must support a consequential recommendation. Model capability should be matched to the purpose and risk of each output.

Context capacity determines how much material can be considered, not whether the reasoning is correct or complete. That approach cannot reliably select different model and review levels for outputs with different purpose, consequence, and timing.

Use the strongest model for the preliminary scan and skip review of the board recommendation.

Strong capability during the preliminary step does not justify removing review from the consequential output. This does not provide a sound way to select different model and review levels for outputs with different purpose, consequence, and timing.

questions.question: An operations team connects Claude to a shared drive for monthly inventory analysis. The drive also contains payroll and legal folders unrelated to the task. Which setup is BEST?

options.label: A
options.text: Connect the entire drive because broader access prevents Claude from missing useful context.

options.label: B
options.text: Use unrestricted access temporarily and rely on prompt wording to keep Claude away from unrelated folders and sensitive files.

options.label: C
options.text: Copy payroll and legal files into the inventory Project so all organizational information is centralized.

options.label: D
options.text: Grant access only to the required inventory folders and assign an owner to review permissions and source relevance.

questions.explanation:
Correct option:

Grant access only to the required inventory folders and assign an owner to review permissions and source relevance.

The setup gives Claude the inventory evidence required for the analysis without exposing unrelated sensitive folders. The connector's access matches the documented business purpose.

Permissions should follow least-needed access. An assigned owner can review whether folders and source assumptions remain appropriate.

The team gains connected context while reducing privacy and governance risk. Future changes do not leave excessive access unnoticed.

Incorrect options:

Connect the entire drive because broader access prevents Claude from missing useful context.

Broad access exceeds the task requirement and includes clearly unrelated sensitive information. This leaves the workflow unable to provide the needed connected information while limiting exposure and maintaining access over time.

A prompt error or workflow issue could expose payroll or legal content. The scenario instead requires the team to scope access to relevant folders and assign permission ownership.

Use unrestricted access temporarily and rely on prompt wording to keep Claude away from unrelated folders and sensitive files.

Prompt instructions do not enforce access boundaries after the connector has been granted permissions. As a result, the option does not provide the needed connected information while limiting exposure and maintaining access over time.

The workflow relies on wording instead of an actual technical and governance control. A dependable response would scope access to relevant folders and assign permission ownership.

Copy payroll and legal files into the inventory Project so all organizational information is centralized.

Centralizing unrelated files increases sensitivity and retrieval noise inside the Project. The underlying requirement remains to provide the needed connected information while limiting exposure and maintaining access over time.

Claude may surface information that should never influence inventory analysis. The stronger course is to scope access to relevant folders and assign permission ownership.

questions.question: An HR team wants Claude to analyze employee-relations notes containing names, medical details, and allegations. Policy permits approved analysis only with minimization and restricted access. Which TWO actions are required?

options.label: A
options.text: Keep the notes unchanged and instruct Claude not to mention sensitive fields in its output.

options.label: B
options.text: Upload the original notes to a general chat because temporary use removes privacy obligations.

options.label: C
options.text: Use only approved access controls and limit the workflow to authorized HR reviewers.

options.label: D
options.text: Remove direct identifiers and unnecessary sensitive details before providing the notes to Claude.

options.label: E
options.text: Share the generated themes with all managers because aggregated output is never sensitive.

questions.explanation:
Correct options:

Use only approved access controls and limit the workflow to authorized HR reviewers.

Approved access controls limit who can use the source notes and inspect the results. The analysis remains within the authorized HR context.

Privacy protection requires both data minimization and controlled access. Authorized reviewers can evaluate whether findings are appropriate for any further action.

The organization gains analytical support without opening the records broadly. Sensitive themes do not circulate beyond the people accountable for the process.

Remove direct identifiers and unnecessary sensitive details before providing the notes to Claude.

Claude receives only the content needed for the approved thematic analysis. Data minimization reduces the amount of personal information exposed to the workflow.

Removing identifiers and irrelevant medical details lowers reidentification and misuse risk. Sensitive information should not be included merely because it exists in the source record.

The output is less likely to reveal or reproduce unnecessary personal details. The team can still analyze recurring themes while protecting employees.

Incorrect options:

Keep the notes unchanged and instruct Claude not to mention sensitive fields in its output.

A prompt to ignore data does not remove the sensitive information from the input. That approach cannot reliably apply data minimization and access controls to an approved sensitive-data use case.

Names, medical details, and allegations remain exposed to the workflow. The task calls for the team to remove unnecessary sensitive content and restrict access to authorized reviewers.

Upload the original notes to a general chat because temporary use removes privacy obligations.

Temporary use does not eliminate privacy, policy, or access obligations. It therefore fails to apply data minimization and access controls to an approved sensitive-data use case.

A general chat may place the records outside the approved workflow. The appropriate alternative is to remove unnecessary sensitive content and restrict access to authorized reviewers.

Share the generated themes with all managers because aggregated output is never sensitive.

Aggregated output can still contain sensitive or identifying patterns. As a result, the option does not apply data minimization and access controls to an approved sensitive-data use case.

Broad distribution may reveal employee information or allegations without proper purpose. A dependable response would remove unnecessary sensitive content and restrict access to authorized reviewers.

questions.question: A marketing team uses Claude to draft social posts from approved campaign material. One post makes a new health-related product claim not present in the source. What should the team do?

options.label: A
options.text: Publish all posts because the campaign material was approved, even when Claude introduces new unsupported claims beyond the source documents.

options.label: B
options.text: Stop using Claude for every marketing task because one output exceeded the source.

options.label: C
options.text: Replace the health claim with stronger promotional wording so it appears intentional.

options.label: D
options.text: Hold the claim for qualified review and source validation while allowing routine compliant drafts to continue through normal approval.

questions.explanation:
Correct option:

Hold the claim for qualified review and source validation while allowing routine compliant drafts to continue through normal approval.

The action isolates the output whose content and consequence differ from the approved campaign material. A qualified reviewer can determine whether evidence and policy permit the new claim.

Routine drafts continue under established approval while the exception receives deeper scrutiny. Human review should be risk based rather than absent or indiscriminately applied.

The team preserves productivity without normalizing unsupported claims. No health-related statement reaches the public before validation.

Incorrect options:

Publish all posts because the campaign material was approved, even when Claude introduces new unsupported claims beyond the source documents.

Approval of source material does not automatically approve claims Claude invents beyond that material. This leaves the workflow unable to separate routine low-risk drafting from a new consequential claim requiring specialized review.

The team could publish a consequential statement with no supporting evidence. The scenario instead requires the team to quarantine the unsupported claim while continuing approved work through normal controls.

Stop using Claude for every marketing task because one output exceeded the source.

One exception does not prove that every routine drafting use case is inappropriate. As a result, the option does not separate routine low-risk drafting from a new consequential claim requiring specialized review.

A complete shutdown sacrifices useful automation instead of improving the review boundary. A dependable response would quarantine the unsupported claim while continuing approved work through normal controls.

Replace the health claim with stronger promotional wording so it appears intentional.

Stronger wording increases the prominence of an unsupported claim. The underlying requirement remains to separate routine low-risk drafting from a new consequential claim requiring specialized review.

The edit can amplify compliance and reputational harm rather than resolve it. The stronger course is to quarantine the unsupported claim while continuing approved work through normal controls.

questions.question: A monthly reporting workflow asks users to paste the same definitions into five prompts and manually reformat identical sections before review. Which optimization is MOST appropriate?

options.label: A
options.text: Keep the duplicated steps because manual repetition guarantees accuracy across every monthly reporting cycle.

options.label: B
options.text: Move stable definitions and formats into maintained Project instructions, then consolidate repeated prompts into a reusable sequence.

options.label: C
options.text: Automate external distribution first while leaving the duplicated preparation, definitions, and formatting steps unchanged for every monthly report.

options.label: D
options.text: Remove all definitions so prompts become shorter and faster to type.

questions.explanation:
Correct option:

Move stable definitions and formats into maintained Project instructions, then consolidate repeated prompts into a reusable sequence.

Users begin each reporting cycle from the same approved definitions and structure. The optimization eliminates repeated context entry and formatting work that does not add judgment.

A consolidated sequence reduces handoffs and inconsistent prompt copies. Stable recurring guidance should be maintained once and reused.

The shared instructions can be reviewed when definitions change. The team saves time without removing substantive validation.

Incorrect options:

Keep the duplicated steps because manual repetition guarantees accuracy across every monthly reporting cycle.

Manual repetition can introduce omissions and inconsistent copies rather than guarantee accuracy. That approach cannot reliably remove avoidable repeated setup while preserving stable standards and review.

Different users may paste different versions of the definitions. The task calls for the team to centralize durable instructions and reuse a consolidated workflow.

Automate external distribution first while leaving the duplicated preparation, definitions, and formatting steps unchanged for every monthly report.

Distribution automation does not address the repeated preparation burden. This does not provide a sound way to remove avoidable repeated setup while preserving stable standards and review.

The workflow sends reports faster while preserving most of the inefficiency. A controlled workflow should centralize durable instructions and reuse a consolidated workflow.

Remove all definitions so prompts become shorter and faster to type.

Shorter prompts without essential definitions sacrifice output consistency. This leaves the workflow unable to remove avoidable repeated setup while preserving stable standards and review.

Claude must infer terms that the workflow should control. The scenario instead requires the team to centralize durable instructions and reuse a consolidated workflow.
